†Aerospace Engineer, Propulsion Laboratory.

temperature aspects were studied. Various mechanisms describing the instabilities were theorized as engine parameters were correlated and empirical stability boundaries defined. Since lowering hydrogen injection temperature at constant flow rate increased the fluid density and reduced the hydrogen injection velocity, one of the earliest engine stability parameters of importance to be recognized was the hydrogen-to-oxygen injection velocity ratio. Operating at high-injection velocity ratios was found to be one of the most effective means to stabilize liquid oxygen/hydrogen combustion for concentric-orifice element injectors. An empirical evaluation of velocity ratio is provided in this chapter.

Another important engine stability parameter to be recognized was the hydrogen injection pressure drop, or flow resistance. At a sufficiently low pressure drop across the hydrogen injection orifice, the orifice would be sensitive to combustion oscillations which could induce oscillations in hydrogen flow rate, leading to the onset of injection-coupled instabilities. Operating at high-hydrogen pressure drop was not a general effective means for stabilization, however, since cases of instability were found with high-hydrogen pressure drop, indicating coupling with other instability mechanisms was possible.

The influence of these parameters and many others are discussed in this chapter. The technical discussion is divided into three sections. A historical overview of liquid oxygen/hydrogen propellant rocket engine testing and development in the United States is first presented. Instability phenomenology is discussed in the next section in four categories based on the injector element type: 1) plain concentric-orifice elements (shear coax), 2) swirling concentric-orifice elements (swirl coax), 3) oxidizer showerhead elements, and 4) oxidizer impinging-jet elements. Last, a brief review of instability phenomena with combustion chamber stabilization devices is presented.

### II. Historical Overview

In the United States, cryogenic oxygen/hydrogen propulsion technology was pioneered in the late 1940s, covering areas of materials technology, propellant handling, test operations, combustor heat transfer, and injector design.<sup>1,76,77</sup> Multitube concentric-orifice element injectors were developed during these very early programs and operated without any indication of combustion instability. They were subsequently used in the development of liquid oxygen/hydrogen propellant rocket engines for flight, which began in the late 1950s with the RL10 and J-2 engines.

The 67-kN (15,000-lbf) thrust RL10 engine<sup>18</sup> was under preliminary development by Pratt and Whitney Aircraft for the upper stage engine of the Air Force Centaur when main development was transferred to NASA. A plain-jet concentric-orifice element injector, with a hydrogen transpiration-cooled faceplate and oxidizer injection tubes flush with the injector face, was designed soon after the NASA contract award in 1958. This version, RL10A-1, was certified for flight in 1961 and flown on the Atlas Centaur in 1963, and became the first production liquid oxygen/hydrogen engine in the United States. There were no combustion instabilities observed during development or preliminary flight rating tests,<sup>17</sup> a fact later attributed to the high-hydrogen injection temperature (161 K).<sup>17</sup> Later testing during investigative programs disclosed that an engine modified for liquid hydrogen operation could be made unstable.<sup>22,23</sup> The injector design was modified in later versions (RL10A-3) by swirling the oxidizer jets in the core elements to increase injector performance.<sup>18</sup>

Development of the J-2 engine under contract to NASA<sup>29-31</sup> began at Rocketdyne in 1960, following some predevelopment.<sup>28</sup> Initial testing was conducted with full size ringed manifold injectors derived from liquid oxygen/kerosene Atlas hardware.<sup>29</sup> Most injectors used showerhead elements with uncooled faces, so injector characteristic velocity performance was poor. More important, all of the ring manifold injector patterns tested initially at conditions simulating the near-liquid hydrogen temperatures expected during the engine start sequence developed spontaneous high-frequency combustion instabilities. This was considered a major technical problem.<sup>29</sup> Radial baffles were installed and appeared to eliminate the instability in most cases, so baffle cooling studies were initiated. Later work showed that a divergence ring from the injector face was also stabilizing at low-hydrogen temperatures, although cooling the ring with these injector patterns proved difficult. Combustion instabilities were also induced by explosive charges at higher hydrogen temperatures than could be induced by hydrogen temperature ramping.

The first concentric-orifice element J-2 injector with a transpiration-cooled faceplate was tested in late 1961.<sup>29</sup> Although still unstable at near-liquid hydrogen temperatures, this injector type was found to be more stable with colder hydrogen injection temperatures than any plain-orifice element injector yet tested without baffles, because vibration levels measured with chamber-mounted accelerometers were considerably reduced. Injector performance was found to be initially similar to the plain-orifice element patterns.

The central oxidizer tubes of these first concentric-orifice elements were flush with the injector face. Further exploration to improve combustion stability and injector performance led to confining the initial unlike propellant contact with various mixing cup designs extended from the injector face. Improvements in combustion stability but difficulty in cooling led to recessing the oxidizer tube back from the injector face. The first recessed concentric-orifice element, introduced in mid-1963, increased injector characteristic velocity performance over nonrecessed by 2% and reduced hydrogen injection temperature for initiating instability to 39 K at mainstage conditions and 32 K at simulated engine start transient conditions.<sup>29</sup> Operation above these threshold temperatures was resistant to the detonation of 200 grain bombs.<sup>29</sup>

This recessed version was eventually selected for the preliminary flight rating test (PFRT) design. The flight rating test (FRT) design added a metering orifice at the inlet of the oxidizer tube, which increased the overall oxidizer pressure drop and improved the low-frequency (chug) combustion stability margin.<sup>29</sup> This change had no noticeable effect on the high-frequency stability margin.<sup>29</sup> The first J-2 engine was flown in 1966.

Despite extensive component development stability testing, engine stability testing of the 1025-kN (230,000-lbf) thrust J-2 engine<sup>31</sup> found a dynamically unstable region between 30 and 50% of full thrust. Acoustic instability was readily induced by thermally detonated nondirectional bombs and did not damp until the engine was shut down.<sup>31</sup> The tested areas outside this region were stable. Between 75 and 100% of full thrust, significant disturbances were difficult to produce, and those produced always damped. At conditions below 20% of full thrust during the oxidizer manifold priming of the start transient, low-frequency (300–400 Hz) chugging occurred, and disturbances were produced which excited acoustic modes; however, oscillations always damped shortly after the manifolds were fully primed. The region between 50 and 75% of full thrust was untested.

The J-2S engine development began in 1966 as an experimental J-2 engine, adding a tap-off engine cycle and uprating thrust to 1180 kN (265,000 lbf), with an accompanying increase in chamber pressure from 5430 KPa (787 psia) to 8690 KPa (1260 psia).<sup>32</sup> A weak but persistent instability made a late appearance in the J-2S program after nearly 6000 s of engine firings had been accumulated.<sup>32</sup> The growth rates of the oscillations were very low and amplitudes were nondestructive. Extensive engine diagnostic testing isolated the cause of the oscillation to coupling between the main injector oxidizer tube flow passage, the injection element recess area just downstream of the oxidizer tube, and the main chamber combustion zone. The oxidizer tubes defined an oscillation frequency which the recessed area, as a precombustor, could amplify. Coupling with main chamber acoustics was unnecessary to create and maintain the instability, apparently only synchronizing the individual injection element responses. The instability was eliminated by adding inserts to the oxidizer tubes,<sup>32</sup> which increased the pressure drop and retuned the hydraulic resonances.

In addition to these flight engine development programs, many investigative combustion stability programs were conducted from the late 1950s through the early 1970s that focused on obtaining fundamental information and developing preventive measures for instability. One of the most informative was the testing conducted at the NASA Lewis Research Center,<sup>46-72</sup> much of it at 89-kN (20,000-lbf) thrust with concentric-orifice element injectors. This research program systematically varied a large variety of geometrical and operational parameters using liquid oxygen/hydrogen propellants and provided the basis for comparison of a significant variety of parameters. Combustion stability margin was rated mainly by hydrogen injection temperature ramping.

Concentric-orifice element injectors were initially found to be more stable with higher fuel-to-oxidizer injection velocity ratios and the use of recessed oxidizer tubes,<sup>57</sup> results comparable to previous J-2 engine injector development experience.<sup>29,30</sup> Later investigation of the stabilizing effects of many element design details that did not change the hydrogen or oxygen injection velocities, such as impingement angle, oxidizer tube base thickness, and, in part, the recess, suggested that the influence of the hydrogen on stability was due to the flow resistance of the hydrogen, especially through the injection pressure drop.<sup>69,78</sup> Identification of the effects on stability of injector pattern layout,<sup>70</sup> combustion chamber geometry,<sup>64,67,70,71</sup> and oxidizer response<sup>55,56,79</sup> led to further refinement of the influence of combustor parameters.

This work supported a cooperative effort with Aerojet Liquid Rocket Co. for the development of the M-1 engine,<sup>8,9,61,66</sup> the largest liquid oxygen/hydrogen propellant thrust chamber tested in the United States. The 6670-kN ( $1.5 \times 10^6$ -lbf) thrust M-1 engine was an upper stage concept terminated in advanced component development. The injector used an injection element derived from the J-2 element,<sup>66</sup> although in a thrust chamber more than twice the diameter. Acoustic instability was initiated by hydrogen injection temperature ramping. The instability appeared abruptly when reducing hydrogen injection temperature and stabilized at a higher hydrogen injection temperature when increasing the temperature from unstable conditions.<sup>7</sup> Different baffle lengths did not change the hydrogen injection temperature at instability,<sup>9,66</sup> similar to experience with J-2 engine development injectors with already superior stability characteristics.<sup>29</sup>

Other liquid oxygen/hydrogen investigative research programs at Aerojet included cryogenic hydrogen technology demonstrations in the 1940s<sup>1</sup> and late

1950s,<sup>2</sup> feasibility of staged-combustion engine cycles,<sup>3</sup> combustion stability investigations at high-chamber pressure,<sup>4-7</sup> advanced injector concepts including platelet injectors,<sup>10,11</sup> development of platelet injectors for candidate SSME preburners,<sup>14</sup> and candidate auxiliary propulsion systems for the Space Shuttle.<sup>15</sup> Cryogenic oxygen/hydrogen propulsion technology was initiated at Aerojet in the late 1940s,<sup>1</sup> evolving from gaseous oxygen/hydrogen rocket research and vehicle performance analyses showing the importance of propellant density. Concentric-orifice element injectors were developed to preclude injector face burning but resulted in the highest injector characteristic velocity performance of all concepts tested.<sup>1</sup> Testing with hydrogen resumed in the late 1950s using Titan hardware for feasibility studies of large engines.<sup>2</sup>

The staged-combustion feasibility program<sup>3</sup> tested hardware that showed the general feasibility of the staged-combustion cycle concept that had been previously recommended for development of higher pressure, higher performance liquid rocket engines. The high-chamber pressure program<sup>4-7</sup> investigated combustion stability at high-chamber pressure (up to 18 MPa), systematically exploring combustion dynamics and providing an experimental evaluation of the sensitive timelag combustion instability theory, using both plain-orifice and concentric-orifice element injectors. The advanced injector concepts program<sup>10,11</sup> developed the transverse excitation chamber, a subscale research tool specially designed to measure the frequency sensitivity of injection elements. Candidate SSME preburners<sup>14</sup> were tested with platelet injector modules with typical orifice dimensions of 0.05 cm. Overpressures of full chamber pressure from 15 to 80 grain bombs damped within 10 ms in both single and combined module demonstrations. Injectors from the Titan hydrogen feasibility program<sup>2</sup> were tested in large "onion-shaped" combustion chambers to provide hot gas for component development on the nuclear propulsion programs NERVA<sup>12</sup> and PHOEBUS-2.<sup>13</sup> High-harmonic mode instabilities occurred in a number of tests.<sup>12</sup>

At Pratt and Whitney Aircraft, liquid oxygen/hydrogen investigative and development programs included feasibility of high-pressure thrust chambers and turbomachinery,<sup>19,20</sup> stability testing with liquid and cold gaseous hydrogen,<sup>21,22</sup> investigation of acoustic, liners,<sup>23,24</sup> and further characterization of the staged combustion rocket engine cycle.<sup>25,26</sup> The high-pressure feasibility program<sup>19,20</sup> investigated injector performance and chamber cooling techniques at high pressure (up to 26 MPa) with plain-orifice and slot element injectors. Most tests were conducted with ambient temperature hydrogen, all of which were stable.<sup>19,20</sup> A pump-fed test at 222-kN (50,000-lbf) thrust with 60-K hydrogen and a circular slot triplet injector developed an apparent instability at the first tangential frequency midway through the test, persisting until shutdown.<sup>20</sup> Warpage of the slot injector through overheating had reduced the hydrogen injector pressure drop to 1/3 of its original value and reduced thrust-based impulse performance 10% during the instability.<sup>20</sup>

The liquid and cold gaseous hydrogen program<sup>21,22</sup> studied the effects of injection momentum ratio, injection velocity ratio, and combustion chamber contraction ratio on stability as functions of the hydrogen injection temperature, using concentric-orifice elements in slab motors and a modified RL10 injector. The mechanical damping devices<sup>23,24</sup> program characterized the stabilizing aspects of combustion chamber acoustic liners. An RL-10 injector modified for less hydrogen injection area that was unstable with liquid hydrogen was stabilized with use of various acoustic liners.<sup>23,24</sup>

Early advanced development of the staged-combustion cycle was demonstrated at 1110-kN (250,000 lbf) thrust at Pratt and Whitney Aircraft.<sup>25,26</sup> Both preburner and main chamber injectors used dual-inlet oxidizer swirl concentric-orifice elements, with the preburner elements laid out in clusters and the main injector elements in radial spraybars.<sup>25</sup> Chamber pressure perturbations from nondirectional 40 and 80 grain charges were readily damped in both combustion chambers at 20 and 100% of full thrust, and with preburner hydrogen injector temperature of 67 K (Ref. 25). The preburner injector layout was changed during the XLR-129 engine development<sup>26</sup> to a hexagonal pattern. Static and pulse tests were stable with a hydrogen injection temperature of 67 K, but nonacoustic low-frequency combustion instability occurred below 25% of full thrust.<sup>26</sup>

At Rocketdyne, liquid oxygen/hydrogen investigative and development programs during this era included photographic combustion studies in large two-dimensional chambers,<sup>33</sup> advanced development of the annular Aerospike<sup>34-37</sup> and linear Aerospike engines,<sup>38-40</sup> development of toroidal thrust chamber concepts,<sup>41</sup> evaluation of high-pressure regeneratively cooled thrust chambers,<sup>42</sup> and investigation of combustor effects on thrust chamber performance.<sup>43</sup> Development of the annular injector of the 1110-kN (250,000-lbf) thrust plug nozzle annular Aerospike Engine,<sup>34-37</sup> nearly 250 cm in diameter, was conducted using segments. Segment tests with 100 to 320-K hydrogen injection temperature and concentric-orifice and oxidizer-fuel-oxidizer (OFO) triplet elements were stable.<sup>34,35</sup> Tests with multiple segments exhibited mixed stability characteristics, with some tests recovering from a bomb in 40 ms (Ref. 34) and some tests displaying moderate amplitude 1800–2000-Hz oxidizer feed system oscillations.<sup>35</sup> Full-scale Aerospike engine tests<sup>35,36</sup> displayed the 1800–2000-Hz oscillation and also high-amplitude (60% of chamber pressure) rotating oscillations in the annular combustion chamber. The amplitudes of these oscillations were later reduced by increasing oxidizer injector pressure drop, isolating oxidizer manifold compartments, and modifying compartment baffles.<sup>36,37</sup>

Segment tests on the linear Aerospike engine were all stable with ambient–500-K hydrogen injection temperature, using triplet and concentric-orifice element injectors.<sup>38,39</sup> Full-scale tests were conducted with no evidence of instability.<sup>40</sup>

Many of these investigations combined to provide the basis for the latest large liquid oxygen/hydrogen propellant flight engine developed in the United States, the 2090-kN (470,000-lbf) thrust Space Shuttle main engine, manufactured by Rocketdyne. The three injector designs, main injector, hydrogen turbopump preburner, and oxygen turbopump preburner, were derived from the J-2S, with added complexity in the main injector manifold due to the high velocities from using the preburner hot gas as the main injector fuel. Preburners were evaluated for temperature uniformity<sup>45</sup> and dynamic stability; tests with bombs were all stable, with and without acoustic resonators but all with injector face baffles. A moderate vibration occurred with some engine tests at the hydrogen turbopump preburner, at a frequency corresponding to the second axial resonance of the oxidizer injection tubes; however, chamber pressure oscillation amplitudes were negligible. Combustion stability was a major consideration in the design of the main injector,<sup>44</sup> so that injector face baffles and chamber perimeter Helmholtz acoustic resonators were included, along with variable oxidizer injection tube lengths to preclude J-2S style instabilities. Nondirectional bomb perturbations in tests with and without the injector face resonators were quickly damped at power levels from 30 to 107% of

full power level (FPL).<sup>44</sup> These tests were recently repeated with an experimental injector with baffles and Helmholtz resonators removed<sup>75</sup> and were equally stable. Additional bomb tests conducted at previously untested regions of the start transient, down to 15% FPL, were also stable. These tests continue the trend that all liquid oxygen/hydrogen staged-combustion tests in the United States have been stable in high frequency.

Efforts in the 1980s to reduce production and launch costs of a heavy lift launch vehicle culminated in the proposal of the Space Transportation main engine (STME), a high-chamber pressure (16-MPa) gas generator cycle with main chamber hydrogen injection temperature of 110 K. Subscale injector component tests were conducted with oxidizer swirl concentric-orifice element injectors,<sup>16, 27, 74</sup> and all were stable, including some with 50-K hydrogen injection temperature and 13-grain nondirectional bombs.

### III. High-Frequency Combustion Instability Phenomena

In the initial rocket test programs with liquid oxygen/hydrogen propellants, combustion was reported to be smooth and without discernable oscillations.<sup>1, 76, 77</sup> There were no instabilities encountered during the development of the RL10 engine,<sup>17</sup> which had a nominal hydrogen injection temperature of 161 K. In one early instability study, oscillations were detected but were sporadic and irregular.<sup>47</sup> In feasibility studies at Aerojet with Titan hardware,<sup>2</sup> however, sustained high-frequency combustion instability was generated and was found easier to excite at fuel-rich mixture ratios with colder hydrogen than at higher mixture ratios with warmer hydrogen. The investigation was not extensive enough to separate the effects of mixture ratio and hydrogen temperature.

In the early phases of the J-2 engine injector development,<sup>29</sup> injector component tests at low-mixture ratio with liquid hydrogen to simulate start transient conditions were always unstable. Tests near the nominal operating conditions with hydrogen injection temperature of 111 K, including bomb stability tests, however, were always stable, even with unbaffled patterns. Hence, stability rating at nominal conditions was abandoned on the J-2 program. At sufficiently high hydrogen temperatures, all injectors could be stabilized. The capability to operate stably over the entire expected hydrogen injection temperature range of 28–167 K was determined to be the most important stability criterion for the J-2 engine. To evaluate stability margin, tests were created which gradually reduced the hydrogen injection temperature until instability occurred, while maintaining constant chamber pressure and mixture ratio. This method, called hydrogen injection temperature ramping, is shown in Fig. 1.<sup>57</sup> A lower hydrogen injection temperature at which acoustic instability occurred implied increased combustion stability margin.

Many physical mechanisms have been hypothesized to explain how temperature ramping causes instability, but all appear to have a limited range of applicability. Engine development, rather, has focused on mapping the stability boundaries with engine parameters to ensure that engines are not designed in regions that are susceptible to combustion instability. The injection velocity ratio, for example, was one of the earliest recognized engine parameters.

The effects of velocity ratio and other rocket engine parameters on combustion instability are discussed in this section. Since the injector element types are strongly influenced by these engine parameters, the discussion is divided into sections based on element type.

#### A. Phenomena with Concentric-Orifice Element Injectors

The concentric-orifice injection element type is used on all flight liquid oxygen/hydrogen propellant rocket engines from the United States, along with a hydrogen transpiration-cooled porous metal face. Geometric and operating conditions of these flight thrust chambers are listed in Table 1. Because of their extensive test history, these designs may be considered to represent very inherently stable conditions.

##### 1. Plain Liquid Oxidizer Jet (Shear Coax)

**Parallel fuel injection.** The J-2 and SSME flight production injectors listed in Table 1 use a concentric-orifice injection element where the liquid oxidizer jet flows full from the injection tube and is not swirled, and the fuel is injected from the concentric annulus parallel to the axis of the oxidizer flow. This element is known conventionally as a shear coax. The liquid oxygen injection plane is usually recessed from the injector face approximately one oxidizer tube exit orifice diameter. On the SSME, the oxidizer is diffused radially due to a slight internal taper at the oxidizer tube exit.

Although used on the very earliest injector testing,<sup>1</sup> the shear coaxial element evolved significantly on the J-2 engine injector development,<sup>29</sup> and current versions of these elements retain all of the basic features derived there. Early in the J-2 program, hydrogen injection temperature was found to influence injector performance and combustion stability of concentric-orifice elements through the momentum and injection velocity ratios,<sup>29</sup> although the nature of the development program limited the generation of investigative correlations.

Investigative testing at Pratt and Whitney Aircraft using a rectangular thrust chamber<sup>21,22</sup> began to develop these relationships in more systematic experimentation. Stability rating was determined by directional pulse testing at fixed hydrogen injection temperatures. Generally, higher values of hydrogen temperature, momentum ratio, velocity ratio, and contraction ratio were found to be stabilizing. The effect of contraction ratio agreed with some later published results<sup>10,62</sup> but contradicted others.<sup>67,70</sup> The best combination of parameters to separate the data was suggested by Fig. 2.

These results agreed with stabilization of the full-scale M-1 thrust chamber, found to depend on maintaining a high-injection velocity ratio, as shown in Fig. 3 for a variety of combustion chamber conditions.<sup>9</sup> Stability rating was determined with hydrogen temperature ramping. The combustion oscillation at the onset of instability appeared more abruptly than usually found with temperature ramping tests.<sup>9</sup> Also, combustion was stabilized at a higher hydrogen injection temperature when increasing the temperature from unstable operation.<sup>9</sup>

at an intermediate thickness.<sup>72</sup> Also, continuous recessing of the oxidizer tube had continuous improvement in stability margin, even to depths of five times the orifice diameter.<sup>72</sup> On J-2 engine injector development, however, increasing the exit wall thickness degraded combustion stability, and continuous recessing did not continually improve stability.<sup>29</sup>

Injection velocity ratio was found to be a key parameter defining stability in many of these studies. To evaluate the effect of injection velocity ratio on stability of shear coaxial elements, data from the J-2 engine injector development,<sup>29</sup> the M-1 sub-scale<sup>61</sup> and full-scale<sup>9</sup> main injector development, NASA LeRC,<sup>36,72</sup> Pratt and Whitney,<sup>22</sup> and SSME<sup>44</sup> were compiled. Figure 4 shows a stability mapping of mixture ratio and fuel-to-oxidizer injection velocity ratio. Stable operation has occurred for injection velocity ratios as low as 1. The maximum unstable velocity ratio at main chamber mixture ratios, with a large variety of design and operating variations, however, has been about 10, which occurred on the M-1 full-scale injector testing. The M-1 instability data, above the diagonal line shown on Fig. 4, are separated from the other instability data, suggesting that chamber diameter is affecting these results. Additionally, not shown on Fig. 4, velocity ratios of about 15 were required to stabilize the M-1 main injector when increasing hydrogen injection temperature from unstable conditions, suggesting hysteresis exists in these stability boundaries.<sup>9</sup>

Higher velocity ratios were also unstable during J-2 engine injector development<sup>29</sup> for main chamber injectors operating off design at low-mixture ratio and low-hydrogen injection temperature and pressure, simulating start transient conditions. These data are shown on Fig. 4 at mixture ratios between 1 and 2. Figure 5 shows a stability mapping of hydrogen injection temperature and fuel-to-oxidizer injection velocity ratio. Instabilities with hydrogen temperatures as high as 83 K, and stable operation with liquid hydrogen, have occurred. The J-2 engine injector development instabilities with the highest velocity ratios occurred with hydrogen injection temperatures ranging from 28 to 42 K and chamber pressures of about 1.5 MPa. At these conditions, hydrogen density can vary two or three times smaller or larger with temperature differences of only  $\pm 5.6$  K about a mean of 39 K. Hence, the potential uncertainty in hydrogen injection velocity for these conditions can be large. Two-phase flow was probably present in these tests. All higher temperature instabilities are found to have occurred at velocity ratios between 3 and 5.

**Impinging fuel injection.** The majority of liquid oxygen/hydrogen investigative stability testing used concentric-orifice injection elements where the liquid oxidizer jet flowed full from the injection tube and was not swirled, and the hydrogen was injected from the concentric annulus convergent to the axis of the oxidizer flow, impinging on the oxidizer shortly after injection.

A large variety of geometrical and operational parameters were evaluated at the NASA LeRC with impinging fuel concentric-orifice elements.<sup>57-60, 62-65, 67-72</sup> An investigation changing propellant injection areas at constant mixture ratio<sup>57</sup> found that reducing the fuel-to-oxidizer injection area ratio was stabilizing because the hydrogen injection temperature at instability was reduced. The effects of injection velocity parameters for these data are shown in Fig. 6.<sup>57</sup> A fuel-to-oxidizer injection velocity ratio of 6.5 and not absolute hydrogen injection velocity or fuel-to-oxidizer velocity differential was found to best define a combustion stability boundary regardless of injection temperature. This boundary held

In subsequent testing at the NASA LeRC, other factors were found that clearly influenced this velocity ratio stability boundary. Recessing the oxidizer tube was always stabilizing by lowering the hydrogen injection temperature at instability for fixed injection area injectors,<sup>57,72</sup> for example, the one shown in Fig. 7.<sup>72</sup> Characteristic velocity performance was also improved. The increase in hydrogen density associated with lower temperatures reduced the critical velocity ratio from 6.5 to about 4.0 at the recessed liquid oxygen tube exit plane for the same mixture ratio. These results were consistent with the J-2 engine injector development, where recessing was stabilizing for both mainstage and start transient conditions.<sup>29</sup>

The test series from Ref. 67 obtained some of the highest unstable hydrogen injection temperatures ever measured for concentric-orifice element injectors, with one test unstable at 195 K. The consistent conditions at instability were low-flow rate per element, high-contraction ratio, and high-mixture ratio.

In other testing at the NASA LeRC, reducing the oxidizer injection temperature was found to be stabilizing.<sup>67</sup> Increasing the impingement angle of the annular hydrogen on the oxidizer jet was found to be stabilizing with no effect on characteristic velocity performance.<sup>72</sup> There was no discernible effect on stability due to hydrogen annulus concentricity.<sup>72</sup> Use of a porous faceplate instead of a solid faceplate was found to be stabilizing.<sup>62</sup> The addition of combustion chamber periphery hydrogen film cooling was marginally destabilizing.<sup>62</sup> The reduction, however of the radial distribution of active elements, i.e., increasing the distance from the outer row of elements to the chamber wall, was also found to be destabilizing, independent of thrust chamber diameter and the number of injection elements.<sup>70</sup> A lower hydrogen injection temperature at instability for the smallest radial distribution

(largest gap between elements and the chamber wall) was considered the result of a change in transverse mode of instability from first tangential to first radial.<sup>70</sup> Decreasing hydrogen injection temperature was also found to be destabilizing to the longitudinal mode in a continuously variable length combustor.<sup>71</sup>

Various correlations have been formulated to explain the variations in these data. One correlation developed from a hydrogen response model<sup>78</sup> is shown in Fig. 11.<sup>67</sup> This correlation was initially generated to help explain the stabilizing effect of recessing the oxidizer tubes. Successful correlation of the data suggested that the contribution of the hydrogen system to stability was due to the hydrogen injection pressure drop,<sup>69</sup> which agreed with the hydrogen response model.<sup>78</sup> Variations in geometrical and operational parameters all affected stability by influencing hydrogen flow resistance<sup>67</sup> or pressure drop.<sup>69</sup> The contribution of the oxygen system to stability was suggested to be due to oxygen density and jet diameter,<sup>67</sup> as shown in Fig. 11. Measurements however, of the periodic behavior of the jet shape during instability<sup>55,56</sup> suggested instead the significant influence of the overall jet dynamics.<sup>79</sup>

An extensive stability investigation with impinging fuel concentric-orifice injection elements was conducted at Aerojet at high-chamber pressure (up to 18 MPa) and hydrogen injection temperatures from 33 K to 69 K.<sup>4-7</sup> Stability rating was conducted with tangential pulsing in the combustion chamber. The measured effects of injection velocity ratio and mixture ratio on combustion stability, suggested as a portrayal of combustion and acoustic processes, are shown in Fig. 12 for low-chamber pressures<sup>7</sup> (7 MPa). Similar to Fig. 2, regions of pulse sensitive operation were identified. At higher chamber pressures (17 MPa), the stable region was enlarged, which was attributed to reduced relative pulse overpressures and the

Impinging fuel concentric-orifice element stability data from the NASA LeRC<sup>58, 62, 64, 67, 68, 70–72</sup> and Aerojet<sup>4–7</sup> were compiled to compare with the parallel fuel shear coaxial data. The significantly increased geometrical and operational variations in the impinging fuel tests increased the maximum hydrogen injection temperature at instability from 83 K in Fig. 5 to 195 K.

The maximum unstable fuel-to-oxidizer velocity ratio at main chamber mixture ratios, however, has increased only from 10 to 13, as shown in Fig. 13, although most of the instabilities are still less than 8, similar to Fig. 4. The high-velocity ratio instabilities have occurred with much warmer hydrogen injection temperatures than in Fig. 5, mostly due to Ref. 67 data as discussed. The smaller number of stable tests in Fig. 13 than in Fig. 4 is due to the nature of investigative stability testing. For each unstable test due to temperature ramping, however, there are implied stable regions at immediately higher velocity ratios, which are not shown in Fig. 13, but would significantly increase the number of stable data.

##### 2. Swirled Liquid Oxidizer Jet (Swirl Coax)

In many concentric-orifice element injectors tested in engine development and investigative programs, the liquid oxidizer was swirled before injection. Swirling was created either by free vortex flow from tangential injection at the entry of the oxidizer tube, in which the swirling flow could be hollow, or by forced vortex flow

This design is known conventionally as a swirl coax. Injection discharge coefficients as low as 0.2 are possible with highly swirled injection. The RL10A-3 engine is the only flight engine with swirl coaxial elements, containing helical ribbon swirlers in all elements except those on the inner row and the outer row near the combustion chamber wall.<sup>18</sup>

Stability test data with swirled jet concentric-orifice element injectors were compiled from the J-2 engine injector development,<sup>29</sup> NASA LeRC,<sup>58</sup> Pratt and Whitney Aircraft,<sup>21,25,26</sup> and STME development subscale injector tests.<sup>16,27,74</sup> In all these hardware designs the hydrogen was injected parallel to the axis of the oxidizer flow.

Two high-temperature instabilities occurred with a helical swirler installed at the oxidizer tube exit.<sup>21</sup> All other instabilities occurred on the J-2 engine injector development,<sup>29</sup> where a variety of oxidizer swirled elements were tested but with the swirl never at the oxidizer tube exit.

A stability mapping of mixture ratio and fuel-to-oxidizer injection velocity ratio is shown in Fig. 14. This figure appears functionally similar to Fig. 4, with instabilities concentrated at low-velocity ratio and low-mixture ratio. Instabilities at main chamber mixture ratios have occurred at lower-velocity ratios than on Fig. 4, however, indicating a larger stable region, albeit one with different element operating characteristics and fewer data points.

#### B. Phenomena with Plain-Orifice Element Injectors

Although they have never appeared on flight production engines, plain orifice element injectors (also known as multiorifice element or ring manifold injectors) have been widely tested with liquid oxygen/hydrogen propellants. Many programs included this type of element because of manufacturing simplicity or prior experience from design and fabrication of liquid/liquid propellant injectors. Between 1958 and 1972, over 1000 plain-orifice element liquid oxygen/hydrogen tests were conducted in the United States. About one-quarter of these were from the J-2 engine injector development,<sup>28,29</sup> one-quarter from Aerospoke development,<sup>34-40</sup> one-quarter from various programs at Aerojet,<sup>2-8,10-15</sup> and the others from various early programs at the NASA LeRC<sup>46-49,51</sup> and Pratt and Whitney Aircraft.<sup>19,20</sup>

About half of the tests were conducted with an oxidizer showerhead element, with either a hydrogen showerhead or a like-on-like doublet element. Of the remaining half, about two-thirds were conducted with OFO triplets, and the rest conducted with pentads (four-on-one OOF00), like-on-like oxidizer doublets with various hydrogen injection methods, and slot elements.

There are sufficient data to compare the stability characteristics of these elements with concentric-orifice elements and, hence, compare the influences of the propellant state and the element types. The following discussion is divided into two categories based on whether the oxidizer is injected as a showerhead jet or self-impinging in some form.

##### 1. Showerhead Liquid Oxidizer Jets

Showerhead oxidizer jet element test data were compiled from J-2 engine injector development<sup>29</sup> and various programs at Aerojet.<sup>2,5-8</sup> Hydrogen was injected

##### 2. Impinging Liquid Oxidizer Jets

Test data for OFO triplet elements were compiled from the J-2 engine injector development,<sup>29</sup> the combustor effects on performance program,<sup>43</sup> and the stability characterization program,<sup>10,11</sup> which used the transverse excitation chamber to generate stability data. A stability mapping with mixture ratio and injection velocity ratio is shown in Fig. 16. Instabilities have occurred at high mixture ratios, high hydrogen injection temperatures, and high injection velocity ratios (up to 25). These conditions are significantly different from any of the unstable conditions presented previously, suggesting the instability mechanisms for this element are different from those for concentric-orifice elements or showerhead elements. This conclusion will be revisited with data from Aerospoke development testing<sup>34-40</sup> and early NASA LeRC testing,<sup>47,48</sup> which were not included in Fig. 16.

Like-on-like oxidizer doublets were tested during the J-2 engine injector development,<sup>29</sup> and various Aerojet programs.<sup>2,8,12,14,15</sup> Insufficient data are available for meaningful presentation in the previous manner. The extensive use of like-on-like doublets with liquid/liquid propellants, however, suggests a comparison with these data. A comparison with combustion stability of storable propellant engines with like-on-like injection elements, using an empirical stability correlation developed by Hewitt (in Ref. 80), is shown in Fig. 17. The characteristic stability parameter  $d/V$ , represents the sensitive or less volatile propellant, which usually is the fuel, but in this case is the liquid oxygen. The slanted lines represent the empirical instability of the storable propellant engine stability data, adjusted for oxygen/hydrogen speed of sound. Correlation of the liquid oxygen/hydrogen stability is found to be good, suggesting the instability mechanism of the like-on-like element is consistent with different propellants and not dependent on the propellant state.

#### C. Combustion Chamber Stabilization Devices

Stabilization (or energy dissipation) devices have not had as extensive use or development with engines using liquid oxygen/hydrogen propellants as with other propellant types, because of the early recognition of stable configurations. As with other rocket engine systems, however, the addition of damping devices can improve combustion stability in liquid oxygen/hydrogen engines, especially for those with generally poor stability characteristics. Some stability devices, however, will not improve the stability margin of engines with already superior stability characteristics.

Radial baffles used in early injector configurations during J-2 engine injector development improved the combustion stability of injectors with poor stability characteristics at low-hydrogen injection temperatures, for both mainstage and

simulated start transient conditions.<sup>29</sup> Baffles tested at the NASA LeRC<sup>65</sup> also reduced the hydrogen injection temperature at instability for a more unstable injector, for example, the one shown in Fig. 18. A variety of baffle patterns successfully stabilized this injector.

The presence of long or very short baffles, however, did not change the hydrogen injection temperature at instability for the M-1 main injector.<sup>9</sup> A temperature of 44 K was unstable from temperature ramping with both 10-cm-long baffles (10% of the chamber diameter) and 1.5-cm-long baffles (1.5% of the chamber diameter). The peak-to-peak amplitudes of the chamber pressure oscillations during instability, however, were reduced by 50–85% with the longer baffles. On the SSME main injector, the presence of baffles did not influence dynamic stability.<sup>75</sup> These results agreed with experience on J-2 engine injector development with injectors with already superior stability characteristics.<sup>29</sup>

Both Pratt and Whitney Aircraft<sup>23,24</sup> and NASA LeRC<sup>59</sup> showed stabilizing aspects of combustion chamber wall acoustic liners in liquid oxygen/hydrogen propellant engines. Liners typically included an axial array of Helmholtz resonators. At Pratt and Whitney Aircraft, an RL10 injector modified for liquid hydrogen injection that was unstable without a liner was stabilized with a liner.<sup>23</sup> At NASA LeRC, a liner reduced the hydrogen injection temperature at instability, as shown in Fig. 19.<sup>59</sup> The presence of the Helmholtz resonators on the SSME main injector, however, did not affect dynamic stability.<sup>44,75</sup>

### IV. Conclusions

The combustion stability history of liquid oxygen/hydrogen propellant rocket engines in the United States is largely represented by the use of concentric-orifice element injectors, which were found to be consistently unstable at off-design conditions with low-hydrogen injection temperatures. All flight engine injectors use concentric-orifice elements with hydrogen transpiration-cooled faces, and all operate with hydrogen injection temperatures in excess of 110 K.

Stability boundaries determined by concentric-orifice element injector testing were initially defined by hydrogen-to-oxygen injection velocity ratio. All flight engine injectors operate with hydrogen-to-oxygen injection velocity ratios in excess of about 10. In this chapter, a comparison of concentric-orifice element injector testing suggested the maximum hydrogen-to-oxygen velocity ratio to develop instability to be about 13. These occurred mostly in the J-2 engine injector development testing at low-chamber pressure and mixture ratio, with a possibility of two-phase hydrogen flow, and in NASA LeRC testing with low-flow rate per element, high-nozzle contraction ratio, and high-mixture ratio. These tests at NASA LeRC provided the most radical departure from the general characteristics, generating instabilities with hydrogen injection temperatures much higher than normal operation for the flight engines, and much higher than usual for investigative testing.

Stabilization at lower velocity ratios was determined in engine development and technology investigations to be possible with many means, including oxidizer tube recessing, higher flow rate per element, higher hydrogen pressure drop, impinging the hydrogen on the oxidizer, and swirling the oxidizer. These results led to the development of stability correlations at NASA LeRC defined by hydrogen injection response, influenced mostly by hydrogen pressure drop. Later, oxygen response and chamber responses were added for more complete formulations of combustion stability.

The general success of concentric-orifice elements in the early engine development precluded widespread later use of plain-orifice elements, except for investigative programs. An empirical examination of the stability characteristics of plain-orifice elements was included in this chapter to attempt to separate the effects of the injection elements from those of the propellant state. The instability phenomena with plain-orifice element injectors appeared to depend on the element type. Showerhead element instability characteristics appeared similar to concentric-orifice element characteristics, especially regarding injection velocity ratio. OFO triplet characteristics were different from concentric-orifice elements, with capability for instability at high injection velocity ratios. Like-on-like oxidizer doublet data compared well with an empirical stability correlation developed for storable propellant injectors.

Stability aids in the combustion chamber have improved the stability of more unstable concepts but generally have not improved the stability margin of more stable concepts for liquid oxygen/hydrogen propellant rocket engines.

### Chapter 3

## Instability Phenomena in Liquid Oxygen/Hydrocarbon Rocket Engines

Jeffrey A. Muss\*

*University of California, Berkeley, Berkeley, California 94720*

### I. Introduction

THE earliest liquid rocket engines used liquid oxygen (LOX) as the oxidizer and various hydrocarbons (HC) as fuels. The propellants were readily available (liquid hydrogen was not), and the theoretical performance characteristics calculated by Olberth in 1917 indicated HC fuels were ideal for booster applications.<sup>1</sup> Goddard's first successful rocket flight in 1926 was powered using the combination of LOX and gasoline.<sup>1</sup> The German V-2 of World War II, the first production liquid rocket, used LOX and an aqueous ethanol solution (75% ethanol by volume) as propellants.<sup>1,2</sup> V-2s captured at the close of World War II served as building blocks for both American and Soviet liquid rocket development programs during the early Cold War period of the late 1940s and early 1950s.<sup>1</sup> The heavy-lift requirements of the early ballistic missile programs necessitated the replacement of the aqueous ethanol fuel with a kerosene petroleum distillate in both countries (known as RP-1 in the United States and T-1 in the former Soviet Union). By the early 1960s, however, storable propellant combinations, such as A-50/N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>, had replaced LOX/RP-1 in many of the American missiles since the vehicle could be stored in a fueled configuration. The original LOX/RP-1 versions of the missiles did, however, serve as the building blocks for the launch vehicles that would open space to mankind. The American Saturn, Delta, and Atlas launch vehicles all use the LOX/RP-1 propellant combination in the high-thrust first-stage booster engines. In the Soviet Union, LOX/RP-1 has been used almost exclusively for launching large payloads. It is the propellant combination for both booster and upper stages of the Soyuz and Proton launch systems.<sup>3,4</sup> The development of LOX/RP-1 engines in the United States essentially ceased with the cancellation of the Apollo space project in the late 1960s and the subsequent development and activation of the LOX/H<sub>2</sub> powered Space Shuttle in the 1970s. The notable exception was Rocketdyne's adaptation of the H-1 engine for use as a booster for the Delta space launch vehicle.<sup>5</sup>
