\*Research Assistant, Department of Mechanical Engineering.

One of the first clear observations of combustion instability in liquid fueled rockets was noted in 1955 in conjunction with the development of the engines for the Thor and Atlas ballistic missiles.<sup>5-7</sup> Prior to this time, many rocket engines were damaged or destroyed during tests and launches,<sup>2,8</sup> but the cause of the failure is not clearly attributed to the feedback coupling between the fluid mechanics and the combustion process that is currently categorized as combustion instability. Detailed studies of the problems of combustion instability and solution techniques accompanied the development of the liquid rocket engines for Jupiter/Thor, Atlas, Titan II, and Saturn IB and V.<sup>5,9,10</sup> Recent reports released from the former Soviet Union indicate that similar problems accompanied the development of many of their liquid rocket systems.<sup>4</sup>

Although these propulsion systems were successful, their development was a long, arduous task. The development process for LOX/RP-1 systems in particular has been characterized by a struggle to achieve stable combustion while maintaining high combustion performance. Often the stability and performance were acceptable in development versions of the engine only to become wildly unstable during engine qualification or flight operation. The American Atlas (MA-1)/Thor(MB-1) and F-1 and the Soviet RD-0110 engines were all plagued by long, costly re-engineering programs.<sup>4,10</sup> The final designs were as much the result of trial and error as an application of firm understanding of the underlying physics. In spite of this apparent drawback, LOX/RP-1 is still considered an attractive propellant combination for booster applications due to its high theoretical specific impulse, relative to storable propellants, and exceptional bulk density relative to other propellant combinations.

In this chapter, the recent advances in the understanding of combustion characteristic of liquid-fueled rocket engines using LOX/hydrocarbon (LOX/HC), particularly LOX/RP-1, propellants are reviewed. The state of knowledge as captured in NASA SP-194 is reviewed, with a special eye toward combustion characteristics and design recommendations for LOX/HC engine systems. The results from recent experimental programs focused on performance and combustion stability issues are chronicled. The development of critical analytical injector design models is discussed. These models facilitate the relationship between injector design features and performance and stability characteristics. As will be shown, recent results indicate that the stability characteristics of oxidizer-fuel-oxidizer(O-F-O) triplet elements are better than previously thought, especially in high thrust LOX/RP-1 applications. The triplet elements will be shown to provide high performance with manageable stability, in contrast to like-doublet injectors where performance goals are often compromised for stability.

### II. Understanding of NASA SP-194

In 1967, Princeton University, under contract to NASA and the U.S. Armed Forces, began assembling a comprehensive reference book on the state-of-the-art knowledge on liquid rocket combustion, with a focus on combustion instability.<sup>7</sup> Published in 1972, NASA SP-194 is the most thorough work on combustion instability in liquid rocket engines to date. The present section summarizes the state of knowledge at the time of SP-194's publication with a special focus on aspects of LOX/HC combustion. Recent advances in the understanding of LOX/HC combustion stability characteristics, particularly LOX/RP-1 combustion characteristics, will then be discussed. Information on developments in the former Soviet

Union available in the open literature are included, although little information is available about the stability characteristics of the staged-combustion LOX/RP-1 systems currently in use. This discussion will not include information from recent LOX/CH<sub>4</sub> studies<sup>11-13</sup> since the engine configurations tend to more closely resemble LOX/H<sub>2</sub> systems.

SP-194 is a comprehensive compilation of combustion instability knowledge. It includes both a history of combustion instability problems in liquid rocket engine development and approaches to the solution of these problems. The chapters discuss the origins and categorization of combustion instabilities, theoretical models to describe stability behavior, guidelines to preclude unstable designs, and experimental techniques for evaluating the stability characteristics of engines.

A historical review of SP-194 indicates that there were two major impediments to a fuller understanding of the relationship between design features and combustion stability characteristics. Without this critical information, the ability to rapidly affect changes in engine designs in response to combustion instability problems was severely hindered. The limited computational power of the early 1970s severely limited the ability to apply all but the simplest models to practical engines. These limitations precluded running detailed parametric studies to understand the effect of input parameters on stability model results. The other significant shortfall was the absence of mechanistic models, or even good correlations, to describe the influence of injector element and thrust chamber design features on the response characteristics of the combustion process. The absence of such models limited the development of clear causal relationships between design and operating conditions and stability behavior. It should be clearly stated from the beginning that these problems affected the development of all rocket engine systems and were not confined to LOX/HC systems.

The following subsections will focus on the understanding contained in SP-194 as it relates to the causal relationship between design features and combustion stability behavior, with a special interest in the relation between injector element characteristics.

#### A. Causes of Combustion Instabilities

At the time of the writing of SP-194, it was clearly understood that combustion instability was the result of coupling between the fluid mechanics (acoustics) in the combustion chamber and the combustion process. The Rayleigh criterion was recognized to be the mechanism through which the combustion could supply the energy to sustain flow oscillations. It was known that a system was required to dissipate oscillatory energy more quickly than it is supplied at all frequencies to have a stable design.

Instabilities were categorized as nonacoustic or acoustic. Nonacoustic or chug instabilities are those where the characteristic wavelength is significantly longer than any characteristic dimension of the combustor. Chug instabilities had been successfully modeled using a lumped parameter chamber and total time lags, although time lags were usually inferred after the fact from engine test data. Acoustic instabilities, both intermediate and high frequency, were assumed to be supported predominantly through combustion mechanisms, although coupling with the feed system was acknowledged as a major driving mechanism for intermediate frequency instabilities. Some of the proposed mechanisms for coupling between combustion and chamber pressure oscillations included resurge, fluctuating

drop vaporization and chemical kinetic rates, and oscillations in the primary and secondary atomization processes. A number of models were developed to describe these processes, but computational complexity usually constrained analyses to investigating the effect of only one phenomenon at a time. It is interesting to note that high-frequency coupling between pressure oscillations and the atomization process was attributed to the interaction between combustion gas velocity perturbations and the atomizing propellant,<sup>14</sup> and most analyses ignored propellant injection flow rate fluctuations resulting from chamber pressure oscillations.

It was felt that stabilization could be achieved by modifying either the combustion process or the chamber acoustics and flowfield. The objective of these changes was to decouple the combustion process from the chamber acoustics, at least enough so that the oscillatory energy input was not sustained. The acoustic field could be modified using a combination of thrust chamber baffles and acoustic cavities. The combustion process could be modified by changing the axial distribution of liquid-phase propellants, distributing the propellant away from pressure antinodes, or isolating liquid streams from the region of vigorous combustion. A common technique used to modify the combustion distribution was to increase the vapor fraction of the most volatile propellant by increasing its injection velocity while decreasing the velocity of the less volatile propellant. This provided both an increased length over which the least volatile propellant vaporized and a reasonably high-velocity gas phase that could presumably isolate the vaporizing drops from acoustic oscillations.

There were only limited models that could relate the combustion response to injector and chamber design and operating conditions. The most widely used of these models were based on the drop vaporization model of Priem and Heidmann,<sup>15</sup> and they were capable of predicting the vaporization-limited combustion response given an initial propellant drop size distribution and a mean axial combustion product distribution. It should be understood that the drop size distribution of sprays formed by practical injectors is disperse, and modeling the spray as being monodisperse is a gross simplification that could possibly lead to completely unreliable stability predictions. There were, furthermore, few models or correlations that related injector design features and operating conditions to the resulting drop size distribution. Rupe<sup>16,17</sup> and his coworkers at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) studied many aspects of the mixing of sprays created with impinging elements and Priem and Heidmann<sup>15</sup> included some simple correlations between orifice diameter and drop size based on data originally collected by Ingebo.<sup>18</sup> With the exception of Abbe et al.,<sup>19</sup> who used Ingebo's drop size correlations as a basis with which to compare the stability characteristics of full-scale combustors that used different injector designs, few works attempted to analyze the causal relationship between element design features and combustion stability. Another major shortcoming was the absence of a model that could predict the effect of thrust chamber baffle geometry on combustion stability. This was especially significant because most large engines of the time required thrust chamber baffles for stable operation.

SP-194 offers a series of design guidelines to bridge the shortage of component models. Some of these are based on empirical correlations of stability data, whereas others are historic rules of thumb. The most notable of the empirical correlations are Reardon's for pressure sensitive interaction index  $\alpha$  and sensitive time lag  $\tau$ . These cover a range of propellant types, injector styles and operating conditions,

but the sparseness of data for LOX/HC propellants led to the lumping of data for similar injectors, e.g., non-hypergolic impinging elements, and wide error bars. The data for  $n$  plotted against orifice diameter  $D_j$  decrease rapidly from nearly 3 at the smallest orifice diameters and asymptote toward 0.6 for orifices larger than 5 mm, but a simple correlation could not be determined. Time lag  $\tau$  was found to correlate with the nozzle entrance Mach number  $M_e$ , reduced pressure parameter  $\beta_p$ , and  $D_j$

$$\tau = 0.165 D_j^{1/2} M_e^{-1/3} \beta_p^{-1} \quad (1)$$

The strong effect of operating mixture ratio (or injection velocity) on time lag is not included in Eq. (1).

Although empirically correlated data were scarce, the design guidelines for LOX/HC engines were even more sweeping and general. Limited data from tests where RP-1 was partially substituted for the hypergolic fuel Hyballine indicated that hypergols may be more stable than LOX/RP-1, implying that combustion instability problems might be easier to solve in engines using hypergolic propellants than in LOX/RP-1 engines. This perception may have resulted, in part, from the fact that many hypergolic systems were designed for low-to-moderate thrust applications and, thus, they could be designed for operation with moderate diameter combustors at low chamber pressures. There is, however, substantial evidence to contradict this belief,<sup>9</sup> since the development of hypergolic engines seem to have a high incidence of chug and longitudinal stability problems, and most hydrazine-based fuels were known to have a strong propensity to produce "pops" that can trigger instabilities during engine operation.

#### B. Injection Element Design Guidelines

It was clearly understood that each type of injector element has its own characteristic response dependent on its design and operating parameters and that the response was independent of the chamber response. There are several subsections of SP-194 concerned with the relative suitability of various injector element configurations for LOX/HC injection. As noted before, the focus was on liquid HCs so there is no discussion of liquid-liquid coaxial injectors, even though they were widely used in the Soviet Union at the time.<sup>4</sup> Element specific design practices that could enhance stability characteristics are also noted.

Since most stability theories only differentiated between like and unlike impinging elements through their axial combustion distributions, it is not surprising that SP-194 concluded that "unlike-impinging jet injectors appear to be more unstable than like-impinging types." This behavior was attributed to more rapid mixing of the fuel and oxidizer for unlike impinging elements and the resultant reduction in the axial combustion distribution. It should be noted that most of the LOX/HC data supporting this premise was obtained on LOX/ethanol research combustors with relatively fine injector elements.

The like-on-like (LOL) impinging element, or like doublet, consisting of like propellant streams that impinge and atomize prior to mixing of the fuel and oxidizer sprays, is the preferred element type for LOX/HC engines. Most LOL data presented in SP-194 were from LOX/RP-1 booster type elements, including the LOL doublets used in the Atlas, Thor, and H-1 engines, and the fuel doublet + LOX triplet configuration used in the F-1 engine. The roughness of the combustion process was found to be significantly reduced if the element layout caused the

atomized oxidizer and fuel streams to come into contact, and the "stability is maximized where unlike fans interact."

However, the unlike propellant mixing characteristics of many LOL element designs resulted in poor overall mixing and low combustion efficiencies (90–95%).<sup>20</sup> There are claims that larger orifices ( $>2.5$  mm) have poorer azimuthal distributions of spray that could lead to clumping of spray around the impingement centerline. The clumping was thought to delay propellant mixing in LOL designs, effectively enhancing the stability by stretching axial combustion distribution. This is a notable difference between like and unlike elements, since clumping in the unlike case will not necessarily delay mixing or axially distribute combustion. The significance of this perceived difference in stability characteristics of like and unlike impinging element types is somewhat suspect since Reardon's correlations of  $n$  and  $\tau$  indicate that all impinging non-hypergolic elements have roughly "the same stability characteristics."

There was no agreement on how to adjust combustion characteristics to improve stability. The goal was a balance of frequency response characteristics with combustion distribution and, possibly, a movement of the sensitive combustion zone. The size of drops in the propellant spray was known to have a large influence on the element's stability characteristics. The proper balance of injection velocity  $V_j$  was not clear, since increasing  $V_j$  produces smaller drops but also may spatially distribute combustion further. The key design guideline for enhanced stability characteristics in LOX/HC engines was that the LOX injection velocity should be at least three times larger than the less volatile fuel injection velocity. This would presumably cause the vaporizing fuel drop to be surrounded by an atmosphere of high-speed oxidizer vapor during the early drop lifetime, when drop vaporization rates are most sensitive to velocity perturbations. This observation may apply equally as well for hypergolic propellant combinations.

There are several discussions on the importance of design of the injection element manifolds. These observations apply to both like and unlike element types, and to all liquid-propellant combinations. Manifold hydraulics, orifice edge conditions, and relative angles between manifold flows and the injector element inlets have all been shown to have strong influences on the propellant stream characteristics, including flow rate through individual elements, stream impingement accuracy, and the spray size and velocity distributions. Contoured orifices were known to increase the orifice discharge coefficients potentially leading to accurate stream impingement and good spray quality as well as efficiently using the available injection pressure drop.

### III. Advancements Since SP-194

Interest in LOX/HC rocket engines was revived in the late 1970s with the envisioned need for heavy-lift capabilities. Vehicle trade studies touted booster engines using a LOX/heavy hydrocarbon (HHC) propellant combinations rather than LOX/ $H_2$  because the fuel is easier to store and handle than  $H_2$  and the increased fuel density could result in smaller vehicles or larger payload capacity.<sup>21</sup> The new engines were expected to operate at high chamber pressures (15–20 MPa) in order to maximize thrust capabilities through optimized exit nozzle expansion ratios.

There were, however, many concerns about the risks associated with the development of such booster class LOX/HC engines. The development of the F-1

had experienced severe problems with combustion instability, performance, thrust chamber cooling, and engine durability.<sup>40</sup> Since the 1970s, advances in understanding in many key areas have been achieved through a combination of experimental technology development programs, advances in computational capabilities, and the development of design feature based spray characterization models. The next subsection chronicles the goals and experimental results of some of these technology programs. This is followed by a description of some of the advances in analysis tools in the area of injection characterization and, finally, a discussion of the net contributions to injection element design practices.

#### A. Experimental Combustor Studies

Beginning in the late 1970s a series of technology development programs was conducted in an effort to resolve the many of the technical concerns raised about the development of large, high-pressure LOX/HC engines. Most of the studies were conducted with classical impinging elements, although Aerojet built several platelet injectors<sup>22</sup> and TRW studied operation of pintle injectors with LOX/RP-1.<sup>23</sup> The bulk of the work focused on stability and performance concerns, but programs also addressed issues associated with gas generator design<sup>24</sup> and thrust chamber cooling.<sup>25,26</sup>

In the mid-1980s the Air Force and NASA organized several research programs to address performance and combustion stability risks identified from the development of the F-1 engine and Space Shuttle Main Engine (SSME). These programs were strongly focused toward devising methods for lowering the risks and costs of full-scale engine development. The following sections discuss the experimental findings of these programs.

##### 1. NASA Lewis Research Center (1978–1979)

Pavli<sup>27</sup> and his coworkers at NASA Lewis Research Center (LeRC) conducted a test program to investigate the suitability of the Priem and Heidmann<sup>15</sup> generalized length vaporization model for the prediction of performance of heavy hydrocarbon fuels. Testing was conducted using LOX as the oxidizer and RP-1, JP-10, and liquefied natural gas (LNG) as fuels. The combustor consisted of a 0.14-m-diam chamber operating at 4.1 MPa chamber pressure. Three basic injector element types were evaluated: like-on-like doublet, O-F-O unlike triplet, and an F-O-O-F unlike split triplet.

The analysis indicated that the model was in good agreement with the performance data when the combustion was vaporization limited. The data indicated that unlike triplet elements were capable of providing excellent combustion efficiency ( $\eta_{C^*} > 99\%$ ) with acceptable high-frequency stability characteristics. Performance with the LOL injector was significantly lower with all propellant combinations. A portion of the performance loss with the like doublet was attributed to poor interpropellant mixing. In addition to the high-vaporization efficiency, the triplet injectors were found to produce good mixing with a relatively coarse pattern.

A radial-inlet 1/4-wave acoustic cavity sized to damp the first tangential (1T) mode was included at the injector plane in some of the tests. Since the focus of this program was performance modeling, no dynamic combustion stability testing (e.g., bombing) was performed. No spontaneous transverse instabilities were observed

with the like doublet or the O-F-O triplet injector operating on LOX/RP-1, even without the cavities present. Spontaneous instabilities were observed without the acoustic cavity present for the O-F-O triplet burning LNG (1T) and JP-10 [first longitudinal (1L)], and the LOL burning JP-10 (1T). Nonlinear 1T instabilities were also noted with the split triplet elements using RP-1 fuel.

##### 2. LOX/Hydrocarbon Injector Characterization Program (1985–1991)

The LOX/hydrocarbon injector characterization program (LHICP) was an Air Force-sponsored technology program focused on the development of analytical methods to reduce development risks, and the associated cost, of booster class LOX/HC engines. Of particular interest were techniques whereby full-sized injector elements could be tested in reduced-scale combustion chambers to significantly enhance the confidence in analytical model predictions of full-scale engine performance and stability characteristics. The program used LOX/RP-1 in large thrust per element O-F-O triplet (5.34 kN/element) and LOL (2.23 kN/element) injectors at high chamber pressures (13.8 MPa). Both subscale (0.18 MN) and full-scale (1 MN) combustors were tested.<sup>28,29</sup> The designs were intended to provide a wide range of potentially unstable operating conditions characteristic of high-performance booster engines, with the triplet injector expected to be higher performing but much more unstable than the LOL injector. The fabrication and testing portions of the program yielded several important observations.

In spite of the large difference in element thrust, the O-F-O triplet element resulted in a significantly higher nominal combustion efficiency than the LOL (99% vs 95%). The performance of the triplet injector showed little sensitivity to changes in mixture ratio, whereas the like-doublet injector exhibited a positive correlation between the oxidizer injection pressure and combustion efficiency. The performance of the triplet injector showed 1.5 and 4.5% decreases in performance as the combustion chamber length was reduced from 20 to 13 and 8 in., respectively.

The O-F-O triplet element showed better dynamic stability characteristics than the LOL, driving only a 1T instability in the subscale chamber, whereas the doublet drove both the 1T and second tangential mode (2T) instabilities. The O-F-O exhibited the only spontaneous instability. Dynamically stable operation was demonstrated for both injectors when 1T monotuned cavities, 1T/2T bituned cavities, or quarter-wave cavities with thrust chamber baffles were included.

The large orifice triplet elements ( $D_f = 3.18$  mm) afforded simplicity in manufacturing over the compound angle of the finer, canted, like-doublet element. It is important to note that the O-F-O element was designed with identical diameter, contoured inlet fuel and oxidizer orifices to minimize misimpingement of propellant streams. This was predicted to result in high intraelement mixing and reduced drop size variation. The normalized oxidizer injection pressure drop ( $\Delta P_{j,o}/P_c$ ) was much larger than what was historically used, about 41%. This may be responsible for the high intraelement mixing efficiency and the enhanced stability characteristics when compared to the triplet designs tested during the ROCCID and HHC programs, described next.

##### 3. Rocket Engine Analytical Design Methodology Development Program (1988–1993)

The subscale (0.18 MN) thrust chamber from the LOX/HC injector characterization program was reworked in conjunction with validation testing for the

NASA Lewis Research Center sponsored LOX/hydrocarbon rocket engine analytical design methodology development program (ROCCID).<sup>30</sup> The objective of the injector redesign was to create a triplet design that could realize high performance (>99%) in a reduced chamber length (0.36- vs 0.51-m chamber length) and that had the capability to drive higher mode acoustic instabilities (2T and the first radial (1R)) in the absence of damping devices. The injector element orifice diameters were reduced to 2.29 mm whereas the number of elements was increased from 39 to 105. The unlike impingement height was slightly reduced so the reduced diameter contoured orifices would mate with the existing propellant manifold channels. The nominal  $\Delta P_{i,o}/P_c$  was reduced to about 0.23.

Manufacturing difficulties precluded detailed evaluation of the stability characteristics of the new design, but instabilities as high as the 1R mode were observed. More notable, however, was the dramatic decrease in overall combustion efficiency. Predicted combustion efficiencies were in excess of 99%, whereas measured values ranged from 93 to 95% at nominal design conditions. These differences were attributed to poorer than anticipated propellant atomization and mixing. The reduction in propellant mixing was attributed to interaction of the propellant fans of adjacent elements before the atomization process was complete.<sup>30</sup>

##### 4. Heavy Hydrocarbon Main Injector Technology Program (1986–1991)

In the late 1980s Rocketdyne evaluated several injector patterns in conjunction with a low-cost design concept for large, high-pressure, baffled combustors using LOX/RP-1 heavy hydrocarbon (HHC).<sup>31</sup> The overall concept was to develop small, stable, high performing combustion modules or cans, and then combine several cans in a single thrust chamber to create a high-thrust engine. Each can would act essentially as an isolated baffle pocket. Six injector patterns were evaluated for performance, stability, and wall heat transfer characteristics in a 0.09-m-diam chamber. The injector designs included a reduced element size derivative of the H-1 engine (fuel doublets and oxidizer triplets),<sup>20</sup> an O-F-O triplet with unlike orifice diameters, two LOL layouts (box and circumferential fans), and two LOX showerhead/fuel doublet configurations. The O-F-O injector was predicted to be more stable than the H-1 derivative, but the analysis did not consider the possibility of injection coupling, which did occur, causing 1L instabilities. The combustion chamber included 7 L-shaped Helmholtz resonators at the injector face tuned to the 1T mode (~8 kHz).

All injectors showed low-to-moderate performance (89–95%  $C^*$  efficiency) and demonstrated spontaneous chamber pressure oscillations (5–50% peak to peak) near the 1L frequency (about 1300 Hz). The largest oscillations occurred for the O-F-O triplet design, with significant oscillations existing prior to main-stage ignition. Comparisons of the phase of the oscillations for the O-F-O showed a strong correlation between pressure fluctuations in the main chamber and the oxidizer manifold, indicating the injection pressure drop may have been inadequate to preclude pressure wave coupling between the combustion chamber and the oxidizer manifold. The amplitude of the 1L oscillations was dramatically reduced for the O-F-O triplet injector when the combustor length was reduced from 0.49 to 0.34 m. The reduction in oscillation amplitude was accompanied by a significant increase in performance (98–99% vs 93%  $C^*$  efficiency), although predictions indicated that performance was mixing limited at 95%.

The dynamic stability of the H-1 derivative injector was evaluated using combustion bombs with and without the resonator ring present. The induced oscillations damped within 5 ms for all cases. Subsequent testing was performed on the other injectors with the Helmholtz resonator blocked closed. The circumferential fan LOL was shown to be statistically unstable in the 1T mode, whereas the box doublet LOL was bombed unstable in the 1T mode. The transition of a 1L instability into a depressed frequency 1T was also observed with the 1T monotuned cavity included. The O-F-O was shown to be dynamically stable in the tangential and radial modes when 1T cavities were used.

A canted fan LOL injector (1.47-mm oxidizer, 0.94-mm fuel, 14-deg included cant angle) was tested in a 0.145-m chamber. The design included a bituned (1T/2T) axial inlet quarter-wave acoustic cavity. The performance was significantly higher than the previous tests (97%  $C^*$  efficiency), but this injector was spontaneously unstable (30% peak to peak) in the 1T mode and bombed unstable (50% peak to peak) in the third tangential (3T) mode. Test data indicated the temperature in the acoustic cavities were much higher than the design value. This caused the characteristic frequencies of the resonators to differ significantly from the resonant frequencies of the chamber.

##### 5. Pressure Fed Booster (1988–1992)

The largest LOX/HC engine tested in the United States during this period was the pressure fed booster,<sup>32</sup> designed and built by Aerojet for NASA Marshall Space Flight Center. The full-scale engine was designed to produce 3.4 MN of thrust at nominal operating conditions, and a wide range of throttling conditions were envisioned. The nominal chamber pressure, 5.0 MPa, was constrained by 7.6-MPa maximum vehicle tank pressure. A subscale combustor (0.49-m chamber diameter, 1-m chamber length, 0.9-MN thrust at 3:1 expansion) was designed and tested with integral radial inlet quarter-wave acoustic cavities. The injector consisted of 12 injection modules. Each module contained five O-F-O triplet injection elements with equal diameter 6.1-mm orifices. Like the triplet injector in the LHCP (see the foregoing), this injector was designed with a high relative injection pressure drop for the oxidizer circuit ( $\Delta P_{o,i}/P_c \sim 0.45$ ). Adjustable flow rate fuel film cooling (FFC) showerhead elements were included at the periphery of the injector.

Performance testing indicated a core  $C^*$  combustion efficiency  $\eta_{C^*}$  of 97–99% at chamber pressures between 5.0 and 6.9 MPa, while overall engine performance was 95–97%  $\eta_{C^*}$  with 15% FFC. The performance was shown to increase nearly linearly as either of the propellant injection pressure drops was increased. The injector was statistically stable but dynamically unstable in the 1T mode without acoustic cavities. Tests with a monotuned and bituned cavity showed dynamic stability at the nominal operating point. Unstable operation also occurred in the 1T, 2T, and 3T modes at high chamber pressures ( $\sim 6.9$  MPa) or low mixture ratios. It is interesting to note that there were no spontaneous instabilities reported regardless of the presence of acoustic cavities.

### IV. Injection Process Modeling for Combustion Stability Analysis

The most important of the component models developed are those that relate engine operating conditions and injector design features to propellant spray characteristics. These characteristics are the critical inputs to all performance and

combustion response models. Foremost of there is the relationship between injector element design parameters and propellant spray characteristics. As with the early work in this field, the main goal of many of the recent modeling efforts was to determine the influence of injector operating and design conditions on propellant spray characteristics so that combustor performance, rather than combustion stability, could be reliably predicted.

The earliest work yielded simple correlations for the dependence of some characteristic drop size and spray distribution on the orifice diameter and element type for impinging injector type.<sup>14-17</sup> Some of the first comprehensive studies were conducted by Dickerson et al.<sup>33,34</sup> at Rocketdyne using hot wax sprays to characterize spray distributions and the influence of impinging element design features. This work was continued into the mid-1970s with increasing geometric sophistication, and both liquid/liquid impinging and gas/liquid coaxial element types were examined. Multidimensional spray distribution characteristics were inferred from flow distribution measurements obtained using a patternator. Ferrenberg et al.<sup>35</sup> compiled a comprehensive summary of the studies undertaken through 1982.

Over the same time span, Ito at Aerojet developed analytical and hybrid analytical-empirical models that related propellant atomization characteristics to element design features for many types of impinging elements.<sup>36</sup> These models permitted the prediction of both spray characteristics relevant to performance (median drop size and distribution) and several time lags, including the impingement and atomization components. The mechanism for analytical prediction of time lag components was of critical importance to the development of predictive combustion stability analysis tools. Fang<sup>37</sup> used the time lags predicted with Ito's models to analyze a range of chug and longitudinal mode combustion instabilities.

Combustion instability data correlation performed at Aerojet also indicated that the sensitive time lag could be correlated with the time it took for the less volatile propellant (usually fuel) to become 20% vaporized.<sup>36,37</sup> This value is much smaller than the 50% vaporization time proposed in SP-194. This correlation was developed from storable propellant engine data, mainly MMH/N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> using the Priem and Heidmann<sup>15</sup> generalized length vaporization correlation. The 20% vaporization concept was subsequently found to apply to a wide range of propellant combinations and operating conditions.

Subsequent work at Aerojet by Hewitt has shown a strong correlation between the observed combustion response frequency and the ratio of the injector orifice diameter to propellant injection velocity ( $D_i/V_i$ ) of LOL injection elements. Whereas most of the data used to establish the correlation were from storable propellant engine systems, Anderson et al.<sup>38</sup> extended the experimental database on which the correlation is based to include the maximum combustion response frequency of LOL injectors using LOX/HC propellants (Fig. 1). The unstable points on Fig. 1 correspond to the highest frequency of combustion instability that was observed in the combustor, whereas the stable points on Fig. 1 correspond to the calculated frequency of the lowest chamber acoustic mode that was not excited by combustion. The correlation as shown in Fig. 1 demonstrates the importance of the injector operating conditions in determining the overall combustion stability characteristics of the engine.

The O-F-O element has a distinct advantage over the LOL element in that it can provide a very high interpropellant mixing efficiency. As demonstrated in the LHCP and LeRC programs already discussed,  $C^*$  efficiencies greater

Furthermore, O-F-O element designs that produce optimal levels of performance (equal LOX and LHC orifice diameters, equal LOX and LHC dynamic heads) are readily achieved with LOX/LHC propellants because of typical propellant mass ratios and typical propellant densities. However, most likely because of the increased energy release rate promoted by the enhanced mixing of the O-F-O element, the O-F-O element also appears to be more prone to spontaneous high-frequency instabilities than does the LOL element. has discouraged rocket developers from using O-F-O elements, and there is a much greater experience level with LOL elements.

It should be noted that much of the perception about the relative stability of O-F-O and LOL elements comes from their comparison on an equivalent thrust-per-element basis, i.e., an O-F-O element can drive higher modes of instability than can a LOL element that injects the same amount of propellant. Since the O-F-O is higher performing than the LOL, however, O-F-O elements with higher thrust-per-element ratios can be used. In light of the ability of the correlation shown in Fig. 1 to match the stability characteristics of LOL elements, the correlation was extended to determine the maximum frequency response characteristics of O-F-O triplet elements with LOX/HC propellants in Fig. 2. Some reasonable trend is seen here as well, but the limited amount of available data makes a clear distinction less certain. It is important to note that these correlations identify the maximum frequency the element can support through a pure burning coupled mechanism, and it is not capable of predicting the stability characteristics if injection coupling mechanisms become important.

### V. Conclusions

The importance of the development of analytical models capable of predicting the characteristics of the spray and combustion response characteristics can not be overemphasized. These models can be used in conjunction with relatively simple steady-state combustion and chamber response models to optimize engine performance and stability characteristics in a short period of time. They also provide tools with which analysts can prescribe hardware modifications to change the performance and stability characteristics of existing hardware designs.

There is strong evidence that large thrust elements can be designed to provide both high performance and good stability characteristics using LOX/RP-1 as propellants. However, it appears that LOL injector designs must trade performance for stability. The LOL injector designs usually provide moderate performance at best if manageable combustion stability characteristics are to be achieved (e.g., Atlas, F-1, HHC, LHICP). The results of the LHICP, LeRC, and pressure fed booster programs indicate, however, that large O-F-O triplet elements can provide very high performance while also possessing manageable stability characteristics. The element response characteristics presented in Figs. 1 and 2 indicate that larger orifice diameters or small injection velocities are required to keep the maximum response frequency low enough (e.g., below the chamber's 3T frequency) to be damped with a combination of acoustic cavities and simple thrust chamber baffle patterns in large-diameter, high-thrust engines. Low injection velocity and low injection pressure drop can lead to injection coupling in triplet designs and poor mixing in doublet designs. Increasing the orifice diameter results in reduced element density, which can result in large mixing losses in like-doublet designs. Since triplet elements result in intimate mixing at impingement, low element density does not seem to significantly affect performance. Low element density can, however, compromise injector face cooling.

The triplet test data indicates that the requirement of equal orifice diameter for the fuel and oxidizer may be desirable but that it is not sufficient condition for good performance. High injector impedance (large  $\Delta P_{j,0}/P_c$ ) seems to be essential to preclude coupling through the feed system. The use of contoured inlet element designs provides for efficient use of the available injection pressure drop

and may partially offset the need for large injection pressure drops. Sparse patterns do not seem to cause performance problems when triplet elements are used, and they may actually lead to better performance and stability characteristics. Triplet and LOL element layouts must carefully consider interaction between adjacent element spray fans since this close packing appears to cause atomization and mixing problems.

Finally, the  $D_j/V_j$  correlations presented in Figs. 1 and 2 can be used in conjunction with the relationship for the resonant frequency of modes in the chamber to guide the injector element sizing early in the development phase for large engines. This type of correlation permits trade studies between stability characteristics, damping device requirements, active cooling, and injector performance to be rapidly conducted.

## Combustion Instability in the RD-0110 Engine

Vitaly R. Rubinsky\*

*Chemiautomatics Design Bureau (CADB), Voronezh, Russia*

### I. Introduction

THE third stage of the Soyuz space vehicle is powered by the RD-0110, a LOX-kerosene liquid propellant rocket engine. During both development and acceptance testing, high-frequency combustion instability was observed. The four-chamber RD-0110 engine (Fig. 1) operates on a gas generator cycle. Propellants are fed to the combustion chamber by the turbopump, whose turbine operates on the combustion products of LOX and kerosene produced by a gas generator. Propellant ignition in both the chamber and in the gas generator is by a pyrotechnic device. Engine control and adjustment is provided by a regulator, a throttle, and a set of valves. The main technical data of this engine are presented in Table 1.

While designing and developing the chamber for RD-0110, a great deal of consideration was given to the analysis of the mixing system, whose scheme and parameters determine the stability and quality of operating process. During the initial injector design analysis stage, a great deal of consideration also was given to the problems of ensuring chamber operating process high-frequency stability using conventional techniques.<sup>1,2</sup> The well-known methods of stabilization, i.e., "extension" of the combustion zone (energy release) along the length or radius of the chamber, changing the mixing elements flow rate/atomizing characteristics, and mounting antipulsation partitions (baffles) at the injector, also were considered.

Proceeding from the idea of the propellants' interaction at the initial section of the chamber and its influence on the dynamics of propellant burnout near the injector, it was supposed that bipropellant centrifugal atomizers had real advantages in this point. It was expected that the propellant burnout dynamics could be influenced by changing the interaction between the oxidizer and fuel cones. At the same time, the necessity of providing the high quality of the propellant mixing system to obtain the requisite specific impulse was taken into account.

During thrust chamber development, occurrences of high-frequency combustion instability were observed to be dependent on the use of different atomizer designs. Studies of the problem confirmed the theory that stability was determined by the interaction between the atomizing cones of oxidizer and fuel, including the core

and peripheral regions of the cone. Spray cone interaction is in turn determined by the design of the centrifugal atomizers. Eventually, an injector that comprised bipropellant centrifugal atomizers was developed and mastered that provided high-quality mixing and high-frequency stability of the chamber operating process over a wide range of pressure and mixture ratio.

High-frequency combustion instability was not observed during the final stages of the chamber off-line development, during the complex development of the whole RD-0110 engine, or during its operation in the third stage of the Soyuz rocket carrier. However, although very seldom (one case per 60–80 engine tests), high-frequency combustion instability began to be observed during engine start in the bench approval tests performed by the production plant. Combustion instability was not noticed during main operation. Studies of these problems were carried out with the goal of eliminating high-frequency instability during the start without changing the engine start scheme or the injector design.

Acoustic and model studies revealed the possibility of stabilizing the operating process by the arrangement of several short longitudinal ribs, made from combustible material, at the inner surface of the chamber; this measure was taken for further development to eliminate high-frequency instability during the start of the RD-0110. It was supposed that the ribs would provide high-frequency stability during the start and burnout for the moment the engine is to transition to the main operating mode. Off-line chamber tests and engine bench tests showed that placement of six longitudinal felt ribs completely eliminated the chamber operating process high-frequency instability during the start of the RD-0110 engine.

This chapter presents the analysis of the high-frequency combustion stability improvement undertaken at different stages of the RD-0110 development as well as the methodology of organization and carrying out of such an analysis. The results of these studies, which were carried out at the time of the chamber's creation, and the conclusions made on their basis were the foundation for further chamber development.

The chapter uses the materials of scientific and technical reports made at the Chemicautomatics Design Bureau and the Research Institute of Thermal Processes. After the completion of these studies the works in Refs. 3–5 appeared. They analyzed the stabilization methods for the chamber's operating process of the liquid rocket engines (LRE). These methods are to some extent similar to the mechanisms that were realized during the creation of the chamber for the RD-0110 engine.

### **II. High-Frequency Combustion Stability Studies During Off-Line Chamber Development**

#### **A. Description and Main Technical Data of the Chamber**

The chamber is a welded detachable construction consisting of two parts, the injector and the chamber itself (Figs. 2 and 3). The chamber injector (Figs. 4 and 5) consists of 91 atomizers (Fig. 6), firing bottom, deflector, and injector housing. The components of the injector are joined by vacuum brazing. The fuel goes through the chamber's cooling duct into the injector and then between the injector face plate and deflector into the atomizer's cavity. This scheme provides reliable cooling of the injector faceplate.

The chamber itself consists of the chamber unit, a throat insert, and a nozzle unit. The chamber unit consists of the outer and inner shells of the cylinder and

#### B. Selection and Bases of the Scheme, Design, and Variants of Injector and Atomizers

Efficient combustion was required taking into account the specific impulse requirements of the RD-0110. Single-propellant and bipropellant atomizers were analyzed. To get the most uniform mixture ratio at the initial section of the chamber (in the scale of spacing between the atomizers), the bipropellant atomizers were chosen. The following points were taken into consideration. In principle, injectors with single-propellant atomizers can provide quite high (small-scaled) uniformity of propellant distribution. The experience of chamber mastering and development showed that, to reach such a goal, one should use a relatively great number of single-propellant atomizers in the injector to provide fine atomization of oxidizer and fuel. It is simpler, however, to get a uniform mixture ratio at the initial section by using fewer bipropellant atomizers, especially with internal mixing. It should be pointed out that the considerations leading to the choice of single-propellant atomizers were connected with the great advantage of such atomizers in case they needed modification and improvement. Such modifications are required in

the process of chamber development if there is a necessity to solve the problems related to operating process high-frequency stability.

Thus, bipropellant atomizers are more convenient for the designer during the chamber development process because they do not need variants modifications, which change the design of atomizers and injector. A basic injector design incorporating the bipropellant atomizers was developed. This injector was subjected to the tests with three types of bipropellant atomizers: centrifugal atomizers (CS), centrifugal-spray atomizers (C), and spray atomizers (S). The location of atomizers is shown in Fig. 10.

For bipropellant centrifugal atomizers, the length of the oxidizer atomizer nozzle face recess relative to the fuel atomizer nozzle face,  $L$ , was taken as a main factor influencing the interaction of propellants at the initial section of the chamber. According to the results of hydraulic tests of centrifugal atomizers with size

$L = 5.0$  mm, mixing and interaction of propellants began in the fuel atomizer nozzle (emulsion atomizer). At the size  $L = 1.5$  mm, mixing and interaction of propellants took place outside the atomizer (outer mixing atomizer). At the size  $L = 2.5$  mm, oxidizer and fuel spraying cones had a contact near the outlet edge of fuel atomizer nozzle.

Thus, it was supposed that the dimension  $L$  can influence the completeness and high-frequency pressure oscillations in the chamber. Five variants of injectors C were developed (Table 3). Design and hydraulic parameters of all C atomizers were identical.

In case increases in the operating process high-frequency stability margins were required for the chamber with injectors C, the injector CS was developed. In its center there were 13 bipropellant spray atomizers with impinging jets of oxidizer and fuel (at a 30-deg angle) to extend the fuel component's initial interaction zone. The geometrical dimensions of the joint places for the spray atomizers were the same as for the joint places of the centrifugal atomizers, which made the process of injector production easier. A variant of injector S with bipropellant spray atomizers (which were used in injector CS) was developed for the case where the operating process high-frequency stability would not be realized on the base of injectors C and CS. The calculated mixture ratio for atomizers of injectors C, CS, and S were kept equal to the value of 2.85. Figure 11 presents the design and parameters of atomizers C and S.

#### C. Results

Off-line firing tests of the chambers were carried out in three stages. The aim of the first stage was the selection of a high-performance injector, providing high quality and stability of operating process in the chamber pressure range  $P_c = 3.0\text{--}8.0$  MPa. The tests were done with the short chamber without supersonic section of the nozzle. Start of the chamber into the main operating mode ( $P_c = 7.0$  MPa,  $O/F = 2.44$ ) was done through the preliminary stage ( $P_c = 3.5$  MPa,  $O/F = 2.44$  or  $O/F = 1.0$ ). Test duration was up to 20 s.

The second stage was carried out to develop reliable cooling. It was done in the chamber with a shortened supersonic section of the nozzle (Fig. 12), providing constant outflow of combustion products under Earth conditions.

The third stage was carried out with the full-sized chamber. The main aim of the tests was to confirm the serviceability of the chamber's final design during its life and the evaluation of specific impulse under the calculated conditions of combustion products outflow from the nozzle ( $P_a = 7.27$  kPa). The test stand for the third stage was equipped with a thrust measuring device and an exhaust device to provide conditions of the combustion product outflow from the nozzle.

The firing tests of the chambers with injectors C1 and C2 were ended by their failure (destruction) by oscillations that appeared in the starting mode with frequency  $f = 4000$  Hz and amplitude more than 1.5 MPa. The duration of the chamber's operation was 0.04–0.1 s. The calculated value of the first tangential mode for the chamber was  $f = 3900$  Hz. Thus, it was evident that tangential mode high-frequency oscillations arose during the tests. Tests of the chambers with reserve variants of injectors CS and S were also ended by their destruction during the start because of the tangential mode high-frequency oscillations. Thus, the approach of high-frequency instability elimination by extending the propellant interaction section in injectors CS and S gave no positive results in the operating process conditions of the oxygen-kerosene chamber of RD-0110. The chamber with injector C5 successfully went through the tests, with a wide range of starting conditions and  $P_c$  and  $O/F$  at the main operating mode value. The specific impulse of the chamber with injector C5 was higher than the chamber with injector C3 by 10–15 m/s and met the technical requirements.

Results of the firing tests of the chambers with injectors C1–C5 confirmed the idea of the influence of propellant interaction in the initial zone (determined by the interlocation of oxidizer and fuel atomizing cones of two-component centrifugal atomizer  $L$ ) on combustion efficiency and high-frequency stability. Thus, the dynamics of propellant burnout near the injector, combustion efficiency, and high-frequency combustion stability can be purposefully influenced by the change of  $L$  in bipropellant centrifugal atomizers located in the center or periphery of the injector.

The studies revealed that mixing between the oxidizer and fuel atomizing cones inside the atomizer over the whole injector field (variants C1 and C2) results in a short initial zone and the dynamics and volumetric energy release rate can create favorable conditions for replenishment of tangential mode oscillations. To change the energy release behavior in the initial zone and to eliminate the conditions for lateral oscillations initiation, it is sufficient to push the mixing zones of the spray cone–spray cone interactions out of the atomizers to the center of the injector. Possibly under these conditions, the mechanism of energy-release “extension” in the center of the injector begins to work, which leads to the stabilization of the combustion process. The analogous processes take place when the peripheral atomizers influence the propellant’s atomizing cones in the same way (variants C3–C5).

Further development tests of RD-0110 confirmed the high-frequency stability and completeness of the operating process in the chamber with injector C5, which was accepted as a standard in the design documentation.

### III. High-Frequency Stability Improvement During Engine Start

#### A. Analysis of High-Frequency Stability at RD-0110 Delivery

At the first stage of RD-0110 engine delivery to customers, during the firing approval tests performed by the production plant, one of the engine’s chambers failed 0.04–0.1 s after start. The time from the beginning of the process to the moment the engine goes into the main operating mode was not higher than 0.18 s. The pattern of failure was similar to the pattern of the chamber’s failure with injector C1 during off-line development tests and indicated that the cause was the appearance of the first tangential mode high-frequency oscillations in the chamber. Such cases were rare, one chamber out of four chambers per engine per 70–80 engines, i.e., one out of every 280–320 chambers. Chamber failure by high-frequency oscillations did not occur during the RD-0110 engine operation on the rocket-carrier Soyuz.

A careful analysis of production peculiarities and possible deviations in the chambers and engines that had high-frequency instabilities and start peculiarities was carried out. No deviations were revealed that were thought to influence high-frequency combustion stability. Prior experience with oxygen-kerosene engine development showed that high-frequency combustion stability is sensitive to the

mixture ratio during start. Thus, special firing tests that provided the measurement of oxygen and fuel flow rate through each chamber to evaluate the mixture ratio deviation range for the four chambers during the start were carried out. The average mixture ratio in these tests was  $0.9 \pm 15\%$ . The spread in the four chambers of one engine also was 15% from the average  $O/F$  value of the engine. The total spread of  $O/F$  during start was 0.7–1.1 for all of the tests. Taking into account these results, off-line firing tests of the chambers were carried out with changes of  $O/F$  during start of 0.6–1.3 over the chamber pressure range 1.5–5 MPa. The aim of the tests was to reveal the stability margin during the start.

Chambers with extreme combinations of oxidizer and fuel atomizer pressure drop were also produced and were tested successfully. To simulate the high-frequency instability, tests with the changes of outer and inner factors at the start of operating mode were carried out; the changes were directed at decreasing the high-frequency instability margins. The engines went through the tests successfully. Thus, according to the results of great number of studies and analyses, the origins of the rare high-frequency combustion instabilities that occurred during the start of the RD-0110 engine were still undiscovered. In so far as the RD-0110 engine operated well on the rocket-carrier Soyuz, the cases of high-frequency instability during approval tests at the production plant were possibly connected with rare occurrences of a certain combination of production engine peculiarities and test stand peculiarities, which are difficult to detect.

Taking into account the fact that the chamber worked well in the main operating mode, it was necessary to find a method of high-frequency instability elimination which would not need a change in the engine start cyclogram (including the start on the rocket-carrier stage), or changes of injector design, which would lead to a great volume of work for engine finishing and mastering. It was also very desirable to find a solution that could be used in engines already produced after their nonsophisticated finishing.

A method that met these requirements and improved high-frequency stability of chamber operating process during the start consisted of the following. Several longitudinal "soft" ribs of middle height and made of combustible material (technical felt) were stuck to the inner cylindrical surface of the chamber beginning from the injector. It was supposed that the ribs would provide reliability at the start and would then burnout up to the moment the engine is to go onto the main operating mode.

#### B. Results of Model Studies on Effectiveness of Ribs

To analyze chamber acoustic characteristics (including the characteristics of the chamber with ribs), a special study was carried out. A chamber purged by air was periodically perturbed in time. Instantaneous measurements of pressure oscillations and injector flow rate oscillations and their phase shifts were measured. To actuate the chamber, an acoustic pulse generator (pulsator) was placed upstream of the injector. Acoustic characteristics of the chamber were determined by the amplitude-phase-frequency characteristic (normalized impedance), which is indicative of the amplitude of nondimensional injector flow rate pulsations,

$$K_A e^{i\phi} = \frac{p'/\bar{p}}{\dot{m}'/\bar{m}}$$

where  $p'$  and  $m'$  are the pulsating components of pressure and flow rate and  $\bar{p}$  and  $\bar{m}$  are the means of these values.  $K_A$  is the chamber amplitude-frequency characteristic and  $\phi$  the phase characteristic.

The function  $K_A$  has the form of a resonance curve. Its maximum value ( $K_A^{\max}$ ) corresponds to the chamber resonance frequency and signifies the acoustic gain factor. A reduction of  $K_A^{\max}$  can be explained by additional dissipation of acoustic energy. The studies showed that mounting of the longitudinal ribs led to a considerable dissipation process. Thus, the felt ribs with the height of 26–28 mm decreased the resonance the acoustic gain factor by approximately three times. Figure 14 demonstrates the amplitude-frequency characteristics of the chamber with and without ribs for comparison. The nondimensional frequency of disturbance input to the chamber,  $\omega R_k / C^*$ , where  $R_k$  is the chamber radius,  $C^*$  the sound velocity in the nozzle throat section, and  $\omega$  the oscillation frequency, is marked at the horizontal axis, and the ratio of the dimensionless amplitude of the pressure fluctuation to the dimensionless injector flow rate fluctuation amplitude is marked at the vertical axis. The maximum value of this characteristic signifies a resonance acoustic gain factor of the first tangential mode oscillations. The acoustic studies showed that the main factor that influences the effect of ribs is the rib height. Neither the number of ribs nor the rib width have a considerable effect. There is a definite length of ribs beginning from which their effectiveness is practically the same. The acoustic study also showed that felt ribs are 50–100% more effective than metallic ribs of the same height.

The following is an explanation of the peculiarities of soft rib behavior in the chamber. Under the influence of oscillations, a submerged body will initiate periodic compression and rarefaction of the surrounding fluid and will be the source of acoustic waves. Energy, carried by these waves, will be obtained from the kinetic energy of the moving body. If the body is immovable and the acoustic wave is incident on it, there would be scattering of sound; together with the incident wave there would appear additional (scattered) waves. If the length of the acoustic wave is large in comparison with the dimensions of the body, the scattered wave can be considered to be a wave radiated by the body. The difference consists in the following: we are dealing not with the body movement in the fluid but with the movement of the fluid relative to the body.

Proceeding from such ideas, the mechanism of acoustic energy dissipation in the chamber with soft ribs can be described in the following way. The rib, on which the acoustic wave is incident (in this case, the wave has the first tangential mode of oscillations), scatters the wave. In so far as the scattered acoustic field will be determined by the geometric dimensions of the rib, the scattered wave pattern will have higher oscillation modes than the main movement. These oscillation modes in the resonance frequency should attenuate very quickly while moving along the chamber. The supposition concerning the higher performance of soft ribs made of felt can then be made: there is an additional dissipation mechanism, one that is possibly connected with the friction loss of felt on fibers under the rib oscillations or with the gas viscosity in the interporous space of the felt.

Special studies were carried out to check the effectiveness of felt ribs under firing test conditions. The special model chamber, working with the propellant combination nitrogen tetroxide + tonka (50% triethylamine, 50% xylidine) was used. The results of the tests showed the presence of the chamber start mode, which always had high-frequency oscillations of the tangential mode. The chamber model was started both with and without ribs. Sensors registered the moment of onset of high-frequency oscillation. The chamber model was equipped with eight ribs,

The influence of rib number, height, and length on the suppression of high-frequency oscillations was checked by demonstrating that shortening rib length from 0.25 to 0.125 m and shortening rib height from 40 to 25 mm did not change the suppression effectiveness of high-frequency oscillations during the start. Decreasing the rib number from eight to four reduced the duration of stable operation by 1–1.5 s.

Tests were carried out to compare the effectiveness of soft ribs (made of felt) and stiff ribs (made of plastic and metal). Tests of a chamber with eight plastic ribs made of plastic ASTT and of the same size as the felt ribs were destroyed by high-frequency oscillations during the start of the chamber at 3.7 s and 3.8 s. The felt ribs stabilized the process up to 7–10 s.

### IV. Test Results on the Use of Combustible Felt Ribs During Firing Tests in Chambers and Engines

Acoustic studies and firing tests confirmed the effectiveness of felt ribs for stabilization during chamber start up to the moment of rib burnout. Full-scale studies were also done in this direction during off-line bench tests of chambers and engines. During the bench tests of the chambers it was necessary to evaluate the effectiveness of combustible felt ribs for stability improvement for at least 0.18 s of the engine start and to allow a decision about rib integration into the standard design. Thus, it was necessary to master a reliable technology to bond the ribs, to define the influence of the rib-bonding process on the reliability of chamber cylindrical section inner wall cooling, to determine the explosion hazard of felt ribs at the initial stage of start under the conditions of advanced liquid oxygen

flowing into the chamber when the cartridge igniters operate, and to confirm the biological shielding of ribs under the long-term storage.

The technology of rib production and adhesion was developed and mastered. It consisted of the selection of an adhesive that could perform satisfactorily in contact with stainless steel without special thermal treatment or great effort to press and stick the ribs, selection of a biological shield for long-term storage, and determination of the optimal felt type.

During the technological mastering and chamber tests, different types of adhesive were tried: adhesive VS-10T, epoxy underpaint hard putty E4020, hermetic Viksint with an underlayer of cold drying P11, and adhesive K300. Fitness of adhesive was determined by the time of stable chamber operation with the ribs, the adhesive and rib remainders at the chamber inner wall, and the state of the chamber inner wall after the tests. According to the analysis of preliminary tests, the best results were given by the VS-10T adhesive and hermetic Viksint with the underlayer of cold drying P11. The samples stuck by the VS-10T adhesive had high-mechanical strength. To bond the ribs, however, required a high drying temperature ( $180^{\circ}\text{C}$  for 2 h) and great effort of pressing, which excluded the use of such an adhesive to bond the ribs in the ready-made engines. Also, the chamber life tests showed that the VS-10T adhesive sometimes did not completely burn off and formed carbonization at the chamber inner wall. Carbonizations disturbing the gas boundary layer lead to wall burnthrough behind ribs.

Hermetic Viksint with underlayer P11 does not need high bonding temperatures; it is polymerized at  $20^{\circ}\text{C}$  during 72 h. The joint was very strong and elastic. Satisfactory resistance and effectiveness of the ribs stuck by the hermetic Viksint with underlayer P11 was confirmed by the chamber firing tests. Reliability of the rib bond was controlled by the samples. Minimum breaking load values were obtained during shear tests of the steel-felt adhesive joint bonded by hermetic Viksint with underlayer P11. Felt samples  $20 \times 20 \times 40$  mm were bonded to the plate from steel IX18H10T. The tearoff force for 25 samples was 65–90 kPa.

Chamber firing tests revealed that the rib resistance depends considerably on the type of felt and on the location of its fibers relative to the bond plane. Ribs made of 3–10-mm-wide layers with fibers parallel to the bond plane and bonded by VS-10T adhesive lost their effectiveness during the chamber firing tests. During the firing tests the ribs made of fibers parallel to the bond plane became larger and were torn off just after the start and consequently did not provide the necessary effect. A rib tear occurred in the felt. Ribs made of 2–15-mm-wide layers with fibers located perpendicular to the bond plane and bonded with hermetic Viksint with one elastic adhesive joint did not change their size, had full burnout, and suppressed the oscillations for more than 0.18 s after the chamber start. This design was considered to be an optimum one.

To provide the biological shield of felt ribs, different coverings were tested: water glass, aluminum enamel C0813, adhesive VS-10T, and hermetic Viksint. The best covering was a fine layer of hermetic Viksint; it was elastic and was not broken while ribs were bonded to the chamber, which allowed the opportunity to cover the ribs before their attachment to the chamber. All of the other coverings must take place after the ribs were attached to the chamber to exclude any damage when pressing the ribs by the rig during their bonding. This fact causes considerable technological difficulties and decreases the reliability of the rib biological shield.

The firing tests showed that the width of covering influences the ribs' effectiveness: increasing the covering width up to 1.5–2.0 mm reduces their effectiveness. The optimum covering was one with 0.2–0.6 mm width.

After the technological mastering and preliminary firing tests (which determined the felt type for rib production, the type of adhesive for their sticking, the technological process, and the rib material) a design variant was chosen for the final stage of off-line chamber firing tests to confirm the effectiveness of ribs in enhancing stability during simulated engine start conditions. Six ribs were located in the chamber. The ribs had the following dimensions: length 0.150 m, height 40 mm of trapezoidal section, top base 20 mm, and lower base (bonding place) 30 mm, with a sharp trailing edge to smooth the gas flow (Figs. 16 and 17). To provide a shield from biological organisms, the ribs were covered by 0.2–0.6-mm-wide hermetic Viksint before their placement into the chamber. The ribs were stuck onto the chamber inner wall by the hermetic Viksint with underlayer P11. Figure 18 shows the chamber with the ribs.

Insofar as the high-frequency instability occurrence rarely arose, it was necessary to develop a method to reliably produce high-frequency oscillations with large amplitude at the initial moment of chamber start up. A method was developed to produce high-frequency oscillations during chamber start up by the use of a cavitating tube (venturi) located at the oxygen inlet to the injector. The cavitating tube (venturi) had converging and diverging parts with a minimum section (throat) diameter of 7 mm. A pressure differential 10–12 MPa provided the cavitating mode oxygen outflow.

During the tests, asymmetric high-frequency oscillations with frequencies of 1100–1600 Hz and amplitudes more than 1.0 MPa arose. Such oscillations made the analysis of effective measures to improve high-frequency stability difficult. The

moment of the onset of high-frequency oscillations also depended considerably on the cavitation intensity at the initial moment of chamber start. Such considerations led to the choice not to use this method of producing high-frequency oscillations.

During off-line mastering tests, injector C1 produced high-frequency tangential mode instability with amplitudes greater than 1.5 MPa at 0.04–0.11 s after the beginning of the chamber start-up process. Therefore, later studies of the effectiveness of ribs were performed in chambers with the injector C1. In so far as the effectiveness of ribs in stabilizing combustion during the start process could be confirmed only during the tests of one chamber without ribs (with high-frequency instability during the start) and with ribs (with high-frequency instability after the ribs tear off or burn out), it was necessary to master the chamber emergency switchoff before chamber failure due to high-frequency oscillations. For that, a signal was given to the emergency switchoff system from the pressure fluctuation piezoelectric transducer, which was put in the combustion cavity in front of the injector atomizers. When the number of pressure fluctuations with the frequency of the first tangential mode  $f = 4000$  Hz and with an amplitude  $\geq 0.5$  MPa exceeded more than 15–20 cycles, the emergency switchoff system gave the signal to switchoff the chamber by closing a quick-acting oxidizer valve located just before the injector. Such a system provided a test shutdown within 0.04 s after the beginning of high-frequency oscillations and kept the chamber intact for repeat tests. The difference in time between the signal from the emergency switchoff system and the moment of ignition determined the time of stable chamber operation. A comparison of these differences during tests of the chambers with and without ribs led to a conclusion about the effectiveness of ribs for stabilization of the operating process. The results from the final stage of chamber off-line firing tests are presented in Table 4. Test results are given graphically in Fig. 19. As seen from the presented materials, during the tests of the chambers without ribs, high-frequency tangential-mode oscillations with frequency  $f \sim 4000$  Hz developed 0.03–0.095 s after ignition. The presence of ribs increased the time of stable operation up to 0.237–0.304 s. Rapid increase in the amplitude of high-frequency oscillations began after the ribs burned out and tore off.

The contacts of the hermetically sealed reed relays were kept in the closed position by the magnets. The measurement system registered the moment the ribs with magnets were torn off by recording the time the contacts broke.

The time of contact break, indicating the moment the ribs tear off, coincided with the time that the signal from the emergency switchoff system was given by sensing high-frequency oscillations with increasing amplitude. Thus, the felt ribs provided stability during the start up to the moment of rib burnout or tearoff. The delay of the appearance of the high-frequency oscillations during chamber start up is 0.17–0.257 s longer with ribs than in the chambers without ribs. Taking into account the fact that the time from propellant ignition to the moment the engine transitions into the main operating mode is less than 0.18 s and the ribs (according to the tests results) stay effective for between 0.237 and 0.304 s, the attachment of combustible felt ribs provided stability during the engine start.

When the engine goes on, the chambers start together with an oxygen advance and with working igniters within 0.4 s. To confirm that there was no explosion hazard and to ensure reliable operation of the chambers with ribs, off-line firing tests of the chambers were carried out with oxygen advance flowing into the chamber during the start up to 1.2 s with operating igniters. The chambers went through the tests successfully.

Vibrational and transport overload tests of the chambers with ribs and with preliminary thermostating of the chambers were also carried out. The levels of

vibrational and transport overload and thermostating conditions corresponded to the engine requirements. Visual inspection after the tests indicated no problems. After the vibrational and transport overload tests, the chambers went through firing tests, during which the appearance of high-frequency oscillations was delayed by 0.24–0.28 s, corresponding to the results presented in Table 4. After the off-line chamber firing tests, qualification life tests of the three-engine RD-0110 were performed. The engines went through the tests successfully, and visual inspection of the chambers did not reveal any defects. The time range of rib tearoff during the engine start was 0.24–0.29 s, which also corresponded to the results of chamber off-line tests presented in Table 4.

The combustible felt ribs were included in the standard chamber documentation of the RD-0110 engine as a method of providing stability improvement during start. After the modification to include ribs, more than 2500 RD-0110 engines, or more than 10,000 chambers, went through the firing approval tests at the production plant. There was not one case of high-frequency combustion instability during the engine start. More than 1000 of the RD-0110 engines successfully took part in the start of the Sojuz rocket carrier, including manned spacecrafts.

### Nomenclature

### I. Introduction

Earth storable bipropellant engines are used extensively in many areas of space flight. In the Apollo program, storable bipropellant engines landed humans on the moon and returned them safely to Earth. In current applications, the Space Shuttle uses Earth storable engines for maneuvering and deorbiting. Many launch vehicles, such as the Titan, Delta, Long March, and Ariane, use Earth storable propellants for boosters and upper stages. Earth storable propellants are also used in most unmanned spacecraft and satellites.

Dynamically stable combustion in Earth storable propellant engines has been obtained through extensive testing of injector element patterns and damping devices, such as baffles and acoustic cavities. Development of stable injector patterns
