and suitable damping devices occurred primarily in the 1960s, during the Apollo program. This chapter describes the development of storable propellant engines in the United States and China. Through these case studies, which include quantitative details of the combustion instabilities experienced, combustion instability phenomena in storable propellant engines can be examined.

Earth storable propellants comprise a family of propellant combinations, which use primarily nitrogen tetroxide (NTO) as the oxidizer, and hydrazine, monomethyl hydrazine (MMH), unsymmetrical dimethylhydrazine (UDMH), or their blends as the fuel. Earth storable refers to the characteristic of being liquid at standard temperature and pressure, and being relatively easy to store for periods of years. Table 1 lists the thermodynamic and physical properties of these propellants, with the maximum theoretical performance evaluated using NTO at an area ratio of 60:1 and optimum mixture ratio.<sup>1,2</sup>

### II. History and Applications of Earth Storable Propellants

Nitrogen tetroxide was first experimentally used for rocket engine research in 1930 by Crocco in Italy and by Glushko in Russia.<sup>3</sup> The fuels were gasoline and toluene, respectively. Hypergolicity, the spontaneous ignition upon contact of oxidizer and fuel, was probably first discovered around 1937, by Walter in Germany, using hydrazine hydrate (N<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub> · H<sub>2</sub>O) and peroxide.<sup>3</sup> The word hypergolic was coined by Noeggerath during experimental work with Sanger and Mueller in Germany on nitric acid and fuels such as aniline.<sup>3</sup>

In the 1950s, hydrazine was considered for use as a propellant because of its high performance, high density, and hypergolicity with storable oxidizers. The only problem was the freezing point, which did not meet military specifications for cold weather applications. A U.S. Navy contract with Aerojet and Metalelectro addressed this problem successfully.<sup>3</sup> This contract evaluated the hydrazine derivatives, such as monomethylhydrazine (MMH, CN<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>), unsymmetrical dimethylhydrazine (UDMH, C<sub>2</sub>N<sub>2</sub>H<sub>8</sub>), and symmetrical dimethylhydrazine (SDMH).<sup>3</sup> MMH and UDMH were found to be suitable; however, SDMH proved to be a low performer. Aerojet later produced Aerozine 50 (A50), a 50/50 blend of hydrazine and UDMH.<sup>3</sup>

Storable propellants are used in applications that benefit from 1) long-term storability, 2) high-bulk density performance, and 3) hypergolicity. These attributes result in space vehicles that are simple, cost effective, and reliable. Because of the

high density, it is practical to use tank pressure to feed the engine. A pressurized engine significantly reduces vehicle complexity, such that engine operation consists of opening only two engine valves. For cost and packaging reasons, many applications use a nonoptimum mixture ratio of 1.6 to make the oxidizer and fuel tanks identical. This results in a lower actual specific impulse, which typically ranges from 280 s to 334 s. Nevertheless, the high-bulk density still provides good overall vehicle performance, since the small tank volumes reduce vehicle structural mass and improve packaging in confined areas. The main drawback is the toxicity of Earth storable propellants, which requires measures to prevent human contact during testing and launch vehicle processing.

Titan 2 was the first major U.S. launch vehicle program to use Earth storable propellants (A50 and NTO).<sup>4</sup> Taking advantage of Earth storability, Titan 2 replaced the Titan 1 and Atlas, due to the possible launch delays inherent with fueling liquid oxygen and kerosene minutes before launch.<sup>4</sup> It went into service in 1962 and was later used in the Gemini program with engine stability improvements, which included baffles and injection distribution modifications.<sup>5,6</sup> Following the Gemini program, the Apollo program used NTO with A50 and MMH. In the 1950s, China began development of storable propellant engines, which led to the Long March Series I and II. In the 1970s, the Space Shuttle program switched entirely to MMH and NTO for on-orbit propulsion. Depending on the requirements of future vehicles, Earth storable bipropellant engines may again be used, if long-term storability, propulsion system simplicity, high reliability, and small packaging are desired.

### III. Combustion Phenomena in Earth Storable Engines

Combustion in Earth storable bipropellant engines has some unique characteristics. One critical characteristic is hypergolicity, in that chemical reaction can start with contact of the liquids and can affect the atomization process. Many instabilities with Earth storable propellants can be related in some manner to 1) popping, 2) resurging, and 3) reactive stream separation. In addition, products that form prior to ignition can cause ignition spikes and disturb combustion. In pressure-fed engines, dissolved gas in the propellant can also affect combustion stability.

The injector type affects the manner in which the propellants come into contact, thereby also affecting combustion stability. Coherent stream injector elements include unlike doublets (UD), triplets [fuel-oxidizer-fuel (FOF) or oxidizer-fuel-oxidizer (OFO)], quadlets, and coaxial elements (pintle or multiple). Self-atomizing elements include the transverse like-on-like (TLOL) and splashplate elements. Examples of these elements can be found in the engine case studies later in this chapter. Additional discussions of storable propellant instabilities can be found in Hefner<sup>6</sup> and Abbe et al.<sup>7</sup>

#### A. Preignition Products

During engine start and prior to ignition, preignition products can form in the chamber. After ignition, these preignition products can detonate and produce a large disturbance to the combustion process that can affect combustion stability. During the Apollo program, Christos et al.<sup>12</sup> examined the explosivity of the preignition products at the U.S. Bureau of Mines, using ballistic mortar and other tests. Christos found that the preignition products had an explosive equivalence of 139% of TNT.

Mayer et al.<sup>8</sup> experimentally studied the preignition of NTO and MMH at low pressures from 10-mm Hg (0.2 psia) to 110-mm Hg (2.2 psia). Using mass spectrometry, Mayer et al.<sup>8</sup> found that unstable nitroamines are created during the preignition phase. Prior to ignition, a flameless reaction occurs between the fuel and NO<sub>2</sub>, which produces a yellow fog in the chamber. Mayer et al.<sup>8</sup> reported that this fog consists of monomethyl nitroamide (CH<sub>3</sub>N<sub>2</sub>HO<sub>2</sub>). Analysis of the residues of this fog found MMH nitrate. The mechanism proposed for the formation of MMH nitrate is

![](2bf9ce14b0eedc810e869da8f46c73df_img.jpg)

$$\text{CH}_3\text{N}_2\text{H}_3 + 2\text{NO}_2 \rightarrow 3\text{H}_2\text{O} + 2\text{N}_2 + \text{CO}$$

![](9a1ae862ac11e6413902bd99441114b1_img.jpg)

$$\text{H}_2\text{O} + 3\text{NO}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{HNO}_3 + \text{NO}$$

![](624be39f0f04e35c5d94d3b7d244b7eb_img.jpg)

$$\text{HNO}_3 + \text{CH}_3\text{N}_2\text{H}_3 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{N}_2\text{H}_3 \bullet \text{HNO}_3$$

Saad et al.<sup>9</sup> examined the mass spectra and infrared spectra of reaction product residues and found, in addition to MMH nitrate, methylnitrosamine (CH<sub>3</sub>NHNO), which is unstable and decomposes to water, methanol, and nitrogen. Takimoto and Denault<sup>10</sup> also examined residues from thrusters and found MMH nitrate and ammonium nitrate. Interestingly, ammonium nitrate formed only during the steady-state firings. They proposed that the mixture containing MMH nitrate also contains heat-sensitive compounds, such as methyl azides and diazomethane, which can trigger sudden MMH nitrate decomposition. MMH nitrate has a low-vapor pressure which allows it to accumulate over successive pulses, especially when the thruster temperature is cold. Takimoto and Denault<sup>10</sup> found that three engine-operation factors increase the formation of MMH nitrate: 1) multiple pulses of short duration, 2) low propellant and engine temperatures, and 3) oxidizer leading the fuel in entering the chamber.

Hydrazinium nitrate and UDMH nitrate is obtained for the fuels, hydrazine and UDMH, respectively. Mayer et al.<sup>8</sup> reported that UDMH nitrate is unstable and decomposes much more readily, suggesting that UDMH may not form deposits which remain on the walls. In general for all Earth storable propellants, many different intermediates can be formed. Mills et al.<sup>11</sup> reported that low-activation energies are involved, which leads to the formation of many complex intermediates. Careful consideration of engine operating conditions and valve timing can limit the formation of preignition products.

#### B. Hypergolic Ignition and Overpressures

During ignition, large overpressures can occur due to the explosion of any preignition products. This is significant primarily because of the potential for damage to the engine or to the stability of the combustion process. Juran and Stechman<sup>15</sup> reported that large ignition overpressures are related to the accumulation of intermediate reaction products on cold chamber walls and that as thruster initial temperature increases, the pressure spike occurs less frequently.

The ignition of hypergolic propellants can be described as a thermal mechanism. The thermal ignition of an NTO and MMH mixture can be computed using the Semenov method or the Frank-Kamenetskii method as described by Glassman<sup>13</sup> and Gray.<sup>14</sup> These methods consider the balance between the rate of heat production by chemical reaction and the rate of heat conduction to the walls. When the rate

###### INSTABILITY PHENOMENA IN BIPROPELLANT ROCKET ENGINES 117

of heat production exceeds the rate of heat conduction, a rapid reaction occurs, which is ignition.

Kerkam and Kahl<sup>16</sup> performed engine tests on the 10,000-lbf thrust A50/NTO Lunar Module descent engine. High-speed photography showed brown viscous low-vapor-pressure deposits on the chamber wall just prior to ignition and the pressure spike. The occurrence of pressure spiking can be controlled by 1) correct oxidizer lead/lag time, 2) engine and propellant temperature, and 3) minimization of manifold (dribble) volume.

#### C. Hypergolic Droplet and Spray Combustion

Combustion of hypergolic propellants can occur in many forms of homogeneous or heterogeneous reactions. Most of the chemical reaction probably occurs as a homogeneous reaction between fuel vapor and oxidizer vapor, typically in which liquid fuel droplets are vaporizing in a gaseous oxidizer-rich environment, since NTO has the lower boiling point. At cooler conditions, heterogeneous reactions between liquid fuel and oxidizer vapor or even homogeneous reactions between liquid fuel and liquid oxidizer can also be expected. Experimental studies have sought to characterize this process, since it can have large effect on performance and stability.

The contact of two hypergolic liquids was experimentally studied by Daimon et al.<sup>18</sup> to measure the time lag of ignition or explosion. The tests were performed by impacting droplets of fuel, at various velocities and drop size, onto a pool of NTO. Upon contact, a layer of fuel and NTO vapor forms due to the gasification of NTO. In this layer a turbulent combustion reaction occurs. The results also indicated that the time lag of ignition decreased as droplet diameter increased.

Allison and Faeth<sup>19</sup> studied the burning of suspended MMH,  $N_2H_4$ , and UDMH droplets at atmospheric pressure in gaseous oxygen. The  $d^2$ -evaporation law plots, where  $d$  is the droplet diameter, were determined for the burning rates. They found that the droplet burns in two distinct regions: the inner region as a monopropellant, and the outer region as a bipropellant. This is especially true for hydrazine and less so for MMH and UDMH.

Eberstein and Glassman<sup>20</sup> experimentally determined the decomposition rates of monopropellant gas phases of MMH,  $N_2H_4$ , and UDMH in an adiabatic flow reactor. They proposed that the two methyl radicals in UDMH increase the chain-branching reactions, which explains why UDMH decomposition has the lowest activation energy. In MMH, however, this chain branching does not occur; hence, MMH has the highest activation energy.

For actual injectors under various operating conditions, Lawver<sup>17</sup> photographed an MMH/NTO unielement unlike doublet. Lawver explained that a yellow flame region occurs near the impingement point due to  $NH_2$  radical emission. Farther down from the impingement point, a blue region indicates methyl radical emission. MMH/NTO thrusters are observed to exhaust a blue-white flame from the nozzle. Lawver<sup>17</sup> also noted that hydrazine burns with a yellow flame over the entire combustion region, due to  $NH_2$  radical emission.

This is a short list of some of the analytical models of the hypergolic spray combustion process that have been made. For an MMH/NTO pintle engine, Krishnan et al.<sup>22</sup> considered both propellants entering as droplets and vaporizing in a Lagrangian frame, which was then mapped into an Eulerian frame and reacted in a simplified single step. Chiu et al.<sup>23</sup> treated the entire process in an Eulerian frame using the codes GEMCHIP and BICOMB. Larosiliere et al.<sup>21</sup> used

a Lagrangian–Eulerian approach and a two-step reaction for hydrazine and NTO and also considered the effects of reactive stream separation.

#### D. Reactive Stream Separation

Impinging streams of hypergolic propellants can be classified by the degree of 1) penetration, 2) mixing, and 3) separation. Penetration occurs when one propellant stream “shoots through” the other, which results in poor mixing. Mixing is the production of an uniformly distributed field of droplets that provides predictable smooth combustion. Blowpart or reactive stream separation (RSS) occurs when a gas layer forms between the impinging streams and prevents proper mixing.

Zung and White<sup>24</sup> and Lawver<sup>17</sup> used high-speed photography to view unelement impinging type injectors under actual engine operating conditions. Lawver studied blowpart for unlike doublets, triplets, and splashplate elements used in the Space Shuttle engines, which are discussed later in this chapter. Mixing is displayed in Fig. 1, and reactive stream separation is shown in Fig. 2, both for the Space Shuttle reaction control engine unlike doublet at actual operating conditions.<sup>17</sup> Reactive stream separation in coaxial injectors has recently been studied by Habiballah et al.<sup>25</sup>

Kushida and Houseman<sup>26</sup> identified criteria for predicting the separation of reactive streams that was based on pressure and the contact time as related to jet diameter and velocity. Lawver<sup>17</sup> correlated the regime of mixing and separation to the fuel orifice Reynolds number, because fuel vaporization was identified as the combustion rate limiting process. Lawver found that increasing chamber pressure and fuel velocity promoted separation. This study also concluded that the transition from mixed to separated modes should be avoided within the engine operational envelope.

#### E. Popping

Perhaps one of the most unique characteristics of hypergolic propellants may be the tendency to generate "pops." These pops can trigger instabilities in the engine, much the same as "bomb" tests used in the stability rating of engines. Although other types of propellants may display this phenomena, popping occurs more frequently with storable propellants. Many of the engines discussed later in this chapter, such as the Apollo Service Module engine, have experienced varying degrees of popping.

Pops are the result of accumulation and subsequent explosion of intermediate products, which are probably nitrates of the fuel, similar to preignition products. The mechanism for the generation of a pop is of considerable interest, since pops have been observed to initiate instabilities. For impinging elements, popping occurs at equal fluid stream dynamic pressures, which causes the streams to simultaneously stagnate. In addition, the temperature range of 297–300 K displayed the highest popping rate, outside of this range the popping rate falls off.<sup>27</sup>

Mills et al.<sup>11</sup> postulated that two conditions must be present for popping to occur: 1) the propellant temperatures must allow the propellants to mix as liquids and 2) the time for full atomization must be long enough to allow ignition to occur. Visual observations of unielement tests indicated that pops occur in the ligaments. These ligaments were observed to explode before fully atomizing. It was also observed in injector tests that two types of pops can occur: 1) smaller explosions within the element and 2) larger two-phase detonations of the entire field of elements.

Based on streak photography observations, Houseman and Lee<sup>28</sup> proposed that popping and reactive stream separation are related. Lawver<sup>7</sup> reported that pops are caused by reaction intermediates formed at the impingement point by surface reactions that occur at low-fuel-vapor pressures or under conditions of high heat

loss, such as with large streams ( $>0.060$  in. diameter) or cold propellants. The reaction intermediates form when the vapor separating the flow streams collapses and allows the liquids to mix. These reaction intermediates then move into a hot region where they detonate or pop.

#### F. Resurging

Resurging causes chamber pressure excursions that can eventually result in high-frequency instability. An example of resurging is shown in the pressure trace<sup>29</sup> in Fig. 3. This particular case is probably best described as a klystron effect,<sup>27</sup> in which sharp pulsing flow stream variations, possibly caused by engine chugging, cause the propellants to clump.<sup>27</sup> These clumps periodically form and then ignite, resulting in resurging that excites an acoustic resonance of the chamber. The example in Fig. 3 shows resurging continuing until it becomes a sustained high-frequency instability.

#### G. Dissolved Gases

The presence of dissolved gas in propellants is a potential problem for Earth storable bipropellant engines, which are pressure fed from screen acquisition tanks, rather than pump fed. In the propellant tank, pressurant gas dissolves in the propellant over time, until the propellant becomes saturated. During engine operation, these gases evolve from the propellants due to 1) the pressure drop in steady flow in the feed lines and the engine injector and 2) the feedline pressure transients at engine startup and shutdown. A significant quantity of helium can be produced which can effect the stability of the engine, as evidenced in the Space Shuttle primary reaction control thruster and the Apollo Lunar Module Ascent engine.

Chang et al.<sup>30,31</sup> provide experimentally determined relationships for the solubility of various gases in storable propellants. Solubility of gas in a liquid is determined from the application of Henry's law, which states that the solubility in terms of the mole fraction concentration  $x_i$  of a dissolved gas  $i$  is proportional to the partial pressure.

$$(\text{ppm})_i = K_i \cdot P_i$$

The amount of dissolved gas in solution can be found using the preceding equation, assuming enough time has been allowed for complete saturation, which could be hours for a typical tank. Figure 4 shows that helium dissolves in the highest concentration in UDMH and NTO.

Visual observations suggest that gas is released rapidly from solution when the pressure is dropped. However, few data are available to determine quantitatively the time rate of evolution of gas from the propellant. Assuming the release is instantaneous as the pressure is dropped, however, a conservative estimate of the volume of gas created can be easily determined.

Perturbation of the combustion process can occur by 1) creating an imbalance resulting in improper mixing of the fuel and oxidizer streams, 2) reducing fuel film cooling, thereby creating a hot chamber, injector, and/or acoustic cavities (depending on configuration of the engine), 3) changing feed system acoustic properties, or 4) creating an oxidizer-rich environment in the chamber leading to an overpressure. In terms of changing the feed system acoustics, Juran and Zwick<sup>32</sup> explored the effects of dissolved gas on small engine injectors. The other possible effects of helium are discussed later in the chapter for the Space Shuttle primary reaction control thruster.

Most storable engine development and certification test programs include some type of entrained bubble and saturated propellant test. Smith<sup>33</sup> provides a method for saturating MMH and NTO propellants and for measuring the degree of saturation of the propellants.

### IV. Storable Engine Case Studies

The engine damage, which was experienced in Apollo development programs, resulted in appreciation of combustion instability. Subsequent testing and experience provided some understanding, which has reduced the number of trial and error injector tests required for recent engines [e.g., the pump-fed Space Shuttle orbital maneuvering engine (OME)]. The following engine case studies for Apollo, Space Shuttle, and Long March programs describe this experience. studies examined. Case studies of these engines provide some understanding of the complex phenomena and the approach taken to eliminate instabilities.

Unfortunately, other significant more recent engines, such as the XLR-132 and the Ariane L7, are not included in the following case studies. A discussion of the Ariane L7 engine is provided by Langel et al.<sup>34</sup> Until recently, small engines (less than 100 lbf) were believed to be immune to high-frequency instability, since the chamber acoustic modes are very high. A recent experience with a 5-lbf-thrust engine is discussed by Crone et al.,<sup>35</sup> which suggests that this is not necessarily always true.

#### A. Case Study 1: Apollo Service Propulsion System Engine

The Apollo service propulsion system (SPS) propelled the service module into lunar orbit and returned it to Earth using a single 91,180-N (20,500-lbf) thrust engine. The development of the Apollo SPS engine required tests on many different injector designs. Much of this was due to high-frequency instabilities that were experienced late in the program as a result of specification changes: 1) the mixture ratio was changed from 2.0 to 1.6, which resulted in increased

popping and 2) a new requirement to demonstrate dynamic stability using bomb tests was added.<sup>36</sup> The problem with high-frequency instabilities was resolved after additional injector modifications.

The BLOCK I engine development program, which specified a mixture ratio of 2.0, tested triplet, unlike-doublet, and quadlet elements in unbaffled injectors. Spontaneous instabilities occurred at the first tangential (1T) of 1650 Hz and the second tangential (2T) of 2700 Hz. When injector face baffles were installed, the high-frequency instability problem appeared to be solved. During a prequalification program, however, a pop caused an instability. This new problem was resolved by extending the baffle tips 2 in., as shown in the testing of the BLOCK I, injectors POUL 41-26 to POUL 41-39, in Table 3.

The BLOCK II engine development program added requirements for dynamic stability and a mixture ratio of 1.6. The first BLOCK II injector, labeled POUL 41-26 modification (Mod.) 0, utilized the 5-4-2 (blade number-hub height in inches-blade peripheral in inches) baffle. The rate of popping for this injector increased from 1.2 to 3.6 pops/min when the mixture ratio was changed from 2.0 to 1.6. These pops resulted in sustained high-frequency instabilities. Similarly, bomb tests also resulted in sustained instabilities.

The high-frequency instability problem was solved by increasing the baffle height. The POUL 41-26 Mod. II injector was tested with a 5-4-2 baffle and a 5-4-4 baffle. The 5-4-4 baffle increased the baffle height at the periphery of the chamber to 101.6 mm. Although the results showed an increase in pops/min from 17.8 to 29.5, the extra baffle height eliminated sustained instabilities.<sup>37</sup>

The popping problem was significantly improved with the POUL 41-26 Mod. IV injector, shown in Fig. 5. Testing found that the injector element was bistable in the operating regime.<sup>38</sup> The discharge coefficient would change dynamically and cause disturbances in the flow. The Mod. IV injector orifices were counterbored to eliminate this problem.

Acoustic tests, using a speaker and microphone, measured the modes of the baffled injector 5-4-4. Corrected for hot-fire conditions, the modes are 1T at 1400 Hz, 2T at 1940 Hz, first radial (1R) at 2050 Hz, 2T + baffle mode at 3000 Hz, 3T at 3200 Hz, 1R + baffle at 3600 Hz, and 1T + 1R + baffle at 5050 Hz. The actual observed modes of instabilities appeared to be about 3600 Hz and 5000 Hz.

In summary, increasing the baffle height by 50.8 mm (2 in.) at the periphery of the chamber appeared to be the most significant stabilizing factor. Overall, the 5-4-2 baffle accumulated 46 instabilities out of 4040 bomb tests, and the 5-4-4 baffle accumulated zero instabilities out of 1898 bomb tests. During the test program, it was also noted that the ablative flight engine chambers damped instabilities much better than the “work horse” steel engine chambers used in development tests.<sup>39</sup> This may have been due to the acoustic absorbercy of the ablative material. Another significant observation was that popping increased with decreasing mixture ratio and increasing fuel film cooling, and that the orifice *L/D* affected the popping rate.

#### B. Case Study: Lunar Excursion Module Descent Engine

The Apollo lunar excursion module (LEM) descent engine landed the two astronauts on the moon. The LEM was propelled by a single engine, which was

supplied propellant by a redundant feed system and which had a requirement for 10:1 throttling. Two engine design programs, conducted in parallel, competed for this engine program. The final design selection was based on combustion stability.

##### *1. Helium Injection Throttled Lunar Excursion Module Descent Engine*

This engine had a unique throttling mechanism, which injected helium into the propellants to reduce the propellant flow rates while maintaining the pressure drop across the injector. It also had an advantage over other designs by having a fully redundant throttling system of propellant and helium valves. This engine design experienced significant low-frequency stability problems, however, possibly caused by the helium in the manifolds.<sup>40</sup>

The specified thrust of this engine was 46704 N, with a throttle ratio of 10:1. The engine chamber used an ablative liner made from a silica tape wrap. The injector consisted of 165 FOE triplet elements. In 1964, tests with helium injection revealed a tendency of the injector to buzz and pop below 70% thrust. The engine

experienced a significant chug instability problem from 35–70% throttle at 30–500 cps. This chamber and feed system coupling was probably caused by the lower injector pressure drop at low-throttle settings and by the helium in the feed system, which changed the acoustic characteristics of the system.

In addition to the low-frequency instability, two types of popping occurred.<sup>40</sup> The first type was isolated pops of 0.698-MPa peak, followed by acoustic oscillations which damped in 20 ms. The second type, probably resurging, occurred in conjunction with the chugging. When the chamber pressure built up in amplitude, a pop occurred. The pop was then followed by a burst of acoustic oscillations which damped with time. Because of these problems, this engine was not selected.

##### 2. Variable Area Pintle Injector Throttleable Engine

The selected LEM descent engine used a pintle injector. This engine development program was relatively free of combustion stability problems. The only problem detected was occasional rough combustion or random pressure spikes characterized by no discernible frequency. A nonredundant throttle mechanism varied the injector flow orifice size of the pintle injector, providing thrust from 4,448 N to 44,480 N at 304 s  $I_{sp}$  (Ref. 41). The feed system valves were also modulated to control propellant flow in addition to the pintle sleeve.

With the pintle injector, propellants are injected radially (orthogonal to axis) into the chamber at the center. A cross section is shown in Fig. 6. The oxidizer flows through the center of the pintle and out through 36 radial slots. The fuel

flows in an axial annular sheet in an outer sleeve of the pintle. Two different pintle configurations were tested: 1) 36 primary and 36 secondary oxidizer slots and 2) 32 primary and 32 secondary oxidizer slots. Although the coarser 32 slot injector had a higher efficiency due to the ability of the coarser oxidizer stream to mix with the fuel sheet, this also produced a rougher combustion.

This engine was certified to be dynamically stable by bomb tests with peak pressures up to 1.03-MPa (150-psi) peak over  $P_c$ . No high-frequency instabilities were encountered. Pressure spikes or combustion disturbances were experienced at full thrust and at 30–50% thrust, depending on specific injection conditions. The rough combustion was associated with very high-fuel-injection velocities and low-oxidizer-injection velocities.<sup>42</sup>

#### C. Apollo Lunar Module Ascent Engine

This engine boosted the LEM from the lunar surface to rendezvous with the orbiting Command and Service Module. Although the single ascent engine was fed by a redundant feed system, an engine malfunction due to chamber or injector structural failure was a major concern, especially to the astronauts. This dictated that the engine be dynamically stable. The engine specifications were for 15,568-N thrust at a mixture ratio of 1.6 NTO/A-50.

The development injector consisted of 84 FOF triplets with 90 fuel-rich unlike doublets at the wall for cooling. The early design did not include baffles. Although the engine initially performed well according to specifications, later on in the program, it developed spontaneous instabilities. When bomb testing was added to the specification, the engine experienced significant stability problems.

The injector, without baffles, had three self-induced instabilities and numerous instabilities during bomb testing. One test run exhibited 12 s of high-frequency instability that resulted in a roughing and bubbling of the chamber wall. The characteristic high-frequency instability occurred at frequencies of 3500 Hz and 7000 Hz at amplitudes of 0.303–1.289 MPa (44–187 psi) peak to peak. Table 4 is a summary of the stability of various engine configurations.

The injector was redesigned in 1965 to include baffles.<sup>43</sup> Numerous tests were conducted using 3- and 4-bladed baffles of different lengths. The baffle design selected used three equally spaced blades. The test results of steel and ablative chambers showed that significant damping was available in ablative chambers. In

fact, high-frequency dynamic stability was achieved only in the ablative chamber.

Although there was success with eliminating high-frequency instability, a problem with low-frequency instability was observed at an amplitude of 0.552–0.621 MPa (80–90 psi) and 350–400 Hz in both the steel and ablative chambers. There is some evidence that gas in solution caused or contributed to the low-frequency problems.<sup>43</sup> This problem was not resolved.

In 1967, due to the stability problems with the initial injector, a backup engine injector for the LEM ascent engine was developed in parallel. This development program began in August of 1967, and culminated in the first lunar landing in July 1969.<sup>44</sup> This engine produced 15,568-N (3,500-lbf) thrust with an  $I_{sp}$  of 3030 m/s (309 s) at a mixture ratio of 1.6 NTO/A50 and used the same chamber developed in the first injector program.

The injector consisted of 177 unlike doublets with a 3-blade baffle and slot acoustic cavities. The 44.5-mm-in-high baffle damped the first tangential mode of instability. The acoustic cavities, located at the outer edge of the injector, were designed to damp the first radial, third tangential, and higher modes.<sup>45,46</sup>

Chug stability was improved by adding a volume to the fuel inlet duct. This injector was successfully bomb tested a total of 302 times, with one exception. On the 99th bomb test, an instability occurred. This was attributed to a damaged injector with plugged and misimpinging orifices caused by the shrapnel from previous bomb testing.<sup>44</sup>

#### D. Case Study: Space Shuttle Primary RCS Thruster

The Space Shuttle primary reaction control system (PRCS) thruster provides control of the Space Shuttle during ascent, on-orbit maneuvers, and re-entry. The PRCS thruster can also de-orbit the Shuttle, if the two orbital maneuvering engines fail. It is a 3870-N (870-lbf) vacuum thrust engine operating at a mixture ratio of 1.6:1 NTO to MMH. Long-life requirements were prime considerations in the design. The duty cycle requirements for this engine are extreme: 1) continuous burn duration from 80 ms to 800 s, 2) total life of 12,800 s, and 3) and cycle life of 20,000 pulses. The engine has proven quite capable of performing this duty cycle.

An extensive ground test program revealed that when helium is ingested in a certain manner, instabilities may sometimes occur. This ground test data can help to understand the effects of helium ingestion on the combustion process. Fortunately, additional ground tests showed that the actual propellant conditions in flight may preclude the occurrence of damaging instabilities. The engine also proved very robust in that sustained instabilities were observed for 40–80 s before causing chamber damage. In addition, an instability protection system was installed to prevent any damage to the Shuttle from a chamber burn through.

The injector consists of a single ring of 84 unlike doublets and an outer ring of 42 fuel film cooling orifices at the chamber wall as shown in Fig. 7. The fuel film cooling accounts for 23–25% of the fuel flow. There are 42 quarter-wave acoustic cavities tuned for the first tangential (5600 Hz). Half of the cavities, 25.4 mm (1.0 in.) in depth, are tuned for startup conditions, and the other half, 27.9 mm (1.1 in.) in depth, for steady state.

Early development testing of this thruster showed that either without the acoustic cavities or with cavities of 4% total injector face area, the engine was spontaneously

unstable in the first tangential mode. Stability was obtained by increasing the area to 8%. Table 5 provides a summary of the development and qualification testing of the engine. During qualification in 1977, the engine was certified dynamically stable using bomb tests.

Later in the program, during the acceptance test of a flight thruster, an instability occurred. Helium bubbles trapped in the feed lines as the result of a poor purge and prime of the system are the suspected cause. This instability resulted in the program taking three basic actions to 1) protect the vehicle from instability, 2) determine the cause, and 3) screen production thrusters for stability problems.

In 1988, the thruster instability protection system (TIPS) was installed to protect the vehicle from chamber burn through. This system consisted of wrapping the valve lead wires around the chamber, in such a way that chamber burn through due to an instability would sever the wires and close the thruster valves. This was demonstrated to be successful by plugging the acoustic cavities on two engines and firing until burn through.

The second action was to determine the cause of the instability. After extensive testing, it was found that helium bubbles injected into the fuel at approximately 8 cc/s could trigger the instabilities. This was of considerable concern, since it is not unusual in a pressure-fed system to have gas bubbles. In order to prevent trapped helium bubbles in the flight system, procedures at the launch processing facility call for a vacuum to be pulled in the system and then to backfill with propellant.

The third action was to screen for manufacturing variation in production thrusters during acceptance tests by injecting helium at 8.19 cc/s steady state in a test consisting of 300 pulses. The acceptance criteria required that no instabilities occur. The criteria defined an instability as an engine acceleration exceeding 20 g at the thruster head end for a duration greater than 12 ms at the 1T of approximately 6000 Hz. In this screening test, the observed rate of instabilities with helium injection was less than 1%, typically around 0.1%. One thruster, which has been set aside for testing, had an observed rate of instability of up to 10%, so that it is statistically different.

In 1990, a test program was conducted at White Sands Test Facility (WSTF) to further examine the effects of helium on stability.<sup>47</sup> The test program found that the instability has several characteristics: 1) the instability always initiates during the start transient, 2) sometimes chugging and an 8000 Hz first longitudinal are seen during this start transient before transitioning to a 6000 Hz 1T, 3) the thrust drops 356–400 N, (80–90 lbf) during the instability, and 4) the injector flange temperature rise rate increases from approximately 5°C/s to 44°C/s.

Two engines were then subjected to sustained instabilities by continuing the pulse after initiation of the instability. The engines were found to be robust, in that sustained instabilities took 40–80 s to damage the chambers. This is significant in that most pulses on the Shuttle are less than 10 s.

Helium was found to be the most significant factor in causing instability. The ingestion of helium caused higher heating rates in the flange and rougher combustion, even when an instability did not occur. It was also observed that the rate of instabilities increased as the thruster flange temperature increased during repeated pulses with helium injected into the fuel. Based on this result, thruster heating could be postulated to affect the tuning of the acoustic cavities or the incidence of popping, thus increasing the number of instabilities.

Another series of tests at WSTF determined that how, when, and where the helium is injected is important. In the first test, when helium was injected into the fuel during the start transient, instabilities occurred. It should be noted that due to the helium injection apparatus, a significant quantity of helium accumulates at the thruster, between pulses, such that the peak flow rate of helium at startup is large (about 245–328 cc/s). In the second test, when helium was injected after the start transient using a slightly different apparatus, there were no instabilities.

In a third test, using fuel saturated with helium rather than helium injection, some albeit fewer instabilities occurred. In a fourth test, when both oxidizer and fuel propellants were saturated, there were no instabilities. The fuel side is obviously sensitive to helium ingestion, and helium ingestion in both the oxidizer and fuel

###### INSTABILITY PHENOMENA IN BI-PROPELLANT ROCKET ENGINES 131

seems to negate the effect. This reduces the probability of an instability on the Shuttle because both propellants are likely to be saturated, since helium dissolves in NTO more than in MMH.

In summary, the physical mechanism for the instability may involve disturbances in the fuel and oxidizer flow caused by helium ingestion. Unielement tests by Lawver<sup>17</sup> found that the PRCS injector element is sensitive to operating conditions from a reactive stream separation standpoint. The higher heating rates experienced during helium ingestion in the engine may also detune the acoustic cavities and increase susceptibility to disturbances. Recently, a limited number of tests suggested that an oxidizer valve lead can cause instabilities. A similar experience is reported by Crone et al.<sup>35</sup> for a 5-lbf engine in which an oxidizer lead caused overpressures that resulted in instabilities. Similarly in the PRCS, helium ingested in the fuel during the start transient would cause an oxidizer lead to some extent. However, direct measurement of an overpressure has not been made with the current low-response instrumentation for chamber pressure.

This case study demonstrates that the solution to a stability problem can require an extensive understanding and consideration of the conditions which cause the instability and a method to deal with the results. The PRCS engine has proven to be quite acceptable in both ground and flight testing based on the fact that 1) the probability of instability is low even under the worst-case conditions, 2) the actual flight conditions are less severe, 3) the engine is robust to damage from instabilities, 4) the time required to damage a chamber is longer than the typical pulse time, and 5) an instability protection system is installed.

#### E. Case Study: Space Shuttle Orbital Maneuvering Engine

The orbital maneuvering engine performs orbit circularization and de-orbit burns for the Space Shuttle. It was selected over the originally proposed LO<sub>2</sub>/LH<sub>2</sub> RL10-based system, when the orbiter configuration required a small propulsion system package.<sup>48</sup> The relatively smooth development of the OME was a result of the extensive predevelopment effort, which included the Apollo experience. The OMS engine is rated at 26,688-N (6,000-lbf) thrust, and operates at a mixture ratio of 1.65:1 NTO/MMH with 316-s  $I_{sp}$ .

After trade studies showed that Earth storable propellants best met Space Shuttle requirements, the early OMS engine development program focused on which storable propellant, cooling method, and acoustic damping device should be used. The optimum design was determined to include an engine chamber regeneratively cooled by MMH, acoustic cavities rather than baffles for easier cooling and longer cycle life, and like doublets rather than unlike doublets or triplets for improved performance and stability.<sup>48</sup>

The early development tests focused on different injection element types, element arrangements, injector manufacturing, and depths of the acoustic cavities, as shown in Table 6. The transverse like-on-like (TLOL), 97.9 N (22 lbf) per element, was found to be stable and, hence, was selected for the design. The injector face is formed by platelets, as shown in Fig. 8. The elements are like-on-like doublets, arranged in 16 alternating rows.

There are 12 acoustic cavities: 8 each 1.5 in. deep for the 1T mode and 4 each 0.5 in. deep for the 2T, 1R, and 3T modes. The significant chamber acoustic modes are 1L, 1100 Hz; 1T, 3200 Hz; 1R, 6400 Hz; 2T, 5200 Hz, and 3T, 7200 Hz.

**Table 6 Aerojet OMS engine development summary**

| Engine configuration                  | Stability | Mode/Freq., Hz |
|---------------------------------------|-----------|----------------|
| 57.8 N (13 lbf/elem.), unlike doublet | Unstable  |                |
| 97.9 N (22 lbf/elem.), like doublet   | Stable    |                |
| 867 Element X doublet                 | Resurge   |                |
| 22 lbf/elem. V doublet                | Unstable  | 1L             |
| 1000+ mixed elements                  | Unstable  |                |
| Acoustic cavities tuned for 1T, 3T    | Unstable  | 2T             |
| 22 lbf/elem., TLOL                    | Stable    |                |

During development of the acoustic cavities, some 2T instabilities occurred when the acoustic cavities were tuned only for the 1T and 3T chamber modes. The chug  $P_c$  limit for this engine was found to be 0.552 MPa (80 psia). The engine is certified dynamically stable per CPIA 247.

stages. Development and test of the injector, which included bomb testing, was successfully completed in 12 months.

Performance and stability design analysis code<sup>49</sup> was used to examine different injectors and size the engine. The chamber pressure was chosen to be 2.413 MPa (350 psia). For the injector selection process, the OMS engine TLOL platelet injector, a quadlet, and a splashplate injector were evaluated analytically. The analysis showed that the splashplate injector was the best injector from a performance standpoint. A stability analysis showed that a chamber diameter of 13.97 cm (5.5 in.) was acceptable, and better than larger diameters. Acoustic cavity depth 22.86 mm (0.9 in.) and injector delta-P were also determined. To achieve the desired goal of 99% energy release efficiency (ERE) without encountering a first longitudinal instability, chamber lengths of 30.48–35.56 cm (12–14 in.) were selected for testing.

The test program was conducted on three different splashplate injectors and three chamber lengths. The 30.48-cm (12-in.) chamber did not achieve 99% ERE. The program goal of 99% ERE was achieved after only 18 total test firings, when the 14-in. chamber was tested. The injectors were all found to be stable above chamber pressures of 1.38 MPa (200 psia). The selected injector was bomb tested and displayed the required damping. In off-nominal tests below 1.38 MPa (200 psia), the first longitudinal instability occurred as predicted by analysis. This successful engine development program demonstrated an improved understanding of Earth storable propellant combustion stability.

#### G. Case Study: Long March FY-20 Engine

All launch vehicle engines of the Long March (LM) series, except the upper stage engine of LM-3, use storable propellant combinations. The most typical is the first-stage engine, FY-20 of LM-3. The FY-20 is a gas generator driven pumped NTO/UDMH engine. Because the FY-20 has never failed in its flight missions, its observed reliability is 100%. Early in the development phase, however, the engine often encountered destructive high-frequency combustion instabilities, which severely affected the development program. The basic performance characteristics of the FY-20 engine and its major components are listed in Table 2.

##### 1. *G Concept Injector for the FY-20*

The original injector design of the FY-20 is called the G concept injector. This injector consists of like-on-like doublets distributed on 15 concentric rings (two rows on each ring). Oxidizer and fuel rings are arranged alternately. The injector face includes a 100-mm-high baffle with six blades and a hub used to eliminate transverse high-frequency combustion instabilities. During early tests on baffle configurations, sometimes one mode of instability would be eliminated, but another would become dominant. Decreasing the chamber contraction ratio and increasing the  $L/D$  tended to excite the longitudinal instability.

Later during off-nominal tests on the G concept injector, intense structural vibrations frequently occurred, with the composite vibration level on the injector head sometimes exceeding 600 g. The intense vibration often caused mechanical failures, such as duct breaks and component weld cracks. The vibration once caused an early shut down of the engine by suddenly closing a valve. Engine exhaust flame flashing could also be seen when the intensive vibration took place.

For storable hypergolic propellants, the propellant inlet temperature is an important factor that can affect combustion stability.<sup>27</sup> During mid-summer, with NTO temperatures higher than 16°C (61°F), statistical data indicated that the incidence of intense oscillations was approximately 66%. At higher engine thrust and mixture ratios, the vibration level increases slightly. A fast engine start with high pump inlet pressures also caused intense vibrations. The severe vibrations often caused a decrease in thrust and performance. The specific impulse loss was about 2%. In general, performance degradation occurs only with low-frequency combustion instability and lower order longitudinal acoustic mode instability. The intense vibration mainly caused structural damage to hardware. Severe erosion of the chamber wall did not occur in most of the chambers tested.

To efficiently monitor combustion instability, accelerometers to measure vibration were placed on the thrust chamber, turbopump, gas generator, and heat exchanger of FY-20 engine. According to the axial vibration recorded for the G concept injector, a predominant vibration of 886–900 Hz existed. At this frequency, the acceleration reached 100–300 g, sometimes even much higher. Pressure measurements upstream of the injector indicated that the frequency of chamber pressure oscillation was identical to the predominant frequency of mechanical vibration. This frequency is consistent with the first longitudinal acoustic mode calculated according to the combustion chamber geometrical sizes and parameters of combustion gas products. The first longitudinal oscillation frequency is not too high (900 Hz), because the combustion chamber size is large. This instability may also have coupled with the fluid pressure oscillation in the propellant feed system.

##### 2. S Concept Injector for the FY-20

Two methods were attempted to suppress the first longitudinal acoustic mode combustion instability in the FY-20 engine: 1) modifying the feed system impedance and 2) modifying the injector axial energy release distributions along the combustion chamber. At first, a cavitating venturi, a throttling orifice, and a hydraulic capacitor were used in the oxidizer ducts to attempt to suppress instability, but test results showed that these were ineffective. The approach to modify the energy release distribution was then attempted. The energy release of combustion was evenly distributed along the chamber axis by modifying the injector element pattern, orifice diameter, flow intensity distribution, and injector pressure drop. This increased the impedance against the pressure perturbation, thereby changing the combustion response. This modified injector is called the S concept injector.

In comparison with the G concept injector, the S concept injector features several changes to the injector element pattern, the orifice diameters, and the flow intensity distribution. The flow intensity is distributed as a steep slope in the core section with a special high-flow intensity within the fourth ring, as shown in Fig. 9. The mass flow rate of the high flow-intensity area is 17% of the total propellant flowrate. The flow intensity is then increased at the number 11 and 12 rings to 1.7 times the average flow intensity of the area, which gives the distribution of flow intensity a hump shape.

The FY-20 engine utilizes a regeneratively cooled baffle, hence, injection at the baffle tips can not be used for axial energy release distribution. The flow intensity adjacent to the radial and circumferential baffles, however, is increased to 1.47 and 1.29 times the fan-shape area average flow intensity, respectively. Thus, the

mass flow rate adjacent to the baffles is 31.9% of the total propellant mass flow rate.

The impingement angles of the basic injecting elements for the G concept injector are 50 deg for oxidizer and 60 deg for fuel. The impingement angles for the S concept injector were reduced to 30 deg for oxidizer and 50 deg for fuel. Adjacent to the baffles, the impingement angle was reduced from 60 deg for the G concept injector to 30 deg for the S concept injector. This moves the impingement points farther from the injector face and distributes the combustion energy release along the chamber axis, thus forming an uneven flame front so as to stabilize the dynamic combustion process.

The number of orifices in the S concept injector is almost equal to that of the G concept injector. Modification of the S concept injector is mainly to the orifice diameter of the injector elements in the high-flow-intensity areas. The orifice diameters were enlarged from 2.1 to 2.3 mm for the fuel and from 2.3 mm to 2.7 mm for the oxidizer. The pressure drop across the injector was reduced to maintain the same total flow rate. At the nominal mass flow rate, the fuel and oxidizer injecting pressure drops were reduced from 1.1466 MPa to 0.8869 MPa and 1.4994 MPa to 1.2397 MPa, respectively. Both enlarging the orifice diameter and reducing the injector pressure drop resulted in increased droplet diameter and facilitated the even distribution of the energy release along the chamber axis. The mixture ratio distribution for the S concept injector is somewhat more uniform than that of the G concept injector in order to compensate for the performance loss caused by modifying the flow intensity.

The axial energy release profile<sup>51</sup> calculated for the FY-20 injector was based on a flow tube combustion model and a droplet vaporization model, and considered UDMH exothermic decomposition and NTO endothermic dissociation mechanisms. In comparison with the G concept injector, the S concept injector has a more uneven combustion flame front and a more even energy release distribution. About one-half of the total propellant energy is released in the region farthest from the injector face. Based on the axial distribution of energy release, the sensitive lag theory of Crocco and Cheng<sup>52</sup> can be used to calculate the stability boundary.

The stability of the S concept injector is enhanced because the energy release is more distributed, and the sensitive lag time is increased.

##### 3. Testing of the S Concept Injector

During tests of the S concept injector, no combustion instabilities were encountered at ordinary environmental temperatures. During test firings conducted in mid-summer ( $T > 20^{\circ}\text{C}$ ), however, four occurrences of intense vibrations were encountered for the S concept injector. As indicated in Ref. 27, when the temperature of the propellant combination, NTO/hydrazine and the like is higher than  $16^{\circ}\text{C}$ , popping is easily excited and can trigger combustion instability. Combustion instability may also be induced by unsteady flow of NTO at a temperature close to its boiling point.

Additional modifications to the S concept injector were made to 1) further modify the mass flow-intensity distribution along the circumferential and radial baffles, and 2) make the pressure drop of the fuel injecting orifice greater than that of the oxidizer injecting orifice. These modifications improved the injection momentum ratio of the two propellants and more evenly distributed the energy release distribution along the chamber axis.

It should be pointed out that the performance of the engine with the S concept injector is identical to that with the G concept injector because the characteristic length  $L^*$  of the combustion chamber is fairly large ( $L^* = 1.12\text{ m}$ ) and the mixture ratio distribution is more uniform. Test firings of the modified S concept injector were successfully repeated in the high-temperature season and at high-thrust levels without occurrence of instability.

#### H. Case Study: Long March YF-1 Engine

The first-stage engine of the LM-1 launch vehicle YF-1 is a pump-fed IRFNA-27\*/UDMH rocket engine with a gas-generator power cycle and with coaxial injection elements. (IRFNA-27 consists of 27% NTO, 71.56%  $\text{HNO}_3$ , and 1.8%  $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ .) Table 2 lists the basic performance characteristics of the latest YF-1 engine and its major components. Early in its development, however, the YF-1 engine utilized the IRFNA-20/MA-50 propellant combination (IRFNA-20 consists of 20% NTO, 77.5%  $\text{HNO}_3$  and 2.5%  $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ; MA-50 consists of 50% triethylamine and 50% dimethyl l-benzamine).

In the initial development, a series of instabilities, causing serious erosion of the injector face, resulted in engine failures. The mechanical vibration acceleration measured on the combustion chamber reached about 300 g. Initially, methods to improve cooling and reinforce components were used, but no obvious effects were observed. Through repeated tests and analysis, it was concluded that the failures were caused by high-frequency combustion instability.

In general, damage to the combustion chamber took place during transitions, e.g., at engine start, operating regime transition, or shutdown. The abrupt change in combustion chamber operating parameters was accompanied by large random disturbances that resulted in instability. These phenomena indicated that the margin of combustion stability was low and could not withstand disturbances.

Instantaneous burnout of the injector face and film cooling ring along the periphery of the combustion chamber often occurred. Erosion traces on the chamber surface were smooth, not rough and uneven as that caused by insufficient cooling and so it was obvious that a spinning gas stream existed simultaneously

with an increasing heat flux. The bulging and dropping off of the injector element covers indicated that high-shock levels also existed in the combustion chamber.

A high-amplitude-pressure oscillation occurred in the combustion chamber and injector manifold at a frequency of 1500 Hz. This frequency is identical to that of the first tangential acoustic mode. The combustion chamber has a strong tendency to trigger transverse combustion instabilities for three reasons: 1) the cylindrical combustion chamber has a large contraction ratio of 5.15:1, 2) the injector face has no baffle, and 3) the flow intensity distribution is uniform.

##### 1. Liquid-Phase Division Modification of the YF-1 Injector

The liquid-phase division method was used to reduce the occurrence of transverse high-frequency instabilities.<sup>33</sup> In liquid-phase division, the entire injector face is divided into several zones by a number of injecting elements which have different atomization characteristics from the basic elements. In this way, energy release is dispersed in the combustion chamber space, and pressure wave propagation is damped because of an insufficient supply of energy.

The liquid-phase division injector pattern is arranged in a honeycomb or concentric circle pattern, as shown in Fig. 10. The principle of division arrangement requires that the energy release points be arranged apart from the oscillatory wave crest and that the atomization characteristics of division injecting elements and basic coaxial elements differ significantly, as shown in Fig. 11. The division elements utilize a double component impinging/coaxial combination. About 30% of the fuel passes through a swirler to form a centrifugal atomization cone which protects the injector face. Division elements are arranged in six rows radially and in two circles peripherally.

To enhance the effects of liquid phase division, the mass flow rate of the division elements is about 1.5 times that of the basic elements. At the same time, the large mass flow rate double-component centrifugal elements, of which the flow rate is 1.5 times that of the basic element, are placed in the core area of the injector face. Thus, the hump-shape distribution of flow intensity is formed radially and peripherally.

After applying liquid-phase division, the results of test firing improved greatly. Within a large range of operating parameters, such as thrust ranging from 78.4 kN

No erosion traces were found in the combustion chamber tested. The combustion stability of the YF-1 injector was improved by liquid-phase division.

##### 2. IRFNA-27/UDMH Propellants with YF-1 Injector

When the propellant combination of the YF-1 engine was changed to IRFNA-27/UDMH, the liquid-phase division method continued to be used because of its significant effects in reducing combustion instability. At the same time, other modifications were made, such as changing the structure of the injector elements, increasing the rows of radial division elements, and improving the flow intensity distribution. But in all five test firings, a high-frequency combustion instability at a frequency of 1600 Hz occurred during the transients (three during start and two during shutdown). The difference in propellant properties changed the sensitive combustion time lag and weakened the ability of liquid-phase division to stabilize combustion.

Although the physical concepts of ignition time delay, combustion time lag, and sensitive time lag are different, they have some inherent relation to the propellant activity. The ignition delay time of the two propellant combinations is listed in Table 7. The ignition delay time of IRFNA-27/UDMH is several times less than that of IRFNA-20/MA-50. Also, UDMH decomposes at a different temperature, which can produce popping and excite combustion instability.

##### 3. Stabilizing the YF-1 Injector with Baffles

To eliminate high-frequency combustion instability, a regeneratively cooled baffle was combined with liquid-phase division. As shown in Fig. 12, a 100-mm-high regeneratively cooled baffle is mounted on the injector face. In a number of test firings, with the thrust increasing from 186.2 to 274.4 kN, no combustion instabilities occurred. Very stable combustion was obtained. The original liquid-phase division and flow-intensity distribution remained unchanged. The baffle concepts were also investigated in another model engine, where the baffle proved very effective in eliminating the transverse mode oscillation.<sup>54</sup>

It should be pointed out that the number of the liquid-phase division elements has an impact on engine performance, as depicted in Table 8. It was once considered that decreasing the number of the liquid-phase division elements, or even removing them might improve the specific impulse while maintaining the stability margin. Three test firings were conducted to demonstrate the feasibility of the concept, but all were unstable. This indicated that the liquid-phase division does have a significant influence on combustion stability even when baffles are used.

Artificial disturbances, using a pulse gun, were induced to rate the YF-1 engine combustion stability. The powder pulse generators, each 3 g of P-45, are mounted

The sensing membrane of one of the transducers is in contacted with the combustion gas in order to calibrate the influence of the mechanical vibration on the performance of the transducer. The test firings were conducted at a main-stage thrust of 245 kN (55,000 lbf). The pulses were initiated during the phases of engine start, main stage, operating regime transition, and shutdown. During the test, the maximum amplitude of pressure was 1.3121 MPa (190 psia), but after rapid attenuation the normal operating state returned in 11 ms. No destructive high-frequency transverse combustion instabilities were excited. The bomb tests demonstrated that the YF-1 engine has a definite stability.<sup>55</sup>

Combining the baffle with the liquid-phase division on the FY-20 and YF-1 engines has proved to be a very effective method to obtain stability, since the axial and transverse energy release distributions are directly related to combustion instabilities. If these methods are properly used, high-engine performance and stability can be best achieved.
