### I. Introduction

**C**OAXIAL twin fluid injectors are widely used in rocket engines, especially for cryogenic engines like the Space Shuttle main engine (SSME) or the European Ariane 5 Vulcain engine, using liquid oxygen and gaseous hydrogen as propellants. The basic mechanisms that atomize the liquid oxygen (LOX) jet into a spray of polydispersed droplets are not yet well modeled nor even completely identified. For this reason the majority of previous work on this subject was purely experimental. Unfortunately, the operating conditions in which the spray characterizations are performed are often very far from actual engine conditions (e.g., cold nonreactive flows instead of hot-burning environment, simulants that are not very representative of LOX, subcritical instead of supercritical pressure). The empirical laws are, therefore, often limited to the operating range where they were derived and do not fit the data obtained with different geometries, or even with the same geometry in different experimental conditions, and consequently often do not apply to actual engine conditions. Despite those limitations, the experiments are useful to compare different designs of a given injector in similar operating conditions, to compare atomization efficiency, and to rate injector performance and combustion stability. A given engine can be stable or unstable by a single injector modification that affects the droplet size. The Ariane Viking engine, for example, has become stable by increasing the mean droplet diameter.

Another important objective of atomization and spray characterizing is the development of computer codes to study the behavior of complete combustion chambers. Because of the prohibitive computation times, it is not realistic to describe all of the elementary processes of atomization or the individual droplets. It is much easier to take spray characteristics near the injectors as the boundary condition at the inlet of the computational domain. Therefore, a purely experimental characterization of atomization may be sufficient. This does not mean that numerical simulation and theoretical studies of atomization processes are of no practical interest. To the contrary, droplet size and velocity as inputs to a chamber model are difficult measurements, and theoretical values, if available, would avoid the problems of nonrepresentative experimental conditions.

The current work includes a literature survey on theoretical aspects and experimental work, part of which is taken from previous reviews performed by Ferrenberg et al.<sup>1</sup> in 1985 and by Ghafourian et al.<sup>2</sup> in 1991. The experimental work on coaxial rocket engine injectors was conducted mainly in the 1960s and early 1970s with a frozen wax technique and in the 1980s with optical particle sizing, first with particle sizers based on the Fraunhofer diffraction theory and more recently with phase Doppler particle analysers (PDPA). Recently a few theoretical approaches have been developed, most often based on linearized equations, but also original ideas like a maximal entropy formalism that seems to be very promising. Numerical simulations of atomization process using the two basic techniques of volume of fluid (VOF) and jet embedding (JE) may also become more important with the increasing performance of modern computers.

The second part of this chapter presents the approach retained at ONERA to characterize the coaxial injectors of both the gas generator and the thrust chamber of the Vulcain engine. This philosophy is, in fact, a progressive empirical method consisting of three steps. First, a series of cold-flow tests were conducted in a pressurized vessel fitted with windows at various chamber pressures up to 30 bar, using the Malvern particle sizer. Water was used to simulate the LOX

and nitrogen or helium to simulate the hydrogen. Second, cold-flow tests were conducted with LOX, at chamber pressures between 1 and 10 bar. The third step used alternative simulants with intermediate physical properties between water and LOX to characterize the change from water to LOX. This third step also aimed at increasing the experimental range of Reynolds and Weber numbers to reach the high values corresponding to engine conditions. Nitrogen or helium were used in all tests to simulate hydrogen.

The last section of the chapter presents the industrial manufacturer's point of view. There the work still to be done to characterize injectors, and to help the manufacturer in designing a new injection element when starting the development of a new engine, will be discussed.

### II. Literature Review

#### A. Theoretical Investigations

##### 1. Early Work

The first theoretical work on the rupture of a round liquid jet into droplets was by Lord Rayleigh<sup>3</sup> as early as 1878. He studied a low-speed liquid jet flowing into vacuum. In this case, the surface tension force is dominating the process, and drops are pinched off from the end of the jet with a diameter comparable to that of the jet. From potential energy considerations, Rayleigh showed that the jet is unstable to symmetrical disturbances with wavelengths larger than the jet circumference. He derived an expression for wavelength and growth rate of the disturbance. Rayleigh's theory was extended by Weber<sup>4</sup> in 1931, who included the liquid viscosity effect and derived an expression for the most favorable wavelength for drop formation in the case of a viscous jet. The analysis was improved by Tyler<sup>5</sup> who added an expression for the size of the droplets issued from this type of low-speed jet breakup.

Ohnesorge<sup>6</sup> in 1936 first identified different regimes of jet breakup by means of a dimensional analysis. The two most important dimensionless numbers in atomization process are the Reynolds number  $Re$ , which represents the ratio of inertial to viscous forces, and the Weber number  $We$ , which represents the ratio of inertial to surface tension forces. The Ohnesorge number is defined as  $Z = We^{1/2}/Re$ ,

$$Re = \frac{\rho_l V_l D_j}{\mu_l} \quad We = \frac{\rho_l V_l^2 D_j}{\sigma} \quad Z = \frac{\mu_l}{\sqrt{\sigma \rho_l D_j}}$$

By plotting  $Z$  vs  $Re$ , the low-velocity and the high-velocity regions can be distinguished. In the low-velocity region, the jet breakup is due to the action of surface tension forces (Rayleigh regime). In the second region, the influence of aerodynamical (inertial) forces increases exponentially with  $Re$  at constant  $Z$ , so that it rapidly dominates the process. In a practical case (injector geometry and propellant given), the orifice diameter as well as the fluid properties are fixed. The Ohnesorge number is consequently defined, so that the initial jet velocity (the injected mass flow rate) becomes the most important variable.

Nukiyama and Tanasawa<sup>7</sup> studied coaxial injectors in 1938 and 1939. They collected drops on a glass slide coated with a lubricant and took photomicrographs to measure the drop sizes. They developed a correlation relating the drop sizes to

operating conditions and also gave an expression of the droplet size distribution function,

$$N(D) = \frac{\beta D^\alpha}{\Gamma[(\alpha + 1)/\beta] \bar{D}^{\alpha+1}} \exp\left[\left(-\frac{D}{\bar{D}}\right)^\beta\right] \quad (1)$$

where  $N(D)$  is the number of droplets having diameter  $D$ , and  $\alpha$  and  $\beta$  are two model constants. In Nukiyama and Tanasawa's experiment  $\alpha$  was found equal to 2, but this is not a general case. This expression is rather rarely used in droplet sizing applications, despite the fact that it often fits the data. Most authors prefer the expression of Rosin and Rammmler,<sup>8</sup> which can be written in the same terms with  $\alpha = \beta - 4$ . The latter expression leads to easier mathematics and simple calculations of mean diameters, but one must notice that the Nukiyama-Tanasawa expression can be derived from maximal entropy formalism, as we will see in a following section. Concerning Nukiyama and Tanasawa's empirical correlation for the Sauter mean diameter ( $SMD$ ), which can be written

$$SMD = 0.585 D_j^{0.5} We^{0.5} + 53. Z^{0.45} D_j^{0.225} (Q_l/Q_g)^{1.5} \quad (2)$$

one can notice that it was expressed in the shape  $SMD = SMD_1 + SMD_2$  with the first term depending on the Weber number and the second on the Ohnesorge number and on the air-to-liquid flow rate ratio. This type of expression, with various exponents, was used by many subsequent investigators of air-blast atomizers.

A coaxial injector is different from a round liquid jet because of the presence of the high-velocity coflowing gaseous jet, which induces disturbances on the surface of the liquid jet in the immediate vicinity of the injection plane. As a first approximation, the jet surface, compared to those small-scale disturbances, can be considered as an infinite flat interface. Consequently, to describe the mechanisms that take place in the atomization process, the instability of surface waves induced by wind must be modeled. This phenomenon is considered to be dominating whereas others, like cavitation and turbulence, are neglected. Kelvin<sup>9</sup> analyzed in 1871 the influence of wind on waves in water under the effects of surface tension and gravity. The Kelvin-Helmholtz instability was defined where waves are generated due to the static pressure perturbation of the air. The pressure and the velocity of the air vary in antiphase at the top and the bottom of the waves, according to Bernoulli's theorem. Therefore, waves are generated on the water surface when the aerodynamical forces overcome the surface tension and the gravity forces that tend to reduce the disturbance. Kelvin derived that the smallest velocity of frictionless air which can raise a ripple on rigorously quiescent frictionless water is 6.6 m/s. Taylor<sup>10</sup> considered the planar wave growth at the surface of a viscous liquid fluid of infinite depth. He showed that if the liquid density is much higher than the surrounding gas density, the growth rate increases and shorter wavelengths become dominant as  $(\rho_l/\rho_g)(Re_l/We_l)^2$  increases. Taylor's analysis constitutes the starting point for the main subsequent wave growth models.

After the waves have broken from the main jet surface, they undergo additional disruption, called secondary atomization. As long as a high relative velocity exists between the surrounding gas flow and some large drops, formed during the jet or ligament breakup, those drops further break up during their flight, into smaller and more stable droplets. Hinze<sup>1</sup> presented a theoretical analysis of droplet breakup. He described the deformation of a liquid sphere caused by normal pressure distribution resulting from a flow of gas over its surface. Hinze postulated the existence

of a critical Weber number as a criterion for drop breakup,  $We = \rho_g D_l V_r^2 / \sigma$ , where  $D_l$  is the original drop diameter. This critical Weber number is approximately 10 for low-viscosity and 20 for high-viscosity liquids. Hinze<sup>11</sup> also gave an expression for the breakup time. This breakup time, together with the initial droplet velocities, is important in combustion applications because it gives the distance to where the secondary atomization takes place compared to the flame position. If droplet breakup occurs before the droplet encounters the flame front, the result of the secondary atomization has to be considered as the correct input for combustion computational fluid dynamics (CFD) codes, where droplets are injected in the computational domain upstream boundary. If the breakup time is too long, the secondary atomization should be modeled in the code, and the result of the primary atomization constitutes the right input.

##### 2. Identification of Phenomena, Classification of Breakup Regimes, and Dimensional Analysis

As indicated by Rice<sup>12</sup> the object of atomization is to increase liquid surface area to accelerate burning. This surface area is increased by various means, until the process becomes unstable, leading to disintegration of the liquid surface into droplets. Such a breakup of round or planar liquid jets is a result of the complex interaction between inertial, viscous, and surface tension forces that can be summarized as follows: liquid viscosity has a damping effect on the growth of disturbances on the surface, aerodynamic forces tend to promote them, and surface tension tends to pull the liquid together. Pressure oscillations and the turbulent nature of the injected fluids and their environment also influence the dynamics of atomization.

Various means may be used to increase the liquid surface area, including the use of a high-speed gas stream in twin fluid gas/liquid atomizers, like the coaxial elements used in cryogenic rocket engines. Similar atomizers are widely used in gas turbine technology. They were reviewed by Lefebvre<sup>13</sup> who classified them in the air-blast and the air-assist types. In the air-blast atomizer, the liquid is atomized by the air that is naturally present in the system and that participates in the combustion, whereas in the air-assist atomizer, an auxiliary air supply, most often at high pressure, is used. A coaxial rocket injector is a combination of the two. Air-blast or air-assist atomizers can also be classified as plain-jet and prefilming types. In the plain-jet type, the liquid is first attenuated into one or several fine jets, before it encounters the gas stream, whereas in the prefilming type, it is attenuated into a thin sheet inside the atomizer. In both cases, the growth of infinitesimal disturbances, generated within the atomizer and/or due to aerodynamic interaction with the surrounding gas, are assumed responsible for the deformation of the original surface of the liquid. The relative motion with respect to the atomizing gas then causes an instability of the liquid stream and a tendency to form waves that rapidly grow in amplitude to critical values at which the liquid stream undergoes a breakup into ligaments and drops.

The hypothesis, however, that the atomization occurs only through aerodynamic interaction between the liquid and the surrounding gas has not found universal acceptance. It is argued that a fully turbulent jet can break up without the application of any external force. Reitz and Bracco<sup>14</sup> considering the case of a high-speed single jet, indicated that several mechanisms, acting simultaneously, are responsible for the jet breakup in the atomization regime. The jet breakup process may occur within the nozzle itself, due to liquid turbulence, so that the radial component of

velocity in turbulent pipe flow could cause the immediate disruption of the jet at the nozzle exit. Liquid cavitation phenomena inside the nozzle could create large amplitude pressure disturbances in the flow, leading to atomization, so that cavitation bubbles may enhance the jet breakup process. The jet breakup may be due to the velocity profile relaxation: high-velocity laminar liquid jets could be more unstable than fully developed turbulent jets because of the rearrangement in the cross-sectional velocity profile of the laminar jet once the constraint of the nozzle wall is removed at the nozzle exit; this redistribution of energy within the jet gives rise to radial velocity components which disrupt the jet. this effect is minimal with fully developed turbulent jets having flat exit velocity profiles. The atomization may also be due to the acceleration experienced by the liquid in the boundary layer on the nozzle wall exit caused by the abrupt change in the boundary condition.

All of these mechanisms refer to the atomization regime of liquid jets, which first has to be defined. In his classification of breakup regimes of a single round liquid jet, in terms of breakup length (or intact liquid core length), Reitz<sup>15</sup> summarized the conclusions of several previous investigators and distinguished four breakup regimes with increasing Reynolds number at constant Ohnesorge number. (For given fluids, liquid and ambient gas, and a fixed nozzle diameter, that is equivalent to increasing jet velocity.) These regimes are (see Fig. 1) as follows.

1) In the Rayleigh jet breakup regime, the surface tension force, which induces axisymmetric oscillations of the jet surface, is mainly responsible for breakup; drops are pinched off from the end of the jet with diameter exceeding that of the jet.

2) In the first wind-induced regime, the aerodynamic forces start playing a role; unstable waves at long wavelengths grow along the jet; drops with diameter of the order of the jet diameter are pinched off from the end of the jet.

3) In the second wind-induced regime, drops, produced by the unstable growth of short wavelength surface waves, are torn off from the jet surface and are smaller than the jet diameter.

4) In the atomization regime, the jet surface appears to break up immediately at the nozzle exit into very small drops.

Surface tension, which enhances the two first regimes, opposes the third one. Liquid viscosity seems to have no effect in the second wind-induced regime.

###### COAXIAL INJECTOR ATOMIZATION

151

The mechanisms involved in the atomization regime are still unknown. Defining the Weber number as  $We = \rho_g d V_l^2 / \sigma$ , where  $d$  is the nozzle diameter and  $V_l$  the initial jet velocity, the second wind-induced regime occurs for  $0.4 \leq We \leq 13$  and the atomization regime for  $We \geq 13$ . Some authors situate the limit for atomization at  $We \geq 40$ , which is not a very important difference when one knows that, for example, in the practical case of the Vulcain engine coaxial injectors, this number is of the order of magnitude of  $10^3$ .

In the wave growth concept, it is generally assumed that the sign of the relative velocity between the gas and the liquid has no effect; i.e., the phenomena are assumed to be essentially the same in the case of a high-speed liquid jet injected into quiescent air and in the case of a low-speed liquid jet exposed to a high-speed coflowing gas stream. As indicated by Lefebvre<sup>16</sup> this might not be exactly true, because in pressure atomizers the various flow phenomena, such as turbulence and cavitation that promote the self-destruction of the liquid jet or sheet and greatly enhance atomization, are highly velocity dependent. In air-blast atomizers, where the liquid speed is as low as possible to increase the relative gas/liquid velocity, liquid turbulence and cavitation are limited, so that atomization consequently becomes almost solely dependent on the air-to-liquid mass flow rate ratio and on the momentum of the atomizing gas. This suggests that a model where only aerodynamic effects are taken into account should be sufficient for coaxial rocket injectors.

Gomi,<sup>17</sup> reviewing previous experimental work on coaxial injectors and adding his own results (Fig. 2), classified the breakup regimes of such atomizers in three categories, depending on the mixture ratio (Fig. 3):  $\dot{m}_l / \dot{m}_g \leq 0.2$ , where the relative velocity determines the drop size;  $0.2 < \dot{m}_l / \dot{m}_g \leq 1$ , where the relative velocity and the mixture ratio determine the drop size; and  $1 < \dot{m}_l / \dot{m}_g$ , where many parameters affect drop sizes. He<sup>17</sup> explained this dependence of drop size by the

potential core, length of the annular gas jet relative to the length of the atomizing region. At a small mixture ratio, the atomization of liquid is completed within the potential core and then drop sizes are determined by the relative velocity. At a large mixture ratio, the atomization terminates downstream because of the rapid decrease of the effective gas velocity which acts on the liquid surface.

Buschulte<sup>18</sup> collected the results of several investigators and plotted the ratio of maximum droplet diameter to jet diameter ( $D_{\max}/D_j$ ) vs an aerodynamical Weber number defined as

$$We_{ae} = \frac{\sigma}{\rho_g D_j (V_g - V_l \cos \alpha)^2 \sin^2 \alpha} \quad (3)$$

where  $\alpha$  is the angle between the jet core velocity and the gas stream velocity. Notice that this Weber number is the inverse of the classical definition. He found that all data whose aerodynamic Weber numbers were less than 0.1 could be correlated by a mean value expression obtained by a least square method,

$$D_{\max}/D_j = 2.2 We_{ae}^{0.5} \quad (4)$$

However, the scatter of the data was as large as an order of magnitude around this mean value.

A new classification of breakup regimes for coaxial airblast injectors was introduced by Farago and Chigier,<sup>19</sup> who carried out an intensive experimental program, using a spark photograph technique, to visualize the rupture of round liquid jets, with or without coflowing gas stream. The Weber number was varied over a range of six orders of magnitude, whereas the Reynolds number was varied over a range of two orders of magnitude. Thus,

$$10^{-3} \leq We = \frac{\rho_g V_r^2 D_j}{\sigma_l} \leq 10^3 \quad 2.10^2 \leq Re_l = \frac{\rho_l V_l D_j}{\mu_l} \leq 2.10^4$$

Detailed analysis of the photographs showed that jet disintegration can be divided into the following three categories (Fig. 4).

1) Rayleigh breakup has the same definition as given earlier. This category can be divided in two subgroups: axisymmetric breakup ( $We < 15$ ) and nonaxisymmetric ( $15 < We < 25$ ).

2) The jet disintegration is produced via membrane-type ligaments ( $25 < We < 70$ ). The round jet develops into a thin sheet (membrane), which forms Kelvin-Helmholtz waves and breaks up into drops, with diameter smaller than the jet diameter. The jet disintegration is completed in one or two wavelengths.

3) The jet disintegration is produced via fiber type ligaments ( $100 < We < 500$ ). Fibers are formed and then peel off the jet. The fibers break into drops via the Rayleigh mechanism. The liquid core is accelerated and develops waves. Breakup occurs via the nonaxisymmetric Rayleigh mechanism or by breaking into ligaments. The ligaments may then break up into smaller drops or ligaments by one of the three disintegration modes. The completion of jet disintegration needs many wavelengths. The produced drops are an order of magnitude smaller than the jet diameter. This category can be divided into two submodes: pulsating jet disruption, which is the normal submode, and superpulsating jet disruption, which is connected to an extremely high periodical change between low- and high-density regions in the spray ( $150 < We < 500$ ).

Care was taken during these experiments to avoid any vibration or pulsation in the feedlines, and the atomizers were designed to uncouple the jet rupture process from the upstream conditions. Despite those precautions, the atomization process was always pulsating, which seems to be a fundamental aspect of atomization. The third (fiber type) process is the most important in practical applications. In this mode, the largest proportion of the liquid is atomized in the secondary atomization region, which is not taken into account in the theories dealing with the onset of the instabilities and the primary atomization region based on wave instabilities at the axisymmetric intact liquid surface. One should also remember that due to the high density of atomizing hydrogen gas and very low surface tension of liquid oxygen, there is still at least one order of magnitude between the highest investigated Weber numbers and the nominal conditions of rocket engine injection.

Lefebvre<sup>20</sup> distinguished two atomization mechanisms in air-blast atomizers, the classical atomization, where the droplet formation is due to wave instability on the liquid surface, and the prompt atomization, which occurs if the gas stream impacts the liquid jet with high angles of incidence or if the gas velocity is unusually high. In this disruption mode, the time necessary for the liquid jet instabilities to develop and form growing waves is not available. Instead, the liquid jet is rapidly torn into small fragments, so that the final drop size does not depend on the initial jet diameter nor on the gas density. The following correlation for the mean drop sizes produced under prompt atomization was proposed:

$$\frac{D_{32}}{D_j} = \frac{1.5}{1 + CWe/(1 + 1/ALR)} \quad (5)$$

where  $C$  is an empirical constant,  $ALR$  is the air-to-liquid mass flow rate ratio ( $ALR = \dot{m}_g/\dot{m}_l$ ) and the Weber number is defined as  $We = \rho_l V_g^2 D_j / \sigma_l$ .

Farago<sup>21</sup> tried to find the maximal possible number of common non-dimensional groups for six different types of aerodynamical atomizers based on two categories.

Coaxial twin fluid atomizers, two-dimensional atomizers (thin-liquid sheet between two parallel gas streams) and thin annular liquid sheet between two gas streams constitute the category A, where nine variables are assumed necessary for a complete description. Disruption of a single liquid drop in a gas stream, atomization of a round liquid jet in quiescent air, and thin liquid sheet ejected into quiescent air constitute the category B, where only seven variables are involved. The identified independent variables for the liquid are the hydraulic diameter, the density, the mean velocity, the dynamic viscosity, and the surface tension. For the gas, they are the mass flow (or an appropriated diameter), the density, the mean velocity, and the dynamic viscosity. The most convenient equation for category A where only common groups are used, is, according to Farago,

$$\frac{\bar{D}}{D_j} = K \left( \frac{\rho_l}{\rho_g} \right)^{b+d+j+f} \left( \frac{V_l}{V_g} \right)^{c+d+j+f} Re_l^{-d-j} We_{ac}^{-e} \left( \frac{\mu_g}{\mu_l} \right)^j \left( \frac{\dot{m}_g}{\dot{m}_l} \right)^f \quad (6)$$

It is obvious from this review that the mechanisms that are involved in the atomization processes of coaxial injectors are not well identified. Several processes seem to be involved simultaneously, their relative importance depending on the specific design or on the operating range of each atomizer. A complete theoretical description valid in all cases may, therefore, be difficult to achieve. Nevertheless, different more or less sophisticated models are available, which are worth being examined, even if their applicability is limited.

##### 3. Linear Models

The successive linear models that can be found in the literature are all improvements at different stages of Taylor's analysis.<sup>10</sup> They examine the stability of a liquid jet surface due to an infinitesimal axisymmetric disturbance with a Fourier form:  $X = X_0 e^{ikz + \alpha t}$ , where  $k$  is the wave number and  $\alpha$  the wave amplitude exponential growth rate, which is governed by the dispersion equation described in detail by Levich<sup>22</sup> or Sterling and Sleicher,<sup>23</sup> for instance. This dispersion equation is obtained from the linearized Navier-Stokes equation by considering the aerodynamic effects with some simplifying assumptions and using the linear stability theory. The result is that  $\alpha$  depends on the local relative velocity, on the gas and liquid densities, on the kinematic viscosity, and on the wave number.

Two important references are the works of Mayer<sup>24</sup> and Dickerson and Schuman.<sup>25</sup> Mayer analyzed the wind-induced capillary waves on a flat, deep liquid surface and obtained an expression for average drop size by assuming that when a wave grows to an amplitude comparable to its wavelength, the crest severs and forms droplets of size comparable to the wavelength,

$$\bar{D} = B_A \left( \frac{\mu_l \sqrt{\sigma_l / \rho_l}}{\rho_g V_g^2} \right)^{2/3} \quad (7)$$

Adelberg<sup>26,27</sup> extended this analysis by including the effect of fluid acceleration on the disturbance wave speed and found that acceleration waves become dominant for large fluid acceleration. This type of breakup should have negligible influence with subsonic flows. Dickerson and Schuman<sup>25</sup> added an expression for

the atomization rates of jets and drops. The mass flow rate torn off from the jet surface was given by

$$\frac{\dot{m}}{A} = C_A \left( \frac{\rho_g^2 V_r^4 \mu_l \rho_l}{\sigma} \right)^{1/3} \quad (8)$$

where the constants  $C_A$ , ranging from 0.003 to 3 and  $B_A$ , had to be experimentally determined.

Dombrowski and Johns<sup>28</sup> considered the stability of a viscous liquid sheet subject to asymmetric waves, complementing Squire's results<sup>29</sup> on an inviscid moving sheet. They<sup>28</sup> gave equations for the sheet thickness, for the wave growth rate of the most unstable frequency, as well as for the corresponding wave number. The breakup of the liquid sheet due to the wave growth concept occurs when the total growth of the wave  $f$ , which is given by the natural logarithm of the ratio of wave amplitude to initial disturbance amplitude, approaches the constant value of 12 ( $f/f_0 = 12$ ). The balance of forces caused by gas pressure, surface tension, liquid inertia, and viscosity, which controls the breakup mechanism of the sheet, can be written as follows:

$$2\rho_g n V_r^2 - 2\sigma n^2 - \rho_l \tau \left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \right)^2 - \mu_l \tau n^2 \left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \right) = 0 \quad (9)$$

where  $V_r$  is the relative velocity,  $f$  the total growth of wave,  $t$  the time,  $\tau$  the sheet thickness, and  $n$  the wave number of the disturbance imposed on the liquid stream,

$$n = \frac{F^2 \rho_g V_r^2}{2\sigma} \quad (10)$$

where  $F$  is the ratio of wave growth of liquid to that of inviscid liquid. The maximum value of  $F$  is given by

$$1 - F^2 - V F^3 = 0 \quad (11)$$

where

$$V = \frac{\mu_l \rho_g V_r^2}{2} \sqrt{\frac{\tau}{2\rho_l \sigma^3}} \quad (12)$$

Reitz and Bracco<sup>30</sup> presented a unified first-order linear theory of the breakup of liquid jets, summarizing the work of Levich<sup>22</sup> and Sterling and Sleicher.<sup>23</sup> They assumed that atomization was primarily due to aerodynamic interaction between the liquid and the gas leading to unstable wave growth on the liquid surface. For the special case of slip at the gas-liquid interface and imposed infinitesimal axisymmetric surface displacement, a nondimensional dispersion equation was derived, which also included the physical and dynamical parameters of the liquid jet and the surrounding gas. Mechanisms of breakup in different regimes could be related to limiting cases in this analysis. At least three regimes were identified, depending on the gas/liquid relative velocity. An equivalent work was presented by Lin and Lian,<sup>31</sup> who showed that the instability of the liquid jet is characterized by three independent parameters: the Reynolds number, the Weber number, and the gas-to-liquid density ratio.

In Taylor's analysis,<sup>10</sup> the gas-to-liquid density ratio was assumed to be very small, but in actual rocket engines conditions, the injected hydrogen is at low temperature and its density is, therefore, not negligible compared to the liquid density. Solving the dispersion equation with  $\rho_g/\rho_l$  varying from  $10^{-3}$  to  $10^{-1}$ , Krülle et al.<sup>32</sup> recently showed that this ratio can have significant influence on the surface wave growth. Increasing gas density, at constant liquid density, had an obvious destabilizing effect on the liquid surface. Also, most probable surface wavelengths were shifted to lower values. The existence of gas velocity profiles, however, leads to an increase of the most probable wavelengths. This latter effect might be substantial and overcome the former, but the result remains that the computed wavelengths and related drop sizes are small compared to the most often reported experimental values which are of the order of  $10^{-4}$  m (100  $\mu$ m).

Caré and Ledoux<sup>33</sup> developed a complete linear model of the instability of a liquid jet in a coflowing air current. They considered the case of swirling and non-swirling flows for both fluids and also discussed the influence of a confinement for the gas flow. But they did not include the effects of boundary-layer velocity profiles and used the equations of inviscid fluids. Because of the high relative liquid-gas velocities this model is, in fact, asymptotic to the classical Kelvin-Helmholtz theory for capillary waves at a simple interface. The dominant wavelength  $\Lambda$  of maximum growth  $\Omega$  is then found,

$$\Lambda = \frac{3\pi\sigma}{\rho_g V_r^2} \quad \Omega = \frac{2\rho_g V_r^3}{3\sqrt{3}\sigma} \left( \frac{\rho_g}{\rho_l} \right)^{1/2} \quad (13)$$

and the propagation velocity of the wave  $c$  is

$$c = (\rho_g V_g + \rho_l V_l) / \rho_l \quad (14)$$

which reduces to  $V_l$  when the gas-to-liquid density ratio is small.

Caré and Ledoux<sup>33</sup> continued the analysis by deriving equations for the mean drop diameter produced by the breakup process. For this they assumed that at breakup the wave had formed a cylindrical ligament of diameter  $\Lambda/2$  and amplitude  $A\Lambda$ , where  $A$  is an unknown constant. By writing the conservation of mass and of surface tension for a ligament and the definition of *SMD*

$$\sum_i N_i D_i^3 = 3A\Lambda^3/8 \quad (15)$$

$$\sum_i N_i D_i^2 = A\Lambda^2 \quad (16)$$

$$D_{32} = \sum_i N_i D_i^3 / \sum_i N_i D_i^2 \quad (17)$$

and eliminating  $A$  they obtained

$$D_{32} = 3/4\Lambda \quad (18)$$

This model was compared to measurements performed near the liquid core (at 5 mm) where it was assumed that no secondary atomization had occurred and good agreement was found.

The number of drops formed  $dN_d$  on a length  $dx$  of liquid jet during the time  $dt$  can be written

$$d^2 N_d = C_1 \frac{64\pi A a}{9t_b \Lambda^2} dx dt \quad (19)$$

where  $C_1$  is another unknown constant,  $a$  is the local jet diameter, and  $t_b$  the lifetime of a ligament that can be written as  $t_b = C_2/\Omega$ . This is equivalent to  $X/X_0 = \exp C_2$ , where  $X$  is the wave amplitude at rupture and  $X_0$  the initial amplitude and  $C_2$  a third constant. Assuming that the jet velocity is constant, equal to  $V_l$ , and writing the mass balance in the liquid core, the jet diameter evolution becomes then

$$\frac{da}{dx} = -0.78 A C_1 / C_2 \Omega \Lambda / V_l \quad (20)$$

In case of total atomization, i.e., all of the liquid is torn off from the jet as droplets, a cone length could be calculated (the average jet surface is assumed to have a conical shape)

$$L = \frac{2\sqrt{3}a_0 V_l}{9\pi C V_r} \left( \frac{\rho_l}{\rho_g} \right)^{1/2} \quad (21)$$

Finally, Caré and Ledoux<sup>33</sup> gave an expression for the initial spray angle that is comparable to similar expressions given by Reitz and Bracco<sup>14</sup> and also by several other authors,

$$\theta \frac{\theta}{2} = \frac{2\pi A V_r}{\sqrt{3} V_l} \left( \frac{\rho_g}{\rho_l} \right)^{1/2} = A \frac{\Lambda \Omega}{V_l} \quad (22)$$

These linear models have proved capable to describe accurately low-speed jet breakup regimes but remain limited in the more practical case of high-speed regimes, especially the atomization regime, because they do not account for the multifarious mechanisms that are involved. Only the initial disturbance may be related to them. Moreover, it is argued that the wave can not be considered small when its amplitude becomes equal to the wavelength and when the rupture occurs. In fact, the formation of a ligament is a highly non-linear phenomenon.

##### 4. Derivation of Droplet Size Distribution Functions

The linear models predict a mean droplet size related to operating conditions but do not predict any kind of polydispersion of droplet sizes. In combustion applications, however, it is critical to know not only the mean diameters but also the size distribution function, because this provides information on the combustion zone extent. Of particular concern for combustion stability, a combustor will have different behavior if the combustion zone is concentrated near the injection plate than if it is distributed over a large volume in the chamber.

Few authors have discussed the problem of polydispersion in sprays. Simmons<sup>34</sup> made an attempt to derive the shape of the distributions when the Sauter mean diameter ( $SMD$ ) or the mass median diameter ( $MMD$ ) were known. He used the results of several experimental works (more than 2000 tests on about 100 different nozzles) on gas turbine injectors, where the droplet sizes were measured

either with a frozen wax technique or by optical sizing (video imaging). Simplex pressure atomizers as well as different types of air-assist and air-blast atomizers were used, and it was noted that in all cases, the ratio of *MMD* to *SMD* was 1.2  $\pm$  5%.

More recently, a new approach has been used, based on a maximum entropy formalism (also called information theory) to derive the shape of the droplets sizes distributions from the first principles: mass, momentum, and energy conservation. Two cases have been studied: the rupture of a thin flat liquid sheet due to the growth of surface waves by Sellens and Brzustowski<sup>35</sup> and the case of an atomizing jet by Li and Tankin.<sup>36-38</sup> The maximum entropy formalism deals with the probabilities of discrete states whose behavior is constrained by the expected values of several quantities  $g_{i,j}$ , which are functions of the set of states  $j$ , and which constitute the physical input to the problem. The probability is obtained by maximizing the entropy, which is the measure of uncertainty arising from information theory, subject to these constraints. The result is  $p_j = \exp(-\lambda_0 - \sum \lambda_i g_{i,j})$  with the normalization constraint  $\sum p_j = 1$ . The  $\lambda_i$  are arbitrary Lagrange multipliers that have to be evaluated in each particular application. This can be extended to the case of a continuous formulation by assuming a uniform discretization of the solution space. The variable  $f$  is then a probability density function (PDF), such that  $p_j = f d\psi_j$ , where  $d\psi_j$  is the small element of solution space  $\psi$  corresponding to state  $j$ . In the case of the breakup of a thin liquid sheet, the constraints are developed from conservation of mass, momentum, surface, and kinetic energy.

Sellens and Brzustowski<sup>35</sup> separated the surface and the kinetic energy in order to take into account some element of irreversibility. Source terms account for transfer between the various modes of energy. A first-order Taylor series expansion transforms the four constraints together with the normalization constraint in a set of five equations that can be solved by means of a Newton-Raphson root solving technique extended to five dimensions, giving the solution for  $f$  as a PDF in the size-velocity space. Integrating  $f$  from zero to a given maximum permitted velocity  $v_m$  over the velocity dimension of the space yields the size PDF. This drop size distribution, called maximum entropy (ME) distribution, was compared to Rosin-Rammler and to upper limit (from Mugele and Evans<sup>39</sup>) distributions for different values of the sheet thickness. All three distributions showed similar features, the Rosin-Rammler and the ME being very close in shape.

Sellens<sup>40</sup> later extended this analysis to an axisymmetrical case by introducing a second component of velocity and applied it to a practical case of hollow cone swirl injector. This type of injector produces a conical liquid sheet which self-atomizes. The predicted distribution was compared to local measurements made with a phase Doppler particle analyser. Very good agreement was found in the initial sections of the spray, where the drag forces had not yet influenced the distributions. As the predicted distribution is in non-dimensional form, some parameters have to be adjusted to get the distribution over a mean diameter related to operating conditions. Consequently, the model has to be combined with another model able to predict the liquid sheet (or the jet, if applied in this case) behavior and the corresponding parameters (thickness, velocity, wave number, etc.) before the final breakup and atomization processes. Sellens<sup>40</sup> obtained these parameters by empirical means in the case of his swirl injector.

Li and Tankin<sup>36</sup> first showed that, with some natural assumptions, the droplets' size distribution produced by a single atomizing jet is a form of the Nukiyama–Tanasawa<sup>7</sup> distribution where the distribution parameter is equal to 3. The derived distribution was compared to some experimental work, and a good agreement was found for the mean diameters as well as for the shape of the distribution. In a second step, Li and Tankin<sup>37,38</sup> extended their analysis by including the velocity distribution of the droplets. Their mathematical procedure was very similar to Sellens' except that Sellens<sup>40</sup> wrote the conservation of kinetic and surface energy separately during the breakup process of the liquid sheet. The obtained equations showed the dependence of droplet size distribution on the Weber number, but actual calculations revealed a very small dependence. This small dependence indicates the predominance of the inertial forces over the surface tension effects in the practical spray formation at high injection velocities and confirms the validity of the first step leading to the Nukiyama–Tanasawa distribution, which corresponds to an infinite Weber number. Nevertheless, care has to be taken that although the nondimensional Sauter mean diameter variation with the Weber number is small, this variation will be increased by the order of magnitude of the mass mean diameter, if the dimensional form is used.

Recent work by Durst and Bhatia<sup>41</sup> showed that a one-dimensional hyperbolic distribution function not only provides an excellent fit to measured size data but also sheds some light on the physical processes that cause the drop size variations downstream of the nozzle. The very satisfactory results obtained by this approach encouraged them to apply a two-dimensional hyperbolic distribution to the coupled droplet size and velocity distributions.

The distribution derived from the information theory, for liquid sheets rupture by Sellens<sup>40</sup> and for single jet disintegration by Li and Tankin,<sup>36–38</sup> could apply to coaxial rocket engines injectors, but the source terms which appear in the conservation equations for momentum and energy may have a significant importance, although they are equal to zero in the aforementioned fully developed works.

##### 5. Numerical Simulations of Atomization Process

The direct simulation of the surface dynamics and jet breakup was recently attempted by several authors, for instance, Fromm,<sup>42</sup> Childs and Mansour,<sup>43</sup> and Shokoohi and Elrod.<sup>44</sup> These analyses show encouraging results, but they were limited to low-speed, long-wave surface disturbances. Because of the horrendous computer time requirements, it may not be feasible to perform today the direct numerical nonlinear simulation of high-speed, short-wavelength atomization process. The alternative is to use approximate modeling techniques, consisting of solving the mean liquid jet flow as well as the gas flow from nonlinear transport equations and computing the breakup rate from semiempirical formulas.

Such a simulation of atomization process in a gas turbine prefilming type airblast injector was presented by Rizk and Mongia.<sup>45</sup> The computer code includes the simulation of the turbulent airflow through and exiting from the atomizer, as well as the successive processes of fuel filming and breakup, secondary atomization, and turbulent fuel dispersion. For the airflow calculation, the turbulent Navier–Stokes equations with source terms for phase exchanges were solved in a boundary-fitted, curvilinear grid. The droplet trajectories were computed by means of a Lagrangian calculation coupled with the Eulerian computation of the gas flow.

The fundamental processes of the fuel atomization include the liquid formation into a sheet and the subsequent disintegration of this sheet into ligaments due to the liquid surface instability. The process is governed by the balance of forces caused by gas pressure, liquid inertia, viscosity, and surface tension and is modeled according to the equations derived by Dombrowski and Johns,<sup>28</sup> which give the sheet thickness, the total growth of wave, the wave number, the time taken for breakup, and the average ligament length. The average initial drop size diameter at ligament breakup is estimated from the conservation of mass of the disintegrated part corresponding to a full wavelength.

The procedure adopted for the calculation of the wave growth on the ligament uses the same outlines as for the sheet rupture. The initial droplet velocity at their formation is assumed to equal the velocity of the ligament at the breakup point. Once the droplets are formed, they are allowed to deform under the effect of relative velocity according to the Weber number level experienced by the drop. The deformation of the drops is modeled considering a change of sphericity with time toward circular disk shapes. The deformed drops may undergo secondary atomization, which is modeled using the stripping breakup concept of Jenkins and Booker.<sup>46</sup> This concept of breakup of a liquid film of uniform thickness into ligaments and drops leads to the formation of a single-size drop spray. To overcome this limitation, the liquid film thickness at breakup, as well as the ligament exit angle and disintegrated length, are considered to vary around the mean value, with a Gaussian probability distribution. The spray characteristics (mean velocities and Sauter mean diameters) predicted by the model were successfully compared to phase Doppler measurements at different downstream axial and radial positions.

For coaxial rocket engine injectors, the first step should be replaced by the calculation of the round jet diameter evolution, but the wave instability concept may remain valid, at least for certain operating conditions, as was shown by Caré and Ledoux.<sup>33</sup> Even if the liquid core is actually very short, and if the ligament formation can not be evaluated by the theory of Dombrowski and Johns,<sup>28</sup> the second step of atomization, namely, the rupture of the ligaments into droplets, should be essentially the same, especially if the assumption of Farago and Chigier,<sup>19</sup> that the final step of atomization is always the same, is true.

Reitz<sup>47</sup> presented an application of the multidimensional numerical model KIVA to study the atomization and vaporization of a liquid jet injected from a round hole into a compressed gas. The liquid was injected in the computational domain as "blobs" with sizes equal to the nozzle exit diameter. The breakup of the blobs and of the resulting drops was modeled using a stability analysis for liquid jets. The product drops were distinguished from the parent drop by having different drop sizes. This had a significant effect on the fuel vapor distribution in the spray. Drop collision and coalescence were also accounted for, as well as the effect of drops on the gas turbulence. Since these phenomena were handled as subgrid scale processes, specific submodels were used. The drop size resulting from the primary atomization of the blobs was determined from the wavelength of unstable waves on the surface of the blobs using the first-order linear theory of Reitz and Bracco.<sup>30</sup> The dispersion relation, however, was not solved in the KIVA code. Instead, the maximum growth rate  $\Omega$  and the corresponding wavelength  $\Lambda$ , valid for Ohnesorge numbers less than 1 and for gas-to-liquid density ratios less than 0.1, were curve fit from numerical solutions. The atomization process was modeled by postulating that new drops were formed with drop radius  $r$  from a parent drop or blob with

radius  $a$  with

$$\begin{aligned} r &= B_0 \Lambda & \text{for } B_0 \Lambda \leq a \\ r &= \min[(3\pi a^2 W/2\Omega)^{0.33}, (3a^2 \Lambda/4)^{0.33}] & \text{for } B_0 \Lambda \geq a \end{aligned} \quad (23)$$

where  $B_0$  was a constant equal to 0.61 and  $W$  the local relative velocity. The second breakup procedure was only allowed once for each injected parcel, to prevent product drops from undergoing further unrealistic size changes. The rate of change of drop radius due to drop breakup was given by

$$\frac{da}{dt} = -\frac{(a-r)\Lambda\Omega}{3.726B_1a} \quad (24)$$

where  $B_1$  was chosen equal to 10, but it must be regarded as an adjustable model constant, possibly with a different value in each breakup regime.

These models were developed for gas turbine or diesel engine injectors, which have different design features from rocket engine elements. A model specially adapted to the latter purpose was developed by Liang et al.<sup>48</sup> and Liang and Schuman.<sup>49</sup> The advanced rocket injector combustor code (ARICC) is based on the volume of fluid technique, which accounts for the mutual volumetric displacement of the gas, the liquid, and the droplets coexisting in the computational domain by means of the variable  $F = v_g/(v_g + v_l)$ , representing the ratio of the cell volume occupied by the gas over the total cell volume, which appears in most of the balance and transfer equations. It is also possible to deduce the location and orientation of a gas-liquid interface cutting arbitrarily across the computational grid, and then to apply the atomization model on a local basis. The atomizing jet is thus explicitly modeled, which is in contrast to the CFD codes in which the atomization model, or its results, is used as an upper boundary condition. The advantage of this more sophisticated model is that a more realistic description is obtained in situations where the atomization process takes place over an extended region of the combustor. However, due to computer costs in practical cases, this model, which needs a very fine grid in the vicinity of the liquid jet core, can only be used in a small section of the combustion chamber, near the injection ceflate. In a first version of ARICC presented in 1986, the atomization model was the same as in the earlier coaxial injection combustion model (CICM) code of Sutton.<sup>50</sup> This model was based on Mayer's analysis<sup>54</sup> and can be expressed as follows: the mean diameter of droplets issued from the jet stripping mechanism and the local mass stripping rate are

$$\bar{D} = B_A \left( \frac{\mu_l \sqrt{\sigma/\rho_l}}{\rho_g V_r^2} \right)^{2/3} \quad (25)$$

$$\dot{M}_A = C_A \left[ \frac{\mu_l (\rho_g V_r^2)^2}{\sigma/\rho_l} \right]^{1/3} \pi D_j \quad (26)$$

where  $D_j$  is the local jet diameter.

In 1990<sup>49</sup> this model was replaced by the wave growth model of Reitz,<sup>47</sup> which is more general, but reduces to Mayer's with very large Weber numbers and viscous liquids. Using Reitz's equations, the complex growth rate  $\omega$  and the wavelength  $\Lambda$  having the maximum growth rate  $\Omega$  were computed from the liquid and gas

properties and from the local relative gas-liquid velocity  $W$ , which has to be evaluated properly first. The atomization model was then postulated in the same terms used by Reitz: if  $B_A \Lambda$  is smaller than or equal to the jet radius, then

$$r = B_A \Lambda$$

if it is bigger, then

$$r = \min[(3\pi a^2 W / 2\Omega)^{0.33}, (3a^2 \Lambda / 4)^{0.33}]$$

where  $r$  is the radius of the formed droplet and  $a$  the local jet radius given by

$$\frac{da}{dr} = \frac{-\Lambda \Omega}{3.788 C_A} \quad (27)$$

The two empirical constants that appear in the preceding equations have to be optimized through numerical experimentation. In fact, two sets of constants may be used, one for the primary atomization of the jet, and one for the secondary atomization of the droplets. Suggested values for the 1990 model<sup>49</sup> are, for the jet atomization,

$$C_A = 0.5, \quad B_A = 5.0$$

and for the droplets breakup,

$$C_A = 10.0, \quad B_A = 0.61$$

The initial droplet velocity is equal to the jet velocity  $V_i$  in the jet axis direction plus a radially outward component of  $V_i \cdot \tan(\theta/2)$  where  $\theta$  is randomly distributed between 0 and  $\Theta$  where  $\tan(\theta/2) = 0.188 \Lambda \Omega / v_i$ .

The jet-embedding technique proposed by Przekwas<sup>51</sup> uses the multigrid concept by employing the regular grid for the gas phase, and the embedded, surface-conforming, adaptative grid for the injected liquid jet core. In work presented in 1989,<sup>52</sup> the conservation equations describing the liquid jet-core flow were numerically solved in a one-dimensional adaptative, surface-conforming grid based on the JE technique. Gravity and internal viscous effects were neglected, but the viscous friction at the gas-liquid interface was accounted for. The solution of the JE method was coupled with the wave breakup model to compute the wave growth and droplet separation process along the predicted jet-core trajectory. Two formulations (linear and approximate nonlinear theory of Yuen<sup>53</sup>) of the wave stability models were used, but the second one was used only for low-speed jet simulation. For the liquid jet atomization, the ligaments or drops were assumed to separate from the liquid jet surface due to the growth of surface wave above critical levels.

As indicated in a preceding section, the linear analysis examines the stability of a liquid jet surface due to an infinitesimal axisymmetric disturbance with the Fourier form:  $X = X_0 e^{ikz + \omega t}$ , which is governed by the dispersion equation. By imposing an infinitesimal axisymmetric disturbance with a spectrum of wavelengths, the dispersion equation was solved to obtain the growth rates for the amplitude of all waves. The criterion for ligaments stripping from the growing waves is based on the assumption that when a given wave has grown to an amplitude larger than its wavelength, the crest breaks off as a ligament. The drop size does not necessarily correspond to the fastest growing wavelength since it is possible for some shorter wavelength  $\lambda$ , with smaller growth rates, to take less time to reach their own

critical amplitude. This time and the corresponding stripping mass of a ligament were expressed as

$$t_n = \ln(\lambda_n / X_0) / \alpha_n \quad (28)$$

$$m_n = \rho_l a (\pi \lambda_n)^2 / 8 \quad (29)$$

The calculation was applied successfully to a low-speed jet (Rayleigh regime) and also to a high-speed single round jet with encouraging results.<sup>52</sup> When applied to a coaxial LOX/H<sub>2</sub> rocket injector jet (without combustion) it gave results comparable to the ARICC code. The predicted intact-core length was about 10 injector diameters.

##### 6. Analytical and Semiempirical Models

Numerical models combining multidimensional gaseous-phase flow simulation with particle tracking may predict detailed features of a spray, but such a complete numerical simulation often needs several hours of computer time and is not suitable for intensive use at the beginning of development of a new atomizer. Therefore, there is a great need for analytical and simplified tools giving a first reasonable approximation in the preliminary phases of a new injector design. Later designs can be improved and optimized with a sophisticated numerical model.

Rizk and Mongia<sup>54</sup> developed a semianalytical model based on the same assumptions as their earlier described numerical model. The same steps of the atomization process are followed, namely, the formation of a thin sheet or fine jets, the appearance of liquid instability, the formation of rapidly growing waves, breakup into ligaments that in turn break up into droplets, secondary atomization, and finally droplet trajectory calculations. Modeling of the atomization process remains exactly the same as in the complete numerical model, which applies Dombrowski and Johns' theory<sup>58</sup> for the sheet or jets and ligaments breakup. The secondary atomization and the droplet trajectories equations that are ordinary differential equations are also the same as in the complete model. The only difference is that the air flowfield is not computed but estimated with analytical formulas based on the concept of velocity components decay along the spray axis of Beer and Chigier,<sup>55</sup> and on detailed measurements in the flowfield of an air swirler. For a coaxial rocket injector, similar expressions can be found in the model of Yatsuyanagi<sup>56</sup> described later. The assumptions that the sheet thickness and the gas velocity vary according to a Gaussian distribution to produce a polydisperse spray are replaced by the use of a modified Rosin–Rammmler distribution function for the droplets sizes. The two parameters  $\bar{D}$  and  $N$  of this distribution are deduced from the final Sauter mean diameter,

$$\bar{D} = (0.91 \text{ } SMD)^{1.18} \quad (30)$$

$$N = \bar{D} / (0.126 \bar{D} + 1.2) \quad (31)$$

The modified Rosin–Rammmler equation can be written as

$$1-G = \exp \left[ - \left( \frac{\ell_n D}{\ell_n \bar{D}} \right)^N \right] \quad (32)$$

whereas the original equation is

$$1 - G = \exp[-(D/\bar{D})^N] \quad (33)$$

where  $G$  is the cumulative volume fraction, i.e., the fraction of the total volume contained in drops of diameter less than  $D$ . Assuming that the liquid density is constant, the volume and the mass fraction are equal.

Yatsuyanagi<sup>56</sup> developed an analytical model for coaxial liquid/gas jets, where the atomization process was modeled with Mayer's<sup>24</sup> and Dickerson and Schuman's laws<sup>25</sup> for the mean diameter and the mass stripping rate but with some corrective factors. For the gas velocity, three regions were distinguished in the jets. In the downstream region, far from the injector outlet, the gas velocity profile was given by an expression proposed by Abramovitch<sup>57</sup>

$$u_g(z, r) = u_c(z) \left[ 1 - \left( \frac{r}{R_g(z)} \right)^{1.5} \right]^2 \quad (34)$$

where  $R_g(z)$  is the outer boundary of the gaseous jet and  $u_c(z)$  is the maximum velocity on the jet axis. In the first region, near the injector outlet and along the liquid core, the gaseous velocity profile had a minimum on the jet axis and two maxima located at a radius  $r_m$  given by

$$r_m = 0.93(D_g - D_l) \quad (35)$$

The velocity profile for  $r \leq r_m$  was then expressed as

$$\frac{u_{\max} - u}{u_{\max} - u_c} = \left[ 1 - \left( \frac{r}{r_m} \right)^{1.5} \right]^2 \quad (36)$$

and for  $r \geq r_m$

$$\frac{u}{u_{\max}} = \left[ 1 - \left( \frac{r - r_m}{R_g - r_m} \right)^{1.5} \right]^2 \quad (37)$$

In the intermediate region, the same shape was used as in the downstream region. The fitting of experimental data in this zone was not as accurate but remained acceptable. The dispersed liquid (droplets) mass flow rate at each  $z$  location was given by a similar expression

$$\dot{m}_l(z, r) = \dot{m}_{lc}(z) \left[ 1 - \left( \frac{r}{2.874\bar{r}_l(z)} \right)^{1.5} \right]^3 \quad (38)$$

where  $\bar{r}_l$  was defined by

$$\dot{m}_l(z, \bar{r}_l)/\dot{m}_{lc}(z) = 0.5 \quad (39)$$

This model was successfully compared to velocity and mass flow rate measurements in water/nitrogen coaxial jets. A very similar model was used at ONERA (for instance, see Barrère<sup>58</sup>) to calculate the upstream droplet size distribution from downstream measurements.

Yeung<sup>59</sup> described a similarity analysis of the far region of a spray, i.e., outside the region where the liquid core exists and where droplets are formed. Following Schlichting's approach<sup>60</sup> for turbulent jet analysis, he<sup>59</sup> obtained a similarity

solution in the case of a flat jet with the assumptions that the droplets are rigid spheres, that the gravity is negligible, and that the droplet equilibration time is very large, which means that the drag force does not affect the droplet motion over a sufficiently large distance. In this case, the droplet motion is entirely inertia dominated, their velocity remains constant, and their trajectories are straight lines. This may be considered a simplistic model, but it gives a first approximation for the velocity field, which may be sufficient in cold-flow experiments.

Several other authors have been interested in the downstream variations of spray characteristics, sometimes taking into account vaporization,<sup>61</sup> sometimes neglecting it.<sup>62,63</sup> Their models were derived for atomizers quite different from coaxial rocket engine injectors, but the main ideas can be easily adapted. Such models may be very useful when one is interested in estimating the initial droplet size distribution near their formation zone from measurements performed farther downstream, which is most often the case due to limitations of the sizing technique.

#### B. Experimental Investigations

Experimental characterizations of coaxial rocket injector elements have been reviewed by Ferrenberg et al.,<sup>1</sup> who presented in Appendix A of their report a complete state of the art in 1983. In their Appendix B,<sup>1</sup> they extended this survey by including the conclusions of Lefebvre,<sup>13</sup> who reviewed the experimental work on air-blast atomizers. They<sup>1</sup> stated that a suitable correlation for such atomizers should consist of the sum of two terms:  $SMD = SMD_1 + SMD_2$ , where the Weber number appears in  $SMD_1$  and the Ohnesorge number in  $SMD_2$ . This correlation provides some theoretical basis for the  $SMD$  equations for air-blast injectors, because the major effects of aerodynamic, surface tension and viscosity forces are taken into account. In the general correlation equation suggested by Lefebvre, however, the factor  $1 + m_l/mg$  also appears with an exponent between 0.5 and 1 for which there is no clear reason.

In experiments performed after Lefebvre's review, Jasuja<sup>64</sup> showed that the second term can be negligible for low-viscosity liquids. A suggested explanation is that at least two different mechanisms are involved in air-blast atomization. For low-viscosity liquids injected into a coflowing gas stream, capillary waves are produced on the liquid surface. These waves grow, become unstable, and break off as ligaments that disintegrate into droplets. For high-viscosity liquids, the capillary mechanism may not be valid. Instead, the liquid is drawn out in the form of long ligaments that break up relatively slowly, in regions of lower gas velocity, into larger size droplets. Water and liquid oxygen are considered low-viscosity fluids.

Ferrenberg et al.<sup>1</sup> also performed tests using droplet sizing interferometry (a technique adapted from laser Doppler velocimetry). Because of severe measurement difficulties (this technique can only be used in low-density sprays), they were unable to obtain measurements in a pressurized vessel. Therefore, they limited their initially ambitious program to investigations of the spray at atmospheric pressure, in unconfined environments. Nevertheless, the precautionary measures they indicated to avoid droplets recirculations in the pressurized chamber will serve subsequent investigators. They did not obtain any new correlation for representative mean diameters with this test program, but they indicated that among the available expressions of previous authors the correlation of Kim and Marshal<sup>65</sup>

should be used for a first rough approximation of droplets sizes, even though when applied to their measurements, the predicted sizes were around 30% too small.

$$MMD = 5.3610^{-3} \frac{\sigma^{0.41} \mu_l^{0.32}}{(\rho_g V_r^2)^{0.57} A_g^{0.36} \rho_l^{0.16}} + 3.4410^{-3} \left( \frac{\mu_l^2}{\sigma \rho_l} \right)^{0.17} \frac{\dot{m}_l}{\dot{m}_g} V_r^{-0.54} \quad (40)$$

We can notice that when applied to the results presented in Sec. II of this chapter Kim and Marshall's expression effectively approaches the experimental values by 30–40% at atmospheric pressure but does not fit all of the values obtained at higher pressures.

To extrapolate the results of water (or other simulants) to actual propellants, Ferrenberg et al.<sup>1</sup> suggested to use the corrective factor proposed either by Ingebo<sup>66</sup>

$$\frac{\bar{D}_{\text{actual propellant}}}{\bar{D}_{\text{simulant}}} = \frac{(\mu_l / \sigma \rho_l)^{1/4}_{\text{actual propellant}}}{(\mu_l / \sigma \rho_l)^{1/4}_{\text{simulant}}} \quad (41)$$

or by Wolfe and Anderson<sup>67</sup>

$$\frac{\bar{D}_{\text{actual propellant}}}{\bar{D}_{\text{simulant}}} = \frac{(\mu_l^{1/3} \sigma^{1/2} \rho_l^{-1/6})_{\text{actual propellant}}}{(\mu_l^{1/3} \sigma^{1/2} \rho_l^{-1/6})_{\text{simulant}}} \quad (42)$$

Gomi<sup>17</sup> investigated the sprays of Japanese injectors, also at atmospheric pressure, using a diffracted light technique (Malvern particle sizer). He did not propose any correlation for his results but indicated qualitative trends that are consistent with other investigations.

The experiments of Farago and Chigier<sup>68</sup> and Eroglu and Chigier<sup>69</sup> attempted to distinguish the different breakup regimes by means of spark photographs of the initial region of the jet. Their conclusions are summarized in an earlier section of this chapter. Some phase Doppler measurements were performed and a maximum of *SMD* near the spray axis was observed in the downstream region. No correlation equation was given.

Vingert<sup>70</sup> presented the results of measurements performed in a pressurized vessel (up to 30 bar), with a Malvern particle sizer, and gave a correlation expression applying to European Vulcain engine injectors (see Sec. II). This expression is currently valid only for water tests, but work is continuing, using alternative fluids to check the influences of liquid density, viscosity, and surface tension. First tests with actual liquid oxygen were performed in 1991 and presented by Gicquel et al.<sup>71</sup>

The same injectors were tested at atmospheric pressure by Gaic et al.<sup>72</sup> The main objective of their work was to compare and to improve several measurement techniques, but they showed that good atomization can only be obtained at atmospheric pressure when the gas-to-liquid momentum ratio approaches its nominal value. This statement was used by Vingert<sup>70</sup> to increase the experimental range where the proposed correlation can be applied.

A similar injector was also investigated at atmospheric pressure by Caré and Ledoux,<sup>33</sup> who used these results to validate the linear model of Caré.<sup>73</sup> As it

is often the case in such atmospheric pressure tests, the liquid-to-gas mixture and momentum ratios were far from actual rocket engine values. The agreement between the predicted and the measured mean diameters, however, was reasonable near the injector exit, typically 10 mm downstream and 5 mm from the spray axis, which is outside of the liquid core but very close to its initial breakup.

Recent experimental work, part of which is currently ongoing, was also presented by Cox,<sup>74</sup> Krülle et al.,<sup>32</sup> Zallen,<sup>75</sup> Zaller and Klem,<sup>76</sup> and Sankar et al.<sup>77</sup> Huynh et al.<sup>78</sup> are interested in a point that is often neglected but which is very important, especially in the field of combustion instability, namely, the influence of large-amplitude pressure waves interacting with the spray.

A major difficulty when comparing data of several investigators is the use of different measurement techniques, which often do not actually measure the same quantities. Ferrenberg and Varma<sup>79</sup> described the difference between temporal distributions obtained, for instance with the wax freezing method or by all the techniques derived from LDV, and spatial distributions obtained mainly from imaging techniques. Dodge<sup>80</sup> indicated the most important error sources when comparing the results of devices based on the diffracted light method and sizers based on the phase Doppler method, that are currently the most widely used techniques. He also indicated<sup>81</sup> a way to compute overall representative average diameters from local measurements. Inversion techniques have also been developed<sup>82-84</sup> to transform line-averaged data obtained with diffraction-based devices into local values given, for instance, by the phase Doppler technique.

### III. Experimental Characterization of the Ariane 5 Vulcain Engine Coaxial Injector Sprays

#### A. General Strategy

ONERA has undertaken the characterization of the spray of a coaxial gas-liquid injector to provide input data for the numerical model PHEDRE, which is a computational fluid dynamics code specially intended to study the high-frequency (HF) combustion instabilities in liquid rocket engines.<sup>85</sup> Coaxial twin fluid atomizers have been extensively studied for several years, but the major part of the available literature deals with gas turbine injectors, which have rather different geometrical designs, different mixture ratio ranges, and lower flow capacities. Moreover, a theoretical model able to describe completely the mechanisms of droplet formation of this atomizer type is not yet available, although progress has been promising. Therefore, it was decided to investigate the spray of the Vulcain engine injectors (Fig. 5) by fully empirical means, because the atomization data were needed early in the HF study program.

At the onset, no cryotechnic research test facility was available to work directly on a liquid oxygen spray (nor even liquid nitrogen). Use of alternative fluids was selected to determine correlations suitable for extrapolation to actual propellants. The first step was to quantify the influence of geometry (LOX post diameter, recess length, annular gap thickness) by testing several elements in similar conditions, using water to simulate LOX and nitrogen or pressurized helium to simulate the cold dense gaseous hydrogen. These tests were also intended to determine the typical mean diameter and the spread parameter as analytical functions of the main parameters (injection velocities, chamber pressure, densities, etc.). In addition, since the boundary condition required by the chamber simulation model

consists of atomization data as near as possible from the injector outlet, a data reduction technique has been developed that permits calculation of the upper mass flow rate drop size distribution (UMD) from the downstream measurements. The technique is specially adapted to coaxial injectors, but the model is very similar to the one described by Brault and Lourme<sup>86</sup> for impinging jet elements. Most of the assumptions on the spray structure are the same as those used by Yatsuyanagi.<sup>56</sup> The next step of this study was to investigate liquid properties effects by using various liquids with values of surface tension, viscosity, and density intermediate between those of water and LOX. Testing with LOX would complete the study.

During a previous characterization of the Viking engine impinging elements, the same strategy was used successfully. Some additional tests were performed with unsymmetrical dimethyl hydrazine (UDMH), which confirmed the correlations established with simulants.<sup>87</sup>

#### B. Water Tests

The water cold-flow test facility is located in the Fauga-Mauzac ONERA Centre (near Toulouse). Water is flowed vertically into a pressurized cylindrical vessel fitted with windows for the optical particle sizing devices. It is able to operate with constant internal pressures up to 30 bar. The injector can be moved horizontally and vertically, which permits measurements at different downstream distances as far as 200 mm and radial locations between 0 and 50 mm from the spray axis. To protect the windows against water splash, a weak airflow was blown from the windows toward the spray. In addition, deflectors, gutters, and capillarity traps were used to avoid the presence of a parasitic spray of small droplets carried back by the gas recirculating at the chamber bottom.

In this study, the Malvern 2600 HSD instrument based on Fraunhofer diffraction was used. For the Société Européenne de Propulsion (SEP) injectors, most of the measurements were made with a 300-mm focal length for the receiving Fourier

transform lens. This choice leads to a measurable droplet size range of 5.6–564  $\mu\text{m}$ . For the Messerschmitt-Bölkow-Blohm (MBB) elements, a focal length of 600 mm was used, which sets the droplet size range between 11.2 and 1128  $\mu\text{m}$ . Specific precautions were taken for the very dense spray measurements. The Malvern instrument is capable of uncorrected dense spray measurement up to obscuration values  $Q$  (defined as the ratio of extinguished light through the spray to the transmitted light when no spray is present) of 0.5. This range can be extended to higher values provided the bias effect due to multiple scattering is taken into account by appropriate corrective functions. The current work used equations derived for the Rosin–Rammmler processing during the Viking study,<sup>87</sup> which are

$$D/D_0 = 0.3 \cos[\pi/4(Q^5 + Q^{8.5})] + 0.7 \quad (43)$$

$$N = N_0 \quad \text{for} \quad Q < 0.8 - 0.1N \quad (44)$$

$$N = 0.8 \frac{0.8 + N_0 - Q}{1.68 - 0.1N_0 - Q} \quad \text{for} \quad Q > 0.8 - 0.1N \quad (45)$$

where  $D_0$  and  $N_0$  are the measured Rosin–Rammmler parameters provided by the Malvern software, and  $D$  and  $N$  are the corrected values. These functions have been validated for  $Q$  as high as 0.97, but they are not valid if local over concentrations higher than  $10^{-3}$  exist somewhere on the optical path of the laser beam. Two different tomographic techniques<sup>82,84</sup> were used to determine the local concentration profiles in the sprays for representative working conditions (Fig. 6). The local values of volume concentrations did not exceed  $5.10^{-4}$  for this testing. An additional method used to reduce the obscuration was to split the spray by moving sleeves inward, in order to reduce the thickness passed through by the laser beam. The edges of sleeves were empirically designed to minimize the perturbation of the flowfield inside the spray and to avoid the presence in the laser beam of the additional spray caused by impingement with the splitter. By dividing the vessel in two parts, the splitter also contributed to eliminate the recirculated droplets, created at the bottom of the vessel, from the probe volume. The vaporization of

droplets (when volatile fluids are used) or the presence of a gas motion around the spray (intended to simulate the combustion gases) create refractive index gradients that can lead to beam deviations. The resulting perturbation of the signals received by the central photodiode shows an increase of obscuration, which is actually not related to an increase of spray density. When the variations of obscuration vs time are recorded during the "steady state" of an injector element operation, one can observe fluctuations that can reach 50% of the mean signal. The droplet sizes do not follow these fluctuations. To obtain stable measurements for the mean obscuration and diameters, a minimum of 200 MALVERN sweeps was chosen.

In actual conditions, the SEP and MBB injectors operate in a high-pressure (80–100 bar) environment with liquid oxygen and cold and dense gaseous hydrogen. Simulating the LOX with water can be satisfactory provided the water injection velocity is sufficient to ensure a fully turbulent flow in the LOX post before the first contact with the gas. A good similarity for the gas injection should consist in keeping the density ratio  $n = \rho_g / \rho_l$  and the order of magnitude of the two velocities as well as their ratio  $m = V_g / V_l$ . The mass flow rate or mixture ratio  $r$  and the momentum ratio  $p$  would then be nominal also. These conditions can be realized easily for the MBB thrust chamber injectors, but some difficulty appears for the SEP elements due to the high density of the hydrogen, which is nearly liquid when injected into the gas generator (70 kg/m<sup>3</sup>). Nitrogen pressure of 50 bar would be required to obtain this density, exceeding the test vessel capacity of 30 bar. For a given back pressure, the three ratios  $m$ ,  $p$ , and  $r$  mentioned previously, can not be nominal simultaneously, but three different working conditions can be defined, each keeping one of these ratios. The test plan was then established with following rules: subsonic gaseous flow in the injector, complete atomization of the liquid near the outlet, and total mass flow rate in the nominal  $\pm 30\%$  range for each element. It was not possible to achieve these three stipulations simultaneously when the back pressure was less than 15 bar (30 bar when helium was used instead of nitrogen) because the gaseous mass flow rate decreased drastically due to the density decrease, and its energy became insufficient to atomize the liquid jet. To increase the mass flow rate by increasing the velocity was not possible because the flow would have become supersonic. Visualizations at atmospheric pressure showed that the atomization was complete if the momentum ratio at injector outlet was nearly equal to its nominal value (Fig. 7). Keeping this ratio  $p$  constant reduced the mass flow rates at lower back pressures and, consequently, allowed a large range of injection velocities. When helium was used, very high injection velocities could be reached with still subsonic flow in the injector. Constant momentum ratio is intermediate between constant velocity ratio and constant mixture ratio. The similarity proposed by Gill,<sup>88</sup> keeping the  $\phi$  parameter defined by Abramovitch,  $\phi = (nm^2 - 1)(n + 1)/2(nm + 1)^2$  is intermediate between constant velocity ratio and constant momentum ratio.

About 200 tests have been performed at back pressures from 1 to 30 bar, with seven different elements for which the nominal operating conditions are shown in Table 1.

None of the droplet diameter correlations from the literature satisfactorily fit the experimental results, so the data were correlated with classical linear multiregression:  $D_{32} = D_{32}^* \Pi(X_i / X_i^*)^{\alpha_i}$  with reference value  $D_{32}^*$  corresponding to specified reference data  $X_i^*$  for the design and operation variables  $X_i$ . For a single injector the most important parameter, which gave the maximum rate of variation  $\tau$  explained by the correlation equation, was the relative injection velocity
