$V_r = V_g - V_l$  (or  $V_g$  because  $V_l \ll V_g$ ). This conclusion is consistent with results from literature. The influences of the injected gas density  $\rho_g$  and the liquid velocity  $V_l$  are much less significant and not well determined. To correlate the diameters measured for the different elements, three geometrical parameters, the LOX post inner diameter  $D_l$ , the annular gap outer diameter  $D_g$ , and the recess length  $R$ , had to be added. Results are summarized in Table 2, where for each test series are included the involved element, the number of tests, the  $\alpha_i$  exponent values, and their standard deviation  $\sigma_i$ , the rate of variation explained by the correlation equation  $\tau$  (for a confidence level of 95%), and the overall uncertainty on the equation  $\sigma$ . The final droplet diameter correlation expression with water and nitrogen or water and helium simulants, having a rate of variation explained of 86% and an overall uncertainty of 12%, is

$$D_{32} = 127 \left( \frac{V_r}{160} \right)^{-0.93} \left( \frac{D_l}{2} \right)^{2.25} \left( \frac{D_g}{3} \right)^{-2.65} \left( \frac{R}{D_l} \right)^{-0.26} \tag{46}$$

The PHEDRE code can handle several droplet classes at injection. Consequently, it is useful to include the whole distribution in reference conditions, instead of a single mean diameter. These correlations have been presented for the Sauter mean diameter, but similar expressions can be found for the Rosin–Rammler diameter  $\bar{D}$  and for the mass median diameter  $D_M$ .  $\bar{D}$  and  $D_M$  are related by  $D_M = \bar{D}(\ln 2)^{1/N}$ . The Rosin–Rammler exponent  $N$  can, therefore, be correlated in the form:

$$1/N = 1/N^* + \sum \alpha_i \ln(X_i/X_1^*)$$

Different equations of this type can be found, which fit the experimental values of  $N$ . To choose between them, the Sauter mean diameter and the mass median diameter calculated with the nominal values predicted for both Rosin–Rammler parameters were compared to the values obtained through the correlations directly established on  $D_{32}$  and  $D_M$ . The best agreement was obtained with

$$\frac{1}{N} = \frac{1}{2.15} - 0.09 \ln\left(\frac{\dot{m}_t}{60.5}\right) + 0.17 \ln\left(\frac{D_t}{2}\right) \quad (47)$$

where  $\dot{m}_t$  is the total mass flow rate in grams per second. The rate of variation explained by this equation and the overall uncertainty are 60% and 7.6%.

The correlation expressions retained are plotted vs measured data in Fig. 8 for both mean diameters and Rosin–Rammler exponent.

#### C. Liquid Oxygen Tests

The initial results of size and velocity measurements under cryogenic conditions are presented in this section of the chapter. The objective of this test campaign was to approach the dimensionless numbers ( $Re$ ,  $We$ ,  $Z$ , etc.) that characterize the liquid and gas flows at the nominal operating point of the thrust chamber or the gas generator of the Vulcain rocket engine (see Table 3). All tests were conducted at the cryogenic facility of the Industrial Chemistry Laboratory of the Liège University (Belgium), which was built by the team of Pr. Germain at the request of SEP for the consolidation program H10. The objectives of this program were to further understand the HM7B cryogenic liquid rocket engine used to propel the third stage of Ariane 4 and, consequently, to increase its performance and reliability. Flow rate capabilities of the facility are 200 g/s of liquid oxygen or nitrogen, 50 g/s of gaseous nitrogen, and 2–3 g/s of gaseous helium. The injection head was designed and fabricated at ONERA to receive a coaxial injection element. It was set up on a pressurized spray chamber with three optical ports, fitted with three fused silica windows for optical applications. Liquid mass flow rate was controlled by a diaphragm orifice. Gas mass flow rate was controlled by a sonic throat. One thermocouple and one pressure probe were mounted on the chamber side to monitor the test conditions. The same one-half scale Vulcain gas generator coaxial injector element previously used on the water/nitrogen testing at ONERA Fauga Mauzac with a pressurized spray chamber was used for the cryogenic testing. Use of the same injector allowed more direct comparisons between water/nitrogen tests and the LOX/nitrogen or LOX/helium tests. The spray characterization was performed with an Aerometrics one-component PDPA system, described by Bachalo and Houser,<sup>89</sup> used in a classical configuration. The laser emission was a helium-neon of 15-mW power. The transmitter was fitted

Four pairs of liquid/gas simulants were tested, which were liquid nitrogen and liquid oxygen with room temperature nitrogen, liquid oxygen with room temperature helium, and liquid oxygen with cold (around 150 K) helium. Tests were conducted with three chamber pressures (10, 5, and 1 bar), different mass flow rates of LOX and gaseous nitrogen and a variable position of the PDPA probe area from 15 to 80 mm downstream in front of the LOX post (on the geometrical centerline). The feasibility of size and velocity measurements in severe conditions (pressure and cryogenic conditions) was demonstrated, but some of the initial tests were invalidated due to problems controlling the LOX injection temperature during the test. Sufficient accuracy on LOX temperature in the injection head was difficult at the considered pressures, and for some tests where the injected oxygen was too hot, cavitation occurred. These are relatively large drops in spite of gaseous flow at room temperature and a spray chamber filled with pressurized gaseous nitrogen also at room temperature. These droplet sizes are not in good agreement with predictions from empirical relations taking into account the surface tension, density, and viscosity of the liquid oxygen. Ferrenberg and Varma<sup>19</sup> have suggested that the empirical relations found with simulants (more often water and nitrogen) be corrected with the ratio

$$K = \frac{(\mu_l^{1/3} \sigma^{1/2} \rho_l^{-1/6})_{\text{actual propellant}}}{(\mu_l^{1/3} \sigma^{1/2} \rho_l^{-1/6})_{\text{simulant}}} \quad (48)$$

Applying this criterion in our case yields  $D_{32, \text{LOX}} \approx 0.3 D_{32, \text{water}}$ ; the water droplets are expected to be much larger than the LOX ones, which was not found to be the case. Another explanation may be the differences between the local PDPA measurements and the line-of-sight integrated MALVERN measurements. Recent tests were performed using the PDPA with water/nitrogen and the same injector at atmospheric pressure to check this point. The observed radial evolutions of mean axial velocity, of volume flux, and of SMD are plotted in Fig. 12. The SMD decreased from the spray axis to the periphery. A line-averaged SMD can be calculated that gives, according to Dodge,<sup>81</sup> a representative mean diameter for an axisymmetric particle field. With this the PDPA results can be compared to the line-of-sight measurements of the Malvern. The following equation is used to calculate line-averaged SMD with local point measurements:

$$D_{32m} = \frac{\sum_{i=-R}^{i=R} W_i (d_{30,i})^3}{\sum_{i=-R}^{i=R} W_i (d_{20,i})^2} \quad (49)$$

where  $d_{30,i}$  is the spatial volume mean diameter,  $d_{20,i}$  the spatial surface mean diameter, and  $W_i$  is given by

$$W_i = \Delta R_i n_i / t_i A_i \quad (50)$$

where  $\Delta R_i$  is the radial displacement step,  $n_i$  the number of droplets,  $t_i$  the acquisition time,  $A_i$  the probe area of radial position number  $i$ .

Figure 13 shows two evolutions of SMD along the axis. There is a good correlation between  $V_r = V_g - V_l$  with the drop size, which decreases when  $V_r$  increases. This result is in agreement with the correlation given for water tests.

The feasibility of drop size and velocity measurements in a cryogenic spray of LOX was demonstrated. The results are self-consistent, but the PDPA point measurement of drop sizes are not in good agreement with the expected values deduced from previous MALVERN measurements in water tests. This difference is likely due to vaporization effects and to line of sight vs local measurements. The PDPA can provide the local velocity of the droplets, and thereby a possibility

### IV. Further Improvements, Industry's Point of View

#### A. Overall Guidelines

The complexity of characterizing the reactive spray from coaxial LOX/GH2 injectors for the Ariane 5 gas generator led SEP and CNES to finance ONERA's experimental work on the simpler problem of characterizing the non-reactive spray of coaxial injectors. The question remains, however, about what kind of knowledge can be gained from cold sprays that can be useful for hot-reactive sprays.

The following assumptions and related options are derived from analysis of the reactive problem, illustrated in Fig. 14.

*Assumption 1:* the flame does not occur in the recess region.

*Assumption 2:* the spray maps obtained in the nonreactive initial region have a major influence on the flame location.

*Assumption 3:* the features of atomization, downstream of the flame detachment position, are lying between two extreme cases. In case 1 the flame surface is positioned radially far from the LOX core, i.e., in the mixing layer between the outer gases and the outer part of a nonreactive annular two-phase jet; then, there will be a region of the LOX core where atomization is produced by the inner part of a nonreactive annular jet. In case 2 the flame reaches the LOX core, which means it is anchored either in the mixing layer between the LOX core and the inner part of a nonreactive annular two-phase jet, or (if the former case 1 allows such a downstream radial evolution) before the end of the LOX core.

These assumptions lead to the following options: cold-flow tests can provide representative spray maps in the nonreactive region and, consequently, be useful

Arrows indicate the flow of hot gas, recirculated hot gas + H<sub>2</sub>, and the diffusion flame. The burning spray zone (4) shows hot gas H<sub>2</sub>O + H<sub>2</sub> at 3000 K and 300 m/s. A legend at the bottom identifies the symbols for Flame, Gas-Gas interface, Dispersed liquid objects (droplets, ligaments), and Liquid core surface.

1 : liquid + cold gas mixing zone, non reactive, confined

for determining the flame position; cold-flow tests can be useful for reactive sprays where regions of case 1 type exist.

To fulfill the objectives, the cold-flow tests have to produce representative spray maps in the nonreactive regions, that is, in the recess zone and in the near outer region (regions 1 and 2 of Fig. 14). As the tests are often performed with fluids rather different from actual ones (ambient temperature instead of cryogenic, for instance), similarity rules are required to design representative tests. The overall strategy is illustrated in Fig. 15.

#### B. First Choice of Similarity Criteria

##### 1. Real Configuration Input Parameters

The recess region spray field is characterized by inner interaction laws and by boundary conditions, mainly geometry and flow at the inlet section (see details in Tables 5 and 6).

**Fig. 15 Overall strategy for cold spray tests.**

In the case of the Ariane 5 Vulcain gas generator, the spray is produced by the atomization of a central liquid oxygen jet (100 K, 12 m/s,  $D_l = 2.5$  mm) by an annular gaseous hydrogen jet [40 K, 170 m/s,  $Y = 0.5(D_g - D_l) = 0.5$  mm] and confined by a recess tube ( $R = 3$  mm,  $D_g = 4$  mm).

##### 2. Similarity Parameters

The spray in the recess zone results from the mixing of two flows and, consequently, depends on the initial profiles of these two flows, mainly the velocity profiles. Hence, the similarity is obtained by keeping the Reynolds numbers  $Re_g$  and  $Re_l$  and the similarity of the upstream injector geometries (including roughness of the walls). This last condition, which is not always fulfilled practically, must be replaced by the similarity of the boundary-layer thicknesses, especially two momentum thicknesses that feed the two-phase wake of the LOX post,  $\theta_g$  and  $\theta_l$ , from where the criteria  $\theta_g^* = \theta_g/b_g$  and  $\theta_l^* = \theta_l/b_l$  came. Moreover, the Mach number condition ( $M = 0.15$ ) can be relaxed to  $M \leq 0.5$  and even more if we ensure that at least  $\theta_g^*$  is kept.

The two-phase mixing layer is developing from a wake of initial equivalent width:  $\bar{b}_s = \theta_g + b_s + \theta_l$ .

The production of dispersed liquid phase (ligaments, droplets, etc.) from the continuous liquid phase (liquid core with turbulent surface) results from the interaction of two kinds of forces: 1) fragmentation forces (mainly gas acting on liquid), i.e., inertial,  $\rho_g V_r^2 b^2$ , and viscosity,  $\mu_g V_r b$ , depending on the scale  $b$  considered and 2) cohesion forces (mainly liquid acting on liquid), i.e., inertial,  $\rho_l V_r^2 b^2$ , and viscosity,  $\mu_l V_r b$ , and surface tension:  $\sigma b$ .

Owing to the six degrees of freedom that are introduced here, and the units involved, three additional criteria must be considered. At this step of estimation, the density ratio  $n = \rho_g/\rho_l$ , the velocity ratio  $m = V_g/V_l$ , and the Weber number  $We = \rho_g V_r^2 \bar{b}_s/\sigma_l$  were chosen for reason of a priori relevance and simplicity.

When the flow enters the chamber, it enters a new environment, and a new set of nondimensional numbers has to be introduced, relating the new to the previous environment parameters, i.e., the chamber conditions to the injection conditions; i.e.,

$S^*$  = chamber section/injector total section

$\rho^*$  = chamber outer gas density/injection gas density

$\mu^*$  = chamber gas dynamic viscosity/injection gas viscosity

$M^*$  = injection gas velocity/chamber gas speed of sound.

Practically, for the recess and the near recess regions, the condition  $M^* = 0.1$  may be relaxed to  $M^* \leq 0.5$ .

For the mean spray characteristics and turbulent main features of the spray, the control of the acoustic boundary conditions appears to be necessary. On the chamber side, it is preferable to have an anechoic acoustic condition. On the injector side, the problem is more complicated, as a consequence the following

##### 3. Practical Use of Similarity Criteria

This choice of similarity criteria can be used to build a test program for further tests using various liquids with lower surface tension and viscosity. They will permit extending the experimental ranges of Weber and Reynolds numbers in order to reach the real configuration values.

### V. Conclusion

In the past, twin fluid coaxial injectors have been used extensively in cryogenic rocket engines, most generally providing high-propulsive efficiency and good combustion stability behavior. The basic atomization phenomena, however, which convert the primary liquid jets into droplets, are not yet fully understood and not yet well modeled, which is required if a numerical simulation of the complete engine is desired.

This chapter is an attempt to get a deeper insight into the state of the art of coaxial injection element characterization in cryogenic rocket engines. Relevant literature on theoretical aspects and experimental work was reviewed and discussed.

A number of theoretical investigations have been carried out on liquid jet atomization, but they have been mainly restricted to low-speed regimes and do not actually apply to rocket engine injectors for drop size prediction. Linear theories, in spite of recent improvements, remain limited in practical applications but can provide useful information on some parametric effects on the mean diameters and, with the help of the information theory, on the drop size distributions. Direct numerical simulations also are not currently suitable for the high-speed regimes of concern, but approximate modeling techniques such as volume-of-fluid and jet-embedding techniques are very promising.

Experimental investigations currently remain the best way to characterize a given injection element. The specific features of the coaxial design make the measurements quite impossible in engine operation conditions and difficult in cold flow ones, with simulation then questionable. Recent progress in diagnostic techniques, however, e.g., Malvern and PDPA, significantly improved the capability of test techniques.

The progressive approach followed by ONERA consisted in cold-flow tests using simulant fluids on both liquid and gas sides, then with LOX as the liquid. The parametric experiments were found to be self-consistent, but the transposition from one to the other did not agree with the findings of former investigators. Discrepancies could arise from different test situations and instrumentation as well as from undesired secondary mechanisms. Further tests with other simulant fluids in fixed experimental conditions are now planned to answer the question.

The industrial manufacturer's point of view has focused on the selection of similarity criteria especially with regard to the incoming flows, the two-phase wake mixing, and the chamber environment. Even if absolute values cannot yet be obtained for hot reactive spray characteristics, a good assessment of the relative influence of the major parameters on these characteristics seems to be reachable, which would considerably help to improve existing hardware or to design new injection elements.

### Shear Coaxial Injector Spray Characterization

Michelle M. Zaller\*

*Sverdrup Technology, Inc., Brookpark, Ohio 44142*  
and

Mark D. Klem<sup>†</sup>

*NASA Lewis Research Center, Cleveland, Ohio 44135*

### I. Introduction

IN combustors fed by shear coaxial injectors, injection of gas and liquid propellants and the formation of liquid droplets provide the initial conditions for calculating the propellant vaporization, mixing, and reaction rates. This makes propellant atomization a critical input to models that predict combustor performance and stability. Coaxial injector spray formation, however, is a complex process that is difficult to model. Analytical atomization models do not yet have the capability to accurately predict injector spray drop sizes. Drop size and velocity measurements, as well as local gas velocity measurements, are needed to validate atomization models, improve modeling capabilities, establish a coaxial injector spray database, and develop empirical correlations. Obtaining measurements of drop sizes produced by liquid propellant rocket injectors has been identified<sup>1,2</sup> as critical to improving the accuracy of computational models that predict the performance and stability margin of liquid propellant rocket engines. Drop size predictions made by available atomization models vary over several orders of magnitude,<sup>3</sup> and none of the models account for the recess of the liquid oxygen post, which separates the central liquid oxygen flow from the annular hydrogen flow and which has been shown to influence engine performance and stability.<sup>4</sup> Significant gains can be made by focusing on improving atomization models, because the drop size and velocity distributions produced at the completion of atomization are the initial conditions for vaporization, mixing, and reaction calculations. Without detailed spray drop size and velocity measurements, accurate liquid rocket engine performance and stability predictions cannot be made. Making accurate performance and stability predictions would contribute to reducing

the expensive testing performed in engine development programs, avoiding combustion instabilities, and optimizing the efficiency of new engines.

Unfortunately, the high-temperature and high-pressure environment of rocket engine combustors has made it difficult to obtain detailed measurements of drop size and velocity in hot firing engines. Because of the lack of hot-firing rocket combustor atomization data, other methods have been relied on to estimate the drop sizes occurring in hot firing engines. One such method has been to use theoretically derived atomization correlations with adjustable parameters in combustor models. These correlations were calibrated by forcing the overall model performance predictions to agree with actual rocket engine performance measurements. This adjustable parameter method assumes that all other processes in the hot-firing rocket engine, such as multiphase mixing and supercritical droplet vaporization, are well modeled. In fact, very little data exist to support models of many significant reacting spray processes. Therefore, this method of inferring drop size distributions based solely on overall performance data does not improve the ability of these models to predict injector spray drop size distributions.

Another technique used to estimate the drop sizes occurring in hot-firing rocket engines is to rely on cold-flow atomization data. Drop size correlations derived from nonreacting test results that have been adjusted to take into account fluid property differences are used as inputs to combustor models. The disadvantage of cold-flow data is that it is obtained at radically different conditions than those existing in a hot-firing combustor. The surface tension and viscosity of the simulants, which influence the drop size distributions, often do not match those of the reactive, hot-fire propellants. It is anticipated that qualitative trends predicted with cold-flow data have some relationship to hot-fire performance. Until extensive drop size measurements in hot-firing engines are performed, however, cold-flow data must be relied on to validate and improve current analytical models.

Because of the high cost and difficulty of obtaining drop size measurements in hot-firing rocket engines, it is desirable to develop cold-flow correlations relating drop size distributions to injection parameters. Optimally, cold-flow databases could be compared to correlations of drop sizes in hot-firing engines, giving a means of estimating performance and stability parameters in future development programs without resorting to hot-fire testing.

#### A. Previous Investigations

Liquid atomization in coaxial injector sprays is primarily due to the aerodynamic shear of the high-velocity gas stream on the surface of the liquid jet.<sup>5,6</sup> Waves of varying frequencies and growth rates form on the liquid jet surface. The dominant frequencies of these waves are functions of the gas and liquid stream relative velocities<sup>7</sup> and liquid jet turbulence levels.<sup>8</sup> Coupling between acoustic disturbances and the natural atomization frequencies is postulated to be a possible combustion instability mechanism.<sup>9</sup> Small mean drop size sprays have rapid vaporization rates that could couple with acoustic waves to induce combustion instability. Efforts have been made by numerous investigators to determine the influence of injection parameters on the drop sizes produced by coaxial injectors. These efforts have confirmed theoretical predictions that the relative velocity between the liquid jet and the surrounding gas stream has a major influence on the resulting drop sizes.

The droplet sizes resulting from the breakup of a liquid jet by a coaxial high-velocity gas stream have been determined by various researchers to depend on the liquid and gas properties, as well as the liquid orifice diameter, and liquid and gas flow rates and injection velocities. The relative influence of each of these parameters on the drop size distribution is not known. Extensive literature surveys are given by Ferrenberg et al.<sup>10</sup> on liquid propellant rocket injector characterization, and Lefebvre<sup>11</sup> on air-blast atomization studies. Some air-blast atomizers break up the liquid stream in a manner similar to coaxial injectors; however, the ratio of liquid to gas flow rate is typically an order of magnitude smaller in air-blast atomizers than in rocket injectors.

One technique used to characterize liquid spray drop size distributions was the wax droplet freezing technique. Hot-liquid wax was injected into ambient pressure air, and the resulting atomized wax droplets froze after being formed. The wax droplets were collected, sieved, and weighed, making it possible to measure large numbers of droplets simultaneously. Empirical correlations were used to account for property differences between the wax and the liquid being simulated. Wax freezing tests could not be used to measure the particle velocities. One difficulty associated with the use of hot wax was the selection of an injection temperature that permitted completion of atomization before the wax particles solidified. Weiss and Worsham<sup>12</sup> used the wax freezing technique to determine the drop sizes produced by the breakup of a liquid jet in a high-velocity coaxial airstream. The tests conducted by Weiss and Worsham<sup>12</sup> examined the influence of varying ambient pressure (air density) and liquid viscosity on the liquid breakup. Kim and Marshall<sup>13</sup> studied the drop size distributions resulting from plain jet air-blast atomizers while varying the wax viscosity. Falk<sup>14</sup> studied the atomization of wax by heated nitrogen gas in coaxial injectors. Although these experiments were conducted at ambient pressure, a gas acceleration ramps was used to simulate the effect of gas acceleration due to chemical reaction in real combustors. Unlike Weiss and Worsham,<sup>12</sup> Falk<sup>14</sup> did not use a sampling probe, and so the data reported by Falk<sup>14</sup> could not include information about the variation in drop size distributions as a function of axial and radial distance from the injector. Use of the wax droplet freezing technique had an advantage over optical spray diagnostics; since the sprays did not need to be kept optically thin, liquid flow rates similar to full-scale launch vehicle injector element flow rates were possible.

Lorenzetto and Lefebvre<sup>15</sup> used diffractively scattered light from a mercury arc lamp to estimate drop sizes in plain-jet air-blast atomizer sprays. Lorenzetto and Lefebvre estimated that their light scattering instrument could measure Sauter mean diameters as low as 20  $\mu\text{m}$ . Gomi<sup>16</sup> applied a laser diffraction technique to low flow rate coaxial injector sprays. Velocities could not be measured with the laser diffraction technique, and only line-of-sight average drop sizes at one radial location were obtained. Like photographic techniques, laser diffraction instruments obtain spatially averaged measurements of drop size, and unless measurements are made for a number of radial locations, the variation of drop sizes throughout the spray cannot be computed. Vingert<sup>17</sup> applied laser diffraction to coaxial injector sprays in a pressurized chamber. Nitrogen and helium were used to atomize water jets. Measurements of sprays with higher flow rates were achieved by using spray splitters and by correcting data with high-obscuration values. Deconvolutions of the line-of-sight data were performed to estimate spray volume concentration profiles. Several different injector geometries and the effect of liquid

post recess were studied, in addition to varying gas properties and gas and liquid flow rates and velocities.

Ferrenberg et al.<sup>10</sup> conducted an extensive study of coaxial injectors using a visibility/intensity droplet sizing interferometry (V/I DSI) technique.<sup>18</sup> The V/I DSI instrument was capable of simultaneously measuring droplet sizes and velocities. This study was limited, however, by the inability of the V/I DSI to reliably measure drop sizes below 18  $\mu\text{m}$ , handle a wide droplet velocity range, or make measurements in dense sprays. Use of the V/I DSI represented one of the first attempts to use a flux sensitive instrument to make rocket injector spray drop size and velocity measurements.

Sankar et al.<sup>19,20</sup> used a phase-Doppler particle analyzer (PDPA) to make detailed coaxial injector spray measurements. The phase-Doppler technique, a laser-based interferometric technique, was similar to the V/I DSI; measurements of drop size and velocity with high spatial resolution could be made. The PDPA represented an improvement over the V/I DSI technique, since the PDPA was insensitive to the relative and absolute intensities of the laser beams, could measure smaller droplets, and could handle a wide droplet velocity range. In the studies conducted by Sankar et al.,<sup>19</sup> the effects of varying gas and liquid flow rates, injection velocities, gas density, and post recess on the spray drop sizes, velocities, and mass fluxes were examined. Measurements were also made of vaporizing liquid nitrogen sprays at atmospheric pressure. Mean drop sizes measured in the liquid nitrogen sprays were much smaller than the water/nitrogen spray drop sizes. Sankar et al.<sup>19</sup> observed that the liquid nitrogen jets atomized without any gas flow. This probably indicated that the liquid nitrogen was boiling in the injector, which could have caused the observed improvement in atomization. PDPA measurements were obtained near the liquid jet breakup point for coaxial injector sprays by Eroglu and Chigier.<sup>21</sup> Goix et al.<sup>22</sup> performed PDPA measurements and obtained OH fluorescence images in reacting methanol/air sprays. Data were obtained for two flow conditions and three different axial locations. One of the tests shows Sauter mean diameter (SMD) radial profiles with a minimum at the spray center. This differs from cold-flow results obtained by other investigators,<sup>19-21,23</sup> which generally have flat profiles or maxima at the centerline.

#### B. Objectives

To obtain the coaxial injector spray data required to improve current modeling capability, a four-phase test program was initiated at the NASA Lewis Research Center. The ultimate goal of this program is to bridge the gap between cold-flow and hot-firing tests by attempting to correlate empirical drop size data acquired under cold-flow and hot-firing conditions. The first phase of the test program was intended to provide an estimate of the capabilities of the droplet sizing instrumentation and provide detailed mappings of the drop sizes produced by nonreacting water/air coaxial injector sprays as a function of liquid and gas flow rates and injector geometry. In the second phase of the program, drop size and velocity measurements were obtained in confined water/nitrogen coaxial injector sprays in a 50-mm-diam cylindrical chamber. Confining the spray permitted the effect of varying chamber pressure to be examined. The third phase of the proposed test program is to obtain drop size and velocity measurements in confined liquid nitrogen/helium sprays. Liquid nitrogen/helium will be used to simulate the fluid

properties of liquid oxygen/hydrogen. The fourth phase of the proposed test program is to obtain drop size data in a LOX/hydrogen rocket engine using the same single-element coaxial injector. The results of the first and second phases of the test program are presented here. These results are expected to be relevant for engines operating at chamber pressures below the liquid propellant critical pressure.

### II. Apparatus

#### A. Facility

The coaxial injector nonreacting spray tests were conducted at the NASA Lewis Research Center. The test facility is described elsewhere.<sup>22</sup> Domestic water at 520 kPa (75 psia) and shop air at 790 kPa (115 psia) were available for the first phase of testing. A 25- $\mu$ m filter was used on the water and air supplies. For these nonreacting atomization tests, the shear coaxial injector was mounted to spray straight down. A catch basin was located 1.2 m (4 ft) downstream of the injector face. Both air and water flow rates and injection velocities were varied. For the confined spray tests, water at 790 kPa (115 psia) and air at 790 kPa (115 psia) were available. The cylindrical chamber was 50 mm in diameter  $\times$  0.3 m long. No coflowing gas was provided, and no attempt was made to prevent droplet recirculation. Three 25  $\times$  62 mm windows were provided to allow optical access. Two of the windows were located at 0 and 150 deg so that the PDPA could be positioned to collect light scattered by the drops in a near forward direction. The chamber pressure for the confined spray tests was controlled using a back-pressure regulator.

#### B. Injector Hardware

The single-element, shear coaxial injector consisted of four parts: a liquid inlet manifold, liquid post, gas manifold, and faceplate (Fig. 1). Each liquid post had four fins to center it within the gas manifold. These fins were located 50 mm (2 in.) upstream of the injector face to minimize their effect on the gas velocity profiles at the injector exit. By changing out the liquid post and faceplate, several injectors could be evaluated using a single gas manifold. The injector elements, designed

for a nominal 330-N (75-lbf) thrust at 5.5-MPa (800-psia) chamber pressure using liquid oxygen and gaseous hydrogen, were smaller than the space shuttle main engine (SSME) main chamber injector elements, but comparable in size to RL-10 injector elements. This injector size was selected to reduce the spray number density and to permit application of optical drop sizing diagnostics. The coaxial injector was operated conventionally, that is, liquid was flowed through the center post, and gas through the injector annulus. The water-to-air mass flow rate ratio ranged from 0.6 to 4.0.

Six injector geometries, with different liquid and gas injection areas, were selected for testing. These injector geometries are listed in Table 1, with illustration of the various diameters provided in Fig. 1. Different injector geometries were tested to examine the effect of varying the gas velocity independently of the gas flow rate on the atomization process. The data were taken using sufficiently low gas flow rates to avoid sonic flow at the injector exit. Conducting tests with the gas gap unchoked allowed the atomizing gas velocity to be varied and the unchoked gas flow in a hot-firing engine to be more closely simulated. The liquid flow rates were reduced from the injector design flow rates to correspond to the reduced (unchoked) gas flow rates.

#### C. Diagnostic Instrumentation

A phase-Doppler particle analyzer was used to obtain drop size measurements in the shear coaxial injector sprays. This instrument is similar to a laser Doppler velocimeter in its use of scattered laser light to obtain flowfield information. The theory of operation of the PDPA is described in the literature.<sup>24</sup> It measures the size and velocity of individual droplets as they pass through a small measurement volume. The measurement volume diameter must be larger than the droplet diameters, yet small enough to detect one droplet at a time at the measurement location. Various moments of the drop size distribution (such as volume mean diameter  $D_{30}$ , and Sauter mean diameter  $D_{32}$ ) are computed from the acquired histograms, instead of fitting curves to the distribution shapes.

For these experiments, the PDPA was configured to provide an overall size measurement range from 4 to 350  $\mu\text{m}$ . A 50:1 maximum diameter ratio setting was available for any given run within the 4–350- $\mu\text{m}$  total size range. A monodisperse droplet generator was used to verify the performance of the phase-Doppler particle analyzer. Refractively scattered light was collected at 30 deg (with 0 deg defined as on-axis forward scatter). Two measurements of droplet size are made for each droplet. If these two measurements do not agree to within a specified tolerance, the droplet is determined to be aspherical, and the measurement is rejected. Signals

with low signal-to-noise ratios, such as signals resulting from multiple particles simultaneously present in the probe volume, are also rejected.

A mass flux patternator was used in open spray tests to estimate the mass flux distribution in the shear coaxial injector sprays. The patternator consisted of 32 square tubes assembled in a row. Each tube was  $6.4 \times 6.4$  mm ( $0.25 \times 0.25$  in.) square. Flexible tubes carried the liquid to collection containers. Measurements were made with the open tube ends 50 mm (2 in.) downstream of the injector face.

### III. Procedure

Drop sizes and velocities were measured using the PDPA in a plane 50 mm (2 in.) downstream of the injector face. Drop sizes and velocities were measured at seven radial locations in the spray until 6000 valid drop sizes were obtained. The smallest drops had mean velocities that were about 20–40% higher than the large drop mean velocities. Data rates (number of drops measured per total measurement time) were 100 times higher in the spray center than at 16-mm (0.62-in.) radius for almost every flow rate and geometry. The radial location of the measurement volume was increased until the valid data rate fell below 60 samples/s. Most of the data presented here were acquired within a radius of 16 mm. For the unconfined sprays, validation rates varied from about 70–100%. Validation rates fell as low as 40% for the pressurized spray tests, largely due to spray accumulating on the windows. To reduce measurement uncertainty, multiple measurements were taken at each location for the confined spray tests. Although the 40% validation rate is low, the drop size and velocity mean values were unaffected. This was checked by acquiring atmospheric pressure data in the chamber, with and without the windows installed, and getting reasonable agreement.

The mean drop size measurement repeatability was determined to be affected mostly by the photomultiplier tube (PMT) gain. The effect of the PMT gain on the polydisperse spray measurements was examined by taking data at one spray location using different PMT high-voltage settings. Mean drop sizes decreased almost linearly with increasing PMT sensitivity, giving no indication of an appropriate PMT gain selection. It was decided to select the PMT high voltage that produced the maximum valid data rate. This criterion for the PMT setting worked well in dense portions of the spray, since the valid data rate reached a maximum value as the PMT gain was varied. While using this procedure, the repeatability of the mean drop sizes were estimated to be  $\pm 10\%$  and velocities  $\pm 4\%$ .

The effect of sample size on the mean drop sizes was determined by taking eight series of measurements at one spray location while varying the number of valid samples collected. The mean drop sizes varied widely for small sample sizes. As the sample size was increased, the standard deviation of the eight measurements of mean drop size reached an acceptable value at a sample size of 6000 (Fig. 2). Larger sample sizes did not lower the standard deviation significantly, so a minimum sample size of 6000 valid drops was selected for all of the tests.

The radial symmetry of the coaxial injector sprays was examined. By traversing across a diameter of the spray<sup>12</sup> tests were conducted since these tests exhibited a high degree of symmetry, the remaining tests were conducted by traversing along only half the spray diameter. A sample measurement illustrating the spray mean drop size and velocity profile symmetry for the entire spray width is shown in Figs. 3 and 4.

A tube patterner was used to measure the spray mass flux using injector 6 with several different water flow rates. The patterner tubes were covered before the spray was turned on. After the flow rates were set, the cover was removed. The water was carried in flexible tubes to the measurement containers, which were weighed before and after each run. Liquid was collected for between 1 and 5 min, with the shorter run times used with the higher water flow rates. Several tests were also conducted using one set of flow rates. The repeatability of the data was exceptionally high, with all of the runs with the same flow rates agreeing to within  $\pm 10\%$ . Although the spray patterner clearly interfered with the spray, the collection efficiencies were between 80% and 100% of the flow meter value.

### IV. Results and Discussion

#### A. Injection Parameter Effect on Spray

##### 1. Gas Velocity Effect on Unconfined Spray

Drop size and drop velocity profiles were measured to determine the effect of varying gas and liquid flow rates on the injector spray. Sauter mean diameters and drop mean axial velocities are presented for injector 1 (see Table 1) as a function of radial location for a constant water flow rate of 0.9 g/s and three air flow rates of 3, 4, and 5 g/s (solid circles in Figs. 5 and 6). Mean drop sizes decreased with increasing air flow rate, in agreement with observations made by numerous investigators.<sup>10-17,19-23</sup> SMD values at the edge of the spray were not observed to be minimum values. For the 3 g/s airflow rate, the SMD measured at the spray edge was actually 20% larger than the SMD measured in the center (Fig. 5). In tests performed by Sankar et al.,<sup>19</sup> slight increases in Sauter mean diameter were also observed at the spray edge. For all three airflow rates, the SMD profiles were flat, with little variation in SMD as a function

##### 2. Liquid Orifice Diameter Effect on Unconfined Spray

Using the same water flow rate of 0.9 g/s and an airflow rate of 3 g/s, mean drop size and velocity data were measured using a smaller liquid orifice diameter (injector 5). These drop size and velocity curves (indicated by open circles in Figs. 5 and 6) are nearly identical to the data obtained for the same flow rates with injector 1, despite the factor of two decrease in the liquid orifice diameter. There was a corresponding factor of two decrease in the liquid jet Reynolds number ( $Re_L = \rho_L V_L D_0 / \mu_L$ ), which has often been used as a correlating parameter for shear coaxial injector sprays.<sup>25,26</sup> This indicates either a weak dependence of the spray drop sizes on liquid jet Reynolds number or the liquid jet Reynolds number might only serve to distinguish among liquid jet breakup or flow regimes. The influence of the liquid jet Reynolds number may be greater for turbulent liquid jet flows.

##### 3. Liquid Flow Rate Effect on Unconfined Spray

A series of tests was conducted with injector 1 using an airflow rate of 3 g/s air and four different water flow rates (Fig. 7). The Sauter mean diameter curves in Fig. 7 are similarly shaped, despite the change in liquid flow rate. The SMD profile shapes are not strongly affected by the change in liquid jet Reynolds numbers, despite the occurrence of both laminar and turbulent liquid flows. For this airflow rate, the largest drop sizes occurred at the spray edge. Little variation in drop sizes is evident near the centerline, as compared with the data presented in Fig. 3, which shows a larger SMD variation along the centerline for the same water flow rates.

To measure spray mass flux, a tube patternator with 6.4-mm-square tubes was used with injector 6. The airflow rate was kept constant at 4 g/s, while the water flow rate was varied from 0.8 to 15 g/s. Collection efficiencies varied from 80

Use of the patternator provided much better mass flux measurements than the phase Doppler for these sprays, especially at the higher flow rate cases, in which large, nonspherical liquid particles were probably present at the measurement plane. The mass fluxes are plotted against radius in Fig. 8. Between 60 and 90% of the spray mass for each case was collected in the center tube, indicating that the sprays are quite narrow, with spray axial velocity components much larger than the radial components.

##### 4. Post Recess Effect on Unconfined Spray

The post was recessed in increments of 1.6 mm from 0.0 to 6.4 mm. The results presented in Figs. 9 and 10 were obtained using a water flow rate of 2.4 g/s and an airflow rate of 4 g/s. As the post recess was increased, the centerline SMD increased. At the same time, SMD measured at 12.7-mm radius decreased with increasing recess, with the exception of the 6.4-mm recess case. Therefore, the general effect of increasing post recess was to increase the slope of the SMD profile as a function of radius. For all cases with post recess, the drop velocity maximum did not occur at the centerline (Fig. 10).

##### 5. Confined and Unconfined Spray

The effect of enclosing the spray within a chamber was examined. Spray mean drop size and velocity data are presented in Figs. 11 and 12 for injector 6. One set of tests was conducted without the chamber present. Another set of tests was performed using the 50-mm-diam  $\times$  0.3-m-long cylindrical chamber, with the chamber pressure maintained at atmospheric. The sprays were quite similar between 0- and 6.4-mm radius. Beyond 6.4-mm radius, the presence of the chamber walls affects the measured spray sizes and velocities. Drop sizes for the enclosed spray are larger than for the unenclosed spray, presumably due to overcounting of large drops recirculating within the chamber. Mean axial velocities were negative at the edge of the enclosed spray, confirming the presence of a recirculation zone.

##### 6. Constant $\rho_g V_g$ for Varying Chamber Pressures

Injector 6 was used with flow rates of 2.3 g/s water and 6.8 g/s air at both 300-kPa and 500-kPa chamber pressures (Figs. 13 and 14). Increasing the chamber pressure while keeping the gas and liquid flow rates constant resulted in larger drop sizes. Since the gas flow rate was the same for both cases, the gas injection velocity for the 500-kPa case was lower than the 300-kPa case, causing the drop sizes to increase with increasing chamber pressure. The drop velocities decreased with increasing chamber pressure near the spray center. Obtaining measurements was difficult due to spray collecting on the chamber windows. Multiple measurements were made at each radial location to minimize the error caused by the presence of the spray on the windows.

###### 7. Constant $V_g$ for Varying Chamber Pressures

Four tests were conducted within the pressurized chamber with 2.3 g/s water and varying airflow rates. The airflow rates were selected to keep the gas injection velocity constant while varying the chamber pressure. Injector 6 was used with chamber pressures from 100 to 500 kPa abs (Figs. 15 and 16). The mean drop sizes at the edge of the spray were similar for all four chamber pressures. Near the spray center, the drop sizes decreased with increasing chamber pressure, probably due to the increased gas stream momentum. The drop velocities were similar for all four cases.

###### 8. Constant $\rho_g V_g^2$ for Varying Chamber Pressures

Additional tests were conducted for the same four chamber pressures using the same injector (injector 6) and water flow rate (2.3 g/s). The airflow rates were chosen to keep the gas stream dynamic head (gas density times gas injection velocity squared) constant for all four chamber pressures (Figs. 17 and 18). The

#### B. Composite Mean Drop Sizes

To make the drop size data obtained for this particular injector more universally applicable and to determine the relative influence of various injection parameters, a correlation between the injection parameters and a composite mean spray drop size was found. First, composite mean drop sizes were computed for each test case. These were based on  $\bar{D}_{30}$  (volume mean diameter) instead of  $\bar{D}_{32}$ .  $\bar{D}_{30}$  is more appropriate because it represents a drop with the average volume (or mass), instead of a drop with the average volume-to-surface area. The composite mean drop sizes were weighted averages of the volume mean drop sizes obtained at the seven radial locations sampled in these tests. The drop sizes at each radial location were weighted by the amount of time required to collect  $N$  samples, and the area of a ring representing an integrated area for each radial location: where  $A$  is the area of a representative ring at that radial location, subscript  $i$  represents each radial location,  $j$  is the number of radial locations, subscript  $C$  designates the composite value,

$$(\bar{D}_{30}^3)_C = \left( \frac{\sum_{i=1}^j \frac{A_i \bar{D}_{30i}^3}{t_i}}{\sum_{i=1}^j \frac{A_i}{t_i}} \right) \quad (1)$$

and  $t$  is the time taken to acquire  $N$  samples. For all of the tests presented here,  $N$  is 6000 samples. Equation (1) assumes the validation rate to be high, which was

true for the unconfined spray data acquired in this study, and neglects the variation of the measurement cross-sectional area with droplet size.

Composite mean diameters from over 80 different tests were correlated with respect to the injection parameters using linear regression. A good fit to the data was obtained with the equation

$$\bar{D}_{30c} = 5.92 \times 10^{-5} \left( \frac{\sigma}{\mu_L} \right)^{0.75} \left( \frac{\rho_L}{\rho_g} \right)^{0.05} \left( \frac{\dot{m}_L}{\dot{m}_g} \right)^{0.25} \frac{V_r^{0.05}}{V_r^{0.8}} \quad (2)$$

where  $\sigma$ ,  $\mu$ , and  $\rho$  indicate surface tension, viscosity, and density.  $V$  is the injection velocity,  $\dot{m}$  is the flow rate, and subscripts  $g$  and  $L$  refer to the gas and liquid phases, respectively. Gas and liquid velocities, flow rates, injection areas, and the gas density were varied. These variable ranges were the following: liquid orifice diameter  $D_0$  1.3–2.5 mm, relative velocity  $V_r$  80–290 m/s, liquid flow rate  $\dot{m}_L$  0.9–15 g/s, gas flow rate  $\dot{m}_g$  1.4–6.8 g/s, and liquid-to-gas flow rate ratio 0.3–4.2. No attempt was made to determine the influence of liquid properties, such as surface tension, density, and viscosity, on the atomization process. These fluid properties were included in the composite mean drop size correlation for nondimensionalization purposes. Also note that the relative velocity appears in the drop size correlation, even though the gas velocity was much larger than the liquid velocity, and the influence of relative velocity was not demonstrated conclusively. The fit of the correlation to the data was checked using linear regression. The square of the correlation coefficient,  $r^2$ , was 0.96. The large value of  $r^2$  that was obtained indicates that the data and the equation are highly correlated. All of the data points are plotted against the correlation in Fig. 19.

The recess data were correlated separately. The influence of post recess was expressed as a fraction of the composite mean diameter value with no post recess,

$$\bar{D}_{30C, \text{recess}} / (\bar{D}_{30C}) (1 + 0.18R - 0.278R^{0.5}) \quad (3)$$

where  $R$  is the dimensionless ratio of recess depth to liquid post outer diameter. This empirical correlation was based on data for  $0 \leq R \leq 2$  and is plotted in Fig. 20.

Previous experiments have shown that the impact of liquid post recess on the drop sizes produced by coaxial injector sprays to be unclear or negligible. Burick<sup>27</sup> reported that recessing the LOX post typically increased overall mean drop sizes for post recesses of less than twice the post diameter. This is not in agreement with the data presented here. Falk<sup>14</sup> found that recessing the liquid post had very little effect on mean drop sizes; however, only one test with a recessed post was conducted in that study. Gomi<sup>17</sup> observed very slight differences in drop sizes between cases with zero recess and cases with a post recess equal to three post diameters. Sankar et al.<sup>19</sup> showed that increasing post recess had a variable effect on drop sizes. Other evidence has indicated that recessing the liquid post might produce smaller mean drop sizes. Hot-firing tests have shown that increased post recess leads to improved combustion efficiency.<sup>4</sup> It is possible that improved atomization was a factor in the observed increase in performance. The data reported here confirms this observation, although it does not take into account the differences between cold-flow and hot-firing testing. Other effects, such as burning in the cup formed by the liquid post recess, may also affect the drop size distributions in hot-firing rocket engines.

#### V. Concluding Remarks

Open air sprays produced by a single-element, shear coaxial injector flowing water and air were characterized using an Aerometrics phase-Doppler particle analyzer and a mass flux patternator. Sauter mean diameter and mean axial drop velocity profiles were examined in detail with the PDPA. The shapes of these profiles were demonstrated to be a function of the water and airflow rates and injection velocities. In all cases, increasing the gas stream velocity resulted in smaller drop sizes. The velocity profile shapes had maxima at the spray center for the lower gas and liquid flow rates; for higher water flow rates, the drops in the spray center did not have the maximum velocities. The liquid orifice diameter was varied by a factor of two in these tests, and was not observed to influence the drop sizes significantly. Sauter mean diameter distributions were flat for low water and airflow rates; the size distributions had maxima at the spray center for higher water flow rates. Recessing the injector post up to twice the injector post outside diameter caused the drop sizes measured at the centerline to increase.

The PDPA was used to make measurements of single-element, shear coaxial injector sprays within a pressurized chamber. Drop sizes measured within the chamber were larger than for open air sprays, especially at the spray edge. Velocities beyond 12-mm radius were negative for almost every test, indicating the presence of a recirculation zone. At higher chamber pressures, the airflow rate had to be increased in order to create a spray without the intact liquid core of the jet reaching the measurement plane. It was demonstrated that keeping the gas dynamic head constant (or Weber number) while varying the gas density created sprays with similar SMD near the spray center. The similarity, however, among SMD or mean velocity profiles obtained at different chamber pressures was not preserved by maintaining a constant gas dynamic head. Therefore, although maintaining the gas dynamic head was a reasonable correlating factor, it was not sufficient to guarantee complete similarity among sprays obtained at different chamber pressures.

A one-dimensional correlation was developed between a composite  $\bar{D}_{30}$  and the injection flow rates and velocities for water/air shear coaxial injector sprays. Fluid properties were included in the correlation in order to nondimensionalize it. The relative velocity appears in the drop size correlation, despite the fact that the influence of liquid velocity alone was not demonstrated conclusively. This correlation should be able to predict shear coaxial injector spray drop sizes only for nonvaporizing, subcritical pressure sprays. It does predict the influence of many injection parameters, however, which should be relevant to other flow regimes. Once appropriate similarity parameters are established, it is expected to be useful for specifying initial drop sizes in reacting spray calculations. Additional testing will be required using fluids with a wide range of properties and a test matrix that includes lower gas/liquid velocity ratios in order to extend the correlation applicability.

### Chapter 8

### Impinging Jet Injector Atomization

William E. Anderson,\* Harry M. Ryan,\* and Robert J. Santoro†  
*Pennsylvania State University, University Park, Pennsylvania 16802*

### I. Introduction

HIGH-FREQUENCY combustion instability in rocket engines occurs when the energy released during combustion couples with an acoustic mode of the thrust chamber and causes amplification of the oscillating pressure field.<sup>1</sup> There is no exact or conclusive proof regarding the specific combustion-based mechanisms that control initiation and sustenance of resonant high-frequency pressure oscillations in liquid rocket engines and, thus, no substantiated predictive model capable of accounting for thrust chamber design and operation on combustion instability. Most work on the coupling mechanism has been based on the underlying assumption that it is traceable to a single one of the principle component processes: injection, atomization, vaporization, mixing, or chemical kinetics.

All of the component processes, with the exception of injection, are determined to a large degree by the event of primary atomization, i.e., the initial fragmentation of an intact liquid core into drops and ligaments. Propellant spray characteristics, which are a direct product of the atomization process, also determine the thrust chamber's combustion efficiency and hot-side heat transfer characteristics. Therefore, it is necessary to understand primary atomization on the basis of its importance in the practical realization of optimal rocket engine operation.

In chemical thrusters powered by liquid propellants, atomization is made to occur efficiently by the use of highly inertial conditions. In rocket engines, where propellants are injected at a high-dynamic head (anywhere from 0.1 and 3 MPa), the greatest source of inertia available for destabilization of an injected propellant stream is another propellant stream. Liquid jet impingement on another liquid jet is a common and effective method to atomize and mix propellants prior to combustion. A number of combinations have been used with up to five impinging jets,<sup>2</sup> but the prevalent element type is the like doublet (Fig. 1), where two geometrically and dynamically similar jets of the same propellant impinge

Impinging jet injector elements are the preferred injector geometry for rocket engines that use storable propellants or liquid hydrocarbons. These injectors are also a desirable substitute for coaxial injectors, typically used with gas/liquid propellant combinations, due to better atomization and mixing characteristics and inherently lower fabrication costs. Present design analysis for impinging jet injectors is not nearly as well developed as it is for coaxial injectors, however, primarily due to the lack of basic knowledge regarding the fundamental atomization mechanisms of impinging jets and their subsequent mixing and combustion processes. This situation is exacerbated by the fact that design and operational effects on combustion stability and performance for impinging jet injectors typically act in opposite directions, i.e., improved performance is achieved usually through sacrificing high-frequency stability margin, and vice versa.

The ability to control combustion instability is clearly dependent on the ability to understand primary atomization and the role it plays in the initiation and growth mechanisms of combustion instabilities in rocket engines. To date, there is not a clear, basic, and quantitative understanding of the processes that control atomization of impinging jets. The purpose of this chapter is to provide a concise report on the current state of knowledge on the primary atomization mechanisms of impinging liquid jets and to explore the roles that primary atomization may play in combustion stability. Results from previous experimental and theoretical studies on impinging liquid jets are summarized. Results from models using linear stability theory to predict certain measurable variables are presented. The results from more recent experimental work on impinging liquid jets are presented and compared with these theoretical results. Explanations for impinging jet behavior in different operating regimes are discussed. The role that primary atomization may play in combustion instability is discussed. In the end, some conjecture is provided regarding the operative mechanisms of impinging jet atomization, and the subject area is summarized.

### II. Background

#### A. General Characteristics of Impinging Liquid Jets

The impingement of liquid jets is a very efficient method of atomization and mixing whereby the dynamic head of the propellant is used to destabilize an opposing liquid propellant stream, thereby fragmenting the liquid into ligaments and droplets. In the typical case of dynamically similar impinging jets, a very high-pressure region exists at the point where the axis streamlines of both jets converge and stagnate. After deceleration at the stagnation point where the static pressure is ideally equal to the total pressure in the propellant manifold, the fluid is accelerated nearly back to the jet's initial velocity. The high pressure in the stagnation region also causes the propellant to spread laterally, creating a fan. Shear occurs in the region between the stagnation streamline of the jet axis and the constant pressure streamline that defines the outer boundary of the impinging jet system. Drop velocity<sup>3</sup> and sheet velocity measurements<sup>4</sup> at atmospheric pressure for a variety of geometric and flow conditions indicate that the liquid downstream of the stagnation point moves at a speed nearly equal to the initial speed of the jets.

A schematic of the like doublet impinging jet injector is shown in Fig. 1. Equal diameter liquid jets impinge and form a fanlike elliptical liquid sheet. For the case of directly opposed jets, a circular disk would be formed after impingement. The angle between the jets,  $2\theta$ , is generally about 60 deg. The impingement point is typically about five length-to-diameter ratios ( $l_j/d_o$ ) downstream of the injector face. Injection orifices are typically fabricated by twist drilling, electrical discharge machining, or laser drilling. In practice, the fan may be inclined at a small angle  $\alpha$  toward an adjacent fan of the opposite propellant to induce large-scale mixing. The angular coordinate in the plane of the sheet is defined as  $\phi$ . At typical rocket operating conditions, Reynolds numbers based on orifice diameter and liquid properties are on the order of  $10^5$ – $10^6$ ; liquid Weber numbers ( $We_l = \rho_l U_o^2 d_o / \sigma$ ) indicating the balance between liquid inertial forces that tend to fragment the propellant and surface tension forces that tend to maintain the integrity of the liquid mass are on the order of  $10^5$ ; and injection pressure drops range from about 0.5 to 3.0 MPa (5 to 30 atm). A vena contracta usually forms downstream of the entrance region of the injector element and subsequently reattaches to the wall. Orifice discharge coefficients typically range between the thin orifice limit of 0.61 and 0.9. The entrance to the orifice is usually sharp, and fabrication cost considerations typically preclude rigorous specification of surface roughness or inlet contour.

The atomization process may be considered to take place in two general steps. Gross fragmentation of the intact liquid stream occurs during primary atomization under the influence of aerodynamic, viscous, inertial, and tensile forces. The shape and size of the liquid fragments are dependent on propellant injector geometry, propellant flow condition, and ambient conditions. During secondary atomization, the liquid fragments further disintegrate into a drop field that is dependent on local relative flow conditions and on the size and shape of the fragments formed during primary atomization. The general trend is for the drop Weber number ( $We_D = \rho_s U_{\infty}^2 d_p / \sigma$ ) to move toward unity in a drop field in a quasi-equilibrium state.

Understanding the relative order of effect of stresses that can disrupt the intact liquid provides insight into the physics of atomization. Following Ranz,<sup>5</sup> order of magnitude estimates of stresses active in the atomization process of a like doublet fuel element in the F-1 engine<sup>2</sup> are presented in Table 1. For this injector, the

fuel was RP-1, orifice diameter  $d_o$  was 7.1 mm, the injection velocity  $U_j$  was 17 m/s, and the total impingement angle  $2\theta$  was 30 deg. Relevant length scales  $L$  to estimate interfacial shear effects are based on the boundary layer depth  $\delta$ ; the calculation of  $L$  was based on a turbulent boundary layer with a nondimensional thickness  $\delta/d_o$  that grows as  $0.16Re_x^{-1/7}$  where  $x$  scales on the orifice diameter  $d_o$ . This leads to a boundary-layer depth estimate of  $\delta \sim 0.06d_o$ , or  $L \sim 0.4$  mm for both liquid and gas. To estimate ambient fluid inertia, a maximum relative velocity is used with the assumption that a quiescent atmosphere surrounds the jets, thus,  $V \sim 17$  m/s. The velocity related to liquid inertial forces is the relative velocity of the two jets; thus, here the relative velocity is 8.8 m/s. The liquid's cohesive forces were estimated with  $d$  based on an injection diameter of 7.1 mm and  $\sigma$  being equal to the surface tension of RP-1 in air, 1.5 mg/s<sup>2</sup>. Only when length scales become extremely small do surface tension effects become important. Based on a local relative velocity of 17 m/s, drop Weber numbers of order one do not occur until drops become submicron size. A measured drop distribution in the dilute spray region of this type of injector would be centered somewhere greater than 100  $\mu$ . It is seen from Table 1 that liquid inertial forces are an order of magnitude higher than the next higher force, the aerodynamic stress. Therefore, it can be expected that the condition of the jet before impingement is very important in determining atomization characteristics and that jet dynamics will play the major role in the breakup of the liquid sheet.

#### B. Previous Experimental Studies

Most previous studies of impinging jet atomizers have emphasized cold-flow pattinator measurements of the mixing characteristics<sup>6-10</sup> using water as a simulant, and drop size measurements using optical techniques either using water as a simulant again<sup>9,10</sup> or by using hot-wax flow and measurement techniques.<sup>11</sup> The results of these studies should be used carefully, since cavitation in the orifice<sup>12</sup> may have occurred in many tests, especially where the jet velocity was high or where a high back pressure was not established. A good summary of the atomization correlations published up until 1984 can be found in a report by Ferrenberg et al.<sup>13</sup>

George<sup>14</sup> used holography to measure monomethyl hydrazine (MMH) drops in a combustng nitrogen tetroxide/MMH environment at a chamber pressure of 156 psia. These measurements were compared with atmospheric cold-flow measurements using the same injectors and using water as a simulant. George<sup>14</sup> found

that the data compared very poorly with Ingebo's correlation<sup>15</sup> for drop size from impinging jet atomizers. George<sup>14</sup> developed correlations for cold-flow and combusting condition drop size as well as a correlation for the change in drop size as a function of distance from the impingement point for the combusting condition. A companion study was conducted at the Air Force Aeronautics Laboratory where injector elements with the same geometry as George's were used in a full-scale rocket test firing.<sup>16</sup> It was likely, however, that in George's cold-flow tests the water jets were cavitating because of the high jet velocities and atmospheric back pressure used in the tests. Other visual studies of impinging jets under combustion flow conditions include holographic studies<sup>17</sup> and high-speed videographic studies.<sup>18-20</sup>

Heidmann et al.<sup>21</sup> undertook an extensive study of impinging jets to characterize the effects of orifice diameter  $d_o$ , jet velocity  $U_j$ , impingement angle  $2\theta$ , preimpingement length  $l_f$ , and liquid properties on the structure of the resulting spray. Liquid velocities between 4 and 30 m/s were studied for orifice diameters of 0.64, 1.02, and 1.45 mm (0.025, 0.040, and 0.057 in.) with  $L/d_o$  ratios of 80, 50, and 35, respectively. Impingement angles in the range  $30 < 2\theta < 100$  deg were studied while preimpingement length was varied between 6 and 60 orifice diameters. Viscosity and surface tension effects were studied by using various glycerol solutions, varsol, and water.

From these studies, Heidmann et al.<sup>21</sup> determined that the liquid jet velocity and impingement angle were critical parameters in determining spray structure and also identified four spray regimes. For low-velocity jets ( $U_j < 4$  m/s), a closed rim regime was observed in which a sheet is initially formed that subsequently contracts into a cylindrical stream. At higher velocities ( $4 < U_j < 6$  m/s), a periodic drop regime was identified in which waves appeared on the surface of the sheet and regularly circumferentially spaced drops were shed from the periphery of the main sheet. At higher velocities ( $6 < U_j < 9$  m/s), in the open rim regime, waves were seen on the surface of the sheet and the leading edge of the sheet fragmented into ligaments and drops. Both open rim and periodic drop patterns were seen at jet velocities between 5 and 10 m/s with periodic phenomena more pronounced for higher viscosity liquids. Above 10 m/s and to the highest velocities tested ( $\sim 30$  m/s), spray patterns were characterized as being in the fully developed regime, where periodic waves of drops projecting from the point of impingement were apparent. Heidmann et al. reported that sheet breakup length  $x_b$  increased with jet velocity over the periodic drop and closed rim regimes, and then approached a constant value in the open rim regime; they were not able to measure breakup length in the fully developed regime with any certainty.

Heidmann et al.<sup>21</sup> recognized that the observed periodicity would be an obvious mechanism of combustion instability if it occurred with the appropriate time scale and if some coherence could be observed between the temporal characteristics of droplet formation and the unsteady gas motions in the chamber. In their studies of the spray formed by two impinging liquid jets, Heidmann et al.<sup>21</sup> noted that the periodic shedding was dependent on injection velocity, impingement angle, and injection orifice diameter. Their study emphasized measuring the "wave frequency" of drops and ligaments and used a pulse meter to measure the rate at which a light beam directed normal to the plane of the sheet was interrupted. Heidmann et al.<sup>21</sup> reported that this wave frequency was linearly proportional to resultant sheet velocity (which was incorrectly defined as  $U_j \cos \theta$ ) and that orifice diameter and

preimpingement length had minor effects on the observed wave frequency. It is important to note that the occurrence of a well-defined single characteristic frequency reported by Heidmann et al.<sup>21</sup> could be determined only over a limited distance with respect to the impingement point and varied in location as operating conditions were changed.

Dombrowski and Hooper<sup>4</sup> studied the disintegration of the sheet formed by turbulent and laminar impinging water jets in air at velocities from about 7 to 20 m/s. Based on the results of Heidmann et al.<sup>21</sup> with respect to the effects of jet diameter and preimpingement length, they chose to study a single orifice diameter (0.5 mm) and preimpingement length (2 mm). A tube length of 200 mm ( $L/d_o = 400$ ) was used to guarantee fully developed velocity profiles at the exit of the tube. The impingement angle was varied from 50 to 140 deg. They concluded that one of three mechanisms was operative in the disintegration of the sheet, primarily depending on the relative jet inertia and whether the jets were turbulent or laminar. For laminar jets at low velocities ( $U_j < 10$  m/s) and low-impingement angles, where large drops were shed off a stationary rim, the leading edge of the sheet was in a state of equilibrium between inertial and surface tension forces. Above 10 m/s for both laminar and turbulent jets, waves formed locally at the point of liquid jet impact. For laminar jets, Dombrowski and Hooper<sup>4</sup> argued that these "impact waves" were associated with the high-velocity jet core, and that for laminar jets with velocities between 10 and 20 m/s, the impact waves were damped by the lower velocity fluid from the laminar jet periphery, which also comprised the peripheral regions of the sheet. Measured reductions in drop size were reasoned to be due to small disturbances introduced by the impact waves that reduced the thickness of the sheet's rim. Furthermore, they reported that at laminar jet velocities approaching 20 m/s, impact waves caused early breakdown of the sheet downstream of the impingement point, whereas waves amplified by aerodynamic stresses controlled the breakdown of the rest of the sheet. At high velocities and large impingement angles, impact waves predominated over the entire sheet. Dombrowski and Hooper<sup>4</sup> reported that in the equilibrium state,  $x_b$  increased with increasing jet velocity at a constant impingement angle, but for sheet breakdown controlled by either impact waves or aerodynamic forces,  $x_b$  decreased with increases in jet velocity at any given impingement angle.

Dombrowski and Hooper<sup>4</sup> reported significantly different behavior for turbulent jets. They attributed these differences to the difference in velocity profile between laminar jets and turbulent jets. For turbulent jets, impact wave effects were seen at velocities as low as 7 m/s for large impingement angles. Dombrowski and Hooper<sup>4</sup> attributed this specifically to the absence of a low-velocity region in peripheral regions of the sheet to damp the impact waves. Drop size decreased with increasing jet velocity and increasing impingement angle. The transition to impact wave-controlled breakup for the turbulent jet case was determined to occur for relative jet Weber numbers,  $\rho_l U_j^2 d_j \sin^2 \theta / \sigma$ , greater than 100.

Huang<sup>22</sup> examined the breakup of axisymmetric liquid sheets formed by the impingement of two directly opposed water jets that covered jet Weber number regimes from 100 to 30,000. Huang<sup>22</sup> used a thin orifice that apparently produced slug flow jets and, thus, were laminar. Two dissimilar breakup regimes connected by a transition regime were documented. The first breakup regime,  $100 < We_j < 500$ , was characterized by stable liquid sheets, increasing breakup length with

increasing jet velocity, and a semicylindrical liquid edge. Huang<sup>22</sup> measured the diameter of drops shed off the outer edge of the sheet from photographs and showed that they were comparable to drop diameters calculated according to Rayleigh jet instability theory using the thickness of the semicylinder at the edge for jet diameter. Huang<sup>22</sup> analyzed this regime by balancing outwardly directed inertial force and inwardly directed surface tension force, and derived a semiempirical relation for breakup radius  $r_b$ ,

$$r_b = 0.167 d_j We_j / 2 \quad (1)$$

The transition regime,  $500 < We_j < 2,000$ , included the critical zone where  $r_b$  was a maximum. Past this point,  $r_b$  decreased with increasing jet velocity. Sinuous waves on the liquid sheet were first apparent in this regime. The second breakup regime,  $We_j > 2,000$ , was characterized by a predominance of antisymmetric waves and steadily decreasing  $r_b$  with increasing jet Weber number. Huang<sup>22</sup> analyzed breakup behavior in this regime using a model of a vibrating membrane and derived a semiempirical relation for  $r_b$ ,

$$r_b = 14.2 d_j s^{-2/3} We_j^{-1/3} \quad (2)$$

#### C. Theoretical Models of Impinging Jet Atomization

Taylor<sup>23</sup> developed a model for low Weber number impinging jets that accurately predicts the overall geometry of the formed sheet and made detailed measurements of sheet thickness and lateral spread of the fan formed by jets colliding at impingement angles  $2\theta$  of 60, 90, and 120 deg, and at jet velocities up to 5.6 m/s to verify his model. His measurements indicated that the sheet thickness  $h$  at any radial location  $r$  on the sheet was of the form  $rh = F(\theta, \phi)$ , which is independent of  $U_s$ . Measured values of  $F$  indicated a symmetric distribution about its peak value at  $\phi = 0$  deg. Taylor<sup>23</sup> noted that the geometry of the sheet formed by the impinging jets was related to the presence of stationary antisymmetric waves within a limiting radius. The limiting radius was defined as the radius where the Weber number based on local sheet thickness is unity. Earlier analysis by Taylor<sup>24</sup> showed that antisymmetric waves move at a speed of  $(2/We_j)^{1/2} U_s$ . Taylor<sup>23</sup> correctly noted that the developed sheet speed and the jet speed are the same. The position of antisymmetric waves on the sheet is defined by

$$\sin^2 \Psi = \frac{2\sigma}{\rho_l U_s^2 h} = \frac{2\rho r}{\rho_l U_s^2 F(\theta, \phi)} \quad (3)$$

where  $\Psi$  is the angle between the wave front and the radial vector from the impingement point. For directly opposed jets,  $2\theta = 180$  deg, the formed sheet is circular and the curves satisfying Eq. (3) are cardioid waves.<sup>23</sup>

Taylor<sup>23</sup> reasoned that the lateral spread of the sheet is due to the high pressure generated around an effective stagnation point and is related to the destruction of the momentum of the impinging jets directed toward each other. Taylor calculated the force required to induce the lateral spread,

$$\rho_l U_j^2 \int_0^\pi F(\theta, \phi) \sin \phi \, d\phi \quad (4)$$
