Four closed, teardrop-shaped curves are plotted, each corresponding to a different impingement angle 2θ: 180°, 140°, 100°, and 60°. The curves are nested, with the 180° curve being the widest and the 60° curve being the narrowest and most elongated towards the right.

**Fig. 2** Sheet shape predictions for water in air from the Taylor<sup>23</sup> model plotted as a function of impingement angle,  $2\theta$  with orifice diameter 0.51 mm and jet velocity 7.1 m/s.

and compared it with the force of impingement

$$\rho_l U_j^2 \sin \theta \int_0^\pi F(\theta, \phi) d\phi \quad (5)$$

and found that the ratio of the force required for lateral spread to the impingement force was a constant independent of impingement angle equal to about 0.65. For the case of directly opposed jets, the ratio is  $2/\pi$ , or 0.64. Results from Taylor's model for sheet geometry are shown in Fig. 2. Taylor's results were used by Hasson and Peck<sup>25</sup> to verify an analytically derived solution of the sheet thickness distribution:

$$h = \frac{d_j^2 \sin^3 \theta}{4r(1 - \cos \phi \cos \theta)^2} \quad (6)$$

Although it has been shown that Taylor's model for the formation of fan sheets by impinging jets and the resulting sheet shape is quite accurate for low Weber number conditions,<sup>26</sup> at higher Weber number conditions ( $We_j > 2,000$ ), where the flow condition can be either laminar or turbulent, there has been much less success in developing an accurate and comprehensive model. This is particularly true for the case where the impinging liquid fans are turbulent. Because the atomization process starts with the primary breakup of the fan sheet formed by the impinging liquid jets, attention has focused mostly on single liquid-gas interfaces, constant thickness liquid sheets, or two-dimensional liquid sheets. Theoretical studies of liquid sheet atomization include numerical simulations,<sup>27</sup> vortex sheet discretization analyses of Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities,<sup>28,29</sup> and linear stability theory-based analyses.<sup>30-36</sup>

The observed periodic nature of the breakup of both jets and sheets and the well-developed basis of linear stability theory has led to its extensive use in modeling

primary atomization for both cases. Linear stability theory is based on the linear growth of small disturbances that can grow due to a variety of sources.<sup>37</sup> For conditions typical of a practical atomizer, the driving force behind the growth of the disturbances on the liquid surface is usually taken to be the aerodynamic stress, which tends to be greater in trough regions and less in crest regions.<sup>38</sup>

In the two-dimensional analysis of liquid sheets, the displacement on the surface of the liquid sheet,  $\eta$ , is modeled as a periodic function of position and time:

$$\eta = A \exp[i(kx - \beta t)] \quad (7)$$

In the temporal theory, waves on the liquid surface with initial small amplitude  $\eta_0$  will grow exponentially according to

$$\eta/\eta_0 = e^{\beta_i t} \quad (8)$$

where  $\beta_i$  is the imaginary part of the complex growth rate factor  $\beta$ . Generally, the gas-liquid interface is regarded as inviscid, and  $\eta$  is calculated by solving the potential flow problem. In practice,  $\beta_i$  is calculated for a spectrum of wave numbers, and the sheet is assumed to take the shape of the fastest growing wave. Wave growth can occur through amplification of either sinuous (antisymmetric) or dilatational (symmetric) waves. Analyses have indicated that for high-speed sheets, sinuous waves always grow faster than dilatational waves.<sup>33</sup>

Squire<sup>33</sup> used this approach to analyze a constant thickness sheet. For high-sheet Weber numbers  $We_s$  and for disturbance wavelengths larger than the thickness of the sheet, he derived an equation for the fastest growing disturbance wavelength,  $\lambda_{\max}$ ,

$$\lambda_{\max} = \frac{2\pi}{k_{\max}} = \frac{4\pi\sigma}{\rho_g U_s^2} \quad (9)$$

and  $\lambda_{\max}$  had a displacement growth rate coefficient of

$$\beta_i = \frac{\rho_g U_s^2}{\sqrt{2}\rho_l h} \quad (10)$$

Thus, from Squire's analysis, the wavelength of the fastest growing disturbance is dependent only on the relative velocity between the gas and liquid for a given fluid combination, whereas  $\beta_i$  is dependent on relative velocity and sheet thickness. Squire<sup>33</sup> compared his analytical predictions of the fastest growing wavelength with apparent wavelengths measured from photographs of thin liquid films and found generally good agreement.

Taylor<sup>23</sup> also compared Squire's analysis to experimental results he obtained on the behavior of liquid sheets formed by impinging jets. He<sup>23</sup> approximated the three-dimensional sheet by considering only the center portion,  $\phi = 0$ , and calculated  $\beta_i$  from his measurements of the thickness distribution along that axis. He compared the predicted fastest growing wavelength to the wavelengths he observed through flash photography of the sheet and reported agreement to within 20%. This comparison was made for a sheet velocity of 5 m/s and was not validated over a range of velocities.

Dombrowski and Johns<sup>34</sup> used linear temporal stability theory to analyze the aerodynamic stress-induced amplification of surface perturbations on a thinning,

two-dimensional, viscous liquid sheet moving with a velocity  $U_s$  relative to the ambient medium. The general dispersion equation they derived in quadratic form is

$$\beta_{i,nd}^2 + \frac{(kh)^2}{Re_s} \beta_{i,nd} + 2s(kh)^2 \left( \frac{1}{sWe_s} - \frac{1}{kh} \right) = 0 \quad (11)$$

where

$$\beta_{i,nd} = \frac{\beta_i h}{U_s}, \quad Re_s = \frac{\rho_l U_s h}{\mu_l}, \quad We_s = \frac{\rho_l U_s^2 h}{\sigma}$$

The first term in Eq. (11) is associated with momentum in the displacement direction, the second term rises from viscous forces, and the first and second parts of the third term account for surface tension forces and aerodynamic forces, respectively.

It may be reasoned that spatial stability theory, i.e., where disturbances grow in space, should be used for these cases rather than the temporal theory, for which it is generally simpler to develop solutions. Chuech<sup>32</sup> compared results from temporal and spatial analyses of disturbances growing on a two-dimensional liquid sheet by using an inertial frame of reference and determined that, for large-sheet Weber numbers,  $We_s > 100$ , the temporal and spatial theories give essentially the same results. At lower sheet Weber numbers, discrepancies start to appear between the two models.

The linear stability theory in itself is not able to predict when the sheet breaks up. Empirical observations of sheet breakup have led to the use of a generally accepted breakup constant to use in conjunction with linear stability theory to predict when breakup occurs<sup>39</sup>:

$$\int_0^{t_b} \beta_{i,m} dt = \int_0^{x_b} \frac{\beta_{i,m}}{U_s} dx = 12 \quad (12)$$

Using this approach, Dombrowski and Johns<sup>34</sup> envisioned the sheet to fragment into ligaments at crest and trough points. The ligaments then contract into cylinders with diameter  $d_L$  given as

$$d_L = \sqrt{4h/k} \quad (13)$$

A second-order relation for the breakup of sheets formed by fan and swirl nozzles was derived by Clark and Dombrowski<sup>40</sup> where the combined growth of sinuous and dilatational modes were considered. Their analysis indicated that the sheet would break at points corresponding to three-eighths and seven-eighths of the fundamental sinuous wavelength.

Further atomization into spherical drops is modeled as a surface tension-controlled mechanism,<sup>34</sup> where dilatational waves grow on the surface of the cylindrical ligament and one drop is formed per wavelength. For water in air,

$$d_D = \left( \frac{3\pi}{\sqrt{2}} \right)^{1/3} d_L \left\{ 1 + \frac{3\mu}{(\rho_l \sigma d_L)^{1/2}} \right\}^{1/6} \approx 1.89 d_L \quad (14)$$

Anderson et al.<sup>3</sup> presented numerically computed solutions to Eq. (11) for the case of orifice diameter equal to 0.64 mm, impingement angle varying from 20

to 100 deg, and jet velocities ranging from 10 to 25 m/s. Following Taylor,<sup>23</sup> Anderson et al.<sup>3</sup> computed growth rates for wave numbers from 0 to 10 mm<sup>-1</sup> at the centerline of the liquid sheet,  $\phi = 0$  deg, where the sheet is thickest. Sheet thickness on the jet axis was calculated using Eq. (6). Temporal growth rates were integrated, and sheet breakup was considered to occur at the first point where the value of the integral in Eq. (12) exceeded 12. The fastest growing wavelength  $\lambda_{\max}$  was also computed in this way. Drop size was calculated using Eq. (14).

Ryan et al.<sup>26</sup> compared the analysis for viscous, thinning sheets developed by Dombrowski and Johns<sup>34</sup> with Squire's analysis<sup>35</sup> of inviscid constant thickness sheets for water jets injected into atmospheric pressure air, which comprises the experimental conditions most commonly employed. Ryan et al.<sup>26</sup> showed that under these conditions Squire's simpler expression for the most unstable wave number, Eq. (9), results in less than 1% deviation from the most unstable wave number calculated using the dispersion equation of Dombrowski and Johns,<sup>34</sup> Eq. (11). Under these conditions of large sheet Weber numbers and low-pressure ratio  $s$ , Ryan et al.<sup>26</sup> showed that the growth rate factor of the most unstable wave number  $\beta_{i,\max}$ , computed using Squire's expression Eq. (10), is essentially the same as that obtained from using Eq. (11). Using the inviscid expressions of Squire<sup>33</sup> for the fastest growing disturbance and growth rate factor [Eqs. (9) and (10)], and Eq. (6) for sheet shape, Ryan et al.<sup>26</sup> identified a nondimensional scaling parameter based on the jet Weber number,  $We_j = \rho_j U_j^2 d_o / \sigma$ , and the half-impingement angle  $\theta$ ;  $We_j (1 - \cos \theta)^2 / \sin^3 \theta$ . Use of this parameter collapses the theoretical dependence of  $x_b$ ,  $\lambda_{\max}$ , and  $d_p$  on orifice diameter, impingement angle, and velocity into a single curve only dependent on the scaling parameter. Results from the model are shown in Fig. 3, where nondimensional lengths, normalized by the orifice diameter  $d_o$ , are plotted against the geometrically scaled jet Weber number.

The persistent use of the aerodynamic instability theory in modeling the atomization of impinging liquid jets may be related to the theory's ability to provide predictions of drop size that fairly match experimental measurements of drop size. Ibrahim and Przekwas<sup>36</sup> compared predicted drop-size using an aerodynamic instability theory with empirical correlations for drop size generated by impinging liquid jets, in which the mass median drop size was approximately proportional to the square root of the orifice diameter and approximately inversely proportional to the inverse of the sheet velocity, which can be shown to be similar to the analytical development for drop size shown earlier in Eqs. (9), (11), and (13). Direct comparisons between results of the linear theory and measured drop size have also been made that show reasonable agreement.<sup>3,26</sup>

The reduction in breakup length  $x_b$  with increasing sheet velocity also agrees with empirical data on liquid sheets formed by swirl or fan nozzles, which tend to show a  $U_s^{-2/3}$  dependency<sup>41</sup> to  $U_s^{-2}$  dependency.<sup>42</sup> The velocity dependence of the breakup length at  $We_j > 500$  predicted by linear stability-based theory, however, does not agree with the results reported by Heidmann et al.,<sup>21</sup> Huang,<sup>22</sup> or more current results obtained by Ryan et al.<sup>26</sup> The inability of the theory to represent the observed trends with respect to breakup length is consistent with the results of Dombrowski and Hooper<sup>4</sup> who suggested that impact wave effects and not aerodynamic force effects controlled sheet breakup for high velocity, turbulent impinging jet conditions. Dombrowski and Hooper<sup>4</sup> did argue, however, that breakup length should decrease with increasing jet velocity for both aerodynamic instability and impact wave mechanisms, although their measurements presented did not support this contention.

### III. Experimental Measurements

#### A. Description of Experiments

A series of experiments have recently been undertaken to clarify the mechanism of impinging jet atomization.<sup>26</sup> The impinging jet injector apparatus was similar to that used by Heidmann et al.<sup>21</sup> and Dombrowski and Hooper.<sup>4</sup> Precision bore glass tubes were used as injectors because they allow visual inspection of the liquid within the tube and ensure that surface roughness is not a factor. Water flow through the glass tubes was driven by a nitrogen pressurized water tank. Individual rotameters were used to monitor the flow rate, and pressure gauges were used to measure the pressure drop across each glass tube. The impinging jet apparatus allowed for substitution of different diameter and length glass tubes as well as variation of impingement angle and preimpingement length and was based on optical mounts so that the tubes could be positioned such that the jets impinged precisely.

The impinging jets studied were formed with either 0.64-mm or 1.45-mm inner diameter glass tubes. In either case, the length of the glass tubes was 51 mm, which corresponds to  $L/d_o$  ratios of 80 and 35, respectively. A shorter  $L/d_o$  of 5 was also tested for the smaller inner diameter (0.64-mm) tube. The  $L/d_o$  ratios tested here, with the exception of the  $L/d_o = 5$  case, are an order of magnitude greater than those used in actual rockets. The glass tubes used in the current set of experiments were attached to 6-mm outer diameter stainless-steel tubes with Swagelok fittings. The ratio of the inlet diameter to the glass tube diameter was approximately five, and the glass tube inlet orifice had either a sharp edge or a

contour to allow the flow to remain laminar into a Reynolds number regime that typically produced turbulent flow.

The impinging jets were studied by image analysis and drop size/velocity measurements over a wide range of parameters. The 0.64-mm inner diameter ( $L/d_o = 80$ ) tube at an impingement angle of 60 deg and a preimpingement length of 25 mm was used as the base case. The impingement angles ( $2\theta$ ) tested ranged from 40 to 100 deg in intervals of 20 deg. The preimpingement lengths were 2.5, 25, and 38 mm. At each of these conditions, the impinging jet sprays were studied at discrete velocities ranging from roughly 5 to 25 m/s.

Studies of high-velocity jets issuing from short  $L/d_o$  injectors must consider the potential for cavitation within the injector. Although no visual effects of cavitation were observed for the majority of the flow conditions tested here, the cavitation number for each flow condition was calculated and compared with Nurick's<sup>12</sup> critical cavitation number. Nurick<sup>12</sup> studied cavitation phenomena in short  $L/d_o$  (2–20) sharp-edged orifices with orifice diameters ranging from 1.52 mm to 3.18 mm. The cavitation number is defined as the ratio of the upstream pressure minus the vapor pressure of the fluid to the pressure drop across the orifice. Nurick<sup>12</sup> observed that for an  $L/d_o$  of 20 ( $d_o = 3.18$  mm), cavitation occurred for cavitation numbers below 1.45. For the present case of an  $L/d_o$  of 80 ( $D = 0.64$  mm), the cavitation number was between 1.1 and 1.4, and no gross cavitation effects were observed. Note that Nurick did not present data for  $L/d_o$  ratios longer than 20 but did observe that the critical cavitation number for the onset of cavitation does decrease for increasing  $L/d_o$  ratios.<sup>12</sup> Cavitation was observed for the  $L/d_o = 5$ ,  $d_o = 0.64$ -mm glass tube at high velocities ( $U_j > 25$  m/s). At this case, the cavitation number was 1.3 and was lower than the critical cavitation number of 1.8 observed by Nurick<sup>12</sup> for an  $L/d_o$ ,  $d_o = 3.18$  mm.

Drop size and velocity measurements were made using an argon-ion laser ( $\lambda = 514.5$  nm) based fast Fourier transform (FFT) version of a phase-Doppler particle analyzer (PDPA) manufactured by Aerometrics, Inc. The theory behind the operation of the PDPA has been discussed extensively in the literature,<sup>43</sup> thus, only a few details concerning the system will be given here. For the present experiments, the collection optics module was oriented 30 deg off axis from the forward propagation direction of the laser beam, which is the best angle for measuring transparent drops.<sup>43</sup> The transmitting and collection optics defined a drop diameter measurement range between 40 and 1400  $\mu\text{m}$ , the maximum range capable with the present system.

Drop size/drop velocity measurements at all parametric conditions were made at two locations downstream of the impingement point, 16 and 41 mm. At each downstream measurement location, drop size/drop velocity measurements were made at 6.4-mm intervals in the plane of the sheet along the line normal to the central axis of the sheet. Lefebvre<sup>44</sup> suggests that at least 5500 data points are necessary for  $\pm 5\%$  accuracy in mean diameter measurements; consequently, 8000 drops were typically taken for the calculation of the various mean diameters.

A charge injection device (CID) solid-state camera with a resolution of  $512 \times 512$  pixels was used to obtain digitized images of the spray field resulting from the two impinging jets. Instantaneous images of the flowfield were obtained using a strobe light with a time duration of  $10 \mu\text{s}$  oriented to provide diffuse back lighting and high contrast. At each flow condition 17 images were recorded, and

the length and width of the intact liquid sheets were measured from the digitized spray images. Standard deviations were calculated for each set of length and width measurements and are reported with the results. Following Heidmann et al.,<sup>21</sup> the length of the sheet was taken from the impingement point to the point where the sheet broke into drops, ligaments, or sheet vestiges. The width was defined as the maximum width of the complete sheet. It is noted that some photographs had cavity-like structures on the periphery of the sheet and that the width was measured upstream of this cavity. It is not clear how Heidmann et al.<sup>21</sup> defined the width of the sheet and, therefore, some ambiguity in definition probably exists between their sheet width results and the current results.

The three limiting cases of fully developed laminar jet flow, fully developed turbulent jet flow, and "plug" jet flow were studied. These cases were chosen because of their well-characterized velocity and turbulence intensity profiles. Absolute plug flow conditions were not obtained but were approached by using orifices with the short length-to-diameter ratio ( $L/d_o = 5$ ). The short  $L/d_o$  orifices did not produce nonturbulent flow as a thin orifice would, and the short orifices were operated either in the laminar or turbulent flow regime. In addition to changing flow condition and  $L/d_o$ , other test parameters included impingement angle  $2\theta$ , orifice diameter  $d_o$ , and freejet length prior to impingement  $l_j$ . Measurements of breakup length, drop size and drop velocity distribution, and periodic wave structures are discussed subsequently.

#### B. Effect of Flow Condition

The flow condition of the jet before impingement, i.e., whether it was laminar or turbulent, had the major effect on atomization. To illustrate the importance of the initial conditions of the liquid jet, consider the instantaneous images of the sheets formed by laminar and turbulent jets impinging at full impingement angle  $2\theta$  of 60 deg shown in Fig. 4 taken under quiescent conditions and at atmospheric pressure. The resultant sheets have distinct characteristics. In the laminar case, Fig. 4a, small but prominent ripples on the surface of the sheet are seen just downstream of the impingement point, and after some distance the sheet suddenly disintegrates into droplets. Small and regular waves can be seen in the outer periphery of the liquid sheet. In many of the images of laminar impinging jets, incipient breakup occurred at midspan of the sheet, downstream of the impact waves. Drops are also seen shedding off the leading edge of the sheet. All of these observations are consistent with those made by Heidmann et al.<sup>21</sup> and Dombrowski and Hooper.<sup>4</sup>

In the turbulent case, Fig. 4b, the amplitude of the waves that appear at impact seem much larger than in the laminar case. (Note that the scale in Fig. 4b is about three times greater than that of Fig. 4a.) Downstream, the sheet disintegrates into ligaments, with incipient breakup consistently occurring at the sheet periphery, where the sheet thickness is least. Periodicity is indicated by the regular spacing between disturbances on the liquid sheet and by the regular spacing between the detached ligaments. Examination of the detached liquid structures reveals irregular liquid shapes that contract into roughly cylindrical ligaments. The cylindrical ligaments appear to contract further into irregularly shaped drops that will eventually take a nearly spherical shape. From these images, it is reasonable to model the ligament-to-droplet formation process as being controlled by surface tension-driven instabilities, as given by Eq. (14).

#### C. Breakup Length

Length measurements of the intact sheet and of periodic structures were made from images such as those shown in Fig. 4. Nondimensional breakup length of sheet formed by impinging water jets from precision bore glass tubes,  $x_b/d_o$ , is plotted against jet Weber number in Fig. 5 for laminar and turbulent impinging jet cases. Clear differences between the two cases can be seen. The nondimensional breakup length of the turbulent impinging jets appears to have some dependence on impingement angle but appears to be relatively independent of jet Weber number. There is a strong dependence on jet Weber number for the laminar impinging jet case, and the general dependence of  $x_b$  on jet Weber number is consistent with that reported by Huang.<sup>22</sup> It is also interesting that the breakup length dependence on impingement angle for turbulent impinging jets is opposite that for laminar impinging jets.

Comparisons of the measured nondimensional breakup length with predictions from the aerodynamic instability model used by Ryan et al.<sup>26</sup> are shown in Fig. 6. Again the differences between the turbulent impinging jet case and the laminar impinging jet case are evident. Laminar impinging jet breakup may be modeled relatively well by a combination of Taylor's model<sup>23</sup> at low jet Weber number and by the aerodynamic instability model at higher jet Weber number, but again the turbulent impinging jet breakup mean shows little dependence on the geometrically scaled jet Weber number, and the conclusion may be made that the aerodynamic instability model is not accounting for an important physical process.

#### D. Drop Size Distribution

Measurements of nondimensional arithmetic mean drop diameters are presented in Fig. 7 for the turbulent impinging jet case. The arithmetic mean drop diameter is used instead of the Sauter mean diameter because the few large drops present in the distribution drastically skews the Sauter mean diameter distribution toward large sizes. A comparison of measured mean drop size with the monodisperse drop size predicted by the aerodynamic instability model is also shown. It should be noted that the measurements using the PDPA instrument yield a mean value for the drop size distribution, whereas the theory effectively assumes that a monodispersed spray is formed. The model predictions match the experimental trend quite well and, as the model predicts, the measurements nearly collapse to a single curve when plotted against the geometrically scaled jet Weber number. An empirical correlation for normalized drop size as a function of the geometrically scaled jet Weber number  $We_j f(\theta)$  was obtained from the experimental data shown in Fig. 7 with a correlation coefficient of 0.964,

$$\frac{dD}{d_o} = 2.217 \cdot \{We_j f(\theta)\}^{-0.354} \quad (15)$$

Drop size measurements were also obtained away from the centerline of the spray to assess the effect of the variation of the sheet thickness on drop size. The variation in the sheet thickness  $h$  with  $\phi$  is represented in Eq. (6) through the  $\cos \phi$  dependence. The results for drop size measured by PDPA shown in Fig. 8 for impinging water jets injected into air have, therefore, been plotted as a function of  $\phi$  for two orifice diameters, the 18.5 m/s jet velocity condition, various impingement angles, and two different downstream locations from the impingement point,  $x = 16$  mm and  $x = 41$  mm. As these results illustrate, for the two lower impingement angles, the measured arithmetic mean drop size decreases slightly as the absolute value of  $\phi$  increases. This trend qualitatively agrees with results of Couto and Bastos-Netto,<sup>45</sup> who applied Eq. (6) to derive the drop size distribution dependence on  $\phi$ . At the two highest impingement angles, however, no discernable decrease in  $D_{10}$  is observed with changes in  $\phi$ , although analysis of Couto and Bastos-Netto<sup>45</sup> indicated that, for  $\phi = 45$  deg, approximately a 30% reduction in drop size should be observed at an impingement angle of  $2\theta = 90$  deg. These results suggest either that the expression for sheet thickness given by Eq. (6) is incorrect, particularly for higher impingement angles, or that the assumption that the sheet breaks up at a constant radial distance from the impingement point is incorrect.

PDPA measured mean drop velocities along the sheet centerline taken at  $x = 16$  mm and  $x = 41$  mm downstream of the impingement point are shown in Fig. 9 for the  $d_o = 1.45$ -mm and  $d_o = 0.64$ -mm diam jets from precision bore glass tubes and for a variety of impingement angles. From the drop velocity measurements, it is seen that the sheet retains nearly all of the dynamic head of the jet before impingement, although a slight reduction in drop velocity with increasing impingement angle can be seen, which may be due to more deceleration resulting from drag on the smaller droplets that are formed at higher impingement angles and/or to less efficient dynamic pressure recovery at higher impingement angles.

###### IMPINGING JET INJECTOR ATOMIZATION

233

#### E. Atomization Frequency

The measured distance normalized by orifice diameter of the separation between periodic structures for turbulent impinging jets is shown in Fig. 10 as a function of jet velocity. The wavelength appears to be primarily dependent on orifice diameter and independent of jet velocity. The observation of independence from jet velocity is contrary to the aerodynamic instability model predictions. The distance between detached ligaments is approximately constant at about four orifice diameters, and the distance between surface wave structures is approximately constant at about two orifice diameters. There was a rather large spread in the data, with a standard deviation of about  $\pm 35\%$ .

The wavelength data was converted to atomization frequency simply by dividing the drop velocity (which was approximated as the initial jet velocity) by the measured wavelength. Atomization frequency data is presented in Fig. 11 based on ligament spacing. Also shown are wave frequency data from experiments of Heidmann

Variations in the preimpingement length of turbulent jets were also studied in terms of its effects on sheet shape at breakup and drop size. As the impingement length of the jet increases, the effects of velocity profile relaxation and of any misalignment will become greater, as will the effects of any growing disturbances on the jets. Preimpingement length was varied from 4 to 60 orifice diameters; the highest values of preimpingement length should have allowed the jet velocity profile to become nearly flat. The visual appearance of the spray structure was sensitive to the preimpingement length, particularly in terms of the breakup length. Breakup length and sheet width measurements for the various preimpingement lengths tested are shown in Fig. 14. Again, orifice diameter of precision bore glass tubes was 0.64 mm and impingement angle  $2\theta$  was 60 deg. The results show that the effect of the preimpingement length decreases with increasing jet velocity. Increased preimpingement length favors longer breakup lengths and slightly narrower liquid sheets. Figure 15 shows drop size PDPA

filters, manifolds, metering orifices, and other flow channels which produce pressure drop and fluid particle rotation. Typically, the jets are analyzed as though they are irrotational; clearly, however, there is a significant amount of vorticity distributed throughout the fluid. Another important observation is the relatively short distances the fluid travels within the orifice and after it exits the orifice on its way to the impingement point. These distances, less than 10 orifice diameters, are insufficient to produce a developed flowfield. Requisite entry length/diameter ratios for developed flows can be estimated for  $Re = 10^5$  anywhere from 12 (Ref. 48) to 2800 (Ref. 49). Engineering rule of thumb estimates place entry lengths at  $L/d_o = 75$ . At any rate, the jet flow at the orifice exit is not developed, and this must be taken into account in theoretical developments as well as in experimental design. The final important point regarding real injector designs is that the entrance to the orifice is usually sharp and that cost considerations related to manufacturing typically preclude rigorous specification of surface roughness

or inlet contour. Since the effects of contour and roughness cannot be predicted with any confidence, the design engineer is hesitant to stipulate specific tolerances even though there is circumstantial evidence in real engine combustors that roughness and contour can effect performance and stability. Studies of orifice geometry effects on jet atomization<sup>50,51</sup> indicated that surface roughness, inlet contour, and orifice  $L/d_o$  all had a major effect on the atomization characteristics. These results do not appear to be consistent with results from impinging jet injectors just presented. Even though the results presented cover a relatively small range of geometric parameters, and only approached the very short  $L/d_o$  and  $l_j/d_o$  geometries used in practical injectors, they provide some evidence regarding the fundamental differences between atomization processes of plain jets and impinging jets.

#### B. Primary Atomization Mechanisms

It is clear from the results of Taylor<sup>23</sup> and Huang,<sup>22</sup> for example, that the breakup mechanism of impinging liquid jets at ambient atmospheric pressure and low jet Weber ( $We_j < 500$ ) conditions is related to a balance between the liquid's inertial force pushing liquid outward and the liquid's cohesive forces that try to maintain the integrity of the sheet. For sheets formed by laminar jets at higher Weber number conditions, atomization may possibly be described by aerodynamic instability theory. For turbulent flow conditions representative of practical injectors, however, the situation is much more complicated. Comparison between experimental results at these conditions and predictions from the theory clearly indicate that there are important physical processes that are not being correctly treated.

The experimental results presented are all consistent with the conclusion by Dombrowski and Hooper<sup>4</sup> that impact waves control the breakup process of impinging liquid jets, although their contention regarding the effects of jet velocity profile on impact wave damping must still be regarded as conjecture. To understand the breakup mechanism, it is necessary to define the source of the impact waves that are reasoned here to be due to fluctuations of pressure and/or momentum at or near the impingement point. It would appear that these fluctuations are either due to disturbances existing within the jet prior to impingement, e.g., turbulence or jet instabilities, or are generated at the impingement point by jet-jet interactions, such as periodic movement about a mean stagnation point, which is a known feature of stagnation point flow.<sup>52</sup>

Although the immediate area of interest is breakup of turbulent jets because practical injector systems produce turbulent jets, a comparison between laminar and turbulent impinging jets may again serve some purpose in clarifying the source of impact waves, or at least help in identifying the appropriate steps that must be taken to resolve the issue. Recall that Dombrowski and Hooper<sup>4</sup> made no distinction between the source of impact waves that appeared on sheets formed either by high-velocity laminar impinging jets or by turbulent impinging jets but concluded that their appearance was due to velocity profile differences, i.e., the slow moving fluid near the outer radius of the laminar jet damped impact waves, whereas the turbulent jets with their "slug flow" profile provided less damping. More evidence regarding these effects could have been obtained by testing impinging laminar jets with flat distribution profiles acquired by using either thin orifices or long preimpingement lengths.

Results shown in Fig. 5 show the very significant differences in breakup length between laminar impinging jets and turbulent impinging jets. To more directly

address the issue of impact wave formation, measurements of the distance between disturbances on the intact sheet and between adjacent detached ligaments were made for the laminar impinging jet case and compared to the data shown in Fig. 10 for turbulent impinging jets. Consistent measurements of wavelength were attainable only for laminar impinging jets with injection velocities greater than about 15 m/s. For laminar impinging jets, where  $U_j = 17.9$  m/s,  $d_o = 0.51$  mm, and  $2\theta = 60$  deg, the measured mean normalized wavelengths  $\lambda/d_o$  on the intact sheet and between adjacent ligaments were  $4.0 \pm 0.3$  and  $5.5 \pm 0.5$ , respectively. These numbers compare well with the detached ligament normalized mean wavelength measured for turbulent impinging jets, which ranged between 3.5 and 5.5. Normalized mean surface wavelengths were on the order of two for turbulent impinging jets.

To evaluate the possibility that disturbances existing on the preimpingement jets are sources of impact waves, it is useful to consider the notion that the disturbances leading to the generation of impact waves and subsequent breakup of impinging jets are essentially the same disturbances that lead to breakup in single jets. An excellent review in this area is provided by McCarthy and Molloy,<sup>53</sup> with some more recent work specifically oriented to the highly dynamic operating conditions of atomization provided by Reitz and Bracco<sup>51</sup> and Wu et al.<sup>54</sup> Reitz and Bracco<sup>51</sup> considered the effects of aerodynamically induced liquid surface disturbance growth, instabilities due to velocity profile relaxation, cavitation, and turbulence as potential mechanisms that control the breakup process of single jets. Reitz and Bracco<sup>51</sup> concluded that the aerodynamic instability model was capable of predicting many of the trends they observed, and they developed a physical model of the breakup process whereby disturbances on the surface of the liquid jet, which are present when the jet emerges from the orifice due to events occurring upstream of the orifice exit, are amplified selectively by aerodynamic forces. The view of single jet atomization that Reitz and Bracco<sup>51</sup> provided was that as the amplitude of these periodic disturbances grew to the same order of magnitude as their wavelength, a drop would be ejected off the liquid surface. The view of Wu et al.<sup>54</sup> of primary atomization was based on turbulence in the liquid, i.e., that large eddies with sufficient energy to penetrate through the liquid surface were the source of drops. In light of the observed similarity between the disturbances on sheets formed by the impinging high-speed laminar jets and impinging turbulent jets, there should be some doubt that turbulence plays the dominant role in the generation of impact waves. The comparison, however, was made only at one condition and should be made over a significant range of conditions before any definite statement related to the role turbulence plays in impact wave generation can be made.

To evaluate the possibility of aerodynamically induced jet instability as a contributing factor, the characteristics of growing disturbances on the freejet surface were calculated. Both long waves ( $kd_j < 2$ ) and short waves ( $kd_j > 2$ ) can grow on the jet.<sup>38</sup> The wavelength of the fastest growing short wave is dependent on relative velocity,

$$\lambda_{\max} = 3\pi\sigma/\rho_g U_j^2 \quad (16)$$

with a growth rate coefficient of

$$\beta_i = 0.4\rho_g U_j^3 \sqrt{s/\sigma} \quad (17)$$

The equation relating the growth rate of long waves on the jet was also derived by Levich<sup>38</sup>

$$\beta_i \sqrt{\frac{\sigma k^2}{2\rho_l r_j} (1 - s^2 - k^2 r_j^2) - \frac{\rho_g k^4 r_j^2 U_j^2 [\ln(kr_j/2)]}{2\rho_l}} \quad (18)$$

In Eq. (18)  $s$  indicates the jet instability mode, where  $s = 0$  for symmetrical long waves and  $s = 1$  for helical long waves. For a 2-mm diam water jet in air traveling at 10 m/s, a plot of Eq. (18) reveals that the fastest growing symmetrical long wave would have a wavelength 3 times the jet diameter, and the fastest growing helical long wave would have a wavelength 4.2 times the jet diameter.

For sufficiently high velocities where the term containing  $U_j$  is much greater than the surface tension term, it can be shown<sup>38</sup> that the length of the fastest growing long wave (regardless of the instability mode) is dependent only on jet diameter,

$$\lambda_{\max} \approx 2d_j \quad (19)$$

and the wave has a growth rate coefficient of

$$\beta_i = U_j \sqrt{s}/d_j \quad (20)$$

The ratio of Eq. (17) to Eq. (20), which is the relative growth rate of short waves to long waves for high velocity jets, is essentially the gas Weber number,  $We_g = \rho_g U^2 d_j / \sigma$ . For the case of a 0.5-mm-diam water jet injected into air,  $We_g = 1$  occurs at a velocity of about 4 m/s. Assuming a phase speed equal to the jet velocity and an impingement length of five orifice diameters, a disturbance on 0.5-mm-diam jet with an injection velocity of 20 m/s would grow by about 20%. It should be noted that since a long wave contains much more mass than does a short wave, a long wave disturbance produces a larger impact wave. It is also interesting to note that the measured detached ligament wavelengths shown in Fig. 10 for turbulent impinging jets and the surface disturbance and detached ligament wavelengths already described for the laminar impinging jet case are both similar to the long wavelength predicted by the Levich<sup>38</sup> theory, i.e., disturbance wavelengths around 2–4 times the jet diameter. Although the linear stability analysis for disturbance growth on jets is strictly applicable for laminar flows, stability theory has also been successfully applied to the growth of wavelike structures in turbulent flows.<sup>55,56</sup>

#### C. Relation of Primary Atomization to Combustion Instability

Given that the breakup periodicity of impinging liquid jets is quite similar to high-frequency combustion instability as shown in Fig. 11, the detailed mechanism of how the process couples with pressure oscillations to modify atomization frequency and generate the requisite interelement coherence across the chamber is still missing. In Levine's remarkable photographic study of LOX/ethanol combustion using impinging jet atomizers, he<sup>18</sup> reported large-scale liquid fan and liquid jet shattering during an actual combustion instability event. Most published investigations of this phenomena used high-amplitude acoustic sources to provide an acoustic field. Longitudinal waves in chambers have been shown to induce periodic jet shortening and droplet formation with frequencies coupled to the sound source.<sup>57,58</sup> Experiments by Miesse<sup>57</sup> with localized high-intensity sound fields

oriented transverse to laminar liquid jets ( $10 < L/d_o < 40$ ) indicated the acoustic field caused the droplets to disperse in a diverging sinusoidal fashion. Miesse<sup>57</sup> reported that the maximum dispersion of the jet occurred when the frequency of the sound was the natural frequency of the jet,  $f_j$ , which he determined empirically to have the approximate form  $f_j \sim 0.03U_j/d_o$  over a frequency range of 10–200 Hz. The periodic effects were observed to decrease with increasing acoustic frequency and jet velocity. This frequency dependence on jet velocity and orifice diameter is the same as that shown in Fig. 10, albeit with frequencies about 3–6 times lower than those shown in Fig. 10. Experiments with three parallel liquid jets in the same cylindrical enclosure used for the longitudinal mode oscillations indicated that the jets were relatively unaffected by radial and tangential mode oscillations; this was considered to be at least in part due to the frequency of the transverse modes, which were not reported. Oscillatory jet displacement from the mean impingement point could also lead to an oscillatory inertial force at the impingement point to generate impact waves.

Buffum and Williams<sup>59</sup> studied turbulent jets in an acoustic field and reported the same sort of sinuous behavior observed by Miesse.<sup>57</sup> An analysis of the jet displacement revealed that the drag coefficient on the liquid jet was three times greater than expected based on solid body data. Tests in which the injector unit was mechanically vibrated demonstrated<sup>60</sup> that periodic intermittencies in a liquid stream and periodic droplet formation could be induced at frequencies up to 4500 Hz using a water jet from a 1.2-mm-diam orifice at velocities up to about 30 m/s. This frequency is very much in line with the atomization frequencies shown in Fig. 10. Thus, there is a significant amount of experimental evidence that supports the theory that acoustically or mechanically forced periodicity of the atomization process may be a driving mechanism to sustain combustion pressure oscillations in a rocket engine. It is natural to expect that acoustic waves can also interact with liquid sheet breakup. In the attempts of Heidmann et al.<sup>21</sup> to show an effect, however, no coupling was evident.

### V. Summary and Conclusions

In summary, experiments contrasting laminar and turbulent impinging jet conditions clearly demonstrate that the jet conditions have a dramatic effect on the atomization process of impinging liquid jets. Specifically, the measured breakup lengths for laminar impinging jets are longer and displayed different trends as a function of jet velocity and impingement angle than those for turbulent impinging jets. In addition, the measured spray width for the turbulent impinging jet case remained approximately constant as a function of jet velocity and impingement angle for a fixed orifice diameter, unlike the laminar impinging jet case. The present results are in agreement with results of earlier studies at atmospheric pressure by Dombrowski and Hooper,<sup>4</sup> who speculated that these differences arose mainly from differences in velocity profiles between laminar jets and turbulent jets and the way that the impact waves were damped. The important question remains, however, of how the impact waves, which determine the breakup characteristics of turbulent impinging jets, are formed in the first place. It appears likely that the source of the impact waves are large pressure and momentum fluctuations that are either accentuated near the impingement point or are a direct result of the impingement. A quantitative assessment of the specific mechanisms controlling atomization remains to be established.

Comparisons of experimental results at atmospheric pressure with results from a linear stability-based theory indicates the use of the aerodynamic instability model for describing the breakup of a sheet formed by turbulent impinging jets appears to be incorrect, at least for atmospheric conditions. The model predicted a monotonically decreasing sheet breakup length with increasing Weber number and a strong dependence of disturbance wavelength on sheet velocity, neither of which were apparent from experimental measurements. It is interesting, however, that the aerodynamic instability model does produce results that match experimentally measured mean drop size quite well.

Variations in the preimpingement length have a measurable influence on the breakup length and drop size. Although these effects are small, they can be associated with the state of the liquid jet prior to impingement. Application of linear stability theory to single liquid jets indicated that long wavelength disturbances are similar to measured disturbances on sheets formed by impinging jets in terms of their magnitude and linear dependence on jet diameter. However, the magnitude of these variations appear to be insufficient to explain the observed difference in breakup length. Measurement of surface wave and periodic ligament formation phenomena for turbulent impinging jets indicates that the observed wavelengths are directly proportional to the orifice diameter and independent of jet velocity and impingement angle. The relationship between the periodic wave and ligament structures observed in these studies needs to be considered in light of their potential to initiate and sustain combustion instability phenomena associated with impinging jet rocket engine injectors. At any rate, combustion instability models should include the effects of the time-dependent nature of atomization, as well as the effects of a realistic distribution of drop sizes.

Based on the results of the studies presented in this chapter, approaches to modeling impinging jet atomization should focus on preimpingement jet conditions and the physics near the jet impingement point, specifically the source of the observed impact waves that appear to control turbulent impinging jet breakup. No current models address these phenomena. Experimentation at higher ambient pressures must be performed to better evaluate aerodynamic effects under conditions comparable to rocket engine environments. More quantitative theories based on the impact wave mechanism are needed for comparison with experimental results.

### I. Introduction

PRIMARY and secondary breakup are important classical multiphase flow problems that have motivated numerous past studies. Primary breakup involves the initial formation of drops and other liquid fragments at the surface of a liquid. Primary breakup is important because it controls the initial dispersion of liquid into the gas phase and, through the strong effect of drop sizes on interphase transport rates, the subsequent mixing properties of sprays. Secondary breakup involves any subsequent breakup of drops or liquid fragments present as dispersed liquids. Secondary breakup is important because drops after primary breakup are intrinsically unstable to secondary breakup, which affects subsequent mixing rates by influencing drop sizes as well. In addition, effects of liquid heating or acceleration of the gas phase can lead to conditions where drops undergo secondary breakup. In spite of their importance, however, current understanding of primary and secondary breakup is limited due to problems of making measurements within

dense dispersions of drops. In particular, measurements of primary breakup involve observations near an undulating liquid surface having protruding ligaments, and frequently generating irregular liquid fragments, which prevents the use of methods convenient for spherical drop fields such as Fraunhofer diffraction and phase Doppler anemometry.<sup>1,2</sup> Additionally, secondary breakup involves the individual drop generating a relatively localized drop field that is not convenient to characterize using line-of-sight or single-point measurements. Recent development of pulsed holography techniques for measurements within dense sprays, however, has provided an alternative experimental approach that has removed some of the experimental limitations.<sup>1,2</sup> Thus, the objective of this chapter is to briefly describe what has been learned about primary and secondary breakup using pulsed holography thus far and to highlight aspects of these phenomena that merit more attention in the future.

Harrje and Reardon<sup>3</sup> review early work on primary and secondary breakup as related to the problem of liquid rocket engine combustion and combustion instability. Other more general reviews of aspects of liquid atomization processes are available as well.<sup>4-9</sup> This chapter will focus specifically on the properties of primary and secondary breakup disclosed by pulsed holography measurements that are not treated in these earlier reviews. The studies of primary breakup focused on breakup along the surfaces of round liquid jets in still gases, whereas the studies of secondary breakup were limited to simple shock-wave disturbances. Thus, the findings do not directly address the complexities of most practical atomization processes. In particular, many instances of primary breakup involve thin liquid sheets, interacting with gas flows having a range of relative velocities, which will not be considered here. Furthermore, practical processes of secondary breakup in sprays often involve gradual variations of disturbances imposed on drops, which will not be addressed as well. Nevertheless, primary breakup of relatively deep liquids, along the surface of round liquid jets, and secondary breakup following shock-wave disturbances, are classical liquid breakup problems that provide well-defined experimental conditions which help to simplify the interpretation of measurements. References 3-9 should be consulted for an introduction to the more extensive literature concerning general processes of primary and secondary breakup.

Some aspects of secondary breakup affect primary breakup; in particular, conditions can be encountered where processes of primary and secondary breakup overlap or merge. Thus, secondary breakup is considered before primary breakup in the following. The discussion is brief, see Refs. 8-15 for additional details.

### II. Secondary Breakup

#### A. Introduction

Because of numerous applications, secondary breakup has received significant attention in the past. Early work in the field is reviewed by Harrje and Reardon,<sup>3</sup> Giffen and Muraszew,<sup>4</sup> Clift et al.,<sup>5</sup> and Hinze<sup>16</sup>; therefore, the following discussion will be limited to more recent studies. The definition of the onset of secondary breakup, secondary breakup dynamics, and the outcome of secondary breakup will be considered in turn.

Most earlier work on secondary breakup has at least touched on the definition and conditions for the onset of various breakup regimes. The breakup regime observed at the onset of secondary breakup has been termed bag breakup; it involves

deflection of the drop into a thin disk normal to the flow direction, followed by deformation of the center of the disk into a thin balloonlike structure extending in the downstream direction, both of which subsequently divide into drops (see Refs. 16–23 for photographs of all the breakup regimes discussed here). The shear breakup regime is observed at higher relative velocities; it involves deflection of the periphery of the disk in the downstream direction, rather than the center, and stripping of drops from the periphery of the disk. The transition between the bag and shear breakup regimes involves complex breakup processes, with portions of this regime termed parachute breakup, chaotic breakup, bag-jet breakup, transition breakup,<sup>19,24–26</sup> etc.; this regime will be denoted the multimode breakup regime in the following. A complex breakup mechanism also has been observed at very large relative velocities, which is called the catastrophic breakup regime<sup>21,22</sup>; however, this regime is associated with very strong disturbances, such as detonation waves, rather than spray processes and will not be considered here.

Existing observations of secondary breakup have generally involved liquid/gas density ratios greater than 500 and Reynolds numbers greater than 100. For these conditions, Hinze<sup>16</sup> has shown that transitions between breakup regimes are largely functions of the Weber ( $We = \rho_g d u_0^2 / \sigma$ ) and Ohnesorge ( $Oh = \mu_f / (\rho_g d \sigma)^{1/2}$ ) numbers, which are measures of the ratios of drop drag and liquid viscous forces to surface tension forces, respectively. He found that progressively larger disturbances, i.e., larger Weber numbers, were required for the onset of breakup as Ohnesorge number increased because viscous forces in the liquid tend to inhibit drop deformation at large Ohnesorge number, which is the first step in the breakup process. In fact, viscous forces essentially suppressed secondary breakup for the available range of Weber number ( $We < 40$ ) for  $Oh > 2$  (Ref. 16). Among others, Loparev<sup>25</sup> showed that the properties of the disturbances also affected the onset of breakup, with more slowly applied disturbances requiring higher values of Weber number for breakup at a particular value of Ohnesorge number. Subsequent considerations will be limited to shock-wave disturbances to avoid this complication. Borisov et al.<sup>24</sup> proposed an alternative breakup regime map in terms of Weber and Reynolds numbers ( $Re = \rho_g d u / \mu_g$ ), considering both the bag and shear breakup regimes, which is best suited to conditions where  $Oh \ll 1$ . Krzczakowski<sup>19</sup> extended the breakup regime map of Hinze<sup>16</sup> to locate transitions to the bag, bag jet, multimode (also called transition breakup) and shear breakup regimes as a function of Weber and Ohnesorge numbers.

Another aspect of secondary breakup that has been studied is the time required to complete breakup. Liang et al.<sup>27</sup> summarize past measurements of breakup times, including the findings of Simpkins and Bales<sup>28</sup> and Ranger and Nicholls<sup>20</sup> for shear breakup, Reinecke and McKay<sup>21</sup> and Reinecke and Waldman,<sup>22</sup> for catastrophic breakup—all for shock-wave disturbances at large liquid/gas density ratios and low Ohnesorge number. For these conditions, breakup times could be normalized by a characteristic breakup time,  $t^* = d_0(\rho_f / \rho_g)^{1/2} / u_{00}$ , finding that the normalized breakup time was constant within experimental uncertainties over a large range of Weber number ( $10 < We < 10^6$ ) that includes both the shear and catastrophic breakup regimes.

Finally, due to the problems of observing drops after secondary breakup, there is very little information available about the outcome of secondary breakup even though this information is vital for understanding the structure of dense sprays.<sup>9</sup>

An exception is some limited results reported by Gel'fand et al.<sup>18</sup> for the bag breakup regime. A bimodal drop size distribution was observed with small drops resulting from breakup of the bag and large drops associated with breakup of the liquid ring at the base of the bag. However, this information is too limited to provide general guidance about the drop sizes produced by secondary breakup.

The preceding review indicates that there are several gaps in the literature concerning secondary breakup. In particular, conditions for the onset of various breakup regimes have been defined reasonably well by Krzeczowski,<sup>19</sup> but analogous deformation regimes have not been defined. Results at large Ohnesorge numbers where liquid viscosity effects are important are also limited. Breakup times and drop deformation have been studied as well, however, available information is limited for the bag and transition breakup regimes that are important for drop breakup in dense sprays. Finally, measurement problems have limited study of the outcome of secondary breakup so that virtually no information is available for this critical breakup property. Thus, the objectives of the present investigation were to extend the earlier work to provide measurements of the onset of various deformation and breakup regimes, the evolution of breakup processes, and the resulting drop sizes and velocities after secondary breakup. Phenomenological descriptions of these processes were used to help interpret the data. The measurements involved pulsed shadowgraph photography and holography limited to conditions which are representative of sprays near atmospheric pressure:  $\rho_f/\rho_g > 500$  and  $Re > 100$ . The following discussion is brief, more details can be found in Refs. 10–12.

#### B. Experimental Methods

##### 1. Apparatus

The measurements of secondary breakup properties were carried out using a shock tube apparatus with the driven section open to the atmosphere.<sup>10–12</sup> The driven section had a rectangular cross section (38 mm wide  $\times$  64 mm high) and a length of 6.7 m with the test location 4 m from the downstream end. This provided test times of 17–21 ms in the uniform flow region behind the incident shock wave. The test location had quartz windows mounted flush with the interior side walls of the shock tube in order to allow observation of drop breakup. Drop breakup was observed in air initially at 98 kPa and  $297 \pm 2$  K in the driven section of the shock tube with shock Mach numbers in the range 1.08–1.31.

Two different drop generator systems were used for the shock tube experiments. Operation at low and moderate Ohnesorge numbers involved use of a vibrating capillary tube drop generator which generated a stream of drops. Electrostatic deflection of a fraction of the drops out of the stream yielded a drop stream with sufficient separation so that interactions between drops during secondary breakup were eliminated.

Drop generation at large Ohnesorge numbers required a different approach because such drops are very difficult to form. Instead, a low Ohnesorge number drop was formed from a liquid solution consisting of a volatile solvent having a low viscosity and a nonvolatile viscous liquid. This drop then was levitated at the test location until the volatile solvent evaporated away. This yielded a small drop of a highly viscous liquid to provide the desired large Ohnesorge number condition. For work reported here, Dow Corning 200 Fluids were used for the viscous liquids with *n*-heptane used as the volatile solvent.

##### 2. Instrumentation

Drops were observed using pulsed shadowgraph photographs and motion pictures to study the overall dynamics of breakup and single- and double-pulsed holography to study the outcome of breakup. The pulsed shadowgraph photographs were obtained using a xenon lamp having a 1- $\mu$ s pulse duration. The image was recorded using a Graphlex camera at a 6:1 magnification. These photographs were obtained in a darkened room with a variable time delay between shock passage and operation of the flash lamp so that various portions of the breakup process could be observed.

Motion picture shadowgraphs were obtained using a copper vapor laser having a 30-nm-pulse duration, in conjunction with a 35-mm rotating drum camera. Laser triggering was controlled to yield 5–14 motion picture shadowgraphs with 120–160  $\mu$ s separation times between images.

The holocamera and reconstruction systems were similar to those described by Ruff et al.<sup>1,2</sup> An off-axis holocamera arrangement was used with a 2–3:1 magnification of the hologram image and a 20-ns-laser pulse time. This arrangement was coupled with reconstruction optics that allowed drop diameters as small as 25  $\mu$ m to be measured with 5% accuracy and drops as small as 10–15  $\mu$ m to be observed. Reconstruction of double-pulsed holograms yielded two images of the spray with separation times as short as 1  $\mu$ s so that drop velocities could be measured.

The diameters of mildly irregular drops were found by measuring their maximum and minimum diameters. It then was assumed that the drop had an ellipsoidal shape, taking the effective diameter to be the diameter of a sphere having the same volume as the ellipsoid. More irregular liquid fragments were sized by finding the cross-sectional area and perimeter of the image and proceeding as before for an ellipsoid having the same properties. The velocity of each drop was found by measuring the distance between the centroid of its two images and dividing by the known time between laser pulses. Results at each test condition were summed over at least three realizations, in order to provide drop size and velocity correlations.

##### 3. Test Conditions

Test drops of water, *n*-heptane, mercury, two Dow Corning 200 Fluids, and various glycerol mixtures were studied. Initial drop diameters were in the range 150–1550  $\mu$ m. Ranges of other variables are as follows:  $\rho_f/\rho_g = 580$ –12,000,  $Oh = 0.006$ –560,  $We = 0.5$ –680, and  $Re = 340$ –15,760. The Reynolds number range of these measurements is higher than conditions where gas viscosity plays a strong role on drop drag properties, e.g., within this Reynolds number range, the drag coefficient of solid spheres only varies in the range 0.4–0.6 (Refs. 10–12).

#### C. Presentation of Results on Secondary Breakup

##### 1. Deformation and Breakup Regimes

The presentation of secondary breakup results will begin with definition of deformation and breakup regime transitions in order to help organize the remainder of the findings. The deformation and breakup regime map, showing transitions as functions of Weber and Ohnesorge numbers similar to Hinze<sup>16</sup> and Krzeczkowski<sup>19</sup> is illustrated in Fig. 1. Present evaluation of the onset of breakup (the transition to

the bag breakup regime) is identical to the findings of Hinze<sup>16</sup> and Krzeczowski<sup>19</sup> within experimental uncertainties. Present results also agree quite well with transitions found by Krzeczowski<sup>19</sup> to the shear breakup regime and the multimode breakup regime (which Krzeczowski<sup>19</sup> called the transition breakup regime). In view of the somewhat subjective identifications of breakup regimes and their transitions, this level of agreement is quite satisfying.

Observations of transitions to the various deformation and oscillatory deformation regimes illustrated in Fig. 1 have not been reported before. The definition of transition to the various deformation regimes was taken to be the condition where the drop deformed so that the ratio of its maximum (cross stream) dimension to its initial diameter was within the given range. Following these transitions, there was a range of Weber numbers at each Ohnesorge number where the drop decayed back to a spherical shape much like an overdamped oscillation. For  $Oh > 0.4$ , this regime ended by the onset of bag breakup, however, for  $Oh < 0.4$ , there was a range of Weber numbers where the drop oscillated with progressively decaying ratios of maximum to initial diameters before the bag breakup regime was reached; this regime is denoted the oscillatory deformation regime in Fig. 1.

The most striking feature of the flow regime map of Fig. 1 is that progressively higher Weber numbers are needed for the various transitions as Ohnesorge number increases. In fact, for  $We < 1000$ , breakup is no longer possible for  $Oh > 10$  whereas 5% deformation is no longer possible for  $Oh > 1000$ . Recalling that Ohnesorge number characterizes the ratio between liquid viscous forces and surface tension forces, the inhibition of deformation and breakup at large Ohnesorge

numbers clearly is due to increased damping by liquid viscous forces. This increased viscous damping slows the deformation process so that drag forces can reduce relative velocities and the potential for breakup. This high-Ohnesorge number regime is encountered during spray combustion processes at high pressures, where values of surface tension become small but viscosity remains finite as the drop surface nears its thermodynamic critical point. Thus, the findings illustrated in Fig. 1 suggest that drops at these conditions would not necessarily shatter due to small surface tension near the thermodynamic critical point as often thought<sup>19</sup>; instead, they might only deform or even remain spherical. However, additional study of drop breakup processes at high pressure is needed before definitive conclusions about this behavior can be obtained. In particular, specific drop trajectories across the flow regime map depend on atomization and mixing properties of the spray whereas near-critical drop processes involve much lower values of  $\rho_f/\rho_g$  than those considered in Fig. 1.

##### 2. Breakup Times

The discussion of deformation and breakup regime transitions highlights the importance of breakup time, which is defined as the time between initiation of the velocity disturbances and the last fragmentation of drop liquid. In particular, as drop velocity relaxation times and breakup times approach one another, the propensity for drop breakup decreases due to reduction of relative velocities between the drop and the gas. Present measurements of breakup times, along with earlier measurements for shock-wave disturbances from Refs. 20–22, 28, and 29, are plotted as a function of Weber number in Fig. 2. The breakup times  $t_b$  in the figure are normalized by the characteristic breakup time for shear breakup defined by Ranger and Nicholls<sup>20</sup> as follows:

$$t^* = d_0(\rho_f/\rho_g)^{1/2}/u_0 \quad (1)$$

Except for the present results, which are grouped according to Ohnesorge number, the measurements are for  $Oh < 0.1$  and effects of liquid viscosity are small. Thus, the deformation and breakup regimes at small Ohnesorge numbers are illustrated in the figure for reference purposes.

A remarkable feature of the breakup time results of Fig. 2 at  $Oh < 0.1$  is that  $t_b/t^*$  varies very little even though Weber number varies over a large range (roughly 10–10<sup>6</sup>) and a variety of breakup regimes are involved. In fact, the breakup time correlation of Ranger and Nicholls<sup>20</sup> developed for the shear breakup regime

$$t_b/t^* = 5.0 \quad (2)$$

provides a reasonably good correlation of all of the measurements for  $Oh < 0.1$ . When the present results for  $Oh > 0.1$  are considered, however, it is seen that  $t_b/t^*$  progressively increases with increasing Ohnesorge number. This reflects the importance of liquid viscosity on breakup evident from the breakup regime map of Fig. 1.

##### 3. Drop Deformation

The first stage of drop deformation, in the period where the drop flattens and first reaches a maximum cross stream dimension, was studied due to its influence on drop velocity relaxation and breakup. In particular, the distortion of the drop should affect its drag properties, and thus relative velocities during the breakup process, which undoubtedly plays a role in the onset of breakup.

Drop distortion correlates reasonably well as a linear function of time with the maximum distortion reached at roughly  $t/t^* = 1.6$  when  $Oh < 0.1$  (Ref. 10). Notably, measurements plotted by Wierzbna and Takayama<sup>23</sup> exhibit very similar behavior. Measurements of drop distortion at  $Oh > 0.1$ , however, show progressive delay in the time required for the drop to reach maximum distortion.

The next parameter of interest is the maximum cross stream diameter of the drop  $d_{c\max}$ . An approximate expression for the variation of  $d_{c\max}$  with flow conditions can be obtained for conditions where effects of liquid viscosity are small,  $Oh < 0.1$ , by considering the interaction between surface tension and pressure forces when the drop is drawn into a flattened shape. This yields the following expression for the maximum deformation<sup>15</sup>:

$$d_{c\max}/d_0 = 1 + 0.19We^{1/2}, \quad Oh < 0.1, \quad We < 10^2 \quad (3)$$

Figure 3 is an illustration of present measurements of  $d_{c\max}/d_0$  as a function of Weber number, with Ohnesorge number as a parameter. The correlating expression of Eq. (3) for  $Oh \leq 0.1$  also is plotted in the figure; it is evident that Eq. (3) provides a reasonable fit of the data. Effects of increasing Ohnesorge number can be seen, with  $d_{c\max}/d_0$  tending to decrease at a particular Weber number as Ohnesorge number is increased. Because the deformation motions of the drop cease at the point where  $d_{c\max}$  is reached, this behavior is not thought to be a direct effect of viscous forces on the force balance fixing  $d_{c\max}$ . Instead, the increased time of deformation due to effects of liquid viscosity is a more probable mechanism. This allows drag forces to act for a longer time before the maximum deformation condition is reached, which tends to reduce the relative velocity, and correspondingly  $d_{c\max}$ .

##### 4. Drop Drag

Drop drag properties were found by measuring the motion of the centroid of the drop in the uniform flowfield behind the shock wave. This approach is only approximate because it neglects the forces involved as the mass of the drop is redistributed during drop deformation, however, this effect is not expected to be large for present test conditions because characteristic velocities in the liquid phase are small as discussed subsequently.<sup>10</sup>

The experiments to find  $C_D$  involved the initial deformation of the drops up to the time  $d_{c, \max}$  was reached for  $Oh < 0.1$  and for a moderate range of Reynolds number (1000–2500) where effects of Reynolds number on the drag of the drops are expected to be small.<sup>8</sup> Thus, it was found that  $C_D$  largely was a function of the degree of deformation of the drop for present test conditions. To highlight this behavior, the results are plotted in terms of  $d_c/d_0$  in Fig. 4. Measurements of  $C_D$  for solid spheres and thin disks, drawn from White<sup>30</sup> for the same range of Reynolds number as the present tests, also are illustrated on the plot. In spite of the relatively large uncertainties of the measurements, the trend of the data is quite clear: for  $d_c/d_0$  near unity,  $C_D$  approximates results for solid spheres and then increases to approach results for thin disks at  $d_c/d_0 = 2$ . Thus, behavior in the period observed appears to be dominated by distortion of the drop, rather than internal circulation which would cause reductions of  $C_D$  from values appropriate for solid spheres. This seems reasonable because liquid-phase velocities are relatively small for present test conditions. In particular, conservation of momentum considerations suggest that characteristic liquid-phase velocities are on the order of  $(\rho_g/\rho_f)^{1/2}u_0$ , see Ranger and Nicholls.<sup>20</sup> Thus, for  $(\rho_f/\rho_g) > 500$ , liquid velocities are roughly 5% of the initial relative velocity.

Past work on the structure of dense sprays and processes of primary breakup of nonturbulent and turbulent liquids<sup>2,13,14</sup> indicated that local drop size distributions generally satisfied the universal root normal distribution function of Simmons,<sup>31</sup> with  $MMD/SMD = 1.2$  (see Belz<sup>32</sup> for a discussion of the properties of the root normal distribution function). This vastly simplifies the presentation of data because the root normal distribution only has two moments, and with  $MMD/SMD$  equal to a constant, is specified entirely by the Sauter mean diameter alone. Thus, initial measurements of drop sizes after breakup focused on evaluating the root normal distribution function.

Typical measurements of drop size distributions are illustrated in Fig. 5 for bag breakup. Results for the other breakup regimes were similar, although for shear breakup trends illustrated in Fig. 5 they were achieved only after removing the core or drop-forming drop from the distribution as discussed in the following (the core drop will be handled separately). The results are plotted in terms of the root normal distribution function, with the function itself illustrated for values of  $MMD/SMD = 1.1, 1.2$ , and  $1.5$ . The data are somewhat scattered at large drop sizes because of the limited number of large drops. The results are represented reasonably well by the universal root normal distribution function with  $MMD/SMD = 1.2$ , similar to the earlier findings.<sup>2,13,14</sup> In contrast to the present findings, Gel'fand et al.<sup>15</sup> observed a bimodal distribution of drop sizes after bag breakup for the two conditions they considered. The reason for this discrepancy is unknown and clearly merits additional study.

A correlating expression for the Sauter mean diameter after secondary breakup is obtained by noting the similarity between primary breakup of nonturbulent liquids<sup>13</sup> and secondary breakup due to stripping originating from the windward

side of the drop in the shear breakup regime. The configuration for secondary breakup in the shear breakup regime is shown in Fig. 6, where the core (drop-forming) drop is illustrated. It is assumed that the relative velocity at the time of breakup can be represented by the initial relative velocity, that drop sizes after breakup are comparable to the thickness of the boundary layer as it reaches the periphery of the drop, that the liquid boundary layer is laminar, and that the Sauter mean diameter is dominated by the largest drop sizes in the distribution. The length of development of the liquid boundary layer is taken to be proportional to  $d_0$ , which should be the condition tending to yield the largest drop sizes.<sup>10</sup>

Present measurements of the Sauter mean diameter after secondary breakup are plotted in terms of the variables from the secondary breakup model in Fig. 7. These results are for  $Oh < 0.1$  and  $We < 10^3$ , including the bag, transition, and shear breakup regimes. A correlation of the data based on the approximate theory also is shown on the plot. The best empirical fit of the data to the theoretical variables is as follows:

$$\rho_g SMD u_0^2 / \sigma = 6.2 (\rho_f / \rho_g)^{1/4} [\mu_f / (\rho_f d_0 u_0)]^{1/2} We \quad (4)$$

with the correlation coefficient of the fit being 0.91. It should be noted, however, that  $\rho_f / \rho_g$  does not vary greatly over the present test range, and additional measurements are needed to explore density ratio effects.

It is probably fortuitous, and certainly surprising, that a single correlation can express the Sauter mean diameter after bag, transition, and shear breakup since the three breakup mechanisms appear to be rather different. On the other hand, similar behavior for the three breakup regimes is consistent with the observation

##### 6. Core Drop Properties

The velocity and size of the core drop at the end of breakup must be known in order to treat it separately from the rest of the drop population after shear breakup. Since drops stripped from the core drop were not observed to undergo subsequent breakup, the end of shear breakup coincides with the end of drop stripping from the core drop. In the following, the velocity of the core drop at the end of breakup will be considered first. Given this information about core drop velocities, subsequent stability considerations yield a method for correlating measurements of core drop sizes. These considerations are limited to the streamwise velocity of the core drop because these drops did not exhibit appreciable cross stream velocities during the present experiments (aside from their cross stream motion due to operation of the drop generator system).

To assist data correlation, a simplified analysis was used to estimate core drop velocities at the end of breakup. The major assumptions of the analysis<sup>11,12</sup> are as follows: virtual mass, Bassett history, and gravitational forces were ignored; gas velocities were assumed to be constant; mass stripping from the core drop was ignored; and a constant average drag coefficient was used over the period of breakup.

Based on the preceding assumptions, the following expression for the absolute velocity of the core drop at the end of breakup,  $u'_b = u_0 - u_b$ , can be found<sup>11,12</sup>:

$$(u'_b/u_0)(\rho_f/\rho_g)^{1/2}(1 + 3C) = 3\bar{C}_D(t_b/t^*)/4 \quad (5)$$

where

$$C = (3\bar{C}_D t_b/4t^*)(\rho_g/\rho_f)^{1/2} \quad (6)$$

Earlier work has shown that  $t_b/t^* = 5$  for  $10 < We < 10^6$  and  $Oh < 0.1$  (Refs. 10 and 27). Thus, the right-hand side of Eq. (5) should be a constant if a constant average value of  $\bar{C}_D$  for the shear breakup process can be found. A reasonable correlation of the present measurements of  $u'_b/u_0$  was obtained by taking  $\bar{C}_D = 5$ , which is comparable to values observed near the maximum deformation condition.<sup>10</sup> This yields  $3\bar{C}_D(t_b/t^*)/4 = 19$  on the right-hand side of Eq. (5).

The measurements of core drop velocities at the end of breakup, normalized as suggested by Eq. (5), are plotted as a function of Weber number in Fig. 8. Measurements are shown for all of the drop liquids over the test range of the shear breakup regime,  $100 < We < 600$ , along with the fitted predictions of Eq. (5). The correlation for  $u'_b/u_0$  is relatively independent of Weber number over this range and is in fair agreement with Eq. (5), based on the estimates of  $t_b/t^*$  and  $\bar{C}_D$  discussed earlier.

The velocity measurements indicated that the relative velocity of the core drop at the end of breakup was 30–40% lower than the initial relative velocity. This implied that the local Weber numbers of the core drop when breakup ended generally were greater than the critical Weber number for the onset of drop breakup due to shock-wave disturbances ( $We = 13$ ). Thus, the criterion for the end of drop stripping from the core drop differs from the criterion for the onset of breakup.
