The dynamic state of a drop at the start of secondary breakup, where the drop is round and the drop liquid is motionless, clearly differs from the state of the core drop when shear breakup ends, where the drop is deformed and liquid motion associated with drop stripping is present. Thus, it is not surprising that local Weber numbers of the core drop at the end of shear breakup were different from (and generally exceeded) the critical Weber number associated with the onset of secondary breakup. Instead, conditions defining the end of drop stripping for shear breakup appear to be related more closely to the onset of breakup for more gradual drop motions, like the breakup of freely falling drops. This correspondence is exploited in the following to find a criterion for the end of core drop stripping and a method for estimating the size of the core drop at this condition.

The deformation and size of freely falling drops generally are correlated in terms of the Eötvös number  $Eu$ . The appropriate expression when the drop acceleration  $a$  is due to gas motion relative to the drop is as follows<sup>2</sup>:

$$Eu = a|\rho_f - \rho_g|d^2/\sigma = a\rho_f d^2/\sigma \quad (7)$$

where the latter approximation follows because  $\rho_f/\rho_g \gg 1$  for present test conditions. It is anticipated that drop stripping ends when a critical value of Eötvös number  $Eu_{cr}$  is reached, based on the behavior of freely falling drops. The values of  $Eu_{cr}$  were found for all shear breakup conditions, as defined in Refs. 11 and 12, and are plotted as a function of Weber number in Fig. 9. The critical Eötvös number of the core drop at the end of shear breakup is seen to be relatively independent of Weber number and liquid type over the range of the measurements, yielding a mean value,  $Eu_{cr} = 16$ . This behavior also is similar to the breakup requirements of freely falling drops, as discussed later.

The previous considerations suggest that Weber number, Eötvös number, and time all are factors in drop breakup events at low-Ohnesorge number. These interactions are highlighted by the local values of critical Weber number, critical Eötvös number, and  $t_{cr}/t^*$  for various breakup events summarized in Table 1.

For abrupt disturbances, like the onset of secondary breakup due to shock-wave disturbances, local values of critical Weber numbers and critical Eötvös numbers were estimated at the time of breakup using measured values of drop drag in the deformation period.<sup>11,12</sup> Thus, these values are lower than criteria normally given for breakup regime transitions due to drop acceleration prior to the onset of breakup. Similar to the normalized breakup time, the normalized time at the onset of breakup for shock-wave disturbances is a constant over a wide range of Weber number,  $t_{cr}/t^* = 1.6$ . For this process, drops in the deformation period have local values of Weber and Eötvös numbers that exceed the limits for the onset of breakup, however, breakup does not begin until the drop has had time to deform and achieve a dynamical condition in the liquid that allows drops to separate from the parent drop. The characteristics of critical Weber number, critical Eötvös number and  $t_{cr}/t^*$  are somewhat different for gradual disturbances.<sup>33-36</sup> In the case

of bag breakup for a freely falling drop, Eötvös number, based on the actual drop acceleration, is a maximum at the start of free fall, whereas  $t_{cr}/t^*$  is large due to the relatively slow acceleration of the drop. Thus, liquid properties are roughly quasisteady at each relative velocity condition and breakup only occurs when forces on the drop surface due to drag are too large to be stabilized by surface tension, i.e., when the Weber number of the drop reaches a critical value. Finally, the end of drop stripping for shear breakup also involves near quasisteady liquid behavior with the dynamical state of the drop being stabilized by surface tension once the forces on the surface, represented by the drop acceleration, became lower than a critical value represented by the critical Eötvös number. A range of critical Weber number is associated with this condition due to the large variation of the drag coefficient with the degree of deformation of the drop. Thus, various breakup events are associated with required minimum values of Weber number, Eötvös number, and time, with one of these parameters frequently serving as the controlling parameter for a particular process.

##### 7. Drop Velocities

The last aspect of secondary breakup considered was the drop-size/velocity correlation at the completion of secondary breakup. These results will include all of the drops in the bag and multimode breakup regimes. The core drop will be excluded in the shear breakup regime, however, because its properties have already been established. A simplified analysis, similar to the approach used for core drop velocities, was used to assist the correlation of drop velocity data.<sup>11,12</sup> Although the analysis was rather crude, it did yield results that were useful for correlating the velocity measurements. Similar to consideration of core drop velocities, attention was limited to streamwise drop velocities.

The drop-size/velocity correlation based on the variables from the simplified analysis is plotted in Fig. 10. The test results involve a variety of drop liquids over the bag, multimode, and shear breakup regimes. Results for the core drops have been shown as dark symbols, for comparison purposes, but they are not included in the following drop-size/velocity correlation. The measured results clearly are independent of the breakup regime and can be correlated reasonably well using the following empirical fit based on the simplified analysis<sup>11,12</sup>:

$$u_0/u_b - 1 = 2.7[(\rho_g/\rho_f)^{1/2}d_0/d]^2/3 \quad (8)$$

Equation (8) appears to be rather robust over the three breakup regimes, the range of liquid types, and the flow conditions considered during the present experiments. Even the results for core drops are in fair agreement with Eq. (8), however, the specific relationships for core drops discussed earlier provide a better estimate of their velocities. Additionally, the results indicate that relative velocities are reduced 30–70% over the period of breakup, with the smallest drops experiencing the largest reduction of relative velocity due to their smaller relaxation times. Finally, this variation of drop velocities with size implies that the secondary breakup process extends over a considerable region of space; for example, core drops move 30–40 initial droplet diameters during the period of breakup.<sup>11</sup> Thus, secondary breakup corresponds to a rate process, somewhat like drop vaporization, rather than to an instantaneous process that can be characterized by jump conditions.

#### D. Conclusions

Drop deformation and secondary breakup after shock-wave initiated disturbances were studied, considering a variety of liquids in air at normal temperature and pressure ( $We = 0.5-600$ ,  $Oh = 0.006-600$ ,  $\rho_f/\rho_g = 580-12000$ , and  $Re = 340-15760$ ). The major conclusions of the study are as follows.

1) Drop deformation and breakup begin at  $We \sim 1$  and 10, respectively, at low Ohnesorge number. Effects of liquid viscosity, however, inhibit deformation and breakup at high Ohnesorge numbers, e.g., for  $We < 1000$ , breakup and deformation were no longer possible for  $Oh > 10$  and 1000, respectively. This inhibition of deformation and breakup should be important for high-pressure combustion processes where drops reach large Ohnesorge numbers as the liquid surfaces approach the thermodynamic critical point, see Fig. 1.

2) Drop size distributions after secondary breakup satisfy the universal root normal distribution of Simmons<sup>31</sup> with  $MMD/SMD = 1.2$ , similar to other observations in dense sprays and after primary breakup.<sup>1,2,13</sup> An exception was shear breakup where the core drop must be treated separately. Thus, the size distribution is completely defined by the Sauter mean diameter alone, see Fig. 5.

3) The Sauter mean diameter after secondary breakup could be correlated in terms of a characteristic liquid boundary-layer thickness for all three breakup regimes, see Fig. 7 and Eq. (4).

4) The streamwise velocity and size of the core drop after shear breakup were correlated successfully based on simplified considerations of drop motion during breakup, and the observation that the Eötvös number at the end of drop stripping was a constant, i.e.,  $Eu_{cr} = 16$ , see Figs. 8 and 9 and Eq. (5).

5) The relative streamwise velocities of the drop liquid are significantly reduced during secondary breakup (30–70%, depending on drop size) due to the large drag coefficients during the drop deformation stage and the reduced relaxation times of smaller drops. These effects were correlated successfully based on variables found from simplified analysis of drop motion, see Fig. 10 and Eq. (8).

6) At low Ohnesorge numbers, criteria for various drop breakup processes can be represented by critical values of Weber number, Eötvös number, and  $t/t^*$ . Although certain minimum values are required for all three parameters, reaching a critical local value of one of the parameters tends to control the onset of particular breakup events:  $t_{cr}/t^*$  for the onset of breakup after a shock-wave disturbance, critical Weber number for the onset of breakup of a freely falling drop, and critical Eötvös number for the end of drop stripping from the core drop during shear breakup.

Aside from the deformation and breakup regime map, the present findings generally were limited to  $Oh < 0.039$ , with results concerning core drop properties limited to  $Oh < 0.011$ . Increasing the Ohnesorge number tends to impede drop deformation and breakup processes and should modify secondary breakup behavior considerably from the results observed during the present study. The liquid/gas density ratios of present work also were relatively limited and are most appropriate for sprays at atmospheric pressure. Effects of both Ohnesorge number and  $\rho_f/\rho_g$  clearly merit additional study in order to better understand secondary breakup properties for practical combustor sprays, particularly at the conditions of liquid rocket engines. Finally, the rate aspects of secondary breakup, e.g., the evolution of dispersed drop liquid as a function of time, needs to be explored because secondary breakup extends over a significant region in space and time and is not completely characterized by jump conditions.

### III. Turbulent Primary Breakup

#### A. Introduction

Primary breakup to form drops near liquid surfaces is an important fundamental process of sprays. Unfortunately, current understanding of primary breakup is limited due to problems of observing the process in dense spray environments, effects of secondary breakup that modify drop size distributions prior to the drop field reaching conditions where drop sizes can be measured readily, and effects of liquid-phase disturbances that can vastly alter primary breakup properties. Recently, pulsed holography techniques have provided optical access to primary breakup properties; thus, findings using these methods will be discussed in the following.<sup>13–15</sup> This work has been limited to primary breakup along the surfaces of round liquid jets in still gases. This region corresponds to the near-injector dense-spray region of pressure-atomized sprays for atomization breakup conditions, in the absence of significant gas velocities relative to the injector passage.

Past studies of pressure-atomized sprays have established that spray properties are influenced by turbulence at the jet exit. First of all, the early studies of pressure atomization by De Juhasz et al.<sup>37</sup> and Lee and Spencer<sup>38</sup> showed that both atomization quality and mixing rates differed for laminar and turbulent flow at the jet exit. Next, Grant and Middleman<sup>39</sup> and Phinney<sup>40</sup> observed that jet stability and the onset of breakup were affected by turbulence at the jet exit as well. Additionally, Hiroyasu et al.<sup>41</sup> studied the length of the all-liquid core near the

jet exit, which resembles the potential core region of single-phase jets. They conclude that turbulence generated in the flow passage has a significant effect on jet breakup properties, with even relatively short injectors exhibiting effects of turbulence due to disturbances generated at the reattachment points of separated flow regions. Chehrودي et al.<sup>42</sup> criticized the measurements of all-liquid core lengths of Hiroyasu et al.,<sup>41</sup> typically finding values roughly half as long. Nevertheless, several other studies with reasonably good characterization of turbulence properties at the jet exit and alternative methods for measuring all-liquid core lengths and jet properties also have reported effects of jet exit turbulence on liquid jet breakup properties.<sup>43-49</sup>

The recent studies of Ruff et al.<sup>1,2,43</sup> and Tseng et al.<sup>44,45</sup> also have helped to quantify effects of turbulence at the jet exit on the mixing rates and structure of the dispersed phase region of pressure-atomized sprays. These studies involved liquid jets in still air at various pressures with both nonturbulent slug flow and fully developed turbulent pipe flow at the jet exit. Measurements of liquid volume fraction distributions showed much faster mixing rates for fully developed turbulent pipe flow than for nonturbulent slug flow. Additionally, drop sizes after primary breakup were larger for turbulent than nonturbulent liquids even though the other properties of these flows were nearly identical. Finally, drop sizes were relatively independent of liquid/gas density ratios for values greater than 500. However, drop sizes progressively decreased as liquid/gas density ratios were reduced below 500, so that aerodynamic effects appear to be limited to this low-density ratio regime.

Other studies also found that disturbances within the liquid phase, i.e., the presence of liquid turbulence, has dominated observations of breakup in pressure-atomized sprays and that aerodynamic effects are not very important at liquid/gas density ratios typical of observations at normal pressure and temperature. First of all, Hoyt and Taylor<sup>46-48</sup> found that the breakup of liquid jets in air at atmospheric pressure was associated with the presence of turbulent boundary layers along the walls near the jet exit. Additionally, large changes in the aerodynamic environment, including both coflowing the counterflowing air, had little effect on breakup properties. Finally, Wu et al.<sup>49</sup> observed the complete suppression of primary breakup along the liquid surface when boundary layers that develop along the injector passage walls for slug flow conditions are removed; instead, the entire liquid column breaks up as a whole at some distance from the jet exit, due to growth of large-scale disturbances. Thus, even the so-called slug flows considered in the past,<sup>1,2,13,44,45</sup> probably involved effects of breakup enhanced by turbulent boundary layers near the liquid surface.

The preceding review of the literature shows that liquid properties affect primary breakup on the surface of the round jet and that aerodynamic effects, or at least the onset of conditions where they are important, are controlled by the liquid/gas density ratio and are not very significant for surface breakup at liquid/gas density ratios greater than 500. Thus, the objective of the present investigation was to observe primary breakup along liquid surfaces with well-defined liquid disturbance levels at various liquid/gas density ratios. Measurements involved round liquid jets in still gases with fully developed turbulent pipe flow at the jet exit. Effects of flow dynamics and liquid physical properties were studied by considering various gases as the jet environment. The measurements included pulsed shadowgraph photography and holography to find the location of the onset of turbulent primary

breakup as well as drop sizes and velocities after primary breakup as a function of distance from the jet exit. Additionally, phenomenological theories were used to help interpret and correlate the results. The following discussion is brief; more details can be found in Refs. 14, 15, and 49.

#### B. Experimental Methods

##### 1. Apparatus

The measurements of primary breakup properties along the surface of round liquid jets in gases were carried out using an injector within a windowed test chamber. The injector consisted of a pneumatically driven piston/cylinder arrangement containing a 600-ml sample of the test liquid. The outlet of the cylinder had a rounded contraction to prevent cavitation, followed by a constant-diameter passage having a length-to-diameter ratio  $\geq 41$ , to yield nearly fully developed turbulent pipe flow at the jet exit. Injection was vertically downward with the liquid collected at the bottom of the test chamber and then discarded.

The windowed test chamber was cylindrical with a diameter of 300 mm and a length of 1370 mm. The chamber could be evacuated and refilled with various gases at pressures of 1 and 2 atm in order to change  $\rho_f / \rho_g$  while avoiding problems of cavitation and flashing at low-chamber pressures. Total test times were 200–10,000 ms, which was sufficient due to short flow development and data acquisition times. Jet exit velocities were calibrated using an impact plate.

##### 2. Instrumentation

Instrumentation consisted of pulsed shadowgraph photography and single- and double-pulsed holography to measure drop sizes and velocities. These observations were confined to the region near the liquid surface in order to characterize the outcome of primary breakup. The holocamera was used for pulsed shadowgraph photography, operating in the single-pulse mode with the reference beam blocked to yield a shadowgraph rather than a hologram; these measurements were used to measure primary breakup properties near the onset of breakup. The arrangement of the holocamera as well as measurement techniques were identical to the secondary breakup measurements discussed in Sec. II. Results at each test condition were summed over 20–400 liquid fragments, to provide drop size and velocity correlations.

##### 3. Test Conditions

The experiments involved relatively large, 3.6–9.5-mm-diam, liquid jets in still gases. Test liquids included water, *n*-heptane, and various glycerol mixtures. Test gases included helium, air, and freon 12 at pressures of 1–2 atm. Jet exit velocities were in the range 16–109 m/s, yielding the following ranges of jet and primary breakup dynamic parameters:  $\rho_f / \rho_g = 104$ –6230,  $Re_{fd} = 90,000$ –780,000,  $We_{gd} = 12$ –3790,  $We_{fd} = 60,000$ –1,090,000, and  $Oh_d = 0.0011$ –0.0052. Most test conditions involved  $We > 8$  and  $We_{gd} > 40$ , which places them in the atomization breakup regime defined by Miesse<sup>52</sup> and Ranz,<sup>53</sup> where primary breakup should begin right at the jet exit. Actually, the onset of primary breakup always occurred at some distance from the jet exit, as will be discussed later in more detail.

#### C. Presentation of Results on Primary Breakup

##### 1. Drop Size Distributions

Drop size distributions after primary breakup were measured for all test conditions. It was found that they satisfied the universal root normal distribution function with the ratio  $MMD/SMD = 1.2$ , similar to results after secondary breakup, discussed earlier. These results also are consistent with numerous other observations in dense sprays.<sup>1,2,31,43-45</sup> Thus, drop size distributions will be specified by the  $SMD$  diameter alone in the following.

##### 2. Drop Velocities

The measurements of mass- (volume-) averaged streamwise and cross stream drop velocities after primary breakup are plotted as a function of distance from the jet exit in Fig. 11. To highlight potential aerodynamic effects, results for  $\rho_f/\rho_g > 500$  are shown as open symbols whereas results for  $\rho_f/\rho_g < 500$  are shown as darkened and half-darkened symbols.

The normalized drop velocities illustrated in Fig. 11 provide crude correlations in terms of  $x/d$  but other factors probably are involved as well. Near the jet exit,  $\bar{u}_p/\bar{u}_o$  has a value of near 0.6, which increases to roughly 0.9 for  $x/d > 20$ . This behavior is consistent with drop velocities after turbulent primary breakup being roughly the same as streamwise liquid velocities near the liquid surface. Thus, the lower streamwise velocities are expected near the jet exit due to the retarding effect of the passage wall, evolving to higher values farther downstream where liquid velocities become more uniform. Superimposed on this behavior,

The plot shows normalized streamwise velocity (u\_p/u\_o) and normalized cross-stream velocity (v\_p/u\_o) on a log-log scale versus normalized distance (x/d). Fig. 11 Mass-averaged drop velocities after primary breakup as a function of distance from the jet exit.

however, is a clear trend that measurements for  $\rho_f/\rho_g < 500$  have significantly lower mean streamwise velocities than the higher density ratio conditions—on the average roughly 20–40% lower. This can be attributed to aerodynamic drag if it is recalled that gas velocities near the liquid surface tend to be relatively low because the dispersed-phase region is very dilute (liquid volume fractions are less than 0.1%) so that momentum transfer to the gas phase is not very effective and relative velocities between the phases are large.<sup>1,2</sup>

Similar trends with respect to density variations are much less clear for the cross stream velocity component  $\bar{v}_p/\bar{u}_0$  in Fig. 11, which are comparable to cross stream velocity fluctuations in the liquid. In particular, maximum values of  $\bar{v}_p/\bar{u}_0 = 0.058$  for fully developed turbulent pipe flow, even in the region near the wall<sup>50,51</sup> which is comparable to the cross stream drop velocity results seen in Fig. 11. An explanation of why the cross stream velocity component does not exhibit a reduction due to drag at low values of  $\rho_f/\rho_g$ , similar to the streamwise velocity component, is provided by an aerodynamic effect other than drag. In particular, the classical aerodynamic theories of primary drop breakup are based on the idea that flow velocities in the radial direction are increased for protuberances from the liquid surface due to acceleration of the gas over the tip of the protuberance,<sup>52–56</sup> which can be seen from the sketch appearing in Fig. 12. This yields a radial pressure drop across the protuberance that should increase the radial velocities of drops near the surface when aerodynamic effects are significant. This mechanism would tend to compensate for drag effects in the radial direction. Thus, it is plausible that radial drop velocities are not significantly changed by the presence of aerodynamic effects within the rather large scatter of the measurements.

##### 3. Onset of Breakup

Phenomenological analysis to find drop properties at the onset of breakup was based on the configuration illustrated in Fig. 12. The onset mechanism was

A drop (typical) is shown above the surface, with dimensions L and theta_0 L. Streamlines (typical) are shown flowing over the surface. A turbulent eddy (typical) is shown below the surface, with dimensions L and U_0. A graph on the right shows the pressure p versus the radial distance r, with a curve indicating a pressure drop across the protuberance, labeled as -rho_g U_0^2 / 2.](ab01758536ec10995738c18cddf9c20c_img.jpg)

Diagram illustrating aerodynamically enhanced turbulent primary breakup at a liquid surface. The diagram shows a cross-section of a liquid surface with a protuberance. A drop (typical) is shown above the surface, with dimensions L and theta\_0 L. Streamlines (typical) are shown flowing over the surface. A turbulent eddy (typical) is shown below the surface, with dimensions L and U\_0. A graph on the right shows the pressure p versus the radial distance r, with a curve indicating a pressure drop across the protuberance, labeled as -rho\_g U\_0^2 / 2.

Fig. 12 Aerodynamically enhanced turbulent primary breakup at a liquid surface.

assumed to involve the formation of a drop from a turbulent eddy having a characteristic size  $\ell$ , and a characteristic cross stream velocity relative to the surrounding liquid  $v_\ell$ . The eddy is shown with an elongated shape because length scales in the streamwise direction are larger than in the cross stream direction for turbulent pipe flow.<sup>50,51</sup> The eddy is assumed to be convected in the streamwise direction at the local mean velocity, which is taken to be  $\bar{u}_0$  based on the results discussed in connection with Fig. 11. The drop formed by the eddy also is assumed to have a diameter comparable to  $\ell$ .

Drops formed at the onset of turbulent primary breakup are the smallest drops that can be formed by this mechanism.<sup>14</sup> The smallest drops that can be formed are either comparable to the smallest or Kolmogorov scales of turbulence,  $\ell_K$ , or the smallest eddy that has sufficient mechanical energy to provide the surface energy needed to form a drop, whichever is larger. For present test conditions,  $\ell_K$  was in the range 1–10  $\mu\text{m}$ , which is much smaller than the smallest observed drop sizes; therefore, only the second criterion will be considered here, even though the first criterion may be relevant for some applications. The second criterion for the smallest drop that can be formed can be approximately quantified based on energy considerations. The mechanical energy available to form a drop includes the kinetic energy of an eddy of characteristic size,  $\ell_i$ , relative to its surroundings, plus the added mechanical energy due to the pressure drop caused by acceleration of the surrounding gas over the tip of the protuberance, as illustrated in Fig. 12. It is reasonable to assume that  $\ell_i$  is in the inertial range of the turbulence spectrum, which implies<sup>53</sup>

$$v\ell_i \sim \bar{v}_0'(\bar{v}_0'\ell_i/\Lambda)^{1/3} \quad (9)$$

where variations of turbulence properties in the liquid have been ignored, similar to Ref. 14. Formulation of these ideas, setting  $SMD_i \sim \ell_i$ , and assuming that turbulence properties in the liquid can be approximated by jet exit turbulence properties, yields the following implicit equation for  $SMD_i$  (Ref. 15):

$$\frac{SMD_i}{\Lambda} \left[ 1 + C_{sa} \left( \frac{\rho_g}{\rho_f} \right) \left( \frac{\bar{u}_0}{\bar{v}_0'} \right)^2 \left( \frac{\Lambda}{SMD_i} \right)^{2/3} \right]^{3/5} = C_{si} \left( \frac{\bar{u}_0}{\bar{v}_0'} \right)^{6/5} We_{f\Lambda}^{-3/5} \quad (10)$$

where  $C_{sa}$  and  $C_{si}$  are empirical proportionality constants. With fully developed turbulent pipe flow at the jet exit,  $\bar{v}_0'/\bar{u}_0$  essentially is a constant<sup>50,51</sup>; therefore, the effect of the aerodynamic enhancement term in Eq. (10) largely is controlled by the liquid/gas density ratio. This helps support past observations that the onset of aerodynamic effects depends on the liquid/gas density ratio rather than dynamic properties related to the liquid velocity.<sup>14,45</sup>

Present measurements of  $SMD_i$  are plotted in terms of the variables of Eq. (10) in Fig. 13. In doing this,  $C_{sa}$  was optimized to a value of 0.04, based on taking  $\bar{v}_0'/\bar{u}_0 = 0.058$  for fully developed turbulent pipe flow.<sup>51</sup> In addition to present results, measurements from Ref. 14 also are shown on the plot, which involve a variety of liquids for conditions where aerodynamic effects are not important. As before, test conditions for  $\rho_f/\rho_g > 500$ , where aerodynamic effects could not be identified, are shown as open symbols. The correlation of the data for all conditions generally is within the scatter anticipated from experimental uncertainties. The power of  $We_{f\Lambda}$  from the correlation of the data is not  $-3/5$  as suggested by

Eq. (9), however, and can be represented by the following empirical fit that is shown on the plot:

$$\frac{SMD_i}{\Lambda} \left[ 1 + 0.04 \left( \frac{\rho_g}{\rho_f} \right) \left( \frac{\tilde{u}_0}{\tilde{v}_0} \right)^2 \left( \frac{\Lambda}{SMD_i} \right)^{2/3} \right]^{3/5} = 76 We_{f\Lambda}^{-0.69} \quad (11)$$

Given  $SMD_i$ , the approach to find the location of the onset of turbulent primary breakup,  $x_i$ , was similar to Ref. 14. To find  $x_i$ , it is assumed that the drop-forming eddy convects along the liquid surface with a streamwise velocity  $\tilde{u}_0$  based on the results of Fig. 11. In addition, it was assumed that the onset of breakup was given by the time for growth of ligaments until their breakup into drops, taken to be the Rayleigh breakup time. The Rayleigh breakup time for a ligament of length  $\ell_i$ , assuming that effects of liquid viscosity are small, is proportional to  $(\rho_f \ell_i^3 / \sigma)^{1/2}$ , as discussed in Refs. 13 and 14. This yields the following expression for  $x_i$  (Ref. 15):

$$\frac{x_i}{\Lambda} \left[ 1 + C_{sa} \left( \frac{\rho_g}{\rho_f} \right) \left( \frac{\tilde{u}_0}{\tilde{v}_0} \right)^2 \left( \frac{\Lambda}{SMD_i} \right)^{2/3} \right]^{9/10} = C_{xi} \left( \frac{\tilde{u}_0}{\tilde{v}_0} \right)^{9/5} We_{f\Lambda}^{-4/10} \quad (12)$$

where  $C_{xi}$  is a constant of proportionality. Similar to Eq. (9), aerodynamic effects on  $x_i$  from Eq. (12) are controlled by the liquid/gas density ratio alone.

Both the present measurements of  $x_i$  and those of Ref. 14 are plotted in terms of the variables of Eq. (12) in Fig. 14, adopting  $C_{sa} = 0.04$  as before. The correlation of the data over the full range of aerodynamic effects is reasonably good in view of

##### 4. Drop Sizes

Aerodynamic secondary breakup times scale proportional to  $\ell_i (\rho_f / \rho_g)^{1/2} / \bar{u}_0$  for an object of size  $\ell_i$ , if the velocity of the gas near the liquid surface is assumed to be small.<sup>10</sup> Thus, for conditions where aerodynamic effects are important, Rayleigh breakup times increase more rapidly than do secondary breakup times as  $\ell_i$  increases. This implies a tendency for secondary and primary breakup to occur simultaneously, or to merge, as distance from the jet exit increases—a mechanism that dominated drop sizes near the liquid surface when aerodynamic effects are important, except near the onset of turbulent primary breakup.

Within the merged primary and secondary breakup regime, turbulent primary breakup properties will be found using the results of Ref. 14 whereas aerodynamic secondary breakup properties will be found from Eq. (4). The variation of  $SMD$  with distance from the jet exit for turbulent primary breakup was found assuming that the  $SMD$  was proportional to the largest drop that could be formed at a particular position with the time of breakup determined from the Rayleigh breakup

time. Thus, the combined formulation yields the following expression for the *SMD* after merged primary and secondary breakup<sup>15</sup>:

$$\rho_g SMD \bar{u}_0^2 / \sigma = C_s C_{sx} (x/\Lambda)^{1/3} (\rho_g / \rho_f)^{3/4} We_{f\Lambda}^{5/6} Re_{f\Lambda}^{-1/2} \quad (14)$$

where  $C_s$  and  $C_{sx}$  are empirical constants.

Present measurements of aerodynamic turbulent primary breakup, along with some results from Ref. 45, are plotted according to the variables of Eq. (14) in Fig. 15. The following best fit correlation of present measurements also is shown in the plot:

$$\rho_g SMD \bar{u}_0^2 / \sigma = 12.0 [(x/\Lambda)^{1/3} (\rho_g / \rho_f)^{3/4} We_{f\Lambda}^{5/6} Re_{f\Lambda}^{-1/2}]^{1.17} \quad (15)$$

Additionally, adopting the best fit values of  $C_s$  and  $C_{sx}$  in Eq. (14), the following theoretical prediction for *SMD* as a function of distance is obtained:

$$\rho_g SMD \bar{u}_0^2 / \sigma = 12.9 (x/\Lambda)^{1/3} (\rho_g / \rho_f)^{3/4} We_{f\Lambda}^{5/6} Re_{f\Lambda}^{-1/2} \quad (16)$$

with the standard deviation of the constant of 21%. Thus, the differences between Eqs. (15) and (16) are not statistically significant, within experimental uncertainties. Present measurements also are in good agreement with the predictions. The measurements of Tseng et al.<sup>45</sup> however, definitely yield smaller drop sizes after merged primary and secondary breakup. An explanation of this behavior is that these flows involved the highest concentrations of drops after turbulent primary breakup within the database, so that drop properties near the liquid surface could be influenced by small drops migrating from other parts of the multiphase mixing layer due to turbulent dispersion.

Fig. 16  $SMD$  after turbulent primary breakup as a function of distance from the injector exit, including inversion of merged secondary breakup effects.

The consistency of the merged primary and secondary breakup process also can be examined by inverting the process; namely, by computing the drop sizes that should have been observed after primary breakup in the absence of aerodynamic effects,  $SMD_p$ , and comparing these results with other measurements at similar conditions. To do this, the nonaerodynamic turbulent primary breakup correlation was refitted to yield<sup>14</sup>

$$SMD_p / \Delta = 0.65 [x / (\Delta We_{f\Delta}^{1/2})]^{2/3} \quad (17)$$

This implies reasonably consistent measurements of turbulent primary breakup with respect to Ref. 14, where the constant of Eq. (17) was 0.64. Then from the fit of the measurements illustrated in Fig. 15, the relationship between  $SMD$  and  $SMD_p$  is given by

$$SMD_p / \Delta = 3.91 \times 10^{-3} (\rho_g / \rho_f)^{1/2} Re_{f\Delta} (SMD / \Delta)^2 \quad (18)$$

The measurements illustrated in Fig. 15, where primary and secondary breakup occurred, were inverted to get  $SMD_p$ , using Eq. (18). These results are plotted in Fig. 16, along with previous results for turbulent primary breakup where aerodynamic effects are not important from Ref. 14. Aside from the few results of Ref. 45 mentioned earlier in connection with Fig. 15, the inverted aerodynamic turbulent primary breakup measurements are seen to be in good agreement with the other results, supporting the idea of merging of primary and secondary breakup.

An interesting feature of the results of Fig. 16 is the progressive increase of  $SMD$  with distance from the injector. The largest  $SMD$  values observed in Fig. 16 approach the order of magnitude of the radial integral scale of the turbulence.

Whereas larger drops are feasible for liquid surfaces in general, this is not the case for round liquid jets due to the finite length of the liquid core. This is indicated in the figure using the correlation for liquid core length from Grant and Middleman.<sup>39</sup> The fact that the  $SMD$  approaches  $\Delta$  near the end of the liquid core is consistent with the liquid column breaking up as a whole in this region.

##### 5. Breakup Regimes

Present measurements suggested three regimes of turbulent primary breakup: 1) nonaerodynamic turbulent primary breakup, 2) aerodynamically enhanced turbulent primary breakup, observed at onset conditions, and 3) aerodynamic turbulent primary breakup, which involves merging of turbulent primary and secondary breakup. The results also indicated that the boundaries of these regimes are fixed by the liquid/gas density ratio and the relative magnitudes of characteristic Rayleigh breakup times of ligaments and the secondary breakup times of liquid fragments. The breakup times used to define these regimes were based on the  $SMD$  after primary breakup, or after the primary breakup stage of merged primary and secondary breakup, for conditions beyond the onset of breakup for present data. Thus, the characteristic Rayleigh breakup time was taken to be  $\tau_R \sim (\rho_f SMD^3 / \sigma)^{1/2}$ , whereas the characteristic secondary breakup time was taken to be  $\tau_b \sim (\rho_f / \rho_g)^{1/2} SMD / \bar{u}_0$ . Then using Eq. (18) to eliminate  $SMD$  from the ratio, the characteristic time ratio was taken to be

$$\tau_R / \tau_b = (\rho_g / \rho_f)^{1/2} (x We_{fA} / \Delta)^{1/3} \quad (19)$$

The resulting turbulent primary breakup regimes based on present measurements, as well as those from Refs. 1, 14, and 45, are illustrated in terms of  $\rho_f / \rho_g$  and  $\tau_R / \tau_b$  in Fig. 17. The total set of measurements yields  $\rho_f / \rho_g = 500$  as the aerodynamic/nonaerodynamic transition, and  $\tau_R / \tau_b = 4$  as the enhanced-aerodynamic/merged transition.

#### D. Conclusions

Primary breakup along the surface turbulent liquids was studied, considering liquid jets in still gases with fully developed turbulent pipe flow at the jet exit ( $\rho_f / \rho_g = 104$ –6230,  $Re_{fd} = 90,000$ –780,000,  $We_{gd} = 12$ –3790,  $We_{fd} = 60,000$ –1,090,000, and  $Oh_d = 0.0011$ –0.0052). The major conclusions of the study are as follows:

1) The presence of aerodynamic phenomena for turbulent primary breakup largely is controlled by the liquid/gas density ratio. When this ratio is less than 500, aerodynamic phenomena affect both conditions at the onset of breakup and drop sizes and velocities (to a lesser extent) after breakup.

2) Aerodynamic enhancement of the onset of turbulent primary breakup was due to the aerodynamic pressure reduction over the tips of protruding liquid elements. This effect assists the kinetic energy of a corresponding liquid eddy relative to its surroundings to provide the surface tension energy needed to form a drop, thus allowing smaller drops to form. Phenomenological analysis based on these ideas yielded reasonable correlations of onset properties, Eqs. (11) and (13), for the enhanced aerodynamic breakup regime (see Figs. 13 and 14).

3) For conditions where secondary breakup times become small in comparison to Rayleigh breakup of turbulence-induced ligaments protruding from the surface,

The reduction of drop sizes at these conditions correlated reasonably well with results for the secondary breakup of drops due to shock disturbances, yielding the correlation of Eq. (16), see Fig. 15.

4) Drop size distributions after aerodynamic turbulent primary breakup approximated Simmons<sup>31</sup> universal root normal distribution with  $MMD/SMD = 1.2$ , similar to observations of other drop breakup processes as well as drops in the multiphase mixing layers of pressure-atomized sprays. Additionally, mass-averaged drop velocities after aerodynamic turbulent primary breakup approximate mean and rms velocity fluctuations of the liquid in the streamwise and cross stream directions, respectively, although there was a tendency for streamwise velocities to be somewhat reduced by aerodynamic effects.

A major issue still open involves primary breakup of nonturbulent liquids and the relevance of the classical primary breakup theories of Taylor<sup>54</sup> and Levich.<sup>55</sup> Current findings, and the observations of others,<sup>46-49</sup> all indicate that it is difficult to observe the nonturbulent primary breakup mechanism. The main problems are effects of liquid disturbances, the intrusion of secondary breakup, and weak aerodynamic effects for most liquids at normal pressure and temperature where measurements are most convenient. Until these experimental difficulties are resolved, understanding of this important primary breakup mechanism will remain limited. This is problematical because the classical nonturbulent aerodynamic primary breakup mechanism is likely to dominate breakup processes within combusting sprays at the pressures typically found in practical transportation and

propulsion systems.<sup>3-9</sup> Finally, the rate properties of primary breakup are not well known, which limits capabilities for rational models of the near-injector region of sprays.

### I. Introduction

**T**HERE are various procedures to estimate liquid rocket engine (LRE) combustor stability to high-frequency (acoustic) oscillations.<sup>1-4</sup> The procedure devised at the Scientific Research Institute of Chemical Machine Building (NI-ICHIMMASH) and some other organizations is based on the combined processing and analysis of records of natural pressure oscillation (noise) and artificial pulse disturbance introduced into the chamber. Such an approach raises the validity of the estimate of stability and provides additional information about LRE combustor processes. The stability estimation procedure is a part of LRE development technology devised at NIICHIMMASH and is aimed at providing engine stability to high-frequency oscillations in a specified range of operation modes.

The technology includes the following stages: 1) laboratory tests of hydraulic, acoustic, and combusting models of combustion chamber and gas generator units; 2) combustion chamber and gas generator component stand tests in actual regimes of the engine assembly; and 3) checking of stability characteristics constancy. Corresponding characteristics defining the stability of the combustion process are devised for all of the development stages.

At the first stage some tentative information should be promptly obtained about combustion process stability with various geometries of actual injection elements (or injectors). This information can be obtained at benign simulated conditions: low pressures and low mass flow rates with simulators instead of actual propellants,

if necessary. The tentative information on stability is used for selecting the most promising injector versions and for devising and implementing changes to the initial injector configuration with the object of stability improvement. The model test results are processed and extended to actual conditions using parametric criteria obtained on the basis of theoretical analysis and on the characterization of energy conditions of exciting self-oscillations.

The qualification of combustion process stability in model combustor tests is carried out by estimating the extent to which the regimes being simulated depart from the boundaries of the self-oscillating excitation region. A comparative estimation of various injector geometries is based on the relative position of the boundaries of the instability region, the hysteresis region, and on other characteristics taken for estimating combustion process stability under actual conditions.

After the transition to stand tests under actual conditions, simplified combustor models can be used to obtain predictive information related to a proposed change to some selected, promising injection element or injector head that is already being tested in actual regimes. Besides defining self-excited oscillation region boundaries for various injector geometries, studies of stability characteristics, gas passage length effects for gas/gas and gas/liquid injection elements, and the influence of harmonic oscillations transmitted from the feed system on the combustion zone properties (the combustion zone may enhance or reduce the oscillations) are performed with combustor models. In injector hydraulic tests at atmospheric and high-pressure discharge conditions, injector dynamic characteristics and injector inlet pressure oscillation influences on atomization parameters may be estimated. Acoustic models may be used for obtaining optimum characteristics of various passive damping devices (acoustic absorbers, dampers) and of active devices preventing the excitation of self-oscillations for which the kinetic energy of flows over straighteners, baffles, and so on may be a source.

At the second stage, an optimum (from the point of view of providing sufficient stability margins under actual conditions of disturbance effects caused by the operation of actual engine components) version of the injector is selected from some of the most promising ones chosen at the first stage. Stability characteristics in actual regimes are defined from parameters of amplitude [frequency spectra at the level of natural chamber pressure disturbances ("noise")] and from the chamber process response to external artificial pulse disturbances generated by a special reusable device. Stability characteristics are derived from measurements of inherent pressure oscillations and from the response to artificially imposed pressure disturbances. The pressure oscillation decrement  $\delta T$ , corresponding to the oscillations in the combustion chamber reaction zone at natural acoustic frequencies, is used as a combustion process stability characteristic. Relaxation time  $\tau$ , at a certain relative maximum value of pressure pulse disturbance peak is also used as a stability characteristic defined by the process response to pulse disturbances. The qualification of chamber process stability is usually performed by statistically comparing these experimental values of stability characteristics with corresponding limit values, based on the practical experience of applying this procedure obtained from prior research and development programs.

The third stage, stability characteristics checking, is carried out in engine manufacturing and operation. Amplitude characteristics of pressure oscillations in cavities upstream of the injector and vibrational accelerations of chamber and gas generator members are used. The limit values of these characteristics are specified for a certain engine on the basis of statistical data accumulated.

Problems of choosing stability characteristics for LRE actual tests and the methods and tools for determining these characteristics are discussed in the present chapter.

### II. Stability Characteristics

A complete theoretical description of dynamic combustion processes in a rocket engine has not been developed. Therefore, an empirically based estimate of combustion chamber and gas generator process stability must be used. The stability degree of a combustion process can be determined from the response of the process to disturbances introduced into the chamber or from natural disturbances present in the chamber.

To obtain a quantitative estimate of stability, the following research work should be performed.

1) Optimum characteristics describing the combustion chamber and gas generator processes should be chosen.

2) Methods of using these characteristics for determining chamber process stability margins for different types of engines should be developed and tested.

3) Relevant instruments and devices for determining stability characteristic numerical values should be developed.

4) The connection of stability characteristics with engine design and operating parameters should be studied.

For choosing optimum stability characteristics, the linearized solution of the combustion chamber's response to both pulsed and stationary random disturbances will be examined. The response of chamber pressure  $P$  to a pulse action (for example, combustion chamber or gas generator pressure oscillations) can be presented as the sum of expressions of the form

$$P' = A_i \exp \left( - \int_0^t \delta_i dt \right) \sin \left( \int_0^t \omega_i dt + \varphi_i \right) \quad (1)$$

where  $A_i$  and  $\varphi_i$  are the initial amplitude and phase of the  $i$ th mode of the natural oscillation, and  $\delta_i$  and  $\omega_i$  are the oscillation damping factor and frequency governed by the system parameters.

Quantities  $\delta$  and  $\omega$ , in general, depend on time, i.e.,  $\delta = \delta(t)$  and  $\omega = \omega(t)$ . These quantities characterize pressure oscillations in combustion chambers at any given time, which is why certain definite values of the quantities correspond to definite characteristic states of the oscillatory system being considered. Negative and positive values of  $\delta$  indicate unstable and stable states, respectively. The stability boundary is indicated by  $\delta = 0$ . This allows one to employ the value of  $\delta$  as a characteristic of the oscillatory system state that can be found in experiments and, in particular, as the system stability characteristic. In LRE development the problem of finding design and operating parameter ranges that correspond to certain combustion process states, i.e., certain states of the oscillatory system being investigated, is of great interest. If these parameters influence the oscillation characteristics, some relationship between them and the values  $\delta(t)$  and  $\omega(t)$  should exist.

On the basis of available experimental data for stationary modes, it is found that the frequency of pressure oscillations in the combustion chamber and gas generator varies only slightly; this allows one to take the oscillation frequency to

be constant or to introduce a certain correction for frequency variation and to use only one characteristic of oscillation, i.e., the damping factor  $\delta$ .

The damping factor has a definite physical meaning; its value equals half of the ratio of the difference between oscillatory energy flux  $E_1$  entering the system and oscillatory energy flux  $E_2$  dissipated by the system to the total energy  $E_\Sigma$  present in the system,

$$\delta = (E_2 - E_1)/2E_\Sigma \quad (2)$$

Thus, the stability characteristic analysis can be associated with the analysis of the energy present in the oscillatory system and the oscillatory energy fluxes entering the system and dissipated by the system.

LRE combustion chambers or gas generators, being nonlinear oscillatory systems, can be represented as two members: an active member and a passive one with direct and feedback coupling. The active member is a source of oscillatory energy, and the passive one is its absorber. Nonlinear properties of these members appear in the dependence of the incoming flux of oscillatory energy  $E_1(A)$  and the energy flux dissipated by the system  $E_2(A)$  on the oscillation amplitude  $A$ . The relationship of these fluxes of oscillatory energy in a certain system defines its stability characteristics. The combustion chamber, being a nonlinear oscillatory system with volume distributed parameters, has some peculiarities that make it different from nonlinear oscillatory systems with lumped parameters. Some of these peculiarities are 1) the existence of a large number of oscillation forms with distinct amplitudes, many of which are realized simultaneously; 2) a possibility of interaction between various modes of oscillation; and 3) parameter fluctuations in the chamber. These peculiarities require defining the oscillation modes for which characteristics should be considered and for which the stability should be estimated.

The parameter fluctuations cause some scatter of oscillatory energy flux and stability characteristic values. To make the concepts and methodological approaches to stability rating clearer, however, in this section oscillations in combustion chambers will be treated from the deterministic standpoint, that is, only mean values of energy fluxes and stability characteristic will be used. Let us consider some peculiarities of the oscillation amplitude dependence of energy fluxes  $E_1(A)$  and  $E_2(A)$ .

The change pattern of the energy flux entering the oscillatory system  $E_1(A)$  is influenced by the propellant transformation conditions and, hence, should be different for combustion chambers with different propellant-phase states (gas-gas, gas-liquid, or liquid-liquid). Besides, the maximum level of the generated oscillatory energy flux depends on the oscillation period, on the amount of energy conveyed by propellants entering the system during this period, on the propellant transformation efficiency downstream of the combustion front, etc. As a consequence, the curve for energy flux  $E_1(A)$  may have one or several more or less distinct bends.

For the qualitative analysis required here, let us plot energy fluxes entering the system and being dissipated by the system against the amplitude of a certain oscillation mode (Fig. 1). Oscillatory energy losses in a combustion chamber (gas generator) include energy losses through the injector, nozzle, and chamber side surfaces, as well as losses due to the chamber medium heterogeneity, viscous effects, etc. Some processes connected with the interaction of disturbances and

the oscillatory system active member (atomization, droplet vaporization, and so on) also cause oscillation energy dissipation.

Each of the curves shown in Fig. 1 corresponds to certain design and operating parameters of the system. Three possible cases of oscillation amplitude dependence of oscillatory energy fluxes are shown. The net energy characteristic, which is the value of the oscillatory excess energy flux  $\Delta E(A) = E_2(A) - E_1(A)$ , defines the amplitude dependence of the damping factor. As  $E_\Sigma$  is always positive, the sign of the damping factor in Eq. (1) is defined by the sign of the difference  $\Delta E(A)$ .

The curve shown in Fig. 1a corresponds to an absolutely stable oscillatory system, and the curve in Fig. 1b corresponds to a self-exciting system with transition to the mode of stable self-oscillations. The curve in Fig. 1c represents the most common case; self-oscillations are excited in such a system when an initial disturbance of an amplitude above the critical value  $A_{cr}$  occurs.

From Fig. 1c, it can be seen that besides the damping factor there is one more characteristic that defines the system stability: the relation between the amplitude of the initial disturbance affecting the oscillatory system and the critical amplitude  $A_{cr}$ .

Variations in the operating mode of the combustion chamber cause changes in the relation between the energy flux entering the system and the oscillatory energy flux being dissipated in the system. These changes then result in a change of the relation  $\delta(A)$ .

Some possible versions of the curve  $\delta = F(A)$  position change are shown in Fig. 2. The case of Fig. 2a corresponds to an absolutely stable system. In the case of Fig. 2b, the damping factor  $\delta$  becomes zero at the oscillation amplitudes that are above the noise level  $A_n$  in the combustion chamber. With the mode changing further, an increase of the amplitude range in which  $\delta$  is below or equal to zero is possible (Figs. 2c and 2d).

It can be seen from Figs. 2 that oscillation excitation is possible in two cases.

1) The oscillation amplitude of random disturbances exceeds the  $A_{cr}$  value (Fig. 2c). This case will be further referred to, as in most papers, as hard excitation.

2) The damping factor  $\delta$  becomes zero at an amplitude corresponding to the level of combustion noise (Fig. 2d). This case of oscillation excitation will be referred to as soft excitation.

Fig. 2 Position variation of damping factor as a function of oscillation amplitude with approaching instability boundaries.

In the case shown in Figs. 2c (if the disturbance exceeds  $A_{cr}$ ) and 2d, the oscillation amplitudes will change in such a way as to finally reach the  $A_2$  level that corresponds to stable oscillations.

In practice, it is convenient to replace the dimensional value of the damping factor with a dimensionless quantity in the form of the product of this dimensional value and the oscillation period  $T$ ; the dimensionless quantity is the oscillation decrement  $\delta T$ .

Let us determine how the dependence of pressure oscillation amplitude on decrement changes with time. Assuming the random processes in an oscillatory system to be stationary, we may write for the rms value of the amplitude change with time

$$\begin{aligned} \overline{[A(t+\tau) - A(t)]^2} &= \overline{A^2(t+\tau)} + \overline{A^2(t)} - 2A(t+\tau)A(t) \\ &= 2\overline{A^2(t)} - 2B_A(\tau) = 2\overline{A^2(t)}[1 - R_A(\tau)] \end{aligned} \quad (3)$$

where  $A^2(t)$  is the rms amplitude,  $B_A(\tau)$  is the correlation function of the envelope  $A(t)$ ,  $R_A = B_A(\tau)/B_A(0)$  is the correlation coefficient of the envelope  $A(t)$ , and  $B_A(0)$  is the correlation function  $B_A(\tau)$  at  $\tau = 0$ .

The correlation coefficient  $R_A(\tau)$  of the envelope of a random process at a simple oscillatory system outlet is known<sup>5</sup> to have the following form:

$$R_A(\tau) = 4/5[1 + (1/4)e^{-2\delta\tau}] \quad (4)$$

Substituting Eq. (4) into expression (3) gives

$$\overline{[A(t+\tau) - A(t)]^2}/\overline{A^2(t)} = 2/5(1 - e^{-2\delta\tau}) \quad (5)$$

From Eq. (5) it is evident that the rms value of the amplitude change for a fixed time interval decreases with a decrease in the damping factor  $\delta$ , i.e., the time dependence of oscillation amplitude becomes smoother.

Let us consider the connection between the oscillation amplitude and the decrement. Let a wide-band random signal  $x(t)$  (which for simplicity is assumed to be stationary white noise) be applied to the inlet of an oscillatory system with the following pulse transient function:

$$h(t) = \begin{cases} e^{-\delta t} \sin \omega t & t > 0 \\ 0 & t < 0 \end{cases} \quad (6)$$

Then at the system outlet we have for the signal  $y(t)$

$$\begin{aligned} y(t) &= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(t-\tau)x(\tau) d\tau \\ y^2(t) &= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(t-\tau)h(t-\tau')x(\tau)x(\tau') d\tau d\tau' \end{aligned}$$

or keeping in mind that the white noise correlation function is

$$\overline{x(\tau)x(\tau')} = \delta(\tau - \tau')\overline{x^2(t)}$$

where  $\delta(\tau - \tau')$  is the Dirac delta function, we get

$$\overline{y^2(t)} = \overline{x^2(t)} \int_0^\infty h^2(\tau) d\tau \quad (7)$$

Substituting Eq. (6) into Eq. (7) gives

$$\begin{aligned} \overline{y^2(t)} &= \overline{x^2(t)} \int_0^\infty e^{-2\delta\tau} \sin^2 \omega\tau d\tau \\ &= \overline{x^2(t)} \frac{1}{2} \int_0^\infty e^{-2\delta\tau} (1 - \cos 2\omega\tau) d\tau = \frac{x^2(t)}{4\delta} \end{aligned} \quad (8)$$

The integration low limit is taken to be zero as the system starts at the time moment  $\tau = 0$ . Presenting the random oscillatory process  $y(t)$  as  $y(t) = A(t) \sin[\omega t + \varphi(t)]$  results in

$$\overline{y^2(t)} = \overline{A^2(t) \sin^2[\omega t + \varphi(t)]} = \overline{A^2(t)/2} \quad (9)$$

Substituting Eq. (8) into Eq. (9) gives

$$\overline{A^2(t)} = \overline{x^2(t)}/2\delta$$

or

$$\sqrt{\overline{A^2(t)}} = (1/\sqrt{\delta})(\sqrt{\overline{x^2(t)}}/\sqrt{2}) \quad (10)$$

Thus, the rms value of the oscillation amplitude at the outlet of an oscillatory system to the inlet where a random wide-band signal is applied is inversely proportional to the square root of the damping factor  $\delta$  of this system.

As indicated by Eq. (10), as the chamber process approaches the soft excitation mode (instability boundary), the decrement (damping factor) decrease is accompanied by a rise in the amplitude of acoustic pressure oscillations. As the system approaches the instability boundary, the energy spectrum parameters vary as well. The oscillations become more regular, i.e., the energy of the oscillations at their natural acoustic frequencies, corresponding to a higher quality factor of the system, gets relatively higher. The change in the spectrum of oscillation energy may be characterized by a number of parameters, all of which can be used in certain cases to indicate that the system is approaching the instability boundary. These parameters provide more information as they become more closely connected with  $\delta T$ .

A hypothetical dependence of pressure oscillation amplitude on operating parameter  $Y$  is presented in Fig. 3. In the parameter range  $Y \in Y_{cr1}, \dots, Y_{cr2}$ , the given dependence has a hysteresis character. The ratio  $A_{cr}/A_n$  defines how far the noise level  $A_n(Y)$  is from the amplitude  $A_{cr}(Y)$ , resulting in excitation of oscillations of the operating parameter ( $Y$ ). Artificial disturbances should be applied to the combustion chamber for determining  $A_{cr}$ . In practice, some problems arise while determining  $A_{cr}$ . Either the critical value of the amplitude could not be attained even at high-disturbance amplitudes or the combustion chamber was damaged as a result of attaining  $A_{cr}$ . Thus, it is taken that the margin to hard excitation of oscillations is sufficient if 1) after applying a pulse disturbance, pressure oscillations decay and 2) the disturbance parameter  $n = A_0/2A_{n,max} \geq N$ . Here,

the initial pressure peak under pulse disturbance  $A_0$ , the maximum value of the total high-frequency signal within a certain time interval before application of the pressure pulse disturbance  $A_{n,max}$ , and a constant  $N$  are found in experiments. The experience of evaluating LRE combustion chamber process stability has shown that this characteristic is informative enough and represents the objective reality adequately.

If  $A_{cr}$  cannot be obtained, which is the most frequent case in practice, it is necessary to show that combustion chamber pressure pulse disturbances that exceed the noise level by a certain factor ( $N$ ) decay sufficiently fast.

For characterizing the decay velocity of pressure oscillations caused by pulse disturbances, the relaxation time  $\tau_r$  (i.e., the time of oscillation amplitude decrease by a factor of  $e$  behind an initial transient region corresponding to a constant time of  $\tau_1$ ) may be used. It should be noted that in evaluating chamber process stability with relaxation time the maximum pressure peak due to a pulse disturbance should distinctly differ from combustion chamber natural noise pressure peaks but not so much so as to distort the essential characteristics of the chamber pressure. Applying disturbances that greatly distort the chamber process may give incorrect information as high disturbances affect the propellant flow to the combustion chamber.

A quantity inversely proportional to the relaxation time is directly proportional to the effective (amplitude-averaged) decrement  $\delta T_e$ . Thus, the stability characteristics that are defined from natural noises  $\delta T$  and from pulse disturbance  $\tau_r$  have the same physical essence based on the damping velocity of pressure disturbances of a different nature (natural or artificial). Sufficiency of the selected stability characteristics and their actual values are confirmed by multiple data obtained with experimental and real LREs.

The injector had 91 pneumatic injection elements of 18 mm diam with eight 1.2-mm holes in the walls for feeding the fuel. The oscillation effective decrement was determined by introducing disturbances of a prescribed amplitude by a shock tube

### III. Disturbance Devices

A device meeting the following requirements had to be developed for rating chamber process stability to hard excitation.

1) The artificial disturbance pulse should be equivalent (in its effect on the combustion chamber process) to most pressure disturbances observed in a combustion chamber.

2) The disturbance device (DD) should function reliably under the firing test condition of the LRE in the required range of combustion chamber and gas generator operating parameters (pressure, temperature, vibration level).

3) The disturbance should be applied to the system at a specified moment.

4) The shock wave amplitude at the device outlet should be constant. It is only in this case that stability quantitative evaluation can be carried out.

5) The disturbance being applied should have a certain form and duration.

In the early work of the design bureaus in Russia and of foreign firms, explosive disturbance devices, in which either an explosive charge was detonated or a powder charge ignited, were used. The large scatter of pulse characteristics was the main drawback of those devices. There were attempts to reduce the scatter by mounting a separating diaphragm with a calibrated burst pressure at the chamber inlet.

Fig. 5 Disturbance devices.

Experts of NIICHIMMASH and the Physical Chemistry Institute of the Academy of Science developed a series of disturbance devices, a shock tube, shown in Fig. 5a being one of them. The shock tube includes a case having a cavity filled with a stoichiometric mixture of methane and oxygen that is separated from the combustion chamber by a burst diaphragm. On initiating detonation in the cavity, the diaphragm bursts, and a disturbance is introduced into the combustion chamber. The cavity filled with the detonable mixture has an "acceleration region" along which the combustion is accelerated after the ignition of the mixture, and then the combustion transition to detonation occurs.

The in-chamber disturbance device shown in Fig. 5b is an explosive charge placed in a case of special heat insulating material; the charge is ignited by a blasting cap (TAT-1-1) with a powder ignitor. The blasting cap is initiated on flame contact after the burnout of the protecting shell, the thickness of which defines the time delay of the device initiation. The possibility of placing the device in the chamber without breaking the chamber integrity and the device independence are its important advantages; the impossibility of introducing disturbances at any desired moment is its disadvantage.

A four-charge DD is shown in Fig. 5c. Four charges that are initiated at prescribed moments are placed in one case. Further improvement of the DD resulted in the development of multicharge devices with slower detonation modes.

A two-pulse DD for gas generators is shown in Fig. 5d. Charge chambers by way of tilted case channels are connected with a channel opening into a trap. At the channel outlet, there is a conical extension immersed into the trap that acts as a shield for repulsing diaphragm fragments.

In a three-charge version of the disturbance device for a gas generator, the charges are separated from the case channels by copper diaphragms to eliminate any oxygen gas effects. To prevent fragments from getting into the gas generator chamber, the body of this disturbance device has a separator with guides made in the form of ribs that prevent the fragments from entering the chamber while the disturbance "flowing over" the ribs enters the gas generator. The diaphragm fragment trap is made in the form of a Y-shaped channel with a decreasing diameter.

A five-charge DD for combustion chambers (Fig. 5e) is a system of disturbance devices placed in one case and connected with tilted channels to form a single outlet channel. Each charge in this device, as in the device for gas generators, is separated from the case channel with a diaphragm. For combustion chambers of small diameter (80–120 mm) a grid is mounted in the device to provide pulse control over a wider range and to trap the diaphragm fragments. The described devices were studied with the aim of analyzing the characteristics of the disturbances being applied. The study results show that the disturbance intensity and uniformity are defined mostly by the device characteristics, the disturbance introduction conditions, and the parameters of the volume being disturbed. Classification of the factors influencing the disturbance amplitude and form is given in Fig. 6. When we speak of DD characteristics, we mean its physicochemical parameters, including its dimensions (channel diameter and length) and configuration features (one charge, multicharge, the existence of damping elements, the explosive mass, and its combustion mode).

The existence of a reactive medium in the combustion chamber often results in an additional replenishing energy effect connected with additional energy release following the moving pressure front. This causes the disturbance amplitude

increase in the combustion chamber. The effect of the volume being excited, however, is defined not only by the intensifying properties of the combustion zone in the chamber but by such parameters as pressure, density, sound velocity, geometry, and other features of the object being analyzed.

To evaluate the influence of the aforementioned factors on the disturbance level  $A_{col}$ , laboratory tests were carried out that gave some quantitative and qualitative relations.

1) For shock wave damping along the channel with a diameter of 4–12 mm and a length of up to 650 mm with various charge masses, the experiment showed that with length-to-diameter ratio increase up to  $l_{ch}/d_{ch} \approx 10$  the disturbance amplitude declines by 20%. With a real channel diameter decrease,  $d_{ch} < 6$  mm, the damping along the channel is greater.

2) For evaluating the chamber pressure, medium density and sound velocity influences, experiments were carried out in volumes filled with air, helium, and pyroxylin combustion products. The experiments showed that the relationship between the medium initial pressure  $P_c$  and the sound velocity is the main factor defining the disturbance characteristics.

3) For the method of introducing the disturbance into the chamber, the experiments showed that at chamber pressures greater than 8 MPa, the influence of introduction angle on the disturbance form is small. The relationships obtained allow one to evaluate the requisite disturbance amplitude value at the chamber inlet for an inert medium. A five-charge DD provides the prescribed value of the disturbance with an accuracy of +10%.

The number of the LRE tests carried out to evaluate the operating process stability to hard excitation of high-frequency oscillations permits one to refine the results of cold tests. When comparing the results of cold tests and tests performed under actual conditions, disturbance amplitude in firing tests was found to be higher than in cold tests. ### IV. Decrement Determination from Natural Disturbances

In evaluating LRE ombustion chamber process stability, combustion chamber noise can also be used as a natural disturbance source. It is natural to suppose that these disturbances are small enough so that the pulsations caused by them can be described with linearized equations. These disturbances are described with random functions, whose spectral densities are of a larger bandwidth than the frequency characteristics of the combustion chamber in the neighborhood of the natural frequencies being studied. Then the chamber pressure pulsations caused

A series of methods is devised for determining the decrement from natural disturbances. The following ones will be considered: spectral, correlational, amplitude, and instantaneous period method.

1) The spectral method defines the decrement from the width of the noise power spectrum (Fig. 10). In an actual case, the filter width  $\Delta_f$  of the spectrum analyzer should be taken into account. For a simple filter,  $\delta T = \pi(\Delta - \Delta_f)/f_0$ , where  $\delta T$  is the oscillation decrement,  $\Delta$  the width of power spectrum  $S(\omega)$  at a level of half that of the maximum amplitude, and  $f_0$  the resonant frequency.

An algorithm was devised for taking  $\Delta_f$  into account for other types of filters as well. In an actual algorithm, more complicated formulas are used to account for neighboring (close) peaks, background, and other interferences (three-point methods). An exhaustive search of point pairs lying to the left and to the right of the maximum is performed, and a pair is selected that gives the minimum sum of the decrement value and its theoretical statistical spread.

2) The correlation method defines the decrement from the rate of decay of the auto- or cross-correlation function  $B(\tau)$  (Fig. 11)

$$\delta T = [1/(m - n)] \cdot \ln[B(\tau_n)/B(\tau_m)] \quad (12)$$

where  $\tau_n$  and  $\tau_m$  correspond to maxima of  $B(\tau)$  for  $n$ th and  $m$ th oscillation periods of  $B(\tau)$ .

3) The amplitude method (Fig. 12) defines decrement  $\delta T$  as a function of the ratio of two amplitudes at the outlet of two different filters tuned to a resonant frequency of the oscillatory process being analyzed:  $\delta T = F(A_1/A_2)$ . In a particular case the decrement is defined from the ratio of amplitudes at the inlet and the outlet of a filter (preferably a rejection one). Discrete values of the function  $F$  are determined by calibration on a simulator that is an oscillatory circuit with a varying decrement. The decrement is calculated from the discrete values by linear interpolation.

4) The instantaneous period method (Fig. 13) defines the decrement from the mean module value  $|T'|$  of instantaneous period fluctuations of the oscillations

There should be a definite idea of the decrement accuracy before using it for quantitative estimation of stability margins. The error of the decrement estimation consists of its statistical error and the error due to interfering factors, such as close frequencies and background noise.

The theoretical estimate of statistical error requires tedious calculations and results in awkward expressions. It is connected with the necessity to account for the relationship between the spectrum points and the correlation function. The results of these theoretical studies are, therefore, given in a simplified form.

For the spectral method, the value of the relative statistical error  $\varepsilon_{\delta T}$  of the decrement estimate is approximately equal to the statistical error  $\varepsilon_{s_0}$  of the power

spectrum estimate  $S(\omega_0)$  (the square of the filtered amplitude) at the resonant frequency  $\omega_0$ ,

$$\varepsilon_{\delta T}^2 \approx \varepsilon_{\omega_0}^2 \approx 1/(\Delta_e \cdot T_a) \quad (13)$$

where

$$\varepsilon_{\delta T}^2 = (\overline{\delta T} - \overline{\delta T})^2 / (\delta T)^2$$

is the square of the relative statistical error of the estimate of the decrement  $\delta T$ ,

$$\varepsilon_{\omega_0}^2 = [\overline{S(\omega_0)} - S(\omega_0)]^2 / S^2(\omega_0)$$

is the square of the relative statistical error of the estimate  $\tilde{S}(\omega_0)$  of the power spectrum at the resonant frequency  $\omega_0$ ,  $T_a$  is the averaging time,  $\Delta_f$  the effective width of the filter amplitude-frequency characteristic raised to the fourth power  $[A^4(\omega)]_f$ . Also  $\Delta''$  is the effective width of the chamber plus filter amplitude-frequency characteristic raised to the fourth power  $[A^4(\omega)]_{f+c}$ , and  $\Delta_e = (\Delta_f')^2 / \Delta''$ . The effective width of the characteristic is the ratio of the area under the curve  $A^4(\omega)$  to the maximum of  $A^4(\omega)$ .

Let us consider two extreme cases of very wide and very narrow filters,  $(\Delta_f' \gg \delta)$  and  $(\Delta_f' \ll \delta)$ , respectively. For the wide filter case, we have minimum statistical error,  $\varepsilon_{\delta T}^2 \approx 1/\delta T_a$ ; however, the frequency resolution is poor and the error due to the existence of closely spaced frequencies, background, etc. is large. For the narrow filter case, we have good frequency resolution and large statistical error,  $\varepsilon_{\delta T}^2 \approx 1/\Delta_f' T_a$ . From the extreme cases just analyzed, it follows that there exists an optimum filter width that gives the least total error.

For the correlation method, the formula of decrement error estimation for the simplest case when the decrement is determined from two points  $B(t_1)$  and  $B(t_2)$  with width  $t_1 = 0$  is  $\varepsilon_{\delta T}^2 \approx [1 + f(\alpha)]/\delta T \alpha$ , where  $\alpha = \delta T n$ ,  $n = \tau_2/T$  (the number of periods), and  $f(\alpha) = (e^{2\alpha} - 1 - 2\alpha - 2\alpha^2)/2\alpha$ . The minimum statistical error of the decrement estimate is achieved with  $n = 1$  (adjacent maxima). In this case,  $f(\alpha) \approx 0$  and  $\varepsilon_{\delta T}^2 \approx 1/\alpha T \alpha$ .

To process an actual signal using the initial part of the correlation function is unreasonable, however, because of the background influence and the filter existence. Using adjacent maxima is unreasonable because of the instrument error influence and closely spaced frequencies; thus, the initial part  $B(\tau)$  is eliminated, and the remaining part  $B(\tau)$  is used more completely by proper averaging of some successive values of  $B(\tau_n)$  ( $\tau_{n+1}$ ).

For the amplitude method, the relative statistical error consists of relative estimates of both filters' squared amplitudes and, as the relative error for the rejection filter is an infinitesimal value, the relative statistical error is actually equal to the relative error of the squared amplitude at the first filter outlet:  $\varepsilon_{\delta T}^2 \approx \varepsilon_A^2$ . Thus, everything that was said about the spectral method relative statistical error also holds true for the amplitude method. As for the instantaneous period method, no theoretical study of the statistical error was performed because of the complexity of the task. Only experimental error estimation with the help of a simulator was carried out. Actual statistical errors for all described methods amounted to about

The results of decrement determination from natural disturbances in component tests of a liquid/liquid engine combustion chamber running nitrogen tetroxide and UDMH are shown as an example in Figs. 14 and 15. The chamber diameter is 0.12 m, pressure 80 bar, and propellant total flow rate  $\dot{m}_\Sigma = 6.2$  kg/s. It should be noted that the spectral density maximum moves to the right while approaching the combustion instability boundary (Fig. 14), which is indicative of an increase in volume-averaged sound velocity at the expense of a decrease in the cold zone volume.

The decrement against the flow rate while testing the chamber as part of the engine is shown for comparison in Fig. 15. The oscillation decrement found from natural noises substantially decreased and reached zero at a flow rate of  $\dot{m}_\Sigma = 8.8$  kg/s. This decrement change can be explained by the change of the combustion chamber operation conditions in the engine. The vibration level increased approximately by a factor of 1.5.

### V. Flame Stabilization Effects

In the course of LRE development, some cases revealed that the scatter of the stability characteristics greatly exceeded their determination accuracy. While evaluating combustion chamber stability with pulse disturbances, differences between pressure oscillation noise spectra and values of the decrement  $\delta T$  (determined from noise) obtained before and after the application of the disturbance were found. The ambiguity appears in the occurrence of spontaneous random transitions from a state of small oscillations (noise) to a state of regular self-oscillations under otherwise fixed conditions. In such cases, an understanding of the physical processes causing the inconstancy of the stability characteristics is necessary for proper modification of combustion chambers and gas generators.<sup>5,6</sup>

The results of an experimental study<sup>7</sup> of the liquid kerosene/gaseous oxygen combustion chamber process bistability nature are presented next. The chamber injector had four emulsifying injection elements. A temperature transducer was mounted in the region where the fuel jet was introduced into the oxidizer flow in the
