The dynamic state of the chamber process was monitored with high-frequency pressure transducers mounted in the reaction zone and in the cavities upstream of the injection elements (Fig. 16).

In the course of the experiment, the following states were recorded depending on the chamber pressure and equivalence ratio: the state of regular self-oscillations at one of the combustion chamber natural frequencies (6300 Hz); the state characterized by alternating combustion modes with noise waves and with self-oscillations, the instant of occurrence and the durability of each dynamic state being random in the series of similar realizations of the operating parameters; and the acoustically stable noise state.

The effect of an introduced disturbance is dependent on the chamber operation regime. The disturbance could have no effect, or organized oscillations could grow from chamber noise. If organized oscillations are present prior to the disturbance, the mode of these oscillations could be changed to random noise by the action of the pulse disturbance. The organized oscillations could also recover their initial amplitude after the pulse.

An analysis of test results revealed that the alteration of the dynamic state was accompanied by transients in the temperature of the gas in the injector passages. At stable operating conditions, with some amount of combustion noise, the measured gas temperature in the injector passage was about 325 K. At the onset of spontaneous instability with a frequency of  $\sim 6500$  Hz and peak-to-peak amplitudes of about 20 kPa, the temperature of the gas in the injector passage increased to approximately 525 K within 0.01 s. A disturbance was introduced, that induced a transition in operation from unstable back to the combustion noise state. With the transition to the combustion noise state, the injector gas temperature went back down to about 325 K. Further analysis of the experimental data leads to a

conclusion that these temperature transients were caused by the variations in the flame stabilization mode of the injectors, which were either spontaneous or were induced by pause disturbances.

The whole complex of the results allows one to explain the observed phenomena if one allows the possibility of multiple combustion zone stationary states within every injection element, which differ in flame stabilization mode, as well as the possibility that the stationary states change, either spontaneously or inductively, by the action of artificial disturbances. The type of dynamic transition that occurs depends on whether the stationary states are stable or unstable with small acoustic disturbances.

In connection with the possibility of combustion zone multiple states occurring under fixed conditions, a question of the nature of dynamic transition arises. Some observations of an open diffusion flame formed by an injector were carried out to reveal physical processes preceding the transition to vibratory combustion. The injector, with a configuration identical to the injector depicted in Fig. 16, had four injection elements with a radial introduction of methane into the flow of gaseous oxygen and air (Fig. 17). The parameter range corresponding to random alternation of flame stabilization modes accompanied by simultaneous wide-band noise level change was studied. Random change of flame stabilization modes occurred at separate fuel holes, both within one injection element and within a group of elements. Flame stabilization could be controlled by varying the air flow rate.

The following two stabilization modes were observed.

- 1) The flame envelops the whole base of the fuel jet over the periphery: the flame has a distinct pattern and a low level of wide-band noise (Fig. 18a).

2) The flame partly separates from the fuel jet, being stabilized in back streams behind the jet: the flame has no definite contour and is characterized by an increase in noise level (Fig. 18b).

It was discovered that after some period of the system being in the regime of random alternation of flame stabilization modes with fixed propellant flow rates, a catastrophic change of the flame pattern takes place on all injection elements simultaneously, and this change is accompanied with a sharp (by an order of magnitude) increase of noise. This combustion mode is characterized by a hysteresis zone in the region of the governing parameters (oxygen, air and methane flow rates). High-level noise has a self-oscillation nature.

Many observations showed that oscillation self-excitation occurs after the transition of the flame stabilization at the jet base to the stabilization in back streams, at least on two opposite jets of one of the four injection elements. Thus, the obtained experimental results demonstrate one of the causes of the irreproducible nature of the stability characteristics.

In practice, chamber process stability can be determined by estimating stability characteristics before and after introducing artificial disturbances. A substantial excess of decrement scatter over the accuracy of its determination at fixed conditions is also indicative of combustion process instability.

### VI. Conclusions

1) Liquid-propellant rocket engine reliability depends largely on the level of combustion chamber and/or gas generator process stability. This level should be rated with characteristics that give objective information about combustion stability. The application of pressure oscillation decrement and oscillation relaxation time as stability characteristics is reasoned theoretically. The decrement is defined from inherent combustion chamber noise at natural acoustic frequencies, and the relaxation time is defined from the decay of pressure oscillations induced by an artificial pulse disturbance at a certain relative maximum pressure peak. The effectiveness of these stability characteristics has been validated by experimental studies and the experience gathered in LRE development.

2) Some methods of oscillation decrement determination from random noise that is always present in the combustion chamber of an operating engine are devised and a theoretical and experimental estimation of their accuracy is made.

3) Disturbance devices were developed and investigated that allow application of pulse disturbances of a prescribed strength to the combustion chamber at a prescribed moment. Up to five disturbances can be applied to the chamber during one test.

4) Problems associated with stability evaluation were studied. It was illustrated by an example that the statistical character of self-oscillation excitation in LRE combustors is caused by the ambiguity of combustion zone stationary states at fixed feed system parameters. The tendency of the combustion zone to change stationary states can be revealed by applying pressure pulse disturbances to the combustion chamber.

## Chapter 11

## Liquid-Propellant Droplet Vaporization: A Rate-Controlling Process for Combustion Instability

W. A. Sirignano,\* J.-P. Delplanque,<sup>†</sup> C. H. Chiang,<sup>‡</sup> and R. Bhatia<sup>‡</sup>

*University of California, Irvine, Irvine, California 92717*

### I. Introduction

THE problem of combustion instability in liquid-propellant rockets is a continuing challenge. Any enclosed or restricted chamber has an infinite number of modes for resonant oscillation. The heat release associated with the combustion processes can potentially provide a driving mechanism for the acoustical oscillation. The acoustical pressure and velocity oscillations tend to cause an oscillation in the local burning rate. If the amplitude of the burning rate oscillation is large enough and if the phase between the burning rate and pressure oscillations is small enough, the instability can be driven. Often the amplitudes are sufficiently large to cause such increased heat transport rates that a structural failure occurs at the injector face or at the nozzle throat. Combustion instability research was very active during the two decades of the 1950s and 1960s, especially in relation to the Apollo program. Experience with liquid oxygen- (LOX-) kerosene propellants and impinging injectors indicated severe instability problems. A general rule is that the instability is more likely and becomes more severe in terms of damage as the energy release rate per unit volume increases or, in other words, as performance increases. The behavior is more complicated than this simple rule; instability probability depends on spatial distribution of the energy release rate, combustion time lag, damping forces, and chamber dimensions (or natural frequencies). The rule, however, is a useful guide.

#### A. Historical Perspective

During the 1950s and 1960s, some limited research was performed on the basic driving mechanism of the instability. Several researchers<sup>1-12</sup> examined fuel droplet vaporization as the rate-controlling phenomenon and as the basic driving

mechanism. Because of limitations of their analyses (explained later in the discussion on spray combustion, Sec. VIII), they could not successfully explain the cause of combustion instability. The most widely used description of the combustion process in analyses was the Crocco time lag description.<sup>1,13-15</sup> This was an ad hoc representation of the combustion process through the use of a small number of parameters (usually two). One of these parameters was the sensitive time lag, which was based on the concept that the combustion process had a time lag so that the burning rate at some instant depended on conditions experienced by the reactants for some short time duration prior to that instant. The time duration or time-lag magnitude itself depended on the conditions prior to the instant of burning. The average time lag and other ad hoc parameters were considered to be functions of propellant combinations and injector design only, yielding the hope for straightforward scaling of results from small combustors to large combustors. This method had limited success.

The most reliable method for preventing large-amplitude oscillations in liquid propellant rocket engines was to damp the oscillations through the use of baffles or acoustic liners. That is, energy was taken from the most unstable modes of oscillation. The science of preventing the addition of energy to the oscillations by modifying or controlling the basic combustion process was never really developed. There is reason to believe, however, that this science now can be rapidly developed and that new technology on the control of combustion instability can be advanced. There is still a need for this new technology since the engineering fixes through damping mechanisms lead to increased volume, increased weight, increased cooling requirements, and decreased performance.

The resurgence in interest in space and the renewed interest in liquid-propellant systems creates the need to re-examine the combustion instability problem in an organized and intense manner. There is recent interest in LOX-methane systems whose instability characteristics are not well understood. LOX-kerosene systems are under active consideration again, and their instability problems are well-known. The LOX-hydrogen systems have not experienced severe instability problems. There is no inherent reason, however, why LOX-hydrogen should be more stable than other systems, and our experience with LOX-hydrogen has been with a very narrow range of designs. New designs intended to improve performance could easily lead to serious instability problems.

Because of limitations in the methodologies of those times, theoretical analyses were performed mostly with small perturbation techniques for linearized or weakly nonlinear oscillations. Other nonlinear approaches involved gross and sometimes nonrealistic simplification of the basic governing equations. On the experimental side, pressure was the only instantaneous and localized point measurement that could be made; even there pressure was measured only at outer walls. Because of the high temperature, high-frequency behavior, velocity, and scalar point measurements could not be made instantaneously in the field.

#### B. Combustion Instability

In this section, a brief outline of the important concepts is given for reference. The sensitive time-lag model is also mentioned for completeness. Details, however, are provided elsewhere.<sup>1</sup>

Combustion instabilities are more likely to occur in systems designed for propulsion because of the high-energy densities and low losses associated with such

systems.<sup>1,13</sup> Combustion instability can be viewed as excitation of acoustical motions by heat addition. They are essentially unsteady motions of compressible gases. There are several types of combustion instabilities, usually classified using the range of frequency of the oscillations created. Of main interest are the high-frequency instabilities (or acoustic instabilities) because they are known to be the most destructive by grossly enhancing heat transfer. Note that the so-called POGO instabilities (coupling between low-frequency pressure oscillations, structural vibrations, and propellant feed system) have also been a major concern in the recent past but will not be discussed here.<sup>1,13</sup> There are other types of instability in a combustion chamber: hydrodynamic, chemical, thermodiffusive, and shock waves to cite just a few. These will not be treated here.<sup>14</sup> Combustion instabilities can be approximated by perturbations of the acoustic modes of the combustion chamber. Therefore, acoustical phenomena must be studied first. Acoustics is quite an ancient science; Lindsay<sup>15</sup> gives a historical perspective. Morse and Ingard give the necessary background of such phenomena.<sup>17</sup>

The issue at stake is to determine which of the many physical processes taking place in a combustion chamber organize into a mechanism that drives the instability. First, one must agree on the definitions of process and mechanism. There seems to be some disagreement in the combustion community regarding these two terms.<sup>2</sup> Our definitions follows. A mechanism is the organized sequence of events whereby a perturbation in the gas field affects a process that results in a change of the energy release rate, which, in turn, modifies the original perturbed quantity. A process is an event or a sequence of events by which a change is produced in at least one of the dependent variables (e.g., pressure, temperature, density, velocity). Vaporization, mixing, and chemical reaction are examples of processes.

The criterion used to assess if a mechanism can drive the instability is the so-called Rayleigh criterion, stated by Lord Rayleigh in 1894 in his pioneering work.<sup>18</sup> This criterion may be summarized as follows: A mechanism can drive the instability if the burning rate associated with it oscillates with a large enough amplitude and with a small enough phase lag with the pressure oscillation. That is, the mechanism's characteristic time is of the same order as the period of pressure oscillations. However, Lord Rayleigh was working on systems much simpler than liquid rocket engines, and the adaptation of his criterion to a more general system with chemical and phase changes is still the object of controversy. First, the response factor can be evaluated at each location in chamber or averaged over the entire combustor. The averaged approach is easier to apply and does provide an evaluation of the stability margin of the engine. The obtained response factor, however, is extremely dependent on the mode and frequency of oscillation and the engine operating conditions.<sup>2</sup>

The candidate mechanisms for liquid-propellant rocket combustion instability involve a coupling of the combustion chamber acoustics with any or some of the following processes: liquid injection, primary atomization, secondary atomization, chemical kinetics, vaporization and liquid heating, and mixing. A discussion of the relative importance of these mechanisms is provided in the next section.

The early attempts at describing analytically combustion instabilities in liquid-propellant engines were of two types: the time-lag model of Crocco and co-workers, and the vaporization model<sup>1-3,6,15</sup> of Priem and co-workers. The time-lag model probably originated in von Kármán's group in the early 1950s. Nevertheless, Crocco and his co-workers at Princeton University applied it to a liquid fuel system

and introduced the idea of a sensitive part of the time lag, which constitutes the highly successful and widely used sensitive time-lag theory. The sensitive time-lag model is heuristic. The basic idea spawns from the observation that, among the exchanges taking place in a combustion chamber, the type most relevant to instability are energy exchanges. Then, the continuous gasification process is modeled as a discontinuous occurrence; it is assumed that there is a finite time interval between the injection of an element of propellant and the release of its chemical energy. The perturbations in the heat release rate at  $t$  are largely due to the pressure and velocity perturbations which occurred at  $t - \tau$  in the reaction zone and are proportional to the intensity of the pressure (or velocity) heat release oscillation coupling modeled by the interaction index  $n$  (Refs. 1 and 15). The time lag is made of two parts: one that is constant and the other sensitive to pressure fluctuations. The existence of a time lag in the combustion process implies that instability is more likely to occur in the frequency range where the oscillation period is of the same order as the characteristic time for combustion. Bypassing the mathematical details, just note that the  $n$ - $\tau$  model accommodates longitudinal and transverse modes and uses both a small perturbation method (linear analysis) and nonlinear analysis for finite (although small) amplitudes.<sup>1</sup> The complete model is presented in a monograph by Crocco and Cheng.<sup>15</sup> The time lag and the interaction index can be regarded as empirical parameters. Hence, experimental data provided the needed parameters (average sensitive time lag and interaction index), yielding quantitatively accurate predictions on the stability of quite a few combustion systems.<sup>1</sup> The stability maps and the behavior of solutions of the  $n$ - $\tau$  model for nonlinear wave motion show how stability depends on the interaction index, the time lag, the type of instability (transverse, longitudinal, with or without shock), and the spatial distribution of combustion. Linear and nonlinear stability limits differ for extreme values of the time lag. This model allowed the treatment of the combustion instability problem without determining a physical link between the combustion rate and the fundamental processes involved.<sup>15, 19</sup> This approach is outdated, however, since today's goal is to understand the instability mechanism in order to model it as well as the resulting instability<sup>2</sup> more accurately. Instead, theoretical models taking proper account of the vaporization process and other physiochemical processes must be developed.

### II. Candidate Driving Mechanisms for Combustion Instability

Many potential mechanisms for combustion instability in liquid-propellant rockets have been identified. They involve coupling of the combustion acoustics with injection coupling, primary atomization, secondary atomization, vaporization, mixing, chemical kinetics, or any combination of these processes.

One may crudely view combustion in a liquid-propellant rocket motor as consisting of a sequence of processes. This sequence would be followed by an infinitesimally small element of propellant. In sequence, injection, primary atomization, secondary atomization, liquid heating, vaporization, gas-phase mixing and heating, gas-phase chemical reaction, and loss of some heat to fresh propellants are the processes. There are some caveats that should be added. The combustion is continuous, so that propellant elements injected at different times would not be necessarily in the same process at a given time. There is also a spatial distribution so that different elements injected at the same time can be in different processes at a given time. The details of any process for a given element can depend on both the

preceding processes for that element and all of the processes for other elements. For example, the vaporization rate for an element depends on the atomization process for that element which determines the droplet size. Vaporization rate also depends on the heat transferred from other propellant elements that have already burned.

Each of the processes has a duration or characteristic time associated with it. The time can vary substantially. If one of the times for the sequential processes is much longer than any of the rest and, in fact, much longer than the sum of the rest, the time for burning of that propellant element is essentially the characteristic time for the longest process. We refer to that particular process as rate controlling because the burning rate approximately equals the rate for that process.

Variation of pressure, temperature, and velocity in the chamber will affect these processes and, in particular, can affect the characteristic times and rates associated with these processes. Dynamic or frequency-dependent phenomena are expected. Any driving mechanism must pass certain tests. In particular, the chemical conversion rate (or burning rate) associated with the mechanism must respond adequately to fluctuations of pressure, velocity, and temperature. That is, for a given amplitude of pressure oscillation, the conversion rate must oscillate with a sufficiently large amplitude and a sufficiently small phase relative to the pressure oscillation. Even if the conversion rate responds to some other quantity, such as temperature or velocity, it is the amplitude and phase relative to the pressure amplitude and phase that is important, since the feedback of energy to the oscillation depends on the relationship to pressure. Because maximum amplitudes of pressure and velocity can occur at different positions in the chamber, this results in a complex relationship for feedback of energy to the combustor oscillation. A change in a parameter generally not only affects the amplitude and phase of the burning rate oscillation but also modifies the spatial distribution of the burning. The most important basic parameters are those related to the injector design or the propellant choice. Three types of mechanisms can be important in combustion instability. The first type is associated with a combustion process that is rate controlling and has a characteristic time of the same order as the period of oscillation. This process can respond strongly to oscillations of the pressure and velocity in the chamber. The question still remains whether the amplitude is sufficient and the phase is proper to overcome the damping mechanisms and to drive the oscillation.

If the process is not rate controlling, oscillations in its rate cannot significantly affect the burning rate and the feedback to the combustor oscillation. If the process has a characteristic time much longer than the period of oscillation, it generally cannot respond to the oscillation. That is, the frequency of the oscillation is too high for the process; there is insufficient time for the particular process to adjust to the oscillations of pressure and velocity. When the characteristic time of the process is very short compared to the oscillation, it can respond. Processes with short characteristic times, however, are generally not rate controlling. If they still are rate controlling, there is the additional difficulty that the process would only respond in a quasisteady manner. The dynamic response could result in larger amplitudes of burning rate than the quasisteady response. The second type of process is one that affects the characteristic time of some other rate-controlling process. An example of this type would be atomization, which has a characteristic time much shorter than the typical period of oscillation; however, pressure and velocity variations produce variations in the initial droplet size distribution which, in turn, affects the characteristic time of rate-controlling processes. This type of process can have a dramatic indirect effect on the oscillatory process.

A third type of mechanism also has an indirect influence. This type of mechanism affects the spatial distribution of the combustion. Therefore, it produces variation in the local response that affects the coupling with a particular mode of oscillation. The second and third types of mechanisms are actually concurrent actions of the same mechanism since a change in characteristic time of a combustion process as viewed from a Lagrangian frame has the impact of a change in combustion distribution as viewed from an Eulerian frame.

Each of the major processes related to combustion in liquid propellant rocket engines is discussed in the following.

#### A. Liquid Injection

The liquid feed system involves storage tasks, pumps, feed lines, and injection parts into the combustion chamber. The lengths and volumes (or components) of the feed system tend to be large so that characteristic response times tend to be much longer than 1 ms.

Injection coupling is defined to mean that oscillations in the combustion chamber and oscillations in the feed system are coupled and reinforcement occurs. If there is no significant coupling, the combustion chamber will oscillate with essentially constant mass flow through the injector ports.

Injector coupling tends to be most significant for low-frequency chamber oscillations because of the large characteristic time for the feed system. That is, the feed system time matches better with the residence time in the combustion chamber than with the period of oscillation for any of the acoustical oscillatory modes. In the low-frequency modes, the chamber pressure is approximately spatially uniform but time varying.

These low-frequency modes have been well understood for decades. Summerfield analyzed these modes<sup>1</sup> using a constant time-lag concept. Injector coupling is relatively easy to eliminate by isolation of the feed system. Increasing the pressure drop across the injection port is a standard process that isolates the feed system since, for large-pressure drops, a given pressure fluctuation in the chamber produces a small variation in pressure drop and, therefore, in the mass flow.

The fluctuation in the feed system could result in modifications of other processes involved in combustion of the propellants. For example, the jet velocity at the port would fluctuate, thus modifying the primary atomization process of one or both propellants. Initial droplet size and droplet velocity fluctuations would vary. This would produce variations in the characteristic times of other processes. Also, it would affect the spatial distribution of combustion in the chamber. Since the characteristic times for these other processes are much shorter than the period of oscillation in the low-frequency cases and since little sensitivity to spatial distribution of combustion occurs in those low-frequency cases, these effects are generally not significant in terms of instability. Of course, some exceptions might exist.

#### B. Primary Atomization

Various atomization schemes are employed in liquid-propellant systems. In one scheme called impinging jets, injection ports are designed to work as pairs or triplets with the jets colliding in order to enhance breakup into droplets. Upon impingement, sheets of liquid in a conical fanlike shape emerge. Here, the conical cross sections are not circular but rather more like ellipses with a very large ratio of semimajor to semiminor axes. Usually, the impinging streams consist of "like"

(identical) propellants so that liquid-phase mixing does not occur. This scheme is commonly used with LOX/RP1 propellants.

In another scheme involving coaxial jets, fuel and oxidizer are injected in parallel streams. This is commonly used for LOX/hydrogen and LOX/methane propellant combinations. In practice, LOX is always placed inside with the fuel on the outside.

At the high-injection velocities employed, the Rayleigh breakup mechanism is not of interest. Rather, the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability is the interesting mechanism. Surface and interface waves form and grow, causing distortion and ultimate breakup of the surface in this mechanism. Very little fundamental experimental and theoretical work<sup>20,21</sup> has been done on this mechanism. The characteristic wavelengths and periods of oscillation for these surface waves on the propellant streams are very small. An estimated frequency for these waves can be more than  $10^5$  cps. This characteristic time can be more than one order of magnitude lower than typical periods of oscillation for chamber instabilities. Variations in chamber conditions due to acoustic oscillations can be treated as quasisteady as far as primary atomization is concerned. The atomization process will not respond in a resonant fashion to chamber oscillations.

Strahle and Crocco<sup>22</sup> have shown by a linearized analysis that, in the absence of a resonant behavior and at low mean flow Mach numbers, fluctuations in droplet size and droplet number density do not cause the instability. The droplets move through the chamber at velocities much less than the speed of sound and carry the effect of initial size and number density. The kinematic wave resulting from the droplet initial conditions undulates more through the chamber than the pressure wave, which travels with an acoustic speed. This results in more undulation of the amplitude of the fluctuating source of burned gases that drives the instability. Because of the substantial undulation of the kinematic wave, there are many regions of both positive and negative reinforcement of the pressure wave. As a result, without a resonance effect, this phenomenon cannot produce a significant global effect since the positive contributions roughly equal the negative contributions.

Primary atomization is not projected to have a major direct effect on the driving mechanism of the instability. If the processes following it in the sequence do not respond significantly to oscillations of pressure and velocity, there would not be any sustained oscillation, according to linear theory. It is possible that a nonlinear perturbation could modify the conclusion. Since the issue relates more to the phase relationship between the source term and the pressure term rather than to an amplitude effect, however, it is not clear how nonlinearities would change the conclusion.

Note that atomization processes are quasisteady and, thus, do not respond differently to different frequencies in the range below  $10^4$  cps; therefore, this mechanism would not explain observed phenomena even if other factors, discussed earlier, were not present.

Atomization does affect initial droplet size distribution thereby influencing substantially droplet heating and vaporization. In this manner, it can affect combustion instability.

#### C. Secondary Atomization

Droplets that are formed by the primary atomization process can undergo further distortion and breakup. When smaller droplets result from a larger droplet, the process is called secondary atomization.

The surface tension tends to keep a droplet intact with a spherical shape. Aerodynamic pressure drag resulting from relative droplet-gas velocity tends to strain the droplet so that it assumes an oval shape with a decrease in the length parallel to the main flow direction and an increase in the transverse lengths. This can result in the "pinching off" of droplets.

Another mechanism involves a Kelvin–Helmholtz instability along the droplet surface. This results in the stripping of smaller droplets from the surface of the larger droplet.

Droplet distortion can significantly affect droplet drag and trajectory since the drag coefficient is modified. The likelihood for distortion, Kelvin–Helmholtz instability, and the pinching-off mechanism increases as the droplet Weber number increases. Secondary atomization tends to occur downstream, away from the dense spray regime.

The characteristic times associated with secondary atomization are much smaller than droplet vaporization and heating times. Also, they are much smaller than the typical periods of oscillation. Therefore, the same general conclusions can be made for secondary atomization as were made for primary atomization. It does not emerge as a strong candidate for direct feedback to the oscillation as a mechanism for combustion instability. There are, however, very important indirect ways in which the instability can be affected by secondary atomization.

#### D. Vaporization and Liquid Heating

Droplet vaporization and droplet heating should be considered as an integrated process. Heat from the high-temperature gaseous environment is transferred to the droplet largely by convective heating. The heat to the surface partially passes to the liquid interior raising the droplet temperature in the interior as well as at the surface. The remainder of the transferred heat sustains the phase change at the surface and increases the temperature of the vapors flowing away from the surface.

In practice, there is generally a relative velocity between the (LOX or fuel) droplet and the surrounding gas. Because of convection, the droplet heating rate and vaporization rate will depend on the Reynolds number based on this relative velocity. There will be a laminar boundary layer over the surface of the droplet. The shear stress at the surface will cause an internal circulation in the liquid droplet. This affects the transient heating of the liquid and the vaporization rate.

Below the critical pressure, a clear distinction can be made between the liquid droplet and the surrounding gas. The surface tension tends to keep the droplet spherical. The characteristic time for the liquid heating tends to be higher than the time for surface-layer heating. For kerosene-type fuel droplets, the heating time and droplet lifetime are of the same order, whereas for LOX droplets, the heating time would be longer than the droplet lifetime. In liquid-propellant rocket motors, periods of acoustic oscillation tend to be of the order of the droplet heating time, suggesting a potential for coupling.

The situation is more complicated at near-critical or supercritical pressures. The reduced surface tension allows deviation from spherical shapes. The increased gas density decreases or removes the distinction between the phases and increases the gas-phase heating time. A coupling with the acoustic oscillations can still be expected, although less is known about the details.

Several investigators<sup>1,3–11,23</sup> have pursued the vaporization as the key process in the driving mechanism for combustion instability in liquid-propellant rocket engines. Generally, vaporization is the slowest of the processes, and, thus, is the

rate-controlling process. A quasisteady response of the vaporization to combustion oscillations cannot provide sufficient feedback to drive the instability. Therefore, a dynamic or resonant response must occur if vaporization were to drive the instability. Strahle<sup>7-11</sup> has examined the gas-phase film and boundary layer surrounding a droplet to determine its oscillatory response. At the frequencies of interest, the heat and mass transport through the gas layer tend to oscillate in a quasisteady manner, without a resonance effect. Transient heating of the liquid interior was examined in Refs. 3-6 and 12. There was a dynamic response with the model<sup>3-6,12</sup> in the frequency range of interest; however, the amplitude of the vaporization rate was not sufficient to drive the instability. It was assumed that liquid temperature was uniform spatially through the interior, albeit time varying. The model effectively employed an infinite conductivity so that the heat transferred through the liquid surface immediately was distributed throughout the liquid interior. This kept the surface temperature unrealistically low; the amplitude of surface temperature and, consequently, the amplitude of vaporization are kept at reduced levels because of this assumption.

In recent years, transient droplet heating and vaporization has been studied<sup>23-37</sup> with a better modeling of heat and mass diffusion in the liquid phase. In particular, spatial gradients of temperature and concentration through the liquid are taken into account. In these more accurate situations, it is found that amplitudes of surface temperature and vaporization rate can be large enough to drive an oscillation.<sup>23,38</sup> The characteristic time for droplet heating is of the order of 1 ms and, therefore, commensurate with the practical periods of oscillation resulting in a strong dynamic response. Droplet heating time is, of course, dependent on initial droplet size. Some recent results<sup>38</sup> for liquid-fueled ramjets indicate that, along a stability limit, initial droplet diameter increases with the combustion chamber length (or the period of the natural oscillation).

The vaporization rate responds to fluctuations of both the ambient pressure and the relative gas-droplet velocity. It tends to be more sensitive to the latter. For transverse oscillations, the pressure and velocity tend to be in phase so that the pressure sensitivity and the velocity sensitivity can be reinforcing.

The theory for oscillatory droplet vaporization can explain the driving of combustion instabilities in situations where hydrocarbon fuels are employed and chamber operating pressures are subcritical. The theory must be extended to understand more fully situations where the pressure is supercritical or the vaporization of the liquid oxygen is rate controlling (hydrogen or methane fuel, for example).

In the supercritical-pressure case, the temperature will vary significantly from the ambient supercritical value to a subcritical value in the droplet. The energy of vaporization is zero in the supercritical-pressure domain. Properties will vary substantially over the droplet, and its surrounding gas film because of the wide variation in temperature; characteristic diffusion times can, therefore, be very different in different zones. This means that the supercritical-pressure case shares certain generic characteristics with the subcritical pressure case with regard to the response to ambient oscillations. That is, transport processes within certain regions of the field could potentially resonate at some frequency. Again, the theory here is not fully developed. Note that the supercritical case allows a greater likelihood for secondary atomization due to the reduced value of the surface tension.

In the case of oxygen droplets at subcritical pressures, the latent heat of vaporization is very low and the transfer number is high so that the droplet vaporization is very fast. The magnitudes of the temperature gradients in the liquid phase remains

to be determined. Potentially, they can be large. The sensitivity to fluctuations also remains to be determined.

In summary, we can model an oscillatory vaporizing spray flow reasonably well for standard hydrocarbon type fuels at subcritical conditions. For supercritical conditions or for oxygen vaporization, the models have greater uncertainties. The vaporization rate is typically rate controlling and responds in a resonant fashion for frequencies of practical interest. Therefore, vaporization is a most prominent candidate as a driving mechanism for instability.

#### E. Mixing

After the two propellants vaporize, they must mix with each other before reaction can occur. The mixing process will be turbulent since Reynolds numbers based on distance between injector elements and propellant velocities will be in the range of  $10^4$ – $10^6$ . This distance is relevant for impinging like-on-like injectors. For like-on-unlike impingement or coaxial injectors, the diameter of the injection orifice or port is more relevant. In that case, we see a one order of magnitude reduction in the Reynolds number.

A characteristic time for turbulent mixing can be estimated to be less than 1 ms at its upper limit and as small as  $10\ \mu\text{s}$ . Some very small fraction of the propellant requires a time to mix that is substantially longer. That small fraction accounts for only a very small amount of released energy. Mixing, then, is generally faster than vaporization so that it cannot be rate controlling. It has minor impact on the distribution of the energy release through the chamber.

In this discussion, only mixing and transport on a scale larger than the droplet size or than the size of the boundary layer around the droplet is considered. The mixing and transport in the boundary layer and near wake of the droplet has been considered as part of the vaporization process. Mixing, as defined here, includes both the process of change of local composition and the transfer of heat from burned propellants to the fresh propellants. Because of the short characteristic time, the mixing process would tend to resonate at higher frequencies than are of practical interest. Mixing is not a promising candidate for a combustion instability driving mechanism.

#### F. Chemical Kinetics

After the propellants are well mixed and heated, they can react. At the high pressures and high temperatures associated with rocket combustion chambers, the chemical reaction rate will be large. The characteristic time for the chemical reaction will be at least one order of magnitude smaller than the vaporization time.

Variations in the chemical reaction time due to fluctuations in pressure and temperature will not be significant compared to variations in the vaporization time. Oscillations in the chemical rate will not, therefore, produce significant oscillations in the overall burning rate. Furthermore, there is no potential for a resonant response of the chemical kinetics in the frequency range of interest.

For these reasons, chemical kinetics is not viewed as an interesting driving mechanism for combustion instability in liquid-propellant rocket motors. Note that, for certain experimental configurations where propellants are introduced as premixed gases, we can see the importance of the chemical reaction as a driving mechanism. The chemistry, however, would respond in a quasisteady manner over a wide range of frequencies. No resonant phenomenon has been observed; for

example, an increase in the chamber length does not modify the stability of the combustion process.

### III. Early Models for Oscillatory Droplet Vaporization

Contrary to the sensitive time-lag approach, these models are based on a tentative description of the actual physicochemical processes. Strahle<sup>7-11</sup> investigated unsteady droplet combustion linearly. He neglected the thermal wave in the liquid, and his results did not provide sufficient evidence to indicate a potential for vaporization to drive the instability. Priem and Heidmann<sup>12</sup> assumed finite thermal inertia and assumed a uniform liquid temperature that was equivalent to an infinite conductivity assumption. Their model was quasisteady and one dimensional and, since the solution procedure was numerical, nonlinearities were less of a challenge. Priem and Guentert<sup>3</sup> and Priem<sup>4</sup> first showed that the stability was affected by vaporization and could be controlled by varying the characteristics of the vaporization process. This model did not yield response factors high enough to reach a clear conclusion on the potential driving of the instability by the vaporization process.<sup>1</sup> Priem and Guentert<sup>3</sup> compared the stability maps obtained by assuming that 1) the local instantaneous burning rate is equal to the local vaporization rate and 2) it is equal to the chemical reaction rate. Their results showed that for large burning rate parameters (which is the case in rocket engines) the vaporization model yields instabilities for smaller disturbances. Of course, due to the limitations of digital computers in the early 1960s, ad hoc assumptions had to be made in order to render the solution tractable. Heidmann and Wieber<sup>5</sup> showed that the  $n-\tau$  model is in good agreement with the response obtained from the Priem-Heidmann model in the region of high response (low frequency). Crocco<sup>19</sup> noted that the conclusions of Priem and Guentert<sup>3</sup> depend more on the ad hoc simplifications than on the original physics of their combustion configuration and that much of the background flow nonlinearities had to be omitted in the computations. Nevertheless, addition of transverse velocity effects to this model could lead to nonlinear instability.

Recently, Nguyen and Muss<sup>39</sup> investigated the open-loop response of the burning rate of a droplet array for specified acoustic oscillations in the combustion chamber. They used an extension of the Agosta-Hammer<sup>40</sup> vaporization response model to mixed radial (R) and tangential (T) modes up to 8R and 8T. This model was basically an evolution of the model used by Priem. Infinite rate chemical kinetics and fast gas-phase mixing were assumed; hence, vaporization and burning rate were identified. Uniform droplet temperature, quasisteady heat and mass transfer processes between the droplet and the surrounding and constant liquid density were also assumed. The droplet temperature is estimated from an overall energy balance. Viscous effects of the gas on the droplets were included, but the reciprocal was neglected. They tested various assumptions concerning heat transfer within the droplet: finite conductivity with spherically symmetric droplet temperature, zero conductivity, and infinite conductivity (uniform temperature). Then they compared their results<sup>39</sup> with experimental measurements of droplet radius history in the case of a droplet vaporizing in a hot cross flowing airstream. The uniform temperature model gave the best fit.

Usually, when the "film" theory is used to model droplet combustion, the film surrounding the droplet is assumed to be quasisteady. To a large extent, this assumption is legitimate, since the characteristic time for heat diffusion through

the film,  $\tau_H$ , is typically two orders of magnitude smaller than the droplet lifetime. This assumption is even more accurate at high Reynolds numbers. However, Williams<sup>41</sup> proved that neglecting the transient of the droplet heating may lead to a 20% error in the evaluation of the total vaporization time in a quiescent environment. Many investigators<sup>42-46</sup> studied transient effects on droplet vaporization and burning. The main conclusion was that although the quasisteady theory gave a good estimate of droplet burning rates, it failed to predict correctly the evolution of the flame-to-droplet diameter ratio. Meanwhile, the unsteady theory predicted that the flame radius increased first and then decreased to zero,<sup>42</sup> thus corroborating experimental observations.<sup>44</sup> Furthermore, at high pressure and temperature, properties in the gas film were significantly modified, and  $\tau_H$  was comparable to the droplet lifetime, which reinforced the intrinsic unsteadiness. The transient character of droplet vaporization and combustion under these conditions cannot be neglected.<sup>47</sup> Some investigators indicated that the quasisteady theory was not valid for reduced pressures above 0.1 in a stagnant environment.<sup>48</sup>

On the other hand, the very high pressures and temperatures encountered in a liquid-rocket combustion chamber imply that both the gas and the liquid phase may deviate substantially from their usual behavior. Specifically, the ideal gas assumption is not valid under these conditions, and the liquid-vapor equilibrium is not correctly represented by the classical laws and approximations. These phenomena complicate significantly the modeling of droplet vaporization and burning in such regimes but may have a critical importance in the liquid-rocket combustion instability phenomenon. As discussed by Wieber<sup>49</sup> over 30 years ago, near the critical point a small change in pressure might lead to violent boiling of the oxygen droplet, thereby supporting the combustion instability. Wieber also noticed that if the chamber pressure is so high that the droplet reached a supercritical state and became a vapor puff, the rate-controlling mechanism for combustion instability might be the vapor diffusion into the gaseous environment. Therefore, determining accurately whether the liquid drop gets close enough to the critical state and exhibits such a behavior is primordial, and a large amount of work was devoted during the past two decades by the combustion community to investigate the vaporization of a spherically symmetric drop in a quiescent environment under high pressure and temperature.

Various researchers have improved on Wieber's work, most of them in the domain of hydrocarbon fuel.<sup>26,27,48,50-52</sup> Lazar and Faeth<sup>50</sup> noted that Wieber did not account for high-pressure phase equilibrium, nonideal gas effects, effects of pressure on physical properties, and gas solubility in the liquid phase. They included these phenomena but considered a simplified droplet model neglecting all transient phenomena and convection. The agreement between the computed equilibrium temperatures and experimentally obtained data on suspended droplet in a microgravity environment was good. Manrique and Borman<sup>51</sup> used a somewhat more sophisticated quasisteady model and showed that if the ambient pressure was high enough, steady-state conditions were not attained. In 1972, Matlosz et al.<sup>48</sup> combined both transient theory and high-pressure effects on the phase equilibrium for a hexane/nitrogen system and provided experimental measurements supporting their results.<sup>51</sup> They<sup>48</sup> concluded that both phenomena must be included for correct predictions. They also noted that accurate methods to compute physical properties, and more specifically mass diffusion coefficients, under such regimes were crucial.

Once the whole droplet has reached a supercritical state, however, modeling is possible. The theory of supercritical combustion for such gas pockets was initially developed by Spalding.<sup>53</sup> He assumed that the droplet can be replaced by a point source of vapor and showed the importance of unsteadiness. He concluded that under supercritical conditions, the burning time increased with the cube root of the pressure. Rosner<sup>54</sup> extended this theory by considering a distributed source. More detailed numerical simulations were performed<sup>55,56</sup> showing that the burning time under supercritical conditions was shorter than under subcritical conditions.

### IV. Opportunities of Modern Times

Now in the 1990s, we can benefit from the methodologies of computational fluid dynamics and of nonintrusive laser diagnostics. Fully nonlinear coupled systems can be analyzed. Measurements of velocity, temperature, and concentration can be made locally under high-temperature, oscillatory conditions. Clearly, the potential exists to learn much more about the driving mechanisms and other characteristics of combustion instability.

As numerical methods and computing power are improving, the mechanistic approaches seem to be able to yield more interesting and insightful results. The limitations of approaches such as the  $n$ - $\tau$  model reside mainly in their heuristic character. They do not provide a description of the combustion process but represent it with a time-lag concept.<sup>15</sup> These approaches are linear so that their response factor really applies to cases where the linear approximation is valid. When nonlinearities are included, the effects of the combustion response nonlinearity are excluded.<sup>1,15</sup> Vaporization models, however, allow the inclusion of vaporization and combustion nonlinearities and, therefore, yield a nonlinear response factor. Furthermore, in the simple version of the  $n$ - $\tau$  model, the interaction index and the sensitive time lag are uniform in the chamber. Crocco and his co-workers extended this analysis<sup>1</sup> to include velocity and displacement sensitivities (in some limited configurations). Because of the phenomenological nature of this approach, however, the values of all of the parameters involved have to be derived from experimental data, which precludes applications.<sup>57</sup> Vaporization models do not suffer from this limitation.

Since the 1960s, there has been substantial advancement in the understanding of basic combustion phenomena. Understanding of spray combustion, including transient droplet heating and vaporization, has advanced tremendously. Mixing of coflowing streams of fluids is now much better understood. Our knowledge of atomization processes and chemical kinetics has also advanced substantially. The research that led to these advancements addressed automotive combustion, gas turbine combustion, ramjet combustion, and industrial combustion problems rather than liquid rocket combustion. Nevertheless, liquid-propellant combustion research can build upon the recently established foundations.

### V. Spherically Symmetric Models

The first step in droplet vaporization and combustion modeling is the simulation of the spherically symmetric vaporization of a droplet in a quiescent environment, with no gas motion other than that created by the Stefan flow and thermal expansion for the reaction zone. These models are considered next with an emphasis on high-pressure and supercritical environments. It should be noted in advance that velocity

coupling is the major influence on droplet vaporization so that spherically symmetric vaporization models have little or no value in explaining combustion instability.

Recent studies<sup>52</sup> concluded that the droplet vaporizes completely before the liquid surface reaches its critical temperature, but the enthalpy of vaporization was approximated by the latent heat of vaporization, which was proven to be quite inaccurate.<sup>48,51</sup> Extension to the case of a multicomponent hydrocarbon droplet was contributed by Hsieh et al.<sup>26</sup> in a detailed numerical analysis that is too computer time consuming to be used in a larger spray combustion code. Umemura<sup>58</sup> showed that the mass diffusion coefficient must be zero at the interface, whereas the mass flux remains finite. This should affect greatly vaporization rate predictions.

Although liquid oxygen (LOX)/hydrogen ( $H_2$ ) systems are currently being used for the Space Shuttle main engine and developed for the European launcher Ariane V because of the higher thrust they provide, only recent contributions<sup>28,59</sup> deal with the case of a LOX droplet vaporizing at high pressure. Indeed, the large molecular weight and temperature differences between the liquid surface and the ambient gas, their consequences on thermophysical property variations, and the disparity of the characteristic times result in increased numerical problems and make LOX/ $H_2$  cases even more complex. Litchford and Jeng<sup>59</sup> used the quasisteady film theory developed for subcritical droplet vaporization and the appropriate high-pressure phase-equilibrium relations. They found that the droplet surface can reach the critical state for reduced ambient pressure slightly above a value of unity.

The singular behavior occurring when a thermodynamic system goes from a subcritical state to a supercritical state has not been thoroughly investigated yet, and the necessary knowledge to model the vaporization and burning of a droplet going through the critical point is still lacking.<sup>58</sup>

The case of an isolated liquid oxygen droplet vaporizing in a supercritical quiescent environment was studied.<sup>29</sup> Effects of the gas-phase unsteadiness and effects of near-critical conditions were studied. First, unsteady spherically symmetric combustion of a single droplet in a quiescent surrounding gas was modeled, which corresponds to a film extending from the droplet surface to infinity. Combustion was included here and, although we were really interested in the unsteady effects on LOX vaporization in gaseous hydrogen, the case of a hexane droplet vaporizing in air was also treated as a reference case to provide a validation of the method used by comparison with classical results. In the cases studied, pressure and temperature were high enough so that unsteadiness in the film had to be considered, but the values near the surface were sufficiently below the mixture critical point for the real-gas mixture effects on phase-equilibrium and latent heat of vaporization to be neglected and for the usual liquid density expression to be used. Nonuniform and time-varying properties were considered. The density of the liquid, however, was assumed to remain constant. The effects of near-critical conditions were predicted using phase-equilibrium relations and thermophysical property expressions valid over the considered range. The pertinence of including each phenomenon specific to near-critical conditions in droplet vaporization modeling was evaluated. Here, relative motion between the droplet and the ambient gas was not considered. Thereby, spherical symmetry resulted.

Yang et al.<sup>27</sup> reported pressure-coupled vaporization results at supercritical conditions for hydrocarbons burning in air. Their model, however, did not allow for relative velocity effects that are known to be predominant. They found the vaporization response changed significantly when the critical mixing conditions were

reached. Nevertheless, it should be noted that they did not indicate clearly how the mass flux was computed at the critical interface.

The exchange of mass, momentum, and energy across the critical interface becomes an important issue in spray calculations. Supercritical sprays can be conveniently described as two-phase fluids. The supercritical fluid can be considered as the continuous phase whereas the subcritical pockets of fluids can be considered as the discrete phase or droplets.

### VI. Convective Droplet Studies

Classical droplet vaporization theory presents the well-known  $d^2$  law. This analysis, however, assumes that the droplet is traveling at the velocity of the gas and that there is spherical symmetry with no transient behavior. It is known that this theory has rather limited applications. The relative motion between the droplet and the ambient gas (which is nonzero in most cases) creates the convection that increases the rates of heat and mass transfer over the values for the spherically symmetric droplet. Furthermore, the shear force on the liquid surface causes an internal circulation that enhances the heating of the liquid. As a result, vaporization rate increases with increasing Reynolds number. For droplets with initial radii of 25  $\mu\text{m}$  and greater, the time for velocity relaxation due to drag is comparable or greater than the droplet lifetime.<sup>24</sup> These and other effects, like internal circulation, neglected by the classical droplet vaporization theory, lead to considerably smaller characteristic lengths and times for liquid-phase heat and mass transfer. The strong coupling among the drag, heat transfer, mass transfer, relative droplet velocity, and internal circulation necessitates a numerical solution.

#### A. Subcritical Environment

Tong and Sirignano<sup>23</sup> examined the effect of an oscillatory field (pressure and velocity) on droplet vaporization. They used an isolated droplet model but combined the vaporization rates, including the effects of the phase at injection, to obtain the equivalent response of the spray. They showed that the oscillatory part of the vaporization rate in phase with pressure is sufficient to sustain instability. Their version of the Rayleigh criterion is that "the growth or decay of the wave is determined by the net in-phase or out-of-phase energy or mass addition." They note that earlier models<sup>3-12</sup> could not prove that vaporization was the driving mechanism for instability, but these models either neglected thermal inertia or assumed a time varying but uniform droplet temperature. In a hot environment, the droplet vaporization rate is large; thus, the heating time and the droplet lifetime are of the same order. Tong and Sirignano's model is one-dimensional and isentropic, and proper account of internal circulation is taken through a vortex model.<sup>25,30</sup> Using this model showed that droplet heating and vaporization are unsteady and that internal temperature profiles are nonuniform during most of the droplet lifetime,<sup>25</sup> thereby refuting the assumptions used by Strahle<sup>7</sup> and Priem and Guentert,<sup>3</sup> Priem,<sup>4</sup> and Priem and Heidmann.<sup>12</sup> Gas-phase heat and mass transfer rates are modeled by an average between the stagnation point and shoulder region. This model was shown to be in good agreement with results of the exact solution of the axisymmetric Navier-Stokes equations. The continuous droplet size distribution is discretized using a finite number of droplet groups.<sup>23</sup> The fuel is hexane (10 atm, 1000 K,  $\Delta V = 25$  m/s, and  $D \simeq 95$   $\mu\text{m}$ ). The frequency range investigated is

100–1000 Hz; hence, the droplet lifetime and period of oscillation are of the same order and, therefore, the droplet behavior is significantly affected by the phase point at which the droplet is injected. This is taken into account here when computing the overall response. To estimate the importance of the component of the vaporization rate in phase with the pressure Tong and Sirignano<sup>23</sup> evaluated

$$G \equiv \int_0^{2\pi} m' p' d\theta \bigg/ \int_0^{2\pi} p'^2 d\theta \quad (1)$$

For vaporization to be able to drive longitudinal mode instability,  $G \geq (\gamma + 1)/2\gamma$  ( $\gamma \simeq 1.2$ ) is needed.<sup>15</sup> (Note that this assumes concentrated combustion. The minimum value of  $G$  to drive instability with distributed combustion will be higher.)

It is assumed by Tong and Sirignano<sup>23</sup> that vaporization is rate controlling; i.e., it occurs much slower than the mixing and chemical reactions, so that the burning rate is identified with the vaporization rate. The model is quasisteady in the gas phase. This is legitimate for frequencies corresponding to an oscillation period much smaller than the diffusion time across the gas-phase boundary layer, hence for frequencies lower than a few kilo hertz. Five types of oscillatory fields were investigated: pressure oscillations only, velocity oscillations only, traveling wave, standing wave, and a one-dimensional shock-wave model.<sup>60</sup> They<sup>23</sup> showed that the effects of velocity oscillations are predominant and that the oscillatory vaporization rate increases as the Mach number of the mean flow decreases. In the traveling wave case, vaporization is found to be driving at all frequencies investigated. In the standing wave case, however, vaporization is driving (marginally) only at low frequencies. Important nondimensional groups were identified in the search for the resonant frequencies:  $f R_0^2/\alpha$ , the Reynolds number based on initial droplet diameter and relative velocity, and the relative pressure and velocity fluctuation amplitudes. The main conclusion of Tong and Sirignano's work<sup>23</sup> is that if droplet vaporization (without coupling to atomization) is the controlling mechanism, self-sustained acoustical longitudinal mode oscillation can occur in the combustion chamber. The oscillations are almost always self-sustained for traveling waves, seldom for standing sinusoidal waves, and sometimes for the shock-wave oscillation.

Culick<sup>13</sup> challenges Tong and Sirignano's conclusions<sup>23</sup> that unsteady rate-controlling droplet vaporization provides a potential mechanism for driving combustion instabilities. Culick argues that if all terms are included and if combustion is ignored, vaporizing droplets cause damping and not driving. We believe that Culick has a semantical difficulty. Certainly, he is correct that vaporization absorbs heat rather than releases heat. Vaporization, however, can control the burning rate so that the characteristic times associated with the energy release are the vaporization times. In this sense, vaporization can be a rate-controlling process that is key to the driving mechanism.

The model used by Tong and Sirignano is valid only at high Reynolds number for the droplet. This precludes its use in situations where the relative velocity might change sign, which is the case in most situations. Assumptions of constant gas-phase thermophysical properties are made in the gas phase, and correction factors are used to account for surface blowing effects on the laminar boundary layer. Since then, Abramzon and Sirignano<sup>31</sup> defined a model that does not have this limitation. This model differs significantly from the one used by Tong and

Sirignano.<sup>23</sup> Internal heating is approximated using the effective diffusivity concept. Influence of Stefan convection on temperature and species profiles in the gas film as well as variable thermophysical properties and nonunitary Lewis number are included. Hence, significantly different results can be expected. Abramzon and Sirignano's model has not been used in a liquid rocket combustion instability study, but the authors could show in a simplified case that the vaporization rate is significantly affected by gas velocity oscillations. Bhatia and Sirignano<sup>38</sup> applied this model to a one-dimensional analysis of ramjet instability. They found that vaporization is rate controlling and identified the ratio of oscillation period to droplet heating time and the ratio of residence time to droplet heating time as important parameters. Turbulent mixing and transverse transport were not included in this study. Molavi<sup>61</sup> and Molavi and Sirignano<sup>62</sup> modeled combustion instability in a two-dimensional dump combustor using this droplet model. Turbulent mixing was included, but due to high numerical diffusion no precise conclusion could be drawn concerning the controlling processes. Note that for transverse oscillations in cylindrical geometries, pressure and velocity tend to be in phase and thus can be reinforcing.

Patnaik<sup>32</sup> and Patnaik et al.<sup>33</sup> developed an axisymmetric model that used a stream function and vorticity approach in the liquid phase and could accommodate variable density in the gas phase. The constant properties used in the calculation, however, were evaluated at ambient conditions and, as a result, the computed quantities were overestimated. Chiang et al.<sup>34</sup> developed an advanced droplet vaporization model with fewer assumptions and with the intention of creating a reference model against which simpler models could be measured. This axisymmetric, single-droplet model includes effects of surface blowing, transient heating, and internal circulation. Variable gas-phase properties are taken into account and viscosity variations in the liquid phase are also calculated. The formulation for the gas and the liquid phases of the axisymmetric droplet problem complete with boundary, interface, and initial conditions can be found in Chiang.<sup>35</sup> A complete primitive variable approach for both gas and liquid phases is given in Chiang and Sirignano.<sup>36</sup> The results given in this chapter are based on that approach.

#### B. Supercritical Environment

Most rocket engine combustors are operated in the very high-pressure domain where fuel droplets may vaporize at near- or even supercritical conditions. Hence, an understanding of fundamental transport processes underlying high pressure fuel-droplet vaporization is needed.

There are several mandatory considerations for both the spherically symmetric and the convective cases to extend the subcritical droplet vaporizing model to deal with the ambient pressure in the range from the near-critical region to the supercritical region. They are summarized in the following. Note that because of various approximations the quantitative accuracy of the model is limited.

- 1) A comprehensive calculation of variations of thermophysical properties with respect to temperature for each species component is necessary. The high-pressure correction, the mixing rules to evaluate the thermodynamic properties, and the quantum gas behavior of hydrogen vapor must be considered.

- 2) The real gas effect in the high-pressure case can be included in the gas-phase equation of state by incorporating a compressibility factor. A modified Redlich-Kwong<sup>63</sup> equation of state with the mixing rules of Chueh and Prausnitz<sup>64</sup> will serve

this purpose. The enthalpy of vaporization is derived from the equation of state by using the fugacity equation. Since the swelling effect of the droplet vaporization at the critical state may be very significant, a primitive variable approach is required to analyze the internal motion and thermal and mass transport within the droplet.

3) The solubility of the fuel vapor in the liquid phase must be considered, and it makes a multicomponent droplet formulation necessary. The principle of equal temperature, pressure, and the fugacity of both phases for phase equilibria is used to compute the surface mass fraction of species for gas and liquid. A brief description of the new phase equilibrium conditions at the droplet interface is given next.

The thermodynamic equilibrium of a mixture gives

$$T^\ell = T^g, \quad P^\ell = P^g, \quad f_i^\ell = f_i^g \quad (2)$$

which ultimately presents the following system of equations to be solved:

$$x_{O_2}^\ell \times \phi_{O_2}^\ell(x_{O_2}^\ell, x_{H_2}^\ell, T, P) = x_{O_2}^g \times \phi_{O_2}^g(x_{O_2}^g, x_{H_2}^g, T, P) \quad (3)$$

$$x_{H_2}^\ell \times \phi_{H_2}^\ell(x_{O_2}^\ell, x_{H_2}^\ell, T, P) = x_{H_2}^g \times \phi_{H_2}^g(x_{O_2}^g, x_{H_2}^g, T, P) \quad (4)$$

A phase equilibrium diagram and enthalpy of vaporization from this analysis is given in Fig. 1. The following interface equations for a multicomponent fluid are taken.

Conservation of species:

$$\left[ \dot{m}_v Y_i - \rho D_{ij} \frac{\partial}{\partial r} Y_i \right]_{r^+} = \left[ \dot{m}_v Y_i - \rho D_{ij} \frac{\partial}{\partial r} Y_i \right]_{r^-} \quad (5)$$

Conservation of energy:

$$\begin{aligned} -k \frac{\partial T}{\partial r} \Big|_{r^-} &= k \frac{\partial T}{\partial r} \Big|_{r^+} + \left[ \dot{m}_v Y_{O_2} - \rho D_{ij} \frac{\partial}{\partial r} Y_{O_2} \right]_{r^+} \\ &\quad \times (\Delta \bar{H}_{v,O_2} - \Delta \bar{H}_{v,H_2}) + \dot{m}_v \Delta \bar{H}_{v,H_2} \end{aligned} \quad (6)$$

where  $\dot{m}_v = \rho(V - \dot{r})_{r^+}$

4) A technique is required to locate the gas/liquid interface and to compute the regression rate due to vaporization as well as phase change across the critical surface with continuous density and temperature gradients at the surface.

Convective effects were considered by Delplanque and Sirignano<sup>65</sup> The extended film model of Abramzon and Sirignano<sup>31</sup> was used here. This model was built on the classical film model to include the effect of blowing on boundary-layer thickness and profile distortion. Internal circulation effects were included using the effective diffusivity model.<sup>31</sup> The high-pressure phase equilibrium computation method already described was used here unmodified. Because the droplet surface temperature may reach the critical mixing value, the surface tension coefficient may become vanishingly small. This allows fluid removal from the droplet surface by shearing, thereby impeding the heating of the droplet surface temperature to its critical mixing value.

The enhanced heat transfer and mass transfer due to convection cause the surface of a LOX droplet vaporizing in hot gaseous hydrogen at a pressure supercritical for

The reviewed literature indicates that the stripping breakup mode would indeed greatly affect the droplet behavior and may not be omitted in the model definition. In addition, the breakup times for the stripping mode found in the literature are much smaller than the droplet lifetime estimated with a simple vaporization and burning model; this could have significant effects on liquid rocket combustion instability study.

Delplanque and Sirignano<sup>65</sup> numerically investigated this phenomenon. The physical properties of liquid oxygen and a surrounding gaseous mixture of oxygen and hydrogen were carefully evaluated to compute the relevant nondimensional numbers and assess if the boundary-layer stripping mode was likely to be dominant according to the criteria found in the literature. Next, a simple analysis<sup>66,67</sup> was used to include, at least roughly, the boundary-layer stripping mechanism in a simple one-dimensional model without increasing unrealistically computation times. They also modified the boundary-layer analysis to incorporate Stefan flow effects.

Their results showed that, in an environment typical for liquid rocket engines, a LOX droplet undergoes boundary-layer stripping, which had two important effects on the droplet behavior. First, stripping significantly reduced the droplet lifetime

(to 0.24 ms in the base case or more than one order of magnitude less than the value predicted without stripping). Hence, the smaller characteristic time introduced by this phenomena must be considered in liquid rocket combustion instability studies. Furthermore, stripping precluded, in most cases, heating of the droplet surface to the critical mixing conditions. Blowing reduced the stripping rate and, therefore, increased the predicted droplet lifetime ( $\approx 13\%$ ). Order of magnitude comparisons with experiment indicated that the stripping rate was controlled mechanically, by the size of the viscous layer, rather than thermally.

In the pressure range investigated ( $Pr = 0.8-2.5$ ), the computed droplet lifetime was shown to exhibit a minimum at  $Pr = 1$  if stripping was not included, whereas  $Pr = 1$  corresponded to a maximum of the droplet lifetime with stripping.

In a recent experimental study,<sup>68</sup> *n*-heptane droplets gasifying at supercritical conditions with forced convection exhibited behaviors similar to those described by theory.<sup>65</sup> At low-convection intensities, the gasification regime was a continuous regression of the droplet surface. At higher convection intensities the droplets underwent what the authors<sup>68</sup> qualified as an "enhanced supercritical" gasification regime where the droplets deformed significantly and were "partially convected away as a dense vapor cloud." This was not quite a secondary breakup in the stripping mode as is described in the present study, but the largest relative velocities considered in these experiments<sup>68</sup> were one order of magnitude smaller than those typical of rocket engine conditions. More experimental studies of this kind are needed to validate the present model. Experimental data are needed to validate the values used for the effective mass flux quality and the mist temperature in the evaluation of the heat transfer effect of stripping.

In the preliminary unpublished work conducted by Chiang and Sirignano,<sup>36</sup> a calculation is performed to study vaporization behavior before the droplet reaches the critical mixing state. The changes of properties at the interface occur very rapidly during the droplet vaporization. Diffusion length scales are reduced at the elevated pressure. The transport rates are faster than those in the low-pressure case; hence, the droplet lifetime is shorter. As a result, a very small time step is mandatory to ensure accuracy. Figure 2 indicates that radius increases with time due to the swelling effect of droplet as well as the condensation of vapor. The reduced enthalpy of vaporization also contributes to the fast vaporization of the droplet.
