The enthalpy of vaporization shown in Fig. 3 is significantly reduced from the conventional "latent heat." A remarkable condensation of gas-phase vapor occurs at the early droplet lifetime. The vaporization begins as the surface temperature increases.

The compressibility factors (averaged around the azimuthal direction) for the gas and liquid phases at the interface become equal when the critical mixing state is reached. The two phases merge into one continuous phase at that point. Since the critical mixing state highly depends on temperature and mass fraction, the droplet surface at different locations will reach the critical mixing state at different times. The diffusivity for the liquid phase is, in general, two orders of magnitude less than that of the gas phase. As a result, most of the diffusing vapors are concentrated in the boundary-layer region at the interface.

To advance this high-pressure droplet model to deal with the vaporization at supercritical conditions, two major difficulties in the calculation must be addressed: 1) the formulation of boundary conditions, especially to trace the location of the droplet interface and 2) more accurate calculation of the near-critical properties for the fluid near the droplet surface.

### VII. Response to an Oscillatory Environment

The model<sup>65</sup> for LOX-droplet vaporization is applied to prototypical cases pertinent to liquid rocket combustion instabilities.<sup>69</sup> The response of a LOX droplet to oscillatory ambient conditions over a wide range of frequencies is computed. The effects of stripping, pressure fluctuation, and mean pressure on the response are evaluated.

In an oscillatory environment, the effects of relative velocity fluctuations are predominant and cannot be overlooked in combustion instability studies. Effects of pressure fluctuations on the critical interface location appear to be minor in the cases investigated.

It was shown that the gasification process, with or without stripping, has enough potential to drive longitudinal mode combustion instabilities, under the simplifying assumptions used in this work. Furthermore, the peak frequency for the computed response factor is correlated to the droplet lifetime. Therefore, secondary atomization, which causes a substantial reduction of the droplet lifetime (one order of magnitude), results in a significant shift of the peak frequency, away from the

common modes for standard rocket engines. This phenomenon could explain the observed better stability of cryogenic rocket engines relative to storable propellant rocket engines because, for cryogenic propellants, most droplets are likely to undergo secondary atomization in the stripping regime. A secondary peak in the response function was identified and linked to both the magnitude of the droplet velocity to sound velocity ratio and the possible occurrence of flow reversal. The computed response factors could be fitted using the simplified expression from the  $n$ - $\tau$  model within a reasonable margin. Various wave patterns (traveling wave, sawtooth wave, and pressure oscillations only) were considered. Results confirm the predominance of velocity effects and show that in a sawtooth wave pattern, when stripping is included, the droplet lifetime is too short for the gasification process to contribute effectively to combustion instability. Supercritical mean pressures have a stabilizing effect if stripping is not included, whereas higher pressures are destabilizing when stripping is included.

All of the previous spherically symmetric oscillatory work did not consider many of the vital effects that would significantly modify the characteristic time or length scales of droplet vaporization. The one-dimensional model<sup>31</sup> was also limited and, therefore, vital information such as the drag coefficient could not be obtained from the Abramzon and Sirignano study. A detailed analysis that includes convection, the transient heating, and variable properties of the fuel droplet vaporization under oscillating conditions is required to identify the role of vaporization in combustion instability.

A preliminary axisymmetric calculation of oscillatory vaporization was made by Duvvur et al.<sup>70</sup> who examined the role of droplet vaporization under oscillating ambient conditions. This extended the previous work by Tong and Sirignano.<sup>23</sup> The advanced model of Chiang et al.<sup>34</sup> and Chiang<sup>35</sup> was employed to study the effects of an oscillating gas phase on the heat and mass transfer processes in the liquid phase. Variable properties were calculated in both the gas and liquid phase. The oscillations of temperature, pressure, and velocity in the gas phase showed significant changes in the heat and mass transfer rates and also in drag coefficients. Droplets were introduced at various times in order to evaluate the combined effect. The response factor of the system was calculated in order to determine if the vaporization process is capable of driving instability.

The problem considered in this study<sup>70</sup> is that of a single  $n$ -octane droplet, injected into the hot gases of a combustor. Gas-phase perturbations are introduced on the velocity, pressure, and temperature. The velocity and pressure oscillations are dictated by the classical standing wave pattern, and the corresponding temperature oscillation is calculated by assuming an isentropic flow. This study<sup>70</sup> examined the effects of variation of critical parameters such as the initial phase of injection, frequency, and amplitude of oscillation on the vaporization history of the droplet. The effects of decreasing relative velocity, varying thermophysical properties, transient heating, internal circulation of liquid, boundary-layer blowing, and moving interface were incorporated into the calculations.

For the governing equations in the liquid and gas phases, one should refer to work by Chiang<sup>35</sup> and Chiang et al.<sup>34</sup> The initial conditions corresponding to the injection of a droplet into an unstable combustor depend on the particular time and location of injection.  $T$ ,  $p$  and  $V_z$  are therefore dependent on the phases  $\phi_i$  and  $\phi_{p0}$ .  $V_r$  and  $Y_f$  are set to zero on the inflow side and the gradients are set to zero on the downstream side. When the flow reverses, the boundary conditions are, in effect, specified downstream with the gradient set to zero on the upstream side.

The inlet conditions of the gas phase are as follows.

Velocity condition:

$$U'_{\infty}(z', t') = \bar{U}'_{\infty} + \epsilon'_u \sin(2\pi z' / \lambda') \sin(2\pi c' t' / \lambda') \quad (7)$$

Pressure condition:

$$p'_{\infty}(z', t') = \bar{p}'_{\infty} + \epsilon'_p \cos(2\pi z' / \lambda') \cos(2\pi c' t' / \lambda') \quad (8)$$

where

$$\epsilon'_u = (a' / \gamma) (\epsilon'_p / \bar{p}'_{\infty}) \quad (9)$$

Temperature condition:

$$\frac{T'_{\infty}}{\bar{T}'_{\infty}} = \left( \frac{p'_{\infty}}{\bar{p}'_{\infty}} \right)^{(\gamma-1)/\gamma} \approx 1 + \frac{\gamma-1}{\gamma} \frac{\epsilon'_p}{\bar{p}'_{\infty}} \cos \frac{2\pi z'}{\lambda'} \cos \frac{2\pi c' t'}{\lambda'} \quad (10)$$

On the outlet side, the pressure is specified in a similar manner, but the gradients of the temperature and velocity are set to zero.

It is known that the driving force behind combustion instability is the energy input from the combustion process. The Rayleigh criterion is the most commonly used criterion to determine whether a particular mechanism is capable of driving the combustor into an unstable mode or not. As previously stated, the Rayleigh criterion for a mechanism to drive the instability is that the associated burning rate oscillates with the proper combination of a large enough amplitude and a small enough phase lag with the pressure oscillation. For the vaporization to be able to drive instability, it is necessary to evaluate the component of the vaporization rate that is in phase with the pressure. Duvvur et al.<sup>70</sup> approached this by evaluating the response factor  $G$  as suggested by the Rayleigh criterion<sup>18</sup>:

$$G = \oint \oint m P \, d\tau_{H_g} \, d\zeta \bigg/ \oint \oint P^2 \, d\tau_{H_g} \, d\zeta \quad (11)$$

where  $\zeta$  is a constant for each droplet during its lifetime. The  $\zeta$  value represents the phase at the time of injection.  $G$  is a nondimensional measure of the integrated (over time and space) product of burning rate fluctuation and pressure fluctuation. This form is consistent with the form for the combustion response developed by linear theory.<sup>15</sup>

The definition of  $G$  just given involves integration in an Eulerian frame of reference. In order to apply this to the present model, it is adapted to a Lagrangian frame of reference. Figure 4 shows the droplets born at various phase values. In an Eulerian time frame (represented by solid lines), droplets injected at different phases are present at different axial locations at a given time. By the preceding definition,  $G$  is calculated by integrating in horizontal sweeps over axial location and then over the Eulerian time. Lagrangian time varies along the dotted lines of constant initial phase value (constant  $\zeta$ ) in the figure.  $G$  can, therefore, be evaluated by integrating in diagonal sweeps over Lagrangian time and then by integrating over the phase value at the time of injection.

Note that the droplets injected into the chamber of a liquid rocket combustor experience varied histories of ambient conditions depending on the phase of the

Droplets injected at phases of  $-\pi$ ,  $-3\pi/2$ ,  $-\pi$ , and  $-\pi/2$  have contributions to the area of interest (marked as A, B, C, and D on the vaporization curves of droplets injected at zero,  $\pi/2$ ,  $\pi$ , and  $3\pi/2$ , respectively). To be able to overcome the losses and to drive combustion instability,  $G$  should be above a certain minimum positive value. For the case of distributed combustion, this value corresponds to 3.72 for longitudinal mode instability.<sup>15</sup>

Four different parametric studies have been conducted or are underway. These involved 1) frequency comparison, 2) amplitude comparison, 3) droplet configuration comparison, and 4) variation in the liquid fuel. Duvvur et al.<sup>74</sup> have not yet completed their effort, but certain conclusions can be drawn from their preliminary analysis.

The imposed oscillations have significant effects on the heat and mass transfer process and on the liquid properties. Droplet vaporization produces enough energy in phase with the pressure to drive longitudinal mode combustion instability. An investigation of the frequency domain showed that droplet vaporization was only capable of driving combustion instability in certain frequency domains. The fre-

Droplet vaporization studies related to combustion instability have neglected to emphasize whether the wake of the droplet is ahead of the droplet or behind it; there is a significant change in the response factor for the two situations. When the droplet is faster than the gas, the system has a high damping, whereas when the gas is faster than the droplet, the response factor is high enough to drive the instability. This is primarily due to the diverse effect the velocity oscillation has on the relative velocity. A variation of the volatility of the fuel has a fairly significant effect on the response factor, though it is not as significant as the orientation of the wake.

### VIII. Spray Combustion Instabilities

#### A. One-Dimensional Analysis

A one-dimensional computational analysis<sup>38</sup> was performed to investigate the liquid-fueled combustion instability with the objective of gaining fundamental

understanding of the effects of various design parameters on the stability of the combustion process in liquid-fueled systems. Spray characteristics, mixture ratio profiles, and combustor geometry were among the more interesting parameters investigated. Effort concentrated on the unsteady solution for the gas and liquid phases, evaluation of the effects of inlet gas velocity perturbations, and the coupling between gas and liquid phases under perturbed conditions.

The physical model studied was a simplified one-dimensional approximation of a ramjet combustion chamber in which vaporization and combustion of liquid spray occurs. Monodispersed, monocomponent, and subcritical liquid spray (*n*-decane) was assumed. The gas phase (air) was taken as unsteady, subsonic, compressible, and exchanging mass, momentum, and heat with the liquid phase. The basic set of equations in the Eulerian approach included continuity, momentum, chemical species, energy, and an equation of state for the gas phase.

The Lagrangian formulation of the liquid-phase equations was based on the effective conductivity model.<sup>31</sup> This droplet model assumes quasisteadiness in the gas film and employs the one-third-averaging rule to evaluate the gas-mixture properties. The assumptions of unity Lewis and Prandtl numbers have been removed. The effect of Stefan flow on the heat and mass transfer is modeled by a correction on the film thickness. For efficient computational time and accuracy, an effective value of the liquid thermal conductivity is used to account for the internal circulation within the droplet. The vaporization model also accounts for the droplet drag and the heat and mass transfer with the gas phase. One-step oxidation kinetics were employed. No assumption was made about a rate-controlling process.

Dirichlet boundary conditions were used at the combustor inlet, where mass flow (time-dependent), gas temperature, and species concentration were specified. The inlet pressure was determined by taking the inlet stagnation pressure to be constant. Overall equivalence ratio was specified at the inlet. At the outlet, Neumann boundary conditions were used, where zero gradients of the density, temperature, and species concentration were employed. The short-nozzle approximation at the combustor outlet (entrance to the nozzle) allowed the exit Mach number to be constant. Initially, the gas-phase temperature, velocity, pressure, and species concentration are specified. For the liquid phase, the droplet radius, location, velocity, and temperature were specified. The numerical solution was based on the modified implicit continuous-fluid (ICE) Eulerian scheme.<sup>71,72</sup>

Results from several cases covering a wide range of parameters were obtained. It was found that when the combustor is free to oscillate, the frequency of oscillations is independent of the frequency of the perturbation function and is solely determined by the length of the combustor, the droplet size, and the overall equivalence ratio. Also, this frequency is found to be very near the fundamental resonant frequency of the combustion chamber.

The results of this study are summarized in Figs. 6–9, which map the domains of stable/unstable combustion with the droplet radius, the combustor length, and the overall equivalence ratio (OER) as the parameters. Figure 6 shows the domain as determined by the droplet radius and the combustor length. With increase of the droplet size (and decrease in droplet number density) for a fixed combustor length and equivalence ratio, the combustion passes from stable to unstable and back to stable. Also evident is the effect of the combustor length. At the lower droplet radius of 50  $\mu\text{m}$ , increasing length moves the combustion process from unstable to stable, whereas the opposite is true at the higher droplet radius of

for the droplet heating ( $\tau_p/\tau_{dh}$ ). For unstable high-frequency cases,  $\tau_p/\tau_{dh}$  is in a range from 0.08 to 0.48. The points in the center of the unstable range vary between 0.14 and 0.16. Therefore, we take 0.15 as the most unstable value of the ratio. Tong and Sirignano<sup>23</sup> in their study of the response of a vaporizing droplet in an unstable combustor, report a maximum gain occurring for oscillations of frequency 200 Hz for 100- $\mu\text{m}$  droplets. Using a characteristic frequency of 30 Hz for 100- $\mu\text{m}$  droplet heating, we obtain  $\tau_p/\tau_{dh} = 0.15$  for the Tong-Sirignano calculation, too.

Figure 7 shows the domain as determined by the droplet radii and the overall equivalence ratio. The domain for unstable operation becomes larger at higher equivalence ratios, as the overtones get excited. The situation is further complicated by the interaction of the simulated injection process. For a fixed rate of injected fuel, the combustion process passes from stable to unstable at lower droplet radius, and again becomes stable at higher droplet radius. Figure 8 shows the stability limits as a function of the combustor length and the overall equivalence ratio. For a given droplet radius, the combustion passes from a stable to an unstable region with increase in the equivalence ratio. In Fig. 9, the low-frequency oscillations are isolated from the high-frequency ones. The figure shows that the low-frequency oscillations are important only in the cases of higher droplet radius. Also shown in the figure is the ratio of characteristic times for residence, taken as  $\tau_f = 2L/\mu_{g,\text{inlet}}$ , to the droplet heating time. It is inferred that to excite the low-frequency modes the characteristic time for the liquid droplet heating has to correspond to the residence time, or  $\tau_f/\tau_{dh} \approx 1.0$ .

Certain general statements can be made. Vaporization is rate controlling in the one-dimensional simulation where turbulent mixing and transverse transport are not considered. The combustion process can occur in either a stable or unstable mode. In the unstable mode, limit-cycle behavior of pressure, temperature, velocity, and gas-phase mass flow rate will occur. The magnitude of these limit-cycle oscillations is determined by the combustor geometry, spray characteristics, and the overall equivalence ratio. Low-frequency or entropy oscillations result when the characteristic time for droplet heating is close to that for the gas residence. High-frequency oscillations result when the ratio of characteristic time for period of oscillation to droplet heating is close to 0.15. At lower equivalence ratios, the frequency of free oscillations is very close to the fundamental resonant frequency of the combustor. At higher equivalence ratios, overtones are present. The frequency of the initial perturbation function has a small effect on the combustor oscillations. When the forcing function is removed, the combustor oscillations return to their natural frequency within a few cycles of oscillation. In cases where the damping of excited acoustic oscillations occurs, the excitations tend to dampen in about 10 cycles. The variation of droplet size, for the same equivalence ratio and combustor length, has a profound effect on the combustor stability. A range of droplet radii for which the combustion is unstable is observed. Below and above this range of droplet size, no limit-cycle behavior is present. This indicates the importance of spray combustion. An intermediate range also exists for combustor length, like the droplet radii, where the combustor operation is unstable. Increasing the equivalence ratio enlarges the domain of unstable operation. In the range of the calculations, all droplet radii and combustor length cases are unstable for the equivalence ratio of 0.7. When the inlet gas velocity is continuously excited, resonance occurs for an excitation frequency close to the combustor natural frequency.

#### B. Idealized Rocket Engine

The single LOX-droplet model<sup>65</sup> was used to investigate the combustion of arrays of LOX droplets in a simplified combustor at supercritical conditions.<sup>73</sup> The simplified configuration considered consists of a two-dimensional rectangular channel closed at one end where discrete LOX droplets are injected in streams (Fig. 10). This configuration, also known as parallel droplet streams, has been extensively used to investigate flame propagation in hydrocarbon fuel droplet streams<sup>74-76</sup> and in hazardous waste incineration.<sup>77-79</sup> A comprehensive review was contributed by Rangel and Sirignano.<sup>80</sup> Using this configuration, the transient effects in the gas phase and the consequences of discrete droplet injection (intermittence) may be included in the model.

Velocity and pressure fields in the channel are prescribed, and species and energy equations are solved. Droplets are followed in a Lagrangian manner and are viewed as point sources (or sinks) from the gas phase. Effects of supercritical ambient conditions on the droplet convective vaporization are included using the model already described.

The LOX droplets are initially in a subcritical state; in the combustor, they heat, vaporize, and burn. Depending on the external conditions, their surfaces may reach the critical mixing point. Note that, hitherto, actual combustion had not been included. The droplets respond to the changing external gaseous field as they travel through the idealized combustor. No direct interaction between drops is included, but the droplets do affect each other through the impact they have on the gaseous fields. Investigation of the influence of these interactions on the droplet transcritical behavior is the main purpose of a recent study.<sup>73</sup>

In the particular case of the LOX droplet in hydrogen, however, the contribution of the mass vaporized to the overall mass flux is not negligible because of the disparities of the molecular weights. To include these effects in the present model while keeping the overall algorithm reasonably simple, the resulting departure of the longitudinal velocity from the uniform profile is evaluated in a quasisteady manner from mass flux conservation. This non uniformity may, in certain cases, affect significantly the computed droplet lifetime (Fig. 11).

The source terms due to vaporization are summed over all of the droplets. The possibility of stripping is included in their evaluation. It was shown<sup>65</sup> that although some of the stripped liquid vaporizes in the film surrounding the droplet (secondary vaporization), thus affecting directly heat and mass transfer to the droplet, most of the stripped liquid vaporizes outside that film. The assumption is made here that, given the high-pressure, high-temperature conditions in the gas phase, and given

the experimentally estimated size of the mist (1–10  $\mu$ m), complete vaporization of the mist occurs within a small region around the parent droplet. Hence, as viewed from the gas flow, the mass source and energy sink due to the vaporization of the remaining mist may be taken as being a point source (sink) at the same location as the parent droplet.

In an attempt to simplify the chemical kinetics of the hydrogen/oxygen system while retaining the principal features of this reaction, the procedure described by Gutheil and Williams<sup>81</sup> and Chung and Williams<sup>82</sup> is followed. A one-step global mechanism is used. The overall reaction rate is approximated by the reaction rate of the first forward elementary reaction of the complete mechanism.

The most consequential result presented in the study<sup>73</sup> is that the combined effects of high temperatures in the reaction zone and reduced relative velocity cause the droplet surface temperature to reach the critical mixing conditions, even when stripping is occurring. This is a significant departure from the behavior predicted for an isolated vaporizing droplet.<sup>65</sup> Nevertheless, it was also demonstrated that stripping is the process controlling the droplet gasification and that the droplet lifetime is at least one order of magnitude smaller than that expected with primary vaporization only.

This simplified geometry was used to gain some insight concerning the consequences of these results on the response of a burning LOX droplet array to an oscillatory environment.<sup>69</sup> Note that the purpose of this comparison is to evaluate the influence of neighbor-induced gas field nonuniformities. High gas velocities, such as those considered in the cases already reported (Sec. VII), could not be used in the present case because they require a much larger domain and significantly more droplets and thus increase unrealistically the computational load. The gas injection velocity used here (1 m/s) is therefore not representative of real engine conditions (the droplet/gas relative velocity was kept unchanged at 20 m/s). Therefore, the values presented in Table 1 are much lower than the threshold value of the response factor for unstable operations.

An important difference between this type of computation and the single droplet evaluation reported earlier, comes from the fact that in the array configuration

the mean velocity of the gas at infinity is affected by the gasification of the neighboring droplets. The stripping rate is, therefore, reduced, and the droplet lifetime increased.

The comparison of the values computed in both configurations (Table 1) indicates that the response spectra obtained with the vaporizing isolated droplet configuration underestimate the driving potential of the gasification process. In Table 1, the values labeled uniform response factor refer to the those obtained using an expression of the response factor resulting from a perturbation analysis as derived by Crocco and Cheng.<sup>15</sup> These values are much lower than those obtained by the other methods. This is attributed to the oversimplification of the vaporization process which such an analysis (linearization and perturbation methods) requires.

No simulation of the droplet-array configuration response could be performed with more realistic gas injection velocities. However, the foregoing argument indicates that such simulations would yield response factors higher than those obtained in the isolated droplet configurations<sup>69</sup> and, thus, confirm the conclusion drawn from these results (cf. Sec. VII).

### IX. Conclusions

Consideration of the characteristic times for each of the major combustion processes in a liquid-propellant rocket motor and comparison with the natural periods for oscillations in typical rocket combustion chambers gives strong circumstantial evidence that vaporization is the major controlling mechanism for combustion instability. Atomization can be a vital coupling mechanism since it affects droplet size distribution that, in turn, directly relates to the characteristic vaporization time. More direct evidence about the prominence of the vaporization mechanism comes from several analyses. Theoretical/computational studies of individual fuel droplets in an oscillatory field indicate that the response of the vaporization to an ambient velocity oscillation is sufficiently large and the phase with the pressure oscillation is sufficiently small to drive combustion instability. Another computational study of combustion of liquid hydrocarbon fuel and air in a chamber with a choked nozzle at the exit confirms the importance of the vaporization process. Calculations by Tong and Sirignano<sup>73</sup> and Bhatia and Sirignano<sup>78</sup> give evidence that the rate-controlling vaporization for hydrocarbon fuels is a critical factor explaining the combustion instability mechanism.

Theoretical studies of oxygen propellant droplets at supercritical ambient pressure indicate substantial differences in the vaporization mechanism from subcritical vaporization. The immediate gas film can become a subcritical, multi-component region. A secondary atomization mechanism identified as stripping can

occur intermittently resulting in an increase in the frequency range for maximum response. Analyses of idealized combustion chamber configurations produced decreasing mass stripping rates with increased droplet lifetimes and a greater potential to drive combustion instability as compared to the isolated oxygen droplet studies.

To a substantial extent, there is need for calculations at more frequency values and over a wider range of other parameters in order to obtain a better picture of the role of vaporization in liquid rocket combustion instability.

### I. Introduction

**L**IQUID-PROPELLANT rocket engines involve the injection of propellants, usually a separate fuel and oxidizer, into a cylindrical combustion chamber. The propellants have a high-energy density and react at a finite rate to release thermal and kinetic energy. The energy release rate includes a variety of time scales due to the many subprocesses that must occur before chemical reaction is completed. Because these subprocesses are dependent on the combustion-chamber pressure and gas velocity, a feedback mechanism for amplifying combustion chamber natural acoustic modes is often encountered. The feedback mechanisms are commonly subclassified into intrinsic and injection-coupled mechanisms. Injection coupling implies that the change in flow rate through the injector due to chamber pressure variation is a significant contributor to amplification. Often times, variation in subprocesses that occur after the propellant has been injected are the dominant mechanisms, and the injector is only passively involved. This is what is commonly referred to as the intrinsic mechanism. This chapter is focused on the unique aspects of the injection-coupled mechanism.

Because of the strong coupling among all of the subprocesses and sparse available instrumentation, it is difficult to clearly determine if injection coupling has occurred when an engine has gone unstable. There is one classic example that can be used to demonstrate a clearly injection-coupled mechanism, the J-2S.<sup>1</sup> The J-2S engine was a liquid-oxygen (LOX)/gaseous-hydrogen engine throttleable between 200-kN and 1140-kN vacuum thrust at mixture ratio from 4.4 to 6.0. The engine was pump fed by pumps driven from a hot-gas tapoff from the combustion chamber. The main injector was made up of shear coaxial injection elements. The initial LOX post design was orificed at the head end with an orifice-to-post area ratio of 0.30, giving it characteristics similar to an opened-end/closed-end acoustic resonator tube (Fig. 1). Although the LOX post lengths varied from 5.59 to 7.87 cm, a combustion instability occurred at 4400 Hz and was attributed to injection coupling between injector flow oscillations and combustion chamber acoustics.

Several unique features of this instability initially flagged this as different from a typical intrinsic instability. 1) The mode shape corresponded to a third tangential mode rather than a fundamental mode. 2) The growth rate of the oscillations was very slow, less than 10/s in contrast to a typical growth rate of an intrinsic instability, which is on the order of 100/s. 3) The oscillations limited at relatively low amplitudes without causing chamber damage. The injection elements used in this engine had staggered LOX post lengths ranging from 5.59 to 7.87 cm that served to spread the bandwidth of the injector response. Injector response calculations reported in Ref. 1 show a resonance at 4600 Hz for the 7.87-cm-long posts, which is very near the observed 4400-Hz frequency. The longer elements make up 237 of the 614 total elements, accounting for a significant percentage of available energy. The remaining elements, all shorter, have higher frequency resonances and contributed less to the instability. This may at least partially explain why the growth rates were slow. A larger contributor to this phenomenon lies in the behavior of the combustion itself. It is often approximated that the

combustion occurs at a fixed axial plane in the chamber (concentrated combustion), allowing a single characteristic time lag to determine when the energy of the injected propellants is released. This time lag controls the phase relationship between the injector oscillations and chamber oscillations. In an actual case the combustion is distributed with some fraction of the burning complete at each instant in time. With this being the case, only a fraction of the available energy may be released in phase. It was believed by the original investigators that the portion of the reaction going on in the cup region provided the proper phase relationship, resulting in a weakly coupled system with the small growth rate. The problem was corrected by altering the resistance of the flow passage allowing most of the loss to occur at the exit of the element. Figure 2 shows the final configuration of the LOX posts, designed to have a considerable pressure drop near the post exit.

The frequency response predictions of these respective elements is shown in Figure 3. The solid line represents the gain of propellant flow rate oscillation as a result of chamber pressure oscillation for the initial J-2S design. The curve has a substantial peak at 4600 Hz, indicative of a resonance condition. The dashed line represents the frequency shift and magnitude reduction that resulted when the post was redesigned. Testing of this design verified that the change was sufficient to stabilize the injector. The methodology used to generate these response curves is described in Sec. II. In this type of instability, injector effects can be isolated to the relatively simple acoustics of the LOX post. In general, however, both the fuel and oxidizer feed systems, including the propellant manifolds, may be coupled.

Another unique aspect of the combustion instability phenomenon with LOX/hydrogen propellants is the strong effect of the fuel injection temperature. Increasing the fuel temperature tends to stabilize the engine. This effect has been studied at least as far back as 1964, but a general agreement does not exist on the

The effect is commonly attributed to either a momentum ratio or velocity ratio effect, which implies an intrinsic instability independent of injector flow rate oscillations. The results of the investigations in the 1960s, however, indicate exactly the opposite argument. The following paragraphs are a brief summary of the studies that lead to this conclusion.

Under NASA contract, an experimental program was conducted to investigate this phenomena.<sup>2</sup> Results of tests involving both a  $2.54 \times 12.7$  cm slab motor and a 25.4-cm-diam cylindrical combustor were evaluated. Fuel injection temperature ranged from 25 to 139 K with chamber pressures ranging from 2050 to 5790 kPa. This program demonstrated high-frequency instability near and below the critical temperature of hydrogen in many tests. The effect was found to be essentially

independent of chamber pressure. An attempt was made to correlate the effect of momentum ratio, and no correlation was found. A trend was found that related stability to the inlet velocity ratio of the fuel and oxidizer.

In 1966 a study was conducted at NASA Lewis Research Center (LeRC) using a 89-kN thrust LOX/hydrogen rocket engine with a 27.36-cm-diam chamber.<sup>3</sup> The fuel temperature was varied from 33 to 107 K and the chamber pressure was held at 2070 kPa. For this engine, the stability boundary could always be defined in terms of a critical velocity ratio, regardless of the fuel temperature. Velocity ratio was controlled by varying the fuel flow areas. It was shown in a later study that velocity ratio correlation does not hold if the element size is changed.<sup>4</sup> A study was conducted to examine the case of varying oxidizer pressure drop independently of the exit velocity. The high-frequency instability limit was found to be independent of oxidizer pressure drop, supporting the argument of an intrinsic mechanism. It was found that in this combustor a LOX post recess of 0.25 cm increased the stability margin by 27.8 K but no conclusions were drawn as to why this was the case. The effects of hydrogen pressure drop were not examined, leaving open the possibility of an injector-coupled instability involving the hydrogen side of the injector. A continued study has shown that the hydrogen velocity ratio correlation actually can be explained by changes in the fuel pressure drop.<sup>5</sup> This information led to the understanding of one of the principal mechanisms of this type of instability. It was concluded that the change in fuel temperature results in a change in injection pressure drop across the fuel annulus allowing oscillations in the fuel annulus/manifold to tune with the chamber resonant oscillations. An empirical correlation was developed to predict the transition temperature. This relation empirically accounts for the closed-looped system that includes the fuel side of the injector. This correlation was found to be rather accurate for a fixed element density. The major shortcoming in this correlation is that the proportionality constant is dependent on the injector/combustor design. It was further shown that the change in hydrogen pressure drop due to LOX post recess accounts for the improved stability that results.

In 1974, NASA LeRC released a report that verified this injector-coupled phenomena.<sup>6</sup> This program involved tests using the same chamber as already discussed operated at 2070 kPa. This study demonstrated that a stability limit dependence on impingement angle and oxidizer tube blunt base thickness may be explained by changes in fuel side pressure drop. These characteristics were later shown also to apply to LOX/methane combustors using shear coaxial injection.<sup>7</sup>

To date a complete analysis of the data has not been conducted with a complete model that includes the fuel side manifold and fuel annulus acoustics. This analysis would be helpful in settling some of the controversy over the controlling mechanism.

It should be noted that injection coupling is never independent of the intrinsic subprocesses, such as atomization, propellant heatup, vaporization, and mixing because these processes determine the phase relationship between the injector response and the chamber response. Also, in the case of an intrinsic instability, where injector flow oscillations do not feed back energy to the chamber acoustic wave, the injector will be passively involved, with the chamber pressure oscillations observable in the propellant manifolds. Careful parametric evaluation and analysis are needed to determine the degree to which the injector is involved in any particular instability.

### II. Modeling

A complete analysis of high-frequency injection coupling involves an evaluation of the interaction between the chamber pressure oscillations and the propellant burning rate oscillations including those that result from flow rate oscillations. The procedure used to perform a linear analysis of this problem is the same as that used for low-frequency, feed system stability with the injector response replacing the feed system response and the chamber acoustic response replacing the bulk chamber response. The model that describes the injector acoustics is unique to this chapter and will be described in the following paragraphs.

For many cases an acceptable level of modeling is to assume one-dimensional flow of a real, single-phase, compressible fluid in an injector element component such as a LOX post or fuel sleeve. The computational domain consists of the propellant flow path from the element inlet to the combustion chamber face. To account for axial variations in the flowfield, the domain is divided into  $n - 1$  computational segments with  $n$  segment faces. The number of computational segments needed is chosen such that the length of a computational element is much shorter than the wavelength of the highest frequency acoustic mode to be considered. The control volume forms of the governing equations of mass and axial momentum can be written as follows.

Mass:

$$0 = \frac{d}{dt} \left( \iiint_{cv} \rho \, dv \right) + \iint_{cs} \rho (\mathbf{V} \cdot \mathbf{n}) \, ds \quad (1)$$

Axial momentum:

$$\sum F_x = \frac{d}{dt} \left( \iiint_{cv} \mathbf{V} \rho \, dv \right) + \iint_{cs} \mathbf{V} \rho (\mathbf{V} \cdot \mathbf{n}) \, ds \quad (2)$$

where the forces are pressure and friction forces. Assuming fully developed plug flow Eq. (1) can be integrated across a computational segment. Decomposing the result into mean and perturbed parts results in

$$0 = \bar{m}'_i - \bar{m}'_{i+1} \quad (3)$$

$$v_{i+1} \frac{d\rho'_{i+1}}{dt} = \dot{m}'_i - \dot{m}'_{i+1} \quad (4)$$

where barred quantities represent mean variables and primed quantities represent the perturbed variables. Assuming small, isentropic perturbations, the density is a function of pressure only. Incorporating this assumption and normalizing by the mean flow quantities, Eq. (4) becomes

$$C_{i+1} \frac{d}{dt} \left( \frac{p'_{i+1}}{\bar{p}_c} \right) = \frac{\dot{m}'_i}{\bar{m}} - \frac{\dot{m}'_{i+1}}{\bar{m}} \quad (5)$$

where

$$C_{i+1} = \frac{\bar{p}_c v_{i+1}}{\bar{m}} \left( \frac{\partial \bar{p}}{\partial \bar{p}} \right)_{i+1}$$

###### HIGH-FREQUENCY INJECTION-COUPLED COMBUSTION INSTABILITY 351

It should be noted here that it is not assumed that the mean flowfield is isentropic, only that an isentropic acoustic field may be superimposed on a real, nonisentropic mean flow. To apply the momentum equation, the wall shear stress is represented empirically as

$$\tau_w = \frac{f}{4} \frac{\rho u^2}{2} \quad (6)$$

Integrating Eq. (2) across the computational element and decomposing into mean and perturbed variables gives, for the mean,

$$\begin{aligned} f_i \left( \frac{l_i}{d_i} \right) \left( \frac{1}{\bar{\rho}_i + \bar{\rho}_{i+1}} \right) \left( \frac{\bar{m}}{S_i} \right)^2 \\ = \frac{(S_i)_i}{S_i} \bar{p}_i - \frac{(S_E)_i}{S_i} \bar{p}_{i+1} + \frac{\bar{m}^2}{S_i} \left\{ \frac{1}{\bar{\rho}_i (S_i)_i} - \frac{1}{\bar{\rho}_{i+1} (S_E)_i} \right\} \end{aligned} \quad (7)$$

Dropping all higher order terms and using the mean equation to eliminate  $f$  results in a manageable, linearized equation for the perturbed axial momentum,

$$\begin{aligned} L_i \frac{d}{dt} \left( \frac{\bar{m}'_i}{\bar{m}} \right) + R_i \frac{\bar{m}'_i}{\bar{m}} + \xi_i \frac{\bar{m}'_{i+1}}{\bar{m}} - \phi_i \frac{\bar{m}'_{i-1}}{\bar{m}} \\ = (1 + D_i - G_i) \frac{\bar{p}'_i}{\bar{p}_c} - (1 - U_i - H_i) \frac{\bar{p}'_{i+1}}{\bar{p}_c} \end{aligned} \quad (8)$$

where the constant coefficients are defined as

$$\begin{aligned} L_i &= \frac{l_i \bar{m}}{S_i \bar{p}_c} \quad R_i = \frac{2(\bar{p}_i - \bar{p}_{i+1})}{\bar{p}_c} + \phi_i - \xi_i \quad \xi_i = \frac{2\bar{m}^2}{\bar{p}_c \bar{\rho}_{i+1} (S_E)_i S_i} \\ \phi_i &= \frac{2\bar{m}^2}{\bar{p}_c \bar{\rho}_i (S_i)_i S_i} \quad D_i = \frac{R_i \bar{p}_c}{2(\bar{\rho}_i + \bar{\rho}_{i+1})} \left( \frac{\partial \bar{p}}{\partial \bar{p}} \right)_i \quad U_i = \frac{R_i \bar{p}_c}{2(\bar{\rho}_i + \bar{\rho}_{i+1})} \left( \frac{\partial \bar{p}}{\partial \bar{p}} \right)_{i+1} \\ G_i &= \frac{\phi_i \bar{p}_c}{2\bar{\rho}_i} \left( \frac{\partial \bar{p}}{\partial \bar{p}} \right)_i \quad H_i = \frac{\xi_i \bar{p}_c}{2\bar{\rho}_{i+1}} \left( \frac{\partial \bar{p}}{\partial \bar{p}} \right)_{i+1} \end{aligned}$$

To evaluate these coefficients the mean pressure and density field as well as the local speed of sound are needed. These may be evaluated using standard one-dimensional engineering equations for internal flow. This generalized formulation allows for the treatment of variable flow area and heat transfer through the element walls.

Combining Eqs. (5) and (8) and taking the Laplace transform gives

$$\begin{aligned} \left( \phi_i s + \frac{1 + D_i - G_i}{C_i} \right) a_{i-1}(s) - \left( L_i s^2 + R_i s + \frac{1 + D_i - G_i}{C_i} \right. \\ \left. + \frac{1 - U_i - H_i}{C_{i+1}} \right) a_i(s) + \left( \xi_i s - \frac{1 - U_i - H_i}{C_{i+1}} \right) a_{i+1}(s) = 0 \end{aligned} \quad (9)$$

where the local admittance is defined as

$$a_i(s) = \bar{p}_c \dot{m}'_i(s) / \bar{m} p'_c(s) \quad \text{and} \quad s = j\omega \quad (10)$$

Equation (9) applies to all of the interior segments. The first and last segments require boundary conditions and can be written,

$$\left( L_1 s^2 + (R_1 - \phi_1)s + \frac{1 + U_1 - G_1}{C_2} \right) a_1(s) + \left( \xi_1(s) - \frac{1 - U_1 - H_1}{C_2} \right) a_2(s) \\ = (1 + D_1 - G_1)s \frac{p'_1(s)}{p'_c(s)} \quad (11)$$

$$\left( \phi_{n-1}s + \frac{1 + D_{n-1} - G_{n-1}}{G_{n-1}} \right) a_{n-2}(s) - \left( L_{n-1}s^2 + (R_{n-1} + \xi_{n-1})s \right. \\ \left. + \frac{1 + D_{n-1} - G_{n-1}}{C_{n-1}} \right) a_{n-1}(s) = (1 + U_{n-1} - H_{n-1})s = 0 \quad (12)$$

The local admittance at the  $n - 1$  segment represents the response in injector flow rate as a result of flow rate oscillations. For clarity we will, therefore, define the injector admittance for either a fuel or oxidizer flow rate as

$$A_o = a_{o,n-1}(s) = \frac{\bar{p}_c \dot{m}'_{o,n-1}(s)}{\bar{m} p'_c(s)} \quad A_f = a_{f,n-1}(s) = \frac{\bar{p}_c \dot{m}'_{f,n-1}(s)}{\bar{m} p'_c(s)} \quad (13)$$

To obtain this admittance the simultaneous solution of the tridiagonal matrix formed from Eqs. (9–12) is required with boundary conditions required at the upstream node. The simplest condition is to set the upstream pressure oscillation to zero, which occurs when manifold effects are decoupled from the injector oscillations.

The goal of this analysis is to predict a coupling between the response of chamber pressure oscillations to burning rate oscillations and the response of burning rate oscillations to chamber oscillations. The burning rate response in this case is a function of the injector flow rate oscillations and the combustion process. The simplest approach for including the effects of the combustion process is to apply the well-known sensitive time-lag model resulting in the following equation:

$$\frac{\dot{m}'_B(s)}{\bar{m}} = \frac{\dot{m}'_o(s)}{\bar{m}} e^{-s\bar{\tau}_o} + \frac{\dot{m}'_f(s)}{\bar{m}} e^{-s\bar{\tau}_f} + A_B(s) \frac{p'(s)}{\bar{p}} \quad (14)$$

where the burning admittance can be used as derived by Crocco and Cheng,<sup>8</sup>

$$A_B = n(1 - e^{-s\bar{\tau}})$$

Equation (14) can be rewritten as

$$\frac{\dot{m}'_B(s) \bar{p}_c}{p'_c(s) \bar{m}} = \frac{\bar{\tau} A_o(s) e^{-s\bar{\tau}_o} + A_f(s) e^{-s\bar{\tau}_f}}{\bar{\tau} + 1} + A_B(s) \quad (15)$$

where the mixture ratio is defined as

$$\bar{\tau} = \frac{\bar{\tau}_o}{\bar{\tau}_f}$$

###### HIGH-FREQUENCY INJECTION-COUPLED COMBUSTION INSTABILITY 353

An overall injector admittance can now be written

$$A_I(s) = \frac{\bar{r} A_o(s) e^{-s\bar{\tau}_o} + A_f(s) e^{-s\bar{\tau}_f}}{\bar{r} + 1} \quad (16)$$

The derivation for the injector admittance was based on a single-injector element. If all of the elements in the injector are identical with the same mean mass flow rates, this equation applies directly simply by using the total injector mean flow rates. The phase relationship due to the element spatial distribution is implicitly accounted for because all of the element oscillations must be synchronized to feed energy into the same acoustic wave if an instability is to be supported. However, if the elements are different, as in the case of variable length elements, the admittance must be written as a mass-weighted summation of the admittance of each individual element.

With these relations the total response of the combustion process to chamber pressure oscillations can now be written as a function of only the injector and burning admittances,

$$[\dot{m}'_B(s) \bar{p}_c / p'_c(s) \bar{m}] = A_I(s) + A_b(s) \quad (17)$$

To evaluate the potential of an unstable feedback of this oscillatory energy back into the chamber acoustic modes, a chamber response function is needed. This function can be obtained from the methods described in Chapter 15 and written as

$$R_c(s) = [p'_c(s) \bar{m} / \dot{m}'_b(s) \bar{p}_c] \quad (18)$$

If the proper magnitude and phase relationship exists between the burning and chamber response, the linear theory results in an unbounded growth in the chamber pressure. The resulting characteristic equation is formed by combining Eqs. (17) and (18),

$$0 = 1 - R_c(s) \{A_I(s) + A_b(s)\} = 1 + F(s) \quad (19)$$

To satisfy Eq. (19), the following must be true:

$$|F(j\omega)| = 1 \quad (20)$$

$$\arg\{F(j\omega)\} = \pm\pi \quad (21)$$

The phase relationship depends on the values of the combustion time lag. Since these values are the weakest part of the analysis, a conservative approach is usually taken where it is assumed that Eq. (21) is always satisfied. To gain insight into the relative contribution of the chamber response and combustion response, a common approach is to graph

$$\left| \frac{1}{R_c(j\omega)} \right| \quad \text{vs} \quad \hat{f} = \frac{\omega}{2\pi} \quad (22)$$

$$|A_I(s) + A_b(s)| \quad \text{vs} \quad \hat{f} = \frac{\omega}{2\pi} \quad (23)$$

on the same plot. Points where the curves cross indicate frequencies that satisfy Eq. (20) and that indicate an instability. Because of the infinite number of mixed

modes and harmonics that are possible from the acoustics, experience must be used to determine which modes should be considered. These are typically limited to the chamber fundamental modes and those up to the second harmonic. Historically, frequencies higher than these are not usually a problem.

The model described was implemented in a stability program conducted at the NASA Marshall Space Flight Center. Tests were conducted in a rectangular chamber with a single row of shear coaxial injection elements. The propellants were liquid oxygen and gaseous hydrogen with mixture ratios of 4.0 to 6.0 running at chamber pressures from 690 to 2760 kPa. The chamber measures 34.29 cm in width and 26.67 cm in length with a thickness of 2.54 cm. The results of plotting expressions (21) and (22) are shown in Fig. 4. The element LOX posts were 11.86 cm in length and 0.35 cm in diameter with a head orifice with a diameter of 0.22 cm. Each of the parabola-shaped curves represents a responsive band around a natural acoustic mode of the chamber. For example, the first widthwise mode has a natural frequency of about 3000 Hz. The bottom curve represents the vector sum of the injector acoustics and the combustion response. The dominating feature of these curves is the peaks representing the natural acoustic modes of the LOX post. For example, the natural frequency of the first mode of the LOX post is about 2750 Hz. This example is typical of what is often seen when analyzing engines with shear coaxial injectors. By strict interpretation of the equations, an instability only can occur when the curves cross. In this plot, the only such points are at the very high-frequency first width-third longitudinal (1W-3L) and 1W-4L modes. Typically, these higher mixed modes do not go unstable, and an instability would not be expected to occur. The 1W mode curve, however, comes very close to

### III. Summary

High-frequency combustion instability in liquid-propellant engines often occurs due to the geometry of the elements that are often used. Shear coaxial injector elements are particularly prone to this type of instability because the resonant acoustic frequencies of the LOX post are often close to the resonant frequencies of the combustion chamber. Linearized acoustic response models of the injector acoustics, chamber acoustics, and the combustion response can be used to evaluate an engine's susceptibility to this phenomena. The preferred frequencies are controlled primarily by the natural acoustic modes of the chamber and injector, and the phase relationship is determined by the combustion process. Since the combustion process is difficult to adequately model, the conservative approach is usually taken that resonant frequency matches between the two components are to be avoided.

### I. Introduction

HIGH-FREQUENCY combustion instabilities are generally characterized by mutual coupling between combustion processes and acoustic motions within a chamber. The study of acoustics in combustion chambers, therefore, constitutes a necessary step in approaching the complete problem. It is the purpose of this chapter to address various important aspects of acoustics in combustion chambers with respect to stability. Issues involving combustion processes and the detailed interactions between combustion and acoustics are treated in other chapters.

The fact that some combustion instabilities are intimately tied to acoustics was recognized early in the development of liquid rocket engines due to striking similarities between the unsteady motions of instabilities and the natural or normal acoustic modes of the chamber. Sometimes called screaming, screeching, or squealing modes, the frequencies of acoustic-coupled instabilities are generally higher than those of feed-system or injector-coupled instabilities, although delineation by frequency alone is not always adequate. An instability is usually classified in terms of the acoustic mode it most closely resembles, with the acoustic motion being either longitudinal or transverse. In rectangular geometries, transverse modes are all basically similar, whereas in cylindrical chambers the transverse modes can be either radial or tangential. Tangential modes can be standing or spinning, depending on whether the pressure node line is stationary or rotating. Besides these simple modes, there are also mixed modes with characteristics of multiple pure modes, each having discrete natural frequencies of oscillation.

Much of the previous theoretical work on liquid rocket combustion instabilities has been limited to linear analysis,<sup>1-3</sup> which is confined to treatment of infinitesimal (or at least sufficiently small) disturbances in the chamber. The global behavior predicted by a linear model will always yield one of three scenarios: the disturbance grows unbounded (linearly unstable), decays completely (linearly stable), or remains unchanged (neutrally stable). Because of the ubiquitous presence of small perturbations in any real system, the latter case is not physically realizable.

Nonlinear analysis deals with finite amplitude fluctuations, offering a wider scope for investigating oscillatory behavior.<sup>4-6</sup> Specifically, the phenomena of spontaneous<sup>7-11</sup> and pulse-triggered<sup>12-14</sup> oscillations may be treated. Spontaneous oscillations are observed in linearly unstable systems in which disturbances grow with no external forcing and eventually reach constant amplitudes, commonly known as limit cycles. Pulsed oscillations occur in linearly stable systems and require an initial excitation with amplitude above some threshold magnitude. For disturbance magnitudes less than the threshold value, the fluctuations decrease to

zero; for those above the threshold, the fluctuations grow to a limit cycle value. Both types of nonlinear phenomena have practical manifestations. For example, the limiting amplitude of spontaneous or pulsed instabilities can determine if the instability warrants design modifications. Also, finding the disturbance threshold for pulsed instabilities is an important part of most engine design programs, since the commonly used bomb stability rating technique basically quantifies the "triggerability" of a system. A firm grasp on modeling, predicting, and analyzing nonlinear phenomena is essential for enhancing liquid rocket engine design and development.

In the remainder of this chapter, the general formulation of acoustic motions in a combustion chamber is explained, followed by a brief summary of normal modes. Several types of nonlinear acoustic waves are then examined in detail, with specific consideration of second- and third-order gasdynamics, mean flow/acoustic interactions, and nonlinear combustion responses.

### II. Formulation

Analytically, a combustion chamber is a complex environment, and the equations which govern the behavior of acoustic fluctuations must be developed with care. The general formulation by Culick and Yang<sup>3</sup> outlined in Chapter 1 of this volume allows consideration of two-phase flow, combustion, and other processes pertinent to acoustic motions. After mass averaging the gaseous and condensed phases into one compressible medium, the conservation equations of mass, momentum, and energy are manipulated to give a nonlinear wave equation in terms of fluctuating pressure,

$$\nabla^2 p' - \frac{1}{\bar{a}^2} \frac{\partial^2 p'}{\partial t^2} = h \quad (1)$$

Boundary conditions on  $p'$  are specified in terms of the gradient of  $p'$  normal to the boundary surface

$$\mathbf{n} \cdot \nabla p' = -f \quad (2)$$

where  $\mathbf{n}$  is the outward unit vector normal to the surface. The exact forms of the source terms  $h$  and  $f$  depend on the order of analysis and the types of processes being considered. Acoustic admittance functions may be conveniently employed to represent  $f$  in actual calculations.

The forcing functions  $h$  and  $f$  represent deviations from unperturbed acoustic modes and provide the mechanism for initiating and sustaining oscillations. Although exact analytical solution of Eqs. (1) and (2) is not feasible for all but the simplest forms of  $h$  and  $f$ , the forcing is typically so small that the unsteady motions in a chamber can be treated as a perturbation of the classical acoustics. Using the approximate method described in Chapter 1, the acoustic pressure and velocity fields are therefore most sensibly expressed as a series of the acoustic normal modes, with arbitrary time dependence accounted for by time-varying coefficients,

$$p'(\mathbf{r}, t) = \bar{p} \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \eta_n(t) \psi_n(\mathbf{r}) \quad (3)$$

$$\mathbf{u}'(\mathbf{r}, t) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{\dot{\eta}_n(t)}{\bar{\gamma} k_n^2} \nabla \psi_n(\mathbf{r}) \quad (4)$$

The normal modes  $\psi_n$  satisfy the homogeneous Helmholtz equation

$$\nabla^2 \psi_n + k_n^2 \psi_n = 0 \quad (5)$$

subject to the boundary condition

$$\mathbf{n} \cdot \nabla \psi_n = 0 \quad (6)$$

Here  $k_n = \omega_n/\bar{a}$  is the wave number and  $\omega_n$  the frequency of the  $n$ th mode. After substituting these expressions into Eqs. (1) and (2), and applying a spatial-averaging technique similar to the Galerkin method, the following set of ordinary differential equations is derived to govern the temporal evolution of each acoustic mode:

$$\frac{d^2 \eta_n}{dt^2} + \omega_n^2 \eta_n = F_n \quad (7)$$

where

$$F_n = -\frac{\bar{a}^2}{\bar{\rho} E_n^2} \left[ \iiint h \psi_n dV + \iint \psi_n f dS \right] \quad (8)$$

and  $E_n$  is the Euclidean norm defined as

$$E_n^2 = \iiint \psi_n^2 dV \quad (9)$$

### III. Normal Modes

Selection of the acoustic normal modes as basis functions for the unsteady pressure and velocity fields not only gives the series in Eqs. (3) and (4) good convergence properties, but also allows Eq. (7) to be written compactly, due to the orthogonality of the normal mode set. For an unbaffled rectangular chamber with length  $L$ , width  $W$ , and height  $H$ , the method of separation of variables may be used to easily find the normal mode shapes,

$$\psi_n = \cos[(\pi l/L)x] \cos[(\pi m/W)y] \cos[(\pi s/H)z] \quad \begin{cases} l = 0, 1, 2, \dots \\ m = 0, 1, 2, \dots \\ s = 0, 1, 2, \dots \end{cases} \quad (10)$$

with

$$k_n^2 = \omega_n^2/\bar{a}^2 = \pi^2[(l/L)^2 + (m/W)^2 + (s/H)^2] \quad (11)$$

Here the subscript  $n$  represents the triplet of indices  $(l, m, s)$ , chosen so that  $\omega_{n+1} \geq \omega_n$  for every mode; in two-dimensional problems,  $n$  would correspond to an index doublet. In an unbaffled cylindrical chamber with length  $L$  and radius  $R$ , azimuthal degeneracy leads to two possible normal modes for each frequency,

$$\psi_n = \cos[(\pi l/L)x] J_m(\kappa_{ms}r) \quad \begin{cases} \cos(m\theta) \\ \sin(m\theta) \end{cases} \quad \begin{cases} l = 0, 1, 2, \dots \\ m = 0, 1, 2, \dots \\ s = 0, 1, 2, \dots \end{cases} \quad (12)$$

$$k_n^2 = \omega_n^2 / \bar{a}^2 = (\pi l / L)^2 + (\kappa_{ms})^2 \quad (13)$$

where  $(\kappa_{ms} R)$  is the  $s$ th positive zero of the function  $dJ_m(r)/dr$  for  $s \neq 0$  and  $\kappa_{ms} = 0$  for  $s = 0$ . In combustors with complicated geometry, as with injector face baffles, the eigenfunction expansion technique explained in Refs. 15 and 16 may be used to find normal mode solutions. The acoustic fields in each baffle compartment and in the main chamber are represented separately using a series expansion in terms of transverse eigenfunctions for each region. An equation governing the axial dependence is subsequently developed. By matching acoustic pressure and the axial gradient of acoustic pressure at the baffle/main chamber interface, a set of equations for the series coefficients in each region can be solved, with the normal mode frequency treated as an eigenvalue. Examination of Figs. 2 and 3 shows that baffles can have a significant effect on the spatial structures of acoustic waves. Whereas a transverse mode shape in an unbaffled chamber varies only in the transverse direction, the baffle introduces longitudinal variation, especially near the head end. Indeed, for longer baffle lengths, the motions within the baffle compartments become almost totally longitudinal for certain transverse modes. Often accompanying this longitudinalization is a concentration of the acoustic pressure extremes toward the injector face. If the combustion processes (atomization, evaporation, reactions, etc.) are sensitive to pressure fluctuations, baffles may actually destabilize the system by increasing the pressure fluctuations in this sensitive region and enhancing combustion response.<sup>15</sup> Given any number of baffles and type of mode, the degree of acoustic pressure concentration may vary substantially among the baffle compartments. In some instances bulk-type pressure oscillations may be found in some compartments, whereas in other cases a baffle compartment may have almost no pressure fluctuations. Since these scenarios have very different implications for stability with respect to pressure-sensitive mechanisms, the global stability of baffled combustors must be considered on a case-by-case basis.

Because of the longitudinalization of the acoustic wave and the partitions between baffle compartments, the transverse component of acoustic velocity is substantially restricted in the compartments. For systems with velocity-sensitive combustion processes, baffles may therefore enhance stability with respect to transverse modes.<sup>15</sup> A region of large acoustic velocity exists just downstream of the baffle, corresponding to the strong acoustic pressure gradient found there. Since the no-slip condition must be physically satisfied at the baffle blade, viscous damping caused by the resulting shear stresses is proposed in Ref. 16 as one way in which baffles stabilize a chamber. The strong transverse acoustic flow may also

result in periodic vortex shedding from the blade. Energy dissipated in these vortical structures or convected with them out of the chamber may be other damping mechanisms of baffles. The vortices could influence local mixing of propellants, affecting the combustion in a periodic fashion. Furthermore, near-wall coupling between fluctuating velocity and combustion processes should be considered in a rigorous stability analysis.

Another important effect of baffles is on the acoustic frequency. Numerous studies have concluded that the frequencies of transverse modes decrease after baffles are inserted.<sup>15</sup> Figure 2 shows how the wave "turns" around the baffle blade, yielding a longer acoustic particle path length and lower frequency. This effect may be stabilizing, destabilizing, or neutral, depending on the frequency response characteristics of the system.

### IV. Second-Order Nonlinear Acoustic Waves

A linear treatment of unsteady motions, such as the stability analysis detailed in Chapter 1, is only meaningful for small disturbances. Investigation of finite amplitude phenomena, such as limit cycles and pulse-triggered instabilities, requires consideration of nonlinear physical mechanisms. The most fundamental nonlinear analysis is a second-order one in which terms having products of three or more fluctuating quantities may be safely ignored. If the mean flow Mach number is reasonably assumed to be small (of the same magnitude as a perturbational quantity itself), then the source terms in Eqs. (1) and (2) become<sup>8</sup>

$$\begin{aligned} h = & -\nabla \cdot [\bar{\rho}(\bar{\mathbf{u}} \cdot \nabla \mathbf{u}' + \mathbf{u}' \cdot \nabla \bar{\mathbf{u}})] + \frac{1}{\bar{a}^2} \left[ \bar{\gamma} \frac{\partial p'}{\partial t} \nabla \cdot \bar{\mathbf{u}} + \bar{\mathbf{u}} \cdot \nabla \frac{\partial p'}{\partial t} \right] \\ & - \nabla \cdot \left[ \bar{\rho}(\mathbf{u}' \cdot \nabla \mathbf{u}') + \rho' \frac{\partial \mathbf{u}'}{\partial t} \right] \\ & + \frac{1}{\bar{a}^2} \left[ \frac{\partial}{\partial t} (\mathbf{u}' \cdot \nabla p') + \bar{\gamma} \frac{\partial}{\partial t} (p' \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}') \right] + \nabla \cdot \mathcal{F}' - \frac{1}{\bar{a}^2} \frac{\partial \mathcal{P}'}{\partial t} \end{aligned} \quad (14)$$

and

$$f = \left\{ \left[ \bar{\rho} \frac{\partial \mathbf{u}'}{\partial t} + \bar{\rho}(\bar{\mathbf{u}} \cdot \nabla \mathbf{u}' + \mathbf{u}' \cdot \nabla \bar{\mathbf{u}}) \right] + \left[ \rho' \frac{\partial \mathbf{u}'}{\partial t} + \bar{\rho}(\mathbf{u}' \cdot \nabla \mathbf{u}') \right] - \mathcal{F}' \right\} \cdot \mathbf{n} \quad (15)$$

where  $\mathcal{F}'$  and  $\mathcal{P}'$  represent the fluctuating influences of mass, momentum, and energy transfer between the condensed and gaseous phases, heat release due to combustion, heat conduction, and viscosity. Substituting these expressions into Eq. (8),  $F_n$  clearly shows the basic physical processes affecting acoustic fluctuations,

$$\begin{aligned} F_n = & -\frac{\bar{a}^2}{E_n^2 \bar{\rho}} \underbrace{\left[ \bar{\rho} k_n^2 \iiint \psi_n(\bar{\mathbf{u}} \cdot \mathbf{u}') dV \right]}_a - \underbrace{\left[ -\bar{\rho} \iiint [\mathbf{u}' \times (\nabla \times \bar{\mathbf{u}})] \cdot \nabla \psi_n dV \right]}_b \\ & - \underbrace{\left[ \frac{1}{\bar{a}^2} \iiint \frac{\partial p'}{\partial t} \bar{\mathbf{u}} \cdot \nabla \psi_n dV \right]}_c + \underbrace{\left[ \frac{\bar{\gamma} - 1}{\bar{a}^2} \iiint \psi_n \frac{\partial p'}{\partial t} \nabla \cdot \bar{\mathbf{u}} dV \right]}_d \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
& \underbrace{+\bar{\rho} \iiint (\mathbf{u}' \cdot \nabla \mathbf{u}') \cdot \nabla \psi_n \, dV}_e - \underbrace{\frac{1}{\bar{a}^2} \iiint \frac{\partial p'}{\partial t} \mathbf{u}' \cdot \nabla \psi_n \, dV}_f \\
& + \underbrace{\frac{\bar{\gamma}-1}{\bar{a}^2} \iiint \psi_n \frac{\partial p'}{\partial t} \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}' \, dV}_g + \underbrace{\frac{\bar{\gamma}-1}{\bar{a}^2} \iiint \psi_n p' \nabla \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{u}'}{\partial t} \, dV}_h \\
& + \underbrace{\iiint \psi_n \frac{\partial}{\partial t} (\bar{\mathbf{u}} \rho' + \mathbf{u}' \bar{\rho} + \mathbf{u}' \rho') \cdot \mathbf{n} \, dS}_i \\
& - \underbrace{\iiint (\mathcal{F}' \cdot \nabla \psi_n) + \left( \frac{1}{\bar{a}^2} \psi_n \frac{\partial P'}{\partial t} \right) dV}_j \Big] \quad (16)
\end{aligned}$$

The terms a–d are linear in the perturbation quantities and represent all influences of mean flow on unsteady motions. Terms e–h are the second-order effects of gas-dynamics, which give rise to cross- and self-coupling among modes of finite amplitude. Term i contains the integrated effects of boundary conditions due to injector and nozzle responses, acoustic liners, etc. The final term j includes any additional linear and nonlinear influences (to second order) of heat conduction, viscosity, interphase momentum and heat transfer, and volumetric combustion response.

By substituting Eqs. (3) and (4) into Eq. (16),  $F_n$  can be written as a function of  $\eta_n$  and  $\dot{\eta}_n$ . Although Eq. (7) could then be directly integrated with numerical techniques, some insight can be gained through application of the method of time averaging.<sup>9</sup> The method basically filters out high-frequency information from the results, leaving a simpler problem to be solved for only the slowly varying behavior, which is of most interest anyway. This filtering feature also decreases the stiffness of the system for numerical solution. To begin,  $\eta_n(t)$  and  $\dot{\eta}_n(t)$  are expressed in terms of  $r_n(t)$  and  $\phi_n(t)$ , measuring the time-varying amplitude and phase of the oscillation, respectively,

$$\eta_n(t) = r_n(t) \sin[\omega_n t + \phi_n(t)] \quad (17)$$

$$\dot{\eta}_n(t) = r_n(t) \omega_n \cos[\omega_n t + \phi_n(t)] \quad (18)$$

where  $\omega_n$  is the radian frequency of the  $n$ th normal mode as found in the linear analysis. The temporal development of the  $n$ th mode may be characterized by two disparate time scales: a fast time scale  $t_f$ , equal to  $\omega_n^{-1}$ , and a slow time scale  $t_s$ , over which the gradual changes in nonlinear oscillations are observed. In Eq. (17) rapid variations of  $\eta_n$  are well captured by the  $\omega_n t$  portion of the sinusoid, leaving only slow variations in the amplitude and phase. Substituting Eqs. (17) and (18) into Eq. (7) yields a set of first-order ordinary differential equations in terms of the new variables  $r_n$  and  $\phi_n$ . If these equations for each mode are time averaged over a time interval  $\tau$ , which is large compared to  $t_f$  but small with respect to  $t_s$ , then slowly varying quantities can be considered as constant during the integration. It can be shown that rapidly varying terms in the  $r_n$  and  $\phi_n$  equations vanish exactly

for longitudinal modes, since the mode frequencies are integer multiples of the first mode frequency. For transverse modes in cylindrical chambers, there is no such relationship between the modes. If, however,  $t_f \ll \tau \ll t_s$ , the effects of rapidly varying terms over many periods of oscillation are quite small, and the terms are neglected.<sup>9</sup>

#### A. Effect of Acoustic Mode Coupling

The linear coupling between acoustic modes is often weak due to disparity of the normal mode frequencies; this implies that linear modes behave independently of one another. For nonlinear waves, however, interactions between modes and self coupling can have profound influences. If only second-order effects of nonlinear acoustics [processes e-h in Eq. (16)] are considered,  $F_n$  can be written as

$$F_n = - \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} [D_{ni}\dot{\eta}_i + E_{ni}\eta_i] - \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} [A_{nij}\dot{\eta}_i\dot{\eta}_j + B_{nij}\eta_i\eta_j] \quad (19)$$

where linear coefficients  $D_{ni}$  and  $E_{ni}$ , and nonlinear coefficients  $A_{nij}$  and  $B_{nij}$  are defined in Refs. 8 and 9. To maintain some degree of analytical tractability, only the first two modes (e.g., either longitudinal or transverse) are retained in the expansions of acoustic pressure and velocity. These common modes adequately capture the major features of nonlinear behavior, since the amplitudes of higher modes are usually small due to the effective viscous damping at higher frequencies. Time averaging then produces the following set for a two-mode system, for longitudinal as well as baffled and unbaffled transverse mode cases<sup>7,9,15</sup>:

$$\frac{dr_1}{dt} = \alpha_1 r_1 + a_1 r_1 r_2 \cos \Psi \quad (20)$$

$$\frac{dr_2}{dt} = \alpha_2 r_2 + b_1 r_1^2 \cos \Psi \quad (21)$$

$$\frac{d\Psi}{dt} = -2\theta_1 + \theta_2 + \Omega_1 - \left( 2a_1 r_2 + b_1 \frac{r_1^2}{r_2} \right) \sin \Psi \quad (22)$$

where

$$\Psi = 2\phi_1 - \phi_2 + \Omega_1 t \quad (23)$$

$$\alpha_n = -(D_{nn}/2), \quad \theta_n = -(E_{nn}/2\omega_n), \quad \Omega_1 = (2\omega_1 - \omega_2)$$

The coefficients  $a_1$  and  $b_1$  arise from the nonlinear gasdynamic coupling between modes. If nonlinear terms are ignored, Eqs. (20–22) become independent, with  $\alpha_n$  and  $\theta_n$  representing the linear growth constant and frequency shift of the  $n$ th mode, respectively.

The mode amplitudes  $r_1$  and  $r_2$  are constant for a limit cycle and cause all derivatives in Eqs. (20–22) to vanish. Limit-cycle amplitudes (denoted by the subscript 0) become

$$r_{10} = \left\{ \frac{\alpha_1 \alpha_2}{a_1 b_1} \left[ 1 + \left( \frac{2\theta_1 - \theta_2 - \Omega_1}{2\alpha_1 + \alpha_2} \right)^2 \right] \right\}^{\frac{1}{2}} \quad (24)$$

$$r_{20} = -\frac{\alpha_1}{a_1} \left[ 1 + \left( \frac{2\theta_1 - \theta_2 - \Omega_1}{2\alpha_1 + \alpha_2} \right)^2 \right]^{\frac{1}{2}} \quad (25)$$

Since  $a_1 b_1$  is always negative in the present study of nonlinear gasdynamics, Eq. (24) requires that

$$\alpha_1 \alpha_2 < 0 \quad (26)$$

In other words, one mode must be stable and the other unstable for a limit cycle to exist. This obviously prevents any triggering to a limit cycle due to second-order gasdynamics alone since triggered instabilities can occur only in a system that is linearly stable. For a limit cycle to be observed, the amplitudes given by Eqs. (24) and (25) must be stable equilibrium points. Conditions for limit-cycle stability may be found by examining the behavior of an infinitesimal disturbance in the neighborhood of the limit-cycle solution.<sup>9</sup>

Analysis of phase in a limit cycle  $\phi_{n0}$  also yields useful insight. For a constant value of  $\Psi$  required for an equilibrium point, the following form of  $\phi_{n0}$  is found:

$$\phi_{n0} = \nu_n t + \zeta_n \quad (27)$$

where  $\nu_n$  and  $\zeta_n$  refer to frequency modulation and relative phase in the limit cycle, respectively. Because one phase is arbitrary,  $\zeta_1$  may be specified with no loss of generality. After several manipulations, expressions for the limiting mode oscillations become

$$\eta_{10}(t) = r_{10} \sin[(\omega_1 + \nu_1)t + \zeta_1] \quad (28)$$

$$\eta_{20}(t) = r_{20} \sin[2(\omega_1 + \nu_1)t + \zeta_2] \quad (29)$$

The second mode, therefore, oscillates at a modulated frequency exactly twice that of the first, even for transverse modes in cylindrical<sup>9</sup> or baffled<sup>15</sup> chambers. With the exception of  $\nu_1 = 0$ , the fundamental mode frequency is shifted from its linear value, even for systems originally having normal mode frequencies, which are already integer multiples of the first.

Nonlinear coupling via gasdynamics within the acoustic modes reveals an energy cascade, which explains the development of limit cycles. The rate of change of time-averaged acoustic energy  $\langle \mathcal{E}_n \rangle$  within each mode is<sup>15</sup>

$$\frac{d\langle \mathcal{E}_1 \rangle}{dt} = \frac{E_1^2}{\bar{\gamma}^2} [\alpha_1 r_1^2 + a_1 r_1^2 r_2 \cos \Psi] \quad (30)$$

$$\frac{d\langle \mathcal{E}_2 \rangle}{dt} = \frac{E_2^2}{\bar{\gamma}^2} [\alpha_2 r_2^2 + b_1 r_1^2 r_2 \cos \Psi] \quad (31)$$

where

$$\langle \mathcal{E}_n \rangle = (r_n^2 E_n^2 / 2 \bar{\gamma}^2) \quad (32)$$

Energy enters the system through linear processes of the unstable (e.g., first) mode and is transferred by nonlinear coupling mechanisms to the stable (e.g., second) mode where it is linearly damped. Substituting results from the limit-cycle analysis

shows that a limit cycle is characterized by constant levels of energy within each mode and the entire system. For systems with  $a_1 = -b_1$  (e.g., longitudinal modes, transverse modes in unbaffled rectangular two-dimensional chambers), the energy extracted in a limit cycle by the unstable mode exactly equals that dissipated by the stable mode; this is not exactly true, however, for cases with  $a_1 \neq -b_1$  (e.g., transverse modes in cylindrical or baffled chambers). Perhaps energy is not directly transferred from mode to mode but, rather, is managed through a kind of energy repository, which may itself have the capacity to modulate energy. The physical manifestation of such an intermediate stage of energy transfer is presently unclear from the time-averaged or complete governing equations. Another strong possibility is that energy is truly conserved in the transfer mechanisms, but the definition in Eq. (32) does not adequately resolve the energy of the system. For example, the effect of frequency modulation is not explicitly accounted for. This question remains somewhat open and deserves further study.

Figure 4 shows the evolution of limit cycles for the first tangential and first radial modes in an unbaffled cylindrical chamber. This behavior is typical of limit-cycle development, with the unstable and stable modes initially showing exponential growth and decay, respectively. As the unstable mode grows, nonlinear coupling mechanisms become more important and eventually form the limit cycles.

Reference 9 also explored a three-mode expansion for a cylindrical chamber, considering the first tangential (1T), first radial (1R), and second tangential (2T) modes. The same basic type of mode coupling was found between the lowest frequency mode (1T) and each of the others, as observed for the two-mode expansion. Furthermore, the nonlinear coupling modulates the mode frequencies in such a way that the two higher modes oscillate at exactly twice the frequency of the first (see Fig. 5). It appears that the three-mode behavior is dominated by the coupling between the 1T and 1R mode due to more efficient nonlinear energy transfer from the 1T to the 1R mode than to the 2T mode.<sup>9</sup> For completeness, coupling between the unstable 1T mode and longitudinal or even mixed modes should be examined to see if other modes are important in the actual transfer of acoustic energy through nonlinear coupling.

It is advantageous to use time averaging and a two-mode expansion in studying nonlinear acoustics because sweeping results can be obtained due to the analytical tractability. If the governing equations were simply integrated with numerical
