techniques, results would be relevant only to specific cases. Jahnke and Culick<sup>10,11</sup> applied dynamical systems theory to nonlinear chamber acoustics and obtained fairly general results without resorting to time averaging or a few-mode expansion. The method utilizes a modified continuation technique to find limit-cycle solutions provided one solution is already known. The power of the technique lies in the ability to compute an entire locus of limit-cycle solutions as a function of system parameters (e.g., linear coefficients of each mode). Furthermore, solutions may be found for many modes in the expansion of Eqs. (3) and (4) only at the expense of increased computational time.

Time-averaged, two-mode solutions were compared with continuation results using different numbers of modes and considering only second-order gasdynamics in a longitudinal mode system.<sup>10,11</sup> Cases with unstable first modes or unstable second modes were treated, with all other modes assumed to be stable. Differences between the two approaches were observed primarily for very unstable systems (large values of  $\alpha_1$  or  $\alpha_2$ ); time averaging caused only quantitative differences, but truncation to two modes yielded qualitative differences. Specifically, in very unstable systems, higher modes can be responsible for a significant share of the total energy dissipation. If these modes are ignored, the amplitude of other stable modes must (unrealistically) increase to compensate for the loss of energy dissipation; in the extreme, the limit cycle in the two-mode system becomes

artificially unstable. Practically, these results may not be too restrictive, since the disagreement occurs for mode amplitudes near the limit of applicability for second-order approximation anyway. Furthermore, the generality of the conclusions may be somewhat confined since only the unstable mode growth constant was varied. The two-mode expansion with an unstable second mode, however, was found to be physically limited, since the natural flow of energy from lower modes to higher modes through gasdynamics is not possible.<sup>11</sup>

#### B. Nonlinear Combustion Response

Although second-order gasdynamics alone are incapable of causing triggered instabilities, nonlinear combustion response to acoustic oscillations is a candidate mechanism in this important nonlinear phenomenon. Previous work<sup>8,12,14</sup> has emphasized combustion response in solid-propellant motors, which enters through the unsteady mass flux in the boundary effects term "i" in Eq. (16). Results thus obtained are still meaningful to liquid rocket engines in which nonlinear effects of the boundary are plausible, due to combustion at the boundary (e.g., "concentrated combustion" assumption or combustion of propellant film at chamber walls), acoustic response of the injector and nozzle, near-injector phenomena such as jet breakup, response of ablative surfaces, or response of acoustic dampers. More important, the effects of nonlinear response of surface combustion are expected to have structural analogs in systems with volumetric combustion (in the limit of concentrated combustion, volumetric and surface burning would have identical influences). In Refs. 8, 12, and 14, combustion response is not formulated from first principles; rather, ad-hoc response functions are used to obtain qualitative results for large classes of physically viable responses. For surface combustion, this amounts to finding a response function for the mass flow normal to the boundary.

In general, the combustion response function should depend on pressure and velocity fluctuations, since these quantities are the primary manifestations of acoustic waves. Two cases are treated here to illustrate the dependence of acoustic characteristics on the type of combustion response function. Case 1 assumes that the fluctuation of propellant burning rate  $\dot{m}'_b$  is proportional to any linear combination of the following quantities:

$$\dot{m}'_b \propto p', \quad u', \quad p'^2, \quad u'^2, \quad p'u' \quad (33)$$

Substituting Eqs. (3) and (4) into the most general form of Eq. (33) will contribute to the forcing function as follows<sup>14</sup>:

$$\begin{aligned} (F_n)_{NC} = & \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} D_{ni} \dot{\eta}_i + \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} E_{ni}^* \eta_i \\ & + \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} A_{nij}^* \dot{\eta}_i \dot{\eta}_j + B_{nij}^* \eta_i \eta_j + M_{nij}^* \dot{\eta}_i \eta_j \end{aligned} \quad (34)$$

where all starred coefficients are constant values. This form of forcing function produces the same basic type of mode coupling as second-order gasdynamics alone, with governing equations similar to Eqs (20–22).<sup>12</sup> Therefore, this rather broad class of combustion response functions is incapable of causing pulse-triggered instability.

Another viable set of nonlinear combustion response functions involves the absolute value of oscillatory quantities. For example, response to  $|u'|$  in liquid engines may be due to enhanced mixing of adjacent fuel and oxidizer streams, accelerated jet breakup, or droplet shattering caused by unsteady gas motions. For case 2 we assume that the fluctuating burning rate is proportional to any linear combination of the following quantities:

$$\dot{m}'_b \propto |u'|, \quad |p'|, \quad u'|p'|, \quad p'|u'| \quad (35)$$

Of all of the possible forms of this dependence, consideration of response only to  $|u'|$  (case 2a) and  $p'|u'|$  (case 2b) is sufficient, since unsteady pressure can be related to velocity fluctuations through a simple phase shift. After expressing these functions in terms of  $\eta_n$  and  $\dot{\eta}_n$  and following the method of time averaging, the equations for the amplitudes and phases of the first two modes become<sup>14</sup> for case 2a,  $\dot{m}'_b \propto |u'|$ ,

$$\frac{dr_1}{dt} = \alpha_1 r_1 + a_1 r_1 r_2 \cos \Psi - 4c_{1a} r_2 \sin \Psi \quad (36)$$

$$\frac{dr_2}{dt} = \alpha_2 r_2 + b_1 r_1^2 \cos \Psi - c_{1a} r_1 \sin \Psi \quad (37)$$

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{d\Psi}{dt} = & -2\theta_1 + \theta_2 + \Omega_1 - \left( 2a_1 r_2 + b_1 \frac{r_1^2}{r_2} \right) \sin \Psi \\ & - \left( 16 \frac{r_2}{r_1} + \frac{r_1}{r_2} \right) c_{1a} \cos \Psi \end{aligned} \quad (38)$$

For case 2b,  $\dot{m}'_b \propto p'|u'|$ ,

$$\frac{dr_1}{dt} = \alpha_1 r_1 + a_1 r_1 r_2 \cos \Psi - c_{1b} \frac{16}{9} \left[ r_1^2 - \frac{4}{25} r_2^2 \cos 2\Psi \right] \quad (39)$$

$$\frac{dr_2}{dt} = \alpha_2 r_2 + b_1 r_1^2 \cos \Psi - c_{1b} \frac{16}{15} \left[ 4 + \frac{7}{15} \cos 2\Psi \right] r_1 r_2 \quad (40)$$

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{d\Psi}{dt} = & -2\theta_1 + \theta_2 + \Omega_1 - \left( 2a_1 r_2 + b_1 \frac{r_1^2}{r_2} \right) \sin \Psi \\ & - c_{1b} \sin 2\Psi \left[ 2 \left( \frac{16}{15} \right)^2 \frac{r_2^2}{r_1} - 7 \left( \frac{4}{15} \right)^2 r_1 \right] \end{aligned} \quad (41)$$

where  $c_{1a}$  and  $c_{1b}$  are parameters (typically negative) measuring the strength of combustion response in each case. Although these equations were derived for longitudinal modes and two-dimensional transverse modes, extension to transverse modes in cylindrical or baffled chambers should present only quantitative differences.

The preceding set of equations may be compared with the case of pure nonlinear gasdynamic coupling, Eqs. (20–22). It has been shown that the linear cross coupling caused by combustion response to  $|u'|$  in Eqs. (36) and (37) and the quadratic self-coupling caused by combustion response to  $p'|u'|$  in Eq. (39) can produce

triggering phenomena.<sup>14</sup> Both cases require strong linear damping of the second mode and weaker damping of the first mode for triggering to occur. For stronger combustion response, damping of both modes must increase for the system to trigger nonlinear instability.

The rates of mode energy are governed by the following equations for case 2a,  $\dot{m}_b' \propto |u'|$ ,

$$\frac{d(\mathcal{E}_1)}{dt} = \frac{E_1^2}{\bar{\gamma}^2} [\alpha_1 r_1^2 + a_1 r_1^2 r_2 \cos \Psi - c_{1a} 4 r_1 r_2 \sin \Psi] \quad (42)$$

$$\frac{d(\mathcal{E}_2)}{dt} = \frac{E_2^2}{\bar{\gamma}^2} [\alpha_2 r_2^2 + b_1 r_1^2 r_2 \cos \Psi - c_{1a} r_1 r_2 \sin \Psi] \quad (43)$$

and for case 2b,  $\dot{m}_b' \propto p'|u'|$ ,

$$\frac{d(\mathcal{E}_1)}{dt} = \frac{E_1^2}{\bar{\gamma}^2} \left[ \alpha_1 r_1^2 + a_1 r_1^2 r_2 \cos \Psi - c_{1b} \frac{16}{9} \left( r_1^3 - \frac{4}{25} r_1 r_2^2 \cos 2\Psi \right) \right] \quad (44)$$

$$\frac{d(\mathcal{E}_2)}{dt} = \frac{E_2^2}{\bar{\gamma}^2} \left[ \alpha_2 r_2^2 + b_1 r_1^2 r_2 \cos \Psi - c_{1b} \frac{16}{15} \left( 4 + \frac{7}{15} \cos 2\Psi \right) r_1 r_2^2 \right] \quad (45)$$

These expressions are similar to Eqs. (30) and (31) but with the addition of energy sources (or sinks) due to the nonlinear combustion response. In the case of linear cross coupling (case 2a), the combustion can add or detract energy from both modes, depending on the mode phases (specifically, the sign of  $\sin \Psi$ ). For nonlinear self-coupling (case 2b), the explicit influence of nonlinear combustion response on mode energy is almost independent of mode phase, except for the relatively small  $\cos 2\Psi$  terms in the energy flow of each mode. Assuming zero phase lag in the response function, nonlinear combustion in case 2b can only drive the second mode but can damp the first mode, if the amplitude of the second mode is sufficiently large and the amplitude of the first is sufficiently small.

Although modal energy transfer plays a key role in system behavior, triggering can occur with energy flow from lower modes to higher modes, or vice versa. For the linear cross-coupling case, the energy source term from nonlinear combustion involves the product of both mode amplitudes, i.e., the presence of one mode is required for the nonlinear combustion to feed (or subtract) energy to (or from) the other. Physically, this might be interpreted as transfer of energy between modes, but it is not the usual transfer associated with nonlinear gasdynamics. In the scenario of nonlinear self coupling, Eqs. (44) and (45) also contain nonlinear combustion response terms with the product of mode amplitudes, but the first mode has the additional  $r_1^3$  term—the first mode can receive energy from nonlinear combustion independent of the second mode.

Examples of pulse-triggered instabilities for cases 2a and 2b are shown in Fig. 6. The typical behavior expected of triggering is observed, with small pulses damping away and larger pulses waxing to limit cycles. An issue of practical concern involves determination of the threshold amplitude, above which an initial pulse causes persisting oscillations and below which it damps out. The bomb test for rating the dynamic stability of an engine experimentally seeks to answer this question. Theoretically, further insight is available through examination of the equilibrium points of Eqs. (36–38) and (39–41). Based on studies of simplified one- and two-degree-of-freedom systems<sup>13</sup> and analysis of nonlinear combustion

response,<sup>12,14</sup> the essence of triggering entails a stable trivial solution ( $r_1 = r_2 = 0$ ) and a stable limit cycle of finite amplitude, with an unstable limit cycle of intermediate amplitude. The stable manifold of this intermediate limit cycle forms the boundary for the basin of attraction of the trivial solution (i.e., the region of initial disturbances which decay). It is reasonably hypothesized in Ref. 12 that initial pulses having energy greater than that of the intermediate limit cycle would grow to the stable limit cycle, but lower-energy pulses would decay. Although the amplitude of the intermediate limit cycle does appear to scale the region of stable pulses, the region is significantly distorted according to the phase and harmonic content (relative amplitudes of the modes) of the initial pulse.<sup>4</sup> In fact, for both cases 2a and 2b, certain stable pulses have initial amplitudes substantially larger than other pulses that trigger the system, but with suitable differences in initial phase and harmonic content. Practically, this means that the idea of a single "threshold" amplitude is physically incomplete—all aspects of the initial disturbance must be considered (e.g., traveling vs standing wave, "bomb" disturbance, harmonic disturbance, etc.).

### V. Third-Order Nonlinear Acoustic Waves

The qualitative effects of third-order gasdynamic interactions are presented in this section. One motivation for originally pursuing third-order mechanisms was the faulty notion that these processes are vital in producing pulse-triggered phenomena.<sup>5,6</sup> It has already been shown that such effects are clearly not necessary.<sup>15</sup> Gasdynamics and mean flow/acoustics interactions to third order are not even completely sufficient for triggering. Investigation of these mechanisms is important, nonetheless, for complete understanding and for extending the analytical treatment to higher amplitude fluctuations.

#### A. Effect of Third-Order Acoustics

If the sources  $h$  and  $f$  are developed to third order (again, treating mean flow Mach number as a perturbation quantity), two new processes arise: third-order acoustics and interactions between mean flow and second-order acoustics.<sup>13</sup> By simply setting the mean flow equal to zero, the effects of third-order acoustics may be isolated for clearer interpretation. The time-averaged amplitude and phase difference equations for the first two longitudinal modes become

$$\frac{dr_1}{dt} = \alpha_1 r_1 + a_1 r_1 r_2 \cos \Psi \quad (46)$$

$$\frac{dr_2}{dt} = \alpha_2 r_2 + b_1 r_1^2 \cos \Psi \quad (47)$$

$$\frac{d\Psi}{dt} = -2\theta_1 + \theta_2 + \Omega_1 - \left( 2a_1 r_2 + b_1 \frac{r_1^2}{r_2} \right) \sin \Psi + 2\beta_1 (r_2^2 - r_1^2) \quad (48)$$

where  $\beta_1 = \omega_1(\bar{\gamma} + 1)/(64\bar{\gamma}^2)$ . It is interesting to note that comparison of the preceding expressions with the governing Eqs. (20–22) for the second-order acoustics shows that third-order acoustics influence only the phase angle of each acoustic mode, with basically identical coupling between the mode amplitudes. For a limit cycle to exist, one mode must still be linearly stable and the other linearly unstable—no triggering is possible due to third-order acoustics alone. The effects of second- and third-order gasdynamics are similar, providing a path for energy exchange between the modes. The only major effect of third-order acoustics is to modify the amplitudes and phases of each mode, with different conditions required for stable limit-cycle oscillations.

#### B. Mean Flow/Acoustics Interactions

The effects of mean flow interactions with second-order acoustics is investigated<sup>13</sup> separately by ignoring all third-order acoustic terms in  $h$  and  $f$ . The mean flow is assumed to be only axial and linearly varying,

$$\bar{u} = (\bar{u}_e/L)x \quad (49)$$

where  $L$  and  $\bar{u}_e$  are the combustor length and mean velocity at the combustor exit, respectively. The equations governing the amplitudes and phase difference of the first two longitudinal modes become

$$\frac{dr_1}{dt} = \alpha_1 r_1 + r_1 r_2 (a_1 \cos \Psi - 7\beta_m \sin \Psi) \quad (50)$$

$$\frac{dr_2}{dt} = \alpha_2 r_2 + r_1^2 (b_1 \cos \Psi + \beta_m \sin \Psi) \quad (51)$$

$$\frac{d\Psi}{dt} = -2\theta_1 + \theta_2 + \Omega_1 - \left( 2a_1 r_2 + b_1 \frac{r_1^2}{r_2} \right) \sin \Psi + \beta_m \left( -14r_2 + \frac{r_1^2}{r_2} \right) \cos \Psi \quad (52)$$

where  $\beta_m = \bar{u}_e/(32\bar{\gamma}L)$ . The mode coupling in this scenario is similar to the second-order acoustics case, but with an important exception; due to the  $\sin \Psi$

However, stability analysis shows that oscillations can trigger only to an unstable limit cycle, as shown in Fig. 7. Since this corresponds to unbounded growth, the ability of mean flow/acoustic interactions to cause triggering to a stable limit cycle is incomplete; other processes must act simultaneously to limit the unsteady motions.

### VI. Conclusions

Because high-frequency combustion instabilities arise from interactions between combustion processes and acoustic motions, studies emphasizing chamber acoustics have added substantially to the general understanding of instabilities. The general two-phase formulation described in Chapter 1 of this volume has proven to be especially fruitful in such investigations. By treating unsteady motions in an integral fashion, it was shown in Chapter 1 that the problem of linear stability can be treated quite generally. Given knowledge of the normal modes of the chamber, the methodology also allows exploration of nonlinear phenomena as well.

The most fundamental of nonlinear processes in a thrust chamber is second-order gasdynamics. The intermodal coupling due to this mechanism allows energy transfer between modes, such that limit-cycle oscillations develop. For this to happen, one mode must be linearly stable and the other unstable, precluding the possibility of triggering due to second-order gasdynamics alone. By additionally considering appropriate nonlinear combustion responses (e.g.,  $\dot{m}'_b$  proportional to  $|u'|$  or  $p'|u'|$ ), triggering to stable limit cycles has been established, suggesting that this mechanism is an important player in pulse-triggered oscillations. The key to triggering is introduction of linear cross coupling between the modes, or nonlinear self-coupling in at least one mode. Results show that initial harmonic content and phase characteristics of the initial pulse (in addition to overall amplitude) are important in determining the nonlinear stability of a disturbance. Third-order gasdynamics have also been treated, yielding behavior basically similar to that of second-order gasdynamics alone (limit cycle may be observed, but no triggering). For assumed small mean flow, another third-order mechanism is the interaction between mean flow and second-order acoustics. Here, the intermodal energy transfer is modified by the mode phase difference so that triggering to an unstable limit

cycle is possible. Since triggered oscillations grow unbounded in this case, other processes must be considered for complete modeling of chamber acoustics.

The majority of the work done on nonlinear acoustics has employed a few-mode expansion to represent the acoustic fields, along with the method of time averaging. Although this procedure has provided key insight into the basic physics of the problem by preserving analytical tractability, the quest for more detailed understanding promotes different solutions. With the current level of computational power available, it seems plausible to simply relax these constraints. A continuation method has been applied to the study of nonlinear acoustics, indeed revealing limitations of a few-mode expansion. Using bifurcation theory, global aspects of system stability and behavior may also be determined with such a methodology. Application of other aspects of modern dynamical systems theory, along with more numerically intensive approaches, is expected to offer further understanding of chamber acoustics.

### I. Introduction

MANY rocket engine development programs have experienced high-frequency combustion instabilities. Elimination of these instabilities is often difficult, calling for a huge number of expensive full-scale tests, and eventually results in redesign of parts of the injector/combustor system at later stages of a project. Consequently, it is important from the very beginning to systematically exploit all possibilities that may help to avoid the occurrence of these highly destructive oscillations.

This chapter provides some experimental procedures that can be employed to aid the design process of acoustic resonators and cavities, i.e., elements that are used as passive means to suppress or limit the destructive potential of high-frequency oscillations. In fact, changing the damping characteristics of a combustion chamber by incorporating acoustic devices is a well-known technique in rocket engine development, even though the actual realization may be quite difficult at times as was the case during the development of the FI-rocket motor.

The mechanism of high-frequency instabilities in rocket engines has been investigated over a period of several decades; however, no general rules have yet

been established for designing inherent stable injector/combustor systems. One reason for this is the enormous variety of existing injector configurations for the different propellant combinations used, all featuring specific atomization, vaporization, mixing, and burning behavior. In contrast to this, it is much easier to formulate general design rules for instability suppression devices since their variability is more limited, at least concerning the general types of baffles, Helmholtz, and quarter-wave resonators discussed here. These damping devices produce good results in stabilizing combustion oscillations. The latter two have the advantage of being less exposed to the adverse core flow conditions within a combustion chamber.

In the first part of this chapter, the role of a full-scale acoustic chamber model in gaining first acoustic data is explained. General baffles as well as cavity design principles are then recalled, and experimental procedures that aid the conventional resonator layout process are described. Experimental data are provided where important to highlight typical resonator characteristics under hot-firing conditions. Finally, several issues addressing the shape of the inlet orifice of an acoustic cavity and its impact on overall resonator absorption behavior are discussed.

### II. Acoustic Tests with Model Chambers

Acoustic resonators and baffles are damping devices successfully used as suppression mechanisms for the reduction or elimination of combustion oscillations. Resonators are narrowband absorbers that must be tuned accurately to discrete acoustic eigenfrequencies of the combustion chamber. These frequencies must be known at the beginning of any preliminary layout of resonating cavities. A full-scale model chamber is a useful tool here for first tests under ambient conditions. Cold-test results can then be used to evaluate the chamber's eigenfrequencies during hot-firing tests.

In the current investigation, a model chamber was equipped with a number of small loudspeakers in the injector faceplate: one in the center and others equally spaced at two different radii. A microphone mounted on a thin rod was attached to a small tube, making it possible to reach any axial, radial, and azimuthal position in the chamber. Additional microphones were mounted flush at the chamber wall immediately behind the faceplate.

Random noise was used as the source for the loudspeakers. Resonant frequencies in the chamber were identified by registering microphone signals throughout the chamber. Once the frequencies were known, a sine generator was used to activate only one particular mode. The shape pattern of the mode was then determined by scanning the chamber in azimuthal and/or radial and axial directions for nodal lines. These lines of minimum pressure can be found, first, by observing the amplitude and second, by locating any phase shift in the chamber. The latter is accomplished by comparing the phase between the measured signal and a reference signal taken directly from the loudspeaker. Each time the microphone moves through a nodal line, the acoustic pressure will be at a minimum and the phase will shift by 180 deg. A schematic layout of the experimental setup is illustrated in Fig. 1.

Another possibility of generating broadband noise in a chamber without loudspeakers is by means of high-speed airflow through the injection holes. This was practiced with smaller liquid-propellant engines where the air pressure in a reservoir behind the faceplate was held constant for the test duration.

#### A. Resonant Frequencies

A typical spectrum of a full-scale model test performed in air under ambient conditions is shown in Fig. 2. The notations 1T, 1L, and 1R stand for first tangential, first longitudinal, and first radial mode, respectively. The combined first longitudinal/first tangential mode is denoted 1L/1T. It exhibits distinct peaks, demonstrating that the chamber itself rarely has any damping effect for transversal modes (tangential and radial) or their combinations with longitudinal frequencies. Longitudinal (axial) modes were not identified during these measurements since they are damped by the convergent part of the nozzle. Only in those chambers with a long cylindrical part and/or short nozzle section were L modes measurable.

Figure 2 depicts two frequency scales: the upper one represents frequencies measured in the model under ambient condition, and the lower one represents frequencies expected in the actual chamber during hot firing. The difference is the speed of sound ratio between these two conditions. Whereas the wavelength of an eigenfrequency is determined by the geometry of the chamber, and thus fixed for a specific model chamber, the corresponding frequency changes with the speed of sound ratio as the hot-gas condition is approached.

Acoustic tests with models have shown that the combustion chamber and nozzle configuration must be treated theoretically as a closed/closed system even though the nozzle is not actually closed. The eigenfrequencies for a cylindrical chamber closed at both sides can be calculated with Eq. (1),

$$f_{\ell mn} = \frac{c}{2\pi} \sqrt{\left( \frac{\lambda_{mn}^2}{R_c^2} + \frac{\ell^2 \pi^2}{L_c^2} \right)} \quad \ell, m, n = 0, 1, 2, \dots \quad (1)$$

where  $\lambda_{mn}$  is the transverse eigenvalue listed in Table 1 for the first few modes.

For rocket combustion chambers,  $L_c$  must be replaced by the effective acoustic length, i.e., the distance between the faceplate and nozzle throat less approximately one-half of the converging nozzle length. Table 2 compares calculated resonant

#### B. Mode Shape

The acoustic modes of a combustion chamber arise from pressure waves traversing the cavity at the speed of sound and reflecting from the chamber walls. If the fluid oscillates freely in the longitudinal  $\ell$ , tangential  $m$ , and radial  $n$  mode, the dynamic component of the fluid pressure is simply the sum of the contributions of the individual modes, and can be expressed in terms of the total velocity potential function:

$$\Phi = \sum_{\ell mn} A_{\ell mn} \frac{c^2}{\omega_{\ell mn}} \varphi_{\ell mn} \sin(\omega_{\ell mn} t + \psi_{\ell mn}) \quad (2)$$

The dynamic variation in the acoustic pressure can be expressed in terms of this velocity potential

$$p = \rho \frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial t} = \sum_{\ell mn} A_{\ell mn} \rho c^2 \varphi_{\ell mn} \cdot \cos(\omega_{\ell mn} t + \psi_{\ell mn}) \quad (3)$$

where  $A$  is a constant that specifies the amplitude,  $\psi$  the phase angle with respect to the other modes, and  $\varphi$  the nondimensional mode shape of the potential function. For a closed/closed cylindrical chamber this mode shape is

$$\varphi_{\ell mn} = J_m(\lambda_{mn}(r/R_c)) \cdot \cos(\ell x \pi / L_c) \cdot \cos m \vartheta \quad (4)$$

$J_m$  is the Bessel function of the first kind and is of order  $m$ .

The acoustic pressure amplitudes of the tangential modes reach their maximum at the chamber wall and are zero in the center, whereas those of the radial modes are largest in the center. This was also observed during measurements in the model chamber where a microphone placed in the combustor's center measured only radial and combined radial/longitudinal modes. From the acoustic pressure field distribution, one can conclude that the ideal placement of acoustic resonators for maximum effectiveness is at the circumference of the combustion chamber if tangential modes are to be damped, and at the center of the faceplate if radial modes are to be damped.

Experience with a number of liquid-propellant engines shows that if a chamber is susceptible to instability, it is usually sensitive to tangential modes. It is also this acoustic mode that may drive the most destructive type of instabilities, since its pressure oscillation shape can destroy the thermal boundary layer and cause immediate chamber wall damage.

Mode-shape measurements in a chamber model under ambient conditions are restricted to the location of nodal lines. Tangential modes are in general unsettled, taking any position in the chamber unless an irregularity in the injection locks them to a fixed location. Cold-gas tests with a limited number of loudspeakers have shown that the nodal pressure lines change their position corresponding to a

change in loudspeaker location. A nodal pressure line always avoids the position of maximum acoustic excitation; i.e., under hot-gas conditions the nodal line spins away from regions of more intensified combustion. Cold tests also showed that the nodal line of a T mode always turns into the position of an acoustic resonator, thus, rendering the absorber ineffective. As a consequence, resonators tuned to a certain mode should be spaced nonsymmetrically around the circumference of an engine.

### III. Baffles

Transverse wave motion in the combustion chamber can be altered by baffles at the injector side. Baffles modify the acoustic resonance properties and change the oscillatory flow pattern in the vicinity of the injector plate. It is further believed that the formation of vortices at the blade edges dissipates energy and, thus, increases damping. This, however, cannot be simulated in an acoustic chamber model.

A two-bladed baffle could, at the most, prevent a tangential mode from spinning. This mode would be fixed in its position, with pressure antinodes at the baffle blades and velocity antinodes displaced at 90 deg. A configuration that damps the first and second tangential mode would be a three-bladed design. A four-bladed concept has little or no effect on the second tangential mode because it can still develop within the baffle arrangement. The five-bladed design used in many liquid-propellant engines is expected to influence all T modes up to the fourth.

Experiments with acoustic model chambers confirm that a five-bladed baffle shifts the resonant frequency to lower values, especially the first and second tangential mode. The baffle used in these acoustic tests had a length-to-radius ratio of 0.33. The first tangential resonant frequency was reduced by 24%, which is in agreement with measurements reported by various investigators.<sup>2</sup> A convenient way to determine the amount of damping present in a system is to measure the decay rate of the oscillating pressure. This measurement is made by abruptly stopping the driving sources—in this case, the loudspeakers installed in the injector plate—which excite the chamber acoustically. Several microphones located in the cavity ring were used to detect the chamber's response. The measured amount of pressure decrease in decibels per second divided by the frequency of the particular tangential mode are plotted in Fig. 3 in line with the damping factor, the determining quantity of the decay rate.

Another useful response measure is the bandwidth method (Fig. 4), which is applicable only if the damping rate is relatively low. Both methods, decay rate and bandwidth measurement, were applied to determine the damping effect of the baffles; results are shown in Fig. 3. Damping increases by a factor of five for the first two modes; however, the five-bladed baffle did not affect the third and fourth tangential eigenfrequency. The diagram in Fig. 5 (taken from Ref. 2) shows the ratio of unbaffled to baffled decay rate vs baffle length for acoustic as well as hot-gas tests. The current experimental data have been added to this diagram. It is surprising that results from acoustic tests agree so well with hot-gas data since the effects of mixing and vaporizing propellant sprays, inhomogeneities in the chamber's gas, and burning rate fluctuations are not present in an acoustic model. The good agreement between cold- and hot-gas decay rates reported in Ref. 2 encourages the use of acoustic chamber models as reasonably accurate approximations of combustion acoustics.

Hot-gas tests with a five-bladed plus hub baffle were performed with an engine operating with the hypergolic propellant combination  $N_2O_4$  and MMH. The baffle

### IV. Acoustic Cavities

#### A. Theoretical Considerations

Acoustic cavities such as Helmholtz and quarter-wave resonators were successfully used as damping devices for the suppression of combustion oscillations. resonator consists of a small volume connected with the combustion chamber through an orifice. If the dimensions of the various resonator elements are small in comparison to the wavelength of the oscillation, the gas motion behavior in the resonator is analogous to a mass-spring-dashpot system. The undamped resonant frequency  $f_0$  can be calculated from the geometrical dimensions (Fig. 6) as

$$f_0 = \frac{c}{2\pi} \sqrt{\frac{S}{V(\ell + \Delta\ell)}} \quad (5)$$

where  $S$  is the orifice area,  $\ell$  the orifice length,  $V$  the cavity volume, and  $\Delta\ell$  the mass correction which is about  $0.85 \cdot d$  for lower noise levels. A quarter-wave resonator (Fig. 6) may also be treated as a mass-spring-dashpot system even if mass and spring must be evaluated differently. The equation for the frequency is

$$f_0 = c/(4(L_R + \Delta\ell)) \quad (6)$$

where  $L_R$  is the length of the quarter-wave resonator.

To study the acoustical behavior of the resonators, and especially its absorption effect, impedance  $Z$  must be determined. This impedance is, in general, a complex unit consisting of the sum of an acoustic resistance  $R$  and an acoustic reactance  $\chi$ ,

$$Z = R + i\chi \quad (7)$$

The acoustic impedance is determined by the geometric and mechanical properties of the resonator, in particular the oscillating mass in the orifice, the spring stiffness of the volume, and the resistive element associated with viscous dissipation in the orifice. The reactance can be written in terms of the cavity dimensions as

$$\chi = 2\pi f \rho (\ell + \Delta\ell) \left(1 - (f_0^2/f^2)\right) \quad (8)$$

The total resistance is a combination of radiation and viscous dissipation at the orifice wall, i.e., internal resistance,

$$R = R_r + R_i \quad (9)$$

The radiation term can be written as

$$R_r = 2\pi \rho S f_0^2 / c \quad (10)$$

According to Morse and Ingard,<sup>3</sup> however, this term is usually neglected for resonators in ducts. The internal resistance is a function of the orifice length and is defined as

$$R_i = 4(\varepsilon_\ell + \varepsilon_{n\ell} + \ell/d) \sqrt{\nu \rho \pi f} \quad (11)$$

where  $\nu$  is the dynamic viscosity and  $\varepsilon = \varepsilon_\ell + \varepsilon_{n\ell}$  is the resistance factor that depends on the quality of the orifice wall surface ( $\varepsilon_\ell$ ), as well as on a nonlinear correction term for high-sound-pressure levels ( $\varepsilon_{n\ell}$ ). This equation also holds true

###### PROCEDURES AIDING THE DESIGN OF ACOUSTIC CAVITIES 387

for quarter-wave resonators, only  $\ell$  has to be replaced by  $\ell_R$  (the length of the effective acoustic mass). The reactance of a quarter-wave resonator is

$$x = -4\rho(\ell_R + \Delta\ell)f_0 \cdot \cot(\pi f/2f_0) \quad (12)$$

When these terms are multiplied by the area ratio  $A/S$  of the combustion chamber, one obtains the specific cavity resistance  $r$  and reactance  $x$  per unit area. For an arrangement of  $n$ , differently tuned absorbers around the circumference of a combustion chamber, the sum of the acoustic impedance is given by

$$Z = \left( \frac{1}{A} \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{S_i}{Z_i} \right)^{-1} \quad (13)$$

Once the impedance is known, the absorption coefficient and the conductance (real part of resonator admittance) can be evaluated:

$$\alpha = \frac{4r}{\rho c} \left/ \left[ \left( 1 + \frac{r}{\rho c} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{x}{\rho c} \right)^2 \right] \right. \quad (14)$$

$$\xi = \frac{r}{\rho c} \left/ \left[ \left( \frac{r}{\rho c} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{x}{\rho c} \right)^2 \right] \right. \quad (15)$$

The reactance vanishes at resonance, thus simplifying this equation in which  $\rho c$  is the specific resistance of the gas in the combustion chamber.

In practice, a cavity layout can be made by either optimizing the absorption coefficient or maximizing the real part of the acoustic boundary admittance (the conductance  $\xi$  is also called the power loss factor). According to Ref. 3, the loss in acoustic power for any surface of local reaction (orifice surface) is the conductance times the dynamic pressure at that surface. Whereas the absorption coefficient has its optimum at 100% (i.e., no reflection of sound intensity at the chamber wall), the conductance term is not limited by definition. Figure 7 may explain this difference in more detail by showing the spectral behavior of the absorption coefficient as well as the conductance for three different absorber arrangements in a closed tube. Optimizing the system's damping by means of the absorption coefficient would suggest, in this example, a three-resonator configuration, in contrast to maximizing the conductance, which suggests the configuration with 12 or even more absorbers. Acoustically speaking, more than three absorbers overdamp this system, which implies less than 100% absorption but increases the bandwidth. Some investigators prefer the use of the conductance term for the combustion process. According to Ref. 2, however, the usual approach attempts to optimize the absorption coefficient, despite the uncertainty of this model, which is the result of the inhomogenous sound pressure field.

The preceding discussion leads to the conclusion that once the basic design of a resonator has been evaluated from acoustic tests that consider the combustion chamber's hot-gas properties, maximization of the absorption coefficient for hot-firing conditions must be done by selecting the right number of resonators within the absorber arrangement. If an increase in bandwidth is desired (see also Fig. 7) because the combustion chamber hot-gas properties either cannot be precisely determined or are expected to shift during engine operation, the number of resonators within the arrangement may be increased.

#### B. Impedance and Absorption Measurements

Impedance and absorption measurements with Helmholtz and quarter-wave resonators were done in a standing wave apparatus. Typical results for a quarter-wave cavity are presented in Fig. 8. Good agreement between calculated and experimental data was achieved by varying the resistance factor [see Eq. (11)]. The absorption maximum at resonance is about 80% for this particular cavity, with a normalized resistance  $r/\rho c = 0.4$ . This means that the system is overdamped. The number of cavities has to be reduced in this case in order to attain 100% absorption.

#### C. Nonlinear Effects

High-fluctuating-pressure levels in a combustion chamber will change the damping behavior of acoustic resonators. Under such circumstances, energy losses as

The main contribution of these losses results from the formation of vortices at the orifice edges, which dissipate into turbulence. These losses are amplitude dependant and dominate the resistance term at high-sound-pressure levels. Consequently, a remarkable change in absorption and bandwidth can be expected.

Acoustic tests in a standing wave apparatus were performed with an increasing sound pressure level (SPL) up to nearly 160 dB. The measured ratio of nonlinear to linear resistance  $(\epsilon_\ell + \epsilon_{nl})/\epsilon_\ell$  vs SPL is shown in Fig. 9 for a Helmholtz and quarter-wave cavity. There are two reasons for this. In the Helmholtz type, the cross-sectional jump between orifice and resonator volume implies a velocity gain and, hence, results in higher resistance values. Second, this cross-sectional jump causes additional turbulence which is not present in a quarter-wave resonator. The effect of such a rising resistance on absorption is that a chamber optimally damped for low SPLs becomes underdamped for high SPLs when Helmholtz resonators are used. It should also be mentioned that a high, fluctuating, pressure level not only influences the resistance but also the resonant frequency. In all experiments, a frequency rise was observed with increasing SPL. This means that the oscillating mass is reduced by shortening the effective orifice length. Again, this effect is negligible in the case of quarter-wave resonators.

#### D. Orifice Shape

The fact that the resistance increases with rising dynamic chamber pressure makes absorption prediction very difficult. A steep increase in resistance provides the absorber with higher damping but with lower absorption. If the design criterion asks for a high-absorption coefficient, however, then the resonator must be designed in such a way that nonlinear effects are kept as low as possible even for high SPLs. Such a criterion usually exists if the eigenfrequency of the combustion chamber does not change during engine operation. On the other hand, if the frequency varies as a result of changing engine operation conditions (as is the case during transients), then the bandwidth should be large in order to supply sufficient damping at any time. Since energy is dissipated in the nonlinear regime due to the formation of vortices at the resonator entrance and the orifice to resonator volume transition area, it is clear that design modifications must focus on these locations.

Several variations of the orifice geometry were tested experimentally. The orifice edges for both types of cavities were rounded with different radii. In addition, the orifice of a quarter-wave resonator received a wedge-shaped constriction, reducing the open area to 50% of its original value. The various orifice geometries are shown in Fig. 10.

A significant reduction in resistance, even in the linear region, was observed with rounded edges for the Helmholtz resonators. The transition from rectangular to rounded edges was especially effective, whereas the radius of curvature had only

a minor influence. Furthermore, it was important to round off both the inner and outer throat edges in order to postpone the onset of nonlinearity. The experimental results are illustrated in Fig. 11a. One can see that the resistance increase is not as rapid for the rounded orifice as for the normal-edged orifice, especially if adjusted at both sides.

Quarter-wave resonators, as pointed out earlier, are less sensitive to nonlinearities. The increase in resistance for a normal-edged cavity is low; nevertheless, the rounding effect is measurable reducing the slope as expected. A greater effect was observed when the orifice-edge was sharpened by applying a thin wedge-shaped constriction at the cavity opening (Fig. 10). As expected, the formation of vortices increased the resistance remarkably, making the cavity more sensitive to nonlinear effects (Fig 11b).

#### V. Hot-Firing Test Results

With the information gained from acoustic tests, a first cavity layout was made. Turning toward hot testing, the engine's dynamic behavior, the cavity performance, and the following parameters need to be observed: dynamic chamber pressure signal, dynamic pressure pressure signal, and cavity gas temperature.

The transfer function between two pressure transducers, installed in the chamber and in the cavity, give the information needed to evaluate the performance of the cavity.

If the complex relation between the dynamic pressure inside the resonator and the excitation pressure at the wall of the combustion chamber are measured, the acoustic properties of the resonator can be calculated with the following equation:

$$\frac{p_2}{p_1} = \frac{-\rho c^2 S}{\omega V} \frac{\omega \rho (\ell + \Delta \ell) (1 - (\omega_0^2 / \omega^2)) + i R}{[\omega \rho (\ell + \Delta \ell) (1 - (\omega_0^2 / \omega^2))]^2 + R^2} \quad (16)$$

At resonance, Eq. (16) reduces to

$$\frac{p_2}{p_1} = -i \frac{\omega_0 \rho (\ell + \Delta \ell)}{R} \quad (17)$$

The resonant frequency and the resistance can now be determined by measuring the phase between the cavity and chamber signal and by the dynamic pressure amplification of the absorber. A typical curve of a transfer function with magnitude and phase taken during a stable combustion period is shown in Fig. 12. This procedure was applied to different tuned quarter-wave absorbers, leading to the curve in Fig. 13, where resonant frequencies are plotted against cavity length. The results are shown together with cold-gas data. From the frequency ratio between hot- and cold-gas data, an effective speed of sound in the cavities was calculated under the assumption of an effective length equal to that measured in the acoustic model chamber. Equation (6) leads to the following relation:

$$\frac{f_{0,\text{hot}}}{f_{0,\text{cold}}} = \frac{c_{\text{hot}}}{c_{\text{cold}}} \cdot \frac{(L_R + \Delta\ell)_{\text{cold}}}{(L_R + \Delta\ell)_{\text{hot}}} \quad (18)$$

Since this frequency ratio remains almost constant for quarter-wave cavities with lengths beyond 30 mm, one can assume that there is no major change in the average speed of sound of a resonator. On the other hand, if resonator tuning requires quarter-wave lengths below 30 mm, the assumption of a constant average speed of sound within those cavities will undoubtedly lead to mistuned resonators. To confirm this, the gas temperature was measured at different depths of a quarter-wave cavity. It was found that the gas temperature drops strongly within the first 15 mm from the orifice inlet but stays almost constant as the depth of 30 mm is exceeded. Hence, care must be taken in tuning quarter-wave resonators to higher modes that call for very short resonator lengths. These cavities are most sensitive to immediate changes of absorber gas properties, particularly when a local change occurs in the combustion process close to the resonator inlet.

An additional feature observed during hot-firing was that the eigenfrequency of a quarter-wave resonator grew with increasing distance of the absorber from the injection plane. According to the preceding statement, the temperature inside the resonators at greater distances from the injector were higher since they are positioned closer to the mean combustion zone. This explains the higher speed of sound and, consequently, the increasing eigenfrequency. With regard to resonator tuning, one can thus conclude that each axial cavity position should be tuned separately in order to optimize overall absorber efficiency.

As mentioned earlier, another important property of resonators is their impedance and, particularly, their resistance. With the measured transfer function and Eq. (16), it is possible to calculate resistance  $R$  as well as resistance factor  $\varepsilon$  at resonance. A necessary condition for applying the transfer function method is a good coherence between the chamber and cavity signal. This requirement will most often be met by placing the two pressure transducers together as closely as possible. If this is not practicable from the design point of view, it may be appropriate to work with the transmissibility rather than the transfer function under insufficient signal coherence. The transmissibility gives the absolute value of the pressure ratio without any correlation between the two signals.

The comparison between the quarter-wave resonators with rounded, normal, and wedge-shaped orifices during hot runs reveals much the same behavior as that found during the acoustic tests. The resistance and resistance factor rise with an increasing sharpness of the orifice edge for both cold- and hot-gas tests at approximately the same SPL, as shown in Table 3.

Figure 14 presents the measured transfer functions for each of the three orifice configurations. The pressure ratio, which corresponds to the resistance magnitude, decreases with increasing sharpness of the resonator edge.

To confirm the slight increase in resistance for quarter-wave resonators at high-sound-pressure levels during a hot-firing test the measured hot-gas data of a

Another series of tests of resonators with two different orifice diameters led to the interesting result that at a constant opening area fraction, a larger number of the cavities with a small orifice area have a lower resistance  $r$  than is the case with fewer cavities with large orifices. Figure 16 shows the specific resistance for resonators with a diameter of 5 and 7 mm. The increased resistance seems to result from the generation of more intense vortices for the larger diameter. Further measurements showed that the resistance of an absorber is highly influenced by the velocity pattern and the gas composition in the combustion chamber.

To judge the effectiveness of absorbers located at different axial chamber positions, a measurement series was made with an unstable combustor. The number of absorbers needed to stabilize the combustion was three, with the absorbers located at a distance of 23 mm from the faceplate. When this distance was increased to 39 mm, the combustor returned to an unstable state. Now, 30% more resonators were necessary to guarantee a stable combustion. A further increase of the distance to 55 mm destabilized the combustion again (see Fig. 17). The effectiveness of resonators in a combustion chamber is, therefore, considerably influenced by its location.

### VI. Conclusion

Combustion instabilities in rocket engines can be eliminated by increasing the damping characteristics of the chamber. Baffles, quarter-wave, and Helmholtz resonators are ideal devices for suppressing combustion oscillations.

To accurately tune these suppression devices, acoustic tests in air under ambient conditions with full-scale chamber models and acoustic absorbers are essential. These tests provide a basic tool for predicting the damping behavior in a rocket engine under hot-gas conditions as well as a general survey of the characteristic quantities of various types of acoustic absorbers under linear as well as nonlinear conditions. With these data and an estimation of hot-gas parameters, a first cavity layout was made.

Transfer function measurements between cavity and chamber dynamic pressure during hot-firing tests yielded additional precise data regarding cavity resonances and impedances. These data confirmed that a high-absorption coefficient can be reached with low-resistance absorbers provided by rounding off the orifice edges. This chapter has further shown that the layout of quarter-wave resonators is more predictable than that of Helmholtz resonators, since the latter are very sensitive to variation of dynamic pressure levels prevailing in combustion chambers.

Further research was carried out through the use of a laboratory combustor. Results gained with this test facility proved that maximum absorption is obtained with a rounded resonator orifice. The test series with variation of the axial cavity position led to the conclusion that the flowfield and gas properties at the resonator opening have a major influence on damping behavior. With increased distance between resonator and faceplate, a decrease in the efficiency of the absorbers could be observed. Small laboratory combustors, such as those described in Refs. 5 and 6 are good tools for optimizing damping devices.
