### I. Introduction and Problem Formulation

THE complex oscillatory phenomena that characterize acoustic or high-frequency combustion instability in liquid-propellant rocket engines pose a challenging problem for those who would model them. In some instances the oscillations grow spontaneously, apparently from combustor background noise or some aspect of the startup sequence, and may eventually reach large amplitudes, of the order of the mean chamber pressure or more. Other engine configurations are spontaneously or intrinsically stable but can be excited into the execution of similar large-amplitude oscillations through the introduction of pulses or disturbances of a certain size and form. The time histories of these oscillations may be more or less sinusoidal, though for the large amplitude waves they are typically steep fronted. In almost all cases the frequency is observed to be within a few percent of that of one of the normal acoustic modes for the basic geometry of the combustion chamber. The stability of a given engine configuration is often

found to be sensitive to relatively minor changes in injector design or sizing. Any comprehensive theory must account for all of these features as well as other, more specific details of the oscillatory fields in order to be a useful tool in designing stable engines, or even in interpreting data and guiding development.

In a general way it must be true that for instability to occur the driving supplied to any particular oscillation mode must exceed the damping available. An accounting and representation of all important driving and damping mechanisms must, thus, be included in a complete stability model. Moreover, their mutual interactions must be interconnected reasonably by satisfaction of the appropriate conservation and state equations. In all engine configurations, the major driving possibility is the combustion of the liquid propellants. Damping can be provided by the mean flow, by interphase damping, and possibly by the supercritical nozzle that must terminate the combustion chamber. There may be, as well, strongly nonlinear interactions between elements of the oscillatory field which produce driving or damping (for example, the presence of a shock wave discontinuity). In more complex engine designs, components such as acoustic liners and slots or injector face baffles may be added to increase damping. Clearly these must also be modeled if a complete stability picture is to be drawn.

Two general approaches to the stability modeling problem just posed can be identified. The first, the one that will be treated in this chapter, is to attempt a direct analytical solution of the partial differential equations and associated boundary conditions that describe the flowfield in the rocket engine. If direct solution is not possible (as it usually is not), then reduction of the system to ordinary differential equations or integral equations and their subsequent numerical integration is also considered to march under the banner of so-called analytical solutions. The second general approach, direct numerical integration of the partial differential equations, is usually termed a numerical analysis, and this type of approach is discussed elsewhere in this volume. The available analytical approaches can themselves be separated into two families. The first of these is devoted to the analysis of small-amplitude oscillations. Specifically, the nonlinear partial differential equations are simplified by assuming that the products of all oscillatory variables are negligibly small. We will place all approaches of this sort under the heading of linear analyses. All other treatments, which include at least some part of the nonlinear terms in the governing partial differential equations, will be called nonlinear analyses. We will classify models for engine components in the same way. For example, the convergent nozzle may be treated by either linear or nonlinear analysis.

A comprehensive review of the status of both linear and nonlinear analysis for liquid rocket engine instability as of about 1970 is available as part of Ref. 1. Chapter 4 of this reference, in particular, deals with the engine stability models available at that time. Analytical models for engine components, such as nozzles and acoustic absorbers, are also included in other chapters. In what follows frequent reference will be made to this book.

The purpose of this chapter is not only to provide a brief review of some of the progress made in liquid rocket instability modeling since 1970, but also to describe in a little detail approaches that represent the state of the art in analytical modeling for the liquid rocket instability problem. To do this, the following scheme of presentation has been adopted. First, the basic equations and assumptions generally used in liquid engine stability analyses will be set down. Following this, linear analysis and methods will be discussed. This discussion will include

some results of calculations made using existing models. A brief presentation of approaches for the nonlinear instability problem will then be made. A few conclusions and a discussion of possible directions for future efforts will conclude the presentation.

### II. Basic Equations and Assumptions

The equations used and assumptions made in analytical approaches since the 1970 review have been no more general than those given in that reference.<sup>2</sup> Consequently, they will be given here in a slightly different form but with the same essential content as presented there. The equations are given in nondimensional form with the characteristic values used in the nondimensional scheme being steady-state values in the gas phase at the injector face. Lengths are made nondimensional using either the chamber radius (circular cross section) or the smaller transverse direction (rectangular cross section).

Continuity:

$$\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot (\rho \mathbf{q}) = Q \quad (1)$$

Momentum:

$$\rho \frac{D\mathbf{q}}{Dt} + \frac{\nabla p}{\gamma} = Q(\mathbf{q}_l - \mathbf{q}) \quad (2)$$

Energy:

$$\rho T \frac{Ds}{Dt} = Q \left[ 1 - T \left( \frac{\gamma - 1}{2} \right) (2\mathbf{q}_l \cdot \mathbf{q} - q^2) \right] \quad (3)$$

State:

$$p = \rho T \quad \rho = p^{-1/\gamma} e^{-s} \quad (4)$$

In deriving these equations, it was assumed that a single-component calorically perfect product gas was produced with nondimensional volumetric rate  $Q$  from the liquid phase whose volume was taken to be negligible. It was also assumed that the stagnation enthalpy of the liquid phase is a constant. Finally it was assumed that drag between the droplets and the gas is negligibly small. Regarding this last assumption, the drag terms were included in the general development of Ref. 2. They were also shown there, however, to have a very minor impact on liquid rocket stability.

### III. Linear Analysis

If the amplitude of the oscillations are small, then a linear analysis, in which products of the oscillatory variables are neglected, is an appropriate mathematical approximation. In a practical sense, a linear analysis can be used to assess the intrinsic stability of a combustor to small amplitude disturbances and to determine the frequency, growth rate, and spatial character of any resulting oscillation. The impact of design strategies, such as the addition of acoustic absorbers or baffles, modifications in the contraction ratio, or the alteration of the steady-state combustion profile on intrinsic stability, can also be ascertained using a linear analysis.

In this section an analytical framework for investigating and describing the linear stability of liquid rocket engines, which includes the flexibility necessary to include acoustic absorbers, baffles, small contraction ratios, and arbitrary axial combustion distributions, will be presented. A few results of calculations showing the impact and interaction of these combustion chamber features on intrinsic stability will also be given.

#### A. Governing Equations

To develop the appropriate linear forms of the conservation equations the dependent variables  $p, \rho$ , etc. are represented as sum of a steady component and an oscillatory component, thus,

$$p = \bar{p} + p^*, \quad \rho = \bar{\rho} + \rho^*, \quad \text{etc.} \quad (5)$$

Here the overbar indicates a steady-state (time-independent) variable whereas an asterisk denotes an oscillatory variable. The set of equations for the steady-state can be solved in a straightforward way if it is assumed that the steady-state flow is one dimensional (axial). The solution gives  $\bar{p}, \bar{\rho}$ , etc. in terms of  $\bar{Q}(z)$ , the steady-state mass source distribution, which can be specified in an arbitrary manner. Steady-state solutions of this type are given, for example, in Refs. 2 and 3 and will not be repeated here. Subtraction of these equations from the complete set leaves the nonsteady (oscillatory) equations which must be solved. These are linearized in the usual way by neglecting products of the perturbation quantities  $p', \rho'$ , etc. In addition, all of the oscillatory components are represented through an exponential time dependence. Thus,

$$p^* = p' e^{i\omega t} \quad \rho^* = \rho' e^{i\omega t} \quad \text{etc.} \quad (6)$$

where

$$\omega = \omega_R + i\lambda \quad (7)$$

where  $\omega_R$  is the nondimensional frequency and  $\lambda$  is the linear decay rate (positive implies exponential decay). The following set of equations results:

$$i\omega\rho' + \nabla \cdot (\rho' \bar{u}k + \bar{\rho}q') = Q' \quad (8)$$

$$\begin{aligned} \bar{\rho}[i\omega q' + \nabla(\bar{u}k \cdot q') - (\bar{u}kx \nabla x q')] + \rho' \bar{u} \frac{d\bar{u}}{dz} k + \nabla \frac{p'}{\gamma} \\ = Q'(\bar{u}_t - \bar{u})k - \bar{Q}q' \end{aligned} \quad (9)$$

$$\begin{aligned} i\omega s' + \bar{u} \frac{\partial s'}{\partial z} = \frac{\bar{Q}}{\bar{p}} [-T' - (\gamma - 1)[\bar{u}k \cdot q' - \bar{u}k \cdot q']] \\ + \left( \frac{Q'}{\bar{p}} - \frac{\bar{Q}p'}{\bar{p}} \right) (\gamma - 1)\bar{u}(\bar{u} - \bar{u}_t) \end{aligned} \quad (10)$$

$$p'/\bar{p} = (\rho'/\bar{\rho}) + (T'/\bar{T}) \quad (11)$$

$$\rho'/\bar{\rho} = (1/\gamma)(p'/\bar{p}) + s' \quad (12)$$

To simplify this system it is observed that the steady flowfield is irrotational and that any vorticity generated in the oscillatory field must be the result of interactions

between the oscillations and the steady and unsteady source terms. Moreover, since the source terms should be of the order of the mean flow Mach number, the vorticity should also be relatively small. Because of this,  $\mathbf{q}$  is represented as the sum of the gradient of a potential function and rotational vector field generated by source and mean flow interactions. Thus,  $\mathbf{q}' = \nabla\phi + \xi$ . Substituting this into the perturbed momentum equation (9) results in the following expressions after a few manipulations:

$$\nabla \left[ i\omega\phi + \bar{u} \frac{\partial\phi}{\partial z} + \frac{p'}{\gamma\bar{\rho}} + \frac{\bar{Q}}{\bar{\rho}}\phi \right] = 0 \quad (13)$$

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial}{\partial z}(\bar{u}\xi_z) + \left( i\omega + \frac{\bar{Q}}{\bar{\rho}} \right) \xi_z = \frac{Q'}{\bar{\rho}}(\bar{u}_l - \bar{u}) + \phi \frac{d\bar{Q}/\bar{\rho}}{dz} \\ + \frac{\rho'}{\bar{\rho}} \bar{Q}(\bar{u}_l - \bar{u}) - \left[ \rho' \bar{u} \frac{d\bar{u}}{dz} + \frac{p'}{\gamma\bar{\rho}^2} \frac{d\bar{\rho}}{dz} \right] \end{aligned} \quad (14)$$

and  $\xi_r = \xi_\theta = 0$  (or  $\xi_x = \xi_y = 0$  for a rectangular cross section). Equation (13) can be integrated directly, with the arbitrary constant set equal to zero to give

$$p' = -\gamma\bar{\rho} \left[ i\omega\phi\bar{u} \frac{\partial\phi}{\partial z} + \frac{\bar{Q}}{\bar{\rho}}\phi \right] \quad (15)$$

It is seen immediately that  $p'$  depends directly only on  $\phi$  and steady flow variables and not on  $s'$  or  $\xi$ .

The vanishing of the components of  $\xi$  in directions perpendicular to the direction of mean flow implies that (as one might expect physically) the vorticity vector must lie in a plane perpendicular to the mean flow direction. Formal integration of Eqs. (14) and (10) can be carried out to give expressions for  $\xi_z$  and  $s'$ , respectively, in terms of  $\phi$  and steady-state variables. Since these integral expressions are somewhat complicated and their exact form is not critical to this presentation, they will not be given here; see Ref. 3 for examples of these expressions.

Substitution of the expression for  $p'$  along with the state equations into Eq. (8) eventually leads to an equation of the following form:

$$\nabla^2\phi + \omega^2\phi = F_1(\phi, \xi_z, \bar{Q}, Q') \quad (16)$$

where  $F_1$  is quite lengthy and complicated. Equation (21) together with the two expressions for  $s'$  and  $\xi_z$  given next form the set of equations to be solved,

$$s' = s'(\phi, \xi_z, \bar{Q}, Q') \quad (17)$$

$$\xi_z = \xi_z(\phi, s', \bar{Q}, Q') \quad (18)$$

To complete the formulation, the perturbation mass source  $Q'$ , must be given in terms of  $p'$ ,  $q'$ ,  $\bar{Q}$ , etc.; that is, some combustion response relationship must be used, though its form is arbitrary.

The approach used to solve this system of equations requires first that Eq. (16) be transformed to an integral equation. This is accomplished using standard techniques (for example, see Ref. 4). A Green's function  $G(\mathbf{r}/\mathbf{r}_0)$  is introduced such that

$$\nabla^2 G + \omega^2 G = \delta(\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_0) \quad (19)$$

where  $\delta(\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_0)$  is the Dirac delta function, and  $\nabla G \cdot \mathbf{n} = 0$  on all bounding surfaces of the combustion chamber. The equation for  $G$  is multiplied by  $\phi$ , whereas Eq. (16) is multiplied by  $G$ . Subtraction of the two resulting equations and application of Green's theorem gives

$$\phi(\mathbf{r}) = \int_{V_0} G(\mathbf{r})/(\mathbf{r}_0) F_1(\mathbf{r}) dV_0 - \int_{S_0} G(\mathbf{r}/\mathbf{r}_0)(\nabla \phi \cdot \mathbf{n}) dS_0 \quad (20)$$

The Green's function is represented by an expansion in orthonormal eigenfunctions for the chamber geometry, thus,

$$G = \sum_N \frac{\Omega_N(\mathbf{r})\Omega_N(\mathbf{r}_0)}{\omega^2 - \eta_N^2} \quad (21)$$

where

$$\nabla^2 \Omega_N + \eta_N^2 \Omega_N = 0 \quad (22)$$

$$\nabla \Omega_N \cdot \mathbf{n} = 0 \quad (23)$$

on all surfaces, and  $N$  is, in general, a set of three integers that depends on the geometry of the chamber. Substitution of this representation for  $G$  into Eq. (20) results in an eigenfunction expansion representation of  $\phi$ ,

$$\phi = \sum \mu_N \Omega_N \quad (24)$$

where

$$\mu_N = \frac{1}{\omega^2 - \eta_N^2} \left[ \int_V \Omega_N F_1(\phi, \xi_z, s') dV - \int_S \Omega_N F_2(\phi, \xi_z, s') dS \right] \quad (25)$$

In the last expression we have assumed a general form for the surface boundary condition, that is,

$$\nabla \phi \cdot \mathbf{n} = F_2(\phi, \xi_z, s') \quad (26)$$

where  $F_2$  varies depending on the boundary surface and may, of course, be zero.

A successive approximation approach is used to solve Eq. (25) as well as the expressions for  $\xi_z$  and  $s'$ . This approximate technique is based on the assumption that the solution for  $\phi$  is close (in some sense) to a known solution for a similar problem, say,  $\hat{\phi}$ . In many cases the choice  $\hat{\phi} = \Omega_{\hat{N}}$  is appropriate, where  $\Omega_{\hat{N}}$  is a particular eigenfunction (acoustic mode). If this choice is made, then

$$\phi = \Omega_{\hat{N}} + \sum_{N \neq \hat{N}} \mu_N \Omega_N \quad (27)$$

This implies  $\mu_{\hat{N}} = 1$  or, using Eq. (25) with  $N = \hat{N}$

$$\omega^2 = \eta_{\hat{N}}^2 + \int_V \Omega_{\hat{N}} F_1(\phi) dV \int_S \Omega_{\hat{N}} F_2(\phi) dS \quad (28)$$

At this point it should be remembered that  $\phi$ ,  $\mu_N$ , etc. are complex quantities as is  $\omega$  ( $\omega_R + i\lambda$ ). Thus, Eq. (28) when solved gives the frequency eigenvalue and the decay rate, whereas Eq. (25) yields a complex coefficient matrix (three dimensional, in general) for the eigenfunction expansion of  $\phi$ . The solution of the system of Eqs. (17), (18), (27), and (28) is then attempted by the technique of successive approximation, using to lowest order  $\phi = \Omega_{\tilde{N}}$ ,  $\omega = \eta_{\tilde{N}}$ ,  $\xi_z = 0$ , and  $s' = 0$ . These are used in the integral terms of all four equations to produce first-order estimates of  $\phi$ ,  $\omega$ ,  $\xi_z$ , and  $s'$ . In turn these are used in the integral terms for the second order, and so on. If the procedure converges so that the  $j$ th approximation is arbitrarily close to the  $(j - 1)$ th, then a formal solution to the integral equations has been found. Of course, there is no guarantee that the technique will converge. In fact, experience has shown that the simple procedure just given, which uses  $\Omega_{\tilde{N}}$  as the lowest order approximation, will only converge for restricted engine configurations. Specifically, it is necessary that the combustion be well-distributed axially (rather than concentrated), that the nozzle effect (admittance) be small, that the total acoustic absorber open area be small and well distributed along the walls of the chamber, that no injector face baffles be present, and that the contraction ratio be sufficiently large (nozzle entrance Mach number less than about 0.2).

When the combustion zone is concentrated, the nozzle effect is large, or the nozzle entrance Mach number is greater than about 0.2, a better approximating function than  $\Omega_{\tilde{N}}$  is required, primarily because of a strong axial variation in the oscillatory field. In these cases a  $\tilde{\phi}$  based on the solution for a chamber with mean flow and nozzle effects but without combustion terms has proved useful. If any  $\tilde{\phi}$  other than  $\Omega_{\tilde{N}}$  is used, it is a straightforward matter to manipulate Eqs. (25) and (28) to produce the following forms:

$$\phi = \tilde{\phi} + \sum_N \mu_N \Omega_N \quad (29)$$

$$\mu_N = \int_V \Omega_N F_3(\phi, \tilde{\phi}) dV - \int_S \Omega_N F_4(\phi, \tilde{\phi}) dS \quad (30)$$

$$\omega^2 = \tilde{\omega} \int_V \Omega_{\tilde{N}} F_5(\phi, \tilde{\phi}) dV - \int_S \Omega_{\tilde{N}} F_6(\phi, \tilde{\phi}) dS \quad (31)$$

where  $F_3$ ,  $F_4$ ,  $F_5$ , and  $F_6$  depend on the choice of  $\tilde{\phi}$ , and  $\mu_N$  is a correction matrix giving the change in  $\phi$  from  $\tilde{\phi}$ .

It must be pointed out that the nonconvergence of the successive approximation technique when  $\Omega_{\tilde{N}}$  is used as the approximating function for a particular engine implies that, for this engine configuration,  $\Omega_{\tilde{N}}$  is an inadequate representation of the wave motion for linear stability analysis. Calculations show that even in those situations in which convergence is obtained using  $\Omega_{\tilde{N}}$  as the lowest order approximation, the final values of  $\omega_R$  and  $\lambda$  often differ from the first-order values (with  $\Omega_{\tilde{N}}$  used in the integrals) very significantly, and the coefficient matrix  $\mu_N$  has considerable content.

Stability calculations require models for combustion response, acoustic damping devices, and the convergent nozzle in order to develop expressions for  $Q'F_1$ , and  $F_2$  in Eqs. (25) and (28). These will be discussed next.

#### B. Combustion Response Models

The state of the art in modeling the response of combustion processes to oscillations in liquid rocket engines has advanced very little since 1970 (as described in Ref. 1). There are still no complete analytical, numerical, or empirical models that represent accurately the major combustion processes, injection, mixing, atomization, vaporization, and chemical kinetics, and their linear or nonlinear response to chamber oscillations. This situation does not result solely from a lack of interest or attention by modelers, though research activity in this area has certainly been very limited. Rather, the current reality is that the critical experiments necessary for such model development have yet to be performed. Until this is accomplished it is hard to imagine how any accurate mechanistic models of the combustion feedback process, suitable for inclusion in an analytical stability model, can be constructed. In the absence of usable mechanistic representations, liquid rocket stability modelers have continued to resort to very simplified two-parameter formulations for combustion response. In the case of linear oscillations, these models take the general form

$$Q' = \bar{Q}\eta p' \quad (32)$$

$Q'$  and  $\bar{Q}$  are the perturbed and steady-state volumetric mass generation rates at a given location, and  $\eta$  represents the so-called (complex) response factor. Since  $\eta$  can be written as  $|\eta|e^{i\alpha}$ , then  $|\eta|$  represents the local gain and  $\alpha$  the phase between mass generation fluctuations and the pressure oscillations. The two parameters  $|\eta|$  and  $\alpha$  depend on the model for  $Q$  and on the frequency of the oscillations. This formulation is quite general and values for  $|\eta|$  and  $\alpha$  must be obtained for a given combustion process as a function of frequency. This has been done in the past, for example, in the case of quasisteady droplet vaporization.<sup>5</sup> Even sophisticated mechanistic combustion response models of the future may well be representable in this form (at least for linear responses), since both of the model parameters can vary with location and their frequency dependence is arbitrary. A response model of this type is easily inserted into the volume integrals of the stability model presented earlier in this chapter.

A widely used simplified model for  $\eta$  that postulates a specific frequency dependence and introduces a characteristic time for the combustion response process was developed by Crocco and Cheng<sup>6</sup> in the 1950s. This so-called time-lag model has the following form:

$$Q' = \bar{Q}n(1 - e^{i\omega\tau})p'/\bar{p} \quad (33)$$

The major assumption in this model is that  $n$ , the interaction index (mainly the gain factor) and  $\tau$ , the time lag (mainly the phase factor) are constants for the entire combustion process (not location dependent) and are independent of frequency. The model was originally proposed solely based on some physical arguments.<sup>6</sup> Subsequently, the existence of a characteristic time (time lag) in liquid rocket instability was demonstrated experimentally.<sup>2</sup> Additionally, for droplet vaporization controlled combustion, averaged values of  $\eta$  for the complete combustion region were shown to match the form of the time-lag model fairly well in terms of frequency dependence.<sup>5,7</sup> Finally, Reardon<sup>8</sup> found that the stability behavior of a range of liquid engine designs could be correlated qualitatively in terms of the time-lag model. Nevertheless, it remains unlikely that the complicated liquid rocket combustion response process can be represented completely and accurately

by this simple two-parameter model. In the absence of more sophisticated formulations, however, the time-lag model can be used to predict and interpret stability trends at least qualitatively. It can be particularly helpful in assessing and quantifying the stabilizing impact of devices such as injector face baffles and acoustic absorbers, as will be done later in this chapter.

#### C. Nozzle Response Model

It has long been the conventional procedure to separate the oscillatory flow in the nozzle from that in the combustion chamber in performing linear stability analyses. The nozzle solution then serves to provide a boundary condition or nozzle admittance relationship for the chamber flow. The work of Crocco and Sirignano,<sup>9</sup> who treated axially symmetric and two-dimensional nozzles, remains the standard reference. Numerical integration was used by them to determine admittance coefficients relating the oscillatory pressure, velocity, and entropy at the nozzle entrance plane. In times past, tables of the admittance coefficients from the Crocco and Sirignano<sup>9</sup> work were used in stability analyses. More recently the increased speed of computers has made direct integration of their equations a common procedure as part of many linear stability analyses. Following this latter procedure really makes the separation between the nozzle and chamber problems mainly formal. In performing stability analyses, however, it is often possible to use a single nozzle calculation for several variations in chamber operating conditions. Consequently, the separation of chamber from nozzle remains a practical convenience. An example of a computer program for nozzle admittance calculations of this type can be found as part of the ROCCID code.<sup>10</sup>

Experiments designed to validate the nozzle admittance predictions at least in cold-flow situations have been performed by Zinn et al.<sup>11</sup> and Bell and Zin.<sup>12</sup> In general, the agreement between theory and experiment has been quite good, especially for longitudinal and mixed longitudinal-tangential mode oscillations. This would seem to indicate that the Crocco-Sirignano approach can be used with some confidence; however, it must be pointed out that actual hot-firing data are lacking.

Some characteristics of the nozzle admittance predictions should be mentioned. The first is that for some ranges of nozzle entrance Mach numbers the admittances are very sensitive to frequency. That is, for the same general mode (say, first tangential) small variations in  $\omega$  away from the normal acoustic mode frequency for the chamber can cause significant changes in the admittance coefficients. If the admittance coefficients were always small (say, of the order of the mean chamber Mach number), this would probably not have a significant impact on stability. It is found, however, that the admittance coefficients frequently are closer to  $\mathcal{O}(1)$  than to  $\mathcal{O}(M)$ . One last but very important prediction of the nozzle theory is that the admittance condition for pure tangential modes is found to be driving rather than damping in many cases. That is, the nozzle admittance tends to drive rather than damp the oscillation. In these driving situations the admittance is typically of  $\mathcal{O}(M)$ , but not vanishingly small. For these situations stability predictions are heavily dependent on the nozzle interaction. Physically the mechanism for producing a driving impact at the nozzle seems to be a conversion of mean flow energy to oscillatory energy in the nozzle convergent section.

The nozzle admittance condition just discussed is appropriate for all nozzles with convergence sufficiently gradual that a quasi-one-dimensional description of the mean flow is appropriate. This includes most nozzles of practical interest. For

the special case of nozzles that are extremely short relative to the wavelength of the oscillation of interest, the well-known quasisteady or short nozzle approximation may be appropriate. For these instances the admittance condition becomes simply

$$u' = [(\gamma - 1)/2\gamma]\bar{M}_e p' \quad (z = L) \quad (34)$$

Since  $(\gamma - 1)/2\gamma$  is small itself, regardless of  $\bar{M}_e$  this will provide a relatively small damping (only) effect. The short nozzle approximation thus provides a simple, frequency-independent boundary condition at the nozzle. Unfortunately, it can hardly be considered a plausible model for real engine nozzles, though it has been used often in the past.

#### D. Acoustic Absorber Models

Given the very incomplete models for combustion response in liquid rocket engines, there has been considerable effort and interest in the use of acoustic damping devices such as slots and liners. The general motivation for this is to provide sufficient damping so that exact knowledge of the driving supplied by the combustion processes to a given mode of oscillation is not a necessity. To effect this strategy, the actual damping provided by a particular absorber design in the complicated oscillatory flow environment of the engine must be assessed. This requires first that accurate models for the absorbers that predict their response to arbitrary oscillations be available. In addition, the impact of these absorbers on the other stability affecting components of the engine and, thus, on the stability of the chamber's complete driving and damping mechanisms must be determined accurately. The latter requirement, in the case of linear oscillations at least, generally can be satisfied using the integral technique given earlier. It remains to discuss response models for acoustic absorbers.

There are several types of acoustic dampers which have been either proposed or actually employed in liquid rocket engines. These include arrays of individual absorbers (generally of the Helmholtz resonator type), which are called acoustic liners. These liners may cover the complete periphery of the combustion chamber or only some fraction of it. In addition to liners, acoustic slots in a wide variety of designs have been used. These include quarter-wave slots, Helmholtz resonator slots, and slots with a design intermediate between the quarter-wave tube and Helmholtz resonators. Beyond these classical devices whose design permits a one-dimensional flow evaluation, L-shaped slots or slots with a more arbitrary two-dimensional geometry have also seen application.<sup>13-18</sup>

Models for acoustic liners and for the classical one-dimensional devices have long been available. These were reviewed in the liquid rocket combustion instability book<sup>1</sup> and also in a slightly later and more complete publication by NASA.<sup>13</sup> More recently slots with an arbitrary two-dimensional geometry and slots with nonuniform mean temperatures have been modeled.<sup>3,19-21</sup> For all configurations the analysis requires that the frequency dependence and damping be predicted. The former problem can be successfully attacked using linear analysis, the latter requires a nonlinear approach, at least for the oscillation amplitudes present in liquid rocket engines.

For use in the type of integral stability model being discussed here, the performance of acoustic absorbers is most conveniently given in terms of an acoustic

admittance  $\beta$ , defined by

$$\mathbf{q}' \cdot \mathbf{n} = \beta p' \quad (35)$$

The condition is to be applied at the absorber–main chamber interface with the unit normal directed out of the combustion chamber. Also,  $\mathbf{q}'$  is the local chamber oscillatory velocity,  $p'$  the local pressure oscillation, and  $\beta$  the (complex) admittance. The real part of  $\beta$  is mainly a measure of the damping provided by the absorber, the imaginary part affects the frequency directly and overall stability indirectly, as will be discussed later. In analyzing the behavior of the absorber by itself, it is somewhat more convenient and consistent with historical practice in acoustics to deal with the reciprocal of  $\beta$ , the acoustic impedance. Clearly

$$\beta = \frac{1}{K} = \frac{K_R - iK_I}{(K_R^2 + K_I^2)} \quad (36)$$

If  $K_I$  is zero then so is  $\beta_I$ . Also, at this point,  $\beta_R$  takes its maximum value and, of course,  $u'$  and  $p'$  are in phase. The absorber is said to be tuned at this point, and the frequency that gives  $K_I = 0$  is called the tuning frequency. In modeling the performance of acoustic absorbers, it has usually been adequate to separate the problems of determining  $K_I$  and  $K_R$ , that is, the tuning and damping problems.

To determine the phasing between  $u'$  and  $p'$  (that is,  $K_I$ ) experience indicates that solving the linear wave equation for the cavity gives a good approximation.<sup>3,20</sup> For one-dimensional geometries this is quite straightforward (i.e., quarter-wave tubes, Helmholtz resonators, intermediate absorbers) and the tuning formulas are well known and validated by much experimental data. For example, in the case of a quarter-wave slot with uniform mean temperature,

$$K_I = -\gamma \bar{\rho}_a \bar{a}_a \cot(\omega L_{\text{eff}}/\bar{a}_a) \quad (37)$$

The parameter  $L_{\text{eff}}$  is equal to the (nondimensional) depth of the cavity plus a small empirical correction, to account for the inertia of the gas in the slot. Somewhat more complicated results for the other one-dimensional cavity flows with uniform temperature are readily available.<sup>13</sup> When a two-dimensional analysis is required, and/or when the mean temperature in the cavity varies, the analysis becomes more complicated and simple closed-form results are not possible. In this case the integral approach described has been used with success for the absorber problem as well<sup>3,20</sup> and results in terms of eigenfunction expansions for  $u'$  and  $p'$  with  $\omega$  as a parameter result.

In developing models to predict  $K_R$  it was recognized early on by Ingard<sup>22</sup> that the basic dissipation mechanism for amplitudes of the magnitude to be expected in liquid rocket engines was related to jet dissipation at the chamber-cavity interface. Quasilinearization of the flow in the interfacial region leads to predictions of  $K_R$  of the following form:

$$K_R = \Gamma \bar{\rho}_a \bar{a}_a \quad (38)$$

In this expression  $\bar{\rho}_a$  is the mean density at the cavity entrance,  $\bar{a}_a$  the amplitude of the oscillatory velocity at the cavity entrance, and  $\Gamma$  a constant dependent on the cavity geometry and the magnitude of crossflow at the cavity entrance.  $\Gamma$  has been predicted by analysis and measured in both cold- and hot-firing environments.<sup>14,23</sup>

With the expressions for  $K_R$  and  $K_I$  already given, the impact of an acoustic absorber on stability can be assessed by inserting these expressions into the integral Eqs. (25) and (28). Note that  $K$  (or  $\beta$ ) has been defined as a strictly local variable, that is,  $\beta = \beta(\theta, z)$ . The design of the absorber can change from place to place on the surface of the chamber. Multiple slots, slots designed for multiple mode tuning, and liners of variable  $\beta$  can all be included. The impact of absorbers of arbitrary design can, thus, be assessed using the stability model. The answers to questions, such as the following, concerning the impact of acoustic absorbers on stability can also be obtained. What geometry tunes a given absorber when the influence of other engine components affecting stability are included? Are combustion zone-acoustic absorber interactions significant? What is the overall impact of a given absorber on linear stability? Does tuning an absorber provide maximum stability enhancement? A surprising result from stability predictions to be presented shortly is that the last question is not always answered in the affirmative.

#### E. Injector Face Baffle Modes

Because the presence of baffles alters the geometry of the combustion chamber to a complicated and frequently irregular form, the wave motions in the baffle cavities and main chamber can be very complex indeed. It follows that including the effects of these baffles is quite a challenging problem analytically. When the liquid rocket stability reference book<sup>1</sup> was written in 1970, only the simplest one-dimensional treatment was available, as given by Reardon.<sup>24</sup> Though this simple model did predict the frequency depression observed in experiments, it made no attempt to describe the complicated three-dimensional wave interactions between the baffle cavities and main chamber. Moreover, no mechanism for dissipation was included, so any damping that occurred could only be the result of indirect effects (such as the frequency depression just mentioned). Oberg et al.<sup>25</sup> attempted the problem of baffled combustors in the early 1970s. In this approach a variational integral method similar to the technique already presented was used. The bulk of this work did not include mean flow, nozzle, or combustion effects. In addition, no dissipation mechanism for the baffled chamber oscillations was included. A surprising and unrealistic prediction of this work was that baffles were found to provide linear driving rather than damping. The work of Oberg et al.<sup>25</sup> did, however, predict the frequency depression observed experimentally.

The first analysis of the baffle problem to provide a mechanism for baffle dissipation was performed by Baer and Mitchell.<sup>26</sup> In this work a finite mean flow, a concentrated combustion zone, and a short (constant Mach number) nozzle were included. The analysis separated the problem into an outer flow region away from the baffle tips and an inner region in the high-velocity region near the baffle blade tips. The outer solution was obtained using an eigenfunction expansion technique. Irrotational, isentropic flow was assumed to exist in this outer region, so the governing equation was simply

$$\nabla^2 \phi + \omega^2 \phi = 2\bar{M}i\omega \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial z} + \bar{M}^2 \frac{\partial^2 \phi}{\partial z^2} \quad (39)$$

with

$$p' = -\gamma \left[ i\omega \phi + \bar{M} \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial z} \right] \quad (40)$$

and

$$\xi_z = s' = 0 \quad (41)$$

In the main chamber,  $\phi$  was represented as an expansion in orthonormal eigenfunctions that satisfied no-flow conditions at the chamber walls and the short nozzle condition at the nozzle entrance plane. For each baffle cavity  $\phi$  was represented as well by a similar expansion. In the cavities the eigenfunctions obeyed zero normal velocity conditions at the baffle blades and the concentrated combustion form of the sensitive time-lag combustion response model at the injector face. Requiring that pressure and axial velocity match at the main chamber-cavity interface then provided the conditions necessary to determine the coefficients in the series for both main chamber and baffle cavities. In addition, a value for the (complex) frequency eigenvalue was determined. The effects of dissipation were included first by performing an asymptotic analysis in a local coordinate system near the baffle blade tip. This inner solution was matched to the outer solution in order to provide an accurate description of the flowfield in this high-velocity region. This solution was, in turn, used to drive an oscillatory boundary layer on the baffle blades near the tips (away from the tips the velocity was small enough that viscous dissipation was negligible). The energy dissipated in the boundary layer was given by a surface integral over the baffle blades area of the form

$$E_{dis} = \int_{\text{blades}} \gamma \sqrt{\frac{\mu_{\text{eff}}(\omega)}{2}} \hat{u}^2 dS \quad (42)$$

where  $\hat{u}$  was the velocity amplitude at the edge of the boundary layer and  $\mu_{\text{eff}}$  was a combined molecular-turbulent effective viscosity coefficient. This dissipation integral was used by Baer and Mitchell<sup>26</sup> in an integral stability determination based on the method of Cantrell and Hart.<sup>27</sup> The complete outer solution was used in volume and surface integrals, similar to Eq. (28), in order to obtain a value for the decay coefficient  $\lambda$ . It is important to note that this procedure assumed that the outer solution is not affected by the dissipation in the boundary layer, that is, no attempt was made to correct  $\phi$ .

More recent work<sup>28</sup> has extended the Baer and Mitchell analysis to include arbitrary combustion distributions, finite length nozzle admittances, and acoustic absorbers. This later analysis is cast in the form of the integral method described in this chapter. The basic solution for the main chamber and cavities (including the inner solution at the tip region) is determined for the no mean flow, no combustion case. That is, the matched inner-outer, main chamber-baffle cavity solutions are all for the no-flow acoustic situation. Taken together they define  $\tilde{\phi}$ , the approximating function of Eqs. (30) and (31). To date only the second of these, Eq. (31), has been used to determine baffled chamber stability. Because  $\nabla \tilde{\phi} \cdot \mathbf{n} = 0$  on all boundaries in the present application this equation can be written

$$(\omega - \bar{\omega}) \int_V \tilde{\phi} \tilde{\phi} dV = \int_V \tilde{\phi} F_1(\tilde{\phi}) dV - \int_S \tilde{\phi} F_2(\tilde{\phi}) dS \quad (43)$$

Using this equation, the effects of mean flow, combustion, nozzle, acoustic absorbers, and dissipation on  $\omega_R$  and  $\lambda$  are determined with the wave represented by  $\tilde{\phi}$ . No attempt has yet been made to successively improve  $\phi$  from  $\tilde{\phi}$  by applying

Eq. (30) to include the mean flow, combustion, nozzle, absorber, and baffle dissipation effects. This remains as an interesting and, perhaps, formidable extension to the theory. It should also be noted that all analyses to date have considered baffles without radial hubs. That is, baffles designed to suppress only tangential and not radial modes have been analyzed. Work is in progress, however, which will treat both hubs and radial blades with hubs.

#### F. Some Predictions

The bulk of the calculations performed using the integral method described have been completed for somewhat simplified forms of the governing equations.<sup>3,19-21,27</sup> This was done both to reduce the cost of the calculations and the complexity of the algebraic manipulations and because the simplifications were found to have relatively minor effects on most predictions. Specifically, in Eq. (16) all terms of  $\mathcal{O}(M^2)$  or smaller were dropped and  $\bar{Q}$  was taken to be approximately constant. The latter assumption implies that the steady-state volumetric mass generation rate was taken to be uniform in the combustion zone. The axial extent and location of the combustion zone were arbitrary, however, as was the corresponding magnitude of  $\bar{Q}$ . Finally, the time-lag model was used to represent the response of the combustion zone to oscillations in the results that will be discussed here.

##### 1. Effects of Combustion Concentration

The impact of the axial extent (distribution) of the combustion zone on stability was examined in a series of calculations.<sup>2</sup> Some results for a particular cylindrical engine configuration are presented in Fig. 1. The two curves shown are neutral stability ( $\lambda = 0$ ) curves for the first tangential mode of oscillation and two different

axial combustion distributions. The curve labeled "concentrated combustion" is for a combustion zone concentrated in the first 10% of the chamber length, next to the injector. The "distributed combustion" curve corresponds to a combustion zone which extends along the entire axial length of the combustion chamber. Points along both curves were generated by solving the integral equations described earlier with the real part of the frequency as the independent variable and the imaginary part of the frequency,  $\lambda_i$ , set equal to zero. The corresponding dependent variables for each solution point were the coefficient matrix  $\mu_N$  (which determines the spatial form of the oscillation) and the combustion response eigenvalues, interaction index  $n$  and time lag  $\tau$ , required to drive the oscillation. A low value of  $n$  for a point along either curve indicates that a relatively small gain is required from the combustion process in order to support the oscillation, whereas a large value of  $n$  requires a high gain.

To illustrate, suppose that the combustion process for a particular engine supplied an overall combustion response characterized by the  $n$ ,  $\tau$  values at point A in the figure. For this value of  $\tau$ , the  $n$  value required for neutral stability in the case of concentrated combustion (as determined by the intersection of a vertical line through A and the appropriate neutral stability curve) is about 1.0. The  $n$  value supplied by the combustion process (point A) is about 1.25. Thus, more gain is supplied than necessary for neutral stability, and the engine with concentrated combustion is predicted to be unstable. Indeed, if the  $n$  and  $\tau$  at point A were used as inputs to the stability model with complex frequency as output (the reverse of what was done to generate the stability curves), one would find that the imaginary part of the frequency,  $\lambda_i$ , would be negative, predicting exponential growth of the oscillation. (The calculated value found using the model for the point in question is  $\lambda_i = -0.036$ .) For an engine with distributed combustion having the same  $n$ ,  $\tau$  values supplied by the combustion process (point A), the  $n$  supplied is less than that required for neutral stability. The engine is predicted to be stable and  $\lambda_i$  is positive (exponential decay). In contrast, if the  $n$  and  $\tau$  supplied by the combustion process corresponded to point B, the opposite situation would obtain: the engine with distributed combustion would be predicted unstable, the one with concentrated combustion predicted stable. Overall, an inspection of Fig. 1 indicates that, at least for the particular engine configuration considered, distributing the combustion zone has an effect on stability which depends on the characteristic time of the combustion process. If  $\tau$  is relatively short (as at point A), distributing the combustion is stabilizing, whereas if  $\tau$  is relatively long (as at B), distributing the combustion is destabilizing. Since there is essentially no upward shift in the minimum of the neutral stability curve with a change in combustion distribution, there is no change in the minimum gain required when phasing is optimal. These results are typical of those found in calculations for other engine configurations.<sup>3</sup>

In Fig. 2 three neutral stability curves are shown. The lowest curve is for the baseline engine with no slot and axially distributed combustion. Above this is the neutral stability curve for the engine with a slot having a depth such that

The third curve is the neutral stability curve for the slot of the depth that produced the largest upward shift in the minimum  $n$  point compared with the baseline engine. This slot had a depth less than that for the tuned slot and was consequently detuned significantly. This was reflected in the fact that the value of  $\beta_R$  (real part of the slot admittance) was about half of the value for the tuned slot.

A more quantitative sense of the damping produced by the addition of slots was gained by making decay rate calculations. Values of  $n$  and  $\tau$  were fixed at the values corresponding to the minimum  $n$  point of the baseline neutral stability curve in these calculations while the depth of the slot was varied. Results of calculations for  $\lambda$ , expressed in terms of percent decay per cycle, are shown in Fig. 3 for two different slot open areas. The large increase in decay rate away from the tuning point is evident in the sharply peaked 10% open area curve. A maximum increase in decay rate of about a factor of three over the tuned slot is predicted.

Addition of a slot was also found to cause a very substantial change in the spatial form of the pressure oscillation. Evidence of this is shown in Fig. 4 where the pressure amplitude is plotted as a function of axial distance. For the baseline engine with no slot a significant decrease in amplitude (about 50%) between the injector and nozzle can be seen. In the case of the tuned slot the opposite is true; injector end amplitude is considerably smaller. In contrast, for the maximum damping untuned slot the amplitude is almost uniform.

of the oscillations discussed is quite different from that of the corresponding simple acoustic mode  $\Omega_{\tilde{N}}$ . This implies that for the significant mean flow, nozzle, and absorber influences present in typical liquid rocket engine configurations it is not an adequate approximation to use  $\Omega_{\tilde{N}}$  as the approximating function in an integral stability equation such as Eq. (28). The impacts of these components can only be included correctly if an accurate representation of the actual waveform is generated. Examination of Eq. (28) shows why. Both nozzle and absorber provide damping through terms like

$$\int_S \Omega_{\tilde{N}} \beta p' dS \quad (44)$$

where  $S$  is the active area over the nozzle or absorber entrance. On the other hand, the leading term in combustion driving is

$$\int_V \Omega_{\tilde{N}} \tilde{Q} \eta p' dV \quad (45)$$

All three integrals are dependent on the local pressure amplitude. Since this varies significantly, according to the calculations just presented, its form must be well approximated in order to give the true stability picture. Certainly if the relative amplitudes of the pressure oscillations at the nozzle and injector change by a factor of four upon the addition of a 10% open area slot as predicted, then a model which assumes that the amplitude is in fact the same at both locations is quite inaccurate.

An important implication of this requirement for a true picture of actual linear wave shape is that it makes no sense to try to separate the complete stability problem into independent calculations for the  $\lambda$  contribution of one component (say, the slot) while ignoring the presence of the others (combustion and nozzle). Adding up the  $\lambda$  values for these problems cannot give an accurate measure of the overall decay coefficient. The fact that a tuned absorber does not provide maximum overall damping is ample evidence of this.

This is not to say that there are no instances in which  $\Omega_{\tilde{N}}$  can be used as an adequate approximating function. It must, of course, be true that if the impacts of combustion, absorber, and nozzle are small enough (that is,  $\tilde{M}$ ,  $\tilde{Q}$ ,  $\beta_{\text{nozzle}}$ , and  $\beta_{\text{absorber}}$  are all small), then  $\Omega_{\tilde{N}}$  will serve. Also, if the impact of one driving or damping element is small (say, the absorber), then the description of the waveform will not be much affected by that element. As an example of this consider a chamber oscillation that is neutrally stable with no absorber present. If an absorber tuned to the frequency of the oscillation without the absorber present is added, then as long as its open area is small enough it should provide optimal damping. At some point, however, the absorber begins to affect the form of the oscillation and the tuning depth may no longer be best. The results of calculations that demonstrate this are given in Fig. 5. Curves are shown for a tuned slot and also for a variable depth slot designed to give maximum  $\lambda$  as the slot width is increased. For small enough open areas (up to about 3%) the curves coincide. For large open areas there is considerable divergence. Note that the effectiveness of the tuned absorber actually decreases with increasing open areas above about 6%. The tuned absorber provides an increase in damping by itself, but also affects the other components so that the net damping decreases.

##### 4. Baffled Chamber Predictions

The calculations to be discussed briefly here were performed for a combustor with a variable length combustion zone and a conical nozzle with admittance predicted by the Crocco-Sirignano<sup>9</sup> theory. As discussed earlier, the approximating function for baffled chamber analysis was described by the solution to the baffled chamber problem without mean flow, combustion, or nozzle. These latter stability components are only included to first order through Eq. (31). A more complete description of these results and the computer code which was used to generate them is given in Ref. 28.

Neutral stability curves in terms of  $n$  and  $\tau$  for a short, three-bladed baffle, concentrated combustion, and the first tangential (1T) mode of oscillation (main chamber) are presented in Fig. 6. The blade length is 33% of the chamber length. It can be observed immediately that the unbaffled chamber is very unstable; that is, the minimum point on the neutral stability curve for the unbaffled chamber is very low, with a minimum  $n$  around 0.25. A major reason for this is that for the particular nozzle design and contraction ratio of this engine, the nozzle admittance has a large, negative real part; it is strongly destabilizing. All combustion zone locations and concentrations are predicted to give identical stability behavior in unbaffled engine. Enhanced stability as reflected by the upward shift of the neutral stability curves is predicted for the same engine with the three-bladed baffle added. Results for two different combustion distributions are shown. The curve labeled "con. combustion" is for a concentrated combustion zone at the injector end of the chamber occupying just 12% of the total axial length. The curve labeled "dist. combustion" is for a uniform distribution occupying the entire chamber length. Comparing the two curves it is seen that the stability enhancement predicted is almost twice as large for distributed combustion as for concentrated combustion.

Why? The plots of the axial dependence of the oscillatory pressure amplitude shown in Fig. 7 give some insight. For the unbaffled engine the pressure profile is just the horizontal line to be expected for the acoustic solution without baffles.

(Recall that the plot is for  $p$  based on  $\tilde{\phi}$ , and  $\tilde{\phi} = \Omega_N$  in the absence of a baffle.) The 33% baffle length, on the other hand, causes a dramatic increase in the pressure amplitude at the injector end relative to the nozzle end. This means that for combustion sources located near the nozzle end, at a location with relatively low amplitude, the contribution of these sources to the combustion driving integral is relatively small. On the other hand, the baffle dissipation integral occurs in a region of relatively high amplitude. The net effect is a considerable stability enhancement. With the combustion zone located at the injector (in the baffle cavities) both dissipation and combustion occur at high amplitude, and the net stabilizing effect is smaller. The general conclusion to be drawn from these calculations is that baffles can provide stabilization both through viscous damping at the blade tips and through a reduction in combustion driving caused by distorting the spatial form of the oscillation.

### IV. Nonlinear Analysis

Though the linear analyses just discussed can be used to assess the intrinsic stability of a liquid-propellant rocket engine including the impact of the major driving and damping mechanisms and components, the linearization of the governing equations that makes the analysis relatively straightforward also precludes the possibility of describing at least two important features of the instability problem. The first of these is a prediction of the finite amplitude waveform (in space and time) that oscillations finally assume. Having a model that can predict these limit cycles is important, not only for a complete description of instability phenomena, but also because of the implications for validation of the theory. Experiments for fully developed oscillations are easier to perform. Measurements of amplitude and waveform for finite oscillation in engines are more straightforward to make than the growth rate or stability boundary measurements for spontaneous oscillations that are generally required for validation of linear theories. The second well-known characteristic of combustion instability that only a nonlinear theory can treat is the phenomenon of triggering. Ample experimental results indicate that in many cases liquid rocket engines which are intrinsically stable to small-amplitude background disturbances can exhibit finite amplitude oscillations upon the introduction of disturbances of sufficient amplitude and of the correct form.

To treat the nonlinear combustion instability problem completely, nonlinearities in all phases of the problem must be included: gas dynamics, combustion response, nozzle admittances, and damping mechanisms including slots and baffles. The lack of a mechanistic combustion response model or even of a viable nonlinear heuristic model which characterizes the nonlinear response of the burning processes to oscillations in pressure and velocity has generally limited analytical work to the treatment of nonlinear gas dynamics and the resulting nonlinear wave motion. In most treatments the combustion response model has remained linear. This is generally true for the early work of Sirignano and Crocco,<sup>29</sup> Mitchell et al.,<sup>30</sup> Crocco and Mitchell,<sup>31</sup> and Zinn.<sup>2</sup> These analyses were reviewed in Ref. 2, and a detailed recapitulation is not needed here. It should be remarked, however, that the analyses were quite successful in predicting the general form of finite amplitude waves, including both shock waves and steep fronted waves for the cases of axial and annular combustion chamber geometries. Triggering was also predicted in this work but only for very narrow ranges of the linear combustion response parameters ( $n$  and  $\tau$ ) close to the neutral stability limit in the region of linear stability. These ranges were, in fact, so narrow that discriminating between the triggered instability predicted and spontaneous instability in an experimental

engine would hardly be possible. Thus, in essence these results indicated that no viable triggering mechanism was to be found in the nonlinear gas dynamics for any geometry common in liquid rocket engines. A few words of caution, however, are appropriate. First, this work was limited to moderate amplitude waves, with terms of the order of the pressure amplitude cubed generally ignored in the equations. Second, the nonlinear form of the short nozzle, constant Mach number boundary condition was used in all of the work except Zinn's, which in turn was limited by an irrotational assumption.

Subsequent work by Zinn and Powell<sup>33</sup> and Powell and Zinn<sup>34</sup> attacked the nonlinear instability problem using a different technique. This approach was an approximate integral analysis based on the method of weighted residuals that they termed a modified Galerkin technique. The basic governing equation used by them can be derived directly from the conservation equations and assumptions presented earlier, if, in addition, an assumption of irrotational motion is made. Noting that the steady-state flow is taken to be one dimensional and that for linear oscillations the influence of combustion generated vorticity is small, this assumption is not as restrictive as it might seem at first glance. Moreover, the early nonlinear work of Crocco and Mitchell,<sup>31</sup> which included vorticity effects in axial and annular mode oscillations, showed that only a modest effect on stability resulted from its inclusion. The velocity potential  $\Phi$  was represented as a (truncated) expansion in terms of appropriate orthogonal eigenfunctions for the geometry in question,  $\Omega_N(\mathbf{r})$ , thus,

$$\Phi = \sum_N A_N(t) \Omega_N(\mathbf{r}) \quad (46)$$

The coefficients  $A_N(t)$  were in turn determined by applying the Galerkin orthogonality condition to require approximate satisfaction of the governing equation and boundary conditions. Substitution of the series representation for  $\Phi$  into these integral conditions resulted in a system of nonlinear coupled ordinary differential equations for the  $A_N(t)$  coefficients. These were then integrated numerically. Results of calculations for both longitudinal and transverse (tangential and radial) mode oscillations showed that limit cycles qualitatively similar to those observed experimentally were predicted. Triggering predictions were consistent with the earlier work just discussed in that triggering was found to exist only for very restricted areas in the linearly stable region of the  $n_r$ ,  $\tau$  plane lying very close to the neutral stability curves. No triggering at all for 1T and axial modes was predicted if only terms to second order in pressure amplitude were retained. A third-order theory was required to predict any triggering. In their work Zinn and Powell<sup>33</sup> found that only a few terms in the series for  $\Phi$  needed to be retained (five terms for axial modes and three terms, 1T, 2T, 1R, for the 1T mode).

There are distinct advantages to the Galerkin approach. It is straightforward, relatively simple, and gives a time history for developing oscillations. In view of the linear results presented earlier, however, one must wonder if it can model adequately the complex interactions between modes that occur for engines with concentrated combustion, strong nozzle effects, and damping components such as slot absorbers. A very complex spatial structure is predicted in these engines for linear oscillations. How can a few modes suffice for the nonlinear case? Certainly for linear oscillations, the Galerkin approximation used by Zinn and Powell<sup>33</sup> leads to a spatial representation through  $\Omega_N$ . As has been shown in the preceding section on linear stability this is rarely adequate.

From the discussion up to this point it can be seen that nonlinear treatments of the gas dynamics in the combustion chamber that include linear combustion response models have not been adequate to predict the observed triggering characteristics of many engine configurations. It is reasonable to suspect then that inclusion of a sufficiently realistic nonlinear combustion response model is required in order to predict triggered instabilities. An attempt was made by Jotiban<sup>35</sup> in the mid-1970s to do this. He pursued an analytical investigation that posited a nonlinear vaporization-based combustion response model as the driver in a liquid rocket engine. Both the combustor model and the response model were quite simplified and, perhaps, quite unrealistic. Nevertheless, some fairly strong triggering was predicted, and the method may bear re-examination for future application. The engine model included a concentrated combustion zone at the injector end, a short nozzle at the nozzle end, a moderate contraction ratio (terms of order  $\bar{M}^3$  were dropped in the analysis) and an acoustic slot with a Helmholtz resonator geometry. Irrotational flow was assumed so that the governing equation was essentially the same as that of Zinn and Powell.<sup>33</sup> The nonlinear short nozzle boundary condition was used as was a nonlinear form of the absorber admittance for the Helmholtz resonator. The concentrated combustion assumption was made for analytical simplicity. It is, of course, inconsistent with a droplet vaporization model requiring a finite droplet lifetime. Consequently, a characteristic time (essentially the droplet lifetime) was artificially included in a monodisperse droplet vaporization model. Though the physical reality of the vaporization model is questionable, it was certainly strongly nonlinear.

To simplify calculations, only terms through second order in  $\varepsilon$ , an amplitude parameter, were kept. Also it was assumed that only traveling tangential ( $\theta$  direction) modes were to be considered. The velocity potential was represented as a harmonic series truncated to two terms, thus,

$$\Phi = Re[\Phi_1 + \Phi_2] \quad (47)$$

where

$$\Phi_1 = \phi_1(\mathbf{r})e^{i\alpha}, \quad \Phi_2 = \phi_2(\mathbf{r})e^{2i\alpha} \quad (48)$$

and

$$\alpha = \theta + \omega t, \quad \omega = \omega_R + i\lambda \quad (49)$$

Substitution into the governing equation and boundary conditions led to two partial differential equations, one for the first harmonic component and one for the second. Following the integral transformation method given earlier, these were, in turn, cast a two integral equations of the form

$$\phi_i = \int_{V_0} G_i F_{1i}(\phi_1, \phi_2) dV_0 - \int_{S_0} G_i F_{2i}(\phi_1, \phi_2) dS_0 \quad (50)$$

where  $i = 1, 2$  and  $F_{1i}$  and  $F_{2i}$  are nonlinear functions of  $\phi_1$  and  $\phi_2$ .  $F_{2i}$  was determined by application of the boundary conditions and included combustion driving terms. The equations were solved by successive approximation. To lowest order  $\phi_1 = \varepsilon \Omega_{\hat{N}}$  and  $\phi_2 = 0$ . Substitution in the integral equations gave improved approximation for  $\phi_1$  and  $\phi_2$  (in terms of eigenfunction expansions) and so on. The requirement that the amplitude of  $\Omega_{\hat{N}}$  be  $\varepsilon$  also gave a successively improved value for  $\omega = \omega_R + i\lambda$ . It is to be noted that  $F_{1i}$  and  $F_{2i}$  contain both the linear

terms due to mean flow, combustion, etc., as well as the nonlinear terms. Thus, if  $\varepsilon$  is set identically to zero, the usual linear solution results.

Results of calculations for one set of model parameters are shown in Fig. 8. To construct this figure, calculations of the type just described were completed for many values of  $\varepsilon$ , starting at  $\varepsilon = 0$ . For each value of  $\varepsilon$ , the functional forms of  $\phi_1$  and  $\phi_2$  were determined and values of  $\omega_R$  and  $\lambda$  were obtained. At  $\varepsilon = 0$ , the linear solution gives a prediction of  $\lambda$  of approximately 0.11. That is, linear stability with a large linear decay rate is predicted. As  $\varepsilon$  is increased,  $\lambda$  decreases, passes through zero, and becomes negative. Negative values of  $\lambda$  indicate growing oscillations. What is shown is, indeed, a prediction of triggered oscillations. For the complete nonlinear solution labeled as "nonlinear wave propagation" in the figure, the curve passes through  $\lambda = 0$  at an amplitude parameter value of about 0.032. For values of  $\varepsilon$  below this the engine is stable, for values larger than this the engine is unstable. Thus  $\varepsilon \approx 0.032$  represents the minimum triggering amplitude parameter required, and the oscillation that occurs at this point represents an unstable limit cycle. Physically the calculation procedure represents a prediction of how the engine configuration would respond to the imposition of a 1T traveling wave of a certain amplitude  $\varepsilon$ . The prediction takes into account all of the driving and damping mechanisms and the nonlinear interactions up to  $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^2)$ . It is a "snap shot" at a particular time; no time history is possible with the technique. The fact that the curve does not recross the axis  $\lambda = 0$  for larger values of  $\varepsilon$  means that stable limit cycles were not predicted. There is, however, a gradual tendency toward the axis. Calculations were not carried out beyond  $\varepsilon = 0.14$  because higher order terms would become important. (Indeed, at  $\varepsilon = 0.14$  the peak-to-peak amplitude of the oscillation was predicted to be more than 50% of the mean.) A third-order analysis might predict stable limit cycles.

The second curve labeled "linear wave propagation" in the figure was generated by repeating the calculation procedure when all of the nonlinear terms in the governing equation (gas dynamics) were neglected. Nonlinearities in the driving and damping boundary conditions were retained. It can be seen that there is a qualitative agreement between the complete nonlinear prediction and that the quantitative differences are not that large, with a slightly higher minimum  $\varepsilon$  for triggering being predicted. Clearly, for the engine model being used, the boundary conditions, and not the nonlinear gas dynamics, dominate. This provides evidence that the required triggering mechanism must reside in the nonlinear combustion response and not in nonlinear gas dynamics.

It is interesting to contrast the Jotiban approach with the Galerkin method of Zinn and Powell<sup>33</sup> (or with the mainly equivalent but more recent and more elegant approach described by Culick<sup>36</sup>). In the Jotiban<sup>35</sup> approach a simple representation of the temporal behavior of the oscillation is combined with a complete description of spatial interactions. For the Zinn and Powell<sup>33</sup> or Culick<sup>36</sup> techniques, a simple spatial representation is combined with a complete investigation of the time-dependent behavior of the oscillation. It would seem that both approaches provide partial pictures of the complete nonlinear situation. Both are of interest; both warrant future application to the liquid rocket instability problem. Finally, both require accurate models for nonlinear combustion response processes before meaningful practical application is possible.

### V. Concluding Remarks

A major conclusion from the review just presented is that, as was the case in the 1970s, the most fundamental need in successful analytical modeling of combustion instability in liquid rocket engines is for mechanistic, realistic models for the combustion process, and for the response of these processes to both linear and nonlinear oscillations. Such models are not currently available. In their absence the other important physical contributors to the stability picture have received the greatest attention. For the case of small-amplitude oscillations especially, a quite complete analytical framework exists, which lacks only the insertion of realistic response models to become a useful predictive tool. The work on these other aspects of the linear stability problem, however is not all done. As mentioned earlier, a more complete description of instability in baffled combustion chambers is required. The mutual influences of baffle dissipation, combustion, and acoustic absorbers on the basic wave pattern generated by the baffle must be modeled. Also baffle hubs to suppress radial instability must be included in the baffled chamber analysis. The profound destabilizing influence of the convergent part of nozzles, which is predicted in some cases by the widely used nozzle admittance analysis of Crocco and Sirignano,<sup>9</sup> needs to be verified. The magnitude of the nozzle driving is predicted to be of the same size as the damping provided by large open area acoustic slots, at least for pure transverse modes in some engine configurations. An extension of the steady-state combustion description to include arbitrary radial and azimuthal variations is a generalization which will better model some real combustion situations and will more readily accept mechanistic combustion response models as they become available.

The state of analytical modeling for large, amplitude spontaneous or triggered oscillations is less well developed. Given the considerable increase in the speed at which computations can be done today as compared to what was possible years ago when the original work was done, a much more general and at the same time

accurate modeling framework should be possible. Both mode history (Galerkin type) and the harmonic analysis approaches should be re-examined and extended as appropriate. Here again, the goal is to develop an analytical framework which can accept quite general nonlinear combustion response models and determine through direct calculation if their driving mechanisms result in stability predictions consistent with the observed phenomena in liquid-propellant rocket engines.
