### I. Introduction

THE purpose of the analysis described in this chapter is to provide a suitable framework for studying the linear instability of acoustic waves in liquid-propellant rocket engines driven mainly by interactions with combustion processes. Most of the discussion here is devoted to the formulation of the problem in a manner that enables us to take into account the effects of the turbulence and spray as well as the chemical reaction. Emphasis will be placed on the mathematical principles for treating wave propagation in random media characterized by stochastic distributions of state variables, velocity, and chemical reaction.

Liquid-propellant rocket acoustic instability was intensively studied during the 1950s and 1960s, the decades of rocket development. Since then, it has undergone a period of de-emphasis during which the fundamental understanding of the related physics remained almost unchanged. Consequently, most of the ideas about acoustic instability can be found in reviews based on information available at that time.<sup>1-3</sup> Because knowledge in turbulent combustion was lacking then, predictions of acoustic instability had to rely on highly simplified models. The most important feature of those models is that the medium of wave propagation is homogenized by taking averages of state variables and assuming homogeneous and empirical chemical reaction rates dependent only on the averaged variables. The problems,

thus, involve only one length scale, i.e., the wavelength. Although from the viewpoint of the acoustic wave such models could give a first approximation, the effects of phenomena taking place at much smaller length scales, such as those of turbulence and influences of interactions with sprays, had to be significantly compromised or ignored. The greatest shortcoming, however, is that the models did not properly include results of the flame-structure analysis. The flame is not only the main energy source for the wave field but also must be located where the actual amplification mechanisms of the acoustic field occur. By ignoring flame-structure analyses, results of the identified amplification mechanisms<sup>4-7</sup> cannot be incorporated into the predictions; therefore, the models had to rely on empiricisms such as time-lag descriptions.<sup>8</sup>

To describe the effects of turbulence and of detailed local flame structure, the basic idea is patterned after the laminar flamelet model of turbulent combustion,<sup>9-11</sup> in which the disparity of the length scales enables us to assume that a turbulent flame is an ensemble of laminar flamelets. Consideration of the length scales involved in the problem indicates that the largest length scale will be the wavelength, whose order of magnitude is the diameter of rocket chamber, denoted by  $d$ . The important length scale for turbulence,  $\ell_t$ , is the integral scale, measuring the distance that a turbulent fluctuation can travel on average. In this analysis, the wavelength is always asymptotically larger than the turbulent length scale. This long-wave assumption allows us to adopt a hypothesis of local homogeneity, which states that the wave is considered to be homogeneous over a distance of the order of  $\ell_t$ . The length scale for the flame is even smaller than the turbulence length scale in the flame-sheet regime, and modeling is needed to resolve all of these length scales.

The modeling in this analysis can occur at two levels, the macroscopic and microscopic levels. At the macroscopic level, the acoustic wave is considered to propagate in a multiphase, turbulent reactive medium. In this case, the resulting wave equation as well as the wave field are stochastic. Using a mathematical method called smooth perturbation,<sup>12-14</sup> the mean wave field is calculated in terms of moments of the stochastic variables. Flame structures are considered at the microscopic level. Since the flame is dominantly a diffusion flame, the mixture-fraction variable can be adopted to simplify the flame-structure analysis. The main objective of this later analysis is to obtain the dependence of variables such as the rate of heat release on acoustic fluctuations as functions of the mixture fraction. The results of the microscopic-level analyses are introduced into the macroscopic level to obtain the moments of stochastic variables through the mixture fraction that is available from the turbulent-flame calculation.<sup>9</sup>

Time scales are relevant to the phenomena. Since the velocity scale of the wave is a representative sound speed, its time scale can be taken to be given by  $d/a_f$  where  $a_f$  is frozen sound speed. On the other hand, the characteristic turbulence time scale is  $\ell_t/u_t$ , where  $u_t$  is the turbulent velocity scale in large eddies. It will be assumed that the time scale of the wave is small compared with that of turbulence, i.e.,  $\ell_t/u_t \gg d/a_f$ , which is true in most rocket engines. The wave is then considered to propagate in a quasistationary random medium so that the time dependence of the turbulent fluctuations is decoupled from the acoustic field. Another important time scale is the chemistry time scale, denoted by  $\tau_c$ , which affects the flame-structure analysis. If the chemistry time scale is shorter than the acoustic time scale, then chemical equilibrium prevails everywhere, so that flame structures can be calculated by considering quasisteady mixing only. The rate of heat release, however, still fluctuates in response to the acoustic field since the rate

of mixing is modified by the acoustic field. As the chemistry time scale becomes equal to or longer than the characteristic turbulence time scale, the dependence of the finite chemical reaction rate on the acoustic fluctuations becomes important for calculating the mean and oscillatory rates of heat release. As an extreme case, flames may be extinguished due to excessively high strain rates exerted by turbulent fluctuation if  $t_c$  is much larger than the turbulent time scale. The amplification mechanisms for the acoustic field can be identified according to these limiting cases.

The amplification mechanisms in acoustic instability can be divided in two groups, boundary amplification and medium amplification. Boundary amplification is more common in solid-propellant rocket engines in which the propellant burns at its surface. In this case, acoustic instability can be analyzed in terms of the acoustic admittance of the burning propellant. Instead, attention is focused on medium amplification driven by combustion, vaporization, atomization, etc. Since the approach is analytic, additional simplifications are introduced. We consider the linear stability only. In later analyses, generalizations to nonlinear stability need to be addressed. With these assumptions, a stochastic wave equation arising from spatial inhomogeneity flow is derived from conservation equations in Sec. II. The stochastic wave equation is averaged by using the method of smooth perturbation in Sec. III. A dispersion relation is obtained to yield turbulence corrections to acoustic frequency and linear-growth rate of acoustic pressure. In Sec. IV, other effects of turbulence on acoustic instability are briefly discussed.

### II. Formulation

#### A. Conservation Equations

Prior to introducing the conservation equations, it is important to clarify the definitions. We let  $\rho_{ji}$  denote the mass of chemical species  $i$  in phase  $j$  per unit volume of phase  $j$  and  $\alpha_j$  the volume fraction of phase  $j$ . Generally  $j = g, f, o$  denotes gas, fuel, and oxidizer streams, respectively. With  $N$  chemical species in the system, the density of phase  $j$  is

$$\rho_j = \sum_{i=1}^N \rho_{ji}$$

and the total density is  $\rho = \sum_j \alpha_j \rho_j$ . From these definitions, we are able to define the mass fractions, namely,

$$Y_j = \frac{\alpha_j \rho_j}{\rho}, \quad Y_{ji} = \frac{\alpha_j \rho_{ji}}{\rho} \quad \text{with} \quad \sum_j Y_j = 1, \quad \sum_i Y_{ji} = Y_j \quad (1)$$

where  $Y_j$  is the mass fraction of phase  $j$  and  $Y_{ji}$ , that of species  $i$  in phase  $j$ . If  $\bar{u}_j$  is the mass-weighted average velocity of phase  $j$  and  $\rho \bar{u} \equiv \sum_j \alpha_j \rho_j \bar{u}_j$ , i.e.,  $\bar{u} = \sum_j Y_j \bar{u}_j$ , then we can define the peculiar velocity of phase  $j$  as

$$\vec{U}_j = \bar{u}_j - \bar{u} \quad \text{with} \quad \sum_j Y_j \vec{U}_j = 0 \quad (2)$$

Overall mass conservation is

$$\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot (\rho \bar{u}) = 0 \quad (3)$$

###### EFFECTS OF TURBULENCE ON LINEAR ACOUSTIC INSTABILITY 435

Mass conservation for phase  $j$  is

$$\frac{\partial \rho Y_j}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \{\rho Y_j (\vec{u} + \vec{U}_j)\} = -w_j \quad (4)$$

where  $w_j$  is the rate of mass loss per unit volume for phase  $j$ . In terms of the diffusion velocity  $\vec{U}_{ji}$  for species  $i$  in phase  $j$ , conservation of chemical species  $i$  in phase  $j$  is

$$\frac{\partial \rho Y_{ji}}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \{\rho Y_{ji} (\vec{u} + \vec{U}_j + \vec{U}_{ji})\} = \alpha_j w_{ji} + \sum_{j' \neq j} w_{j'} \beta_{jij'} \quad (5)$$

where  $w_{ji}$  is the mass rate of production of chemical species  $i$  in phase  $j$ , and  $\beta_{jij'}$  is the mass of species  $i$  added to phase  $j$  from phase  $j'$  per unit mass loss of phase  $j'$ . Vaporization and droplet combustion laws determine  $w_j$  and  $\beta_{jij'}$ , whereas diffusion equations determine  $\vec{U}_{ji}$  and chemical kinetics  $w_{ji}$ . Overall momentum conservation is

$$\frac{\partial \rho \vec{u}}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \left\{ \sum_j \rho Y_j (\vec{u} + \vec{U}_j) (\vec{u} + \vec{U}_j) \right\} + \nabla p = \nabla \cdot \left( \sum_j \alpha_j \vec{T}_j \right) \quad (6)$$

where  $\vec{T}_j$  is the viscous stress tensor in phase  $j$ .

Overall energy conservation written in terms of the total (thermal plus chemical) enthalpy per unit mass, denoted by  $h$ , is

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{Dh}{Dt} &= \frac{1}{\rho} \frac{Dp}{Dt} + \frac{1}{\rho} \left[ \vec{T} : \nabla \vec{u} + \nabla \cdot \left( \sum_j \alpha_j \vec{U}_j \cdot \vec{T}_j \right) - \nabla \cdot \left( \sum_j \alpha_j \vec{q}_j \right) \right] \\ &\quad - \frac{1}{2} \frac{DU^2}{Dt} - \frac{1}{\rho} \left[ \nabla \cdot \left( \sum_j \rho Y_j H_j \vec{U}_j \right) + \vec{u} \cdot \nabla \cdot \left( \sum_j \rho Y_j \vec{U}_j \vec{U}_j \right) \right] \end{aligned} \quad (7)$$

where  $h \equiv \sum_j Y_j h_j$ ,  $\vec{T} \equiv \sum_j \alpha_j \vec{T}_j$ ,  $\vec{q}_j$  is the heat flux vector for phase  $j$ , and the material derivative is defined as

$$\frac{D}{Dt} \equiv \frac{\partial}{\partial t} + \vec{u} \cdot \nabla$$

In addition, the stagnation enthalpy per unit mass for phase  $j$ , denoted by  $H_j$ , and the overall stagnation enthalpy per unit mass  $H$  are defined as

$$H_j \equiv h_j + u_j^2/2 \quad H = h + u^2/2 + U^2/2$$

respectively, in which  $u^2 \equiv \vec{u} \cdot \vec{u}$  and  $U^2 \equiv \sum_j Y_j \vec{U}_j \cdot \vec{U}_j$ .

Focus on the mechanical phenomena that occur in acoustic waves can be achieved by invoking two thermodynamic identities<sup>10</sup>

$$T \frac{Ds}{Dt} = \frac{Dh}{Dt} - \frac{1}{\rho} \frac{Dp}{Dt} - \sum_{j,i} \frac{\mu_{ji}}{W_i} \frac{DY_{ji}}{Dt} \quad (8)$$

and

$$\frac{Dp}{Dt} = \left( \frac{\partial p}{\partial \rho} \right)_{s, Y_{ji}} \frac{D\rho}{Dt} + \left( \frac{\partial p}{\partial s} \right)_{\rho, Y_{ji}} \frac{Ds}{Dt} + \sum_{j,i} \left( \frac{\partial p}{\partial Y_{ji}} \right)_{s, \rho, Y_{kl}(\neq ji)} \frac{DY_{ji}}{Dt} \quad (9)$$

where  $s$  is the entropy per unit mass,  $W_i$  the molecular weight of species  $i$ , and  $\mu_{ji}$  the chemical potential per unit mass of species  $i$  in phase  $j$ . Equation (7) may be used to eliminate  $Dh/Dt - \rho^{-1}Dp/Dt$  from Eq. (8), which may then be employed to remove  $Ds/Dt$  from Eq. (9), leaving many source terms, a number of which involve  $DY_{ji}/Dt$ , which is eliminated in favor of other source terms by use of Eq. (5). Employing Eq. (3) for  $D\rho/Dt$  in this reduced form of Eq. (9) then yields

$$\frac{1}{\rho a_f^2} \frac{Dp}{Dt} = -\nabla \cdot \vec{u} + \frac{\beta_f}{c_{p,f}} Q \quad (10)$$

where  $a_f$ ,  $\beta_f$ , and  $c_{p,f}$  are defined by

$$a_f^2 \equiv \left( \frac{\partial p}{\partial \rho} \right)_{s, Y_{ji}}, \quad \beta_f \equiv -\frac{1}{\rho} \left( \frac{\partial \rho}{\partial T} \right)_{p, Y_{ji}}, \quad c_{p,f} \equiv \left( \frac{\partial h}{\partial T} \right)_{p, Y_{ji}} \quad (11)$$

It is usually physically more relevant to use the overall adiabatic compressibility defined by

$$K_f \equiv \frac{1}{\rho} \left( \frac{\partial \rho}{\partial p} \right)_{s, Y_{ji}} = \frac{1}{\rho a_f^2} \quad (12)$$

instead of  $a_f^2$ . A simplified recipe to estimate the molecular properties in a mixture of the ideal gases and liquid spray is presented in the Appendix.

The composite term  $Q$  denotes the rate of heat exchange per unit mass and for convenience is taken to be separated into four terms,  $Q_v$ ,  $Q_t$ ,  $Q_c$ , and  $Q_e$ , which represent, respectively, various contributions from molecular transport, contributions from peculiar velocities, contributions from homogeneous chemical reaction, and contributions from phase change. They are expressed as

$$\begin{aligned} Q_v &= \frac{1}{\rho} \left[ \vec{T} : \nabla \vec{u} + \nabla \cdot \left( \sum_j \alpha_j \vec{U}_j \cdot \vec{T}_j \right) \right. \\ &\quad \left. - \nabla \cdot \sum_j \alpha_j \vec{q}_j + \sum_{j,i} h_{ji} \nabla \cdot (\rho Y_{ji} \vec{U}_{ji}) \right] \\ Q_t &= -\frac{1}{2} \frac{DU^2}{Dt} - \frac{1}{\rho} \left[ \nabla \cdot \left( \sum_j \rho Y_j H_j \vec{U}_j \right) + \vec{u} \cdot \nabla \cdot \left( \sum_j \rho Y_j \vec{U}_j \vec{U}_j \right) \right. \\ &\quad \left. - \sum_{j,i} h_{ji} \nabla \cdot (\rho Y_{ji} \vec{U}_j) \right] \\ Q_c &= -\sum_{j,i} h_{ji} \alpha_j \frac{w_{ji}}{\rho}, \quad Q_e = -\sum_{j,i} h_{ji} \sum_{j' \neq j} \frac{w_{ji'}}{\rho} \beta_{ji'} \end{aligned} \quad (13)$$

An applicable wave equation may be derived by linearization of Eqs. (6) and (10). For convenience, expressing Eq. (6) in a form similar to that of Eq. (10), conservation equations for the overall energy and momentum are

$$K_f \frac{Dp}{Dt} + \nabla \cdot \vec{u} = Q, \quad \rho \frac{D\vec{u}}{Dt} + \nabla p = \vec{F} \quad (14)$$

where

$$Q = \frac{\beta_f}{c_{p,f}} Q, \quad \vec{F} = \nabla \cdot \left\{ \sum_j \alpha_j (\vec{T}_j - \rho_j \vec{U}_j \vec{U}_j) \right\}$$

Here  $\vec{F}$  represents the momentum transfer resulting from the viscous stresses and from the peculiar velocities of the different phases. It also can be viewed as a kind of external force applied to the ideal multiphase fluid. Analyses at the microscopic level will provide the most useful avenues for modeling of the source terms  $Q$  and  $\vec{F}$ .

#### B. Scaling and Derivation of Wave Equation

It is important to recognize that variations of the mean field and of the acoustic field scale differently, since changes in the mean field are scaled by a characteristic flow velocity  $u_0$ , whereas the acoustic field is scaled by a characteristic sound speed  $a_0$ . The fact that the Mach number  $M = u_0/a_0$  is small provides a scaling that ultimately yields a much simplified wave equation.<sup>15,16</sup>

To nondimensionalize the variables, characteristic values for the length, density, and velocity need be selected. First, reference values for the density and adiabatic compressibility are obtained by volumetric and time averages to be

$$\rho_0 = \lim_{t' \rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{V t'} \int_0^{t'} \int_{\mathcal{V}} \rho \, d\vec{x} \, dt, \quad K_0 = \lim_{t' \rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{V t'} \int_0^{t'} \int_{\mathcal{V}} K_f \, d\vec{x} \, dt \quad (15)$$

where  $\mathcal{V}$  denotes the integration domain and  $V$  is the total volume of the integration domain  $\mathcal{V}$ . The mean chamber pressure is similarly defined as

$$p_0 = \lim_{t' \rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{V t'} \int_0^{t'} \int_{\mathcal{V}} p \, d\vec{x} \, dt \quad (16)$$

From  $\rho_0$  and  $K_0$ , the characteristic velocity scales for the mean and acoustic fields are found to be

$$u_0 = \dot{m}/\rho_0, \quad a_0 = 1/(K_0 \rho_0)^{1/2} \quad (17)$$

where  $\dot{m}$  is the area-averaged axial mass flux and is independent of the axial coordinate. Then the Mach number  $M$  is defined as

$$M \equiv u_0/a_0 = \dot{m}/\rho_0 a_0 = t_a/t_r \quad (18)$$

which is also the ratio of the characteristic acoustic time  $t_a = d/a_0$  to the characteristic flow time  $t_r = d/u_0$ , where the chamber diameter  $d$  is taken to be the characteristic geometric length.

The nondimensional spatial coordinates  $\vec{x}$  and temporal coordinate  $\tau$  are

$$\vec{x} \equiv \vec{x}/d, \quad \tau \equiv t a_0/d \quad (19)$$

The nondimensional dependent variables are

$$\wp \equiv \frac{p}{\rho_0 a_0^2}, \quad \mathbf{u} \equiv \frac{\vec{u}}{a_0}, \quad Q \equiv \frac{Q \beta_f d}{a_0 c_{p,f}}, \quad \mathbf{F} \equiv \frac{\vec{F} d}{\rho_0 a_0^2} \quad (20)$$

and the density and the adiabatic compressibility are scaled by

$$\varrho \equiv \rho / \rho_0, \quad \kappa \equiv \rho_0 a_0^2 K_f \quad (21)$$

Scalings for variations of the mean field variables are

$$\begin{aligned} \wp_s &\equiv \frac{p_s}{\rho_0 u_0^2} = M^{-2} \frac{p_s}{\rho_0 a_0^2}, & \mathbf{u}_s &\equiv \frac{\vec{u}_s}{u_0} = M^{-1} \frac{\vec{u}_s}{a_0} \\ Q_s &\equiv \frac{Q_s \beta_f d}{u_0 c_{p,f}} = M^{-1} \frac{Q_s \beta_f d}{a_0 c_{p,f}}, & \mathbf{F}_s &\equiv \frac{\vec{F}_s d}{\rho_0 u_0^2} = M^{-2} \frac{\vec{F}_s d}{\rho_0 a_0^2} \end{aligned} \quad (22)$$

where the subscript  $s$  denotes variations of the mean field. In addition, the mean chamber pressure is scaled by

$$\wp_0 \equiv \frac{p_0}{\rho_0 a_0^2} \quad (23)$$

We now decompose the nondimensionalized variables into sums of the mean and acoustic components. The acoustic field can be sought in order of  $\epsilon$  where the small parameter  $\epsilon$  measures a small amplitude of the acoustic pressure relative to the mean chamber pressure. Although  $\epsilon$  is, in general, a function of Mach number  $M$ , an arbitrary small number can be taken as  $\epsilon$  if only linear instability is considered. Then we seek a solution in the form

$$\begin{aligned} \wp &= \wp_0 + M^2 \wp_s + \epsilon \wp', & \mathbf{u} &= M \mathbf{u}_s + \epsilon \mathbf{u}', \\ Q &= M(Q_s + \epsilon Q'), & \mathbf{F} &= M^2(\mathbf{F}_s + \epsilon \mathbf{F}') \end{aligned} \quad (24)$$

where  $\wp'$  and  $\mathbf{u}'$  are acoustic fluctuations of the pressure and velocity, and  $Q'$  and  $\mathbf{F}'$  are the acoustic responses of  $Q$  and  $\mathbf{F}$ , respectively. Here the orders of magnitude for the acoustic responses are assumed to be the same as the orders of magnitude for the corresponding mean field variations. All of the quantities in the right-hand side of Eq. (24) except the small parameters  $M$  and  $\epsilon$  are of order unity.

Since  $\wp'$  and  $\mathbf{u}'$  are the dependent variables, the acoustic responses  $Q'$  and  $\mathbf{F}'$  have to be expanded as linear functions of  $\wp'$  and  $\mathbf{u}'$  such that

$$Q' = \varrho R_p \wp' + \varrho \mathbf{R}_v \cdot \mathbf{u}', \quad \mathbf{F}' = \mathbf{B}_p \wp' + \vec{\mathbf{B}}_v \cdot \mathbf{u}' \quad (25)$$

where  $R_p$ ,  $\mathbf{R}_v$ ,  $\mathbf{B}_p$ , and  $\vec{\mathbf{B}}_v$  are defined as

$$\begin{aligned} R_p &= \frac{1}{\varrho M} \frac{\partial Q}{\partial \wp} = \frac{\rho_0 a_0^2 d}{u_0} \frac{1}{\rho} \frac{\partial Q}{\partial p}, & \mathbf{R}_v &= \frac{1}{\varrho M} \frac{\partial Q}{\partial \mathbf{u}} = \frac{\rho_0 a_0 d}{u_0} \frac{1}{\rho} \frac{\partial Q}{\partial \vec{u}} \\ \mathbf{B}_p &= \frac{1}{M^2} \frac{\partial \mathbf{F}}{\partial \wp} = \frac{a_0^2 d}{u_0^2} \frac{\partial \vec{F}}{\partial p}, & \vec{\mathbf{B}}_v &= \frac{1}{M^2} \frac{\partial \mathbf{F}}{\partial \mathbf{u}} = \frac{a_0 d}{\rho_0 u_0^2} \frac{\partial \vec{F}}{\partial \vec{u}} \end{aligned} \quad (26)$$

###### EFFECTS OF TURBULENCE ON LINEAR ACOUSTIC INSTABILITY 439

Here  $R_p$ ,  $\mathbf{R}_v$ ,  $\mathbf{B}_p$ , and  $\vec{\mathbf{B}}_v$  are, in general, complex functions of  $\wp'$  or  $\mathbf{u}'$ , and subjects of analyses in the microscopic level.

Substituting Eqs. (15–25) into Eq. (14), and collecting the terms of  $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon)$  and  $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon M)$  only, conservation equations for the acoustic pressure and velocity are found to be

$$\begin{aligned} \kappa \frac{\partial \wp'}{\partial \tau} + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}' &= -M(\kappa \mathbf{u}_s \cdot \nabla \wp' - \varrho \mathbf{R}_p \wp' - \varrho \mathbf{R}_v \cdot \mathbf{u}') \\ \varrho \frac{\partial \mathbf{u}'}{\partial \tau} + \nabla \wp' &= -M(\varrho \mathbf{u}_s \cdot \nabla \mathbf{u}' + \varrho \mathbf{u}' \cdot \nabla \mathbf{u}_s) \end{aligned} \quad (27)$$

If the density and adiabatic compressibility are constant, and the terms on the right-hand side are not present, then Eqs. (27) reduce to a Helmholtz equation upon eliminating  $\mathbf{u}'$  from the equations. It is important to note that the nonhomogeneous terms are responsible for amplification (or attenuation) and refraction of the acoustic pressure and that they are only of order of  $M$ . Therefore, growth or decay of the acoustic pressure amplitude can occur only in the characteristic residence time  $t_r$  that is longer than the characteristic acoustic time  $t_a$  by an order of  $M^{-1}$  (Ref. 16). Such multiple time-scale behavior is found in evolutions of the sustaining acoustic oscillations in rocket engines. From time to time, it has been questioned whether the order of magnitude for the acoustic velocity response  $\mathbf{R}_v$  is  $M^{-1}$ . This question stems from the observation that relative amplitude of the acoustic velocity to its mean velocity is larger than that of the acoustic pressure by an order of  $M^{-1}$ , so that the acoustic response can be much larger than assumed in the present analysis. If such ordering for the  $\mathbf{R}_v$  term exists, then the acoustic oscillations will grow or be damped in less than a few cycles, so that no sustaining acoustic oscillations can be observed. Since our interest is restricted to the sustaining acoustic oscillations in liquid-propellant rocket engines,  $\mathbf{R}_v$  must be of order unity.

To investigate acoustic waves, it is more convenient to introduce complex representations of the acoustics variables, in terms of the complex wave number  $k$ , as

$$\wp' = \psi \exp(-ikt), \quad \mathbf{u}' = \mathbf{v} \exp(-ikt) \quad (28)$$

where the wave number  $k$  is an eigenvalue of the problem. If the imaginary part of  $k$  is positive, then the acoustic oscillation grows, thereby leading to the instability. The wave number is related to the dimensional frequency  $\omega$  by

$$\omega = \frac{k}{d} \sqrt{\frac{1}{K_0 \rho_0}} \quad (29)$$

From the second of Eqs. (27),  $\mathbf{v}$  is found in terms of  $\psi$  as

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{v} &= \frac{1}{i\varrho k} [\nabla \psi + M(\varrho \mathbf{u}_s \cdot \nabla \mathbf{v} + \varrho \mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla \mathbf{u}_s)] \\ &= \frac{\nabla \psi}{i\varrho k} - \frac{M}{k^2} \left[ (\mathbf{u}_s \cdot \nabla) \left( \frac{\nabla \psi}{\varrho} \right) + \left( \frac{\nabla \psi}{\varrho} \right) \cdot \nabla \mathbf{u}_s \right] + \mathcal{O}(M^2) \end{aligned} \quad (30)$$

Substituting Eq. (30) into the first of Eqs. (27), a single scalar wave equation is obtained as

$$\begin{aligned} \nabla \cdot \left( \frac{\nabla \psi}{\varrho} \right) + \kappa k^2 \psi \\ = \frac{iM}{k} \left\{ -k^2 \kappa \mathbf{u}_s \cdot \nabla \psi + \nabla \cdot \left[ (\mathbf{u}_s \cdot \nabla) \left( \frac{\nabla \psi}{\varrho} \right) + \left( \frac{\nabla \psi}{\varrho} \right) \cdot \nabla \mathbf{u}_s \right] \right\} \\ + M \left[ ik\varrho R_p \psi + \varrho \mathbf{R}_v \cdot \left( \frac{\nabla \psi}{\varrho} \right) \right] \end{aligned} \quad (31)$$

Here the term involving the acoustic pressure response  $R_p$  is usually the main amplification effect, whereas the terms involving the mean field velocity  $\mathbf{u}_s$  on the right-hand side of Eq. (31) are responsible for the possible damping effect arising from the convection in the longitudinal direction. It appears from Eq. (31) that all of the perturbations in the right-hand side vanish as the Mach number  $M$  approaches zero. However, the acoustic source terms that do not involve  $\mathbf{u}_s$  explicitly may be rescaled in an alternative way at zero  $M$ , since the mean axial convective transport is no longer the dominant transport mechanism for the acoustic source terms. If the turbulent mixing becomes more important than the mean axial convective transport, a new scaling can be introduced by a new Mach number based on the characteristic turbulent velocity, and the resulting equation will be identical to Eq. (31).

Wave equation (31) is applicable even for more realistic nonuniform acoustic media. We limit our interest, however, to the case in which the acoustic medium is uniform in the leading order, the assumption that is commonly adopted in most of the acoustic instability analyses. This simplification may give rise to significant error in evaluating the eigenfunctions and eigenvalues, but such error estimates have not yet been made, although it might be simple to do so. Since our main interest is to analyze the effects of the turbulence, the nonuniformity of the acoustic medium is assumed to be only of order of  $\varepsilon$  for the purpose of circumventing the lack of knowledge about acoustics in nonuniform deterministic media. Here the new small parameter  $\varepsilon$  measures the intensity of the turbulent fluctuations. Also the wave equation is subject to the simplest boundary condition, namely, the Neumann condition,

$$\mathbf{n} \cdot \nabla \psi = 0, \quad \text{for } \mathbf{x} \in B \quad (32)$$

where  $\mathbf{n}$  is the unit normal vector at the boundary.

#### C. Introduction of Turbulent Fluctuations

This analysis is based on the limit in which  $u_t/a_0 \ll \ell_t/d$ , so that the characteristic acoustic time is shorter than the characteristic turbulence time. The acoustic medium is then considered to be quasi-stationary, and the time dependence of the turbulent fluctuations is decoupled from the acoustic field. Only the spatial inhomogeneity of the mean field needs be considered. In liquid-propellant rocket engines, the spatial inhomogeneity arises from a variety of sources, such as turbulent combustion, or fluctuations of phase or velocity fields. Although the spatial fluctuations associated with these effects have the same characteristic time and length scales, their orders of magnitude are different. Since the order of magnitude

###### EFFECTS OF TURBULENCE ON LINEAR ACOUSTIC INSTABILITY 441

for the temperature fluctuations associated with turbulent combustion far exceeds those associated with the phase and flow turbulence, only the spatial inhomogeneity arising from turbulent combustion needs to be considered in order to obtain the first approximation to influences of the turbulence.

Not all of the mean-field variables are directly coupled with turbulent combustion. For instance, if the medium is assumed to be a mixture of the ideal gases and spray,  $\kappa$  is proportional to the volume fraction of the gas phase, since only the gas phase is compressible. The volume fraction of the liquid phase is usually small, so that inhomogeneity of  $\kappa$  can be ignored. The density  $\varrho$  and the acoustic responses,  $R_p$  and  $\mathbf{R}_v$ , however, are directly influenced by turbulent combustion, and their fluctuations must be included. On the other hand, the velocity field is predominantly longitudinal with a constant mass flux. Since the longitudinal velocity is inversely proportional to the density, fluctuations of the longitudinal velocity also needs to be included.

Prior to introducing the expansions for the fluctuation fields, it is convenient to introduce a coordinate transformation that will significantly simplify the algebra involving the variable density. This can be achieved by introducing new nondimensional coordinates that are weighted by the nondimensional density. The new coordinates  $\xi$  are then defined by

$$\xi_i = \int_0^{x_i} \rho dx'_i, \quad i = 1, 2, 3 \quad (33)$$

where the origin of the coordinate is placed at the center of the injector assembly. The wave equation in the new coordinate system is

$$\begin{aligned} \nabla^2 \psi + \frac{\kappa}{\varrho} k^2 \psi = \frac{iM}{k} \{ -k^2 \kappa \mathbf{u}_s \cdot \nabla \psi + \nabla \cdot [(\varrho \mathbf{u}_s \cdot \nabla) \nabla \psi + \varrho \nabla \psi \cdot \nabla \mathbf{u}_s] \} \\ + M[i\kappa R_p \psi + \mathbf{R}_v \cdot \nabla \psi] \end{aligned} \quad (34)$$

where  $\nabla$  now denotes the gradient operator in the  $\xi$  coordinate.

Letting  $\varepsilon$  be the intensity of the temperature-field fluctuations, we now expand the mean-field variables into sums of their mean and fluctuating values,

$$\begin{aligned} \varrho = 1 + \varepsilon \varrho_1, \quad \kappa = 1 + o(\varepsilon), \quad R_p = R_{p0} + \varepsilon R_{p1} \\ \mathbf{R}_v = \mathbf{R}_{v0} + \varepsilon \mathbf{R}_{v1}, \quad \varrho \mathbf{u}_s = \mathbf{e}_\zeta, \quad \mathbf{u}_s = \mathbf{e}_\zeta (1 - \varepsilon \varrho_1) \end{aligned} \quad (35)$$

where  $\zeta$  is the longitudinal coordinate in the  $\xi$ -coordinate system and  $\mathbf{e}_\zeta$  denotes the unit longitudinal vector. Substituting the expansions (35) into Eq. (34), we then obtain

$$\begin{aligned} \nabla^2 \psi + k^2 \psi = M \left[ i\kappa R_{p0} \psi + \mathbf{R}_{v0} \cdot \nabla \psi - 2i\kappa \frac{d\psi}{d\zeta} \right] + \varepsilon \varrho_1 k^2 \psi \\ + \varepsilon M \left[ i\kappa R_{p1} \psi + \mathbf{R}_{v1} \cdot \nabla \psi + 2i\kappa \varrho_1 \frac{d\psi}{d\zeta} - i \frac{d}{d\zeta} (\nabla \varrho_1 \cdot \nabla \psi) \right] \end{aligned} \quad (36)$$

where the first line corresponds to the mean-field part of the wave equation, whereas the second line is the fluctuating part. Since  $\xi_i \rightarrow x_i + o(\varepsilon)$  for  $x_i \gg \varepsilon$  with the density profile given in Eq. (35), the boundary condition remains the same as Eq. (32) even in order of  $\varepsilon$ .

### III. Mean Wave Field

#### A. General Consideration for Stochastic Averaging

Since the wave equation in Eq. (36) is a random field, the resulting wave is also a random field. Then the terms in the second line of Eq. (36) involve multiplicative randomness, which is not necessarily vanishing by averaging. Therefore, the resulting mean wave field is different from the wave field without randomness. An averaging technique is discussed to obtain the mean wave field.<sup>14</sup>

Let us consider a simple linear stochastic wave equation given by

$$L_r(r)u(r) + X(r, \mu)u(r, \mu) = 0 \quad (37)$$

where  $L_r$  is a given deterministic differential operator in the  $r$  coordinate,  $X(r, \mu)$  is a given random-field operator arising from a random process  $\mu$ , and  $u(r)$  is the resulting random wave field. Averaging Eq. (37) yields

$$L_r\langle u \rangle + \langle Xu \rangle = 0 \quad (38)$$

where the average operator  $\langle \cdot \rangle$  can be understood in an ensemble-average sense. The equation includes not only  $\langle u \rangle$ , but also the second moment  $\langle Xu \rangle$ . To find the equation for  $\langle Xu \rangle$ , one may multiply Eq. (37) by  $X(r_1, \mu)$  and take averages, giving

$$L_r\langle X(r_1, \mu)u \rangle + \langle X(r_1, \mu)X(r, \mu)u \rangle = 0 \quad (39)$$

which now contains the third-order moment. To describe the subsequently occurring higher order moments, an infinite set of hierarchy equations is necessary. Clearly, it is not possible to obtain a finite and closed system of equations just as has been encountered in the averaged Navier–Stokes equations. One is then forced to introduce closure procedures by postulating that the higher order moments can be expressed in terms of the lower order moments.

One of the closure schemes is the correlation-discard approximation, namely,

$$\langle X(r_1, \mu)X(r, \mu)u \rangle = \langle X(r_1, \mu)X(r, \mu) \rangle \langle u \rangle \quad (40)$$

This hypothesis is equivalent to

$$\langle X(r_1, \mu)X(r, \mu)\Delta u \rangle = 0 \quad \text{with} \quad \Delta u = u - \langle u \rangle$$

which means that the product of the field fluctuation with a random coefficient is independent of the random coefficient at a different location. This approximation is also known as the local-independence hypothesis. Substitution of Eq. (40) into Eq. (39) gives

$$\langle X(r_1, \mu)u \rangle = -L_r^{-1}\langle X(r_1, \mu)X(r, \mu) \rangle \langle u \rangle = -\langle X(r_1, \mu)L_r^{-1}X(r, \mu) \rangle \langle u \rangle \quad (41)$$

where  $L_r^{-1}$  denotes the inverse of the operator  $L_r$ . Substituting Eq. (41) into Eq. (38), the resulting equation becomes

$$[L_r - \langle X(r_1, \mu)L_r^{-1}X(r, \mu) \rangle] \langle u \rangle = 0 \quad (42)$$

which describes the mean wave field.

###### EFFECTS OF TURBULENCE ON LINEAR ACOUSTIC INSTABILITY 443

If the stochastic operator  $X$  is of order of  $\varepsilon$  as found in the present analysis, a more systematic closure scheme, called smooth perturbation,<sup>12-14</sup> can be adopted. There exists a solution  $u_r$  obeying

$$L_r u_r = 0 \quad (43)$$

Then, a solution of a linear stochastic wave equation  $L_r u + \varepsilon X u = 0$  can be iterated, in a form of a perturbation about  $u_r$ ,

$$u = u_r - \varepsilon L_r^{-1} X u_r + \varepsilon^2 L_r^{-1} X L_r^{-1} X u_r + \dots \quad (44)$$

Taking the average and solving for  $u_r$ , we find

$$\begin{aligned} u_r &= \{1 + \varepsilon^2 L_r^{-1} \langle X L_r^{-1} X \rangle\}^{-1} \langle u \rangle + \dots \\ &= \langle u \rangle - \varepsilon^2 L_r^{-1} \langle X L_r^{-1} X \rangle \langle u \rangle + \dots \end{aligned} \quad (45)$$

Application of  $L_r$  to the both sides of Eq. (45) yields an equation for  $\langle u \rangle$  as

$$\{L_r - \varepsilon^2 \langle X L_r^{-1} X \rangle\} \langle u \rangle = 0 \quad (46)$$

which is identical to Eq. (42) considering that  $X$  in Eq. (42) is now scaled by a small parameter  $\varepsilon$ .

In the present analysis, the operators  $L_r$  and  $X$  are the composite terms of order unity and of order of  $M$ . When a solution is sought in the neighborhood of an eigensolution of the Helmholtz equation, the operators can be decomposed as

$$L_r = L_0 + M L_1, \quad X = X_0 + M X_1 \quad (47)$$

where the Helmholtz operator  $L_0$  is

$$L_0 \equiv \nabla^2 + k_n^2 \quad (48)$$

whereas the other higher order operators are

$$\begin{aligned} L_1 &= \frac{(k^2 - k_n^2)}{M} - i k_n R_{p0} - \mathbf{R}_{v0} \cdot \nabla + 2 i k_n \frac{d}{d\zeta} \\ X_0 &= -\varrho_1 k_n^2 \\ X_1 &= -i k_n R_{p1} - \mathbf{R}_{v1} \cdot \nabla - 2 i k_n \varrho_1 \frac{d}{d\zeta} + i \frac{d}{d\zeta} (\nabla \varrho_1 \cdot \nabla) \end{aligned} \quad (49)$$

Here the subscript  $n$  denotes the  $n$ th eigenmode ordered from the smallest wave number. The difference of the eigenvalue  $k$  from  $k_n$  is of order of  $M$ , so that the term  $(k^2 - k_n^2)/M$  is of order unity. Substituting Eq. (47) into Eq. (46), we obtain a new symbolic equation for the mean wave field as

$$\begin{aligned} &\{L_0 + M L_1 - \varepsilon^2 \langle X_0 L_0^{-1} X_0 \rangle \\ &- \varepsilon^2 M [\langle X_1 L_0^{-1} X_0 \rangle + \langle X_0 L_0^{-1} X_1 \rangle - \langle X_0 L_0^{-1} L_1 L_0^{-1} X_0 \rangle]\} \langle u \rangle = 0 \end{aligned} \quad (50)$$

To obtain the mean wave equation, it is necessary to evaluate the terms involving the inverse Helmholtz operator  $L_0^{-1}$ . The inverse operator  $L_0^{-1}$  may be represented by an integral operator of Green's function defined by

$$L_0 G(\xi, \xi') \equiv \delta(\xi - \xi') \quad (51)$$

where  $\delta(\xi)$  is the Dirac delta function. Green's function for the Helmholtz equation in cylindrical coordinates<sup>17,18</sup> is given by

$$G(\xi, \xi') = \sum_{i \neq n} \frac{\varphi_i(\xi) \varphi_i(\xi')}{k_n^2 - k_i^2} \quad (52)$$

where  $\varphi_i$  are the orthonormal eigenfunctions for  $(\nabla^2 + k_i^2)\varphi_i = 0$ . As seen from the summation, which excludes the eigenmode  $\varphi_n$ , a role of Green's function is to resolve the particular solution whose functional form can be decomposed into a sum of the eigenmodes that differ from the homogeneous solution  $\varphi_n$ . In terms of Green's function,  $L_0^{-1}$  becomes

$$L_0^{-1} f(\xi) \equiv \int_V G(\xi, \xi') f(\xi') d\xi'$$

Then a representative term in Eq. (50) involving  $L_0^{-1}$  becomes

$$\langle X_0 L_0^{-1} X_0 \rangle \langle u(\xi) \rangle = \left\langle X_0(\xi) \int_V G(\xi, \xi') X_0(\xi') \langle u(\xi') \rangle d\xi' \right\rangle \quad (53)$$

The other functional operations involving  $L_0^{-1}$  can be evaluated in the same manner.

#### B. Mean Wave Equation

First, we evaluate the second-order moments of the random operators. Considering  $\langle X_0 L_0^{-1} X_0 \rangle$ , it is found to be

$$\begin{aligned} \langle X_0 L_0^{-1} X_0 \rangle \langle \psi(\xi) \rangle &= k_n^4 \left\langle \varrho_1(\xi) \int_V G(\xi, \xi') \varrho_1(\xi') \langle \psi(\xi') \rangle d\xi' \right\rangle \\ &= k_n^4 \int_V \langle \varrho_1(\xi) \varrho_1(\xi') \rangle G(\xi, \xi') \langle \psi(\xi') \rangle d\xi' \end{aligned} \quad (54)$$

which brings in two-point correlation of two scalar fluctuations by using commutativities of the  $X_0(\xi)$  and average operators with the integral in the  $\xi'$  coordinates. Since the turbulent length scale  $\ell_t$  is much shorter than the typical wave length, i.e.,  $k_n \ell_t \ll d$ , the correlation  $\langle \varrho_1(\xi) \varrho_1(\xi') \rangle$  behaves like a delta function. Green's function  $G(\xi, \xi')$  and the mean wave  $\langle \psi(\xi') \rangle$  can then be approximated by their values at  $\xi' = \xi$ . We find  $\langle X_0 L_0^{-1} X_0 \rangle$  as

$$\langle X_0 L_0^{-1} X_0 \rangle \langle \psi(\xi) \rangle = k_n^4 G_n(\xi) \langle \psi(\xi) \rangle \int_V \langle \varrho_1(\xi) \varrho_1(\xi') \rangle d\xi' \quad (55)$$

###### EFFECTS OF TURBULENCE ON LINEAR ACOUSTIC INSTABILITY 445

where the modified Green's function  $G_n(\xi)$  is

$$G_n(\xi) = G(\xi, \xi) = \sum_{i \neq n} \frac{\varphi_i^2(\xi)}{k_n^2 - k_i^2} \quad (56)$$

To complete the averaging procedure, the two-point correlation is introduced as a function of the distance vector  $\mathbf{r} = \xi' - \xi$ ,

$$\langle \varrho_1(\xi) \varrho_1(\xi') \rangle = \langle \varrho_1^2 \rangle C(\mathbf{r}) \quad (57)$$

where  $\langle \varrho_1^2 \rangle$  is the correlation value at  $\mathbf{r} = 0$  and measures the intensity of the fluctuations. The functional form of the correlation function for two arbitrary scalar fluctuations may be approximated as

$$C(\mathbf{r}) = \exp(-r_a^2/\ell_a^2 - r_b^2/\ell_b^2) \quad (58)$$

where  $r_a$  and  $r_b$  denote the nondimensional longitudinal and transverse distance between two points, respectively, and where  $\ell_a$  and  $\ell_b$  are their corresponding nondimensional correlation distances normalized by the chamber diameter  $d$ . If the turbulence is isotropic, then the correlation distances  $\ell_a$  and  $\ell_b$  are the same and can be denoted by  $\ell_c$ . Also, if the turbulence is homogeneous, the intensity  $\langle \varrho_1^2 \rangle$  is not a function of  $\xi$ . Since these approximations affect the algebraic results by only a small degree, the turbulence is assumed to be homogeneous and isotropic in order to simplify the algebra. Then the two-point correlation for the density fluctuations where  $r = |\xi - \xi'|$  is expressed by

$$\langle \varrho_1(\xi) \varrho_1(\xi') \rangle = \langle \varrho_1^2 \rangle \exp(-r^2/\ell_c^2) \quad (59)$$

The volumetric integration of the correlation is found to be

$$\begin{aligned} \int_V \langle \varrho_1(\xi) \varrho_1(\xi') \rangle d\xi' &= \langle \varrho_1^2 \rangle \int_0^\infty \exp(-r^2/\ell_c^2) 4\pi r^2 dr \\ &= \langle \varrho_1^2 \rangle \sqrt{2\pi^3} \ell_c^3 \end{aligned} \quad (60)$$

The final expression for  $\langle X_0 L_0^{-1} X_0 \rangle$  then becomes

$$\langle X_0 L_0^{-1} X_0 \rangle \langle \psi(\xi) \rangle = \sqrt{2\pi^3} \ell_c^3 k_n^4 \langle \varrho_1^2 \rangle G_n(\xi) \langle \psi(\xi) \rangle \quad (61)$$

A similar procedure can be applied to yield

$$\langle X_0 L_0^{-1} X_1 \rangle \langle \psi(\xi) \rangle = i\sqrt{2\pi^3} \ell_c^3 k_n^3 G_n(\xi) \left[ \langle \varrho_1 R_{p1} \rangle + 2 \langle \varrho_1^2 \rangle \frac{d}{d\xi} \right] \langle \psi(\xi) \rangle \quad (62)$$

$$\langle X_0 L_0^{-1} X_1 \rangle \langle \psi(\xi) \rangle = i\sqrt{2\pi^3} \ell_c^3 k_n^3 \langle \psi(\xi) \rangle \left[ \langle \varrho_1 R_{p1} \rangle + 2 \langle \varrho_1^2 \rangle \frac{d}{d\xi} \right] G_n(\xi)$$

where the correlation function  $C(\mathbf{r})$  is identical for each of the two-point scalar correlations because the fluctuations arise from a single random process, i.e., the turbulent flame. The second-order moments associated with the random vector fields  $\mathbf{R}_{v1}$  and  $(d/d\xi) \nabla \varrho_1$  vanish, because their correlations with  $\varrho_1$  are first-order

tensors that are in general odd functions with zero volumetric integrals. Finally, the last second-order moment  $\langle X_0 L_0^{-1} L_1 L_0^{-1} X_0 \rangle$  is not important in linear analyses because the contributions that can be decomposed by  $\varphi_n$  are filtered out after a successive application of Green's function. This term thus cannot affect the mean wave  $\langle \psi \rangle$  that is extremely close to the eigenmode  $\varphi_n$ , although it may be important in nonlinear analyses.

By collecting the terms in Eqs. (61) and (62), the equation for the mean stochastic wave field is found to be

$$\begin{aligned} [\nabla^2 + k^2] \langle \psi(\xi) \rangle &= iM \left[ k_n R_{p0} - i\mathbf{R}_{v0} \cdot \nabla - 2k_n \frac{d}{d\xi} \right] \langle \psi(\xi) \rangle \\ &+ \varepsilon^2 \sqrt{2\pi^3} \ell_c^3 k_n^4 \langle \varrho_1^2 \rangle G_n(\xi) \langle \psi(\xi) \rangle \\ &+ i\varepsilon^2 M \sqrt{8\pi^3} \ell_c^3 k_n^3 \left[ \langle \varrho_1 R_{p1} \rangle + \langle \varrho_1^2 \rangle \frac{d}{d\xi} \right] \{ G_n(\xi) \langle \psi(\xi) \rangle \} \end{aligned} \quad (63)$$

Here the term of order of  $\varepsilon^2$  describes the effective variation of the acoustic frequency arising from the random density profile, whereas the terms of order of  $\varepsilon^2 M$  give the correction for the growth rate. Since the mean linear-growth rate is of order of  $M$ , the turbulent corrections to the acoustic frequency and linear-growth rate are both of order of  $\varepsilon^2$ . Taking the average of Eq. (32) gives the appropriate boundary condition as

$$\mathbf{n} \cdot \nabla \langle \psi \rangle = 0 \quad \text{for} \quad \xi \in B \quad (64)$$

#### C. Dispersion Relation for a Cylindrical Chamber

To calculate the wave number  $k$ , we consider a mean wave that is extremely close to an eigenmode  $\varphi_n$ . Now multiply Eq. (63) by  $\varphi_n$  and the Helmholtz equation  $(\nabla^2 + k_n^2)\varphi_n = 0$  by  $\langle \psi \rangle$ , subtract the results, and integrate over the chamber to obtain

$$\begin{aligned} &\int_V \{ \varphi_n \nabla^2 \langle \psi \rangle - \langle \psi \rangle \nabla^2 \varphi_n \} d\xi + (k^2 - k_n^2) \int_V \langle \psi \rangle \varphi_n d\xi \\ &= iM \int_V \left[ k_n R_{p0} - i\mathbf{R}_{v0} \cdot \nabla - 2k_n \frac{d}{d\xi} \right] \langle \psi(\xi) \rangle \varphi_n d\xi \\ &+ \varepsilon^2 \sqrt{2\pi^3} \ell_c^3 k_n^4 \int_V \langle \varrho_1^2 \rangle G_n(\xi) \langle \psi(\xi) \rangle \varphi_n d\xi \\ &+ i2\varepsilon^2 M \sqrt{8\pi^3} \ell_c^3 k_n^3 \int_V \left[ \langle \varrho_1 R_{p1} \rangle + \langle \varrho_1^2 \rangle \frac{d}{d\xi} \right] \{ G_n(\xi) \langle \psi(\xi) \rangle \} \varphi_n d\xi \end{aligned} \quad (65)$$

Green's integral theorem shows that the first integral of Eq. (65) vanishes. Integrating the leftover terms in Eq. (65), the dispersion relation is obtained, namely,

$$\begin{aligned} k &= k_n \left\{ 1 + \frac{1}{2} \varepsilon^2 \ell_c^3 \Xi \langle \varrho_1^2 \rangle \right\} + \frac{M}{2k_n} \int_V (\mathbf{R}_{v0} \cdot \nabla \varphi_n) \varphi_n d\xi \\ &+ iM \left\{ \frac{1}{2} \int_V R_{p0} \varphi_n^2 d\xi + \varepsilon^2 \ell_c^3 \Xi \langle \varrho_1 R_{p1} \rangle \right\} \end{aligned} \quad (66)$$

###### EFFECTS OF TURBULENCE ON LINEAR ACOUSTIC INSTABILITY 447

where the factor  $\Xi$ , of order unity, is

$$\Xi = \sqrt{2\pi^3} k_n^2 \int_V G_n(\xi) \varphi_n^2(\xi) d\xi \quad (67)$$

The first term on the right-hand side of Eq. (66) is the main contribution to the real part of the wave number  $k$  which corresponds directly to the acoustic frequency by Eq. (29). The last term carrying  $iM$  is usually the main amplification effect, whereas the second term comes from the acoustic velocity response. Since  $R_{n0}$  is a complex vector function, it is not clear whether its dominant consequence will be amplification or refraction.

Whether turbulence will increase or decrease the linear-growth rate and acoustic frequency depends on the signs of  $\langle \varrho_1^2 \rangle$ ,  $\langle \varrho_1 R_{p1} \rangle$  and  $G_n(\xi)$ . Whereas  $\langle \varrho_1^2 \rangle$  is positive definite,  $\langle \varrho_1 R_{p1} \rangle$  tends to be negative. The acoustic pressure response occurs mainly in relatively thin reactive layers, and its real part is generally positive because reaction rates increase with pressure. Since the density is lower in the reaction zone, the correlation  $\langle \varrho_1 R_{p1} \rangle$  is likely to have a negative real part. The sign of the factor  $\Xi$  will be negative for a few lowest eigenmodes. Putting these results into Eq. (66), it can be seen that turbulence tends to increase the amplification rate and decrease the acoustic frequency for lower eigenmodes, and otherwise for higher eigenmodes.

The turbulent corrections to the acoustic frequency and amplification rate are both of order of  $\varepsilon^2 \ell_c^3$ . Although the corrections have a fifth-order dependence on the small parameters  $\varepsilon$  and  $\ell_c$ , their actual values can be much larger. First, a typical value for  $\varepsilon$  is about one-half, since temperature fluctuations in the turbulent flame are sometimes as large as the mean temperature. If the average distance between the injectors is taken as the characteristic turbulent length, a typical value of  $\ell_c$  is of order  $10^{-1}$ . On the other hand, the actual value of  $\Xi$  is about  $10^2$ , because  $k_n^2$  is usually larger than 10, and an additional factor 10 comes from  $\sqrt{2\pi^3}$ . Combining all of these numbers, a realistic turbulence correction can be a few percent of the mean value. Moreover, the turbulence correction increases with the cubic power of  $\ell_c$ , so that it can be much more important in flows with larger turbulent length scales. It is also worthy of note that the dispersion relation in Eq. (66) is still valid even if  $\varepsilon$  is a value of order of unity, because the mean equation obtained from the local-independence hypothesis is identical to that obtained from the smooth perturbation.

A few percent correction of the acoustic frequency may not be considered of great importance; however, such a correction to the linear-growth rate is found to be significant in some circumstances. Acoustic instabilities in rocket engines can be seen in general as a Hopf bifurcation, which occurs when the imaginary part of the wave number begins to be positive. For systems that are far from the onset condition of Hopf bifurcation, effects of the turbulence will be qualitatively insignificant. Near the critical condition of Hopf bifurcation in which the mean linear-growth rate is of the same order as the turbulent correction or smaller, however, the turbulence correction can have a dominant amplification contribution. It is the stochastic acoustic pressure evolution regime in which Clavin et al.<sup>16</sup> found that, combined with a subcritical Hopf bifurcation, evolution of the acoustic pressure is qualitatively different from what has been obtained from deterministic analyses.

### IV. Other Effects of Turbulence on Acoustic Instabilities

Turbulence effects on acoustic instabilities in rocket engines manifest themselves in a variety of ways, such as the spatial and temporal randomnesses, and engine variation of test results. Up to now, this chapter has been devoted to describing the averaging technique that is capable of treating spatial randomness. Other consequences of turbulence on acoustic instabilities are briefly discussed in order to help the readers understand the current status of development concerning acoustic instabilities in turbulent flows.

In general, turbulent flows in rocket engines are statistically stationary but only on time scales much longer than the characteristic turbulence time. The linear-growth rate is expected to fluctuate about its mean value with a typical fluctuation time corresponding to the characteristic turbulence time. The spatial averaging presented here is still valid when the characteristic turbulence time is longer than the characteristic acoustic time. Considering an acoustic mode  $\varphi_n$ , the time-dependent mean wave can now be expressed as

$$\langle \psi \rangle = A_n(\tau') \varphi_n(\xi) \exp(-ik_n \tau) \quad (68)$$

where  $A_n$  is the acoustic pressure amplitude and the new temporal coordinate  $\tau'$  is defined by

$$\tau' = M \tau \quad (69)$$

where  $\tau'$  is normalized by the characteristic instability growth time that is equivalent to the characteristic flow time. Nonlinear evolution of the acoustic pressure amplitude is described by a Landau–Stewart equation, namely,

$$\frac{dA_n}{d\tau'} = (\lambda + \eta) A_n \pm A_n^3 + \text{higher order terms} \quad (70)$$

where the deterministic and stochastic linear-growth rates in the  $\tau'$  coordinate, i.e.,  $\lambda$  and  $\eta$ , can be, respectively, given by

$$\lambda = \frac{1}{2} \text{Im} \left\{ \int_V (\mathbf{R}_{v0} \cdot \nabla \varphi_n + i R_{p0} \varphi_n) \varphi_n d\xi \right\}, \quad \eta = \text{Im} \{ i \varepsilon^2 \ell^3 \Xi_{(Q1} R_{p1}) \} \quad (71)$$

This nonlinear amplitude evolution equation is a single-mode approximation of general acoustic amplitude evolution equation.

Comparing the characteristic turbulence time with the characteristic instability growth time, Clavin et al.<sup>16</sup> identified two distinct interaction regimes, depending on whether the turbulence time is or is not much smaller than the characteristic instability growth time. Larger instabilities are associated with the second of these classes in which evolution of the acoustic pressure during each fluctuation exhibits a deterministic behavior. The transition behavior in the first class involves random walks of the stochastic linear-growth rate  $\eta$ , requiring a statistical description that was performed by approximating the stochastic linear-growth rate by a white noise. A key feature of Eq. (70) is that influences of the stochasticity on the acoustics appear as multiplicative noise rather than additive noise.

In a white-noise approximation, the Stratonovich rather than Ito interpretation of the stochastic integral must be employed, and the Markov property of the white-noise process then enables the evolution of the probability density of the pressure

###### EFFECTS OF TURBULENCE ON LINEAR ACOUSTIC INSTABILITY 449

amplitude to be described by a Fokker–Planck equation. The stationary solutions of the Fokker–Planck equation lead to the results shown in Fig. 1, which demonstrates that the transition behavior depends on the character of the bifurcation. The results shown in Fig. 1 were highlighted by the bimodal behavior seen in the metastable region of subcritical bifurcation, thereby suggesting that resurging patterns of the pressure amplitude signal may occur near the transition regime of subcritical Hopf bifurcation. In other cases, the probabilities of the acoustic pressure amplitude are unimodal, and the most probable pressure amplitudes are close to the deterministic pressure amplitudes.

Results of the analysis can be related to engine variation of acoustic instability characteristics. Suppose that we run a series of rocket engine tests for different chambers which are all built in the same way and working under the same condition. Some of them may exhibit strong instability which could lead to the destruction of the engines, whereas others maintain only a weak level of acoustic instability. In such cases, a statistical description is necessary to investigate the chance of the strong instability occurring. Once random evolution of the acoustic instability becomes stationary, the resulting statistics are equivalent to that measured in ensemble average sense due to the ergodicity. Then the bimodal probability density function could explain strong engine variations of test results.

Similar analyses were performed by different authors. Culick et al.<sup>19</sup> wrote a two-mode approximation different from Eq. (70) and identified a corresponding

Fokker-Plank equation. They reported results of a Monte Carlo simulation that exhibited only unimodal probability density functions. Because no subcritical bifurcation case was considered, they were not able to obtain the bimodal probability density functions. In an analysis of Roudakov,<sup>20</sup> a bimodal probability density function associated with subcritical bifurcation was obtained from an electrical analog. Although a number of his observations are similar to those of Clavin et al.,<sup>16</sup> there is a fundamental difference in that Roudakov employed an additive (rather than multiplicative) noise arising from random turbulent pressure fluctuations. Since the additive noise associated with turbulent pressure fluctuations is smaller than the multiplicative noise coming from the noisy linear-growth rate by order  $M$ , his results may not represent the main route to the bimodal probability density function.

Another promising avenue to study nondeterministic behaviors of acoustic instabilities<sup>5,16,19</sup> is chaotic transition in dynamical systems, which developed considerably during the past two decades. As is well known, nonlinear terms of relatively simple deterministic equations can lead to chaotic evolutions, and turbulence in nonreacting flows is considered to be an example of such transitions. The noisy behavior is here associated with a strange attractor (which can occur already in low-dimensional systems) that introduces, as a consequence, a strong sensitivity to initial conditions. Thus far there is no conclusive evidence that acoustics in rocket engines exhibit chaotic behaviors, although Jahnke and Culick<sup>21</sup> reported a Poincaré intersection map suggesting the possible existence of a toroidal attractor arising from a quasiperiodic bifurcation. If chaotic acoustic oscillations ever occur in rocket engines, the resulting dynamic behaviors can provide different routes to complicated evolution patterns of acoustic instabilities. Since chaos can occur usually in sufficiently nonlinear systems, bimodal probability density functions might be produced without involving the metastability of the subcritical Hopf bifurcation, the necessary condition from which Clavin et al.<sup>16</sup> obtained the bimodal probability density functions. Therefore, a more extensive and systematic search for chaotic acoustic oscillations is warranted.

Until now, we have discussed the turbulence effects on the dynamic behaviors of acoustic pressure amplitude evolution. However, the most important turbulence effect on acoustic instability lies in combustion by which the actual amplification mechanisms occur. Difficulties in including turbulent combustion effects come from the fact that no general theory describing such flows is currently available. To make progress, it is therefore necessary first to limit attention to specific types of combustion and to introduce simplifications of the combustion models. One of the simplified models is the reaction-sheet model<sup>9-11</sup> of turbulent combustion, in which the turbulent flame is considered to be an ensemble of laminar flamelets. Provided that the statistics regarding distributions of the elementary laminar flamelets throughout the chamber and their response functions to acoustic excitation are known, the linear growth rates can be calculated from the spatial averaging procedure demonstrated in this chapter. Although a few models<sup>9</sup> exist that enable us to describe turbulent combustion statistically, in many respects the acoustic response functions of laminar flamelets are still unknown and deserve more attention.

Pioneering work concerning laminar-flame acoustic response was performed by Strahle.<sup>4-7</sup> However, all of these works postulated infinite rate chemistry, thereby precluding study of the interaction of finite-rate chemical kinetics of the flame with

the acoustic waves. Since the dominant nonlinear term in combustion processes arises from the chemical reaction, neglecting finite rate chemical-reaction effects may lead to significant underestimation of amplification rates under some conditions. In earlier attempts to address acoustic-chemistry interaction, applications of activation-energy asymptotics (AEA)<sup>22</sup> can be found in the works of McIntosh<sup>23</sup> and Clavin et al.<sup>24</sup> in which the stabilities of one-dimensional premixed flames were studied. Recently, Kim and Williams<sup>25</sup> and Im et al.<sup>26</sup> extended AEA to problems related to amplification mechanisms in rocket engines. In their analyses, particular attention was focused on near-extinction flames, a condition that can be caused by strong turbulent fluctuations of the velocity field. The amplification rates near extinction are found to be larger by an order of magnitude than those near equilibrium, thereby once again suggesting the significant underestimation of the amplification rate obtained from equilibrium flames.

Analytical improvements for AEA have recently been developed for alkane-air flames<sup>27-29</sup> and for hydrogen-air flames<sup>30</sup> by use of reduced chemical-reaction models systematically deduced from the detailed chemistry, followed by application of the methods of rate-ratio asymptotics (RRA). With sufficient effort, these methods can be applied to analyses of acoustic amplification. Since phenomenological chemistry parameters, such as the overall activation energy and the overall frequency factor, are no longer needed in these approaches, the RRA methods may provide more fundamentally based, quantitative predictions for acoustic amplification mechanisms.

### V. Concluding Remarks

The present chapter deals with effects of spatial inhomogeneities in the acoustic medium associated with two-phase flow and with turbulence. Attention is restricted to a particular class of interaction in which the characteristic time scale of turbulence is asymptotically large compared with that of acoustic waves, so that the acoustic medium can be considered to be a quasistationary random medium. In addition, it is assumed that the acoustic wavelength is long compared with any scale of inhomogeneity within the chamber, motivating a homogenized description, in which averages of the state variables become appropriate. On the basis of these assumptions, the Navier-Stokes equations for two-phase flows were reduced to a nonhomogeneous stochastic Helmholtz equation. Source terms of the equation were identified as arising mainly from homogeneous chemical reaction and from the resulting spatial variations of molecular properties such as density.

To handle the stochastic wave equation, the method of smooth perturbation was used and resulted in a Helmholtz equation for an equivalent deterministic acoustic medium. With use made of Green's integral theorem, the dispersion relation for transverse acoustic modes in cylindrical chambers was obtained in the form  $k = k_n[1 + \varepsilon'(\varrho_1^2)/2] + iM\{(\langle R_{p0} \rangle/2 + \varepsilon'(\varrho_1 R_{p1})\}$  where  $(\varrho_1^2)$ ,  $(\langle R_{p0} \rangle)$ , and  $(\varrho_1 R_{p1})$  are calculated from appropriate averages of the source terms. In particular, the  $\varepsilon'(\varrho_1 R_{p1})$  term corresponds to the main stochastic contributions to the linear-growth rate arising from the spatial correlation of the density with the pressure response function. Compared with the deterministic contributions to the linear-growth (or damping) rate and the acoustic frequency, the ratios of the stochastic contributions,  $\varepsilon'$ , are both found to be of the order of  $\varepsilon^2 \ell_c^2$  where  $\varepsilon$  is the intensity of the temperature fluctuations and  $\ell_c$  is the ratio of the characteristic length scale

for turbulence to the chamber diameter, thus implying that most of the stochastic contributions comes from the larger turbulent eddies. The stochastic effects are expected to be significant in the transition regime in which the deterministic growth rate is close enough to zero for transition between stable and unstable domains to occur reasonably frequently by stochastic variations of the growth rate.

A number of other aspects associated with turbulence are discussed in the preceding section regarding dynamic behaviors of nonlinear acoustic instability. Recent analyses by Clavin et al.<sup>16</sup> and Culick et al.<sup>19</sup> and Jahnke and Culick<sup>21</sup> suggested that extremely complicated evolution patterns of acoustic instability can occur if the acoustic oscillatory systems are situated in a metastable region of subcritical Hopf bifurcation or chaotic transition regime. However, the most important and challenging aspect of turbulence on acoustic instability is the turbulent combustion. Since turbulence can enhance nonequilibrium chemistry, the dominant nonlinear process of flows in rocket engines, the presence of strong turbulence may lead to an order-of-magnitude increase in the overall amplification rate. In order to predict the turbulence effects on amplification mechanisms, emphasis must be placed on two aspects of turbulent combustion: 1) what type of flame element produces the largest flame response to acoustic oscillations and 2) how many of these flame elements exit in the rocket engine. The first problem is currently being investigated by a model chemical mechanism employing AEA.<sup>25,26</sup> However, detailed chemical kinetic mechanisms, perhaps simplified by reduced chemical kinetics, need to be introduced to obtain quantitative predictions of amplification rates coming from elementary flames. The second problem can be addressed by statistical description of turbulent flames in rocket engines, which is in turn dependent on progress of modeling for general turbulent flames. In these studies, special emphasis on multiphase effects is warranted since they introduce the most pronounced difference in statistical description of turbulent flames in rocket engines.

#### Appendix: Molecular Properties in Multiphase Mixture

In this Appendix, we discuss a way to estimate the molecular properties of a multiphase system consisting of a number of liquid phases dispersed in an ideal-gas mixture. To consider  $a_f$ , we first write the overall density as

$$\rho = \frac{m}{V} = \sum_j m_j / \sum_j V_j \quad (\text{A1})$$

where  $m_j$  is the mass of phase  $j$  in a small control volume  $V$  and  $V_j$  is the volume of phase  $j$  in that control volume. Since the differential operator acts only on the  $V_j$ ,

$$\frac{1}{a_f^2} = \left( \frac{\partial \rho}{\partial p} \right)_{s, Y_{ji}} = - \sum_j \frac{m_j}{V^2} \left( \frac{\partial V_j}{\partial p} \right)_{s, Y_{ji}} = \sum_j \frac{\alpha_j^2}{Y_j} \frac{1}{a_{f,j}^2} \quad (\text{A2})$$

where the frozen sound speed of phase  $j$  is

$$\frac{1}{a_{f,j}^2} = - \frac{m_j}{V_j^2} \left( \frac{\partial V_j}{\partial p} \right)_{s, Y_{ji}} \quad (\text{A3})$$

In liquid-propellant rocket engines, the volume fraction of each liquid phase is usually small, and the sound speed is higher in the liquid phase than in the gas

###### EFFECTS OF TURBULENCE ON LINEAR ACOUSTIC INSTABILITY 453

phase, so that the overall sound speed can be approximated as being determined by that of the gas phase only. Since the gas phase is assumed to be an ideal-gas mixture, the overall frozen sound speed is expressed as

$$a_f^2 \approx \frac{Y_g a_{f,g}^2}{\alpha_g^2} \approx \frac{Y_g \gamma_g R T_g}{\alpha_g^2} \quad (A4)$$

where  $R$  is the gas constant per unit mass. Then the adiabatic compressibility  $K_f$  is correspondingly approximated as

$$K_f = \frac{1}{\rho a_f^2} \approx \frac{Y_g}{\alpha_g} \frac{1}{\rho_g a_g^2} \approx \frac{\alpha_g}{\gamma_g p_0} \quad (A5)$$

which shows that  $K_f$  is proportional mainly to the volume fraction of the gas phase.

Similarly,  $\beta_f$  is expressible as

$$\beta_f = \sum_j \alpha_j \beta_{f,j} \approx \frac{\alpha_g}{T_g} \quad (A6)$$

On the other hand,  $c_{p,f}$  is given by

$$c_{p,f} = \sum_j Y_j c_{p,f,j} \quad (A7)$$

which shows that  $c_{p,f}$  is weighted by the mass fraction rather than by the volume fraction, so that contributions from liquid phases are not generally negligible.

### I. Introduction

A NY review of liquid rocket combustion instability model development in the United States prior to 1972 inevitably leads to Ref. 1. This publication is a compendium of the combustion instability modeling efforts by industrial, academic, and government teams from across the nation. Their efforts were aided by the considerable financial support these groups received during the 1960s due to the perceived threat of combustion instabilities to achieving national space goals. The work of these groups also benefitted from the considerable experimental studies of combustion instability phenomena including liquid rocket combustion tests.

After 1972, financial support for combustion instability research was drastically reduced and very little effort was devoted to the subject. In the interim, major advances were made in the computational capability of computers and in numerical solution techniques for nonlinear partial differential equations. This increase in capability has permitted investigators to make calculations that were only dreams in the early 1970s. Increased computational capabilities also allowed the development of new quantitative spray measurement techniques.

#### A. Status as of 1972

The majority of the modeling efforts prior to 1972 used linear or nonlinear acoustics but very cursory combustion models. Modeling efforts representative of this era were made by Crocco and Cheng,<sup>2</sup> Crocco et al.,<sup>3</sup> Crocco and Mitchell,<sup>5</sup> Culick,<sup>6</sup> and Priem and Rice.<sup>7</sup> These models were used to gain an understanding of instabilities and guide engine design changes intended to achieve stability. In general, the differences between the chamber response obtained with linear and nonlinear acoustic models were small.<sup>3,4</sup> Some models for chamber acoustics included the separate effects of baffles (radial baffles or hub baffles, but not combinations of hub and radial baffles) and acoustic absorbers but not the combined effects of baffles and absorbers. With these models of chamber acoustics, designers had a greater ability to predict the need for and proper design of acoustic absorbers.

The combustion models used in the frequency-domain codes related the local instantaneous combustion rate to the local pressure using two constants. Reardon<sup>8</sup> did correlate time-lag parameters with engine design and operating parameters. These correlations were also used as a guide to obtaining stable engine configurations. Individual combustion processes such as injection, atomization, and vaporization were too computationally intensive to model, and in the case of atomization detailed models were not available. Movies of the combustion zone in experimental combustors<sup>9-11</sup> have shown the highly nonlinear nature of the combustion process during an instability. During a full-blown instability, it almost appeared as if a shock wave was traversing the combustion zone. It is not surprising that the simple two-constant combustion models could not provide a detailed understanding of instability or a quantitative evaluation of the influence of design and operating changes on stability.

Numerical studies<sup>12,13</sup> were conducted to examine the response of individual combustion processes (injection, atomization, vaporization, and chemical reaction) to idealized chamber acoustic waves. These acoustic waves corresponded to the resonant frequency of cylindrical chambers with no stability aids, axial velocity profiles, and ideal nozzles. The studies demonstrated that all of the individual processes were capable of driving an instability. The results of these studies were

correlated to provide values for the two constants,  $n$  and  $\tau$ , used in the simple acoustic models. None of the frequency-domain models of this era attempted a comprehensive model that tracked the propellant from the injector until it was completely burned. Simple one- and two-dimensional time-domain combustion instability models<sup>14-16</sup> were developed prior to 1972. Although these codes typically modeled injection, a mechanistic treatment of atomization was omitted. The combustion rate was usually modeled as an empirical function of pressure. None of these early time-domain codes had a "complete" combustion model. The codes were able to demonstrate the existence of a minimum disturbance amplitude necessary to initiate an instability. The wave characteristics calculated with these codes were similar to those observed from dynamic stability tests. These codes had considerable problems with numerical stability, particularly the two-dimensional codes.

#### B. Design Tools for the 1990s

The goal of current stability code development efforts is to produce a collection of analysis tools to allow a designer to assess the stability margin of candidate combustor designs. This collection of codes may include fast, acoustic  $n$ - $\tau$  codes for preliminary design screening. Fourier time expansion and simple time-domain codes could be utilized for stability margin evaluation and stability aid design for candidate combustor designs. Rigorous time-domain codes could be used for final design evaluation. The features of these codes are summarized in Table 1 and are discussed next.

**Table 1 Three approaches to instability modeling**

| Acoustics:<br>simple combustion              | Time domain<br>CFD                                    | Fourier time<br>expansion            |

| <i>Features</i>                              |                                                       |                                      |
