| Continuity and momentum<br>conserved         | Continuity, momentum,<br>and energy conserved         | Continuity and<br>momentum conserved |
| Simple two-parameter<br>combustion model     | Mechanistic<br>combustion model                       | Mechanistic<br>combustion model      |
| Stability aids modeled                       | Stability aids modeled                                | Stability aids modeled               |
| <i>Advantages</i>                            |                                                       |                                      |
| Identifies problem<br>modes                  | Includes all<br>nonlinear effects                     | Determines stability<br>margin       |
| Results obtained<br>quickly                  | Direct comparison to<br>stability tests               | Simulates resulting<br>oscillation   |
| <i>Disadvantages</i>                         |                                                       |                                      |
| Poor modeling of<br>combustion               | Computationally<br>intense                            | No real time history<br>generated    |
| Difficult to determine<br>instability source | Different runs for<br>each disturbance<br>level, type | No interaction<br>between modes      |

Any analysis of combustion instability in rocket engines is only as accurate as the specification of the boundary conditions (in particular, the injection and atomization rates at the injector face) for the problem. Unfortunately, the boundary conditions for stability analyses in liquid rocket engines are highly nonlinear and not very well understood. The rate and location at which injected propellant is atomized and the resulting size and velocity of the droplets is crucial input to any instability analysis. The subsequent behavior of the propellant as it burns or undergoes further breakup is critically linked to the atomization boundary condition. This boundary condition is also part of a highly nonlinear feedback loop in which the combustor gas field influences atomization and atomization influences burning and the combustor velocity profile. Accurately modeling this phenomena is the paramount challenge of rocket combustor modeling.

Typically, a shear coaxial element is modeled using correlations developed from cold-flow tests.<sup>17,18</sup> These correlations provide a relationship between global parameters (gas velocity, liquid flow rate, jet diameter, etc.) and drop size or atomization rate. Unfortunately, in many models, these global correlations have been applied in a subgrid fashion. The overall significance of droplet coalescence and secondary breakup phenomena has not been demonstrated. Secondary breakup is typically modeled using a spring-mass oscillator analogy or linear-surface wave growth rates even though the majority of experimental evidence suggests a violent stripping phenomena.<sup>10</sup> One can imagine the difficulty in trying to model the drop size produced by an impinging element subject to a high-amplitude transverse wave.

The biggest advantage of time-domain codes is that they can provide a complete time history of any parameter of interest. These time histories allow for a direct comparison with engine test results. Physical submodel development and code validation is also facilitated by use of these time histories. Interaction between different modes of oscillations is handled automatically, within the filtering limits of the finite difference method. Updating of one- and two-dimensional time-domain codes to take advantage of the increase in knowledge of the stability characteristics of various finite differencing techniques is underway.<sup>19-23</sup> However, most instabilities due to injector design or the wave dynamics are inherently three-dimensional. A fully three-dimensional simulation of the Space Shuttle main engine (SSME) (manifolds, baffles, absorbers, and 600 injection elements) is beyond current computational capabilities, even if atomization could be modeled adequately. Computational time remains a major drawback of the time-domain approach.

The Fourier time-expansion (FTE) approach is something of a hybrid between the numerical time-domain approach and the semianalytical acoustic-modeling approach. In the FTE approach, the thermodynamic variables and velocity components are expanded in a Fourier time series and substituted in the appropriate conservation equations. The resulting equations are differenced and solved numerically to determine the gas-phase oscillations. All of the basic combustion processes are modeled as they would be in a time-domain approach and then converted into complex responses for use with the FTE approach. Solutions are obtained at different oscillation amplitude levels for the complex frequency (observed frequency and decay rate). The oscillation amplitude at which the decay rate changes from negative to positive is the minimum disturbance amplitude required to excite that mode of instability. The oscillation amplitude at which the decay rate changes back from positive to negative is the equilibrium or limit cycle amplitude of the instability. A disadvantage of the FTE approach is that it does not

permit having oscillations present with different basic frequencies, i.e., chug and a high-frequency oscillation or two transverse modes with different frequencies that beat. Another disadvantage is that no time history of flow parameters is calculated directly for comparison with experiments.

### II. Theory for the Fourier Time Expansion

In this chapter, the theory for the Fourier time expansion model will be discussed and calculations made using the method will be presented for an SSME combustor. The results of the FTE approach were developed for incorporation into the high-frequency injection coupled combustion instability program (HICCIP).<sup>24-26</sup> The code described in Ref. 24 was restricted to using wave characteristics derived from a pseudo-three-dimensional theory. The code assumed uniform combustion response at all radial and tangential positions for a given axial position. Also, the wave model used could not account for the presence of baffles and discrete absorbers. Therefore, a three-dimensional model for the chamber gas oscillations was required for HICCIP to predict the characteristics in a typical rocket engine.<sup>25,26</sup>

The gas-phase oscillations calculated with the three-dimensional FTE approach are used to determine burning-rate oscillations throughout the combustor. This is an open-loop calculation where burning-rate oscillations are assumed and used to calculate gas-phase oscillations. The gas-phase oscillations are then used to calculate burning rate oscillations. If the final calculated burning-rate oscillations agreed with the assumed values, a consistent, complete solution would have been obtained. To close the loop and obtain the complete solution would require iterating the procedure described earlier. Work is continuing toward completing the closed-loop model.

The basic conservation equations used to define flow in a cylindrical chamber are as follows.

Conservation of mass:

$$\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot (\rho v) = w \quad (1)$$

Conservation of momentum:

$$\frac{\partial (\rho v)}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \rho v v + g \nabla p = w v_{liq} \quad (2)$$

Adiabatic ideal gas:

$$\frac{p}{p_0} = \left( \frac{\rho}{\rho_0} \right)^\gamma \quad (3)$$

It is assumed that viscous and gravitational forces are negligible. To simplify the analysis, it is further assumed that the radial and azimuthal steady-state flow are minimal and are, therefore, zero. This avoids requiring a three-dimensional steady-state solution to determine radial and azimuthal flow and pressure profiles. As in HICCIP, all of the variables ( $p$ ,  $\rho$ ,  $v_z$ ,  $v_r$ ,  $v_\theta$ ,  $w$ ) are expanded in a Fourier time series given by

$$F = F_0 + F_1 e^{i\omega t} + F_2 e^{2i\omega t} + \dots + F_n e^{ni\omega t} + \dots \quad (4)$$

where  $F$  is a dependent variable in the conservation equations.

Consistent with the preceding assumptions,  $\rho_0$  and  $p_0$  vary only in the axial direction,  $v_{r0}$  and  $v_{\theta 0}$  are zero (no radial or tangential average flow), and  $v_{z0}$  and  $w_0$  are variable in all three space dimensions.

In the remaining portion of this chapter, only the terms through  $F_1$  are used. When Eq. (4) is substituted into the conservation equations the terms with the  $\omega t$  dependence are the only ones with  $F_1$  coefficients, and these terms are, therefore, not influenced by  $F_2$  and higher harmonic terms. After determining the  $F_1$  values, the equations could again be solved using the known  $F_0$  and  $F_1$  values to find the  $F_2$  values. This process could be continued to determine as many  $F_n$  values as required to completely and rigorously define the oscillations. Solutions for the  $F_1$  values, however, define the complex frequency of the oscillations (both the observed frequency and the damping or growth rate for a specified pressure amplitude at a single point and combustion response). Substituting the Fourier time series into the conservation equations and retaining only the terms containing  $F_0$  and  $F_1$  yields the following set of equations.

Continuity:

$$i\omega\rho_1 + \frac{1}{r} \frac{\partial(r\rho_0 v_{r1})}{\partial r} + \frac{1}{r} \frac{\partial(\rho_0 v_{\theta 1})}{\partial \theta} + \frac{\partial(\rho_0 v_{z1})}{\partial z} + \frac{\partial(\rho_1 v_{z0})}{\partial z} = w_1 \quad (5)$$

Axial momentum:

$$i\omega\rho_0 v_{z1} + i\omega\rho_1 v_{z0} + 2 \frac{\partial(\rho_0 v_{z0} v_{z1})}{\partial z} + \frac{\partial(\rho_1 v_{z0} v_{z0})}{\partial z} + \frac{1}{r} \frac{\partial(r\rho_0 v_{r1} v_{z0})}{\partial r} + \frac{1}{r} \frac{\partial(\rho_0 v_{\theta 1} v_{z0})}{\partial \theta} + \gamma \frac{p_0}{\rho_0} \frac{\partial \rho_1}{\partial z} = w_1 v_{\text{liq}} \quad (6)$$

Radial momentum:

$$i\omega\rho_0 v_{r1} + \frac{\partial(\rho_0 v_{z0} v_{r1})}{\partial z} + \gamma \frac{p_0}{\rho_0} \frac{\partial \rho_1}{\partial r} = 0 \quad (7)$$

Azimuthal momentum:

$$i\omega\rho_0 v_{\theta 1} + \frac{\partial(\rho_0 v_{z0} v_{\theta 1})}{\partial z} + \gamma \frac{p_0}{r\rho_0} \frac{\partial p_1}{\partial \theta} = 0 \quad (8)$$

Adiabatic ideal gas:

$$p_1 = \gamma \frac{p_0}{\rho_0} \rho_1 \quad (9)$$

The boundary conditions at the chamber wall for the combustor are

$$v_{r1} = \gamma A_w p_1 \quad (10)$$

where the wall admittance  $A_w$  is zero for hard walls and is an input value for wall absorbers.

At the centerline of the chamber ( $r = 0$ ) all radial fluxes are zero as the area is zero.

The boundary conditions at the injector face are

$$v_{z1} = \gamma A_f p_1 \quad (11)$$

###### CALCULATIONS OF COMBUSTION RESPONSE PROFILES 461

where  $A_f$  is zero for a solid injector face and is input for absorbers on the injector face.

At the end of the combustion chamber the boundary conditions are

$$v_{z_1} = \gamma A_n \rho_1 \quad (12)$$

where  $A_n$  is the nozzle admittance. In this chapter, it is assumed to be zero (short compact ideal nozzles).

For the two baffle surfaces, the radial baffle  $v_{\theta 1} = 0$ , and the baffle is at an azimuthal momentum cell face; the hub baffle  $v_{r 1} = 0$ , and the baffle is at a radial momentum cell face.

It is also possible to model the oscillations as one- or two-dimensional phenomena. This is accomplished by assuming that the oscillations in the radial and/or azimuthal directions can be specified by an analytic wave equation solution in the desired direction. With this assumption, the conservation equations in that direction are not necessarily satisfied. The solution can be obtained in terms of the potential function given as

$$\Phi = f(z)e^{i\omega t}e^{in\theta}J_r(mr) \quad (13)$$

and the variables are determined by<sup>27</sup>

$$\rho_1 = C_1 \frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial t} \quad (14)$$

$$v_{z_1} = C_2 \frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial z} \quad (15)$$

$$v_{r_1} = C_3 \frac{1}{r} \frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial r} \quad (16)$$

$$v_{\theta 1} = C_4 \frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial \theta} \quad (17)$$

For one cell in the radial direction, the radial derivatives in Eqs. (5–8) are given as follows:

$$\frac{1}{r} \frac{\partial}{\partial r} (r \rho_0 v_{r_1}) \equiv \frac{\rho_0}{r} \left\{ \frac{\partial^2}{\partial r^2} [r J_n(mr)] \right\} / \frac{\partial}{\partial r} [J_n(mr)] \Big\} v_{r_1} \quad (18)$$

$$\frac{1}{r} \frac{\partial}{\partial r} (r \rho_0 v_{z_0} v_{r_1}) \equiv \frac{\rho_0 v_{z_0}}{r} \left\{ \frac{\partial^2}{\partial r^2} [r J_n(mr)] \right\} / \frac{\partial}{\partial r} [J_n(mr)] \Big\} v_{r_1} \quad (19)$$

$$\gamma \frac{p_0}{\rho_0} \frac{\partial \rho_1}{\partial r} = \frac{\gamma p_0}{\rho_0} \left\{ \frac{\partial}{\partial r} [r J_n(mr)] \right\} / J_n(mr) \Big\} \rho_1 \quad (20)$$

where the derivatives of the Bessel functions are determined from Bessel function tables (at a radius equal to half the chamber radius) for different Bessel function indices  $m$  and  $n$ , which describe the mode in the radial direction and the tangential mode ( $n$ ). The calculations then correspond to a very thin annular ring at half the distance to the chamber wall.

Similarly for only one cell in the azimuthal direction the azimuthal derivative in Eqs. (5–8) are given as follows:

$$\frac{1}{r} \frac{\partial \rho_0 v_{\theta_1}}{\partial \theta} = i \frac{n}{r} v_{\theta_1} \quad (21)$$

$$\frac{1}{r} \frac{\partial (\rho_0 v_{z_0} v_{\theta_1})}{\partial \theta} = \frac{\rho_0 v_{z_0}}{r} i n v_{\theta_1} \quad (22)$$

$$\frac{1}{r} \frac{\partial (\rho_0 \rho_1)}{\partial \theta} = \frac{\gamma \rho_0}{r} i n \rho_1 \quad (23)$$

where  $n$  specifies the number of modes in the azimuthal direction. The calculations then correspond to a very thin “pie” section cut out of the chamber.

### III. Sample Calculations for the Space Shuttle Main Engines

To demonstrate the capability of the FTE approach, calculations were made for the SSME at nominal operating conditions with and without baffles and absorbers for different oscillation modes. The configuration used to represent the SSME is presented in Table 2.

A time-averaged combustion profile was used similar to that obtained with a vaporization limited model (50% combustion completed 0.058 m from the injector, 90% in 0.191 m, and 99% completion within the chamber). The time-averaged combustion profile remained constant. This is not a realistic assumption as the gas oscillations do influence the time-averaged burning rate. The influence of these oscillations will be evaluated when the FTE approach is combined with the combustion models in HICCP.

The definition for combustion response is

$$R_p = \frac{W_1 / W_0}{p_1 / p_0} \quad (24)$$

The combustion response is a vector in the complex plane. The real portion is the magnitude of the nondimensional burning rate oscillation that is in phase with the pressure. The imaginary portion indicates the phasing of combustion relative to pressure. A positive imaginary response indicates that the combustion is leading the pressure oscillation, a negative response indicates combustion is lagging.

In the present work, the combustion response is assumed to be spatially invariant. The simplifications of the burning process, although not rigorous, allow a demonstration of the FTE approach and indicate how some of the combustor design variables influence stability of the SSME.

The combustion response needed to drive various waves in the SSME were calculated iteratively. For a given frequency, a combustion response was assumed

and a burning rate oscillation was approximated using an analytical acoustic wave solution. This initial guess at the burning rate oscillation was used to determine oscillating pressure and velocity profiles in the combustor. With the calculated pressure profile and assumed burning rate oscillations, an average combustion response was calculated (based on the fraction of propellant burned at each location) which was then used to calculate a new burning rate oscillation. This process was repeated until the change in the average combustion response between successive iterations was minimal. With the assumptions and procedure outlined, a combustion response for any frequency can be determined. The combustion response was calculated (using a grid size of 4 radial, 10 azimuthal, and 8 axial cells) for the first tangential (1T) mode and the results are shown in Fig. 1. The complex combustion response is plotted as a function of frequency between 1860 and 2060 Hz. Three curves are shown in Fig. 1, corresponding to damping rates (imaginary portion of the complex frequency) of +628, 0, -628 /s. As the frequency is increased, the combustion response changes from combustion lagging pressure to leading pressure and crosses the in-phase (1.39 real and zero imaginary) plane at 1960 Hz with neutral damping. Normally, this is considered the natural frequency for the 1T mode in this engine. Depending on the combustion response, however, oscillations in the engine can occur at other frequencies as shown in Fig. 1. Larger combustion responses make the engine unstable; lower values result in a stable engine. Negative imaginary response lowers the frequency from the natural, and positive imaginary responses increase the frequency. Similar plots can be obtained for all of the modes possible in the chamber. The mode type is determined by the initial assumption for the pressure profile or burning rate oscillations in the chamber.

To illustrate how the FTE approach can be used to determine the influence of design parameters on stability and stability modes, calculations were made

to determine the frequency and combustion response for neutral stability at the natural frequency, i.e., where the combustion response has no imaginary value and the oscillations have zero growth or decay rate. The results of these calculations for different stability aid configurations and modes are presented in Table 3.

Table 3 illustrates how the acoustic absorber improves stability in the SSME. The original absorber design is tuned to the 3T mode and increases the required combustion response of the 3T mode for neutral stability from 1.64 to 2.63, which is equivalent to going from neutral stability to a damping rate of  $-628$  1/s in Fig. 1. This damping rate would decrease the amplitude of a 100% chamber pressure peak-to-peak wave to the allowable 10% amplitude in 3.6 ms. The damping time as required by Ref. 28 is 18 ms. Therefore, the SSME absorber design provides damping five times that required for the 3T mode.

The original absorber design provides a very small change in frequency and response for the 1T and first longitudinal (1L) modes because the absorber is tuned to a much higher frequency. The 2T mode is actually made more unstable by the absorber because it reduces the frequency and decreases the chamber response. Retuning the SSME absorber to the 1T and 1L modes by decreasing the absorber opening in the chamber from 0.009 to 0.003 m and increasing the aperture length from 0.013 to 0.025 m will produce a large increase in stability, more than enough to meet the damping requirements of Ref. 28. The increase in stability at the 1T and 1L frequencies is less in comparison to the stability of the original design at the 3T because the absorber open area has been reduced to obtain tuning at these lower frequencies.

Adding the baffle to the SSME changes the tuned frequencies and decreases the response required for neutral stability. The frequency change is 105 Hz for the 1T mode and 380 Hz for the 2T mode. The reduction in response is also greater for the 2T mode.

These calculations demonstrate that oscillations can occur in baffled chambers. Oscillations with either standing or spinning wave characteristics are possible. With the baffle, the wave is distorted within and near the baffles, but an acoustic-like wave does exist. Downstream of the baffles, the wave is similar to the acoustic wave for a pure cylinder. Near the baffles, they become distorted and within the baffle compartment, the oscillations are predominantly axial with small variations in the radial and azimuthal directions. The decrease in response occurs because of the wave distortion produced by the baffles coupled with the steady flow profile within the chamber. The baffles reduce the loss associated with the steady flow convecting spinning oscillations out of the chamber by producing axial oscillations.

To test the capability of the FTE approach to predict observed acoustic phenomena, calculations were performed to compare with the results published by Wieber<sup>29</sup> and the GEMSIP program.<sup>30</sup> Good agreement with this data was obtained. Calculated results for the SSME were somewhat dependent on grid size, especially for the baffled chambers.<sup>25,26</sup>

### IV. Space Shuttle Main Engine Burning Rate Oscillations

Local burning rate oscillations resulting from the gas-phase oscillations just described were calculated using the HICCIP model described in Ref. 24. These calculations were performed at the resonant frequency (zero imaginary part of the combustion response and no damping rate) for the SSME chamber and for the SSME with stability aids removed. The HICCIP model includes: 1) fuel flow oscillations, 2) oxidizer flow oscillations, 3) atomization in the recess and chamber,<sup>7</sup> and 4) vaporization using an onion skin model.<sup>20</sup> With these models, the propellant is followed from the time it enters the fuel or oxidizer dome, through the injection element, recess, and combustion chamber (as a function of time and space). Mass is always conserved throughout the combustion process. The processes are dependent on the local conditions as required by the available equations.

To make the burning rate oscillation calculations, a proper selection of the constants in the atomization models for the rate of atomization and drop size is required. The atomization rate constant was selected so that 50% of the oxidizer was atomized in the recess. This resulted in an atomization plane (the effective location where vaporization starts) at the injector face. The drop size constant was selected to produce a steady-state gas velocity profile similar to that used in the gas-phase oscillation calculations already described (99% vaporized in the chamber). This resulted in a steady-state drop size of 507  $\mu$  being formed at the injector face.

The oscillations in injector flow rates as given by a flow response for different rows in the injector are shown in Table 4. The large fuel response is due to the very low fuel-injection pressure drop (2.1 MPa). The variation in oxidizer response is due to the different lengths of the oxidizer tubes connecting the oxidizer manifold to the combustion chamber in the SSME injector. Oxidizer tube length varied from 0.127 m near the center to 0.228 m at the chamber wall. Local combustion responses are shown in Fig. 2 as a function of axial position for five different radial and tangential positions. To compare the local combustion rate oscillation at different locations they are nondimensionalized as follows:

$$R_c = \frac{p_0 \sum_i w_i p_i}{p_{f1}^2 \sum_i w_0} \quad (25)$$

where  $w_1$  is the local oscillating burning rate,  $w_{01}$  the average burning rate in the first axial cell,  $p_0$  the average chamber pressure, and  $p_{11}$  the oscillating pressure in the first axial cell. Thus, cells with very low burning rates and/or pressure amplitude do not contribute to the oscillations and are reduced proportionally in combustion response. The responses are referred to as normalized local combustion responses in Fig. 2. This weighting eliminates large values of the combustion response at the end of the combustor where only a few drops remain to burn, and the combustion response is very dependent on when in the pressure cycle these remaining drops are vaporized.

The gas oscillations and combustion response field repeat around the chamber with each baffle compartment. Therefore, only the first four tangential locations, corresponding to one baffle compartment, are shown in Fig. 2 and discussed herein. Profiles inside the hub baffle are presented in Fig. 2 as well as within a baffle compartment.

The responses for radial positions near the centerline and within the hub and all tangential positions are very similar as the oscillations are spinning. Next to the hub (radius = 0.098 m) the influence of the radial baffles outside the hub are noticed, and the responses corresponding to the cells near the radial baffles (radius = 0.098 m) are shown. Within the baffle compartment, the responses at the corners and the center show the extreme variations calculated.

At the first axial position, the real part of the response is always a large positive number, and the imaginary part is a larger negative number. This is a result of the large variation in drop size produced by the oscillation in fuel flow during a cycle. In the baffle compartments, the drop size varied between 270 and 950  $\mu$  during a cycle. With the large negative fuel response listed, the axial velocity is very low when the pressure is high. Thus, large drops are being produced when the pressure is high, resulting in low burning rates for these drops. Within the first cell 40–50% of the oxidizer is burned (depending on the oscillation amplitudes). The average time for the oxidizer to travel from the injector face (atomization plane) to the center of the first axial cell is 0.40 of a cycle. Therefore, on average the large drops produced at the high-pressure portion of the oscillations are burning at the low-pressure portion of the oscillation in the first cell. This produces the large positive combustion response in the first cell. The fact that the combustion response has a larger negative imaginary response indicates that the time delay has resulted in the large drops burning closer to the period when the pressure is near zero and increasing.

**Fig. 2** Normalized local combustion responses at various radial and tangential locations.

The real part of the combustion response in the first cell varies between 1.78 and 3.41 whereas the imaginary part of the combustion response varies between  $-5.30$  and  $-7.67$ . It is evident that these combustion responses cannot be considered constant as is assumed in the simple combustion models discussed earlier.

The normalized combustion response drops very fast after the first cell, due to the decrease in burning rate axially and to the fact that the drops take different amounts of time to arrive at downstream cells. The effects of the variation in drop size with time are being smeared by the drops having different life times. It takes several cycles for the drops to arrive at these downstream cells. As a result, the contribution of the oscillating burning downstream is minimized. However, the variation in combustion response with radial and tangential directions is very large. Again, this violates the assumption used in the simple combustion models that the combustion response is uniform throughout the chamber.

To determine the best representation of a combustion response for the entire chamber, the burning rates were summed over the full chamber volume. For the baffled chamber, the normalized full chamber combustion response was  $(1.358, -2.084i)$ . This is in contrast to the value of  $(1.35, +0.0i)$  determined using the FTE approach to drive the 1T mode. Obviously, the combustion response will not drive the oscillations at the natural frequency since the phasing of the two vectors are not the same (the tuning frequency would be lower as indicated by Fig. 1 for negative imaginary response). In addition, the local combustion oscillations calculated in the two stages are very different, which means we do not have the correct oscillation profiles.

Similar local combustion response calculations were made for the unbaffled SSME with no absorber. For the 1T mode in an unbaffled chamber, all of the angular positions see the same oscillation. Therefore, all of the combustion responses are the same for a given radial position. The normalized stream tube (an axial row of cells at a fixed radial location) combustion responses are shown in Table 5 for the SSME with stability aids removed.

Table 5 again shows the large variation in combustion response with position with an unbaffled chamber. Since the wave is spinning, there are variations in only the radial and axial directions. The first axial position again has a very large value (twice the normalized stream tube value) and then rapidly drops, as seen in Fig. 2 for the baffled chamber. The largest response values are located near the chamber wall where they are most effective in driving an oscillation. The

calculated response for the full chamber has a slightly lower real value for the unbaffed chamber compared to the baffled chamber. This would indicate that the unbaffed chamber is more stable than the baffled chamber. With the SSME, the large combustion response is due to the varying atomization produced by the large injector fuel flow response.

The results and discussions indicated that the fuel response is responsible for a large portion of the combustion response in the SSME. This result was checked by performing calculations with different portions of the combustion model turned off. Calculations were also performed with different oscillations amplitude levels to show the nonlinear characteristics of the combustion process. The results of these calculations are shown in Table 6.

Table 6 confirms the importance of fuel flow oscillations on the combustion response. It is the phenomena making the largest contribution to combustion response at all amplitudes. The influence is very nonlinear, decreasing with increasing amplitude. At higher oscillation amplitudes the velocity of the fuel in the injector element reaches sonic velocity during a portion of the oscillation. Since the velocity cannot exceed sonic velocity, this reduces the fuel flow oscillation. To account for this fact, the fuel response in HICCIP is decreased by the square root of the oscillation amplitude at which sonic velocity is first achieved divided by the actual amplitude. For the 20% peak-to-peak chamber pressure oscillations, sonic condition is reached in the four rows within the baffle compartment and the response is reduced to 0.8 of its value at low amplitude. At 80%  $P_c$  peak-to-peak rows 2–10 reach sonic velocity and the fuel response in the baffle compartment area is reduced to 0.4 of its value at low amplitude (values in Table 6). As a result of this feature, the contribution of the fuel flow response decreases with increasing amplitude. The other terms are relatively insensitive to the oscillation amplitude at low amplitudes but do change at very high amplitudes.

Axial velocity oscillations are the next most important influence on combustion response after the fuel response. With the presence of the baffles, an axial wave is present in the baffle compartments, thereby producing large axial velocity oscillations. With a steady axial velocity in all cells, the axial velocity produces a sinusoidal oscillation in burning rate (the burning is Reynolds number dependent). The baffles also reduce the frequency of the oscillation. Within the hub, the reduced frequency combined with the smaller diameter results in a large amplitude increase

from the injector to the tips of the baffle. This is accompanied by large axial velocity oscillations within the hub. The contribution of the axial velocity is out of phase (imaginary response) as the axial velocity oscillations are generally 120-deg out of phase with the pressure.

Density oscillations always produce a 0.4 contribution to the combustion response. This is associated with the density term in the Reynolds number, which influences the burning rate in proportion to the square root of the Nusselt number. Since density is proportional to pressure divided by the ratio of specific heats, the predicted influence of density on response is about 0.4 and is independent of amplitude, frequency, drops size, etc.

Oxidizer flow oscillations have a nominal influence on the combustion response in the SSME. Oxidizer injector pressure drop is not excessive, and as Table 4 shows, the oxidizer flow response is as large as  $-1.2$  at some rows. The negative flow response results in a positive combustion response because the time lag between injecting the oxidizer and burning is close to a half-cycle. The oxidizer flow response is reduced due to the smearing of the flow oscillations through many cycles in the combustion process. The influence of the oxidizer flow oscillations increases with amplitude due to the change in drop size and velocity, which changes the time lag between injection and burning, as well as the burning rates.

Radial and tangential gas velocity and pressure oscillations have little influence on the combustion response. Without steady state or time-averaged radial and tangential velocities, the effect of these oscillations on burning rate cancel (burning rate is a function of the magnitude of velocity). The radial and tangential gas velocities would contribute to the harmonic terms in the Fourier expansion. The pressure oscillation also has little influence as it changes the surface temperature of the drop, which slightly changes the heat required to vaporize the drop. Pressure also slightly influenced the drop size and atomization rate via the density influence in the atomization process, which was considered as a pressure oscillation influence. These factors were all small and not very dependent on oscillation amplitude.

Contributions of the various factors toward the total combustion response is additive at the lower amplitudes. The entry "linear sum of all" in Table 6 is the value obtained by adding all of the individual contributions. At the 5 and 20% peak-to-peak levels, the actual calculated response using all of the terms is within 5% of the individual sums. At higher amplitudes, the factors interact, as one would expect, and the sum appears to be quite different than the actual. The major influence, however, has been to change the phasing of the combustion response (larger imaginary and lower real values). Basically, this means that the time lag has changed.

All of the results presented are very dependent on the constants used in the atomization process to determine drop size and atomization rates.<sup>17,24,25</sup> The atomization constants are premultipliers for the drop size and mass stripping rate equations. The drop size and stripping rate are functions of the relative velocity of the fuel and oxidizer, the densities and viscosities of the fuel and oxidizer, and the surface tension of the oxidizer. These constants will change the steady-state profiles as well as the time lags between injection and burning. To show this influence, calculations were made with the same gas-phase oscillations but with different atomization constants. These results are shown in Table 7.

With either larger or smaller rate constants the baffled chamber is more stable than the unbaffled. At the rate constant used in the previous results, the baffled chamber is more stable than the unbaffled. At smaller size constants, the unbaffled chamber becomes much more stable than the baffled.

### V. Summary

A brief review of instability modeling prior to 1972 was made. Current approaches to instability modeling were outlined, and the advantages and disadvantages of each approach were discussed. The theory for the Fourier time-expansion approach was outlined in detail. Calculations were made for the combustion response profiles in the SSME combustor (with a five-bladed hub baffle and absorbers). The contributions of various physical phenomena (atomization, injection, etc.) to the combustion response profiles were assessed.

### I. Introduction

COMBUSTION instability results from the coupling between combustion and the fluid dynamics of the system. Several types of instability have been observed. They are all characterized by chamber pressure oscillations, although the frequency and amplitude of the oscillations and their external manifestations normally vary with the type of instability.

Oscillatory operation of an engine is undesirable for many reasons. One of the most important effects is the very high vibration levels that may impair the operation of the guidance system and severely affect payloads. Another detrimental effect of oscillatory operation is the highly increased heat transfer. This increase often leads to destruction of the engine. Several different classes of instability have been identified and studied experimentally: low-frequency (chug, pogo), intermediate-frequency (buzz), and high-frequency instability (screaming, screeching). High-frequency instability, also called resonant combustion or acoustic instability, is the most destructive type of instability.

Combustion instability problems have been encountered in almost all of the propulsion system development programs, for example, during the development programs of the F-1, J-2, and J-2S in the United States, and the Viking engine in Europe. Although a considerable effort has been given to understanding and controlling this undesirable phenomenon over the last 40 years, it continues to present significant challenges in reliable engine design. An unforeseen instability problem can cause engine loss and facility damage, and it can result in cost over-run and program schedule slippage. Stabilizing devices often used to solve the instability problem impose additional cost, weight, and complexity to engine technology.

A significant amount of work on combustion instability was performed in the United States in the 1950s and the 1960s during the Apollo development program. Much of this work was compiled by Harrie and Reardon.<sup>1</sup> Since then, due to limited development programs, research on combustion instability has been reduced significantly. Culick<sup>2</sup> has reported more recent work on the subject.

This chapter focuses on the numerical analysis of engine instability. After a short review of the numerical analysis of combustion instability, we describe the

research we have been carrying out on combustion instability in the framework of the Ariane European launcher development program.<sup>3</sup>

Until now, stability assessment of rocket engines has relied on qualitative tools and full-scale testing. The complex nature of the combustion instability phenomenon and the lack of computational capabilities precluded any attempt to describe it in the past. Most of the effort put into understanding, predicting, controlling, and eliminating combustion instability in rocket motors has been devoted to linear analyses.<sup>4-6</sup> These analyses, which must make assumptions such as small-amplitude oscillations and single-frequency sinusoidal oscillations to solve the problem, are not always consistent with observed instability phenomena. Finite disturbances are often required to excite instability, and waves are usually steep fronted. Linear analyses can predict neither the large-amplitude oscillations often observed in case of instability nor the limiting cycle behavior.

Comparatively limited work has addressed the solution of nonlinear combustion instability problems in liquid rockets. Over the past decade, substantial applications of computational fluid dynamics (CFD) techniques to solid rocket and ramjets instabilities have been reported,<sup>7-11</sup> whereas these techniques have received only limited attention for liquid rocket combustion instabilities.<sup>12,13</sup>

With the limited resources available today, more economical quantitative analysis tools and subscale testing must be used to rate the stability of an engine. The advent of large supercomputers, CFD modeling capabilities, and progress in diagnostic techniques make numerical analysis of combustion instability a promising new approach to the problem.

Numerical analysis of combustion instability requires the solution of the differential conservation equations that describe the flow in a typical liquid rocket engine. Thus, it is necessary to describe in detail potential mechanisms involved in the instability phenomenon. Such mechanisms are recognized as injection, atomization, vaporization, mixing, and combustion of liquid propellants.

Priem and Guentert<sup>14</sup> were the first to address combustion instabilities in liquid rockets by solving the conservation equations numerically. Their approach was later adopted by others, like Hoffman et al.<sup>15</sup> Only one- or two-dimensional problems were treated. The two-dimensional problem was formulated for an annular ring in the combustion chamber. The nonlinear conservation equations were solved with source terms representing vaporization and combustion. Hoffman et al.<sup>15</sup> improved the Priem model; they treated variable oxidizer/fuel mixture ratio, included the droplet drag and momentum transfer between the liquid and gas phases, and adapted the vaporization model by including the Reynolds number dependence.

In these works, numerical analysis was initiated by a pressure wave having sinusoidal amplitude distribution around the annular ring. Its time evolution was calculated as it propagated around the ring, which could be placed anywhere along the axis of the chamber. Axial propagation of the wave was not treated.

The approach just described was motivated by the analysis of tangential acoustic modes, the most destructive kind of instabilities. Burstein et al.<sup>16</sup> carried out a similar numerical analysis. They also treated wave propagation in an annulus, including the influence of axial baffles, and were able to treat wave propagation in the axial direction. This appears to be the last work reported in the 1970s.

More recently, some research effort on numerical analysis of combustion instability was initiated in a few laboratories, either by adapting existing numerical

models to the problem of combustion instability<sup>17-19</sup> or by developing specific models (See Chapter 19).

### II. Approach to the Numerical Analysis of Combustion Instability

In the early 1980s, as part of the European Ariane rocket development program, a research activity on high-frequency combustion instability in liquid-propellant engines was begun. At that time, computational resources were sufficiently advanced to make it possible to address the problem numerically. The complex processes involved in the combustion chamber of a rocket engine that needed to be modeled were many. Emphasis was placed on those processes recognized to be involved in combustion instability phenomenon: atomization, droplet vaporization, and burning. Submodels resulting from atomization and droplet vaporization studies were implemented in the simultaneously developed numerical model.

Although the approach is general and may be used for any liquid propellant engine, the analysis presented herein was carried out with the Ariane liquid rocket engines in mind. Two engine types were considered: the Viking engine using UDMH/N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> propellants and a radial impinging injector system, and the cryogenic Vulcain engine using LOX/H<sub>2</sub> and a coaxial element injector system.

#### A. Atomization Model

The intent of the research on atomization was to describe the spray characteristics resulting from the injector system. More precisely, attention was focused on the measurement of droplet size and velocity distributions. The lack of a theoretical model to describe droplet formation for an impinging or coaxial injector dictated an experimental approach. Measurements were performed with a Malvern sizer. In most cases, simulant fluids were used to replace actual propellants. Different parameters were investigated, such as fluid properties, working pressure, and mass flow rate. The injector element geometry was also investigated. The spray characterization output was given in a compact form which described drop size distribution as a function of working conditions and geometry. Both impinging and coaxial injector elements were considered, and the results were described in several papers<sup>20-23</sup> (see also Chapter 6).

#### B. Vaporization Model

Droplet vaporization and burning have been recognized as playing a fundamental role in combustion instability phenomenon. Research was undertaken to provide insight into this process and to determine how it affects combustion instability. The approach taken dealt with detailed numerical analysis of the flowfield of vaporizing and burning droplets. It included both one-dimensional (burning droplet in a quiescent atmosphere) and two-dimensional (burning droplet in a convective field) analyses.<sup>24</sup> The mathematical formulation includes multispecies gas-phase equations and liquid-phase equations, which are solved numerically. Special attention was paid to the analysis of vaporization and burning of droplets in a high-pressure and high-temperature atmosphere that represented the actual working conditions of rocket engines. The analysis was applied to storable (UDMH, N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>) and cryogenic (LOX) propellant droplets. The effects of pressure and velocity waves on

vaporization and burning were investigated for both UDMH and  $N_2O_4$  droplets. For liquid oxygen droplets, vaporization has been considered under subcritical and supercritical conditions.<sup>25</sup> Results of these analyses were summed up in analytical laws that were implemented in the numerical model.

#### C. Phedre Numerical Model

Despite progress made in computing capabilities, it was not realistic at the time the present research started to deal with the development of a three-dimensional code that would describe the flowfield in a typical rocket engine. Limitations resulted from both computational time and memory requirements. The alternative was to develop a two-dimensional annular model, Phedre, to analyze combustion instability. This approach was suggested by the concern for describing acoustic tangential modes, which are by far the most critical ones. This numerical code is discussed in the following section.

### III. Numerical Analysis of Combustion Instability

The two-dimensional numerical model Phedre was developed to describe the unsteady, turbulent, two-phase reacting flow in a liquid rocket engine combustion chamber such as that represented in Fig. 1a. The model formulation, presented in this section, enables the treatment of different engine types. It includes axial or radial propellant injection, baffles, and acoustic resonator modeling. The injected propellants may be either both liquid or one liquid and one gas.

The axisymmetric chamber geometry is transformed into an equivalent annular geometry as shown in Fig. 1b. This transformation consists of spreading out the actual geometry according to the following rules. The axial lengths ( $x$  axis), such as the chamber length  $L$  and the baffle length  $L_b$ , are kept unchanged. The chamber transverse length  $l$  ( $y$  axis) is adjusted so that the  $n$ th tangential mode frequencies of the real and equivalent chambers are the same ( $n$  being the order of the mode being analyzed). The width in the third direction ( $z$  axis), which varies only with  $x$ , is determined so that the cross-sectional areas of the two chambers match, enabling the axial flow evolution to be the same in both chambers. The flowfield is not resolved in the  $z$  direction.

An  $n$ -bladed baffle is represented by placing evenly spaced  $n$  plates in the transverse direction. To represent acoustic resonators distributed at the chamber periphery, surface boundary conditions are applied at the chamber-resonator interface. These conditions, simulating a gas flow incoming or leaving the chamber through the cavity aperture, consist of solving a set of equations which describe the resonator response to the chamber flow disturbances.

To model radial injection and acoustic resonators, the two-dimensional model equations were written in a form that enables the injection of gas and/or liquid through the chamber lateral walls. Later, these flows will be referred to as lateral flows.

With this formulation, it is also possible to describe two-dimensional planar flows useful for pure longitudinal-mode analyses, provided the relevant boundary conditions are implemented. Then, the transverse length is typically chosen equal to the chamber diameter, and the width is determined as for the annular geometry.

#### A. Governing Equations

##### 1. Gas-Phase Equations

The gas phase is described by solving the Favre-averaged Navier–Stokes equations with specific source terms. These terms are the result of the interaction of the gas phase with the liquid phase and the injection of a lateral gas flow when present. The gas phase consists of three species: fuel, oxidizer, and burnt products. Additional transport equations for the fuel and the oxidizer are also solved. The gas-phase equations are written in the following two-dimensional form.

Conservation equation of mass:

$$\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{b} \frac{\partial \rho u b}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial \rho v}{\partial y} = \dot{W}^v + \dot{W}^{lf} \quad (1)$$

where  $\dot{W}^v$  and  $\dot{W}^{lf}$  are the mass source terms due to droplet evaporation and lateral flow, respectively.

Conservation equations of momentum:

$$\frac{\partial \rho u}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{b} \frac{\partial \rho u^2 b}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial \rho uv}{\partial y} = -\frac{\partial p}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial \sigma_{xx}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial \sigma_{xy}}{\partial y} + f_x + S_x^v + S_x^{lf} \quad (2)$$

$$\frac{\partial \rho v}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{b} \frac{\partial \rho uv b}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial \rho v^2}{\partial y} = -\frac{\partial p}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial \sigma_{xy}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial \sigma_{yy}}{\partial y} + f_y + S_y^v + S_y^{lf} \quad (3)$$

where  $f_x$  and  $f_y$  are the drag force components,  $S_x^v$  and  $S_y^v$  are the components of the momentum exchange  $S^v$  between the two phases due to droplet evaporation, and  $S_x^{lf}$  and  $S_y^{lf}$  are the components of the momentum source term  $S^{lf}$  due to lateral gas flow.

Conservation equation of energy:

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial \rho e}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{b} \frac{\partial \rho e u b}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial \rho e v}{\partial y} = & -p \left( \frac{1}{b} \frac{\partial u b}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} \right) \\ & + \sigma_{xx} \frac{1}{b} \frac{\partial u b}{\partial x} + \sigma_{yy} \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} + \sigma_{xy} \left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} + \frac{1}{b} \frac{\partial v b}{\partial x} \right) \\ & - \frac{1}{b} \frac{\partial q_x b}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial q_y}{\partial y} + S_e^v + S_e^{dw} + S_e^{lf} \end{aligned} \quad (4)$$

where  $S_e^v$ ,  $S_e^{dw}$ , and  $S_e^{lf}$  represent the energy source terms due to droplet evaporation, drag force, and lateral flow, respectively;  $q_x$  and  $q_y$  are the heat flux components due to both conduction and species enthalpy diffusion expressed according to Fick's law,

$$\begin{aligned} q_x &= -\lambda \frac{\partial T}{\partial x} - \rho D \sum_k h_k \frac{\partial}{\partial x} \left( \frac{\rho_k}{\rho} \right) \\ q_y &= -\lambda \frac{\partial T}{\partial y} - \rho D \sum_k h_k \frac{\partial}{\partial y} \left( \frac{\rho_k}{\rho} \right) \end{aligned} \quad (5)$$

Conservation equations of species concentrations:

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial \rho_k}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{b} \frac{\partial \rho_k u b}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial \rho_k v}{\partial y} = & \frac{1}{b} \frac{\partial}{\partial x} \left[ \rho b D \frac{\partial}{\partial x} \left( \frac{\rho_k}{\rho} \right) \right] \\ & + \frac{\partial}{\partial y} \left[ \rho D \frac{\partial}{\partial y} \left( \frac{\rho_k}{\rho} \right) \right] + \dot{W}_k^v + \dot{W}_k^c + \dot{W}_k^{lf} \end{aligned} \quad (6)$$

where  $\dot{W}_k^v$ ,  $\dot{W}_k^c$ , and  $\dot{W}_k^{lf}$  are the source terms of species  $k$  due to droplet evaporation, gas-phase combustion, and lateral flow, respectively.

This system of equations is closed by the perfect gas equation of state,

$$p = RT \sum_k \frac{\rho_k}{M_k} \quad (7)$$

where the temperature is derived from the internal energy using

$$e(T) = \sum_k \frac{\rho_k}{\rho} \left[ h_k(T) - \frac{R}{M_k} T \right] \quad (8)$$

Turbulence model equations: Turbulence effects are taken into account using the Boussinesq approximation. Thus, the transport coefficients are expressed as the sum of a laminar coefficient and a turbulent one. The turbulent viscosity is given by the Deardorff subgrid scale (SGS) turbulence model<sup>26</sup>:

$$\mu_t = \rho c_t \delta^2 \left[ 2 \left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} \right)^2 + 2 \left( \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} \right)^2 \right]^{\frac{1}{2}} \quad (9)$$

where  $c_t$  is a dimensionless constant  $c_t = 0.04$  and  $\delta$  the minimal cell size.

Turbulent thermal conductivity and species diffusivity are, thus, obtained from the turbulent Prandtl and Schmidt numbers,

$$\lambda_t = \mu_t C_p / Pr_t, \quad D_t = \mu_t / \rho Sc_t \quad (10)$$

##### 2. Liquid-Phase Equations

The liquid phase is represented by droplet groups. Each group includes droplets having the same composition, diameter, velocity, and temperature at injection. As the droplets move through the chamber, they remain in their initial group and, as a result, there is no mass transfer between groups. For each group, equations describing the Eulerian motion of the droplets are solved. Only the drag forces are considered. Coalescence, droplet breakup, and interaction forces between droplets are neglected. The liquid-phase equations are, thus, written in the following two-dimensional form.

Conservation equation of mass: For each group  $m$ , partial density  $\rho_m$  is defined as the mass per unit volume of droplets belonging to group  $m$ ,

$$\frac{\partial \rho_m}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{b} \frac{\partial \rho_m u_m b}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial \rho_m v_m}{\partial y} = \dot{W}_m^v + \dot{W}_m^{lf} \quad (11)$$

where  $\dot{W}_m^v$  and  $\dot{W}_m^{lf}$  represent the mass loss of group  $m$  caused by evaporation and the mass source due to lateral injection, respectively.

Conservation equations of momentum:

$$\frac{\partial \rho_m u_m}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{b} \frac{\partial \rho_m u_m^2 b}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial \rho_m u_m v_m}{\partial y} = f_{mx} + S_{mx}^v + S_{mx}^{lf} \quad (12)$$

$$\frac{\partial \rho_m v_m}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{b} \frac{\partial \rho_m u_m v_m b}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial \rho_m v_m^2}{\partial y} = f_{my} + S_{my}^v + S_{my}^{lf} \quad (13)$$

where  $f_{mx}$  and  $f_{my}$  are the group  $m$  drag force components,  $S_{mx}^v$  and  $S_{my}^v$  the momentum exchange terms between the two phases due to group  $m$  evaporation, and  $S_{mx}^{lf}$  and  $S_{my}^{lf}$  the momentum source terms due to lateral injection.

Conservation equation of droplet number:

$$\frac{\partial n_m}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{b} \frac{\partial n_m u_m b}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial n_m v_m}{\partial y} = S_{m,n}^{lf} \quad (14)$$

where  $S_{m,n}^{lf}$  represents the rate of change of the number of droplets resulting from lateral injection.

The droplet diameter is thus derived from the following expression, assuming spherical droplets:

$$D_m = \left( \frac{6\rho_m}{\pi\rho_L^*n_m} \right)^{1/3} \quad (15)$$

No droplet energy equation is solved as we neglect the transient heating time of the droplets and consider that the droplet surface temperature immediately reaches the vaporization temperature at local pressure and remains constant. This assumption is consistent with those made to establish the droplet vaporization model. It assumes that the heat transfer within the droplet is slow, which is valid for a vaporizing droplet in a high-temperature quiescent atmosphere. In the presence of convection where internal circulation tends to homogenize temperature inside the droplet, however, this assumption is not satisfactory. Indeed, some limited numerical analyses, including transient heatup and convection, showed that the surface temperature and the minimum temperature, which correspond to the vortex center, increase continuously. The analyses also showed that even with convection, a temperature gradient still exists inside the droplet. This suggests use of an effective conductivity model to account for this gradient. Improvement of the droplet heating model will be addressed in future work.

#### B. Source Terms due to Liquid and Gas-Phase Interaction

##### 1. Mass Source

*Vaporization.* As mentioned earlier, the one-dimensional droplet combustion model provides an analytical expression for the unsteady vaporization mass flow rate of a nonmoving droplet. The Ranz–Marshall correction is then applied to account for convection effects. This finally gives an expression of the vaporization mass flow rate  $\dot{m}$  for one droplet as a function of the droplet diameter, temperature, and local gas flow conditions. The mass loss term for group  $m$  may be given by

$$\dot{W}_m^v = -n_m\dot{m} \quad (16)$$

Consequently, the mass source terms are

$$\dot{W}^v = -\sum_m \dot{W}_m^v = \sum_m n_m\dot{m} \quad (17)$$

for the gas phase, and

$$\dot{W}_k^v = -\sum_{m_k} \dot{W}_{m_k}^v = \sum_{m_k} n_{m_k}\dot{m} \quad (18)$$

for those gaseous species  $k = 1, 2$ . The index  $m_k$  refers only to those groups of droplets with the same chemical composition as the  $k$ th species.

*Combustion.* A one-step chemical reaction is assumed to describe gas phase combustion:  $v_1 \text{ fuel} + v_2 \text{ oxidizer} \rightarrow \text{burnt products}$ .

The chemical reaction rate  $\dot{\omega}$  is given by the Arrhenius law,

$$\dot{\omega} = CCe^{-\frac{E}{T}} \prod_{k=1,2} \left( \frac{\rho_k}{M_k} \right)^{\alpha_k} \quad (19)$$

where  $CC$ ,  $T_u$ , and  $\alpha_k$  are coefficients to be given later for each propellant combination.

The species mass source terms due to gas-phase combustion are expressed as

$$\dot{W}_k^c = -v_k M_k \dot{\omega} \quad (20)$$

##### 2. Momentum Source

*Vaporization.* Assuming the vapor has the same velocity as the droplet when leaving the droplet surface, the momentum loss components for a group  $m$  may be written as

$$S_{mx}^v = \dot{W}_m^v u_m \quad S_{my}^v = \dot{W}_m^v v_m \quad (21)$$

and the momentum source components for the gas phase as

$$S_x^v = - \sum_m S_{mx}^v = - \sum_m \dot{W}_m^v u_m \quad (22)$$

$$S_y^v = - \sum_m S_{my}^v = - \sum_m \dot{W}_m^v v_m$$

*Droplet drag force.* The total droplet drag force appearing in the gas momentum conservation equations is given by

$$f = - \sum_m f_m \quad (23)$$

and the droplet drag force for a group  $m$  is

$$f_m = (\pi/8) \mu_l n_m D_m C_{Dm} Re_m (V - V_m) \quad (24)$$

where  $Re_m$  is the Reynolds number based on the relative gas-droplet velocity,

$$Re_m = \frac{\rho D_m}{\mu_l} |V - V_m| \quad (25)$$

The expression of the droplet drag coefficient  $C_{Dm}$  was corrected using the detailed droplet vaporization and burning analyses. Results obtained with the two-dimensional combustion model indicated that the drag coefficient of an evaporating droplet was approximately one-half the drag coefficient of a nonevaporating droplet. This is due to blowing of the boundary layer by the vaporized mass flow, which results in reduction of the friction forces.

The following relations have thus been used for the drag coefficient:

$$C_{Dm} = 12/Re_m (1 + 0.15 Re_m^{0.687}) \quad \text{if} \quad Re_m \leq 1000 \quad (26)$$

$$C_{Dm} = 0.22 \quad \text{if} \quad Re_m > 1000.$$

##### 3. Energy Source

**Vaporization.** To derive the internal energy source term, first the exchange of total energy  $E = e + V^2/2$  between the two phases is evaluated. The gas-phase energy source is a balance between the heat loss due to heatup and vaporization of the droplets and the energy increase due to the vaporized gas. The total energy source term is given by

$$S_E^v = S_E^{\dot{W}^v} - \Phi = \sum_{m_k} S_{E,m}^{\dot{W}^v} - \Phi_m \quad (27)$$

where  $\Phi$  is the heat flux absorbed by droplets.

According to the assumptions relative to droplet temperature and vapor velocity, the total energy produced by a group  $m$  may be written as

$$S_{E,m}^{\dot{W}^v} = -\dot{W}_m^v [e(T_m^v) + (V_m^2/2)] \quad (28)$$

The heat flux  $\Phi_m$  needed to increase the droplet temperature from the injection temperature to the vaporization temperature and vaporize the droplet is given by

$$\Phi_m = -\dot{W}_m^v \left( \int_{T_m^i}^{T_m^v} C_{p_m}^L dT + L_m^v \right) \quad (29)$$

where  $C_{p_m}^L$  is the specific heat at constant pressure and  $L_m^v$  is the latent heat of vaporization for the liquid constituting the group  $m$ .

The following expression is then obtained for  $S_E^v$ :

$$S_E^v = - \sum_m \dot{W}_m^v [h_m^i - r_m T_m^v + (V_m^2/2)] \quad (30)$$

where  $h_m^i$  is the specific enthalpy of group  $m$  at injection temperature and  $r_m = R/M_m$ , with  $M_m$  being the molar mass of the group  $m$  vaporized gas.

Deriving the internal energy conservation equation from the total energy and momentum conservation equations results in the following expression of the internal energy source term:

$$S_e^v = S_E^v + \dot{W}^v (V^2/2) - \mathbf{V} \cdot \mathbf{S}^v \quad (31)$$

This relation and the foregoing results lead to the following expression for  $S_e^v$ :

$$S_e^v = - \sum_m \dot{W}_m^v [h_m^i - r_m T_m^v + \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{V} - \mathbf{V}_m)^2] \quad (32)$$

**Drag force.** The work of the drag force  $S_e^{dw}$  appearing in the energy equation is expressed as

$$S_e^{dw} = \sum_m \mathbf{f}_m \cdot (\mathbf{V} - \mathbf{V}_m) \quad (33)$$

#### C. Source Terms due to Lateral Flow

Because the model cannot resolve the flow in the third direction ( $z$ ), a lateral mass flow (due to injection or the presence of an acoustic resonator) is handled as source terms (superscript  $lf$ ) in the conservation equations. This is achieved by integrating the liquid- and gas-phase equations in an elementary volume of the computational domain. Note that lateral flow assumes no tangential ( $y$  axis) velocity component.

The expressions of the source terms are written next in the general case of a lateral flow which may be gaseous (mass flowrate  $\dot{m}^{lf}$ ) or liquid (mass flow rate  $\dot{m}_m^{lf}$  for each group  $m$ ).  $V_{\text{cell}}$  refers to the computational cell volume.

The source terms for the gas phase are, for mass source,

$$\dot{W}^{lf} = \dot{m}^{lf} / V_{\text{cell}} \quad (34)$$

and, for momentum source,

$$S_x^{lf} = \dot{m}^{lf} u^{lf} / V_{\text{cell}} \quad S_y^{lf} = 0 \quad (35)$$

where  $u^{lf}$  is the longitudinal component of the lateral flow velocity  $V^{lf}$ .

The energy source is

$$S_e^{lf} = \frac{\dot{m}^{lf}}{V_{\text{cell}}} \left( h^{lf} + \frac{(V^{lf})^2}{2} - uu^{lf} + \frac{V^2}{2} \right) \quad (36)$$

where  $h^{lf}$  is the enthalpy of the lateral gas flow. The  $k$ -species mass source is

$$\dot{W}_k^{lf} = y_k^{lf} (\dot{m}^{lf} / V_{\text{cell}}) \quad (37)$$

where  $y_k^{lf}$  is the mass fraction of  $k$  species in the lateral flow.

The source terms for the liquid phase are for the mass source

$$\dot{W}^{lf} = \dot{m}^{lf} / V_{\text{cell}} \quad (38)$$

for the momentum source

$$S_{mx}^{lf} = \dot{m}_m^{lf} u_m^{lf} / V_{\text{cell}} \quad S_{my}^{lf} = 0 \quad (39)$$

and for the droplet number source

$$S_{m,n_m}^{lf} = \frac{1}{V_{\text{cell}}} \frac{6\dot{m}_m^{lf}}{\pi (D_m^{lf})^3 \rho_L} \quad (40)$$

where  $D_m^{lf}$  is the diameter of the group  $m$  droplets injected laterally.

Acoustic resonator modeling is discussed next. When lateral flow is due to gas flow exchange between the chamber and its acoustic resonators, the mass flow rate is given by a system of differential equations. This system describes the inflow and outflow of gas at the resonator orifice in response to chamber pressure fluctuations, according to the Helmholtz theory.<sup>1</sup> This theory assumes that the motion of the gas in the resonator is analogous to that of a mass-spring-dashpot system. The mass of the system is the gas in the orifice and its immediate vicinity, which is considered to move as a unit. This theory also assumes that the dimensions of the

acoustic resonators are small enough compared to the wavelengths of the chamber acoustic modes.

Therefore, the lateral mass flow rate  $\dot{m}^{lf}$  is given by the following ordinary differential equations:

$$l_{\text{eff}} \frac{d\dot{m}^{lf}}{dt} + R_0 \frac{\dot{m}^{lf}}{\bar{\rho}} + \frac{\bar{\rho} \bar{a}^2 A_{\text{ori}}^2}{V_{\text{cav}}} \bar{z} = A_{\text{ori}} p' \quad (41)$$

$$\dot{m}^{lf} = \bar{\rho} A_{\text{ori}} \frac{d\bar{z}}{dt} \quad (42)$$

where  $\bar{z}$  is the gas displacement along the orifice axis,  $\bar{\rho}$  and  $\bar{a}$  are the mean gas density and sound velocity in the resonator,  $p'$  is the chamber pressure fluctuation,  $A_{\text{ori}}$  is the cross-sectional area of the resonator orifice, and  $V_{\text{cav}}$  is the resonator cavity volume.

The effective orifice length  $l_{\text{eff}}$  is the sum of the orifice length  $l_{\text{ori}}$  and a length correction  $l_c$  that accounts for the flow effects in the vicinity of the orifice ends. An empirical equation for  $l_c$ , the most suitable for all conditions when the ratio  $A_{\text{ori}}/A_{\text{cav}}$  is less than 0.15, is

$$l_c = 0.96 \sqrt{A_{\text{ori}}} (0.5 - 0.7 \sqrt{A_{\text{ori}}/A_{\text{cav}}}) \quad (43)$$

The resistance per unit orifice cross-sectional area  $R_0$  accounts for nonlinear effects. Its expression is obtained from nonlinear analyses of Helmholtz resonator behavior,

$$R_0 = \Gamma \bar{\rho} \bar{U} \quad (44)$$

where  $\Gamma$  is a constant and  $\bar{U}$  the amplitude of the orifice gas velocity oscillations. In our model the instantaneous gas velocity is used instead of the amplitude.  $\Gamma$  is taken equal to 1, a commonly used value.

The quantity  $p'$  appearing in the acoustic resonator equations is taken as the chamber pressure fluctuation, and couples the resonator flow to the chamber flow.

Some assumptions have to be made with regard to the temperature and chemical composition of the flow in acoustic resonators.

#### D. Boundary Conditions

Because of the hyperbolic nature of the convective part of the gas-phase equations, the number of physical boundary conditions to be specified is based on the method of characteristics. At a boundary, this number is thus equal to the number of characteristics running into the computational domain. For the running-out characteristics, numerical boundary conditions, which depend on the computed flow, must be formulated.

Let us first consider the case of a gas flow injected at the inlet boundary. The subsonic conditions at this boundary imply that only one characteristic is running out of the computational domain. Thus, we chose to specify the gas momentum components, the species mass fractions, and the temperature, whereas the pressure is extrapolated from downstream flowfield. When no propellant or only droplets are injected at the inlet boundary, this boundary is considered as a solid wall for the gas.

At the outlet boundary, the flow being supersonic, all characteristics are out running, so that boundary conditions need not be set. All variables are extrapolated from the computational domain. When the exit flow is subsonic at the outlet of the computational domain, which was the case for some computations, the Mach number is imposed.

Considering now droplets at the inlet boundary, a complete set of independent parameters is specified. For each group  $m$ , we impose the velocity components, volume concentration, and diameter.

Solid walls may be present at the inlet, inside the combustor for baffle modeling, or at the lower and upper boundaries for planar two-dimensional analysis. At these boundaries, the normal component of gas and droplet velocity is set to zero, along with an adiabatic wall assumption. Wall shear stress is determined by a wall function matching approach as

$$\tau_w = \beta_f \mu_l u_T^0 / \Delta \quad (45)$$

where  $\Delta$  is the distance to the wall at which the shear stress is evaluated and  $\beta_f$  is a friction coefficient given by an analytical law as a function of the local Reynolds number:

$$\beta_f = 1 + 0.0236 \frac{(Re/80) + (Re/240)^2}{1 + (Re/80) + (Re/240)^2} (Re/4)^{0.811} \quad (46)$$

The Reynolds number is expressed as

$$Re = \rho u_T^0 \Delta / \mu_l \quad (47)$$

where  $u_T^0$  is determined directly or by an iterative method, depending on whether or not  $\Delta$  is in the viscous sublayer.

For tangential modes analysis using the annular geometry, the lower and upper boundary conditions are irrelevant in that it is only necessary to ensure periodicity.

#### E. Numerical Method

The partial differential equations for the gas and the liquid phases are solved by means of a finite difference method using the explicit predictor-corrector MacCormack<sup>27</sup> scheme. This is combined with a staggered grid; fluxes are defined at the cell sides, whereas scalar quantities are defined at the cell centers.

#### F. Instability Triggering Methods

To simulate unsteady behavior of the combustor, the model just described must be completed by a method of instability triggering. Different methods, based on industrial combustion stability rating techniques, have been investigated. They are all applied once the chamber steady-state flow has been computed.

The most commonly used method to rate engine dynamic stability is using explosive bombs. To model the finite amplitude pressure wave generated by a bomb, a sinusoidal pressure disturbance is initially imposed in a limited zone. Thus, the pressure distribution in this zone is given by

$$p(x, y) = \bar{p}(x, y)[1 + \alpha_p \sin(\beta_1 x + \beta_2) \sin(\gamma_1 y + \gamma_2)] \quad (48)$$

where  $\bar{p}$  is the steady-state pressure and  $\alpha_p$ ,  $\beta_i$ , and  $\gamma_i$  are constants to be set. Similar equations are used for densities  $\rho$  and  $\rho_k$  and internal energy  $\rho e$ , assuming

that the bomb-supplied mass has the same temperature and composition as the gas in the chamber.

Since this excitation method simultaneously triggers longitudinal, tangential, and combined acoustic modes of the chamber, an alternative version has been used to trigger exclusively tangential modes. In this case, the disturbed pressure applied on the chamber generatrix is given by

$$p(x, y) = \bar{p}(x, y)[1 + \alpha_p] \quad (49)$$

Another triggering method intended to simulate siren tests, which were performed in small divergentless chambers, was implemented in the numerical model. During such siren tests, longitudinal acoustic modes are triggered by successive partial closing up of the throat by means of a rotating wheel. This excitation method was implemented in the code as a time variation of the throat width ( $b_t$ ) at the longitudinal mode frequency during a few cycles.

### IV. Assessment of Engine Stability

In this section, numerical analysis of the stability of a cryogenic engine, including the effect of baffle and acoustic resonator, is presented. The investigation concerned the gas generator and the thrust chamber of the Ariane V main-stage engine. Both the gas generator and the thrust chamber use liquid oxygen and gaseous hydrogen injected through coaxial injector elements.

#### A. Physical Submodels

Let us first describe the atomization and vaporization models used for the analyses.

##### 1. Atomization Model

A cold-flow test program has been carried out to characterize coaxial injector sprays for both the gas generator and thrust chamber (see Chapter 6). Hardware configuration and test conditions were selected to make cold-flow simulant testing correspond as closely as possible to the engine operating conditions. Results of this program have led to the following correlation for the Sauter mean diameter  $D_{32}$  (in micrometers):

$$D_{32} = 127 \left( \frac{V_r}{160} \right)^{-0.93} \left( \frac{D_I}{2.10^{-3}} \right)^{+2.25} \left( \frac{D_g}{3.10^{-3}} \right)^{-2.65} \left( \frac{rec}{D_I} \right)^{-0.26} \quad (50)$$

where  $V_r$  is the relative gas-droplet velocity (in meters per second), and  $D_I$ ,  $D_g$ , and  $rec$  are the LOX post inner diameter, hydrogen annulus diameter, and recess, respectively (in meters).

This correlation, established with water/nitrogen and water/helium simulant combinations, is corrected for actual fluids (according to Ferrenberg et al.<sup>28</sup>), by multiplying the obtained diameter by the following coefficient  $K$ :

$$K = \frac{(\mu_L^{1/3} \sigma_L^{1/2} \rho_L^{-1/6})_{\text{actual propellant}}}{(\mu_L^{1/3} \rho_L^{1/2} \sigma_L^{-1/6})_{\text{simulant fluid}}} \quad (51)$$

where  $\sigma_L$  is the liquid surface tension.

##### 2. Vaporization Model

Analyses of oxygen droplet vaporization and burning in a quiescent atmosphere were carried out under supercritical conditions. Different ambient conditions (pressure, temperature, and hydrogen mass fraction) were investigated. An analytical law for the droplet instantaneous diameter evolution was derived from numerical results. As the droplet surface reaches supercritical conditions, droplet diameter was defined as that of the sphere bounded by the critical isotherm. This law is similar to those obtained in subcritical combustion

$$D^2(t) = D_i^2 - (K_v t)^{\alpha_v} (D_i^2)^{1-\alpha_v} \quad (52)$$

Coefficients  $\alpha_v$  and  $K_v$  depend on local pressure, temperature, and hydrogen mass fraction.

The vaporization rate in the absence of convection is then derived as

$$\dot{m}_0 = \rho_L \frac{\pi D(t)}{4} (D_i^2)^{(1-\alpha_v)/\alpha_v} \alpha_v K_v [D_i^2 - D^2(t)]^{(\alpha_v-1)/\alpha_v} \quad (53)$$

The Ranz–Marshall correction is then applied to take into account the convection effects.

##### 3. Combustion Model

To describe the  $H_2/O_2$  combustion, the parameters appearing in the Arrhenius law were taken as<sup>29</sup>

$$CC = 1.210^6, \quad T_A = 800 \text{ K}, \quad \alpha_1 = 1, \quad \alpha_2 = 1 \quad (54)$$

#### B. Effect of Damping Devices on Engine Stability

Numerical analysis of combustion stability of both the Vulcain thrust chamber and gas generator was carried out for different operating conditions. We illustrate these results by presenting those corresponding to nominal working conditions.

The reference operating points in terms of total mass flow rate and overall  $LOX/H_2$  mixture ratio are as follows. For the gas generator  $\dot{m}_T = 8.25 \text{ kg/s}$ , and  $r_m = 0.9$ . For the thrust chamber  $\dot{m}_T = 232 \text{ kg/s}$ , and  $r_m = 5.9$ .

The analysis was performed, using only one group of droplets to represent the spray. Injection droplet diameter and velocity were chosen as the Sauter mean diameter and the liquid-jet velocity, respectively. Droplets and gaseous hydrogen were uniformly injected at the chamber inlet.

To trigger instabilities, the computation was initiated by a bomb explosion as described earlier, the pressure perturbation having a sinusoidal form. The  $\alpha_p$  constant, which represents the maximum overpressure, was  $\alpha_p = 0.8$  for the gas generator and  $\alpha_p = 0.5$  for the thrust chamber.

To illustrate the results, the time evolutions of pressure in a cell close to the inlet boundary are given. Reduced values are used; the reference pressure is the steady-state pressure, and the reference time is of the order of the millisecond.

The graph shows a highly oscillatory pressure signal that starts at 1.0, drops sharply to about 0.75, and then exhibits large, sustained oscillations between approximately 0.8 and 1.8, with the amplitude of the initial peaks decreasing over time.](094a35044054a0b21a90a4cf571ff236_img.jpg)

##### 1. Gas Generator Results

Figure 2 shows undamped pressure oscillations in the gas generator without any damping device. The corresponding Fourier analyses are presented in Fig. 3. This figure shows that all the first harmonics of the chamber acoustic modes are initially excited, but the longitudinal and combined modes are rapidly damped. Unstable modes are the tangential ones, especially the first tangential (1T) and second tangential (2T). Conversely, when the gas generator is equipped with a baffle (Fig. 4) or acoustic resonators tuned to the first tangential mode frequency (Fig. 5), its behavior is stable.

##### 2. Thrust Chamber Results

The thrust chamber was found to be stable even without a damping device. A stable behavior was obtained at this operating point with overpressure intensities up to  $\alpha_p = 2$ .

#### C. Effect of Initial Droplet Size on Engine Stability

In the earlier analyses the gas generator without a damping device appeared to be the most sensitive to combustion instability. Thus, this chamber configuration was used to point out the effects of the spray injection parameters on the results. This problem was studied by varying the droplet injection diameter.

Computations were performed at the following operating point:  $\dot{m}_i = 4.13 \text{ kg/s}$ , and  $r_m = 0.94$ . Three different values of injection diameter were used.
