is an intermediate value. The unsteady computations were initiated using the bomb explosion method with a coefficient  $\alpha_p = 1.5$ .

Figures 6–8 show the pressure evolutions in a cell close to the inlet boundary using reference values as first defined. The two larger drop diameters lead to unstable operation whereas in the third case the fluctuations are damped. The larger the droplet size, the higher the amplitude of the pressure fluctuations. In the three cases, a large number of acoustic modes are initially excited, but most of them are quickly damped since the pressure signal rapidly appears well organized on one frequency. Spectral analysis of this signal indicates the presence of the second tangential mode and its harmonics. A second tangential combustion instability is thus associated with the largest droplet diameter, and to distributed vaporization. Injection of smaller droplets, which corresponds to high-vaporization rates in the injection zone, does not sustain instabilities. This result was confirmed by simulations for which the vaporized mass flow rate was artificially increased or decreased. An increase of this rate favors engine stability with regard to tangential modes.

### V. Comparison of Test Results with Numerical Analysis

In this section, we discuss comparisons between experimental data and numerical results. Experimental data were obtained for the storable propellant Viking engine, a one element LOX/H<sub>2</sub> combustor, and the Vulcain gas generator.

#### A. Viking Engine

After a combustion instability problem occurred during the operation of the Viking engine, a campaign was waged to rate the engine stability for different operating conditions, propellant nature, and injector geometries. These tests, carried out by Société Européenne de Propulsion (SEP),<sup>30</sup> enabled the characterization of

engine stability. The engine was more stable with the Viking injector type 2 (VI2) than with the Viking injector type 1 (VI1), the stability margin decreased as the working pressure increased, and the engine was more stable with the UH25 (75% of UDMH + 25% of hydrazine hydrate) than with UDMH.

Numerical computations were carried out to check whether these features could be recovered by the code.

The spray was represented by one group size of droplets with the Sauter mean diameter  $D_{32}$  derived from spray characterization studies.<sup>12</sup> Droplet injection velocity was set equal to the liquid-jet velocity. Droplet vaporization was described by analytical laws obtained from detailed droplet combustion analysis.<sup>13</sup> Gas-phase combustion was represented by the Arrhenius model with the following set of coefficients:

$$\begin{aligned} v_1 = 1, \quad v_2 = 1.203, \quad CC = 10^5, \quad T_A = 0 \\ \alpha_1 = 1, \quad \alpha_2 = 1.203 \end{aligned} \quad (55)$$

Different operating conditions were investigated, including injector geometry and working pressure. Instabilities were triggered by the bomb method. In the present analysis the disturbance had the following form:

$$p(x, y) = \bar{p}(x, y)[1 + \alpha_p] \quad (56)$$

Depending on the strength of the overpressure (value of  $\alpha_p$ ), the engine may or may not recover a stable operation. For given operating conditions, numerical analysis showed stable operation for small values of  $\alpha_p$  and unstable operation

Numerical simulation shows that, for unstable operation, oscillations develop and reach a limiting cycle regime. The resulting peak-to-peak pressure level  $\tilde{P}$  depends on the working pressure  $P_s$ .

Figures 9 and 10 present the final results of the engine stability assessment. Figure 9 shows the critical value  $\alpha_{plim}$  vs the reduced working pressure  $P_s/P_{ref}$ , and indicates that the stability margin decreases as the operating pressure increases. Figure 10 presents the pressure level  $\tilde{P}/P_{ref}$  vs  $P_s/P_{ref}$ . Peak-to-peak pressure level is increased with increasing working pressure. What is quite clear from these figures is the stabilizing effect of the VI2 injector. In another study, (not reported here) the propellant (UH25 instead of UDMH) caused the stability margin to increase. These results fit quite well with the experimentally observed engine behavior.

#### B. Vulcain Engine Gas Generator

During the development program of the gas generator of the Vulcain engine, SEP conducted a stability rating program, including subscale and full-scale tests. Subscale tests were performed using a one-element LOX/H<sub>2</sub> combustion chamber designed to operate at the same conditions as the gas generator. Full-scale tests were performed with the gas generator.

In this section we discuss the numerical analysis carried out for both combustors and compare the analysis with experimental data.

Comparison between predicted and experimental results indicated a higher experimental damping ratio than had been calculated but relatively good agreement on the evolution of this damping with the mixture ratio. The damping ratio of both first and second longitudinal modes decreased with increased mixture ratio. Even if absolute values were not recovered, the results were useful in comparing the stability of the engine under different working conditions.

Differences between predicted and experimental damping ratios may be caused by nozzle geometry representation, atomization, and vaporization models that must still be improved.

##### 2. Full-Scale Tests

These tests concern the assessment of dynamic stability of the gas generator. A series of bomb tests was carried out with a baffled and an unbaffled gas generator for this purpose. Different bomb sizes were used. The stability rating was determined for different working conditions. The tests were simulated with the Phedre numerical model, and results were compared with those of experimental tests.

The bomb is modeled using a group of cells called the bombed area, where the initial overpressure is imposed. The center of this area corresponds to the actual position of the bomb center.

Figure 13 is an example of the computed pressure evolution in a cell corresponding to the actual location of a pressure transducer. Figure 14 presents the same curve, filtered around 9000 Hz with a band width of 2000 Hz. The actual frequency of the second tangential mode was approximately 9600 Hz.

After adjusting the initial overpressure at the center of the bombed area on one experimental operating point to recover the initial level recorded on the pressure transducers, the entire pressure-mixture ratio domain was explored, i.e., all operating points where a bomb test was performed were numerically analyzed.

The conclusion reached from this work was that although the absolute value of the experimental damping ratio was not recovered by the numerical model, relative trends were well predicted. Differences between the numerical model and test results may be due to the vaporization and atomization models. Moreover, the Vulcain gas generator has a three-dimensional outlet, which cannot be modeled with the Phedre code. Only the evolution of the section along the curvilinear abscissa on the generator axis could be represented.

### VI. Conclusion

During the last four decades, liquid-propellant rocket engine development programs have been hampered by combustion instability problems. These problems remain a major concern for any rocket engine development program, particularly when a new design is involved.

Despite efforts to control and understand this phenomenon, rating the stability of an engine still relies on full-scale testing and semiempirical tools. Stabilizing devices such as baffles and acoustic resonators are often required to ensure stability.

The need for engines with high reliability and efficiency continues to increase. With limited funding for development programs, the instability problem cannot be solved by a trial and error method alone. Increased testing and more quantitative tools are needed.

Recent progress in diagnostic methods and computational resources offer new opportunities to develop tools that would help solving the problem. To control combustion instability, it is necessary to understand basic mechanisms; this requires extensive experimental research. Such efforts should involve both laboratory facilities accustomed to dealing with small-scale testing and intermediate- and full-scale test facilities. The latter are necessary to validate and complete data obtained by subscale testing, especially when laboratory experiments alone cannot cover the entire range of engine operating conditions.

Numerical analysis appears to be the proper direction toward better control of combustion instability. Current and future computers offer the means to achieve a better physical understanding of the detailed processes involved in liquid rocket operation from injection to combustion. Close contact must be maintained between research on basic mechanisms, numerical analysis, and full-scale testing. With this in mind, it should be possible to obtain predictive tools beneficial to the design of efficient and reliable engines.

The approach developed for liquid rocket combustion instability analysis involves development of a numerical model and research on physical modeling, with emphasis on spray characterization and detailed description of droplet vaporization and burning. A two-dimensional numerical model, Phedre, which incorporates various physical submodels (atomization, vaporization, and chemical reaction) is now available. It also includes baffles, acoustic resonators, and triggering methods.

Numerical analysis of combustion instability was performed for different combustors using storable and cryogenic propellants. Numerical results were compared with available data obtained from subscale or full-scale firing tests. Comparison

between experiments and numerical analysis almost always revealed/ good qualitative agreement and identical general trends. The fact that quantitative agreement is not always satisfactory highlights the need for physical modeling improvement and more realistic geometries (i.e., a three-dimensional numerical model).

Currently efforts are being made to develop a three-dimensional numerical model for combustion instability analysis.<sup>30</sup> Investigations on basic processes to obtain more relevant physical submodels are also being conducted on the ONERA cryogenic bench MASCOTTE.

## Chapter 19

## Application of Computational Fluid Dynamics Techniques to Engine Instability Studies

J. M. Grenda,\* S. Venkateswaran,<sup>†</sup> and C. L. Merkle<sup>‡</sup>

*Pennsylvania State University, University Park, Pennsylvania 16802*

### I. Introduction

OUR present understanding of liquid rocket combustion instability has been achieved through a combination of experimental investigations and approximate analytical models. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) has now advanced to the point where it can potentially complement these existing methods. The purposes of this chapter are to assess the potential role of CFD in combustion instability research and to explore the issues that are involved in bringing CFD methods to bear on combustion instability problems.

One of the advantages of computational analyses is that they permit very detailed physical descriptions of the liquid- and gas-phase processes to be coupled with the acoustics of the combustion chamber. Consequently, a most promising role of CFD is to serve as a computational testbed for demonstrating the effect of new analytical models of important subprocesses such as atomization and vaporization on the stability characteristics of a combustor. Similarly, such a computational testbed can be used to investigate the impact of experimental findings on stability behavior.

The development of a computational testbed for combustion instability requires careful validation against both analytical solutions and experimental results. Validation against analytical solutions is necessary to ensure that the numerical results represent accurate solutions to the equations and submodels that are chosen to represent the physics of the instability process. Validation against experimental data is necessary to ensure that the equations and submodels are physically meaningful.

In the present chapter, we discuss some of the fundamental characteristics that computational instability models must possess and identify some computational problems that are encountered in modeling the instability process. We also discuss the necessity for ensuring that computational models are sufficiently accurate and present methods for validation. Finally, to demonstrate current capabilities of

<sup>‡</sup>Professor of Mechanical Engineering.

computational instability methods, we present some representative results based on currently available physical submodels.

Computational instability models for liquid propellant engines are currently being developed in several groups. The model developed by Habiballah et al.<sup>1</sup> and Refs. 2–4 at ONERA, which has been applied to real engines perhaps more extensively than any other, solves the Navier–Stokes equations for the gas phase plus Eulerian formulation for the liquid phase. Their model considers annular geometries and includes comprehensive submodels for atomization, vaporization, turbulence, and finite rate chemistry. A similarly detailed model by Liang et al.<sup>5,6</sup> likewise includes atomization, vaporization, secondary breakup and droplet agglomeration, turbulence, species diffusion, and chemical kinetics. This model has been applied to both steady-state combustion and instability simulations.

In more recent work, Kim et al.<sup>7</sup> have reported solutions of the reacting Navier–Stokes equations for both axisymmetric and annular geometries, and Litchford and Jeng<sup>8</sup> have coupled an unsteady vaporization model based on a simple pressure-sensitive response with a two-dimensional annular geometry. In addition to these CFD models, Priem and Breisacher<sup>9</sup> have developed a three-dimensional, frequency-domain analysis that incorporates injection, atomization, and vaporization submodels. Their model provides the linear response to single-frequency disturbances although the physical subprocesses are incorporated as full nonlinear models.

The CFD analysis of the present authors<sup>10–12</sup> is philosophically similar to the Priem–Breisacher approach except that it is a time-domain method, and all nonlinear terms are retained. The time-domain solution enables the direct simulation of experimental events such as spontaneous disturbance growth and the response to bombs, but requires larger CPU requirements than does the linearized frequency-domain method. To circumvent this and to provide validation of our fully nonlinear analysis, we also have developed a companion linear time-domain analysis that is competitive with the Priem–Breisacher<sup>9</sup> analysis in CPU requirements. Wang et al.<sup>13</sup> have recently presented similar CFD results for the Euler equations utilizing a two-parameter collapsed combustion zone assumption analogous to that previously used by the current authors.

In the following section, we present the governing equations for the two-phase flowfields in liquid rocket engine combustors and outline appropriate models for the contributing physical subprocesses. Following this discussion, the important issues and numerical aspects of computational combustion instability are addressed.

### II. Governing Equations

Computational analyses of combustion instability require equation sets for the gas and the liquid phases along with appropriate interaction terms. The formulation for the gas phase entails standard equations although there may be some argument as to which terms should be retained. The analysis of the liquid phase requires a description of the continuous liquid as it enters the chamber, the ensuing atomization process, and the dynamics of the droplet cloud as it traverses the combustor, as well as expressions for droplet vaporization, mixing, and combustion. The submodels for these processes entail substantial physical modeling. Here, we concentrate upon employing available descriptions of the atomization and vaporization processes.

###### APPLICATION OF COMPUTATIONAL FLUID DYNAMICS TECHNIQUES 505

#### A. Selection of the Gas-Phase Equations

The first major issue in modeling gas-phase phenomena is whether to start from the Navier–Stokes equations or the Euler equations. The Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes equations coupled with species diffusion and chemical kinetics represent the most complete description of combustion instability, but the simpler Euler equations accurately describe the wave dynamics while omitting only the effects of viscous wave dissipation. The primary diffusive effects occur in the boundary layers along the combustor walls where they have little effect on the wave dynamics. Consequently, boundary layers may profitably be ignored and replaced by slip boundary conditions regardless of whether diffusive and turbulence effects are included elsewhere in the flowfield.

The dominant diffusion processes in the instability problem are those associated with the coupling between the energy release process and the gas dynamics. These include microscale mixing on the droplet level and mean flow recirculation effects near the injector face on the scale of individual injector elements. The microscale mixing phenomena between the vaporizing droplets and the surrounding hot gases most certainly affect the instability mechanisms, but their scale is too small to be resolved with either an Euler or a Navier–Stokes formulation. Consequently, their effect must be included globally in either representation so that their presence does not detract from the choice of an Euler formulation.

The mixing on the scale of injection elements may, however, be compromised by the choice of the Euler equations. Individual elements introduce oxidizer/fuel (O/F) striations into the flow whose convection and redistribution by acoustic disturbances could provide driving mechanisms. In addition, the recirculation zones near the injector face on the individual element scale could impact both steady and unsteady atomization. Unfortunately, these scales are also probably too small to be resolved in unsteady Navier–Stokes solutions.

In view of the preceding arguments and the computational requirements needed for the spray dynamics, we choose here to focus on the Euler equations. We emphasize that an accurate, validated Euler solution is a necessary precursor to a reacting Navier–Stokes solution. This extension requires few additional new concepts in terms of numerics or physics although the required computational resources are larger.

The Euler equations in cylindrical coordinates take the form

$$\frac{\partial \mathbf{Q}}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial \mathbf{E}}{\partial x} + \frac{1}{r} \frac{\partial \mathbf{F}r}{\partial r} + \frac{1}{r} \frac{\partial \mathbf{G}}{\partial \theta} = \frac{1}{r} (\mathbf{H}_{\text{gas}} + \mathbf{H}_{\text{liq}}) \quad (1)$$

where  $x$ ,  $r$ , and  $\theta$  are the axial, radial, and azimuthal coordinates. The vectors,  $\mathbf{Q}$ ,  $\mathbf{E}$ ,  $\mathbf{F}$ , and  $\mathbf{G}$ , are given by

$$\mathbf{Q} = \begin{bmatrix} \rho \\ \rho u \\ \rho v \\ \rho w \\ e \end{bmatrix} \quad \mathbf{E} = \begin{bmatrix} \rho u \\ \rho u^2 + p \\ \rho uv \\ \rho uw \\ (e + p)u \end{bmatrix} \quad \mathbf{F} = \begin{bmatrix} \rho v \\ \rho uv \\ \rho v^2 + p \\ \rho vw \\ (e + p)v \end{bmatrix} \quad \mathbf{G} = \begin{bmatrix} \rho w \\ \rho uw \\ \rho vw \\ \rho w^2 + p \\ (e + p)w \end{bmatrix} \quad (2)$$

Here,  $u$ ,  $v$ , and  $w$  are the velocity components in the axial, radial, and azimuthal directions, respectively. The density and pressure are given by  $\rho$  and  $p$ , and the total

energy is defined in terms of the internal energy  $e = \rho\varepsilon + 1/2\rho(u^2 + v^2 + w^2)$ , where  $\varepsilon = RT/\gamma - 1$  and  $R$  and  $\gamma$  represent the gas constant and specific heat ratio. For simplicity, we use constant specific heats and close the system by means of the perfect gas formulation  $p = \rho RT$ . Although written here in cylindrical coordinates, it is assumed that generalized coordinates are used throughout.

The source terms appearing on the right-hand side of Eq. (1) include radial and azimuthal effects,  $\mathbf{H}_{\text{gas}}$ , that arise from placing the governing equations in cylindrical coordinates, and the coupling terms,  $\mathbf{H}_{\text{liq}}$ , between the liquid and gas phases. These vectors are given as

$$\mathbf{H}_{\text{gas}} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ p + \rho w^2 \\ -\rho v w \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \quad \mathbf{H}_{\text{liq}} = \begin{bmatrix} S_c \\ S_{mx} \\ S_{mr} \\ S_{m\theta} \\ S_c \end{bmatrix} \quad (3)$$

The terms in  $\mathbf{H}_{\text{gas}}$  are standard. The quantities in  $\mathbf{H}_{\text{liq}}$  represent mass, momentum, and energy transfer from the liquid to the gas. It is through these terms that effects such as droplet vaporization and combustion energy release are coupled to the gas phase. These terms are defined subsequently.

#### B. Liquid-Phase Equations

For the liquid phase, we divide the droplet size distribution into bins of class  $k$ , partition the entering liquid among each droplet class at each instant of time, and track each class in Lagrangian fashion. As the droplets vaporize in the chamber, they transfer mass, momentum, and energy to the gas phase, thereby determining the source term  $\mathbf{H}_{\text{liq}}$  in Eq. (3).

The dynamic equations that govern each droplet class include an appropriate force balance and companion mass and energy conservation statements, written in vector form as

$$\frac{d\mathbf{Q}_\ell}{dt} = \mathbf{H}_\ell \quad (4)$$

where

$$\mathbf{Q}_\ell = [m_{d,k}, \mathbf{v}, T_d]^T \quad \mathbf{H}_\ell = \left[ -\dot{m}_{\text{vap},k}, \frac{\Sigma \mathbf{F}}{m_{d,k}}, \Delta \bar{E}_s \right]$$

Here,  $\mathbf{v}$  is the droplet velocity,  $\mathbf{F}$  the drag forces associated with the relative velocities between the phases,  $m_{d,k}$  the mass of a droplet in class  $k$  (kilogram per droplet),  $T_d$  the droplet temperature, and  $\dot{m}_{\text{vap},k}$  the vaporization rate of the droplet (kilogram per second per droplet).

The temperature distribution within the droplet is obtained from an energy balance whose form is dependent on the particular approach. Here we use  $\Delta \bar{E}_s$  to represent an appropriate difference between the energy arriving at and leaving the droplet surface. Options for treating the droplet temperature are considered in more detail subsequently.

#### C. Coupling Between the Liquid and Gas Phases

The source term  $\mathbf{H}_{\text{liq}}$  in Eqs. (1) and (3) is determined by dividing the combustor into finite volumes and summing the mass and energy generation rates and the

###### APPLICATION OF COMPUTATIONAL FLUID DYNAMICS TECHNIQUES 507

forces in Eq. (4) over all classes of particles in each volume. When expressed in the vector form used for the gas-phase equations, Eq. (1), these relations become

$$\mathbf{H}_{\text{liq}} = r \begin{bmatrix} \sum_k n_k \dot{m}_{\text{vap},k} / \Delta V \\ \sum_k \left( n_k \dot{m}_{\text{vap},k} u_k - \frac{1}{6} \pi \rho_k d_k^3 n_k \frac{du_k}{dt} \right) / \Delta V \\ \sum_k \left( n_k \dot{m}_{\text{vap},k} v_k - \frac{1}{6} \pi \rho_k d_k^3 n_k \frac{dv_k}{dt} \right) / \Delta V \\ \sum_k \left( n_k \dot{m}_{\text{vap},k} w_k - \frac{1}{6} \pi \rho_k d_k^3 n_k \frac{dw_k}{dt} \right) / \Delta V \\ \sum_k n_k \dot{m}_{\text{vap},k} [\bar{c}_{p,f}(T_k - T_g) - \lambda + h_{\text{comb}}] / \Delta V \end{bmatrix} \quad (5)$$

Here,  $\Delta V$  is the local cell volume,  $u_k$ ,  $v_k$ , and  $w_k$  are the droplet velocities,  $d_k$  is the droplet diameter,  $n_k$  is the number of droplets, and  $T_k$  and  $T_g$  are the entering vapor temperature and the ambient gas temperature. Remaining quantities in the energy source are the appropriately averaged specific heat of the vapor/gas mixture  $\bar{c}_{p,f}$ , the latent heat  $\lambda$ , and the heat of combustion  $h_{\text{comb}}$ .

#### D. Phenomenological Models for Physical Subprocesses

The evaluation of the sources in Eqs. (4) and (5) requires an atomization model and a vaporization model. Here, we take these models from the available literature.

##### 1. Atomization Models

Typical atomization models include both a mean drop size correlation and a droplet distribution function. Some representative mean drop size correlations<sup>14-16</sup> for coaxial injectors are provided in Table 1. In these expressions,  $u_{\text{rel}}$  is the relative velocity between the velocity and the gas phase; the bulk properties include the liquid viscosity  $\mu_\ell$ , the surface tension  $\sigma$ , and the gas and liquid densities  $\rho$  and  $\rho_\ell$ . In addition,  $D_1$  and  $D_2$  are post and injector diameters, and  $B$  is an empirical constant. From these mean drop size correlations and the liquid density, the mass per droplet and the number of droplets formed can be found.

**Table 1 Summary of atomization models for collapsed liquid zone**

| Model                | Mean dropsize correlation                                                                                                          |
|----------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Ingebo <sup>14</sup> | $d = 0.123 D_1 \left[ \left( \frac{\rho}{\rho_\ell} \right) \frac{\rho^2 D_1^2 u_{\text{rel}}^2}{\sigma \mu_\ell} \right]^{-0.44}$ |
| Mayer <sup>15</sup>  | $d = 9\pi \sqrt[3]{16B} \left[ \frac{\mu_\ell \sigma^{\frac{1}{2}}}{\rho u_{\text{rel}} \sqrt{\rho_\ell}} \right]^{\frac{2}{3}}$   |
| Nurick <sup>16</sup> | $d = 3.3 \times 10^{-5} \left[ \frac{\mu_\ell^{0.61}}{(u - \mu_\ell)^{1.4}} \right] \left[ \frac{D_1}{D_2} \right]$                |

The application of any steady-state atomization model in a quasisteady sense in an unsteady CFD code gives time-varying drop sizes, but this quasisteady treatment is only a stop-gap measure. Unsteady transverse disturbances are expected to have an important effect on droplet size, and models that include unsteady effects are urgently needed. Research aimed at providing more detailed models of the atomization process from first-principles calculations is currently underway. Although such calculations offer promise of providing improved atomization models, the effects of crossflow velocities and unsteady gas-phase conditions are beyond near-term computer capabilities, and they will probably have to be obtained from experiments. In the interim, the present quasisteady implementations must serve as a logical starting point for CFD-based instability analyses.

##### 2. Droplet Vaporization

Once the liquid droplets have been formed by atomization, they are convected through the combustor by the high-temperature gases while they simultaneously vaporize and burn. Substantial effort has gone into developing phenomenological models of spray vaporization. Most models are based on global heat and mass transfer balances over an isolated droplet in a quiescent environment that are later adjusted for convective effects. As a representative model, we consider the Priem and Heidmann model<sup>17</sup> that expresses the vaporization rate  $\dot{m}_{\text{vap}}$  and the heat feedback  $q_v$  as

$$\dot{m}_{\text{vap}} = \pi d \bar{\rho} D Sh \ln[p/(p - p_{v,s})] \quad (6)$$

$$q_v = [\dot{m}_{\text{vap}} \bar{c}_{p,v}(T_g - T_{d,s})/(e^e - 1)] \quad (7)$$

For clarity, the bin subscript  $k$  has been dropped. The parameters in Eqs. (6) and (7) include the mass diffusivity  $D$ , the partial pressure of the vapor at the droplet surface  $p_{v,s}$ , and the Sherwood number for mass transfer  $Sh$ . Additional predictions given later also include the Abramzon-Sirignano model.<sup>18</sup>

The expressions for the vaporization rate and the heat flux in Eqs. (6) and (7) require a knowledge of the droplet temperature. There are several levels of sophistication that can be used to model the droplet temperature variation. These range from an unsteady, two-dimensional treatment of the internal droplet fluid dynamic processes to the simple assumption of a uniform fixed droplet temperature. For a multidimensional computation with a large number of droplets, a full solution of the flowfield within each droplet is computationally prohibitive. At the other extreme, however, it is likely that a fixed droplet temperature will not allow appropriate stability predictions. A tractable compromise is the rapid-mixing limit in which the droplet temperature remains uniform because of strong liquid convection effects, but its time rate of change varies according to the difference between the energy leaving the surface due to vaporization and the energy arriving due to heat transfer,

$$\frac{dT_d}{dt} = \frac{q_v - \dot{m}_{\text{vap}} \lambda}{m_d c_{p,e}} \quad (8)$$

where  $T_d$  corresponds to the droplet temperature. In an unsteady gas phase, this model allows temporal oscillations in the droplet temperature that induce a phase

###### APPLICATION OF COMPUTATIONAL FLUID DYNAMICS TECHNIQUES 509

difference between the vaporization and gas oscillations. This is an important instability driving mechanism as is demonstrated later.

##### 3. Other Potential Coupling Mechanisms

In addition to atomization and vaporization mechanisms, other phenomena including injector coupling, droplet-turbulence interactions, chemical kinetics, and secondary droplet breakup can also drive combustion instability. As with the work discussed here, algebraic correlations for any of these phenomena could, in principle, be incorporated in numerical simulations of combustion instability.<sup>19</sup>

### III. Computational Fluid Dynamics Aspects of Combustion Instability

#### A. Separation of the Equations into Mean and Disturbance Components

The computational resources required for solving the Navier–Stokes or Euler equations in three-dimensional unsteady flowfields restricts the number of solutions that can be practically computed. Consequently, it is important to be able to rely on some simpler analyses for obtaining initial qualitative understanding and for providing a guide and validation procedure for the full numerical solutions. We obtain a simple analysis by splitting the flow variables into mean and fluctuating quantities and linearizing the results. Accordingly, expand the vectors  $\mathbf{Q}$ ,  $\mathbf{E}$ ,  $\mathbf{F}$ ,  $\mathbf{G}$ , and  $\mathbf{H}$  as

$$\begin{aligned}\mathbf{Q}(x, r, \theta, t) &= \bar{\mathbf{Q}}(x) + \mathbf{Q}'(x, r, \theta, t) \\ \mathbf{E} &= \bar{\mathbf{E}} + \mathbf{E}' = \bar{\mathbf{E}} + \bar{\mathbf{A}}\mathbf{Q}'\end{aligned}\quad (9)$$

and similarly for the flux vectors  $\mathbf{F}$ ,  $\mathbf{G}$ , and  $\mathbf{H}$ . In these expressions, overbars refer to the mean and primes to unsteady fluctuations, and  $\bar{\mathbf{H}}$  indicates the sum of  $\mathbf{H}_{\text{liq}}$  and  $\mathbf{H}_{\text{gas}}$ . The Jacobians are given by  $\mathbf{A} = \partial \mathbf{E} / \partial \mathbf{Q}$ ,  $\mathbf{B} = \partial \mathbf{F} / \partial \mathbf{Q}$ ,  $\mathbf{C} = \partial \mathbf{G} / \partial \mathbf{Q}$ , and  $\mathbf{D} = \partial \mathbf{H} / \partial \mathbf{Q}$ .

Substituting Eq. (9) into Eq. (1) gives separate equation sets for the mean flow and the unsteady portion. The mean flow equations are uncoupled from the unsteady part and can be solved before the perturbation solution. The perturbation equation takes the linear three-dimensional form,

$$\frac{\partial \mathbf{Q}'}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial \bar{\mathbf{A}}\mathbf{Q}'}{\partial x} + \frac{1}{r} \frac{\partial \bar{\mathbf{B}}\mathbf{Q}'r}{\partial r} + \frac{1}{r} \frac{\partial \bar{\mathbf{C}}\mathbf{Q}'}{\partial \theta} = \frac{1}{r} \bar{\mathbf{D}}\mathbf{Q}' \quad (10)$$

Although this equation is linear, its solution takes nearly as much effort as solving the entire nonlinear equations.

To obtain an equation whose numerical solution can be obtained very rapidly, we restrict the mean flow to one-dimensional (axial) variations and take the radial and azimuthal mean velocities  $\bar{v}$  and  $\bar{w}$  as zero so that the equations admit a separable solution,

$$\mathbf{Q}' = \begin{bmatrix} \hat{\rho}(x, t) RZ \\ \hat{u}(x, t) RZ \\ \hat{\rho}v(x, t) R'Z/\lambda \\ \hat{\rho}w(x, t) RZ'/\lambda r \\ \hat{e}(x, t) RZ \end{bmatrix} \quad (11)$$

where  $R$  is a Bessel function of order  $\mu$ ,  $R = C_3 J_\mu(\lambda r)$ , and  $Z$  is the trigonometric function,  $Z = C_1 \cos(\mu\theta) + C_2 \sin(\mu\theta)$ . (Superscript primes denote differentiation with respect to the arguments.) The wave number  $\lambda$  is determined by requiring that the normal velocity fluctuations vanish at the wall,  $J_\mu(\lambda r_w) = 0$ , where  $r_w$  denotes the wall radius.

After substituting Eq. (11) into Eq. (10) and separating variables, we obtain the equation for the amplitude function,

$$\frac{\partial \hat{Q}}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial \bar{A} \hat{Q}}{\partial x} + \bar{B} \hat{Q} = \bar{D}_{\text{liq}} \hat{Q} \quad (12)$$

where the vector  $\hat{Q} = (\hat{\rho}, \hat{\rho}u, \hat{\rho}v, \hat{\rho}w, \hat{e})^T$ , and the matrices  $\bar{A}$ ,  $\bar{B}$ , and  $\bar{D}_{\text{liq}}$  are given elsewhere.<sup>19</sup> Note that the solution requires that  $\hat{\rho}v$  and  $\hat{\rho}w$  be identical.

As Eq. (12) suggests, the three-dimensional perturbation relation has been reduced to an unsteady equation in one space variable, even though the resulting solutions represent full three-dimensional disturbances. This equation can be solved at a small fraction of the effort of the fully three-dimensional set in Eq. (10) and can be used very effectively as a diagnostic tool. Further, it provides an efficient means of performing exploratory three-dimensional stability surveys prior to attempting nonlinear computations. The full nonlinear calculations can then be validated against these small amplitude results in the small disturbance limit.

#### B. Constant Coefficient Equation and Analytical Solution

By requiring the mean flow and the atomization, vaporization, and combustion models to be independent of  $x$ , Eq. (12) can be solved analytically. These solutions are restricted in the physical problems they simulate, but they are useful for qualitative understanding and numerical validation. The restrictions on the analytical solution can later be removed in the numerical code to test the impact of simplifying assumptions on the overall physics. Representative comparisons of this type are given in Sec. IV. The analytical solution also requires a formal linearization of the physical submodels for atomization, vaporization, and injector coupling.

If no mean axial variations are present and the liquid-phase source term is taken as constant, Eq. (12) admits solutions of the form

$$p' = \text{Re}[(P_1 e^{-k^+ x} + P_2 e^{-k^- x}) J_\mu(\lambda r) e^{i\mu\theta} e^{i\omega t}] \quad (13)$$

with similar relations for the remaining variables. Here,  $\omega$  is the frequency,  $k^\pm$  are the axial wave numbers of the disturbance,  $P_1$  and  $P_2$  denote the amplitude of the pressure, and  $\text{Re}$  refers to the real part.

Because our reason for obtaining an analytical solution is to understand the physical aspects of the instability problem and to validate the numerical algorithm, we choose a two-zone, distributed combustion model as depicted in Fig. 1, and linearize the atomization and vaporization submodels in this region. We start from the atomization relations given in Table 1 that show that the droplet size depends on the liquid- and gas-phase velocities, the physical properties of the liquid, and the thermodynamic state of the gas. To represent the gas, we choose its pressure and entropy  $s$ . We then express the atomization relations in the functional form,  $d = d(p, u, s, T_\ell, u_\ell)$  where  $u$  here represents the velocity magnitude, and the subscript  $\ell$  refers to the liquid. For simplicity, we ignore variations in the liquid and droplet velocity and consider an isentropic gas-phase fluctuation. These are

$\dot{m}_{\text{vap}} = (p, u, s, T_\ell)$ , and here again, we omitted variations in the droplet velocity and are restricted to isentropic gas fluctuations. Note that the vapor-pressure dependence in Eq. (6) can be expressed implicitly as a dependence on the liquid temperature through the Clausius–Clapeyron equation,  $p_v = f(T_\ell)$ .

Equation (15) can be reduced to two variables by combining it with an analogous linearized expression for the heat feedback to the droplet [Eq. (7)],

$$\frac{q'_v}{\dot{q}_v} = \left[ \alpha_q \frac{p'}{p} + \beta_q \frac{u'}{u} + \delta_q \frac{T'_\ell}{T_\ell} \right] \quad (16)$$

where the constants  $\alpha_q$ ,  $\beta_q$ , and  $\delta_q$  represent the partial derivatives for the heat transfer relations. Expressions for these coefficients are given in Table 3 for the Priem–Heidmann model. Here,  $Re$  is the droplet Reynolds number, and  $Pr$  and  $Nu$  are the Prandtl and Nusselt numbers, respectively.

To eliminate the temperature dependence in Eq. (16), we linearize the energy balance in Eq. (8) to give

$$\frac{dT'_\ell}{dt} = \frac{1}{\bar{m}_d \bar{c}_{p,\ell}} \left[ q'_v - \dot{m}'_{\text{vap}} \bar{\lambda} - \bar{m}'_{\text{vap}} \frac{d\lambda}{dT_\ell} T'_\ell \right] \quad (17)$$

where the derivative of the heat of vaporization with respect to the liquid temperature is here retained to allow expressions that depend on both  $T'_\ell$  and its time rate of change. Then, combining Eqs. (15–17) and using complex notation, we obtain the two-parameter vaporization expression,

$$\dot{m}'_{\text{vap}} = \bar{m}_{\text{vap}} \left[ \alpha^* \frac{p'}{p} + \beta^* \frac{u'}{u} \right] \quad (18)$$

**Table 3 Summary of Priem–Heidmann linearization constants**

|-------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
|       | $\alpha_v(X_1/\gamma) - (p_{v,s}/Y)$                                                                                        |
|       | $\beta_v(uX_1/ u - u_d )$                                                                                                   |
|       | $\delta_v = \frac{T_\ell}{Y} \frac{dp_{v,s}}{dT_\ell}$                                                                      |
|       | $\alpha_q = \alpha_v + \frac{\gamma - 1}{\gamma} \frac{T}{T - T_\ell} + \frac{Z^2 p_v}{Y} - \frac{Z^2}{\gamma} (X_1 - X_2)$ |

###### APPLICATION OF COMPUTATIONAL FLUID DYNAMICS TECHNIQUES 513

where the complex coefficients  $\alpha_v^*$  and  $\beta_v^*$  are given by

$$\alpha_v^* = \alpha_v + \frac{\delta}{\phi} \left[ \alpha_q - \bar{\lambda} \frac{\bar{m}_{\text{vap}}}{\bar{q}_v} \alpha_v \right] \quad (19)$$

$$\beta_v^* = \beta_v + \frac{\delta}{\phi} \left[ \beta_q - \bar{\lambda} \frac{\bar{m}_{\text{vap}}}{\bar{q}_v} \beta_v \right] \quad (20)$$

and the quantity  $\phi$  is given by

$$\phi = \frac{\bar{m}_{\text{vap}} \bar{T}_\ell}{\bar{q}_v} \frac{d\lambda}{dT_\ell} + \frac{\bar{m}_{\text{vap}} \bar{\lambda}}{\bar{q}_v} \delta_v - \delta_q + i w \frac{m_d c_{p,\ell} \bar{T}_\ell}{\bar{q}_v} \quad (21)$$

Equation (18) provides a relationship for the rate of vaporization from a liquid droplet as a function of pressure and velocity fluctuations. The expressions  $\alpha_v^*$  and  $\beta_v^*$  are functions of the complex frequency of the gas-phase oscillations. Because Eq. (17) is a differential rather than an algebraic expression, the vaporization response is not in phase with the pressure and velocity oscillations. This out-of-phase component arises from the temperature fluctuations within the liquid droplet and has a major impact on stability characteristics.

In the absence of droplet temperature fluctuations, Eq. (18) reduces to Eq. (16), with the  $T_\ell$  variations set to zero. In this case,  $\alpha_v^*$  and  $\beta_v^*$  become real and reduce to the linearization coefficients  $\alpha_v$  and  $\beta_v$ . The values of  $\alpha_v^*$  and  $\beta_v^*$  along with corresponding values for  $\alpha_d$  and  $\beta_d$  directly determine the stability characteristics of a combustor.

Finally, we note that the effects of atomization and vaporization can be combined with other physical phenomena such as injector coupling or secondary breakup to obtain a complete instability model. The overall linearization coefficients relating unsteady responses to disturbances in the chamber can be combined as

$$\alpha = \alpha_v^* - 3\alpha_d + \alpha_{inj} + \dots \quad (22)$$

with an analogous expression for  $\beta$  where the factor of three multiplying the droplet fluctuation changes the droplet size fluctuation to a vaporization fluctuation.

#### C. Nonlinear Finite Difference Spectral Procedure

The solution of nonlinear three-dimensional transient flowfields remains non-trivial from the standpoint of computational resources. Finite difference solutions of the three-dimensional unsteady equations given in Eq. (1) coupled to the liquid phase may become prohibitively expensive. Because of limitations in grid size and difficulties caused by the presence of the axis of symmetry, economical solutions to the three-dimensional Euler equations are perhaps most efficiently obtained through a spectral decomposition of the tangential direction. Traditional finite differences are used in the axial and radial directions. This mixed character approach utilizes a Fourier expansion of the primary variable  $\mathcal{Q}$  represented by truncated series of the form

$$\mathcal{Q} = \sum_{m=0}^M \left[ \hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{m,c}(x, r, t) \cos m\theta + \hat{\mathcal{Q}}_{m,s}(x, r, t) \sin m\theta \right] \quad (23)$$

where the amplitude coefficients are

$$\hat{\mathbf{Q}}_{m,c} = (\hat{\rho}_c, \hat{\rho}u_c, \hat{\rho}v_c, \hat{\rho}w_c, \hat{e}_c, 0, 0, 0, 0)^T \quad (24)$$

$$\hat{\mathbf{Q}}_{m,s} = (0, 0, 0, 0, 0, \hat{\rho}_s, \hat{\rho}u_s, \hat{\rho}v_s, \hat{\rho}w_s, \hat{e}_s)^T \quad (25)$$

These coefficients corresponding to the Fourier mode  $m$  are time-dependent functions of both the axial and radial directions. The general series formulation permits both spinning and standing mode wave solutions to be calculated.

By substituting these expressions into Eq. (1), the general dynamic equation governing the development of the flowfield in Fourier space can be written as

$$\frac{\partial \hat{\mathbf{Q}}_{m,T}}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial \hat{\mathbf{E}}(\hat{\mathbf{Q}}_{m,T})}{\partial x} + \frac{1}{r} \frac{\partial \hat{\mathbf{F}}(\hat{\mathbf{Q}}_{m,T})^r}{\partial r} = \mp \frac{m}{r} \hat{\mathbf{G}}(\hat{\mathbf{Q}}_{m,T}) + \frac{1}{r} \hat{\mathbf{H}}_{\text{tot}}(\hat{\mathbf{Q}}_{m,T}) \quad (26)$$

Here, the vectors  $\hat{\mathbf{E}}$ ,  $\hat{\mathbf{F}}$ ,  $\hat{\mathbf{G}}$ , and  $\hat{\mathbf{H}}_{\text{tot}}$  are written as functions of the amplitude coefficients  $\hat{\mathbf{Q}}_{m,T}$ . In this expression, the variable  $\hat{\mathbf{Q}}_{m,T}$  is defined as the sum of the amplitude coefficients  $\hat{\mathbf{Q}}_{m,c}$  and  $\hat{\mathbf{Q}}_{m,s}$ , and  $\hat{\mathbf{H}}_{\text{tot}}$  is a combination of the gaseous- and liquid-phase source term vectors. This relationship reduces the three-dimensional equations for the continuum gas phase to  $2M + 1$  sets of two-dimensional equations. For standing mode calculations, the equations can be recast in a form in which each of the dynamic equations decouple in the tangential direction. This results in only  $M + 1$  sets of two-dimensional equations.

In both the standing and spinning mode computations, the calculation of the shape functions in the Fourier domain provide the flow variables in three-dimensional physical space. These are defined by the summation of the truncated series of the primary vector  $\hat{\mathbf{Q}}$ . In either situation, the spectral decomposition procedure should result in a decrease in computational time required over three-dimensional finite difference calculations since the Fourier series representation in  $M + 1$  or  $2M + 1$  modes replaces the discretized azimuthal direction. The solution of the general dynamic equation given in Eq. (26) is obtained through an explicit four-step Runge–Kutta time integration. A more detailed discussion of the mixed finite difference/Fourier spectral scheme can be found in Ref. 19.

### IV. Representative Results

In this section, we present representative results to give concrete examples of the concepts just discussed and to illustrate how available models of atomization and vaporization can be combined with CFD analyses to study instability characteristics. The use of existing physical submodels enables instability characteristics to be tied to specific hardware configurations such as injector type and size, engine operating conditions, and combustor geometry. In addition, the identification of the most sensitive parameters in the models points the way for further diagnostic experiments, whereas the computational tools provide a testbed in which the effects of these findings on stability characteristics can be determined. We begin with an investigation of the global topology of the unstable regions of combustion instability models based on representative atomization–vaporization descriptions. Chamber conditions for the following predictions are: chamber diameter and length (chamber of length 0.36 m and radius 0.23 m), mean flow Mach number, 0.10 (150 m/s), droplet injection velocity 100 m/s and temperature 125 K, and mean pressure 40 atm and temperature 3000 K.

#### A. Global Stability Characteristics of Atomization-Vaporization-Based Models

The nondimensional coefficients  $\alpha^*$  and  $\beta^*$  represent a two-parameter combustion response function that defines a complete stability map. To apply such two-parameter analyses, both the range of  $\alpha^*$  and  $\beta^*$  values that lead to instability and the range of values that is physically realizable must be determined. The stability characteristics of an engine are then defined by the overlap between these two  $\alpha^*$ - $\beta^*$  regions. To facilitate understanding, we begin by considering the case where the droplet temperature is fixed so that the parameters  $\alpha$  and  $\beta$  become real so that the analysis can be presented on the  $\alpha^*$ - $\beta^*$  plane.

The magnitude of the atomization parameters can be inferred directly from Table 2, but the vaporization parameters require some calculation. To demonstrate their magnitude, representative ranges are given in Figs. 2 and 3 for both the Priem-Heidmann<sup>7</sup> and Abramson-Sirignano<sup>18</sup> models. Figure 2 shows that  $\alpha_v^*$  is negative for both models ( $\dot{m}'_{\text{vap}}$  decreases as pressure increases) and is a weak function of droplet Reynolds number, whereas Fig. 3 shows that  $\beta_v^*$  is positive and decreases with Reynolds number. The rapid decrease in  $\beta_v^*$  at low Reynolds numbers reflects the increased sensitivity as the mean relative velocity approaches zero.

Given these physically realizable ranges of  $\alpha_v^*$  and  $\beta_v^*$ , we now compare them with the companion stability characteristics obtained by solving the two-parameter model. Results for the most unstable (or least stable) mode selected from the first tangential (1T), first radial (1R), and arbitrary longitudinal (nL)(typically first or second) mode are shown in Fig. 4. These results are obtained from a combination of the analytical and linearized numerical models.

The two-parameter formulation shows an unstable region in the upper left hand corner of the  $\alpha$ - $\beta$  plane as indicated by the neutral stability curve (solid line). Note that  $\alpha = \alpha_v$  and  $\beta = \beta_v$  for this constant droplet temperature case. The dashed lines show contours of constant growth (decay) rate, with positive values indicating growth and negative values attenuation. The magnitude of these numbers indicates the percent amplitude change per cycle. Realistic ranges of the  $\alpha$ - $\beta$  parameters corresponding to the two vaporization models (Figs. 2 and 3)

The vaporization-only results are more stable than the combination of atomization plus vaporization, but neither the Abramson-Sirignano model nor the Priem-Heidmann model predicts instability for the constant temperature droplet case. The  $\alpha$ - $\beta$  parameter range for combined atomization-vaporization results is, however, close enough to the neutral stability curve to suggest that the addition of a third effect (for example, injection coupling) could lead to instability in this constant droplet temperature case.

Before leaving this initial example, we pause to reflect on the difficulty of verifying that a given instability model is absolutely stable while using only a CFD code. Proof of absence of instability without analytical guidelines is essentially impossible, even though it is critical to establishing instability mechanisms by turning various effects "on" and "off" as is so easy to do with CFD analyses. This observation is the primary reason for pursuing the present synergistic modeling philosophy.

#### B. Validation and Error Estimation of Numerical Solutions by Comparison with Analytical Solutions

The analytical solution described can be used to validate both the linearized numerical procedure and the full nonlinear analysis in the small amplitude limit. The validation referred to here has only to do with ensuring that the numerical results represent the correct solutions to the stability model. The issue of verifying the accuracy of the stability model must be done by comparison with experiment.

In validating the numerical procedures, we use an initial condition corresponding to a single-mode analytical solution. The resulting amplitude growth and phase error can then be determined by comparing with the exact solution. We consider an instability model based on vaporization effects alone. We also include the effects of temperature fluctuations. Inlet conditions for the LOX droplets are 120 K and a monodisperse droplet diameter of 90  $\mu\text{m}$ . These conditions result in a vaporization length of about half the combustor. This operating condition is subject to an unstable 1T, 1R, 1L mode that grows approximately 20% per cycle as shown in Fig. 5.

Comparisons of the numerical and analytical pressure oscillations are given in Fig. 6 for two angular positions near the wall and the injector face for the linearized numerical analysis with 201 grid points in the axial direction. As can be seen, the numerical and analytical solutions are nearly indistinguishable. Quantitative evaluation of the difference indicates an amplitude error of 0.1% per cycle and a

An analogous study of numerical accuracy in the nonlinear code is presented in Fig. 6. These grid refinement studies show that second-order algorithms require some 40 grid points per wavelength. This grid density requirement can be reduced by switching to fourth-order systems that require only about 10 points per wavelength.<sup>20</sup>

#### C. Response to Arbitrary Disturbances

Unstable disturbances in liquid rocket engines generally arise from broadband disturbances within the chamber. With a broadband initial condition, each mode grows or decays according to its individual stability character, and the long-time solution will be dominated by the most unstable mode. The analytical solution predicts the most unstable mode (apart from nonlinear effects) for any set of operating conditions and can again be used as a check on the numerical results. Long-term nonlinear calculations should differ from linear calculations thereby displaying effects of finite amplitude.

Solutions obtained with the linearized numerical model to verify that it will pick out the most unstable mode are given in Fig. 8. Figure 8a is for the fluctuating droplet temperature case whereas Fig. 8b is for the constant droplet temperature case. The initial condition for the fluctuating temperature droplet is an arbitrary

The short-term response to this disturbance contains low-frequency waves that slowly propagate through the flowfield. As the disturbances interact with the distributed combustion process, the oscillations grow, and a beat frequency appears as the selective wave amplification by the instability model begins to take over. When carried out for long times, the final growth rate agrees with the analytically predicted maximum growth rate to within 1/2%, thus giving further validation of the analysis.

Corresponding calculations for the constant temperature droplet result in stable response over the entire spectrum as can be seen from Fig. 8b. To obtain a nontrivial problem, this case is started with a combination of a single-mode solution plus an arbitrary disturbance.

The preceding examples have relied on the two-zone, constant mean flow conditions that were used to obtain analytical solutions. A uniform mean flow assumption is not necessary for the linearized numerical solutions (or the full Euler equations), and we now relax this restriction. Because a variable mean flow does not allow analytical solutions, we lack an appropriate initial condition for single-mode solutions, and so all results are limited to the response to arbitrary disturbances.

### V. Conclusions

It would appear that the most promising role for computational fluid dynamics in combustion instability research is to serve as a testbed for determining the effect of various physical mechanisms on the instability process. This testbed would then evaluate analytical models of individual processes that had been developed through diagnostic experiments and approximate analytical procedures to ascertain their effect on stability. The capability for turning various mechanisms on and off in the CFD testbed should be particularly useful in understanding fundamental mechanisms.

For a CFD analysis to be used in combustion instability, it is imperative that it be validated carefully. Validation at small amplitude is most effectively made by comparing with analytical results from simplified, closed-form analytical expressions, including linearizations of the atomization and vaporization models. Additional validation against experimental measurements is then needed to verify submodel predictions.

In addition to using linearized models for validation purposes, these models are also useful for identifying the basic instability features of a given instability model. These features are difficult to identify with a full, multidimensional, nonlinear computer model, but a simplified small amplitude numerical procedure that permits full three-dimensional disturbances in a one-dimensional mean flow is given that can rapidly provide a complete map of instability solutions to define an entire engine operating regime. The full nonlinear analysis can then be used to ascertain finite amplitude effects, more realistic mean flow variations on more

detailed submodels in specific locales of the parameter space that makes up the instability hypersurface, rather than having to compute the entire multidimensional surface.

As a demonstration of the types of results that can be obtained from a CFD testbed, this hierarchy of synergistic models has been used to compute the instability characteristics as determined by classical atomization and vaporization models. This choice of submodel ties the combustion model directly to observable physical phenomena and ensures that the parameters used in the model are realistic. The results again point out the importance of phase lags introduced by unsteady vaporization effects in the droplets. The results also point out the necessity for developing models that describe unsteady atomization effects and more accurate dynamic models of droplet vaporization.

#### Introduction

**C**OMBUSTOR process high-frequency stability refers to the ability of a process property to continue without developing oscillations that correspond to acoustic frequencies. The spectral analysis of pressure pulsations upstream of the injector and combustor shell vibrations is a common way of studying stability in liquid rocket engines (LREs) both in stand-alone tests and in tests where the LRE is part of a stage. Measurements of pressure pulsations upstream of the injector and measurement of combustor shell vibration, rather than direct measurement of pressure pulsations in combustors and gas generators, are done primarily for two reasons. 1) The measurements of pulsations and vibrations upstream of the injector are sensitive enough to various phenomena in the combustor, the engine fluid systems (including the cooling system), and others that influence engine high-frequency stability to provide information with which to estimate stability margin. 2) Provision of engine test safety is easier while using these types of measurement, as they do not require any additional holes in the combustion zone.

There are various ways of applying results from the spectral analysis of these measurements to the study of engine high-frequency stability. Several features of a spectral analysis are 1) the number of measured parameters being analyzed (it may be only pressure pulsations upstream of the injectors, only shell vibration,

or both); 2) the bandwidth of frequencies being analyzed, i.e., a narrow band of frequencies specified a priori in an interval not more than  $\pm 10\%$  of natural acoustic frequencies, or a wide band of several thousand hertz within which all narrow bands mentioned are analyzed; 3) single amplitude-frequency spectrum parameters, e.g., amplitude and oscillation decrement; 4) characteristics that are used for subsequent solutions, single measurement results (maximum values when amplitude measurements are used for solutions, minimum values if decrements are analyzed), or statistical estimates of these parameters; and 5) the possibility of comparing the reduced results from the formal analysis.

Combinations of these features form a matrix of conceptually possible ways of using spectral analysis data to study LRE high-frequency instability. Such a matrix is shown in Table 1. Of course, the matrix does not include all possible situations; for example, there is no division by the number of similar measurements (pressure pulsations upstream of injection elements of one or both propellants, one- or many-directional vibrations). The matrix, however, does contain the main methodological peculiarities connected with obtaining initial information for subsequent analysis and the engine state qualification as acceptable or nonacceptable from the standpoint of high-frequency stability. Generalized data on the application of spectral analysis in the practice of engine development are given in Table 1. This chapter describes one of the most frequent methods, which has the following features: 1) spectral analysis of pressure pulsations upstream of the injector, and vibrations of the combustion chamber and gas generator shell; 2) investigation of a wide frequency band (0.2–15 kHz) by successive analysis of narrow intervals composing the band; 3) use of statistical characteristics that are obtained by spectral analysis; and 4) comparability of information found in narrow intervals.

This last feature, the comparability of information found in separate narrow intervals, is one of the main advantages that distinguishes the spectral analysis method from others given in Table 1. This method relies not on a priori models of processes, which may finally result in a loss of combustor stability, but rather on the basis of newly established relations of amplitude-frequency spectrum parameters to create models characteristic of specific situations.

The spectral analysis method shares certain features with other methods presented in Table 1, but the use of quantities characterizing the relations between the results obtained in relatively narrow frequency intervals is a peculiarity of the spectral analysis method. The method's main drawback is the amount of initial information associated with a narrow band that will appear unnecessary after finding the cause of the anomaly. It will be particularly evident if the same effect is obtained within one or two frequencies defined a priori. However, the spectral analysis method tends to be most reliable, and the superfluous information that is obtained may be useful for other cases, including other engine designs.

The main methodological principles used by the authors in LRE high-frequency stability analysis on the basis of information obtained in full-scale tests of these engines may be of some interest to specialists in other fields as well. With this in mind, it is appropriate to expound on the following issues: 1) the procedure that comprises primary processing of the pressure pulsation and the shell vibration amplitude-frequency spectrum, 2) the procedure of using data from the primary processing step to estimate LRE high-frequency stability, 3) examples of the procedure application in practice, and 4) recommendations on ways to improve the method.
