#### Amplitude-Frequency Spectrum Primary Processing

The amplitude-frequency spectrum is the expansion of the total signal into its components in which certain amplitudes correspond to certain frequency values. The expansion into a series (in this case a Fourier series) is carried out anywhere from about 200 Hz to 15 kHz. The primary processing is performed in the following sequence.

1) At each LRE operating regime, from 10 to 100 magnetogram (magnetic tape record) data samples are taken of pressure pulsations and/or shell vibrations. Each sample is expanded into a Fourier series within the stated frequency band.

2) The frequency band under study is divided into subranges (usually not less than three, e.g., 200–1000 Hz, 1000–5000 Hz, 5000–10,000 Hz). Each subrange is analyzed further separately.

3) While investigating a subrange, the following information is recorded for each separate spectrum: the amplitude maximum value  $A_i$  and the corresponding frequency intervals  $f_i \pm \Delta f_i$ , where  $\Delta f_i$  is approximately 2–3% of the interval of the frequency subrange  $\Delta f_s$  taken for analysis.

4) From the spectra obtained for the engine operation regimes the following determinations are made. Estimates are made of the mathematical expectation of amplitude  $\bar{A}_{fi}$  for each narrow frequency intervals ( $f_i \pm \Delta f_i$ )

$$\bar{A}_{fi} = \sum_{N_{fi}} A_{fi} / N_{fi} \quad (1)$$

where  $A_{fi}$  is the current value of the maximum amplitude in the frequency interval  $f_i \pm \Delta f_i$ , and  $N_{fi}$  is the number of samplings taken for the operation regime under study in which maximum amplitudes were realized in the frequency range  $f_i \pm \Delta f_i$ . The rate is ascertained at which a maximum amplitude appeared in each narrow frequency interval that will be later referred to as regularity  $R_{fi}$ ,

$$R_{fi} = N_{fi} / n \quad (2)$$

where  $n$  is the number of samplings for the engine given operation regime. The estimate of mathematical expectation of amplitude  $\bar{A}$  is made in the narrow frequency interval being studied

$$\bar{A} = \sum_n A_i / n \quad (3)$$

Finally, the maximum regularity,  $R_{\max}$  is determined in the frequency band under study and in the narrow frequency interval ( $f_i \pm \Delta f_{i,\max}$ ) corresponding to this regularity.

Special attention should be paid to the necessity of studying each subrange of the overall frequency band separately to define all of the mentioned characteristics for each subrange. Special attention should also be paid to the significance of regularity in the whole analysis. It is regularity that defines the contribution of various frequencies to the overall process or, rather, the level at which various frequencies affect the process. The examination of Eq. (2) shows that changes in regularity with engine transition from one regime to another, even without changes in amplitude of pressure pulsations or shell vibrations, represent changes in the spectrum structure that are often indicative of physical changes in the system.

Regularity to some extent may be treated as a characteristic of the process “band-narrowness,” i.e., of the oscillation energy concentration in a relatively narrow interval of frequencies.

It is useful to compare regularity with another LRE process stability characteristic, the oscillation decrement. The following interpretation of these characteristics seems reasonable: oscillation decrement is a characteristic uniquely related to the probability of sustained self-oscillations of a certain frequency without any connection to its amplitude; regularity is an estimate of the probability of self-oscillations appearing at a certain frequency at an amplitude maximum for the frequency band under study. The differences between these two characteristics, decrement and regularity, are most apparent at relatively low-amplitude oscillatory conditions. It is interesting to define possible regions in which the mentioned characteristics can be applied most effectively.

The use of decrement as a primary chamber process stability criterion is quite well justified for the analysis of combustion chamber and gas generator component tests where there is no connection to the engine state, in which case stability is defined to a high degree by pressure pulsation and vibration amplitude level. When the engine stability is analyzed, however, then both the amplitude value characteristic of self-oscillations and the probability of self-oscillation excitation at the maximum amplitude level are of importance. If the engine stability is evaluated without amplitude value being taken into account, the so-called producer risk will be, as a rule, too high.

Thus, in evaluating LRE high-frequency stability the authors give preference to regularity. At the same time it should be emphasized that in selecting criteria for defining LRE high-frequency stability, the variety of mechanisms that can lead to instability and the lack of theoretical knowledge of the problem makes a priori preference of a specific characteristic unwarranted. The main methodological principles used in the choice of high-frequency stability criteria and the procedures used to process these parameters will be discussed in the next section.

#### **Estimating High-Frequency Stability Using Spectral Processing: Systematic, Essential, and Preventative Conditions**

The problem is reduced to the consideration of the following two situations.

1) The combustion chamber process stability loss was accompanied by an increase in pressure pulsation amplitude and vibratory overload and by the appearance of some other indications of the intensification of instability.

2) The process stability loss was not confirmed by available information.

The same problems arise in both cases; that is, which characteristics of those obtained in primary spectral processing are most suitable for the estimation of high-frequency stability of the design. It is evident that the task is easier in the first case.

Theoretically any characteristic (estimate of mathematical expectations of amplitudes, or regularity of certain frequencies and maximum regularities corresponding to them) obtained may be used as an effective means of engine stability control if this characteristic can be used to identify a disposition toward stable or unstable operation, and has the properties of being systematic, essential, and preventative; these three terms will be explained in detail.

The term systematic refers to a situation whereby features found in certain series of tests are systematically (without any exclusion) observed in other independent

test series, including experiments with different specimens carried out simultaneously. For example, if a multichamber engine is tested and high-frequency instability is found with a given rate in each of its chambers, then being systematic implies that the character of the parameter chosen for high-frequency stability control changes for successful and failed tests for each chamber in a reproducible fashion.

If the parameter is chosen to be the estimate of the mathematical expectation of amplitude in a certain frequency band, the requirement of being systematic is fulfilled if, for each chamber, the estimate value in successful engine tests is lower than in failed tests. Attention should also be paid to the systematic correspondence between the character of the parameter change and the change of certain design, manufacturing, and/or operation factors.

Another feature of the parameters that may be used for high-frequency stability evaluation is essentiality. One may speak of an essential difference if its value can be accounted for with an acceptable significance level on the basis of statistical data. Here, the significance level value is equal to  $1 - \gamma$ , where  $\gamma$  is the fiducial probability specified by the user for evaluating the lower boundary of the confidence interval of failure-free operation probability. In the authors' experience the significance level is usually about 5–10%. Let  $\bar{X}_1$  and  $\bar{X}_2$  be the estimates of mathematical expectation of the parameters to be compared and  $S_{\bar{X}_1}$  and  $S_{\bar{X}_2}$  be the mean square errors of the mathematical expectations. The requirement of essentiality is fulfilled if the following relationship holds:

$$\frac{|\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2|}{\sqrt{S_{\bar{X}_1}^2 + S_{\bar{X}_2}^2}} - t_{st}[1 - \gamma; N_1 + N_2 - 2] \geq 0 \quad (4)$$

where  $t_{st}$  is the quantile of the student distribution, corresponding to  $(N_1 + N_2 - 2)$  degrees of freedom at a significance level of  $1 - \gamma$ ;  $N_1$  and  $N_2$  are the number of measurements in the samples being compared.

In cases where the parameter  $X_i$  used for high-frequency stability estimation has a certain quantifiable dependence on some test condition or design factor, e.g.,  $X_i = f(j_i)$ , the estimate of essentiality is virtually an estimate of the certainty of the dependence and is based on the comparison of an estimate of the variance of separate parameter measurements relative to the relationship  $[S_X = f(j_i)]$  and an analogous estimate made with the assumption that there is no such relation ( $S_{X_0}$ ). The requirement of essentiality is met if

$$\frac{S_{X_0}^2}{S_{X=f(\varphi_i)}^2} - t_F(N_2; N_1; 1 - \gamma) \geq 0 \quad (5)$$

where  $t_F$  is the quantile of the Fisher distribution corresponding to the number of experiments in each sample and the chosen significance level.

It should be noted that unlike the systematic condition estimate, negative results of the essentiality estimate do not mean that the proposed parameter is inadequate for checking the engine state; such results indicate that there is insufficient information to state for certain that the observed difference is not a random realization of the same relationship. These results do not necessarily eliminate the proposed parameter as being adequate for high-frequency stability control. However, it should be known to what extent the search is promising, i.e., what is the chance that the experiment continuation will not finally result in the loss of being systematic. Here the following statement may be helpful: Further search (statistics

accumulation) is not promising if relationship (6) holds and Eq. (4) does not hold for the samples being compared,

$$[N_2/(N_1 + N_2)]M_2 + (\gamma - 1) \leq 0 \quad (6)$$

where  $N_2$  is the total number of samples,  $N_1$  is the number of samples in which no cases of high-frequency instability were observed, and  $M_2$  is the number of observations of high-frequency instability.

Equation (6) is an estimate based on an alternative characteristic ("success or failure") of the product state. The application of parametric methods instead of alternative ones is justified only in cases where the former are more informative. The number of engines or tests required for defining the effect of various factors on the engine high-frequency stability is the informativeness measure. This means that application of a certain parameter is justified only in a case in which it allows a reduction in the number of engines required for finding certain relationships. When relationships (4) and (5) are not met and Eq. (6) is met, two versions are possible: 1) the parameter is not informative, 2) the proposed parameter does not characterize the process under study.

In both cases any attempts to confirm the parameter adequacy will lead nowhere.

If Eqs. (4) or (5) hold, and the requirement of being systematic is met, the parameter may be reasonably considered as a basis for further application for an estimate of engine instability.

Here a question arises: at what engine state (how far from the stability boundary) does the amplitude-frequency spectrum of pressure pulsations or/and vibrations allow the systematic and essential distinction of negative changes of the hardware state and engine processes? It is most important that the requirement of being preventative mentioned at the beginning of this section is met. The preventative condition is the parameter's ability to reveal negative tendencies before they are found by more simple means, i.e., before the occurrence of serious damage.

It is only with these parameters that a probability (or improbability) of high-frequency engine instability occurrence can be estimated before the engine failure and without testing a large number of specimens. This possibility of being able to estimate the probability of ensuring high-frequency stability with reasonable accuracy and certainty is the main motive stimulating the application of parametric methods.

It should be underlined that only parameters directly connected to and governed by design, technological, and some other engine features can be used for estimating the probability of ensuring high-frequency stability.

If an estimate is based on the measurement of parameters that are not direct characteristics of the engine, the extension of the estimate to subsequent products is valid only in the case that the features defining the high-frequency stability are constant. If direct engine properties are checked, such confirmation is easy and does not require failure tests (in this case a failure caused by disturbance of combustion process). If out-of-engine characteristics (external and test conditions) are used as parameters of an operable state, the guarantees may be confirmed only by systematic tests of driving the combustion chamber and gas generator process to an unstable state or by tests carried out under conditions promoting such anomalies. This makes the application of amplitude-frequency spectrum parameters more attractive than other parameters even when the latter are better in terms of being systematic and essential. The application of out-of-engine parameters for the probabilistic prediction of high-frequency stability may be accepted only as a temporary, forced

measure and are not suitable for either high-frequency stability control in the course of full-scale production or for the estimate of high-frequency stability margins.

Any amplitude frequency spectrum parameter may be used for checking high-frequency stability without restrictions. Theoretically it may be a parameter related to pressure pulsations upstream of a single injection element or analogous parameters related to combustion chamber or gas generator shell vibrations. Complex parameters, i.e., parameters practically duplicating each other, to some extent can be used as well. Common parameter combinations will be considered presently. The requirements of being systematic, essential and preventative are to be met in all situations. If these requirements are fulfilled for several parameters, the one that best meets the essentiality requirement should be chosen. Because state differences are expressed by complexes of a type

$$\frac{|\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2|}{\sqrt{S_{X_1}^2 + S_{X_2}^2}}$$

where two states are analyzed or

$$S_{X_0}^2 / S_{X=f(\varphi)}^2$$

where relationships are analyzed, one may (designating parameters to be compared by indices  $a$  and  $b$ ) express the conditions under which one of the parameters,  $a$  for example, is more preferable than the other by

$$\left\{ \frac{|\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2|}{\sqrt{S_{X_1}^2 + S_{X_2}^2}} \right\}_a - \left\{ \frac{|\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2|}{\sqrt{S_{X_1}^2 + S_{X_2}^2}} \right\}_b > 0 \quad (7)$$

$$\left\{ \frac{S_{X_0}^2}{S_{X=f(\varphi)}^2} \right\}_a - \left\{ \frac{S_{X_0}^2}{S_{X=f(\varphi)}^2} \right\}_b > 0 \quad (8)$$

Thus, the choice of amplitude-frequency spectrum parameters for subsequent control of high-frequency stability is a formalized problem. However, this normalization prevents only the rough mistake of choosing a parameter not adequate for the problem solution. The choice in the most simple case (one of the parameters is suitable) is a laborious task, i.e., a complete exhaustive search of all parameter possibilities. The selection of a complex parameter on the basis of theoretical concepts may be a very difficult task.

In the simplest case when enough experience has been gathered in the study of the unstable state of a certain engine configuration, a parameter obtained from the primary processing of the amplitude-frequency spectrum may be chosen. It may be the regularity of pressure pulsations in a narrow interval of frequencies upstream of an injection element  $R_f$ , the estimate of the mathematical expectation of amplitudes in the narrow interval upstream of an element  $A_f$ , or the estimate of the mathematical expectation of amplitude in one of the frequency bands being studied  $\bar{A}$ .

The regularity of pressure pulsations upstream of an injection element is a frequent choice due to the fact that the underlying mechanisms of high-frequency instability are unknown a priori. Therefore, a frequency band in which a certain instability mechanism manifests itself should be found. As a rule the regularity  $R_{f1}$  parameter is most suitable for stability investigation when its value is less than

0.1. In cases qualified as being disposed to high-frequency instability, its value increases.

The estimate of the mathematical expectation of amplitude in a certain narrow frequency interval  $A_{fi}$  is not always suitable for stability study because of its low preventativity. The same may be said about the estimate of the mathematical expectation of amplitudes in the frequency band under study  $\bar{A}$ . In the case when the investigated process is accompanied by a regularity greater than 0.7 in the narrow frequency interval characterized by the chosen values of  $\bar{A}_{fi}$ , methods based on  $\bar{A}_f$  and  $\bar{A}$  are practically the same. These methods are widely used in investigating a possibility of high-frequency instability appearing under the existence of pressure self-oscillations in combustion chambers and fluid lines. A regularity level close to 1.0 is characteristic of such situations, and failure-free operation depends on the ability not to permit anomalous amplitude increase. In cases when self-oscillations are not systematic in time and have a tendency to increase in duration, the most simple complex parameter, the product  $\bar{A}_{fi} \cdot R_{fi}$  or  $\bar{A} \cdot R_{fi}$  is often preferable. This quantity may arbitrarily be called a mean integral amplitude in a narrow frequency interval,  $f_i \pm \Delta f_i$ . The arbitrariness of the definition is because in the first case ( $\bar{A}_{fi} \cdot R_{fi}$ ), for samplings where no maximum amplitudes were observed, their values were equal to zero, and in the second case ( $\bar{A} \cdot R_{fi}$ ), their values were equal to those observed in other frequency intervals. Mean integral amplitudes are applied to study processes characterized by self-oscillations developing in time and, as a consequence, by developing amplitude. If the regularity value at a qualified stable state is taken as a reference, then the development of regularity from the range 0.2–0.4 to the range 0.5–1.0 is characteristic of a state being inclined to instability.

For the cases just discussed when only one parameter may be taken for the stability study, the following expression defining the amplitude value vs the engine operation durability and the relevant parameter (the observed regularity, for example) is typical:

$$A_\tau = A_0 + B_0 \tau^\beta \left[ 1 / (\nu - R_{fi}^\alpha) \right] \quad (9)$$

where  $A_\tau$  is the amplitude value at time  $\tau$ ,  $A_0$  is the amplitude value at the start, and  $B_0$ ,  $\beta$ ,  $\nu$ , and  $\alpha$  are constants characteristic of the development of certain mechanisms of instability.

With Eq. (9) in mind, guidelines for applying each of the abovementioned amplitude-frequency spectrum parameters given in Table 2 where  $R$  is the regularity value characteristic of the situation when no failures are caused by combustion instability. It is clear that in the first case a quick process stability loss occurs, whereas in the others a relatively slow development of the event occurs.

**Table 2 Guidelines for applying amplitude-frequency spectrum parameters**

| Initial conditions  |                 |                     | Most informative parameter              |
|---------------------|-----------------|---------------------|-----------------------------------------|
| $\nu \rightarrow 1$ | $\alpha \leq 1$ | $R_0 = 0-0.05$      | Regularity $R_{fi}$                     |
| $\nu \ll 1$         | $\alpha \gg 1$  | $R_0 \rightarrow 1$ | $\bar{A}_{fi}; \bar{A}$                 |
| $\nu \ll 1$         | $\alpha \gg 1$  | $R_0 = 0.2-0.4$     | $\bar{A}_{fi} R_{fi}; \bar{A}_i R_{fi}$ |

#### Complex Parameters

It is clear that after determining the dependence of constants  $A_0$ ,  $B_0$ ,  $\beta$ ,  $\alpha$ , and  $\nu$  at certain test conditions one may define the character of the development of processes leading to instability under various conditions. However, it should be kept in mind that the possibilities of the scheme described by Eq. (9) are rather limited. It defines the self-development of the process. At the same time experiment shows that in many cases the interaction of processes in the engine fluid systems and mutual influence of hydraulic, thermal, and mechanical effects are the governing factors of high-frequency instability. It is clear that for investigating such processes the parameters describing the interaction of these factors should be used. These complex parameters are based on parameters determined during primary processing.

The following notion of a possible mechanism of high-frequency instability is the basis of this complex parameter: various factors defining chamber and gas generator high-frequency stability act independently according to the laws of random independent events before the oscillations reach a certain level. When each of the factors reaches a certain limit value they influence each other unfavorably, thereby promoting high-frequency instability. Since high-frequency instability results in high levels of pressure pulsation and vibration amplitudes, the search and qualification of various engine states should be based on the investigation of the connection of the amplitude-frequency spectrum and engine parameters as a function of increases in pressure pulsations and shell vibration amplitude.

Complex parameters may be used for high-frequency stability analysis if the following relationships are satisfied (while meeting all other conditions already formulated):

$$\frac{\partial \bar{A}_i}{\partial X_i} \geq 0 \quad (10)$$

$$P[\bar{r}A_i = \varphi(A_i)]_{\text{lim}} \quad (11)$$

where  $(\partial \bar{A}_i / \partial X_i)$  is a derivative of pressure pulsations or vibration amplitude with respect to any component ( $X_i$ ) of the complex parameter. The derivative of the amplitude of pressure pulsations upstream of an injection element and shell vibrations with respect to each other should be positive. Equation (11) is the probability that the estimate of the mathematical expectation of the correlation coefficient of the interdependence of pressure pulsation and vibration amplitude differs from zero at the limit and higher values of amplitude.

Approximate equations, implying that full-size tests do not always give enough information for full correlation analysis, may be used for calculations. With the minimum required amount of information (two intervals, i.e., relatively low and higher level of amplitude), the following operations should be carried out for determining pressure pulsation or vibration limit values.

1) For each of the amplitudes being analyzed the difference between their values  $\Delta A_i$  should be analyzed,

$$\Delta A_i = A_{i_1} - A_{i_2} \quad (12)$$

where index  $i_1$  denotes the amplitude of any measured parameter (pressure pulsation upstream of an injection element or vibration) at an initial time interval and index  $i_2$  is the value of the same parameter at the next interval.

2) The relation  $K_i$  of the amplitude changes of engine parameter in each separate test is determined,

$$K_i = \Delta A_{i1} / \Delta A_{i2} \quad (13)$$

where the indices 1 and 2 denote different engine parameters.

3) The mathematical expectation  $\bar{K}_i$  and its mean square error  $S_{\bar{K}_i}$  are evaluated from well-known relations. If  $\bar{K}_i \leq 0$  the calculation is ceased as the relationship (10) is not satisfied. If  $\bar{K}_i > 0$ , the probability of the characteristic lying in the region of positive values is estimated; it is this condition that allows the results to be a consequence of certain relationships,

$$P = \varphi_{st}(K_i / S_{K_i}; N) \quad (14)$$

where  $\varphi_{st}$  is student's function.

At  $P > \gamma$  the estimated expectation of the amplitude used in the calculations may be taken as a value at which various parameters mutually increase the tendency to development of high-frequency instability. The case  $P > \gamma$  suggests that the estimated expectation lies in the superlimit range, i.e., in the range where the relationship is certain. If  $P < \gamma$ , the validity of the relationship is not confirmed. With enough data the dependence of the probability on the estimated expectation of amplitude could be found, and the estimated limit value ensuring  $P = \gamma$  could be determined. Since this is not always possible, amplitude limit values may be found from relations of the form in Eq. (15) that imply that the probability asymptotically approaches unity when the value of the relevant amplitude tends to infinity, and the probability approaches zero when the amplitude tends to zero:

$$1 - P = e^{-\lambda A_i} \quad (15)$$

where  $\lambda$  is a constant.

With the preceding condition an equation may be written for the limit value of the amplitude of a parameter  $A_{lim}$ :

$$A_{lim} = A_p \frac{\log(1 - \gamma)}{\log(1 - P)} \quad (16)$$

where  $A_p$  is the amplitude value satisfying the probability  $P(1 - P)$ .

It is clear that the limit amplitude value  $A_{lim}$  can be easily found if the probability  $P$  is known. In the same way the limit values of each amplitude-frequency spectrum characteristic for each parameter connected to an instability may be found. A complex parameter connected with the characteristics of the engine's amplitude-frequency spectrum may be based on various possible combinations: pressure pulsations upstream of one injection element and shell vibrations in one direction, the same pulsations and vibrations in another direction, the same combinations for an injection element of another propellant, or combinations of the same parameter (pulsation-pulsation, vibration-vibration).

In contrast to situations characteristic of simple cases when the analysis is based on one parameter, in the more complex cases when the analysis is based on the relationships of several amplitude frequency characteristics, the parameter combinations do not compete with each other. There is no preferable combination. Any combination should be taken into account if it satisfies the requirements of being systematic and essential and it satisfies the condition  $P > \gamma$  at the amplitude

values that took place. It is clear that if this condition was satisfied the possibility of finding an anomaly was confirmed.

While studying high-frequency stability in full-size tests the same problems are solved by means of simple and complex parameters. The engine state is qualified as stable, disposed to instability, or unstable. The effectiveness of measures taken to increase stability and the probability of stability assurance are evaluated.

Qualification criteria are actually the same: no failures due to chamber process instability, and the values of the parameter used for stability analysis must remain within a certain so-called sublimit range. These are considered sufficient to qualify the engine as stable; maintaining the operable state with control parameters lying in the superlimit range qualifies the engine as being disposed to instability; conditions when the engine is qualified as unstable are evident. However, there are some differences between the approaches used, for example, to define the limit level of parameters being controlled. In the simplest case, this is a quantity characterizing an amplitude-frequency spectrum parameter. For a complex parameter the limit value is an aggregate of limit values of a parameter combination. For example, if a parameter combination is made of the pressure upstream of an injection element and one value of shell vibration, parameters of the amplitude-frequency spectrum should include the estimated computed expectation in the frequency band being studied  $\bar{A}$  and their maximum regularity  $R$ , the limit values of the estimated expectation of pressure pulsation and vibration amplitudes, and the limit value of the maximum regularity of these parameters. If it turns out that a high correlation of these parameters (e.g., pressure pulsations upstream of an injector element and vibration) appears beginning from some minimum frequency difference ( $f_i \pm \Delta f$ ) corresponding to maximum regularities, then the complex parameter limit should include the minimum allowable frequency difference as well.

If, in the example just given, all complex parameter components except one reach or exceed the relevant limit value, the engine still should be qualified as stable if it maintains its operable state in the absence of other faulty circumstances.

Some peculiarities of the complex parameter appear when the stability margin is estimated. Such calculations are necessary for each new measure introduced to ensure engine stability. In the simplest case, i.e., when the stability is analyzed with an amplitude-frequency spectrum parameter found in primary processing or with a parameter of mean-integral amplitude type, the margin is determined as the difference between the parameter's current and limit values from the estimated expectation of the parameter's critical value. For the versatile complex parameter it is clear that its margin can not be estimated the same way. First of all, separate parameters comprising the complex one should be made commensurable. There are several ways for solving the problem; the one applicable in this case follows.

- 1) All limit values of parameters that make the complex parameter are assigned the same value, that is, zero.

- 2) Value intervals are set for each parameter, and each interval is assigned a value that increases by a unit with a departure from the limit value toward the direction of favorable stability.

- 3) The dimensionless characteristic of each parameter making the complex parameter is the sum of intervals separating the current value from zero in the direction of favorable stability.

This way to make the parameters forming the complex parameter commensurable with each other can not be considered certain as it is based on arbitrary intervals taken for each parameter. However, any possible detrimental effects due

to this approach can be partly compensated by the commensurability of intervals for similar parameters.

The estimate of the margin of the complex stability parameter is defined as the sum of dimensionless estimates of all parameters that comprise the complex parameter. Using margins calculated in such a way, the effectiveness of measures taken for assuring high-frequency stability and the probability of its realization are estimated. Both problems are solved in accordance with reliability assurance and control documents. The dimensionless estimate of the complex parameter is formally the estimate of the probability of this estimate lying above zero.

The validity of using dimensionless complex parameters to calculate stability probability may be confirmed by comparing these results with estimates based on assumptions about the character of the sublimit range of the complex parameter values. In the sublimit range, factors governing stability act independently and, consequently, the probability  $q_0$  of reaching the limit state is defined by

$$q_0 = \prod_{i=1}^Z q_{0i} \quad (17)$$

where  $q_{0i}$  is the probability of achieving the limit state of the single amplitude-frequency spectrum parameter, and  $Z$  is the number of complex parameter components.

The value of  $q_0$  is defined from well-known equations of probability parametric estimates. The estimated probability of stability using dimensionless complex parameters may be considered acceptable if the following relation is met:

$$P_{l_a} < P_{l_{cp}} \leq 1 - \prod_{i=1}^Z q_{ui} p_{0i} \quad (18)$$

where  $P_{l_{cp}}$  is the lower confidence interval boundary of the probability of the dimensionless complex parameter lying in the range above zero (all confidence interval boundaries being defined with the fiducial probability set for engine reliability estimate),  $P_{l_a}$  is the lower confidence interval boundary of the probability of stability determined by the alternative method, and  $q_{ui} p_{0i}$  is the upper confidence interval boundary of the probability of reaching the limit value of the single amplitude-frequency spectrum parameter.

Failure to satisfy the left-hand side of Eq. (18) means that the proposed parameter is not informative enough and, consequently, it cannot be used. Failure to satisfy the right-hand part of the relation means that the initial preconditions of the process development model do not conform to each other or, rather, the significance of the intervals of dimensionless estimates is chosen incorrectly. Such situations are possible for states close to the limit. In this case a review of the scale of the dimensionless estimates is necessary. In conclusion it should be said that when there are several possible combinations of single parameters for making a complex parameter, the margin of such a parameter is estimated from the least sum of the dimensionless combination of the estimates of the single parameters.

#### Application of the Described Methods

In the application of the described methods two basic problems should be considered: 1) actual situations when two parameters that had not been widely used before turned out most effective; pressure pulsation regularity in a certain narrow frequency interval and a complex (versatile) parameter; 2) some information about

the reproducibility of high-frequency stability level obtained with the application of complex parameters.

As an example, consider the logic of selecting the regularity and a complex parameter for estimating the stability margin in two different cases. In the first case, an amplitude-frequency spectrum parameter must be found that conforms to the following observations: until a certain propellant temperature at the engine inlet was reached, no high-frequency instability was observed; instability was observed many times on reaching this temperature; and the rate of instability differed for two chambers of a two-chamber engine. In the second case the preferable parameter conforms to the following observation: instability appeared when the chamber pressure was changed. In this case, as in the first one, the instability appeared when the propellant at the engine inlet achieved a certain temperature. In both cases, the essentiality of statistical characteristic difference for different conditions was evident enough, i.e., the influence of the conditions on the engine stability seemed well grounded. In both cases the regularity of pressure pulsations in a narrow frequency interval upstream of an injection element was the most effective amplitude-frequency spectrum parameter. In the first case fuel injection elements were used, and the frequency interval was identified with the first modes of longitudinal and transverse oscillations. In the second case the oxidizer injection elements were used, and the interval differed from frequencies that usually accompany high-frequency instability.

In the first case the regularity of pressure pulsations upstream of the oxidizer injection elements competed with the chosen parameter. The competing parameter was rejected as inconsistent with differences of instability frequencies.

In the second case no other parameter of the amplitude-frequency spectrum of pressure pulsations and vibrations could compete with the chosen one as no other parameter conformed to statistical requirements. It should be noted that the frequency interval in which pressure pulsation regularity was most effective coincided with the interval of maximum vibration regularity through the engine's operation cycle.

Some data on parameter reproducibility are given in Fig. 1. The rms scatter of the measured pressure pulsation and vibration spectrum at engine start and during steady-state operation are presented. The ordinate is the ratio of the observed estimate of the rms scatter of the complex parameter obtained in tests of multiple

combustors to the observed estimate of the rms scatter of the parameter in repeated tests of a single combustor. The estimate was based on the analysis of statistical data of versatile parameters composed of amplitude-frequency spectrum parameters.

In connection with the data presented in Fig. 1 it should be noted that there are two equally important aspects in the problem of assuring stability reproducibility. The first is stability reproducibility in a single specimen (engine, combustor, gas generator). It may be expected that the engine that successfully (from the standpoint of stability) underwent acceptance tests will reproduce satisfactory characteristics in operation. The second problem is the reproducibility of satisfactory levels of stability in all engine specimens. The solution of the first problem is a necessary condition of the solution of the second problem.

The following observations can be made from Fig. 1.

- 1) The reproducibility of stability characteristics at the start and during the steady-state operation is higher for repeated tests of the same specimen than for tests of different specimens.

- 2) The differences observed in steady-state operation are well founded by statistical data; the differences observed at the engine start are found only in approximately half of the cases.

- 3) The ratio of the unreproducibility characteristic from specimen to specimen to that for repeated tests of the same specimen is higher in steady-state operation than at the start. This is attributed to the fact that repeated tests, which were accompanied by a change of elements affecting the start, were also taken into account.

The presented data could be grounds for a review of the design and technology documentation and the production process with the objective of providing higher reproducibility of design characteristics from specimen to specimen. It should be remembered, however, that the presented results cannot be taken as a generalization but serve to illustrate the application of complex parameters for the solution of a particular problem.

#### Conclusions

In conclusion, the following points should be stated:

- 1) Various mechanisms of high-frequency instability excitation are observed in full-size tests and their investigation is not always possible with a priori established parameters.

- 2) The procedure of applying parameters of the amplitude-frequency spectrum of pressure pulsations upstream of injection elements and combustor shell vibrations may promote the ability to find the most informative parameters for specific cases of high-frequency stability.

- 3) The effectiveness of the procedure may be increased by using amplitudes lower than the maximum amplitude. Though the experience in using the method for the analysis of high-frequency stability can be considered as a whole, some drawbacks of the method are evident. In particular, the method uses only a limited part of the spectral information. This limits the potential of the method for early detection of peculiarities leading to high-frequency instability. The potential of the method may be extended by using not only the largest amplitudes (the so-called major maxima) but also second-order amplitudes in the analysis. This should present no major problems considering the computational power presently available. The amount of information will be enlarged considerably, and the criteria used for qualifying liquid rocket engine stability will be modified. The modification of the current method by using second-order amplitudes may be the subject of a significant study.

## Chapter 21

## Scaling Techniques for Liquid Rocket Combustion Stability Testing

Steven C. Fisher,\* Fred E. Dodd,<sup>†</sup> and Robert J. Jensen<sup>‡</sup>

*Rockwell International, Canoga Park, California 91303*

### I. Introduction

THE development of liquid rocket combustion devices has historically been a costly effort when combustion instability is encountered. To prevent this unnecessary cost, typical programs are structured to deal with the issue of combustion stability through a balance of analysis and stability rating testing. If properly incorporated into the development methodology, subscale testing can be quite beneficial in eliminating configuration and design problems early in the development program. Subscale development efforts will never result in complete confidence in the full-scale design, but with a properly structured program full-scale development risks can be reduced. Stability modeling is an important tool in establishing low-cost and low-risk stability development programs. A variety of different subscale combustors are discussed in this chapter. The combustors reviewed include single-element, three-dimensional round, and two-dimensional configurations. The information that can be gained from each type of combustor is included in the discussion along with examples. Typically, various mechanisms of combustion instability can be studied more effectively with specific subscale combustors. Finally, suggestions are provided relative to maximizing the amount of information that can be extracted from a subscale program in order to minimize the cost of the full-scale program.

### II. Injector Combustion Stability Development Issues

Combustion instability has proven to be a formidable issue in liquid rocket engine development programs. As demonstrated by many incidents, combustion

instability can cause significant damage or loss of the combustor, the test facility, or even the vehicle and launch pad within fractions of a second. One example is a liquid oxygen (LOX) and methane injector<sup>1</sup> that was severely damaged after about 0.8 s of unstable operation at 2000 psia (Fig. 1). Figure 2 shows an F-1 engine injector with major damage following an instability during development testing. In back-to-back incidents, two early Atlas vehicles equipped with bafflesless MA-2 booster engines were lost together with their respective launch pads due to unstable combustion. From the standpoint of an engine or engine combustor component development program, combustion instability is a critical issue along with performance and injector/chamber compatibility. As a result, significant resources are typically set aside to analyze and experimentally demonstrate the stability of the injector design selected.

Combustion instability has been defined as the occurrence of pressure fluctuations of a well-defined frequency (or set of frequencies) within a combustion chamber that are coupled with the combustion process.<sup>2,3</sup> Often these frequencies can be readily identified with characteristic acoustic modes of the combustion chamber. However, the amplitudes of these oscillations are typically orders of magnitude above that of environmental acoustic noise sources. Peak-to-peak pressure wave amplitudes as high as 150% of the average chamber pressure have been measured during fully developed combustion instabilities.<sup>1</sup> For the LOX/methane injector shown in Fig. 1, the peak-to-peak amplitude during unstable combustion was as high as 3000 psi (Fig. 3). For certain types of instabilities the propellant feed system is also coupled with the chamber oscillations, such that the dynamics of the entire propulsion system may dictate the oscillation growth rate, mode, and frequency. Combustion processes such as transient atomization, vaporization, and propellant mixing may occur causing locally enhanced burning rates and pressure-wave amplification. As a result of such mechanisms combustion instability can grow to full amplitude within milliseconds. Chamber and injector damage associated with combustion instability result from the high localized heating rates caused by the oscillatory motion of the combustion gases. Often minor changes in configuration (such as LOX post length) or operating conditions may cause a previously stable injector to exhibit an instability.

Because of these concerns, the design process within industry has been structured to address the issue of stability in a stepwise manner which is fully integrated with other design objectives. As indicated in the process outlined in Fig. 4 a full-scale injector concept is developed based on available data and analyses. Although the conceptual design is often relatively similar to the final configuration, many details must be defined that can significantly affect combustion stability. These details are dependent on characteristics that can only be established with confidence through hot-fire testing. For example, cavity design is driven by the instability frequencies that must be suppressed. This frequency is typically calculated based on the assumption that the chamber acoustic velocity is equal to that of combustion products at the injected mixture ratio based on equilibrium chemistry.<sup>4,5</sup> In some cases, instabilities have occurred at frequencies significantly above or below that assumed frequency. There are several reasons why the measured frequencies may not correspond to the equilibrium speed of sound of the product gases. Since data indicate that most of the acoustic energy and damage is localized near the injector face, it is reasonable that the frequency of oscillation of the transverse modes is dependent on the speed of sound at the injector face. The near injector speed of

sound may vary from the equilibrium product gas sound speed for reasons including a two-phase composition at the face, unreacted gaseous propellants that have a substantially different speed of sound than the combustion gas, and heat transfer to the wall, for example. Although the exact causes of a shift in frequency may not be immediately obvious from the data, hot-fire testing is critical to confirm what frequencies the cavities should be designed for.

As indicated earlier some occurrences of combustion instability can be traced to minor changes in operating condition or hardware design that may occur during combustor development. Ideally the impact on stability of such changes should be anticipated through analyses. However, whereas modeling techniques have proven useful in describing stability trends, these analyses are by no means fully matured and anchored. One of the key current limitations of analytical stability tools is the inability to predict the magnitude of the combustion instability gain. Often it is not even possible to determine which mechanisms are responsible for a given combustion instability, much less model it. Such experiences reinforce the need to conduct stability rating hot-fire testing with representative hardware.

It would be desirable to conduct all such testing at the full-scale level to match the stability-controlling characteristics of the final engine configuration (including the chamber acoustic modes and frequencies and the injector pattern) as closely as possible. For small (for example, upper stage class) engines and thrusters, testing is typically conducted at the full-scale size and thrust level. It is difficult if not impossible, however, to conduct all of the desired stability development testing for booster class engines at full-scale because of cost and schedule considerations. Because of test operations and hardware costs, only a limited number of

full-scale injector configurations and tests can be conducted with actual engines. Most often, initial testing is accomplished using pressurized facility propellant tanks rather than actual engine pumps to minimize test hardware costs and to facilitate testing early in the engine development program. In addition, the potential for failure of a large test article and the associated safety, cost, and schedule issues if such a failure were to occur must be considered. Finally, other combustion related characteristics such as combustor performance and the impact of the injector flowfield on chamber life and cooling (injector/chamber compatibility) may be of greater concern than stability for a given program. Like stability, these concerns motivate the engine developer to seek some measure of confidence in his design prior to committing to full-scale booster testing.

To provide an intermediate, cost-effective evaluation of full-scale booster stability and performance characteristics, lower thrust subscale combustor hardware is typically hot-fire tested as part of the full-scale design effort. As shown in Fig. 4 the subscale effort is embedded within the detailed full-scale design effort and follows the conceptual design phase. The thrust level is often dictated by the maximum flow rates available at a given (subscale) facility. Typical industrial facility thrust levels are on the order of 20,000–100,000 lbf (89,000–445,000 N) at sea level.

### III. Development of a Stability Program Utilizing Subscale Testing

Fundamental to the entire stability development effort is the fact that the injector and its associated stability aids (baffles and cavities) are the primary stability and performance controlling components in the engine. Hence, subscale test programs must be structured to evaluate the stability related characteristics of the full-scale injector. In particular, to be successful, subscale test programs must preserve those characteristics to the greatest extent possible. However, certain subscale design features are often the result of tradeoffs between stability, performance, and heat flux characterization objectives. Depending on the subscale approach selected, these tradeoffs may result in adjustments to the subscale injector pattern, the combustion chamber constant diameter section length, nozzle inlet geometry, and the amount of wall film cooling, for example. In addition, the desire to have a modular thrust chamber assembly to facilitate a wide range of injector and chamber parameters may result in baffles and cavities that are geometrically dissimilar to those in the full-scale design. For instance, the modular subscale thrust chamber hardware may utilize a removable spool with radial aperture cavities whereas the full-scale engine may have axial aperture cavities that are integral with the injector body. If possible, subscale chamber dimensions are selected such that full-scale baffle compartment and/or chamber frequencies are matched. Even if no pertinent mode of the full-scale combustor is matched, the occurrence of a combustion instability in subscale testing would indicate that further stability improvements are necessary before committing to a full-scale injector. The probability of an instability occurring in a full-scale combustor with an injector pattern from an unstable subscale combustor is very high. The higher frequency transverse modes of a full-scale combustor may match the range of frequencies in the subscale hardware. In addition, depending on the bandwidth of mechanisms relevant to subscale instabilities, these same mechanisms may easily support growth of lower frequency tangential oscillations characteristic of the larger chamber diameter hardware.

Although the subscale combustor diameter (or transverse dimensions) are typically smaller than the full-scale design, operating conditions (mixture ratio and

chamber pressure) are usually close to that of the full-scale design for both performance and stability considerations. Injector element dimensions, injector to wall spacing, combustor length, and contraction ratio also usually match full-scale values for similar reasons. Throat heat flux simulation requirements dictate that the convergent section wall radii be smaller than full scale, potentially resulting in a chamber contour quite unlike the full-scale design. To correctly make such trades and accommodate subscale data requirements, a systematic design approach is necessary.

To fill this need, a judicious selection of stability and performance modeling techniques is required. Modeling can be employed to establish both appropriate (including off-nominal) ranges of operating conditions and hardware configurations to evaluate performance and stability characteristics of the subscale hardware. This is particularly true for cases where some tradeoffs between stability and performance design requirements are being considered. The results of a parametric modeling study can be used to structure a test plan and a test logic in parallel to establishing the subscale design and the required instrumentation. In addition, the results of subscale testing can later serve to better anchor the stability and performance models for conditions and configurational details typical of the full-scale design. Stability codes can be incorporated to evaluate spontaneous stability characteristics and acoustic cavity effectiveness. These codes can also be used in a correlative technique to quantify the combustion response (combustion induced gain and characteristic frequency). Theoretically, the combustion response is independent of the combustor scale. Hence, when anchored to subscale data these models can then be applied to estimate the performance and stability of a full-scale combustion device, provided that the injector and operating conditions tested at the subscale level are similar to that of the full-scale hardware.

Together with the subscale database, anchored stability and performance models supply a basis for confidence that the full-scale combustor will meet the design requirements. Far from eliminating the need to verify these characteristics at full scale, subscale testing and associated analyses provide an ability to cost effectively eliminate unsatisfactory designs early in the development process and to partially characterize the remaining candidates.

Critical to the subscale test program and the analytical efforts is an understanding of the key stability parameters and mechanisms. Subscale testing that is conducted at conditions similar to that of the full-scale design will exhibit similar combustion physics. For example, atomization rates, droplet size distribution, vaporization, and mixing should be reasonably similar between subscale and full-scale combustor conditions. If full-scale chamber or baffle compartment acoustic frequencies are matched by the subscale hardware, the interactions (including the relative characteristic times of the various processes) between the combustion and the oscillations in the full-scale design should be reasonably simulated in the subscale testing. With respect to stability modeling, although exact functional forms describing instability mechanisms are not required, predicting the preferred coupling frequencies and gain exhibited by injection and combustion processes as a function of geometry and operating conditions is essential to structuring a meaningful subscale stability test plan. Furthermore, the degree to which the key instability mechanisms are represented in the modeling will be reflected in the a priori accuracy of stability predictions for an untested full-scale combustor. A code that is well anchored to the subscale data across a range of operating conditions and configurations will be more likely to correctly model the effect of key

stability physics for the full-scale design. Hence, part of the subscale test effort is typically aimed at gaining understanding of the controlling stability mechanisms and representing them in the codes.

An understanding of the mechanisms (feed system dynamics, atomization, vaporization, mixing, or chemistry) associated with instabilities may be isolated by performing tests at selected operating points. Mixture ratio excursions and throttling may expose feed system mechanisms. Chamber pressure excursions typically aid in the evaluation of the atomization/vaporization process as a controlling mechanism. Measured performance (and sometimes heat flux profiles) are compared with trends predicted by performance codes to attempt to determine the relative influence of each of the physical mechanisms modeled. At times, however, a single controlling mechanism cannot be isolated.

Examples and discussion of the more common subscale test approaches and modeling tools that are matched to the data obtained from such testing follow. Emphasis is placed on current industrial practice. Recommendations for future test and analysis technology improvements are also presented.

### IV. Subscale Experimental Techniques

During most rocket engine development programs, series of subscale tests are typically performed to mitigate risk. As discussed earlier, typical subscale rocket engine development tests include cylindrical chamber hardware that is geometrically smaller with respect to the full-scale hardware, has similar contraction ratio and injector elements, and operates at similar pressures and mixture ratios. More generally, subscale combustors include single-element, subscale three-dimensional cylindrical combustors, two-dimensional "slab" combustors, and a variety of more obscure combustors, such as wedge-shaped combustors.

The experimental testing must be carefully planned in order to efficiently obtain as much information as possible. The stability considerations of a given full-scale design are not the only reasons for performing subscale development tests. Typically, performance information, heat transfer data, and injector-chamber compatibility data can also be generated during subscale testing depending on the combustor. The next section discusses the various subscale combustors and the information that can be obtained from each to reduce full-scale development risk.

#### A. Single-Element Combustors

Single-element combustors are also called labscale devices. The injector is composed of one or a few elements. Single-element combustor testing represents the most convenient and lowest cost form of subscale testing. However, only a very limited amount of stability information (relating to full-scale stability trends) can be generated. The most obvious information that can be obtained from single-element testing is the flow and combustion characteristics of an isolated injector element (intraelement flow characteristics). Several design features influence on the intraelement flow properties of the combustor. For a typical coax injector these include the fuel annulus dimensions, the oxidizer post tip thickness, and the oxidizer post inner diameter. The combustion dynamics may be evaluated by disturbing the flow with a high-explosive charge or by periodically interrupting the flow-field. Some of the physical results that can be obtained include approximations of the relative combustion time lag (using advanced photographic diagnostics), an approximation of the average combustion distribution, the propensity of the

single-element injector to react to artificially generated high-amplitude disturbances, and single-element spontaneous stability characteristics. One example of the use of artificial disturbances was a set of experiments conducted in France with a rotating wheel to interrupt the combustor exhaust.<sup>6</sup> The specific results of these tests were not scaled to larger liquid propellant hardware. It should also be noted that element-to-element interactions that affect performance and stability are not simulated in single-element experiments. Specific evidence of a single-element spontaneous instability has not been obtained, but a 5 lb, three-element Marquardt engine was found to be spontaneously unstable.<sup>7</sup>

Single-element testing has limitations. Because the single-element chamber residence time and the propellant manifolding are quite different from the full-scale combustor, very little is offered with respect to chug stability information even though the element hydraulic response is the same as for the full-scale combustor. The chamber length can be increased with subscale hardware to represent full-scale chamber residence time and heat transfer aspects, but the increase in length of the combustor is destabilizing with respect to the longitudinal mode. Another disadvantage of single-element testing is that the tangential acoustic modes associated with the combustion chamber are not usually representative of the full-scale combustor. The tangential mode acoustic frequencies of a single-element combustor are higher than typical full-scale baffle compartment and main chamber frequencies. In addition, the injection density is typically lower than full scale which may affect the instability physical process relevant to full-scale instability behavior.

Instrumentation is critical with single-element hardware as with all combustors. Single-element chambers, however, can offer additional instrumentation opportunities not easily available to full scale. Typical instrumentation includes chamber pressure, steady flow rate, propellant and chamber temperatures, and some noninvasive diagnostics. Windowed combustors facilitate a variety of both qualitative and quantitative combustion measurements. Qualitative visual information regarding general combustion zone structure, ignition and flame holding characteristics, and intraelement mixing characteristics may be obtained. Quantitative information includes droplet sizing and velocity data, liquid stream length, and temperature measurements. Such information can be useful for the determination of combustion performance characteristics that are typically needed to conduct an analysis of the combustion stability of a particular injector. Current single-element combustors allow uncooled windowed chamber sections to facilitate optical diagnostics that include Raman spectroscopy, planar laser-induced fluorescence, laser schlieren, droplet sizing measurements, and other optical techniques that characterize the combustion process. Window cooling can be a significant issue especially at high pressure. The aforementioned diagnostics have been applied to the single-element windowed combustor<sup>8</sup> shown in Fig. 5. Key objectives of this program were to collect data for use in evaluating Space Shuttle main engine (SSME) preburner ignition processes and validating a mechanistic [computational fluid dynamics (CFD)] combustion model.

#### B. Three-Dimensional Cylindrical Subscale Chambers

Unlike a true single-element combustor, a typical three-dimensional chamber has multiple injector elements of the same basic element size, geometry, and pattern as the full-scale. The number of elements, however, is reduced to match the smaller injector face area and lower overall flow rate. Three-dimensional round

The background shows other laboratory equipment and structural elements.](93ca802a16bc521f0fac76fcc3d1083b_img.jpg)

The combustor is a large, rectangular metal structure with various pipes, valves, and instrumentation attached. Bright light is visible from the combustor's exit, indicating it is operating. **Fig. 5** Turbine drive single-element combustor with Raman and schlieren instrumentation.

subscale chambers can provide information on inter-element interaction that is characteristic of the full-scale design. In addition, the transverse wavelength of subscale hardware may approximate that of a full-scale baffle compartment. The full-scale mass flux, contraction ratio, and operating conditions (chamber pressure and mixture ratio) are specified for the three-dimensional subscale test article. Performance and heat flux information (using water cooled calorimeter chambers) may be obtained to aid in the design of the full-scale combustor. Care should be taken, however, in the design of the subscale hardware in order to not jeopardize the stability development program.

There are several advantages to using subscale three-dimensional round hardware. These advantages include reduced flow rates (and thrust) relative to full scale, a large hardware experience base from which to draw, and a large test database to compare with. All of these factors make it relatively easy to plan and execute a successful development program. Similar to single-element combustors, combustion characteristics can be obtained experimentally and later applied to the analysis of a full-scale combustor. The response of the combustion process to high-amplitude steep-fronted waves can be examined with three-dimensional round chambers via stability rating bomb tests similar to those typically used in full-scale tests. This rating technique has been successfully incorporated on many full-scale rocket engine programs including the J-2, F-1, and the SSME. During bomb tests, a small charge of high explosive is installed in the chamber combustion zone and detonated during combustor operation. The response of the combustor to the bomb pressure pulse has been shown to be a reproducible stability rating technique. The amplitude of the induced pressure wave can be controlled by the amount of explosive placed in the bomb.

Three-dimensional round chamber subscale testing also has some limitations. The most prominent limitation is that the hardware is geometrically smaller than the full-scale hardware. As a result, frequencies observed are not the same as

the lower frequency transverse modes of the full-scale combustors. Another limitation is that the subscale combustor may have a larger length-to-diameter ratio than the full scale. The reason is that to preserve the same combustion residence time and allow for complete droplet vaporization, the subscale length is made identical to that of the full-scale engine. Combustion chambers with relatively large length-to-diameter ratios are susceptible to longitudinal instabilities.

Key stability results obtained in three-dimensional cylindrical hardware include basic stability data such as fluctuating pressure and acceleration levels, cavity temperature measurements, high-frequency time-lag data (which is calculated from the ring-down of a pressure perturbation), and the dynamic response (pulse induced pressure wave amplitude growth) associated with a specific injector pattern. Other data typically include chamber pressure measurements, calorimeter temperature measurements (heat flux), propellant flow rates, and external high-speed motion pictures of the plume. If the framing speed of the film is fast enough, some low-frequency (e.g., chug stability) information may be obtained from plume motion pictures. Plume spectroscopy is sometimes incorporated with subscale three-dimensional round hardware testing to detect the onset of combustor erosion or compatibility problems. Propellant flow rates are typically measured with cavitating venturis, ASME type venturis, or turbine flow meters. Typically, high-frequency pressure measurements in the manifolds and combustion chamber are made with piezoelectric pressure transducers. Since acoustic mode high-frequency instability is defined as oscillations in chamber pressure at a specific frequency and amplitude, chamber high-frequency pressure measurements should be made on all subscale and full-scale hardware. Typically, combustion instability pressure oscillations are at their maximum amplitude at the injector face. Hence, high-frequency pressure transducers should be located at various circumferential locations close to the injector face to provide accurate information on the mode and peak amplitude of those oscillations.

Many examples exist with respect to three-dimensional cylindrical subscale hardware. The 82-element  $\text{LOX}/\text{CH}_4$  hardware<sup>1</sup> is displayed in Fig. 6. The combustor diameter was 5.66 in., the main stage operating pressure was approximately 2000 psia, and the mixture ratio ranged from 1.9 to 3.7. The nominal propellant flow rate was approximately 90 lb/s. During the testing of the 82-element  $\text{LOX}/\text{CH}_4$  injector, two separate types of stability rating tests were performed in order to evaluate the stability margin of a combustor with this particular injector. The first tests performed were fuel temperature ramp testing. The combustor was found to be unstable at methane temperatures ranging from  $-16$  to  $-23^\circ\text{F}$ . During the J-2 program, it was discovered that instabilities would occur with the engine when the nominal fuel temperature was lowered to a specific value for a given injector. As a result, this technique was established as a stability rating approach for liquid/gas coaxial injectors. Many such subscale ramping tests were conducted at NASA Lewis Research Center in the 1960s and 1970s.<sup>9</sup> Two mechanisms can account for the temperature ramp instabilities observed. The first is that the gaseous fuel density decreases appreciably with temperature and results in a loss in hydraulic resistance across the injector. The loss of resistance results in increased combustion chamber sensitivity to fuel side feed system oscillations. The second mechanism is that the fuel injection velocity decreases linearly with temperature and results in poor atomization, improving the potential for combustion coupled acoustic instability.<sup>10</sup>

Figure 7 shows the varying LOX dome frequency spectrum that was typical of these tests. Each spectrum trace corresponds to a "slice" (short sampling period) of time during the test. Note that the characteristic combustion frequency shifts as the test proceeds and the fuel temperature continues to decrease. The start of the instability that is noted corresponds to the onset of high-amplitude chamber oscillations. Subscale fuel temperature ramp tests can provide direct input into the development of the start sequence of a full-scale engine.

Some programs that have implemented three-dimensional subscale hardware include the SSME 40,000-lb test article,<sup>11</sup> the heavy hydrocarbon main injector technology program,<sup>4</sup> Marshall Space Flight Center RP-1 and methane tests<sup>12</sup> and Lewis Research Center RP-1 hot-fire tests.<sup>13</sup> A large amount of useful data has been collected with three-dimensional cylindrical subscale hardware.

#### C. Two-Dimensional Subscale Combustors

Two-dimensional slab combustors represent perhaps the most representative means by which full-scale acoustical stability can be evaluated with subscale hardware. Two-dimensional subscale combustors are typically sized such that the first width or "slosh" mode of the two-dimensional combustor matches the first tangential mode of the full-scale hardware. This is done in order to expose the combustion process to pressure perturbations of the same frequency that occur in the full-scale hardware. It should be noted that the two-dimensional tests do not yield exact combustion stability simulation to the full-scale hardware, because the spatial pressure waveform differs between two-dimensional and full scale due to the differences in geometry of each type of combustor. Furthermore, a spinning type full-scale instability cannot physically occur in the two-dimensional hardware.

The main advantage of two-dimensional subscale testing is that it is possible to have the same acoustical frequencies as the full-scale hardware at much

lower flow rates (compatible with a smaller test facility) than the full-scale design. The injector elements match the full-scale hardware. The two-dimensional hardware can also be used for acoustic cavity sizing configuration evaluation efforts.<sup>14</sup> Baffle length studies can also be performed with two-dimensional subscale combustors. The damping rates and frequencies of combustors can be evaluated as a function of baffle length.<sup>15</sup> The damp time of bomb disturbances typically decreases as the baffle length increases, but longer baffles require more coolant which detracts from performance. Two-dimensional combustors afford the developer an opportunity to optimize baffle length for full-scale hardware by means of relatively lower cost testing. Two-dimensional subscale hardware has also been manufactured with transparent chamber walls that facilitate flow and combustion visualization. The transparent wall J-2S two-dimensional combustor is shown in Fig. 8.

Two-dimensional combustors have some limitations. Besides the facts that spinning tangential instabilities are precluded and that the waves exhibit different spatial pressure distributions relative to full scale, the other drawback is that the surface area to volume ratio of two-dimensional hardware is much larger than the corresponding full-scale combustor. The large surface area results in somewhat greater acoustic damping relative to full-scale hardware. However, the amount of damping occurring at the wall is thought to be small in comparison to the convective damping through the combustor throat.

Typical instrumentation with the two-dimensional combustor includes high- and low-frequency pressure transducers, thermocouples, accelerometers, flow meters, and high-speed motion picture cameras. Various low-pressure two-dimensional

The chamber is a complex, cylindrical device with various ports and instrumentation. It is mounted on a stand, and the background shows laboratory equipment and structural elements.

combustors have incorporated transparent walls.<sup>10,14,16</sup> Nonintrusive optical instrumentation such as schlieren, shadowgraph, or direct combustion photography can be used if a transparent wall is incorporated in the hardware. One particular advantage is that two-dimensional combustors have two large surface area regions that are easily accessible for multiple instrumentation ports and windows if needed.

A significant amount of information was generated during two-dimensional testing that directly supported the design of the F-1 engine. In particular, the effectiveness of various baffle lengths, the occurrence of the resurge instability mode, and the stability of innovative injector concepts were all studied in two-dimensional combustors as part of Project First, which supported F-1 engine development.<sup>15</sup> Additionally, good corroboration was noted between two-dimensional and full-scale chambers in a study of the dynamic stability of an injector using various fuels.<sup>16</sup> J-2S slab motor testing was conducted to study the flow characteristics in the region of a hot-gas tap-off port.

A recent example of a two-dimensional subscale device is the two-dimensional stability research combustor (SRC). The SRC was designed to aid in the understanding of predominant physical mechanisms associated with unstable combustion. Either coaxial or impinging injectors may be installed. The combustion chamber is highly modular and permits combustor widths up to 13.5 in. long to be tested. The combustion chamber includes instrumentation ports for various test measurements and also incorporates a wall with windows to facilitate optical diagnostic techniques discussed earlier. The hardware is shown installed at NASA Marshall Space Flight Center in Fig. 9.

#### D. Other Subscale Hardware

Other types of subscale hardware have also been used to a limited degree to aid in understanding how full-scale hardware should be designed to maximize stability margin. Three subscale configurations that have been tested in the past are annular, barrel, and wedge combustors. Examples of all three combustors are displayed schematically in Fig. 10.

As depicted, the annular chamber has an outer chamber, a centerbody, and a spud or ring type injector pattern located at the head end of the annular gap. This design is intended to facilitate the study of full-scale frequencies in a reduced thrust combustor. The annular combustor can be used to model spinning instabilities in the outer zone of the combustion chamber. Assuming the annular chamber has the same diameter as the full-scale hardware, the spinning or racetrack mode frequencies are typically lower than the full-scale combustor. Annular combustor radial modes will be at significantly higher frequencies. The annular chamber, however, poses significant fabrication issues (high cost and design complexity for thermal load management on the centerbody) that should be considered in the subscale program planning. In addition, like the two-dimensional combustor, wall losses are higher than in cylindrical chambers.

The barrel (or pulse type) chamber is another subscale alternative that offers full-scale acoustics with reduced flow rates. The barrel chamber is similar to the annular chamber but without the centerbody. As before, spud or ring type injectors are located near the chamber wall to study the influence of the near-wall elements on stability. Like the annular chamber, this is a relatively low-thrust

The top right diagram, labeled 'Annular Chamber', shows a cylindrical chamber with a 'Centerbody' in the middle and 'Nozzles' at the front.
