**Fig. 10 Annular, barrel, and wedge combustors (from NASA SP-194).**

device. Because the chamber diameter is essentially full scale, the combustion instability frequencies approximately match those of the full scale. The drawback to the barrel chamber is that the mass flux in the combustion chamber is significantly lower than a full-scale chamber. This leads to contraction ratio (or chamber pressure) discrepancies that can affect the convective loading and diffusion characteristics of the propellant sprays. Such compromises may result in misleading information with respect to the combustion response. A high-contraction ratio may reduce convective damping of the nozzle and result in a significantly different stability margin than the corresponding full-scale hardware. Major differences in stability characteristics have been noted between barrel and full-scale hardware in the study of various propellants.<sup>16</sup>

Wedge chambers have also been previously used to investigate baffle compartment acoustics. Previous programs have displayed baffle compartment modes and ring down frequencies that match the predicted compartment acoustics. The wedge-shape chambers give an exact representation of the full-scale baffle compartment but fail to give information on the interaction between the compartment and chamber.

One final method of testing that may be considered is cold-flow acoustic response testing. Information can be gained from these tests, but careful extrapolation must take place to utilize cold-flow subscale test results to project hot-fire combustor characteristics. The information that can be gained from these tests includes the complex acoustic modes of the full-scale geometry, the hydraulic resistance of the injector, and visual flow representation. Additionally cold-flow

droplet vaporization and breakup studies have been conducted with the purpose of obtaining a better understanding of combustion instability mechanisms and developing a database for code anchoring efforts. However, combustion effects can be substantial such that cold-flow mixing and atomization test results must be interpreted analytically to properly extrapolate to hot-fire conditions.

### V. Analytical Approaches

As stated earlier, subscale engine component testing is used to mitigate the risk associated with full-scale combustor development. A key application of the subscale test results is to validate analytical tools that will be used in the extrapolation to full scale. Several analytical approaches have been used to model the aspects of combustion instability in liquid-propellant rocket engines. The approaches include the correlative sensitive time-lag analysis and multidimensional mechanistic time-domain numerical models. All of the analyses lend credibility to the full-scale design when properly validated.

The sensitive time lag approach was first introduced in 1956 by Crocco and Cheng.<sup>17</sup> The approach incorporates mechanistic modeling of the gas acoustic field in the combustion chamber and correlative modeling of the gain and characteristic frequency (combustion response) of the propellants. The time-lag approach has been used successfully on a number of rocket engine programs. Because of the mechanistic approach to the acoustics modeling, combustion stability aids such as acoustic cavities and injector face baffles can be evaluated analytically. The time-lag theory assumes that all of the combustion processes can be correlated to the unsteady pressure in the combustor. The drawback to the time-lag theory is that any new rocket engine design analysis must be based on extrapolated data. If subscale tests are run and combustion response growth or decay data are obtained such that the time-lag database can be extended, the amount of extrapolation is minimized.

The combustion response can be calculated from the pressure oscillation decay rate (ring-down) of an artificial or naturally occurring disturbance during hot-fire testing. Alternatively, the combustion response can also be related to changes in instability margin if the instability damping characteristics are parametrically varied, say, by varying the cavity open area. Using a linear stability model the decay rate measured from the ring-down of the pressure disturbance is then used to calculate the gain and overall combustion response.<sup>17,18</sup> Nonlinear combustion response stability models have also been developed which predict the steep-fronted pressure perturbation amplitude required to drive a given combustion process unstable.<sup>19</sup> Both modeling techniques require inputs that can be obtained from subscale testing and/or combustion performance modeling, such as the combustion profile and droplet sizes.

Time-lag theory was used to predict the available stability margin as a function of cavity tuning and open area on a high-pressure LOX/RP-1 subscale test program and on the full-scale (upper stage) XLR-132 storable propellant engine.<sup>4,20</sup> Linearized theory was also used in scaling the XLR-132 to a higher thrust storable upper stage (SUS) engine. Quantitative results were generated based on the scaling technique. When tested, the SUS combustor was spontaneously and dynamically stable without need for changing the predicted stable acoustic cavity configuration.<sup>21</sup>

The second approach that has been taken to model unstable combustion in liquid propellant rocket engines is mechanistic numerical analysis. This includes

a limited amount of transient CFD analyses of the combustion process.<sup>22,23</sup> The relevant combustion processes include injection hydraulics, atomization (both primary and secondary), mixing, vaporization, and chemical reaction. Recent efforts have concentrated on the development of submodels that describe these processes based on first principles. These analyses also have to be anchored with detailed spatial data (both time averaged and transient) which are used to validate the predicted values. Subscale testing (especially single-element tests and cold-flow tests) provides an excellent means to collect the necessary data to accomplish the anchoring process. Advances in combustion diagnostic instrumentation (particularly nonintrusive optical diagnostics) facilitate acquisition of the required data. Key data that can now be measured in reacting flows include droplet sizes and velocity and gas-phase species, temperature, and velocity.

All of the data also aid in the validation of current and future steady-state performance codes. These codes also yield information that can aid in the evaluation of the stability characteristics of a combustion chamber. An example discussed earlier is the steady near injector acoustic environment for a given injector. Parametric performance design analysis codes, such as the standardized distributed energy release model (SDER), can be used to approximate the conditions. However, three-dimensional CFD analyses in principle can provide the most accurate and detailed near injector acoustic profile necessary for this calculation.

### VI. Technology Improvements

There are many areas of rocket engine scaling that can be improved. The most important aspect of a stability development or a scaling program is to establish the direction from the beginning of the program. A well-defined subscale test methodology will enable the program to progress to the desired results on time and within budget. The current design methodology should be enhanced so that the most advanced analytical and instrumentation technologies are incorporated early in the test planning and hardware design. If properly structured, the design methodology related to combustion stability scaling efforts could become a self-improving test and analysis effort. This can only occur if state-of-the-art technology is constantly being included in the scaling effort.

The capabilities of combustion instrumentation are constantly being improved and enhanced. The current technology includes nonintrusive techniques for measuring flow velocity, flow rates, drop sizes, chemical species, and temperature distribution within the combustor. Development hardware needs to be designed to facilitate the application of advanced diagnostics to provide direct insights of the impact of design parameters on stability and performance. This would ideally include full-scale development hardware as well as subscale test articles. In this manner more information could be obtained from each test. This is an important consideration since test costs continue to rise. It is not an uncommon event for full-scale hardware to be manufactured with a fraction of the instrumentation (especially high-frequency pressure transducers) that the subscale development hardware had. A lack of instrumentation in the full-scale hardware makes it very difficult to cross reference the full-scale results to that of the subscale testing.

### VII. Conclusions

Subscale test techniques can be used to gain substantial insight relative to full-scale hardware combustion stability characteristics. The purpose of the subscale

hardware is to mitigate as much as possible the risk involved with unstable combustion in the full-scale design. Absolute stability characteristics of the full-scale hardware cannot be determined without testing the full-scale hardware, but subscale hardware can greatly reduce the cost of a full-scale stability development program.

In addition, subscale testing can serve to better anchor performance and stability analyses that can be utilized to assess the stability of the full-scale design before it is built and tested. In particular, where specific mechanisms such as injector element hydraulic coupling with the combustion process can be studied, key stability mechanism models can be anchored. Currently, the approach to achieving a successful full-scale design is to perform a portion of the development work at the subscale level and enter the full-scale design with as much information as possible. Some previous development programs started with full-scale hardware and backed into subscale stability tests to examine particular mechanisms as they arose. This practice has proven to be very costly. Careful planning of experiments and use of analysis techniques is required to produce the design information needed to develop a full-scale configuration within program schedules and budgets.
